Level Z2

101 books · 10 pages each

1. 1865 and the Close of the Civil War

1A map for the year 1865 can set the Union beside the Confederate states. Later parts tell how the fighting stopped. Slavery and the Union come first in the story behind that ending. A form of war that struck farms, towns, and armies comes next. Surrender by the South follows. The killing of President Lincoln comes after the surrender. What the war left behind closes the book, along with a word list. Early spring of 1865 had arrived, and so had the finish. General Robert E. Lee could see the truth about his Confederate Army. The men were exhausted, and the army could give no more. Lee had once said a thousand deaths would be easier than giving up. No path remained except surrender. Forces of the Union had beaten the forces of the South. He had to accept that result. April 9 was the day he put on a clean uniform. Tired, he rode his horse to a private home. The town was Appomattox Court House, in Virginia. The meeting was with General Ulysses S. Grant, who led forces for the United States. Half an hour passed after Lee got there. Then the U.S. commander came in. Mud spattered the old uniform Grant had on. The generals spoke in a friendly way at first. After that talk, they took up the work of stopping the war. In the decades before this war, North and South had split so deeply that the whole nation was shaken. Plenty of people doubted the United States could stay whole. Slavery had turned into a major line of division. Growing industry marked the North. Farms there were small. Big farming counted for less in that region's economy. Slavery was not unknown in the North in earlier years. Every Northern state had made the practice illegal by 1804. The South was another world entirely. Cotton ruled an economy built on farming.

2Plantation owners in the South picked enslaved labor on purpose. Growing cotton, and gathering it, cost the least that way. Near the middle of the 1800s, the Southern states held nearly four million Black people. Those people worked without pay. Death was the threat hanging over them. Many kinds of jobs were forced on them. Cotton plantations were home and workplace for most. Freedom was refused to them. The houses they were given were usually filthy. Cruel treatment was common. Inhumane treatment was common too. During those same years, abolitionists in the North spoke against bondage in the South. An abolitionist was a person who fought slavery. A second argument grew out of the argument over slavery. The second argument was about the rights of states. One federal law was the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850. Under that law, a fugitive in a single state counted as a fugitive everywhere. People in free states had to send escapees back to the people who enslaved them. Help went the other way from some Northerners. They aided people who had gotten away, rather than returning them. Juries in the North sometimes would not convict anyone who broke that act. An enslaved family, like the one pictured together, could be broken apart whenever an enslaver chose. Contact might then be lost for good. This war might not have started if the country had stayed a small cluster of eastern states. The 1800s were a time of push into huge western lands. Native peoples had lived on those lands for thousands of years. The lands were taken from them by force. Territories were turning into states. Congress had to choose whether slavery would be legal in each new state. A rough balance was what the Southern states wanted. States that permitted slavery should not fall far behind free states in number. Otherwise Southern votes in Congress could be outnumbered.

3Political power for the South would shrink. Deals in Congress kept a rough balance for several decades while new states were made. Tension between the two regions kept rising anyway. November 1860 brought the break. That month held the election for president. Abraham Lincoln won, to the dismay of the South. His party was the Republican Party, and that party opposed slavery. A government run by Republicans frightened the Southern states. They feared ruin for their economy. They feared an end to slavery as well. Seven Southern states quit the Union once the election was over. South Carolina was one of the seven. Mississippi was another. Then came Florida, Alabama, and Georgia. Louisiana and Texas made the list complete. February 1861 was the month they officially created the Confederate States of America. Their hope was a nation that would last, apart from the United States. Fighting started in April 1861. The place was Charleston, in South Carolina. Fort Sumter stood in Charleston Harbor as a Union fort. The Confederacy treated that fort as a foreign post on its own land. April 12 was the day the Union commander refused to hand the fort over. Confederate guns then bombarded it. Four further Southern states quit and joined the Confederacy. Virginia was one of the four. Arkansas was another. North Carolina and Tennessee joined as well. War's arrival brought joy to most people in the South. How horrific the war would become was clear to no one, North or South. The first two years went badly for the Union. One weak general after another troubled President Lincoln. September 17, 1862, brought a kind of victory the Union could claim. The battle was Antietam, in Maryland. Both sides suffered terrible casualties. Lee, who commanded the Confederate Army, had to fall back to Virginia. Because of that retreat, the North treated the battle as a win.

4That same win let Lincoln send out the Emancipation Proclamation. Freedom for enslaved people inside the Confederacy was what that order granted. Saving the United States as one country had been Lincoln's main aim when fighting began. He now started to consider a final end to slavery in every state. A fuller Northern triumph at Antietam was possible. George B. McClellan, the Union general in command, would have had to obey. Lincoln's order was to chase Lee and wreck Lee's army. McClellan was always hesitant, and he ignored that order. Lincoln, exasperated, took the command away in November 1862. Ambrose Burnside replaced him. Burnside would prove even worse. The Emancipation Proclamation, standing alone, did not finish slavery in the United States. Freedom applied only inside Confederate state areas the Union did not already control. Enslaved people in those Confederate areas could now fight on the Union side. Soldiers of that kind were badly needed by the North. The war's meaning changed too. It became a crusade against slavery. Slavery's final end still needed two more years. It also needed an amendment to the Constitution. Close to 200,000 Black Americans fought on the Northern side during this war. Fighting continued, and the count of casualties climbed. December 1862 brought disaster for the North. The battle was Fredericksburg, in Virginia. Under Burnside, Union losses were staggering. One man who survived on the Union side compared the falling soldiers to autumn leaves. Escape for any of them seemed, to him, like a wonder. Killed, wounded, or missing: the Union total passed 12,500 by the battle's end. Another man spoke of the wounded and their cries. He called those cries eerie and dreadful, hard to hear and hard to endure. Frederick Douglass was a famous speaker who had lived in slavery. News of the Emancipation Proclamation was something he celebrated. In his view, the order made every person free.

5He named the white man and the Black man. He also named the brave soldiers then fighting rebels and traitors for their country. He still understood the limit. Freedom and equality for every Black American would take a long road beyond this first step. July 1863 brought a turning point. The battle was Gettysburg, in Pennsylvania. General George Meade now led the Union forces. His army won a decisive victory against Lee. Invading the North was something Lee could never do again after that battle. From then onward, the Confederacy had to stay on the defensive. The human cost was horrendous once more. About 51,000 were killed, wounded, or missing. As many as 28,000 of them were on the Southern side. Meade shared a failure with McClellan. Neither man chased Lee's army after a victory. Feeling in the North turned more strongly against the fighting as the war stretched on. The year 1864 put General McClellan up as the Democratic candidate for president. Stopping the fight was what the Democratic platform demanded. A negotiated finish to the war was the other demand. That 1864 election would decide the war's whole direction. Lincoln thought he would be the loser. The winner was Lincoln. A mandate came with reelection. He could keep the war going so the country might be joined again and slavery might end. January 1865 was the month Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment. Slavery would end in the United States. A crime's punishment was the only case left out. The generals Lincoln needed were finally in place. One was Ulysses S. Grant. The other was William Tecumseh Sherman. Both men were professional. Both were effective. Destroying the Confederacy was their aim. Ending the war quickly was their aim too. Sherman's campaign ran through the deep South. Late in 1864, much of Atlanta was burned. His soldiers then crossed Georgia.

6Rail lines were torn up. Bridges were destroyed. Many homes were set on fire. A picture shows General William Tecumseh Sherman in 1865. North of that march, Grant pressed Lee without pause. Cold Harbor, in Virginia, was the site of one especially horrible battle in the middle of 1864. Grant ordered his men to attack Confederate lines that were strongly dug in. About seven thousand Union soldiers became casualties in twenty minutes. A Union soldier later said the charge was murder, not war. Women joined the armies in disguise. More than four hundred of them dressed as men so they could fight for the Union or for the Confederacy. Other women, in the tens of thousands, also served. White women did this work. Black women did it too. Laundry, cooking, and nursing were the jobs. Susan Baker King Taylor was born in Georgia in 1848, into slavery. At fourteen she taught school to other Black Americans who were newly free. She also washed clothes and nursed Black soldiers on the Union side. Northern anger at the bloodshed produced a bitter name for the Union commander. People called him Grant the Butcher. Lee's army was still being worn down. Early in 1865, trenches outside Petersburg, in Virginia, held Lee in a trap. Grant had already shown his skill in the western campaigns. March 1864 was when Lincoln placed him over every Union force. Five years after that, Grant became president. He took office as president number eighteen. His portrait is on the fifty-dollar bill. Dawn had not come on April 3 when Lee quit Petersburg. Only the ragged remains of his army went with him. Staying longer, he knew, would mean ruin. Another Confederate army was marching north out of Tennessee. He hoped to join it. Union Private Jacob Haas kept a diary of that day. The Confederacy was close to falling apart. Haas wrote that April 3 began with a hard shaking of the ground, which woke him early.

7The cause became clear soon after. Lee's men blew up the gunpowder they had stored, then fled the town. A little later, Haas wrote of Union troops taking Petersburg. The taking brought huge joy. Thousands of voices cheered and filled the air. A band played the tune Yankee Doodle. Lee's army, falling back, was chased without a rest. Grant had decided Lee must not slip away. On April 6, Grant's army inflicted casualties on the Confederates. The number was about eight thousand. Surrender was the only reasonable choice Lee could see. Four bloody years had passed, and the Civil War was nearing its finish. April 9 brought Grant and Lee together again. The place was a private home in Appomattox Court House, Virginia. History remembers that meeting. The terms Grant offered the South were generous. Every Confederate soldier could go back home. Horses and mules could stay with Lee's troops. Those troops were close to starving. Grant therefore ordered food for them, twenty-five thousand rations. Other Confederate forces farther south had not quit yet. Surrender came from all of them soon. April 2 was the day Confederate President Jefferson Davis left Richmond. Richmond was the Confederate capital. May 10 was the day he was captured. Prison would hold him for two years. The Civil War had ended. A different offer had come at the war's start. President Lincoln asked Robert E. Lee to command the Union armies. Lee said no. Fighting his beloved Virginia was something he would not do. He left to join the Confederacy. Once he had gone, his estate was seized by the government. The estate was named Arlington. Washington, D.C., stands across the Potomac River from those grounds. Those grounds became Arlington National Cemetery. February 1865 was the month Abraham Lincoln sat for a photograph.

8His death would come two months later. The United States was still one country. Victory brought joy in the North, and that joy soon turned back into mourning. April 14, 1865, was the night a man entered the Lincolns' private box. The place was Ford's Theatre, in Washington, D.C. The whole nation would soon know the name John Wilkes Booth. A play was on. The president watched it beside his wife, Mary. One shot from Booth struck Lincoln in the head. Booth then leaped to the stage. Men carried the unconscious president across the street. A private house received him. Early the next morning, he died. Booth worked as an actor. He sympathized with the South. He also belonged to a band of conspirators. Revenge for the Confederacy's defeat was what they wanted. Harriet Tubman had been born into slavery in Maryland. At twenty-seven she escaped to the North. Trip after trip brought other family members north as well. Dozens of further people then followed her guidance to freedom. The Union Army used her as a cook, a nurse, a scout, and a spy. She led fighters on a raid inside South Carolina. Enslaved people set free by that raid numbered over seven hundred. The plot was wider than one victim. Lincoln was to be killed. Vice President Andrew Johnson was to be killed. Secretary of State William Seward was to be killed. Only Lincoln died by assassination. Seward did suffer serious wounds from a knife. Troops of the Union followed Booth to a farm in Virginia. A fellow conspirator, David Herold, was with him. Booth died by gunshot. Herold was captured. A trial came later for Herold and the other conspirators. Four were judged guilty and hanged. Herold was one of the four. A funeral train carried Lincoln's body to Illinois, his home state. Burial was in Springfield. That city was where he had worked as a lawyer before politics.

9Lincoln himself was gone. His main goals had been reached while he lived. One goal was keeping the Union together. The other was ending slavery. A new chapter in United States history opened when the Civil War closed. December 6, 1865, was the date by which enough states had ratified the Thirteenth Amendment. The amendment then became law. Slavery was what it ended. Five years after that, two further amendments passed. Civil rights for people who had been enslaved came with the Fourteenth. Voting rights came with the Fifteenth. The year 1870 put Hiram Revels of Mississippi into the U.S. Senate. He was the first Black American elected there. Protection for formerly enslaved people, after the war, came through a system called Reconstruction. The U.S. government ran that system. The year 1877 ended Reconstruction. Southern states then found paths around the Fourteenth Amendment and the Fifteenth. New rules appeared. Some were called Black codes. Others were called Jim Crow laws. Racial segregation was enforced by those rules. The power of Black voters was reduced by them too. Intended rights from the Fourteenth and Fifteenth finally reached Black Americans through two later laws. One was the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The other was the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Attack on those rights has not stopped. Advocates still push for equality. They still push for protection under the law. A principle was set, beyond the end of slavery. The United States cannot be divided into separate nations. Complaints, however serious, do not give a state the right to secede. Since this war, the country has faced other periods of severe conflict and stress. Americans still split over issues of many kinds. The splits show up in daily life as well. One nation remains. That nation is the United States of America. A timeline lists key dates.

10December 20, 1860: South Carolina left the Union. It was first. Ten more Southern states would leave too. November 6, 1860: Abraham Lincoln was elected president. June 8, 1861: Tennessee seceded, the last of the eleven. April 12, 1861: the Civil War began. September 16 to September 18, 1862: the Battle of Antietam was fought. January 1, 1863: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. November 8, 1864: Lincoln won reelection. January 31, 1865: Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment. April 14, 1865: John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln. April 9, 1865: General Robert E. Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant. December 6, 1865: Congress ratified the Thirteenth Amendment. Special words can be set out plainly. An amendment is a change added to a law or other document, the U.S. Constitution included. Assassinated describes a killing that was planned, often for a political reason. A campaign is a string of planned actions aimed at one goal. Casualties are the people hurt, killed, or lost in a war, an accident, or a disaster. Cessation means a pause in something, or a full stop. Confederate points to the Confederacy, meaning the Southern states that broke away during the Civil War. The Emancipation Proclamation was Lincoln's 1863 order. It declared freedom for every enslaved person under Confederate authority. A fugitive is someone running, usually from the law. Indivisible describes something that cannot be split apart. Mourning is the showing of grief, above all for a person who has died. Relentless describes effort that stays just as strong, intense, or determined when obstacles appear. Representatives are the people picked to speak, vote, or act for someone else or for a group. Roiled means stirred up, agitated, or made angry. Seceded means a formal withdrawal from a group or an organization. The Union was the side that fought the Confederacy in the American Civil War. That side was the United States.

2. A Hidden City Cut from Rose Rock

1Hundreds of artifacts are on display in the Petra Museum. Many other objects have been lost to thieves over the centuries. A visitor can see Petra in two days. People who live nearby say five days are ideal. They tell tourists to be ready for a great deal of walking. They tell them to wear sturdy shoes. They tell them to bring sunblock, sunglasses, a hat, and a camera. Water is another necessity. The desert can become extremely hot in summer. Petra is vulnerable to erosion by wind and by water. It is also vulnerable to weathering from salt. Wind carries that salt from the Red Sea. The salt can enter small pores in the stone. It can then crystallize and cause damage. Tourists wear surfaces down by touching the structures. They also wear them down by sitting and walking on them. In 1985, the Rose City was given the status of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. That status helps ensure protection and conservation. A mosaic from the floor of the ancient Christian church shows a spotted giraffe. The animal looks like a camel. Historians believe the mosaic is meant to be a giraffe. They believe it was made by a person who had never seen one. The account moves from the hidden city to a desert treasure, then to the Rose City, a busy trade center, the work of building, a visit, and more still to discover.

2British author T. E. Lawrence wrote about Petra. He said that a person who had not seen it did not yet have even a faint idea of how beautiful a place can be. In the early 1800s, Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt grew fascinated. He had heard about a hidden city in the Middle East. The city was carved from red sandstone cliffs streaked with gray and black. It lay in a narrow mountain valley in a remote part of Jordan. Only the Bedouin knew it well. The Bedouin are Arab nomads who lived in the area. Burckhardt disguised himself as an Arab for his own safety. The area had periodic conflicts with neighbors. He arranged to be taken to the mysterious city. His hard journey in 1812 brought a reward. He passed through a narrow canyon and entered the secluded valley. Burckhardt became the first European since the Crusades, from 1095 to 1291, to look upon the striking stone city of Petra. Petra is Jordan's most popular tourist attraction. More than four hundred thousand visitors made the trip in 2015. The Rose City gained a great deal of publicity in 2007. That year it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

3Petra was also placed on a 2008 Smithsonian magazine list of 28 places to see before you die. Travelers buy tickets at the Visitor Centre. They enter through the Siq by horse cart or on foot. They may also enter on a horse, a donkey, or a camel. No motorized vehicles are allowed in the ancient city. People mainly explore Petra on their own. They start with the Treasury. They move on to tombs, the museum, and other sights. Nabataean architecture is a synthesis of many styles. Those styles reflect cultural influences from the region. The influences include Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt. Design elements of the Treasury reflect many different influences. Little Petra is a smaller archaeological site. It lies 8 kilometers (5 mi.) north of Petra. Like Petra, it can be entered only by traveling through a narrow canyon. Nabataeans created it by carving the buildings directly into the sandstone. Many historians believe ancient traders stayed in Little Petra. They stayed there when they visited its larger and more famous neighbor to the south. A second theory concerns the carvers. They may have set strong rods into the rock. The rods would have held a wooden board. The carvers would have stood on that board while they worked.

4After they finished a level, they would have placed the rods lower in the rock face. Then they would have moved the board. Scientists still look for clues. They hope to learn more about how Petra was built. Nabataean tools included picks, chisels, mallets, and hammers. Claw chisels have teeth. Their use could explain the coarse diagonal lines visible in many places in the stonework. Many stairways and water channels were also carved by hand. Other features were carved into the natural shapes of the cliffs and canyons. Petra lies in southwestern Jordan. It sits in a valley between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba. The gulf is a northern extension of the Red Sea. The ancient city is about 185 kilometers (115 mi.) southwest of Amman. Amman is Jordan's capital. Petra stood on routes that used to be important for trade among the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. It lies in one of Earth's driest deserts. Dramatic red sandstone cliffs and gorges surround it. The Siq, pronounced SEEK, is a canyon 1.2 kilometers (0.75 mi.) long. It rises as high as 80 meters (262 ft.). It leads to Petra from the east. It is the city's main access. The nearest water supply that lasts all year is Ain Musa, or Moses's Spring.

5That spring is about 8 kilometers (5 mi.) away. Now and then, a dry riverbed close by fills in a sudden flash flood. A map of the region marks Syria, Iraq, Amman, the Dead Sea, Israel, Jordan, Egypt, Ma'an, the Gulf of Aqaba, and Saudi Arabia, with Europe, Asia, and Africa labeled around them. The city of Petra takes its name from the Greek word for rock. People call it the Rose City because of the color of that rock. Petra covers 264 square kilometers (102 sq. mi.). The city center along the Colonnaded Street measures about 6 square kilometers (2.3 sq. mi.). The stone city is mainly carved from sandstone cliffs. Some construction was involved as well. Among the features are hundreds of tombs. Many of the tombs are adorned with sacred writings. Civic buildings recall the city's former role as an influential trade center. The structures also include temples, monuments, altars, and houses. Many of them are over 30 meters (100 ft.) tall. The unfinished monuments have helped scientists understand carving methods at Petra. One theory says the builders removed large blocks of sandstone one level at a time. That work left a huge step. It also provided rock for the freestanding structures. Carvers presumably used the rock step as a platform.

6They stood on it while they worked on the highest level. Once that level was done, they removed another layer of raw material. The new layer gave them access to a lower level. Petra's structures fall into two main types. One type is freestanding. The other type is the rock-cut monument. Each type brought its own building problems. The rock-cut monuments were carved into the cliffs. They surely presented the greater challenge. They also produced by far the more impressive results. These architectural masterpieces were remarkable for their sheer size. The towering Monastery is 45 meters (148 ft.) tall. They were also remarkable for their striking beauty and elaborate designs. Freestanding structures were built from the bottom up. The opposite was true of the rock-cut monuments. Unfinished monuments confirm the top-down method. Those monuments are carved only on top. Petra's topography and geology left sandstone as the only abundant raw material for buildings. No one is certain exactly how the Nabataeans carved the rock-cut monuments. A shortage of trees in the area rules out a plentiful supply of wood for scaffolding. Another major part of the infrastructure is a wide system of water management. Dams, channels, aqueducts, cisterns, reservoirs, and tunnels are all evidence. For that time, the technology was highly advanced.

7It collected water, stored it, controlled it, and distributed it. A dam at the start of the Siq kept floodwaters from flowing through the canyon and reaching Petra. The system let Petra's inhabitants thrive in a barren area. The technology is especially impressive because the city supported at least twenty thousand people at its peak. In 1993, Petra was named an archaeological park. Jordan's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities manages it. The park includes ancient trade roads around the city. Rock-cut channels along both sides of the Siq held pipes. Those pipes carried water to the people who lived in Petra. The most notable structures in the city center include several famous stops. The Treasury, called al-Khazneh in Arabic, is Petra's most famous monument. It is the first one visitors see when they come out of the Siq. The Street of Facades leads into the city center. Tall tombs with large facades line it. Some smaller tombs line it as well. The Theatre was cut from solid rock. It has suffered extensive damage. The Royal Tombs are where kings were buried. Some of them are very ornate. Through the middle of the city runs the Colonnaded Street. Petra Museum was founded in 1994. It holds more than six hundred artifacts. Those objects trace Petra's history across various eras.

8The Monastery, called al-Deir, is among Petra's largest monuments. Mosaics on the floor of the church show many kinds of animals. They also show figures that stand for the seasons, the ocean, Earth, and wisdom. In 330 ce, Roman emperor Constantine I, a Christian, moved the empire's capital. He moved it from Rome to Byzantium. That city was later called Constantinople, and it is now Istanbul. His goal was to spread Christianity. Petra's inhabitants slowly adopted Christianity. The change showed in their city. Petra Church was built around 450. It was remodeled in the years 500 to 550. Large mosaics were installed then. During that time, some tombs were turned into churches. An enormous earthquake in 363 ce damaged much of the water-management system. It also damaged nearly half the city. Petra's decline likely had a significant cause in that earthquake. A second large earthquake struck in 551. In the early 600s, Arab rulers took control of the region. When that century ended, the last people living in Petra had gone. Petra was thriving at the same time the Roman Empire pushed east into the Middle East. In 106 ce, the Romans took control of Petra in a peaceful way. Evidence suggests that life in Petra went on much as it had before.

9Roman rule still changed the city in many ways. The changes included architectural design. They also included new roads lined with columns. The Romans ruled Petra for three hundred years. Then they moved the focus of their trading north. They turned much of that trade into water routes. Those changes made Petra less important as a trade center. The columns of the Colonnaded Street show Roman influence. The street has suffered extensive flood damage over the centuries. A walk through the site can be traced from east to west. It passes the Visitor Centre, the entrance to the Siq, and the path through the Siq. It continues to the Treasury, the Street of Facades, and the Theatre. It continues to the Royal Tombs, the Colonnaded Street, the Monastery, and Petra Museum. Walking from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery takes about twenty minutes at a normal pace. Most visitors take much longer. They stop to examine each new location. The Petra area has been occupied since at least 7000 bce. The rock city was founded by the Nabataeans, pronounced nab-uh-TEE-uns. They were a nomadic Arabian tribe. They herded camels, goats, and sheep. Their standing in the ancient world grew during the first millennium bce. Slowly they became successful traders. They gained control of trade routes that linked parts of the Middle East with Asia and Africa.

10The goods included incense from Arabia. They included spices from India. They included silks from China. The Nabataeans gave water and shelter to traders who carried goods across the desert. They charged tolls to foreigners. For hundreds of years they were nomads who lived in tents. Then they began carving dwellings out of stone. At sunset on the winter solstice, sunlight lights the central podium of the Monastery. Over time the Nabataean traders grew wealthy. They built Petra and settled down. No one knows why they left their nomadic life and became sedentary. Petra was their capital. They called it Raqmu. It is thought to have been founded around 300 bce. It flourished starting in the first century bce. The city became a hub for people, for goods, and for money. It also became a cultural center. At its peak, the Nabataean empire grew to include parts of lands that are now Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Israel. Not much is known about the Nabataeans beyond one clear fact. They worshipped the Sun. On the winter solstice, and at certain other times of the year, the Sun lights or lines up with 80 percent of Petra's main structures.

3. A Look at Argentina

1A picture shows a gaucho riding his horse. The topics are where the country sits, its people, its land, its history, its celebrations, its food, and a closing word. A glossary follows. A map names the neighbors Paraguay, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay. Buenos Aires is marked. The Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean are labeled. North America, Africa, and South America appear on the wider view. Argentina is the second-biggest country in South America. In the whole world it ranks eighth. The area is 2,736,690 square kilometers. That is 1,056,642 square miles. The Andes Mountains stand on one side. No mountain chain on Earth is longer. The Atlantic Ocean stands on the other side. Five countries touch Argentina. Brazil touches it. So do Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Chile. Twenty-three provinces make up the country. Each province has its own government. Each has its own laws. Each has its own constitution. National law still rules. Every province must follow those laws and answer to them. Buenos Aires is the capital. It is also the largest city. The name means fair winds, or good winds.

2More than fifteen million people live there. The city claims the widest street on Earth. People call that street Avenida 9 de Julio. In English that is July 9th Avenue. The date is the day Argentina became free of Spain. The city is among the biggest ports in South America. Banking is centered there. So is food processing. So is the automobile industry. Residents are known for being friendly. Many different groups of people live in this multicultural city. Its middle class is among the largest in Latin America. A great many residents like city life and what the city offers. Traditions carried by those residents make the streets look much like a city in Europe. An obelisk stands on Avenida 9 de Julio. It was built in 1936. It marks four hundred years since Buenos Aires began. Farming has a strong place in the country's past. Pictures show farmers gathering wheat and gathering grapes. Argentina's people number more than forty-three million. More than 90 percent of them live in the four biggest cities. In Latin America, this economy ranks third.

3Brazil is larger. Mexico is larger. Farming is a strength. The ground holds silver and gold. It also holds oil and natural gas. Goods sent abroad include wine and beef. Lemons go out too. So do grapes, peanuts, tea, and wheat. Service jobs employ most Argentines. Work also exists in cars, cloth, energy, communications, and appliances. Film work is another path. Dozens of motion pictures are made there every year. Roman Catholic faith is the country's official religion. Freedom of religion is still guaranteed. People also practice Muslim, Jewish, Protestant, and Mormon faiths. Argentina can be called a melting pot, as many countries can. Peoples from all over the world came together and formed a new nation. New immigrants have always been welcome. Today, most Argentines have roots in Europe. Spanish is the official language. Because those roots are European, some people also speak Italian. Some speak German, French, or English. Visitors see European buildings in Villa General Belgrano. Córdoba is the province that holds this district. The land is shaped like a long triangle. It holds mountains, deserts, and plains. It holds glaciers, huge lakes, and seashores.

4Five big regions make up this varied land. The Andes form a high wall between Chile and Argentina. The Pampas are a wide stretch of flat, fertile ground. Many crops grow there. Patagonia is the largest region. Oil and gas industries are based there. The region is known for ecotourism. The Littoral region lies in the north. It has jungles and swamps. Northwest of the other regions sits a lowland called the Gran Chaco. A land map marks Iguazú Falls, the Iguazú River, and the Paraná River. It also marks Mount Aconcagua, the Pampas, and the Andes. The Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean frame the drawing. Brazil and Paraguay meet Argentina at a place called the Triple Frontier. The Iguazú River and the Paraná River form that meeting. There the Iguazú River drops over falls shaped like a horseshoe. The falls stretch 2.7 kilometers, or 1.7 miles. Iguazú Falls stand taller than most waterfalls in the world. They also stand wider. Millions of years ago, a volcano erupted and split the ground with a huge crack.

5The falls formed from that crack. Native people of the region named them in their own language. The name means big water. People count these falls among seven natural wonders worldwide. Many habitats keep the country full of birds and mammals. Toucans live here. So do Andean condors, penguins, and pumas. Tapirs, howler monkeys, and jaguars live here too. The towering Andes run the whole length of western South America. They are one of Earth's great natural features. Length is about 7,242 kilometers. That is 4,500 miles. It crosses seven countries. Its highest peak is Mount Aconcagua. That peak is 6,962 meters tall, or 22,841 feet. No peak in the Americas stands higher. Argentina's history has been long. It has also been troubled. For thousands of years, native peoples have made this place home. A Spanish invasion in the 1500s was followed by disease and by war. Many native people died. Argentina declared itself free of Spain in 1816. Spanish rule was at last driven out. Founding of the Argentine Republic came in 1853. Buenos Aires became the official capital in 1880. A Golden Age is what some people call 1880 through 1914.

6Railroads spread. Sheep farming grew very important. Cattle ranching did too. New roads appeared. New buildings and parks appeared too. The Great Depression arrived in 1929. The economy struggled. Military dictators rose to power. Dictatorships lasted from 1929 until 1943. Then another military leader helped throw out the government. His name was Juan Perón. A painting shows the 1816 meeting that said Spain no longer ruled the land. Voters chose Juan Perón as president in 1946. His popularity grew as he brought in reforms. Health services were one reform. Retirement money for most Argentines was another. He and his wife, Eva, brought these gains to the working classes. He also ignored human rights. He behaved like a dictator. A second term in office brought a drop in that popularity. In 1955 he fled to Spain. A picture shows Juan and Eva Perón. He came back in 1973. He ran for president again. He won by a decisive margin. Death came the next year. The Peróns have critics. Even so, many Argentines today remember them as good leaders.

7They helped the working classes. They helped modernize the country. The decades after Perón brought more takeovers by the military. They also brought economic turmoil. Since 1983, democracy has held. The economy has grown. New jobs number in the millions. The past was rocky. The future still looks promising. Modern Argentina comes alive each year in its festivals. Carnival often falls in February or in March. People dress as clowns, as animals, and as cartoon characters. Huge, colorful floats roll down the street. Musicians play. Dancers move. Onlookers enjoy the day. Festivals also honor wheat, the tango, and gauchos. San Antonio de Areco hosts a popular gaucho festival. It happens every November. Gauchos show how well they ride. The party lasts ten days. Bronco riding is part of it. Parades and dancing are part of it too. Independence has a national day on July 9. Families and friends gather to honor what happened in 1816. Traditional food and parades mark the day. In earlier times, cattle herds moved across the Pampas with gauchos. Today the Argentine spirit is what these riders represent.

8They are proud of their horses. A saying compares a gaucho who lacks a horse to a person who lacks feet. Spanish immigrants brought their own tastes to the table. French immigrants did too. So did Italian immigrants. Foods from all three cultures are popular now. Meat is easy to get. Eating beef twice in one day is not unusual. Steak and other cuts are always on hand. They are often cooked on an open pit. A barbecue is another common way. Empanadas are served almost everywhere. They are tasty pastries. The filling may be meat, vegetables, cheese, or fruit. Italian dishes are popular as well. Ravioli is one. Pasta is another. Pizza is another. Besides food, Argentines drink a tea called yerba maté. The plant is called yerba maté. Its leaves are dried, then brewed into the drink. People say it gives them energy. They say it keeps the mind alert. A dance called the tango uses complicated steps. Those steps can tell of love. They can also tell of political unrest. Every August, people travel to Argentina from around the world.

9They come for a tango festival. In Buenos Aires, fountains stand before the buildings of the national government. Those buildings are in Buenos Aires. European roots have shaped the country in a solid way. It has much to offer. The land is beautiful. The population has grown to include people from China. It includes people from South Korea and from other Asian nations. Argentines are committed to democracy. They feel the country will keep prospering. The country looks ahead. It sets strict rules to protect the environment. Women are urged to join the work of government. Equal rights, for every person, are part of what it stands for. Political unrest filled much of the past. Citizens still hold great hope for the future. The rest of the world shares that hope. A facts box lists key numbers. The population is 43,646,358. The land is 2,736,690 square kilometers, or 1,056,642 square miles. The capital city is Buenos Aires. The primary language is Spanish. The primary religion is Roman Catholic. The primary exports are beef, wine, soybean meal, cars, and corn.

10The currency is called the Argentine peso. The source is the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook from 2016. The word list gives plain meanings. Middle classes are groups who are neither rich nor poor and who earn an average income. Decisive means able to choose quickly and firmly, or ending in a clear way. A dictator is a ruler who holds all power. Force is the usual tool. Multicultural means including many different groups, each with its own ideas and customs. Diverse means different from one another, or made up of different people or things. Provinces are the largest areas into which some countries are divided. Ecotourism is travel to natural places to watch wildlife and to explore, without causing damage. Reforms are acts or processes that change things in order to improve them. Turmoil is a state of disorder, confusion, or agitation. A gaucho is a cowboy of the grassy plains of South America. Volcanic describes a spot in the crust of Earth. Gases, ash, and lava pour out there. Habitats are the natural homes of plants or of animals.

4. A Marble Tomb for a Beloved Wife

1A map can place Agra in India beside the Yamuna River. It can also mark Burhanpur, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal. Contents. The White Tomb. The Mausoleum at the Center. The Story of the Taj Mahal. Raising the Great Tomb. The Taj Mahal after Shah Jahan. A Memorial That Lasted. Words to Know. The Taj Mahal is known for perfect symmetry. It is the most magnificent creation of the Mughal dynasty. The White Tomb. Imagine a family so wealthy that its name means riches and power. That picture fits the Mughal (MOO-guhl) dynasty. These rulers governed northern India in the 1600s. The Mughals competed with one another. Each wanted the most beautiful mansions. Each wanted the most beautiful memorials. Their family name gave rise to the word mogul. A mogul is someone as wealthy and powerful as the richest king and the most famous rock star joined into one person. Today the Mughals are famous for jewel-encrusted works of art. They are famous for extravagant architecture. Their most famous creation is a tomb. The fifth Mughal emperor, Shah Jahan, built it. People call it the Taj Mahal. When people think of the Taj Mahal, most picture the mausoleum and its immense white dome. The Taj Mahal is actually a wider place. It covers 16 hectares, or 42 acres. The design stood for the paradise home of Mumtaz Mahal, who was Shah Jahan's favorite wife. Buildings, walls, gates, and gardens are laid out in a symmetrical way. The layout represents the Islamic idea of a perfect heaven. Grass now fills the grounds. Flowers and fruit trees once suggested the gardens of paradise.

2The garden is split into four equal parts by four water channels. The parts meet at a pool in the garden's center. The channels symbolize the four heavenly rivers described in the Koran. The Koran is the Islamic holy book. A plan of the complex can label an assembly hall, called a jawab, and a forecourt. It can label a water channel, a central pool, and the Great Gate. It can label a riverfront terrace, the mausoleum, a minaret, a mosque, and the gardens. Octagonal towers stand on either side of the Great Gate. White marble domes top those towers. The mausoleum's onion-shaped dome sits perfectly framed in the Great Gate's archway. The Mausoleum at the Center. Today, visitors enter the Taj Mahal through the Great Gate. The building is like a fortress. It is constructed of red sandstone and marble. Welcoming words from the Koran are spelled out in letters. Enormous archways adorn the Great Gate. So do domed ceilings. So do octagonal niches like the ones in the mausoleum. Those details hint at the luxury beyond the gate. The many structures and gardens all point visitors toward the mausoleum. Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan are buried there. Visitors who stroll through the gardens see the mausoleum reflected in the central water channel. The mausoleum sits on a raised marble platform. It dominates the landscape. Four minarets rise from the platform's corners. They look like guards standing at attention. Each minaret is more than 40 meters tall. That height is 130 feet. Translucent white marble covers the mausoleum. It covers the platform that holds the mausoleum.

3It covers the surrounding minarets. The marble's crystalline structure makes it change color as the light changes. Sometimes the building appears to shine with a glow that hardly seems of this world. White is the Islamic color of mourning. On a tomb, white is intended to show the faith of the person buried within. Other structures on the grounds are red sandstone. Those structures include the mosque (MAHSK). They include the assembly hall that flanks the mausoleum. A picture can show the white marble seeming to change color with the light and with the air. Inside, the public sarcophagus of Emperor Shah Jahan stands next to the sarcophagus of his third wife, Mumtaz Mahal. The mausoleum was designed as a holy building. It is a reflection of Mumtaz Mahal's mansion in the gardens of paradise. In Muslim belief, paradise is what the number eight stands for. Mughal tombs were often octagonal for that reason. Mumtaz Mahal's mausoleum follows this tradition. It has four long outer walls. It has four short outer walls. Entry on each of the four long walls comes through a massive arch. Smaller arches flank them on either side. Within, rooms and passages honeycomb the building. They are laid out in perfect symmetry. Mumtaz Mahal's sarcophagus (sar-KAH-fuh-guhs) sits at the center of an octagonal room. That room is at the center of the building. A second sarcophagus rests beside it. It is the only element that is off center. It marks her husband's burial site. Both rest inside a marble screen full of small openings. Both sarcophagi are cenotaphs.

4A cenotaph is a fake burial site for visitors to view. The real burial sites are in a private chamber on the lower level. They lie directly below the cenotaphs. Taj is a Persian word, and it means crown. Some experts suggest that the mausoleum stands for Mumtaz Mahal's jewel-covered crown. It is the most richly decorated structure in the Taj Mahal. It is meant to honor her in death. Almost every inch of the floor carries a geometric design. Vines decorate the walls. So do flowers and butterflies. The designs shine with precious stones and semiprecious stones. Those stones include jade, jasper, turquoise, and lapis lazuli (LAP-is LA-zuh-lee). Artisans also set thousands of diamonds into the designs. They set rubies, amethysts, and other gems. A thin sheet of pearls was made to cover Mumtaz Mahal's sarcophagus on holy days. A picture can show artisans' floral patterns and the costly colored stones set into the interior walls. The Story of the Taj Mahal. The Taj Mahal was not the first tomb that Mughal rulers created. It was one of the few such monuments created for a woman. The tombs of Shah Jahan's other two wives stand on the Taj Mahal grounds. They are in unmarked buildings near the Great Gate. What moved Shah Jahan to build such a magnificent memorial for Mumtaz? Shah Jahan met Mumtaz Mahal when he was a fifteen-year-old prince. She was fourteen. Her name then was Arjumand Banu. They were engaged shortly after they met. They married five years later, in 1612. The title he gave her was Mumtaz Mahal. The title means Chosen One of the Palace.

5A Custom That Hid Her Face. Poets of the time said Mumtaz Mahal's great beauty made the moon hide its face when she was near. Few people were permitted to see that beauty. Public life required Mumtaz, a noblewoman, to keep her face covered. No paintings survive that show her appearance. Painting noblewomen was an Islamic taboo. Later paintings show only artists' ideas of how she may have looked. A picture can show Emperor Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal as artists imagined them. Shah Jahan was a powerful military leader. He lived at the peak of Mughal rule. He showed skill in battle at an early age. For the following eighteen years, she went wherever her husband went. She even went with him when he traveled to war. Death came while she was in his battle camp. In 1631 she died as their fourteenth child was born. Her age was only thirty-eight. Shah Jahan was heartbroken. He gave up jewelry. He gave up fancy clothes. He gave up music. He even delayed his sons' weddings for two years. Mumtaz had died on a Wednesday. Every Wednesday, Shah Jahan banned celebrations. Each year, the whole month of her death anniversary had to pass with no celebrations. He required his court to wear white in her memory. The western bank of the Yamuna River is where Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal. Water in the garden channels comes from that river. He chose a site for the memorial shortly after he returned to his capital. The capital was Agra. The land he picked lay beside the Yamuna (YAH-moo-nah) River.

6Mughal royalty lived there in large garden mansions along the river. The mausoleum would stand along a bend in the river. Slower water at that bend protected the riverbanks from erosion. There the river creates a natural mirror. It reflects light onto the white marble walls. It reflects light onto the towers. In that era, a mausoleum usually stood in the middle of a garden. Mumtaz's mausoleum stood at one end of the gardens. That position was unusual. Ruins of a second garden property were later found on the opposite riverbank. People called it the Moonlight Garden. Today, archaeologists see the Moonlight Garden as an important piece of the Taj Mahal grounds. Visitors could view the mausoleum by moonlight from that spot. The Moonlight Garden lies to the east, on the far side of the Yamuna River. It was restored in the 1990s. Shah Jahan liked to look at his wife's memorial from this spot. Raising the Great Tomb. The year 1632 is when construction of the Taj Mahal began. That was about a year after Mumtaz Mahal's death. The project was the largest architectural work of the Mughal dynasty. It required more than twenty thousand workers. It required more than a thousand elephants. Shah Jahan brought in architects from all over the world. He brought stoneworkers and painters as well. Facts Worth Remembering. The mausoleum is about 70 meters tall, or 240 feet. Its dome is 44 meters tall, or 144 feet. The dome is estimated to weigh 11,000 metric tons, or 12,000 tons. The Taj Mahal took 22 years to build.

7It cost about 32 million rupees in the money of 1632. Building the Taj Mahal today would cost about 1.6 billion dollars. That is four times the cost of building Disney World. A slight slant was built into the minarets. If they ever fall, they will fall away from the mausoleum. Gems came from China, Tibet, Afghanistan, and other countries. Semiprecious stones came from those places too. So did different colors of marble. The slabs of white marble that cover the mausoleum had to travel hundreds of miles. Carts pulled them. Teams of twenty to thirty oxen pulled each cart. At the building site, workers built a dirt ramp. The ramp was 4 kilometers long, or 2.5 miles. They also built a complicated system of scaffolds, ropes, and pulleys. That system moved the marble into position. The next twenty-two years were spent continuing the work. Late in his life, three of Shah Jahan's sons fought among themselves. They fought over who would be the next emperor. Shah Jahan was imprisoned in Agra Fort. The victor was Aurangzeb (aw-ruhng-ZEB). He kept his father in the fort until Shah Jahan's death in 1666. From the time his son imprisoned him, Shah Jahan could view the Taj Mahal only from afar. A picture from a room at Agra Fort can show that distant view. The Taj Mahal after Shah Jahan. From sunrise to sunset, the public may enter the Taj Mahal today. It is open every day except Friday. Friday is the Islamic holy day. Local Muslims may use the Taj Mahal for religion on Fridays. They can offer prayers from the mosque near the mausoleum.

8Moonlight offers visitors another way to see the Taj Mahal. They may come on the night of a full moon. They may come on the night just before a full moon. They may come on the night just after. They may not come for those moon views during the holy month of Ramadan. The Taj Mahal today is not the same building Shah Jahan finished in the seventeenth century. In the years after his death, it was practically abandoned. Looters chiseled out many gems. Vandals did the same with semiprecious stones that decorated the mausoleum. Gold lamps disappeared. Persian carpets disappeared. The pearl overlay for Mumtaz Mahal's sarcophagus disappeared. Other decorations disappeared too. The gardens became overgrown. Buildings fell into disrepair. No one cared for them. Late in the nineteenth century, Agra's British viceroy started to restore the site. He planted neat lawns where the former gardens had been. He fixed broken marble inlay. He replaced missing screens. He replaced missing lamps. Looters and vandals were stopped. New enemies still arose to threaten the Taj Mahal. Iron foundries came to Agra. Factories and other industries came too. They emitted high levels of air pollutants. The white marble grew worse because of acid rain. A yellow fungus called marble cancer began to discolor the soft marble. Pollutants cause that fungus. It eats away the surface. Behind the mausoleum, the Yamuna River now carries raw sewage from upstream cities. It carries garbage as well. Scientists suspect that gas from these contaminants may add to the marble's discoloration. More and more visitors brought more attention to the monument.

9They also brought problems. Moisture from the breath of thousands of visitors promoted algae. That algae damages the marble. A picture can show artisans restoring marble artwork made hundreds of years ago. In the 1980s, the Indian government put measures in place to protect the monument from pollution. One measure was the Taj Trapezium. Major industries that pollute would not be allowed in this area around Agra. It was created in 1982. Two years later, the government created a zone around the Taj Mahal where emissions were not allowed. The zone extends 2 kilometers, or 1.2 miles. The Indian Supreme Court added more measures in 1996. Air pollution in the city had remained high. Polluting industries near the Taj Mahal had to switch to a cleaner fuel. That fuel was natural gas. Otherwise they had to move beyond the protected zone. In 2001, several organizations joined together. They formed the Taj Mahal Conservation Collaborative. The group is dedicated to conservation of the Taj Mahal. It is dedicated to restoration. It is dedicated to beautification. The group has taken on projects such as removing stains from the white marble. Workers use detergents for that job. They use absorbent clay packs. The Taj Mahal faces numerous challenges. It has survived earthquakes. It has survived lightning, wars, and floods. Those trials cover the past several centuries. Luck, plus a great deal of hard work, can carry it through the centuries ahead. Early in the morning, and later in the day, visitors see the light change across the Taj Mahal. Those views are hard to forget.

10A Memorial That Lasted. Shah Jahan wanted a memorial for his beloved wife. He wanted it so magnificent that the entire world would admire it for all time. Today the Taj Mahal sees thousands of visitors each day. It sees millions each year. They come from all over the world. The United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, called UNESCO, declared the Taj Mahal a World Heritage Site. A vote by people of many nations named it one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Centuries after the building work, the Taj Mahal is still among the most beautiful memorials ever made. Words to Know. conservation (n.) the protection and preservation of historical or cultural items, structures, or places. dominates (v.) has continuing power over something or someone, or a commanding presence. dynasty (n.) a series of rulers of a country who come from the same family. Islamic (adj.) of or relating to the monotheistic faith of Muslims. mausoleum (n.) a large tomb, or a structure that holds several tombs. memorials (n.) things that stand for the memory of a person, a place, a thing, or an event. minarets (n.) slim towers beside a mosque, used when worshipers are called to prayer. mosque (n.) a place of worship in the Islamic faith. restoration (n.) the act of returning something to its original condition. sarcophagus (n.) a stone coffin or tomb, often inscribed and richly ornamented. symbolize (v.) to represent an idea with an object, a picture, or a sign. symmetrical (adj.) having sides that match in shape and size, like a mirror image.

5. A Railroad Across the Continent

1This book follows one great building job, a railroad from the Atlantic side of the country to the Pacific. First it explains why the land journey west was so hard. Then it asks who could pay for the line and who would do the heavy work. Next it asks which company would lay rails faster. After that it asks how a path was cut through high mountains. Then it asks where the two crews finally joined their rails. A last look sums up what the finished line changed. Hard words are explained after that. A topic list closes the book. Until the 1860s, a land journey that began in New York City and ended in San Francisco might last half a year. During those months, travelers had to bring all the food they would eat. Hunting and gathering along the way was the other choice. People went hungry. They also went thirsty. Storms and heat made the trip harsher. Sickness spread. Wild animals were a threat. Maps of the region were scarce, so a wrong turn was easy. The western paths crossed country already lived in by Indigenous peoples. Outsiders had treated those peoples badly many times. Trust had worn away. Settlers still poured toward California, thousands of them each year. Farmland there was rich. The climate was wonderful. Gold was a further lure. A belief called Manifest Destiny shaped many of these travelers. It claimed that God meant the United States to grow. Democracy was supposed to spread with that growth over all of North America. Capitalism was supposed to spread too. People already living on the land paid the price. The land itself paid a price as well. Through the 1800s, settlers hunted for a western journey that would bring less danger. Speed mattered to them just as much. Rail travel was the quickest option then.

2Eastern lines already ran in a crisscross pattern. Chicago, Illinois, was as far west as some of them went. Omaha, Nebraska, was another western end. Average speed was 25 miles an hour, which is 40 kilometers an hour. One unbroken line to the Pacific would cut the time settlers needed to reach California. People settled in the West could also return east sooner. Goods would be simpler to order. Mail would move both ways with less delay. Family members unseen for years could be visited again. Business in California was booming. A rail link would join that boom to eastern companies. It would join California to the eastern government too. The East would share in the western boom. Gains would not stop at the two coasts. Communities would grow beside the route. Men made up most of each new town. Women arrived with them. A stubborn problem remained. Who could pay for, and actually build, a line across so much rough western country? One photograph shows people posing beside a train in a crowded eastern station. A coast-to-coast railroad had been wished for over many years. Several barriers stopped it. The price was too high for one person. It was too high for one company. The machines and methods of the day also looked too weak for the job. No calculators helped the engineers. Computers did not exist for them. Airplanes were not available to survey the ground. War made planning even harder. Northern states and Southern states were already fighting the Civil War. While they fought, they could not agree on a railroad. Owners tried to hold down wages by hiring immigrant laborers. Some came from China. Others came from Ireland. Many Black workers were hired too. Pay for all of them was low. The chosen route followed the 41st parallel. The Mason-Dixon line lay farther south.

3In the Civil War, soldiers often tore up rail lines. They also put lines back together. A map dated 1862 shows the United States, with Oregon, Sacramento, Omaha, and California labeled. Northern states, territories, Southern states, and disputed areas are marked. So is the Mason-Dixon line. The wide yellow region of land that was not yet states had no rail lines. California therefore stood apart from the rest of the country. Oregon did too. Congress acted in July 1862 by passing the Pacific Railroad Act. The law required a railroad spanning the continent. A telegraph had to run with it. Both were to stretch from the Missouri River out to the Pacific Ocean. Track laying toward the east was assigned to the Central Pacific, starting at Sacramento, California. Track laying toward the west was assigned to the Union Pacific, starting at Omaha, Nebraska. Each company received enormous grants of land beside the planned line. The Cheyenne held that land. So did the Sioux. So did the Arapaho. Treaties with those tribes were broken by the U.S. government. Soldiers used violence to force people off the ground. Sale of the land then raised cash for the railroad. The same act required that government use of the rails be protected. Government use of the telegraph had to be protected as well. Thomas Durant was the Union Pacific owner. Four men owned the Central Pacific. They were Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker. Leland Stanford was one of them. Collis Huntington was the fourth. A portrait groups Durant with those four. The heaviest labor fell largely to immigrants. Competition was built into the plan so the line would grow fast. More track meant more government money. Durant was a businessman, and he also had a medical degree. The four Central Pacific partners had made their money in the gold rush.

4Their crews started in January 1863, just beyond Sacramento. Accidents and natural disasters killed hundreds during the work. Many of the dead were never counted. Construction did not stop. Which side would finish more track? War and a shortage of money delayed the Union Pacific for two years. Iron that the crews needed was going to the war. Gunpowder was going there too. So were workers. Building began only after fighting ended in 1865. By 1866 the Union Pacific looked sure to win. West of Omaha, Irish immigrants pushed rails quickly over the Nebraska prairie. Preparing the ground took several careful steps, and the order mattered. Survey crews came first. They studied the ground and drove stakes to show the exact line. Graders came second. They cleared plants, filled hollows, and dug until the bed was smooth and level. On flat prairie the graders sometimes found little to change. Tracklayers came last. Most of them were Chinese immigrants, and their pay was severely low. One picture shows surveyors measuring how far and how high the land ran. Another shows Chinese crews in Utah in 1869, setting rails by hand. Several teams shared the laying itself. One team placed wooden ties across the bed. Another team hauled iron rails onto those ties. Gaugers measured the gap so the rails stayed the right distance apart. A further team swung heavy sledgehammers. Spikes and bolts of iron locked each rail to the ties. Sand and gravel, known as ballast, came last, moved by wheelbarrow and by wagon and packed around the new line. On a good day the Union Pacific finished 2 to 3 miles. That is about 3 to 5 kilometers. An illustration from the 1860s shows crews, many of them immigrants, building across Nebraska. Behind them a supply train already rolls on fresh rails.

5That train was storage. It was also a place to live. The first train to follow the new line came right after the work gangs. Steam drove its locomotive. Wood for the job rode on board. Rails, spikes, tools, and ballast rode there too. Some cars held bunks. One held a kitchen and stored food. Repair shops filled other cars. Clothing and similar goods were carried as well. The whole train worked like a town that crept forward and built the road under its own wheels. Most of its people had immigrated from Ireland, from Germany, or from the Netherlands. Veterans of the Civil War rode with them. Black people who had once been enslaved were part of the crew. Papers painted these Union Pacific men as tough and proud. All week they were said to work diligently. Sunday was free, and they gambled. Prairie miles fell behind them at a startling pace. The Rocky Mountains came into reach quickly. For Plains peoples the new rails meant their old life kept collapsing. The railroad devastated the Sioux. It devastated the Arapaho and the Cheyenne. The herds they needed were American bison. Another name for that animal is buffalo. Herds could not cross the rails on their old migrations. Officials urged settlers to slaughter bison by the thousands. Extinction nearly followed. Plains communities could not live without the herds. Disease took huge numbers of people. Hunger took more. Conflict that followed the killing took still more. A picture shows settlers shooting bison until almost none remained. Settlers flooded in behind the rails. Wherever a crew paused, a town appeared. Some towns vanished as soon as the work moved on. Others lasted and became major cities. Reno, in Nevada, was one. Cheyenne, in Wyoming, was another. Broken treaties had already handed Sioux, Cheyenne, and Arapaho land to the railroad companies.

6Those companies sold it onward to settlers. Farms started. Houses went up. Trains left litter behind them. They made noise. They dirtied the air. Engines burned wood or coal, and their sparks started prairie fires. Indigenous fighters resisted the illegal seizure of their country. Before a railroad posse could form, the fighters were gone. Supplies were taken. Livestock was taken. Some railroad workers were killed. Army protection was what the Union Pacific demanded, both for crews and for the line. General Ulysses S. Grant answered by sending many soldiers to ride beside the surveyors. General William Tecumseh Sherman gave the same order. Skirmishes with Indigenous people followed again and again. Marksmen hired by railroad officials guarded certain stretches. One picture shows the line being forced through the rugged Sierra Nevada. Far to the west, the Central Pacific crawled. Its first task was a roadbed in steep, snowy Sierra Nevada rock. The path crossed California's Donner Pass, a place with an infamous story. Pioneers stranded there in the fierce winter of 1846 starved. Locomotives of that era could not mount a sharp slope. Tight curves were impossible for them too. Jagged peaks had to be reshaped into a smooth trail with only a gentle rise. Solid granite was cut back from the slopes. Gorges and ravines were packed with rock and soil. Each load moved by wheelbarrow. Few workers would stay at such slow, painful labor. Most newcomers of European descent had come west for gold. A portion of them tried railroad jobs. Nearly every one of those Central Pacific hires quit inside a week and went looking for riches elsewhere. The company, unwilling at first, then tried about fifty Chinese workers. Many Chinese immigrants, like others, hoped America would make them rich. California's draw for a great number of them was the Jinshan, said jeenshahn, the Mountain of Gold.

7A picture shows Chinese crews tipping ballast under the rails. Racism met them almost everywhere. Employers stole wages. Housing was refused because of who they were. Even then, they outlasted the white workers on the same jobs. In 1868 they were 80 percent of everyone the Central Pacific employed. The railroad advanced because of them. Their health was a large part of that success. Other crews sickened. Chinese crews more often stayed well. Food was one reason. They carried fresh fruit and vegetables and ate a low-fat diet. Other camps ate a heavier meal that was less healthy. It was built from meat and potatoes. Cabbage was added, and so were bread and butter. Drink was another reason. Tea replaced water and beer. Heat from the tea warmed the men. Boiling also killed germs in the water. Bathing mattered too. Chinese custom at that time prized cleanliness more than American custom did. Frequent washing slowed the spread of germs in camp. One picture catches loose gunpowder as it blows a piece of mountain apart. Fifteen tunnels through solid rock were required before rails could cross the Sierra Nevada. Hand drills did the boring. Sledgehammers drove them. Loose gunpowder split the stone. No other tools were used. Winter buried the peaks in forty-four separate snowstorms. Under snow that averaged 18 feet, or 5.5 meters, the men dug tunnels. They also dug rooms for sleep and for work. These were grading crews only. Track had not arrived, so no train could haul freight up to them. Ox wagons carried the loads up the slope. Hands carried what the wagons could not. Cape Horn was their most famous job, a cliff so huge they gave it that name. Stories of the work describe a method brought from China. It was old, and it was dangerous.

8Reed was woven into baskets that could carry two people. From the cliff top, crews lowered those baskets. Men inside drilled holes in the rock face. Black powder filled each hole. A fuse was lit. A shout warned the team above. Baskets were yanked upward at full speed. The hope was that every person would clear the blast in time. Another picture shows a tunnel being cut by Chinese workers in a wall of rock. Success and disaster arrived together. Hands were crushed in accidents. Feet were crushed. Whole bodies were crushed. Cold killed many by freezing. Avalanches buried whole parties alive, and some bodies stayed hidden until spring. At Strong's Canyon one slide erased an entire camp, crews and buildings together. The Central Pacific never recorded how many Chinese laborers died on the transcontinental job. One estimate puts the number near 1,200. A winter picture shows crews fighting mountain cold. The year 1867 finally brought the line out of the peaks. Utah's dry deserts waited beyond the peaks. That was the Central Pacific's next ground. A record fell on April 28, 1868. Crews laid 10 miles in a single day, equal to 16 kilometers. Charles Crocker said the men looked like an army crossing the land, with finished track appearing behind the march. Where would the rivals meet? Rocky Mountain country was far kinder to the Union Pacific than the Sierra Nevada had been to the Central Pacific. The older Oregon Trail led them along Nebraska's Platte Valley. The grade stayed gentle. South Pass, in Wyoming, carried them over the Rockies. Utah's deserts came soon after. During 1869 the two fronts drew close. The join was set at Promontory Point in Utah. The Great Salt Lake lay south of that spot. Brigham Young, who had governed the territory, was dismayed.

9He had wanted the rails to bend south and pass through Salt Lake City. Tourists in one picture stand by a locomotive and cars built before the 1930s, parked on a historic mountain line. The celebration day was May 10, 1869. Workers, owners, journalists, and politicians all came to Promontory Point. Racing was finished. Union Pacific rails measured 1,086 miles, or 1,748 kilometers. Central Pacific rails measured 689 miles, or 1,109 kilometers. Extra pay went to the Central Pacific because its route had crossed the Sierra Nevada. Chinese workers fill one picture, a reminder of how large their role was. For the ceremony, leaders of both companies were to hammer the final four spikes. Gold and silver made those four. Mines in California supplied some of the metal. Mines in Nevada and Arizona supplied the rest. Long inscriptions covered the spikes. A special hammer was required for a light ceremonial tap. Ordinary spikes went in after that show. Crews from each company dragged the final rails into line. Leland Stanford, leading the Central Pacific, lifted a sledgehammer. Thomas Durant, leading the Union Pacific, lifted one too. Each man swung and missed. Cheers came from the crowd all the same. The coast-to-coast railroad now existed. A route map uses red for the Central Pacific, which built from the west toward the east. Blue marks the Union Pacific, which built from the east toward the west. Labels include Promontory Point, Wyoming, Nebraska, Omaha, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Sacramento, and California. Years of danger and labor had changed distance itself. New York to California was now a trip of only a few days. More lines reached Salt Lake City. Others reached Oregon Territory and the Southwest. Towns kept forming beside the rails once goods and mail moved so freely. Millions of dollars went to the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific.

10The money came from land sales. Along the route, that land had been taken from Indigenous peoples. Laborers got no added payment later. Families of the dead received none either. Even so, east and west were tied together by rail for the first time. The harder words in this book can be read this way. If someone works diligently, that person shows care, determination, and attention to small details. Discrimination is unfair treatment aimed at a person or a group over gender, race, age, religion, or some other difference. An engineer designs, builds, or repairs machines, buildings, bridges, and similar structures. An immigrant is a person who arrives to live in another country, often to settle for good. Indigenous refers to the earliest peoples of a place, or to what belongs to them. A person or event called infamous is famous because of evil, harm, or danger. A laborer earns pay by physical work. To have portrayed someone is to have described or shown that person in one particular way. Racism is unequal treatment that rests on a belief that one race outranks another. A settler makes a lasting new home in a place that was not originally home. A telegraph sends written messages as simple electric signals moving through wires. A veteran is someone who has served in the armed forces. Readers of this book will meet these topics: the Arapaho, avalanches, and a booming economy. Also the Cheyenne, China, and Chinese workers. Also the Civil War, Charles Crocker, deserts, and Donner Pass. Also Thomas Durant, gaugers, government, and graders. Also Ulysses S. Grant, Mark Hopkins, and Collis Huntington. Also locomotives, Manifest Destiny, and the Mason-Dixon line. Also the military, mountains, mail, and the prairie. Also Promontory Point, William Tecumseh Sherman, and the Sioux. Also sledgehammers, Leland Stanford, technology, and transport.

6. A Stone City of the Maya

1A map of the region can mark Cancún, Maya territory, Uxmal, and the Gulf of Mexico. It can mark Cozumel, the Yucatán Peninsula, Palenque, and Belize. It can mark Tikal, Mexico, Guatemala, and the Pacific Ocean. It can mark Honduras and El Salvador. A key can show a Maya archaeological site, Maya territory, and a modern city. Contents. Where the City Began. Buildings of Stone. Buildings near the Water. A Northern Stronghold. From One Building Style to the Next. Roads Left from Earlier Times. Secrets of Maya Science. The Maya Today. A Visit to Chichén Itzá. The Search Goes On. Words to Know. Where the City Began. In the jungle of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula lie the ruins of Chichén Itzá. The city has massive stone structures. It has a network of paved roads. The Maya built the city. They are a people native to the area in what is now Mexico. Mayan speakers understand Chichén Itzá as at the mouth of the well of Itzá. The Itzá are a Maya ethnic group. They lived in the northern part of the Yucatan Peninsula. The well in the name refers to the city's water sources. Those sources were practical sites for the Maya. They were sacred sites as well. A picture can show statues found at Chichén Itzá. A dozen or more of them were found. Offerings for the gods were placed in them. The early 400s ce is the founding date given by some historians. Whenever it was constructed, the city was an important center by the 600s ce. It served many different Maya ethnic groups. Nearly one thousand years passed with Maya people living in Chichén Itzá.

2That span runs from around 450 ce to 1450 ce. Then populations shifted away from the city. It became mostly abandoned. It was never entirely abandoned. Archaeologists have studied the area from the nineteenth century onward. The area covers more than 7.5 square miles, or 19.4 square kilometers. Only 2 square miles have been completely mapped. That mapped part is 5.2 square kilometers. A Maya artist carved a jaguar on a temple. In Maya culture the jaguar is Ruler of the Underworld. In the carving, the jaguar eats a human heart. The large stepped pyramid stands in the center of Chichén Itzá. Buildings of Stone. Today, many impressive buildings in Chichén Itzá have been restored. They look as they would have when they were first constructed. Maya people used stone tools. They made intricate carvings on stone buildings throughout the city. From these carvings, scientists learn about the early days of Maya culture. A giant stepped pyramid is the monument people know best. On top of it is the Temple of Kukulcán (koo-kool-KAHN). Kukulcán is a god depicted as a winged serpent. Maya culture names Kukulcán as the god who created the world. He is the god of rain, wind, storms, and life. In this temple, priests led ceremonies. They led ceremonies in many other temples in Chichén Itzá as well. Gifts were offered to Maya gods. A stone ring on the ball court suggests one goal of an ancient game. Players may have tried to hit a ball through this ring and through others like it on the field. Another well-known feature is the Great Ball Court.

3A game the Mayan language calls Pitz was once played there. Scholars have looked at art and artifacts. They know that the game involved two teams of players. The players used their elbows, hips, and knees to hit a rubber ball. People harvested latex from rubber trees in the surrounding forests. They made the ball from that latex. Scholars are still piecing together the rules. One sure fact is that people often played the game for fun. The Maya creation story was acted out in the game as well. It re-enacted the triumph of good over evil. Chichén Itzá also has observatories. Astronomy mattered deeply to the people of the city. They carefully designed several buildings to align with significant astronomical events. Those events include solstices. They include eclipses and lunar shifts.
