A plan of the city can label the Sacred Cenote and the Great Ball Court. It can label the Venus Platform and the stepped pyramid. It can label the Temple of the Warriors and the Ossuary. It can label the fresh-water cenote, El Caracol, which means the Snail, and Casa de las Monjas, which means the Nunnery. Buildings near the Water. Scholars have wondered why the Maya chose this spot for a city. Many think the Maya may have chosen it because of two cenotes (say-NOH-tayz). Water rising from underground is what makes a cenote. Fresh water came from one of the cenotes. The other is called the Sacred Cenote. It had religious significance. The Maya believed the Sacred Cenote was a pathway. It led to the home of the rain god Chac.

4They believed that offerings placed in the water could win his favor. His favor could help him send enough rain for their crops. Cenotes have yielded a number of interesting artifacts to archaeologists. The finds include tools, pottery, gold, and incense. Human bones found in the Sacred Cenote indicate a further practice. Human sacrifice was sometimes part of ancient Maya religion. Archaeologists have found artifacts on the rock ledges around cenotes. Those objects were likely placed there centuries ago. Warriors in canoes appear in a copied wall painting from the Temple of the Warriors, in a scene of a Maya village by the water. Warriors sit in canoes. A Northern Stronghold. Chichén Itzá was just one of many large cities the Maya built. Over the course of four thousand years, the Maya empire spread widely. It extended across land that is now five different countries. Those countries are Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. Related languages were spoken by different Maya tribes and ethnic groups across this region. They prayed to similar gods. They also shared a system of writing. They shared calendars. Archaeologists call one era the Preclassic. It runs from 1000 bce to 250 ce. They call the next era the Classic. It runs from 250 to 900 ce. In those periods, many cities appeared in what is now southern Mexico and Guatemala. Palenque (pah-LEN-keh) is one. Tikal (tee-KAHL) is another. By around the year 1000, the center of the Maya world moved north. It moved to the Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) Peninsula. Scholars still debate the reasons. Some experts think war may have caused the ruin of southern Maya cities.

5Drought may have caused it. Overcrowded cities may have caused it. Populations in the south dropped. In the north, Chichén Itzá grew. It became the most powerful city in the region. Aside from the large city of Mérida, much of the Yucatán Peninsula is still wild or farmed. Coastal resorts and a few other urban areas are the exceptions. The land is still jungles, forests, and farmland. Successful farming methods are still used by some Maya farmers. The methods were passed down from their ancestors. The milpa system plants staple crops in the same plot. Those crops include corn, beans, and squash. Farmers harvest each plant as it ripens. To replenish the soil, they burn dead vegetation. Or they leave the land unplanted for years. A statue dating back to the eleventh century shows a Chac priest. Chac is the Maya rain god. He gives rain, or he withholds it. A building known as Casa de las Monjas, the Nunnery, is built in the Puuc style. From One Building Style to the Next. Over the centuries, different groups of Maya invaded Chichén Itzá. They conquered it. Other parts of the Yucatán sent ruling families. They came from the lowlands to the south. They came from the Gulf of Mexico. Another group came from Central Mexico. That group may have been Maya. It may not have been Maya at all. Many architectural styles grew out of that mix of cultures. Many of the earlier buildings are in the Puuc (POOK) style. They were constructed between the sixth and tenth centuries. The Puuc region lay west of Chichén Itzá in the Yucatán Peninsula.

6The Maya city of Uxmal (oos-MAHL) was located there. The Puuc style features strong horizontal lines. The bottom half of a Puuc building is often plain. The upper halves are elaborately carved. During the tenth century, a group of outsiders conquered Chichén Itzá. They brought new architectural styles. Archaeologists are not sure who the conquerors were. They may have been the Toltec. The Toltec were a group of non-Maya natives from Central Mexico. The conquerors may have been an ethnic group of Maya called the Itzá. The city is named for the Itzá. In either case, structures built after this time often include both Maya features and Toltec features. Many buildings are carved with images of winged snakes. They are carved with jaguars. The stepped pyramid has these carvings. So does the Great Ball Court. The same carvings appear on Toltec structures 930 miles to the west. That distance is 1,497 kilometers. Statues known as Chacmools (chahk-MOOLZ) may also be signs of Toltec influence. A Chacmool is a reclining human figure. It holds an offering dish on its stomach. Gods received offerings that were set on the Chacmools. The offerings included tamales, tobacco, or flowers. The heads of all Chacmool statues face outward. Columns surround the Temple of Warriors. Each column has carvings of Toltec warriors. The columns were originally painted. Some paint still remains. The people of Chichén Itzá did not maintain every structure built in earlier styles. They did not necessarily demolish those structures either. A common Maya choice was to raise a larger building on top of an older one. They kept the older building inside.

7Scholars think this was a way to hold onto an old temple's holiness. It may have held onto a palace's power. It may have brought attention to history and to time passing. Or it may simply have reduced the labor needed to construct an entirely new structure. In Chichén Itzá, workers built the stepped pyramid on top of an earlier structure. They built the Temple of the Warriors that way as well. Roads Left from Earlier Times. Maya architects did not limit themselves to buildings. The elevated roads they built are also impressive. People call the roads sacbeob (sahk-bay-OHB). Boulders formed the base layer of each sacbe (SAHK-bay). Finer and finer layers covered that base. The layers were stone, gravel, and powdered limestone. Seventy to eighty sacbeob formed a network at Chichén Itzá that linked the buildings with the cenotes. Longer roads, built by architects, tied the city to communities nearby. The sacbe that leads to the Sacred Cenote is still there centuries later. Maya Calendars. The Haab is a 365-day solar calendar. It is divided into eighteen months of 20 days and one month of 5 days. The Tzolk'in has 260 days. Those days may represent nine cycles of the Moon. The Calendar Round is a 52-year cycle. A day in the Haab is paired with a day in the Tzolk'in. The same pairing does not come back until 52 years have passed. Secrets of Maya Science. The Maya calendar systems clearly show an understanding of astronomy. The Maya invented the concept of zero. They developed complex calendars based on the movements of planets. The calendars are called Haab (HAHB), Tzolk'in (ZOHL-kin), and the Calendar Round.

8These calendars are still in use in some Maya communities. Astronomy that the Maya understood also shows in the stepped pyramid. It has four staircases. Each staircase has ninety-one steps. Count the platform at the top as well, and the steps match every day of the year. One of the four seasons may be what each staircase stands for. The people of Chichén Itzá may have built the pyramid so they could use it as a calendar. It could help them know when to plant crops. It could help them know when to harvest. El Caracol (EL kah-rah-KOHL) is Spanish for the snail. It is a carefully designed round tower. It is the observatory in Chichén Itzá. It provides more clues. The ancient Maya understood the movements of the planets and the stars. No other structure in the city faces the same direction as this building. It is perfectly angled for viewing Venus. The view matches Venus at its northernmost point in the sky. Small windows remain in the ruins of El Caracol. They are aligned with the northernmost position of Venus. They are aligned with its southernmost position. A high platform is what El Caracol stands on. It rises above vegetation that could block views of the heavens. The Maya carefully planned their stepped pyramid. The plan let them track the movement of the Sun. The Maya Today. Central America is home to more than six million Maya people. They live in Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and southern Mexico. They speak more than thirty languages. Across Mayan languages, the words for house, sun, time, mother, and corn sound almost the same.

9These similarities show that some concepts are valued across all Maya cultures. Some of those concepts include the importance of family. They include the importance of community. They include the relationship to corn. The Maya people continue to keep an important connection to the sky. That connection helps them know when to plant crops. Maya people take an active part in the wider world. They often integrate modern practices with ancient traditions. Language is one way Maya people keep their culture alive. They preserve it through their traditions. They preserve it through connections to the land and the sky. A picture can show a Maya woman and children walking through a traditional marketplace in Guatemala. Visits by so many people have worn the stepped pyramid's stairs away. The steps have become too dangerous to climb. A Visit to Chichén Itzá. Few sites in Mexico draw more people than Chichén Itzá. Each year, the site is toured by more than one million people. The Mexican government restored the site in large part to promote tourism. Tourism brings money to the government. It also brings money to the local Maya communities that still surround the city. Visitors may enter many buildings. Access to some structures has been restricted. The limits protect the ruins. They also protect the visitors. Since 2006, climbing the stepped pyramid has been forbidden. In that year, a tourist died in a fall down one of its steep stairways. An estimate from that era puts about fifty thousand people in or near Chichén Itzá. Scientists continue to learn from the treasures those people left behind.

10The Search Goes On. Digging at Chichén Itzá has uncovered a great deal. There is still a great deal to learn. Only five years ago, archaeologists made a discovery in the Holtun cenote. The cenote is not far from the stepped pyramid. They found jade beads. They found knives. They found animal bones and ancient human remains. They also found evidence about the pyramid's alignment. The pyramid was built to line up exactly with the Sun's path over the cenote. If the landscape of Chichén Itzá has more to tell, people are still listening. The descendants of the Maya who built it may have more to tell as well. Words to Know. abandoned (adj.) left behind and uncared for. archaeologists (n.) scientists who study the remains of ancient cultures. artifacts (n.) any objects made or used by humans long ago. astronomy (n.) a field of science that studies the stars, the planets, comets, and other things found in space. excavation (n.) the process of uncovering something or digging it out. intricate (adj.) very detailed or complicated; complex. Maya (n.) a people and a civilization from ancient Central America and southern Mexico, known for stone pyramids. offerings (n.) things offered as contributions or gifts, including gifts that worshippers give to a god or to gods. restored (v.) returned to its original condition. ruins (n.) the remains of an old or destroyed building or other structure. sacrifice (v.) giving something valuable to a god, often by killing a person or an animal during a ceremony. temples (n.) buildings that are places of worship.

7. A Tiny Life That Feeds the Sea

1A speaker too small to see opens this book. Later pages trace who eats whom, then walk from bright water into dim water and finally into black water. The last story climbs back up. A word list finishes the book. Residents of the sea, and plenty of land animals too, treat the ocean as one huge table of food. Think of a great white shark, fierce, taking prey. Think of a blue whale, the largest animal on Earth, swallowing tons of krill. Think of seaweed in giant stands, grazed the way a salad bar is grazed underwater. A quieter fact sits under those pictures. In the end, some other sea animal eats more than 90 percent of sea animals. The voice here belongs to the little organisms that nearly always get eaten. They themselves eat nothing. No ocean species is more microscopic. The wide, complicated food web still has them at its middle. These phytoplankton include forms called diatoms, and a picture shows how small they are. Call the speaker phytoplankton. It is an alga, close to a plant, only far smaller. Plants grow roots. This life does not. It is not fastened to the sea floor or to any ground. Every ocean on Earth carries it in currents close to the surface, where it basks. Sunlight is not optional. Without that light it cannot live. Photosynthesis is the name of the food-making process.

2Chlorophyll, which is green, grabs the Sun's energy. Nutrients drawn from seawater are changed into food. Oxygen leaves as a byproduct and enters both water and air. Another picture shows that green substance inside plant cells, taking the light those cells need for the change. Billions upon billions must gather before the green can be seen, because each cell is so small. Luckily for everyone else, gatherings of that size are common. Thousands can sit in one cup of seawater. Put together, this photosynthesis gives the atmosphere well over half the oxygen Earth has. From space, light streaks mark a bloom where phytoplankton and zooplankton crowd together. How many of them live in a place also tells scientists whether the ocean is healthy. Algal blooms are the large green patches visible from orbit. How often those patches show up, and how far they spread, is a clue to pollution levels. Other sea creatures need those healthy numbers. Directly or indirectly, this life feeds every marine form, the largest and the smallest alike. The whole ocean's food web turns on that center. Picture a simple sandwich made with tuna. Tuna count as relatively large fish. Mackerel, a smaller fish, is what they eat. Flesh weighing 1 kilogram, or 2.2 pounds, costs the tuna about 10 kilograms of mackerel, or 22 pounds. Herring, smaller still, supplied those mackerel. The herring total was 100 kilograms, or 220 pounds.

3Zooplankton amounting to 1,000 kilograms, or 2,200 pounds, fed that herring. Microscopic animals make up the zooplankton. Some are krill, shrimp-like and tiny. Others are larvae, the young of jellyfish, crabs, shrimp, and further fish. Phytoplankton weighing 10,000 kilograms, or 22,000 pounds, had already fed that zooplankton. Read the links in order. Phytoplankton feed zooplankton. Zooplankton feed herring. Herring feed mackerel. Mackerel feed tuna. Zones of the ocean appear in a cross-section picture. A short tour can show how much life hangs on this speaker. It begins in surface water and ends in the trenches, the deepest cuts in the sea floor. Otters, one picture notes, both live and feed where sunlight still reaches. That top layer is called the euphotic zone, or the sunlit zone. From the surface it extends downward about 200 meters, a depth of 660 feet. Plants of the ocean, and phytoplankton, find the strong light ideal. Animal species mostly live here as a result. Shallow floor is often covered by seaweed, some of it green and some of it red. Giant kelp grows in thick forests and shelters many animals. Sea urchins are among them. Otters eat the urchins. At rest, an otter wraps kelp in long strands about its body. The wrap keeps sleep from turning into a drift. Seafood on human plates comes, nearly all of it, from the euphotic zone.

4Oysters, mussels, and clams occupy shallow floors. Crabs and lobsters move through seaweed beds and through coral reefs. Hunting light is good here, and food is plentiful, so most fish species stay. Swordfish are here. So are cod, mackerel, tuna, and salmon. People also eat squid and octopuses that mostly reside in this same water. A hammerhead shark in one picture is a familiar fish of the zone. Reefs of colorful coral are the places visitors like best. Plant and animal species of the ocean are concentrated there more than anywhere else. Clear tropical water with plenty of sun is where small animals called coral polyps live. Their skeletons pile up and form the reef. The community includes lobsters and crabs, plus shellfish and sharks. Lion fish are there, and angelfish, and clown fish. Brain coral and sea fans are there. Moray eels are there. Anemones look like flowers in bloom, yet they are animals. Zooplankton is caught on tentacles that sting. Huge swarms of jellyfish draw sea turtles, which are eager to eat them. Young animals shelter on the reef, then move into the open ocean when they grow up. Biodiversity this rich pulls in tourists and people who love the outdoors. Snorkeling and diving are favorites, above all around coral. Thousands of tons of fish also leave these surface waters. Some become food.

5Some become pets in aquariums of the tropics. Pollution joins that human pressure. Reefs and other parts of the zone are at risk. A polyp can be killed by dirty water. An engine can break it. A diver's step can crush it. After the coral is gone, every other reef animal suffers. Sea life here can feel the damage at once, and the damage can be devastating. The coast feels it too. During a severe storm, reefs act as shields and slow the erosion of the shoreline. That value makes care and protection urgent. Can a damaged food web be repaired? Delaware's Red Bird Reef says yes. The unlikely material is retired subway cars. Beginning in 2001, barges carried hundreds of those cars, emptied and cleaned, out of New York City. They were dropped on empty Atlantic floor off the Delaware coast. Life soon thrived on the metal. Grasses of the sea covered floors and walls. Sponges and mussels held to the sides. Fish passed in and out through the windows. Fishermen, both for sport and for sale, now treat the spot as a hot spot. Harm also falls if explorers stay gentler. Looking into a tide pool samples this zone without a destructive visit. When the tide goes out, leftover pools can hold snails and barnacles. Clams, urchins, and sea stars may be there. Mussels may be there.

6A hermit crab may hurry past in a shell it did not grow. An octopus may show up. You can watch all of this and stay dry. Every one of these lives leans on phytoplankton, whether the link is direct or runs through other eaters. Leave the euphotic zone and the water changes. Darkness increases. Cold increases. The water feels heavier. Twilight begins near 200 meters down, which is 656 feet. Another name is the disphotic zone. It reaches about 1,000 meters, or 3,280 feet. A person would be crushed by the pressure. Residents have adapted instead. Plants cannot live here, and photosynthesis cannot run. The light is too weak. Squid and octopus still keep homes in this band. Whales come down on visits from brighter water. Fish that stay all the time look unlike the fish above. Dark red or black helps them vanish into the gloom. Each species has adaptations suited to chill and dimness. One predator, the viperfish, is a frightening sight. Curved teeth, large ones, rim a mouth that gapes. Active chasing is pointless when almost nothing can be seen. The mouth waits open for a swimmer to come close enough. Hatchet fish stay small. Their bodies are thin and strangely shaped, and silvery scales cover them. Shine on those scales matches the weak light falling from higher water. Counterillumination is the name of that trick. A bigger hunter looking upward struggles to pick them out.

7Bodies that are nearly transparent hide other animals just as well. Giant squid, famous and seldom seen, also keep to this zone. Undersea canyons are their neighborhood. Living ones went unseen until fairly recent years. Now and then a body washed up. Now and then a sperm whale's stomach held the remains. A research ship working the Gulf of Mexico in 2009 caught one in a trailing net. The squid weighed 47 kilograms, equal to 103 pounds. Depth at the net was 457 meters, or 1,500 feet. Biology and daily habits of this mystery animal may become clearer because of that catch. One picture shows an angler fish, small and still scary. Another notes that octopuses belong to both zones, the bright one and this dimmer one. Phytoplankton still end up as food down here, unlikely as that sounds. Scientists use a soft name, marine snow, for the diet. What falls is dead. It is phytoplankton that have died, and zooplankton that have died. The bodies sink in a slow drift, layer after layer, like snow crossing air on the way to the bottom. Being eaten does not require living in that deep place. In the black water, tiny animals glow with their own light. Midnight water has no sunlight at all. Depth runs from 1,000 meters down through 5,000 meters, and farther still.

8In feet, that span is 3,280 to 16,404. Water here is 90 percent of the ocean. Life is almost absent. Most submarines would be crushed. Nearly anything else would be crushed too. The cold sits close to freezing. Look carefully and life still appears. Aphotic zone is the other name. Lantern fish, and many other tiny animals, wear small lights along the body. Fireflies shine by the same process. It is called bioluminescence. Bacteria can carry this light. Fish, squid, and jellyfish can carry it too. Without the Sun, the glow lets animals see. It lets them signal. Mates can be found. Food can be found. The deep-sea angler fish is a famous neighbor, and the name suits it. Females grow a stalk from the top of the head. Bacteria that glow cover the tip, bright like a bulb. Prey comes close, drawn as if the stalk were a fishing pole, and the jaws wait. Hot minerals pour from a chimney in one picture. That chimney is a black smoker. Crabs use the warmth and the nutrients. Tube worms use them. Other animals use them too. Oceanographers sometimes cut this dark region into two further zones. Trenches are one. The abyssal zone is the other. Darkness there is complete. Much of the floor lies in it: canyons, valleys, mountains, and wide plains. Faults are where trenches open.

9Great plates in Earth's crust collide along those cracks. Canyons and splits can reach 10,000 meters, or 32,808 feet. Cold is severe. Blackness is total. Pressure is huge. Nothing, you would think, could live there. Hot water and minerals still jet from openings in the trench floor. They rise from deep in the Earth. The warmth is enough to sustain life. Hot magma meets seawater, and the openings take shape. Warmth and nutrients from those openings are used by the animals much as sunlight is used up above. Chimneys is another word for the openings. Bacteria around them feed giant clams. They feed shrimp and tube worms. The year 1977 was the first time scientists found these hydrothermal vents. The place was the ocean floor beside the Galapagos Islands. A trench bottom has enormous pressure. Few submersibles, small submarines, are strong enough to bear it. One picture shows a craft built for exactly that. Back at the surface, the point is clear. Home for phytoplankton is only the top of the sea. The food web still has them in the middle, holding up every other life in the water. Size is microscopic. Impact is not. Ocean meals depend on them. Human meals depend on them. Maybe you come for reefs. Maybe you come for the dark unknown of the abyss. Maybe you come for fish and chips. Thank phytoplankton either way.

10Words in this book can be read as follows. Within the aphotic zone, the deep floor is the abyssal zone. An accumulation is a pile that builds as time goes on. An anemone is a sea animal with a plantlike form, and the tentacles often mimic petals. No sunlight enters the aphotic zone, the lowest band of the ocean. Biodiversity means how many kinds of life share Earth, or share one habitat or ecosystem. When a living body makes light by a biochemical process, that light is bioluminescence. Plant cells hold a green substance called chlorophyll. During photosynthesis it absorbs the light energy used to make food. Counterillumination hides an animal by matching a lit background with light of its own. A demise is a death, a failure, or an ending. Damage that is devastating is great and physical. Little sunlight reaches the disphotic zone, the ocean's middle band. Plants do not live there, and animals are scarce. Almost all ocean life sits in the euphotic zone, the top band. A fault is a crack in the crust of Earth, and the crust moves along it. In photosynthesis, plant cells absorb sunlight and spend that energy changing carbon dioxide and water into food. A phytoplankton is an alga of one cell, living in water. A submersible is a small craft able to work underwater, above all at great depth.

8. A Wall Through the Middle of Berlin

1A map places Berlin inside Germany. Around it sit Europe, the Atlantic Ocean, Denmark, Africa, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Poland, Belgium, Czechia, France, Austria, Switzerland, and Italy. Seven sections shape this account. They cover a hated wall, the Cold War, the rise of the barrier, life in a split city, ways past the wall, the wall's fall, and a word list. In 1987, before West Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, President Ronald Reagan delivers the speech in which he demands that the wall be torn down. A wall people hated June 12, 1987, brought a memorable address from United States President Ronald Reagan, given in West Berlin, Germany. Behind him stood the Brandenburg Gate, famous in that city. The gate was very near and still impossible to reach. The reason was its place on the far side. That barrier was the Berlin Wall, already infamous. Few symbols of the Cold War were more visible, or more detested. That struggle set a communist East against a democratic West. Some of Reagan's words were aimed at Mikhail Gorbachev, leader of the Soviet Union. Reagan's voice rose. He told Gorbachev to pull the wall down. Gorbachev was absent and offered no answer. The wall stayed up. Anyone there that day could imagine it standing forever. A portrait shows Mikhail Gorbachev. The Cold War From 1939 to 1945, during World War II, the United States kept an uneasy tie with the Soviet Union. France and Great Britain shared the unease. They still joined forces to beat the Axis, a coalition joining Japan, Italy, and Germany. Once Germany surrendered in May 1945, the partnership began to break.

2The Soviet Union tightened its hold on Eastern Europe, lands its troops had occupied while chasing the German army in retreat. Those controlled nations became the Eastern Bloc. East Germany belonged to that region, and Berlin sat entirely inside Soviet territory. Once Nazi Germany was beaten, the victors split Berlin into four sectors. One victor would govern each sector: the United States, France's partner Britain, the Soviet Union, or France. The city's eastern sector was the Soviet share. A map of the split city shows the wall and the zones of France, the Soviet Union, Great Britain, and the United States, labeled West and East. Four nations controlled Berlin once World War II had ended. Late in the 1940s, distrust between Moscow and the nations of the West had deepened. Commitment to communism defined the Soviet Union, and wanted that ideology to spread. Democracies included the United States and Western Europe's nations, and they opposed communism strongly. During 1947, a policy called the Truman Doctrine was adopted in the United States. President Harry S. Truman gave it his name. It promised aid to any nation threatened by Soviet expansion. Because the two ideologies differed completely, hostility settled into a stalemate. People called that stalemate the Cold War. Full control of Berlin was the Soviet aim. In June 1948 the Soviets tried to get it by cutting every road into the city's western parts. An answer came from Great Britain and from the United States with the Berlin airlift. A picture shows a ragged group of Berliners among ruins while a cargo plane brings food during that airlift.

3Portraits show President John F. Kennedy and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. Food, fuel, and other necessities flew into the city around the clock. Western powers had shown they would stand for West Berlin's freedom, so in May 1949 the Soviets lifted the blockade. The airlift no longer had to continue. That first Berlin crisis was settled, yet the city stayed tense. Through the decade of the 1950s and then the 1960s, both East and West still found Berlin a headache. Washington feared the standoff could become an armed clash, and that clash could become a full war. Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev, on November 10, 1958, demanded in a speech that France, Britain, and the United States quit West Berlin. Talks linking Moscow with the United States produced no progress. Berlin was a crisis nobody seemed able to defuse. The barrier rises Another trouble pressed the Soviet Union and East Germany's government. East Germany was losing people in crowds. Many Germans in East Berlin, and in the rest of East Germany, rejected communist rule. Basic rights were missing, including the vote and freedom of speech. Wages were low, supplies were thin, and prices were high. Thousands moved to West Germany through West Berlin, which worked as an escape hatch. The border between the two Germanys was sealed tight, but Berlin itself stayed an open city. A person in the East could ride a streetcar, or hire a taxi into West Berlin, then board a plane for a West German city. Many who left were young and well educated, so the outflow threatened East Germany's economy.

4Some 2.5 million people, by 1961, had relocated west. East Germany's population fell by about 15 percent. Soviet leaders and East German leaders decided something had to be done. Their 1961 answer was an impenetrable wall built around West Berlin. Bricklayers from the East German side are shown raising the wall, a barrier meant to stop refugees from reaching West Berlin. Construction started without warning on August 13, 1961, a day later called Barbed Wire Sunday. Concrete blocks and barbed wire made the first wall. Later, concrete slabs replaced them. Those slabs rose as high as 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, with barbed wire on top, and with watchtowers and gun posts as guards. In the end there were two walls. The outer one faced West Berlin. An inner wall stood behind it. Open ground between them was about 143 meters wide, or 469 feet. People named that ground the death strip, because crossers were often shot. Through Berlin the wall ran about 45 kilometers, or 28 miles, then another 120 kilometers, or 75 miles, beyond the city, ringing it completely. Guards had orders to fire on any person who tried an escape. A picture shows cars passing the crossing called Checkpoint Charlie, headed into West Berlin. The scene is ten days after laws on crossing the border were eased. East Germany's government denied that the wall was built to stop emigration. It claimed the wall kept opponents of communism from entering and undermining the state. Walter Ulbricht, an East German leader, said they had closed every crack running through the fabric of their house and closed the holes where the German people's worst enemies might creep.

5With the wall up, West Berliners could enter the eastern sector only at several checkpoints. Those gates mainly served diplomats and military personnel. Fame belonged most of all to Checkpoint Charlie. Tourists had that gate as their only portal. Many people asked why Western allies of the United States did not stop the building. Truth was different. Seeing the barrier rise did not make President Kennedy or the other Western leaders unhappy. They had feared violence breaking out inside Berlin, or a fresh attempt to cut West Berlin off, as in the late 1940s. Nikita Khrushchev, the Soviet leader, had threatened a fresh blockade if Western forces refused to leave. When the building started, Kennedy felt relief. The wall, he said, was not a fine answer for Berlin, but it beat a war. He declared the Berlin crisis finished. A picture shows East German troops guarding the wall, with West Berlin marked on one side and East Berlin on the other. Life in a split city. Once the wall was a settled part of the landscape, acceptance came from people living on either side of it. What other choice was there? The division was inconvenient. Streets were cut. Public squares were cut. Certain districts saw the barrier run down the middle of a street or along a row of houses. West Berliners showed contempt by covering the wall's length in colorful graffiti. Daily life in West Berlin changed little.

6People were free to follow whatever interested them. At last they were free of the risk of a military clash. A vibrant society grew. Lights and neon blazed. Shops, restaurants, and department stores offered what a modern city offers its people. Arts thrived. Theater and music flourished, and the music embraced the youth movement of the 1960s. As time passed, West Berliners developed what they called a mentality like an island. In their own eyes they were a bastion, isolated, of freedom and of Western values, ringed by communism, which surrounded them like a dark sea. East Berlin was dark in a literal way. Streets were poorly lit, with no neon and no billboards. State department stores stocked only a sparse range of goods. Jobs, when they existed, were limited. Worse, secret police were everywhere. They were called the Stasi. About a hundred thousand employees worked for them, plus informers who may have reached two million, hunting people labeled enemies of the state, both inside East Berlin and across the rest of that state. Colleagues, neighbors, and friends were pushed to report on one another. Files covered citizens of East Germany numbering about five million, roughly a third of the population. Life in East Berlin, and in the rest of East Germany, grew repressive and often dangerous. Escape became a desperate wish for many. A picture shows East German police watching a photographer in West Berlin while the wall goes up. Near the Brandenburg Gate, a hole in the fence let 150 people flee west. Getting past the wall Across the wall's lifetime, East Berliners numbering about ten thousand made attempts to reach the West.

7About half succeeded, and that half included some six hundred border guards. Of the other five thousand, nearly all were captured and arrested. Sentries killed approximately two hundred, or fatal accidents did. Some estimates put the dead closer to seven hundred. Methods varied. In the first days, people jumped from windows or from roofs of buildings close to the wall. Falls killed some of them. Further attempts used hot-air balloons, or sewer pipes, or cars driven at weaker stretches. Some intrepid people simply clawed at the barbed wire and tried to climb over. Once watchtowers and gun posts made the wall a formidable barrier, some East Berliners tunneled. They dug with painful care, across spans that reached 190 meters, or 600 feet. Many tunnels failed. Some collapsed. Some flooded. Before anyone could use them, guards posted on the border, or else the secret police, discovered the rest. About three hundred people still escaped through tunnels. Arrest for an escape attempt could mean three years in prison, and prisoners could face hard labor or torture. People who fled, and political prisoners besides them, also turned into a lucrative source of money for East Germany's government. Ransoms from West Germany, running from 1964 to 1989, covered political prisoners numbering nearly 34,000, along with 250,000 members of their families. The sums brought in German marks amounting to some 3.5 billion. That was nearly 1 billion dollars in the dollars of 1965, or close to 8 billion dollars now. Those who were ransomed could leave with nothing but their clothes.

8In West Germany they gained something far more precious: freedom. The wall falls. Late in the decade of the 1980s, Soviet control of Eastern Europe began to weaken. Nation by nation, the Eastern Bloc announced freedom from domination by communists. The Soviet Union could not stop them. The Cold War was ending at last. On November 9, 1989, a spokesman of East Germany's Communist Party announced that city residents could now pass into the western half. His intention had been an orderly change, with long paperwork. Jubilant Berliners on both sides ignored him. Thousands flocked to the wall in celebration. Many passed the checkpoints. Others climbed up with hammers and picks and knocked chunks from the barricade. People called them wall woodpeckers. Across that weekend, East Berliners numbering some two million poured into West Berlin for a joyous party. A journalist on the scene called it a street party larger than any the world had seen. One picture shows a wall woodpecker at work. In November 1989, thousands of Germans from east and west celebrate the Cold War's end along that barrier, on the East Berlin side of Germany. Months passed while the wall came down. Woodpeckers kept up their small demolitions. East Germany's government brought cranes and bulldozers to tear out large sections. Germany's reunification date was October 3, 1990. East Germany and West Germany were no longer separate. One nation stood again, under a democratic government. The capital returned to Berlin. The capital had not sat there since 1945. Even more astonishing was the end of the Soviet Union itself.

9December 8, 1991, was the day the Soviet Union was formally dissolved. A body under the name Commonwealth of Independent States replaced it, made of Russia plus several republics that had been Soviet. Truly, the Cold War was finished. Germany was unified again, yet growing pains came with integrating the sectors of east and west. Communism had been the life of two generations, who knew little of democracy or of life in the West. In time the country became whole. Today the country is a powerful European force and holds the continent's biggest economy of all. The wall that once split Germany ended by strengthening it and binding it together. Where pieces of the wall rest. The barrier was broken into many pieces. Most of the material was ground up and used in German highway building. Many chunks passed into private hands. Others were sold in Berlin souvenir shops or by sellers working online. In 2013 a large slab brought 23,500 dollars when Atlanta, Georgia, auctioned it. One piece stands inside a Rome garden belonging to the Vatican. Maybe the oddest home for a section is a men's restroom in one casino of Las Vegas. The biggest piece still intact is Berlin's East Side Gallery, 1.3 kilometers long, or 0.8 miles. Other fragments around the city remind people of a troubled past. A section is also on display inside New York City, at the United Nations. Words from the book. A bastion is a place or a situation where certain ideas or practices survive and thrive. Demolitions are acts that destroy something completely, often with explosives.

10A blockade is any obstacle meant to stop passage through an area. Dissolved, a verb, means brought to an end. Communist, an adjective, concerns a belief that the government should run the economy and that individuals may not own property. Emigration is the act of leaving a country or a region to settle elsewhere. Formidable, an adjective, means impressive or powerful enough to stir respect or fear. A crisis is a dangerous, unstable time that demands attention. An ideology is the set of beliefs under an economic system, or a social or political one. Democratic, an adjective, concerns government through elections that are free and frequent, by the people themselves. Impenetrable, an adjective, means impossible to see through, or impossible to pierce. Infamous, an adjective, means famous for evil, harm, or danger. Occupied, a verb, means took or held a district using military force. People called informers secretly pass word of a crime, and a reward is often the reason. Payments called ransoms are payments demanded or made so a captive person or thing will be released. Integrating means bringing different groups or ideas together. Repressive describes rule that blocks free expression and uses force to keep people down. Intrepid, an adjective, means fearless and daring. Jubilant, an adjective, means full of great joy. Reunified, a verb, means joined again. Sectors are distinct divisions of a place. Lucrative, an adjective, means able to produce a great deal of money. Negotiations are talks aimed at a formal agreement. A stalemate is a deadlock in which neither side can win.

9. Abraham Lincoln and the Nation He Held Together

1The parts of this book follow one path. An introduction comes first. Early years come next. Law and politics follow. A divided America comes after that. The years of war come last. A word list closes the book. Lincoln grew a beard only after he had won the presidency. He had not yet moved to Washington, D.C. An 11-year-old girl was the person who suggested the beard. One picture shows the Lincoln Memorial. Washington, D.C., is the city. Millions of people visit that monument each year. In the story of American presidents, few matter more than Abraham Lincoln. He led the United States through the Civil War. The war lasted from 1861 to 1865. Northern states and Southern states fought over what the country would become. People call him the Great Emancipator. Enslaved people across the South gained freedom because of what he did. When the fighting stopped, the country stood as one nation again. It has stayed one nation ever since. Americans treat Abraham Lincoln as a great folk hero. Stories and legends gather around him. Pictures often show him tall. They show him lanky. They show him solemn. Memory keeps him as a common man. Regular schooling in his life was slight. A log cabin in Kentucky was his birthplace. Humble beginnings did not stop him. He became an outstanding lawyer. He became an outstanding speaker. He became an outstanding political leader. Speeches of his, eloquent ones, speak of freedom. They speak of justice. They speak of bringing all Americans together. Those words are cut into stone at the Lincoln Memorial. The memorial stands in Washington, D.C. His belief can be put in plain words. He would not accept being enslaved. He would not accept being a master either. That pair of refusals was his meaning of democracy. A picture shows a cabin built from logs. People believe those logs came from the cabin where he was born. The cabin stands at the Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site. Hodgenville, Kentucky, is the town. Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln were his parents. February 12, 1809, was the day of his birth. The place was a small farm of log cabins near Hodgenville, Kentucky.

2The family later moved to Knob Creek, close by. School there included Abe. Sarah, his older sister, went as well. The schooling came only in short stretches. Those stretches fell in the winters. Nancy, their mother, pushed them to learn. Tom, their father, wanted Abe at the chores instead. Abe was seven when the family moved to Indiana. They hoped Indiana would give them a better life. A fresh cabin made of logs was Tom's work. Two years after that cabin, Nancy died. Milk sickness was the cause. Milk sickness is poisoning. The poison comes from milk or meat of cows. Those cows have eaten a certain plant. Abe mourned his mother. Sarah mourned her too. She had been hard-working. She had been loving. Soon afterward, Tom married Sarah Bush Johnston. She was a widow. She was already mother to three children. Tom had known her back in Kentucky. Love and care from her made a warm home for Abe. The same care made a warm home for Sarah. She encouraged Abe as he grew. He grew tall. He grew awkward. Hours in the woods went to his ax. He felled trees. He split logs for fences. He split logs for wagons. He split logs for farm equipment. Friends noticed a moody quiet in him. Even so, he told stories that were homey. The stories were humorous too. Winter school for Abe lasted only a few weeks. Each day he walked 18 miles. That distance is 29 kilometers. Most of his learning was his own work. He borrowed books from neighbors. He borrowed newspapers from neighbors. He borrowed them from travelers too. These were frontier days. People were moving west. Daniel Boone was one pioneer they followed. Johnny Appleseed was another. Other pioneers went ahead as well. Stories of those travelers widened Abe's view. Books he read did the same. The world began to look bigger than his backwoods. As a teenager he stood 6 feet 4 inches tall. That height is 2 meters. A flatboat carried him along the Mississippi River. Produce filled the boat. He floated with the current. A pole was how he steered. New Orleans, a busy port, was the end of the trip.

3He saw the wonders of that city. He saw its diversity. For the first time he saw Black men in holding pens. He saw Black women in those pens. He saw Black children there too. They were caged. They were chained at auction blocks. White enslavers bought them. White enslavers sold them. His feelings about ending slavery changed across his life. Hatred of the institution itself never changed. The year 1841 put him on a steamboat. The Ohio River was the route. That river was a border. Several free states met several slave states along it. A dozen enslaved people were on board. Shackles held them together. He called that sight a continual torment. The same torment returned whenever he met that river. Any line that separated enslaved Black people from free people brought the torment back. Early campaigns taught him to communicate with skill. After the river trip, his father moved the family again. The new home was in central Illinois. Decatur was the nearby town. Abe helped his father raise another log cabin. He left the homestead soon after that. He was twenty-two. New Salem was a frontier village. He worked there as a storekeeper. He worked as a surveyor. He worked as a carpenter. People also knew him as a wrestler. Inside the New Salem Debating Society, people knew his skill as an orator. The Illinois state legislature was the office he sought. The 1832 race was a loss. Two years later he won. John Todd Stuart, a lawyer and a fellow legislator, urged him to study law. Abe read law books. March 1837 was the month he passed the law exams. He joined Stuart's law practice. Springfield became his home. The Illinois legislature met in that city. Democratic rights for every person were the base of Lincoln's views. Wealth did not decide a person's importance. Privilege did not decide it either. Respect inside the Whig Party grew around him. Whigs wanted a strong central government. Washington, D.C., was where that government sat. Democrats were the other leading party. They believed in states' rights. In that view, a state should run its own affairs. Washington should not interfere.

4Lincoln was thirty when he met Mary Ann Todd. She would become his wife. She was fashionable. Her father was a wealthy banker in Kentucky. Her background and his were far apart. They fell in love anyway. Her parents objected. The couple married once those objections were overcome. November 4, 1842, was the wedding day. Robert, the couple's first son, arrived in 1843. In 1846 Lincoln won election as Illinois representative. The seat was in the U.S. Congress. The family moved to Washington, D.C. A picture shows Mary Todd Lincoln in 1846. During his time in Congress, North and South grew more polarized. Slavery was the issue pulling them apart. The North relied on paid laborers. Those laborers worked in factories. They also worked on small farms. The North wanted a strong central government. Northern states had already made slavery illegal. King Cotton ruled the Southern economy. Large plantations grew that cotton. The work was done by enslaved people. Those people had no personal rights. They had no civil rights. Most lived in very poor conditions. Treatment of them was inhumane. Southern state laws allowed slavery. Those laws protected it. Western territories were asking to become states as the country grew. One question mattered most. Would a new state be free, or would it be a slave state? The South wanted the new land for cotton. Enslaved labor was how that cotton would be grown. The North wanted independent farms. The North wanted paid labor. A picture shows a building in Atlanta, Georgia. Sales of enslaved people took place in that building. Lincoln was against slavery. As Illinois's representative in Washington, he still saw a legal limit. State law in the South, he believed, protected the practice there. He did fight to stop slavery from spreading into the western territories. The abolitionist movement grew during the 1840s. Its goal was to outlaw slavery. White people were among its followers. Free Black people were among them too. They called for the horrors of human bondage to stop. They demanded an end to the inhumanity of holding humans that way. Two years in Washington were enough. Lincoln went back to Springfield. For the next few years he shared a law practice.

5William Herndon was his partner. The practice did well. People spoke of Lincoln's honesty. They spoke of his skill in law. They spoke of his wit. They spoke of his fine oratory. February 1850 brought a family tragedy. Eddie, their boy, died of tuberculosis. He was nearly four. Both parents sank into deep depression. Signs of emotional imbalance appeared in Mary. December of that year brought another son. His name was Willie. Three years later another son arrived. His name was Thomas. Tad was his short name. Lincoln stayed very close to his sons. He was a proud father. He was a loving father. The 1850s were years of struggle between proslavery and antislavery forces. The Kansas-Nebraska Act won passage in Congress during 1854. An earlier law had forbidden slavery in those territories. The new act cancelled that ban. Residents themselves could now choose. They could choose to be a free state. They could choose to be a slave state. Popular sovereignty is the name of that idea. Letting the people decide is what it means. Stephen Douglas introduced it. Lincoln and Douglas had been political rivals for years. He was now a U.S. senator from Illinois. A map gives the picture of slavery in the country once the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 was law. Nebraska Territory appears on it. Utah Territory appears on it. Kansas Territory appears on it. New Mexico Territory appears on it. The map marks free states and territories. It marks areas allowed to choose. It marks slave states. It marks unorganized territory. Lincoln decided the spread of slavery had to be opposed out loud. He also decided to seek office again. The new Republican Party was against slavery. He joined it. In 1858 that party nominated him for senator. Senator Douglas, his old enemy, was the opponent. The Lincoln-Douglas debates were held during the campaign. The whole country paid attention. A picture shows Lincoln in 1858. The picture was made two weeks before his last debate with Douglas. With great skill as a speaker, he said slavery had put the nation in crisis. A house split against itself, he said, cannot keep standing.

6He said this government could not last forever if half of it stayed enslaved. The other half, in that picture, would be free. Black people, he argued, held the same claim as white people. That claim was the right to life. It was the right to liberty. It was the right to the pursuit of happiness. Douglas answered from the Constitution. Equality, he said, was guaranteed only to white people. Each state, he asserted, could choose slavery or freedom for itself. A picture shows Stephen A. Douglas. Lincoln lost that election. The debates still made him popular. The Republican Party felt that popularity most. By 1860 the party wanted him for president. Rallies and parades gave him nicknames. One name was Honest Abe. Another was the homespun rail-splitter. People called him a man of the people. Equality was what he stood for. Freedom was what he stood for. The rail-splitter name came from work he had done as a young man. On November 6, 1860, voters made Lincoln president. The nation was the United States. The North rejoiced. The western territories rejoiced. The South was outraged. His inauguration was set for March 4, 1861. Seven states in the South cast votes to secede before inauguration day. They were leaving the United States of America. February saw a government formed by the states that supported slavery. Confederate States of America was its name. Jefferson Davis was its president. Those states prepared for war. Lincoln still hoped to avoid bloodshed. In the inauguration speech he placed the choice with the unhappy states. The momentous question of civil war, he said, was in their hands. It was not in his. A picture shows that inauguration. The date was March 4, 1861. The place was the U.S. Capitol. The Capitol was still under construction. Events then moved fast. By April 14, Northern troops had given up Fort Sumter. Cannons from South Carolina had fired on the fort. Both sides mobilized quickly. The Union was one side. The Confederacy was the other. They called for volunteers. They gathered arms. They gathered supplies. Lincoln's home and office were in Washington, D.C. That city belonged to the Union. Across the river he could see Virginia.

7Virginia belonged to the Confederacy. Superior military leadership on the Southern side won the first battle. That battle was at Bull Run. Union forces lost it. Strong commanders were hard for Lincoln to find while the war lasted. General George B. McClellan led Union armies to some successes. By 1862 those armies were stopped. Confederate General Robert E. Lee was the one who stopped them. Union forces did control New Orleans. They controlled the Mississippi River. Victories beyond that were few. The North called for action. Lincoln took on more of the military planning. Young soldiers died in enormous numbers on both sides. Others were wounded. Others were missing. The war moved into its second year. Personal loss struck Mary and Abraham Lincoln in February 1862. Fever took their son Willie. Mary never fully recovered from that grief. Abraham carried the same sadness into meetings with families. Those families were mourning their own war dead. A picture shows President Lincoln talking with General McClellan at Antietam. Replacement of McClellan would come soon. Bull Run's second battle went against the Union. No engagement in the war was bloodier than Antietam. Both sides suffered there. Powerful Republican senators pressed the president. They wanted abolition of slavery to become a goal of the war. Their argument was practical. The Union, they said, had to remove the issue that had caused the war. Only then could the fight succeed. Lincoln at last accepted a claim about his own power. As president, he could order abolition in the South. The Emancipation Proclamation became active on January 1, 1863. From that day forward, and for all time, it freed enslaved people in the Confederacy. The proclamation freed many enslaved people. It did not free all of them. Freedom on that first day of January 1863 covered enemy territory. Black men just freed inside Confederate areas could then join the Union fight. The North badly needed those soldiers. The war's meaning changed. It became a crusade against slavery. Border states were left out. Delaware was one. Maryland was one. Kentucky was one. Missouri was one. Those states still held enslaved people. They had never seceded from the Union.

8Lincoln feared a result if he freed people there. Those states might join the Confederacy. The United States would be very likely to lose the war if that happened. It would lose the South. It would lose the chance to end slavery in every state. Enslaved people who remained would wait two more years for freedom. A map shows the border states in 1863. It marks Union free states. It marks Union slave states. It marks Confederate slave states. It marks territory. Maryland, Delaware, West Virginia, Missouri, and Kentucky appear on it. No other state was created the way West Virginia was, by breaking away from a Confederate state. That Confederate state was Virginia. From 1863 to 1865, the new Union state ended slavery step by step. After Fort Sumter, free Black men hurried to join the Union army. At first they were turned away. They had served in earlier wars. A federal law from 1792 still blocked them. The law said they could not bear arms for the U.S. Army. By the middle of 1862, the Union needed more volunteers badly. That need pushed the government to lift the ban. By the war's end, Black men serving as soldiers numbered nearly two hundred thousand. A picture shows Company E of the 4th U.S. Colored Infantry. Former enslaved men made up that company. Other free Black men served in it too. Many people call Lincoln the Great Emancipator. For many Native peoples, the record he left is not a good one. He was president during a great push westward. His policies hurt Native peoples who already lived on those lands. The harm was disastrous. The Homestead Act of 1862 was one cause. Another law was the Pacific Railway Act, passed in 1862. Together they led to building the transcontinental railroad. Lost land was one result of that railroad for a great many Native peoples. It meant lost natural resources. It meant the loss of a whole way of life. Lincoln forced Native peoples onto reservations. In doing that, he carried on harsh policies of presidents before him. Those policies were discriminatory. A picture from 1864 shows Manuelito on the left. He was a Navajo chief.

9Notrossia and Pattia stand on the right. They were two Navajo girls. That year the Lincoln administration oversaw a removal. Navajo people were taken from their home. Some Apache people were taken too. The home region was northeastern Arizona. The march they were forced to make covered hundreds of miles. People came to call that march the Long Walk. Many died along the way. Summer of 1863 brought a Union victory at Gettysburg. Gettysburg turned the direction of the war. Lincoln dedicated a cemetery there to soldiers who had died. The speech he gave is the Gettysburg Address. The speech took only two minutes. People still remember its simple beauty. They remember its eloquence. He described the war as a test. He asked whether a nation built as a democracy could last. He asked the living to finish work the dead had left undone. A government of the people, he said, must not vanish from the earth. A government by the people must not vanish. A government for the people must not vanish. General Ulysses S. Grant was newly appointed. Under him, Union armies won in the West. They won in the South. Georgia saw Confederate troops go down to defeat late in 1864. They were defeated in Virginia. Lincoln began to hope the war would end. He was re-elected president. Early in 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. He cheered that passage. Slavery inside the United States was banned by that amendment. That amendment was only a first step toward equal rights for Black people. Denial stayed routine through the years of the civil rights movement in the 1960s. Jobs were denied. Voting rights were denied. Basic human respect was denied. April 9, 1865, brought the war to a close. Four years had passed since it began. Six hundred thousand lives was the cost. The Union was preserved. Slavery was abolished. Only six days later, Abraham Lincoln was dead. An assassin's bullet had killed him. John Wilkes Booth was the shooter. Booth sympathized with the Confederacy. Lincoln was at a play in Ford's Theatre. The theatre is in Washington, D.C. A funeral train carried his body back to Illinois, the state he loved.

10Mourners along the road saluted in silence. They were saluting a great American hero. A picture from February 1865 is among the last photographs of him. A timeline marks the main dates. His birth date on the timeline is February 12, 1809. Kentucky is the state listed. In 1818, his mother, Nancy, died. In 1819, his father, Thomas, married Sarah Bush Johnston. In 1834, Lincoln was elected to the Illinois state legislature. In 1837, he opened a law practice in Springfield, Illinois. In 1842, he married Mary Todd. In 1846, he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. In 1850, his son Edward died at age four. In 1858, the Lincoln-Douglas debates were held. Lincoln became a leader on the anti-slavery issue. In 1860, he was elected president. In 1861, the Civil War began. Confederates fired on Fort Sumter to start it. In 1862, his son William died at age twelve. The Battle of Antietam was fought that year. In 1863, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. The Union won at Gettysburg that year. In 1865, Confederate forces surrendered. That surrender ended the Civil War. The shot came on April 14, during the evening. He died the following day. The word list gives meanings from this book. An abolitionist worked to put slavery outside the law. Civil rights are legal rights. They are also social rights. They are also economic rights. They guarantee freedom and equality for every citizen. Eloquent speech or writing is simple, powerful, and elegant. An emancipator is a person who sets other people free. Equality means every person holds the same rights. Homespun means humble. It means a person comes from a simple rural background. To act inhumanely is to act with no dignity and no kindness. Momentous means hugely important. It means something of great consequence. An orator is a public speaker. An eloquent speaker is the kind the word points to most. To secede is to withdraw in a formal way from a group or an organization. Solemn means serious. It can also mean sad. Sovereignty means a person or a state is free to handle its own affairs.

10. Africa's Heavyweight Beetles

1Male Goliath beetles grow Y-shaped horns that they use when they fight. This book begins with the biggest beetle on Earth. It then asks what kind of beetle a Goliath is. The scarab family comes next. An African home follows. The life cycle comes after that. Speed and other wonders close the story. A word list sits at the end. About a million insect species are known. Beetles account for close to half of that total. Goliath beetles sit inside that huge group. Common does not mean ordinary, though. These beetles are fast, and they live mostly alone. People are still learning about them. Finding them is hard. Studying them is hard too. Size sets them apart from a ladybug cousin. Beside a ladybug cousin, a Goliath measures over two thousand times the bulk. The young form is even bigger. A developing Goliath, called a larva, weighs nearly twice what an adult weighs. That bulk makes these beetles the heavyweight champions of insects. They are amazing insects in every way. A size chart shows the larva at 5 inches (12.7 cm) long. The larva weighs 3.5 ounces (99.2 g). The adult beetle is 4.33 inches (10.99 cm) long. The adult weighs 1.7 ounces (48.2 g). A human hand on the chart is 7.44 inches (18.89 cm) long.

2The hand is 3.3 inches (8.4 cm) wide. A rhinoceros beetle, a Hercules beetle, and a Goliath beetle can be lined up for a look. Beetles come in every shape and size. The Goliath still wins on weight. Centipedes of huge size appear in fossils three hundred million years old. They also show dragonflies whose wings stretched as wide as a hawk's wings. Today the air carries less oxygen than it carried in that distant past. Insects and some other animals have simpler systems for moving fluid through the body. Those systems cannot carry oxygen to every part in an efficient way. Because of that, a Goliath body cannot reach the sizes seen in those ancient times. More oxygen in the old air allowed greater growth. A few beetles alive today are longer than a Goliath. The Hercules beetle can reach 7 inches (18 cm). That length includes 4 inches (10 cm) of horn. The rhinoceros beetle is 6 inches (15.24 cm) long. Most of that length comes from the huge horns on its head. The Goliath beetle is about 4 inches (10 cm) long. Other beetles cannot match its body weight. That weight is a full 1.7 ounces (48.2 g). The name Goliath beetle covers six related kinds. Telling the six apart is hard.

3Even inside one kind, the markings are never the same on two beetles. Early nature scholars thought they had found more than two dozen separate kinds. Each beetle looked so different that a new name seemed right. Later they learned the truth. Those specimens were only different examples of the six Goliath types. The first type is Goliathus cacicus. Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part KA-sih-kus. Another type is Goliathus goliatus. Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part go-LY-uh-tuhs. A third type is Goliathus regius. Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part REJ-ee-us. A fourth type is Goliathus orientalis. Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part or-ee-en-TAH-lis. A fifth type is Goliathus "atlas". Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part AT-luhs. The sixth type is Goliathus albosignatus. Say the first part go-LY-uh-thus. Say the second part al-bo-SIG-nuh-tuhs. Early British nature scholars called Goliath beetles zebra beetles. Bold black-and-white stripes and other marks earned that name. Scientists suspect the strong pattern may hide the beetle. Enemies may miss it. Researchers may miss it too. The marks break up the body's outline. A leafy background then hides the insect more easily. All beetles share some body traits. Two pairs of wings are part of that shared plan.

4The rear wings are the flying wings. They are dark. They look like leather, yet they are thin and like a membrane. Those rear wings are strong enough to lift the beetle's full weight in the air. The front wings are called elytra. They are smaller, harder, and tougher than the flying wings. When the beetle is not flying, the elytra form a suit of armor over the folded rear wings. In many beetles, the elytra also shield the body. Mouths in some insects have changed for special ways of eating and drinking. A Goliath beetle does drink sap. Its mouth is built more for chewing than for sipping nectar the way a butterfly does. It is not built for piercing skin the way a mosquito does. Many smaller beetles sit on flowers and eat pollen or petals. A Goliath weighs too much for a flower to hold it. Scientists think these giant insects probably do not feed on flowers. Sharp claws, called tarsi, help them climb trees instead. Tree sap and rotting fruit are the food they seek. A diagram of the body shows several insect traits. Antennae can spread open so the beetle senses its surroundings better. Hard wings guard the thin flying wings. The body has a head, a thorax, and an abdomen.

5Male Goliath beetles carry Y-shaped horns used in fights. Sharp claws give a firm grip for climbing. Every insect has wings. Every insect has jointed legs, and most have six legs. Every insect has three main body parts: a head, a thorax, and an abdomen. Every insect has a skeleton on the outside. Beetle remains in a London museum puzzled people for a long time. Recent X-rays cleared the puzzle up. Holes in the remains were gunshot wounds. The scientist used the entry hole and the exit hole to judge the angle. The report said the beetle was hit while it flew upside down. Beetles are sorted into more than one hundred families. Scientists use the word family for animals whose traits match. Scientists think each beetle family comes from one shared ancestor. Hundreds of millions of years have passed since that shared ancestor lived. The scarab family is where Goliath beetles fit. Rhinoceros beetles are in that family too. Dung beetles are in it as well. A giant beetle might seem slow and awkward. Goliath beetles are the opposite. They fly with such skill that early collectors shot them out of the sky just to see one up close. Even now, insect scientists have trouble getting close enough in the wild to watch what they do.

6Insect specialist Dr. Brett Ratcliffe says that watching them in nature is very hard. Speed may come from a special change in the elytra. Some beetles must swing the wing covers aside before the flying wings can open. A Goliath does not. It can unfold the flying wings while the covers stay in place. Scientists think that shortcut lets it leave the ground faster. All beetles use antennae to pick up smells, chemicals, and other signals. Goliath antennae, like those of other scarabs, have a shape of their own. Experts think that shape makes the senses sharper. Separate pieces at the antenna tips overlap. They can spread like a fan. A larger surface helps the beetle find food. It helps the beetle find feeding places. It helps the beetle pick up smells. It even helps the beetle find a mate. You can feel an object better with your whole hand than with one fingertip. The fan works in a similar way. Antennae can be shown closed, partly open, or fully open. No other beetles spread their antennae in this fan shape to take in more of their surroundings. Goliath beetles live in the tropical rainforests and savannas of Africa. Those places stay warm all year. A dry season lasts for several months of every year.

7People mostly see the beetles in the wet season. Heavy rain then makes the air warm and damp. Plants grow well in that weather. Trees put out plenty of fruit and sap, which is good news for a hungry Goliath. Plenty of leaves also give cover. A predator that wants a crunchy snack has a harder time finding the beetle. No one knows for sure which animals eat Goliath beetles. Some experts think monkeys might, if they can catch one. Large birds might do the same. These fast fliers hide so well in the treetops that the question stays open. A trunk or branch with plenty of food may draw several Goliaths together. Such meetings are only occasional. Most of the time they seem to prefer being alone. A search for a mate is the main exception. Dr. Ratcliffe says they are not insects that live in a social group. Males guard feeding spots with great force. Every male Goliath has Y-shaped horns on the head. The horns are used to shove other males away. The fights are not only about food. Insect scientists suspect that the best feeding spots also draw females. A male who holds such a spot may have a better chance to attract a mate. The life cycle can be drawn as a loop.

8Eggs lead to a first larva after hatching. A second larva follows the first molt. A third larva follows the second molt. Then comes the pupa, and then the adult. Shedding of the larva's outer skin happens in the pupal stage. Wings and legs take shape. Wet seasons and dry seasons set the timing of this cycle. The months of those seasons change with the exact place. Like other beetles, Goliaths pass through a complete metamorphosis. The stages are egg, larva, pupa, and adult. Most of an adult life is given to mating. Egg-laying begins with a dig. Her wedge-shaped head is the tool. The burrow goes deep into rainforest soil. She often lays more than one hundred eggs under the ground. She dies soon after. Her work is finished. Several further months pass with the young still below ground. About two weeks pass, and then the eggs hatch. Young larvae come out at that point. Grubs is another name for them. They have no eyes and no wings. Eating and growing fill all their time. No one knows the exact wild diet. Rotting plant matter in the soil is the most likely food. When people keep them, the larvae will also feed on beetle larvae of a smaller size. They also eat adult insects.

9Growth is fast. Growth to full size takes about four months. The timing falls near the wet season's close. The larger kinds can reach 5 inches (12.7 cm) in length. A dollar bill has nearly the same length. Weight can hit a full 3.5 ounces (100 g). Once the wet season closes, the larvae dig farther down. Sandy soil is where they stop. There they build thin-walled cells from the soil. The cells are like the cocoons of butterflies. Inside, the pupal stage begins. Metamorphosis goes on inside those cells for several months of the dry season. Legs take shape. Wings take shape too. Each one folds into position. The outside of the pupa hardens into a protective shell. The new adult sleeps through the dry season inside the earthen cell. When moisture soaks deep enough to reach it, the beetle wakes. It climbs out of the soil. The cycle starts again. The fast Goliath beetle is a giant that is hard to find and even harder to catch. Bold stripes and huge size still make it a favorite of people who love insects. A few admirers even raise these beetles at home. Scientists gain from that habit. Much of what is known comes from the study of beetles kept in captivity. Think of a songbird's size.

10Add a zebra's stripes. Add the agility of a trick flyer. That combination fits this beetle. The Goliath beetle is that insect. In one picture, the beetle nearly matches a person's hand in size. Another view shows how quickly these beetles fly, and how hard they are to catch. A word list can lock in the special terms. Captivity is the state of being held in, or of living without freedom. Modified describes something that has been changed. Circulatory systems carry blood, or some other fluid, around inside a body. Naturalists are people who study nature and the history of the natural world, especially plants and animals. Elusive means hard to catch or hard to find. Pupal is the word for a young insect that has left the larva stage and is not yet an adult. Entomologists are scientists who study insects. Scarab names a large beetle. The shell is hard. The color is often black. Larval names a young animal whose body must change in a major way before the adult look appears. Solitary describes a creature that prefers to spend its time alone. Metamorphosis is a change from one body shape to a completely different shape. A species is a set of living things with similar bodies that can produce young together.

11. Albert Einstein and the Hidden Pattern

1The book follows Albert Einstein through these parts. A hidden puzzle opens the story. A talented, curious boy comes next. Work at a patent office follows. A miracle year follows that work. His rise as a star comes after. He then uses his fame. A move to America comes next. His influence is traced. A well-lived life closes the story. A word list and a topic list end the book. Hermann, Albert's father, showed him a magnetic compass when Albert was five. The needle's floating motion woke the boy's curiosity. He wanted to know the cause of that motion. His father turned the casing again and again in one hand. The needle hardly moved. He wondered why the needle kept aiming north. It was as if a hand no one could see were steering it. Answers were beyond a child that young. The feeling of wonder stayed with him. The feeling of mystery stayed too. Years later he wrote down the lesson of that compass. Something hidden, he said, had to sit behind the things we see. The curious child became a curious scientist. His life went into a search for that hidden something. Curiosity, kept alive, changed how people picture the universe we live in. One picture links his curiosity about hard problems with later discoveries. The violin stayed with Einstein from boyhood into adult life. A line he liked said happiness asks for little: simple furniture, fruit, and the violin. March 14, 1879, was his birth date. Ulm, a small town in Germany, was the place. A move came the following year. Munich, a larger city, was the new home. Maja, his younger sister, was born there. She became his closest friend in childhood. The whole family shaped his life. Pauline, his mother, played the piano. She passed a love of music to him. The violin was the instrument she wanted him to learn. He disliked the strict shape of those lessons.

2Playing itself became something he loved. For as long as he lived, the violin stayed beside him. A way of speaking he had as a child made his parents worry. It is a habit many children show. Words he had just said aloud, he often said again to himself. The second saying was very quiet. He seemed to be checking whether the words were right. He grew out of the habit. He later became a skilled speaker in public. One picture shows him with his sister Maja. His father was an electrical engineer. Two uncles were electrical engineers too. They brought him math and science while he was still young. Algebra's basics came as a game. A medical student ate dinner with the family once a week. That student brought books. Some books were about science. Some were about math. Some were about philosophy. Einstein would pore over them for hours at a time. A geometry book held him most of all. Philosophy books helped form him too. Even as a child he could concentrate deeply. He stayed with a hard problem until every solution he could imagine had been considered. Math talent showed at once in school. Science talent showed at once too. So did a strong individual streak. To the boy, teachers resembled army sergeants. They drilled pupils to memorize information. They drilled lifeless facts. They did not push students to think on their own. They did not push students to hunt for new answers. Einstein wanted a creative kind of thinking that was his own. His objections in class broke the lesson's flow. One teacher finally told him to leave the school. The reason given was his attitude. The teacher said the class was losing respect for him because of Einstein's attitude. Einstein felt relief when he left. The teachers felt relief too. He was 15. Italy, where his parents were, became his next stop. A new business was the reason the family had gone to Italy.

3Soon after they settled, he moved once more. Switzerland was where he would finish school. At only seventeen he was accepted by a university. It was one of Europe's finest schools for science. Routine lectures were often skipped. He used the time in a laboratory. His own ideas grew there. Most of his professors saw a brilliant student. They also saw a bright future only if he would follow rules already in place. A job was hard to find after he finished school in 1900. No one doubted that he had been a bright student. His degree came from one of Europe's finest universities. Independence and curiosity had a cost. The teachers who might have helped him find work did not like him. A teaching post would have left him free to study further. He was dismayed. He was not discouraged. He did not quit. Ideas were waiting to be thought through. They were waiting to be tested. He needed time. He needed a place. Both arrived in 1902. A patent office hired him as a clerk. Bern, Switzerland, was the city. His task was unusual. Devices sent in for patent approval had to work as their inventors said they did. He was the one who checked. The job let him do what he did best. He could follow curiosity. He could question.
