Between 1963 and 1977 she played in 171 golf events. Tennis alone would have secured her place among top athletes. She was not finished. Golf was the next sport. At that time it was played almost only by white people who had money. Black golfers had not held membership in the Ladies Professional Golf Association before her. She joined in 1964. People call that group the LPGA. Many golf clubs in the country still refused Black golfers. Membership was closed. The course was closed. Clubs that let her play often shut her out of the clubhouse. Bathrooms were shut too. She changed clothes in her car. Death threats arrived. Racist insults came from the crowd. She was not swayed. Some courses on the tour changed an open event into an invitational. The change was a way to keep her out. LPGA players voted to boycott those events unless everyone was welcome. The clubs backed down. Another color barrier broke. She was a fantastic athlete and a hard competitor.

9Two different sports gained a way in for pros who were players of color, and she was the one who opened it. She also cleared a path for later Black tennis greats. Arthur Ashe was one. Venus Williams was one. Serena Williams was one. A different legend begins with speed. James Cleveland Owens, called Jesse, was born in Alabama in 1913. He burst onto the sports scene in junior high. The city was Cleveland, Ohio. For his age group he set world records in the high jump. He set them in the long jump too. A high school track coach asked him to join the team. Family support fell partly on Jesse, so he worked after school. Showing up with the squad at the usual practice hour was impossible. Training happened at 5:00 a.m. His coach was there with him. A picture shows Jesse Owens. The legend kept growing. High school athletes from around the country met for a track contest. There he matched a world record. The race was the 100-yard dash. The time was 9.4 seconds. The long jump brought a new world record. The mark was 22 feet 11 3/4 inches, or 7 meters. College brought a championship meet in 1935. New world records fell in the 220-yard dash. They fell in the long jump. They fell in the 220-yard low hurdles. The 100-yard dash gave him another match of the existing world record. The time was again 9.4 seconds. No track and field athlete had ever done so much. The burst of records took about an hour. A back injury was already with him. He had fallen down a flight of stairs. Even with all those records, larger triumphs still waited. A picture shows him at the 1936 Olympic Games, several strides ahead of the field. Those Games were the Summer Olympics in Berlin, Germany. The year was 1936, just before World War II began. He was not welcome there. Adolf Hitler, the Nazi leader, ruled Germany. Hitler believed that white people who were not Jewish formed a master race. He believed that race stood above all others.

10Their label for Black people was the word primitive. Hitler expected the Games to prove his ideas. Owens was not intimidated by Hitler's attitude. Threats did not intimidate him either. The track in Berlin was his answer, and he gave it four times. Four gold medals were his. Olympic history had never seen that. Track and field would not match the feat for twelve years. Homecoming brought a ticker-tape parade. Admiration came with the cheers. He toured the United States. He toured the world. Young people heard a push to give a full effort. Leaders of the United States government gave him a title. He was America's Ambassador of Sports. Later life brought the Presidential Medal of Freedom. President Gerald R. Ford awarded it in 1976. A 1953 picture shows him at home, smiling widely. The twentieth century was an astonishing time. The professional sports world we know grew up in those years. Along the way, certain athletes stood apart from a crowd that was already full of talent. Their abilities astonished the world. Their sports changed for good. Their societies changed for the better. They helped make sure the highest level of competition would be open to everyone. Memory will keep them as American sports legends. A few words help a reader of their stories. Accomplished means to succeed at doing or achieving something. Dominated means standing above the rest through success, influence, or power inside a contest. Achievements are successes reached through effort. Integrate means to bring different ideas, or different groups of people, together. Astonishing describes something that causes surprise. Intimidated means fear, or a sense of being swamped, was pressed onto someone. Determination is the drive to keep working toward a hard goal. Omissions are things or people left out. Dignity is the quality of being worthy of respect and of honor. Revolutionized means made enormous changes. Versatile means able to serve in lots of different ways. Discriminated means given unfair treatment over race, over age, over sex, over religion, or over another kind of difference.

16. Blue Whales, Giants of Every Ocean

1The parts of this book begin with an introduction. Body structure comes next. Diet and feeding follow. Range and homes come after that. The huge calves have a part of their own. The calls of these whales come later. A conclusion and a word list close the book. A size chart sets a person beside a blue whale. The person is 6 feet (1.8 m) tall and weighs 175 pounds (79.4 kg). The blue whale is 100 feet (30.5 m) long and weighs 200 tons (181.4 mt). A research ship moves across the smooth Pacific Ocean off the California coast. Marine biologists on board keep scanning the horizon. They are looking for the largest creature on Earth. Soon a water spout rises about three stories high. The spout is what they hoped to see. Balaenoptera musculus is the source. That is the blue whale. Blue whales live in every ocean. One of the largest groups lives in the northeastern Pacific Ocean. An estimated 2,800 blue whales travel each year between Alaska and Costa Rica. Costa Rica is a country in Central America. The trip is a search for mild water and for food.

2Scientists try to find the whales so they can learn more. Behavior is one subject. How these giant mammals migrate is a further subject. Several traits show why a blue whale is a mammal. It breathes air through blowholes on top of the head. A fat layer called blubber helps keep it warm. Baleen, made of hairlike plates, lines the inside of the upper jaw. Every mammal breathes air. Every mammal has hair at some stage of development. Every mammal is warm-blooded. Every mammal makes milk for its babies. No animal known to have lived on Earth is larger than the blue whale. Even the most enormous dinosaur was no match. One of these sea animals equals four brontosauruses. A typical adult weighs 200 tons (181.4 mt). Length is about 100 feet (30.5 m). An elephant is a fair match for the weight of the tongue. Main blood vessels of the heart are wide enough for a person to crawl through. A body this huge could not live on land. Gravity would make the body collapse under its own weight. Buoyancy comes from the water.

3It pushes back against gravity and helps hold the body up. Life in the sea is the only way a blue whale can be this gigantic and still survive. Huge as they are, they move with ease and grace. A usual cruising speed is 5 miles per hour (8 kmph). Speed can rise to 20 miles per hour (32 kmph). The body is long and graceful. A flexible spine and long pectoral fins help it steer through changing ocean water. The tail carries a pair of enormous flukes, which are lobe-like parts. When the whale dives, the flukes lift out of the water. They leave a round mark on the surface called a flukeprint. Whale watchers look for those marks when they want to find whales. The two blowholes on the head work like human nostrils. Lungs let blue whales breathe air. People do the same, but the whale's scale is far greater. More than 1,000 gallons (3,785.4 L) of air can fit in the whale's lungs. About 1.3 gallons (5 L) is all that adult human lungs hold. The whale rises and breathes out through the pair of blowholes.

4Air and condensed water vapor shoot 30 feet (9.1 m) into the air. A quick breath then fills the huge lungs in under two seconds. The blowholes connect to the lungs through the trachea. Breathing through the mouth is impossible for a blue whale. Several breaths are taken before the dive. A flap covers the blowholes once the whale goes under. A typical dive lasts twenty to thirty minutes. These whales are classed as shallow divers. They rarely go deeper than 700 feet (213.4 m). Depths reached by a sperm whale can be more than four times as great. Even the shallowest tropical water can feel cool. That coolness is not a problem. Fatty tissue lies in a thick layer just under the skin. That layer is blubber. Every cetacean has it, blue whales included. Blubber insulates them from cold. It is less dense than water, so it also adds buoyancy. Floating and swimming become easier. A diagram of the body wall shows epidermis, dermis, blubber, connective tissue, and muscle. Blubber insulates the whale and helps it keep food reserves.

5A female builds extra blubber before she gives birth. She will not have to leave her newborn to search for food. Energy stored in that extra blubber carries her until she can feed again. Krill are the main food of a blue whale. The tiny animals often swarm near the surface. On a dive, the whale is hunting that favorite meal. Krill are small crustaceans that look a bit like shrimp. It may seem odd that the largest animal eats one of the smallest. There is a good reason. The whale is huge, but the throat is quite narrow. The esophagus is only inches wide, so nothing big can be swallowed. Blue whales also lack teeth. Food must be swallowed whole. Scientists split whales into two groups. Some, such as sperm whales, have teeth. They are placed in the suborder Odontoceti. Others, such as blue whales, have baleen. They are placed in the suborder Mysticeti. Hundreds of baleen plates line the upper jaw instead of teeth. Keratin is what baleen is made of. Human hair is made of that material. Fingernails are too. The ends are fringed, so the inside of the mouth looks as if a mustache is growing there.

6The baleen works as a strainer. The whale takes a huge gulp of seawater full of krill. The throat expands to hold thousands of gallons. The mouth then closes. The massive tongue pushes the water out through the baleen. Krill cannot pass through, so they stay in the mouth and are swallowed whole. About forty million krill are eaten each day. A feeding whale dives again and again into a swarm. Huge amounts are required because the whale burns up to 3 million calories (300,000 kcal) per day. A close look shows baleen. As many as eight hundred plates can line the mouth. A world map marks North America, Asia, Europe, Africa, South America, Australia, and Antarctica. The Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean are labeled. Shading shows where blue whales live. These whales glide through the deep water of every ocean. Some whale species travel in groups called pods. Blue whales usually travel alone or in pairs. In winter they move from higher latitudes to lower latitudes in search of krill.

7Pacific blue whales favor a place called the Costa Rica Dome. It lies off Central America's southern coast. In summer, currents there force cold water to the surface. Plankton then shows up in large amounts. Krill does too. Grooves on the throat expand so the whale can gulp up to 17,000 gallons (64,352 L) of water at one time. Females give birth while they spend the winter in warm water. Gestation lasts about one year. At birth, a calf weighs more than 5,000 pounds (2,268 kg). Length is about 25 feet (7.6 m). Minutes later, mother and calf are at the surface. The calf draws a first breath there. Birth happens in warm water because a newborn has little insulating blubber. A female gives birth every two or three years. The calf remains near the mother through the opening six months, at minimum. In that time it drinks up to 100 gallons (378.5 L) of milk each day. It gains over 200 pounds (90.7 kg) every day. Weaning comes once the pair has reached the summer places where they feed. A search for krill then begins, with the young whale on its own.

8Maturity is counted as reached by age ten. No animals in the world are larger. None are louder, either. A jet engine falls short of these sounds for loudness. Miles of water do not stop the calls. Even so, people have trouble hearing them. The sounds are made at extremely low frequencies. Those frequencies are too low for a human ear unless special equipment is used. Some scientists think the sounds, or songs, work as a kind of sonar. That would help the whales find their way in dark water. Other scientists think the songs are messages about where the whales are and what they are doing. A leap out of the water is called breaching. A loudness chart compares everyday sounds. A conversation is 70 dB. A jet engine is 140 dB. A rock concert is 150 dB. A blue whale call is 180 dB. Loudness and softness are measured in a unit called a decibel. The short form is dB. Researchers know that only males sing. Songs from one region differ a little from songs sung in other regions.

9In calm seas, other blue whales can detect the songs from as far as 1,000 miles (1,600 km) away. Indian Ocean blue whales have the most musical and varied songs. Four distinct notes show up in the song. Blue whales still fascinate researchers around the world. Hunting from the early twentieth century into the middle years killed so many that disappearance was close. Other dangers remain, including crashes with ships on the open ocean. Endangered status brings protection under the International Whaling Commission. Hunting bans are still hard to enforce. The population has not fully recovered. Migration patterns are studied by marine biologists and by other scientists. Feeding patterns are studied too. The goal is a better understanding of how these deep-ocean giants live. Those studies also look for lessons about staying alive in the ocean. Watching threats from the environment and from people may still meet a further goal. That goal is to keep blue whales safe and to help their numbers rise again. Estimates put the living population between ten thousand and twenty-five thousand. The old total stood above three hundred thousand.

10A word list explains the special terms. Certain whales carry baleen in the mouth. It strains food out of seawater. Buoyancy is the ability or the tendency to float. Cetaceans are mammals of the ocean. Whales belong to the group. Dolphins and porpoises do too. Crustaceans are mostly invertebrates that live in water. Crabs are examples. Lobsters and shrimp are examples too. Flukes are the two halves of a whale's tail. A frequency is how fast a sound wave vibrates. Gestation is the span before birth, while a baby develops inside the mother. The growth during that span is part of the meaning too. Some animal bodies make a strong material called keratin. Hair can be made of it. Hooves, claws, and feathers can too. Fingernails can as well. Krill are tiny ocean crustaceans that many other animals eat. Pectoral describes something of, related to, or located on the chest. Plankton are tiny living things, both plants and animals, at or near the surface of the ocean. Sonar sends sound waves of high frequency through water. It then records the vibrations an object sends back.

17. Brothers Who Sent a Balloon Up

1A map of early balloon flights sits near Paris, in France. Labels include Gonesse, Saint Denis, Belleville, and the Tuileries Garden. Versailles and Paris are marked too. England, Germany, Italy, and Spain appear on the wider view. The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea are named. Four dates are printed on the map. They are August 27, 1783, September 19, 1783, November 21, 1783, and December 1, 1783. A scale runs from 0 to 1 in miles and in kilometers. The topics begin with people watching a new age start. Two brothers and their big ideas come next. Then come balloons driven by smoke, a rivalry, a climb into the blue, and what lighter-than-air flight left behind. A word list ends the book. September 19, 1783, fell on an afternoon when a thrilled crowd packed the grounds. The place was the Palace of Versailles. The palace stands just outside Paris, in France. The count of people was 130,000. The event was a trial of a big balloon lifted by heated air. Two French brothers had built it. Their names were Joseph-Michel Montgolfier and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier. King Louis XVI watched from the palace courtyard. Queen Marie Antoinette watched with him. Silk and paper formed the balloon. Gold designs lay on a blue field. The air felt tense. Nobody yet knew how dangerous flight might be. Humans were not the riders. Three animals shared the hanging wicker basket. One was a sheep.

2One was a rooster. One was a duck. The animals were part of a science test. A sheep's body was judged near enough to a human body to make a fair trial. The rooster came along for a different reason. It is a bird, yet it cannot fly very far up. The duck, which does fly high, was there to reveal any other danger in the trip. A pit fire supplied smoky heated air, and that air went into the balloon. Release came a little past 1:00 in the afternoon. Watchers stared as it climbed. The height was about 460 meters, or 1,500 feet. Eight minutes after that, it came down to Earth. The landing was 3.2 kilometers away, which is 2 miles. The animals were not hurt. A dream as old as people, flight, had begun at last. The path was open for humans to rise into the clouds. Much of the credit belonged to the Montgolfiers. Those two brothers were among sixteen children. Their parents were Pierre Montgolfier and Anne Montgolfier. Home was Annonay, a town in the south of France. Pierre made paper and did well at it. Writing paper for King Louis XVI's court came officially from his factories. That contract kept the family financially safe. Joseph and Etienne took charge of the family firm in the 1770s. Spare hours were plentiful for other interests. Flight began to fascinate Joseph when he was in his early forties.

3From the 1600s onward, scientists had hunted for a craft lighter than air. Buoyancy would be what held it up. Nobody had yet learned how to build that craft. The ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes was the first to understand buoyancy. Density is the weight of an object for a set amount of space. Buoyancy compares that density with the density of a fluid the object sits in. A fluid here may be a liquid. It may also be a gas. If the object is less dense than the fluid, an upward force acts on it. Joseph had a theory. A gas lighter than air, held inside a light shell, might push upward hard enough to matter. He read about hydrogen. People then called it inflammable air, because it can explode. Scientists had known of this gas for quite a while. Early chemists sometimes made a gas that could burn. They did not know what the gas was. In 1766 an English chemist, Henry Cavendish, showed that the gas was an element. Inflammable air was the label he chose. A French chemist, Antoine Lavoisier, gave it a new name in 1783. The name was hydrogen. Joseph packed small paper balls with hydrogen and let them go. The tests disappointed him. The balls rose only a few meters, then sank. Hydrogen atoms are tiny enough to slip through paper. They then spread out into the air around them.

4Elements are the chemical pieces that build the universe. Atoms make up every element. An atom is the smallest bit that still acts like that substance. Oxygen is an element. Hydrogen is an element too. One atom of oxygen can join two atoms of hydrogen. Together they make one molecule of water. Joseph searched for a different way to build what he called an ascending machine. One day he watched shirts dry over a smoky fire. The cloth puffed upward. Like most people, he had watched smoke leave chimneys. Smoke, he decided, was the answer. A picture shows Joseph-Michel Montgolfier. Early in 1783 the brothers burned many materials that can catch fire. They wanted the ones that made the most smoke. Damp straw mixed with chopped wool won that test. The smell was awful. The smoke still lifted any light container. A picture shows Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier. The brothers decided the smoke held some unknown part that could lift things. They named that wonderful stuff Montgolfier gas. No such stuff existed. Hot air itself did the lifting. Heat makes the molecules in air move faster. The air then spreads out and grows less dense. Inside a balloon's envelope, that lighter air carries the balloon up. The brothers still did not grasp the real science of hot-air balloons. They kept trusting Montgolfier gas. They kept making smoke that smelled foul. Their test balloons worked, so they had no cause to doubt the idea.

5They tried several materials for the envelope. Silk was one. Paper was another. Linen was another. The balloons also grew larger as the work went on. Each one climbed higher than the last. Crowds started to notice. On June 4, 1783, the town square in Annonay was full. The test used a large balloon of cloth with a paper lining. Nobody rode in it. Amazed watchers saw it climb some 2,000 meters, or 6,560 feet. The flight lasted ten minutes. It came down about 2 kilometers away, which is 1.2 miles. Tests like this one set off a balloon craze across France. The excited French first called the craft ascending machines. Later they said aerostats. The word balloon came only after the Montgolfiers had made history. It was taken from the French word ballon. In French it names a big play ball. The brothers wanted the French Academy of Sciences to recognize the work in an official way. A seal of approval from that famous body helped inventors a great deal. It raised their prestige. It won admiration. They hoped it would also win the king's support. The ruler, in turn, would enjoy public praise for backing a striking step in technology. The academy refused to approve them yet. It chose to wait, in case a better balloon appeared. Jacques Charles, a physicist, was the chief competitor. He wanted to build a balloon that used hydrogen.

6The Montgolfiers had dropped hydrogen long before. Hot air was their choice. Charles still saw strong promise in hydrogen. In July 1783 he started building. Public gifts paid for the work. Two brothers helped him. They were Nicolas-Louis Robert and Anne-Jean Robert. Both were professional engineers. The three made a small test balloon of silk. A rubber coating kept the hydrogen from leaking out. Meanwhile the Montgolfiers won a large victory. Reports of their tests reached King Louis. He asked them to come to Paris. He wanted a dazzling balloon that would show his glory to every part of France. As favorites of the king, the brothers now got money from the government. Charles had to settle for kind words from the Academy of Sciences. Public money, at least, was already his. Both teams raced to be first to send people up in a balloon. The contest stayed fairly friendly. As summer faded, each side was nearly ready to show its balloon. Hydrogen is the lightest element. It weighs only one-fourteenth as much as air. At first it looks like the ideal gas for a balloon. It is dangerous, though. It catches fire. It explodes with ease. Helium is a clearly better gas for this use. It is the second-lightest element. It does not burn. It does not explode. Lighter-than-air flight with helium is fully safe. Helium stayed unknown until the 1880s. Balloon makers in the 1700s could not get it.

7August 27, 1783, brought a big crowd to a lawn inside Paris. The Eiffel Tower stands on that ground today. People had come to see the Charles balloon leave the ground. A famous American was in the crowd. Benjamin Franklin was serving as ambassador from the United States to France. The balloon was fairly small. Its width was about 4 meters, or 13 feet. Red stripes took turns with white stripes. The white ones had gone yellow. A rubber mix rubbed on the silk had stained them. Charles and the Robert brothers made the hydrogen on the spot. They poured sulfuric acid onto half a ton of scrap iron. The brothers Montgolfier and Jacques Charles shared one question. Could people build a device lighter than air that would let humans fly? They followed a set of steps called the scientific method. First, ask a question. Next, study what is already known. Then build a hypothesis. Test that hypothesis by watching or by experimenting. Study the data and decide what it shows. Last, tell others what you found. Late in the afternoon, the balloon with no pilot was set free from its ropes. It climbed fast. It flew toward the northeast for under an hour. The landing was about 15 kilometers away, or 9 miles, in the village of Gonesse. Frightened villagers saw a strange monster from the sky. They attacked it with pitchforks. Paris then waited for the Montgolfiers.

8On September 19 they sent up the test balloon and its animal riders at Versailles. The animals came down safe. A trial with humans could finally happen. The king feared a failure in the air. He suggested prisoners already sentenced to death as the first human riders. Others talked him out of that plan. A science teacher volunteered instead. His name was Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier. A soldier volunteered with him. That soldier was the Marquis d'Arlandes. Their famous flight was on November 21. This time the start was on the edge of Paris. The balloon was grander than the one before. It stood 23 meters high, or 75 feet. Gold designs covered it. One design was Louis's monogram, two capital L letters wound together. Another was a ring of fleurs-de-lis. Those are lilies drawn in a formal style. They stood for French royalty. Airships of our time include blimps. A blimp keeps its shape only by the pressure of the gas inside. Dirigibles are different. They have a frame on the inside. A picture shows a modern blimp. De Rozier stood on one side of a platform at the balloon's base. The marquis stood on the other side. The craft, called an aerostatic globe, lifted off. The landing came after twenty-five minutes. The distance was about 8 kilometers, or 5 miles. It settled between two windmills outside the city. People hailed both men as heroes.

9Benjamin Franklin watched that flight. Another watcher asked what use the balloon had. Franklin's reported reply compared the question to asking the good of a baby just born. December 1 came only ten days after the Montgolfier success. Jacques Charles rose with a partner on that hydrogen balloon. The partner was Nicolas-Louis Robert. No people had gone up in a hydrogen balloon before them. They left from the Tuileries Garden in Paris. The flight lasted more than two hours. A town about 36 kilometers off, or 22 miles, was where they came down. In later years the Montgolfiers sent up several more balloons. The French Academy of Sciences honored the brothers. King Louis raised their father, Pierre, into the nobility. Love of ballooning soon moved across Europe. The dangers showed themselves before long. In June 1785, de Rozier tried to cross the English Channel by balloon. His copilot was Pierre Romain. Both were killed. Pioneers still kept improving balloon designs. The work went on well past the early excitement that faded late in the 1700s. In the 1800s, craft lighter than air gained rudders. They also gained propellers run by motors. By the 1930s, giant airships carried passengers back and forth over the Atlantic Ocean. That golden age of airships stopped short in 1937. Fire broke out on a German airship called the Hindenburg. It crashed as it tried to land in New Jersey. Airships today are used mostly for advertising.

10You can often see them over open stadiums at big sports events. Balloons filled with gas are used mostly to collect weather facts. Hot-air balloons are used mostly for fun. Many places hold a festival each year. The sky fills with hundreds of bright balloons that ride on heated air. The scene can make balloon fever look as if it never stopped. The word list gives plain meanings. Immersed means dipped or set into a fluid, or into anything that surrounds a thing completely. Airships are aircraft with no wings. They can be steered and powered, and gas inside the body makes them lighter than air. Inflammable means able to catch fire easily and burn fast. Buoyancy is the ability, or the tendency, to float. Intrigued means very curious or deeply interested. Chemists study the elements of chemistry. They also study how chemicals affect each other. A molecule is the tiniest piece of a substance able to stand alone. One atom or several atoms form each molecule. Combustible means catching fire or burning with ease. A physicist is a scientist who studies what energy and matter are like. An envelope is the outside bag on an airship. A balloon that uses heated air is one example. The bag holds gas or heated air. It holds gas or heated air. Prestige is a high level of respect. An experiment is a scientific test or trial.

18. Changed Genes on the Plate

1Tucson, Arizona, is where demonstrators protest foods made as GMOs. The Monsanto company is part of what they protest. Sale of a new tomato inside the United States was approved in 1994. Approval came from the FDA, the Food and Drug Administration. Flavr Savr was the tomato's name. Its seeds had been altered by researchers in a laboratory. Ordinary tomatoes soften after they ripen. This new kind stayed firm for a long time. Pickers could leave it on the vine longer. Markets still received it in good shape. Labels stated clearly that the seeds were genetically modified. Sales were strong at the start. Safety worries flipped public opinion within two years. The tomatoes left the market. Argument about genetically modified organisms, GMOs, had started. Doctor Virginia Ursin, shown in the main photo, worked on those first genetically modified tomatoes. A smaller photo shows the fruit. Farming began, and people started breeding plants so food crops would exist that the wild does not offer. Corn as we know it never grew wild. A wild grass called teosinte was the starting point. Farmers saved seed only from plants that had the qualities they wanted, then planted that seed again. Fields today are still improved by that same method. Newer methods, built over the past few decades, let scientists introduce foods that had never existed. Look, taste, and behavior can change without waiting through generations of plants. A new gene, placed in a seed in the laboratory, can give a new trait.

2Another kind of plant can supply the gene. A wholly different organism can supply it too. USDA, the agriculture department of the United States, describes most corn the country now grows. A soil bacterium called Bt supplied genes that were added. Insects that ingest Bt are killed by it. Insects that feed on the new corn can be killed by the corn as well. Genetic engineering is the making of a brand-new organism. Genes of existing organisms that are not related are combined. The new varieties are called genetically modified organisms, or GMOs. Everyday shopping in the United States already includes some of them. Where are these foods, and what are they? The USDA puts genetic modification at about 40 percent of every crop the country grows. Alfalfa is among the crops changed most often. Cotton is too. Canola is on the list as well. Corn is on it. Sugar beets are on it. Soy is on it. Zucchini is on it. The corn crop is about 90 percent GMO. Cotton matches that share. Soybeans match it too. Modified foods show up in surprising places. Corn is more than a cob roasted for a treat. It is more than a snack popped for the movies. The kernels go further. Corn meal is one product made from those kernels. Corn syrup is another. Cereal then uses those products as ingredients.

3Cookies use them. Pet foods use them. Countless other foods use them too. An estimate says GMOs show up in 60 to 80 percent of processed foods sold across the country. A GMO food of some kind has already been eaten by most Americans, often without their knowledge. A full reading of a label can still hide which ingredients were changed in a lab. Change is what some people seek. They want the U.S. government to force a label on every product that includes a GMO ingredient. Most products must already carry a label. The label lists ingredients. It lists nutrition facts. Shoppers, these people argue, deserve to learn whether they are eating a GMO. Every food in the picture above is made with corn. Benefits and risks both attach to these foods. By the middle of the 1990s, these products were part of what people in the country ate. Speakers for the technology listed many gains for farming worldwide. Families and the environment, other people fear, may face risks from the modified foods. Most GMO crops on the market were changed by added genes. The genes help the crop resist pests that eat it. They also help it resist chemicals that kill weeds. Fewer pesticides on the fields are possible, some experts say. An herbicide can cover a whole field. Unwanted weeds die. GMO crops built to survive those chemicals do not. Time and labor drop when farmers spray whole fields of GMO crops with herbicides.

4Fewer chemicals, some scientists say, can make farming less harmful to the environment. Food can be safer for people to eat. Yields can rise, and profit can rise with them. Other researchers see a different total. Chemical weed killers, they say, have been used in greater amounts since GMO planting began. Insects and weeds may grow stronger. They adapt to insecticides built into the crops. They adapt to heavier herbicide use. Stronger chemicals may eventually be needed against these new superbugs and superweeds. Humans and the environment could face new safety risks from that cycle. Supporters answer that unknown risks are smaller than a larger hope. Genetically engineered crops might solve world hunger. Earth's human population is growing, and bigger yields will be needed to feed it. Researcher David Weisser says a limit on GMOs hurts only the people who are starving. Opponents answer with a different danger. The same few GMO varieties, planted by more and more farmers, leave the food supply easier to hurt. A warning comes from experts at Princeton University. Disease can move faster through plants when fewer varieties are grown. Picture one GMO corn seed used by everyone. A disease that destroys that corn would destroy a whole key source of food. Scientists at Cornell University record how fast genetically modified plants grow. Petri dish lids are where those rates get written down. Seeds for GMO crops are developed in laboratories.

5Growing them in real life is part of the experiment. Effects on the surrounding environment, and on the plants and animals living there, show up only then. Wind can move pollen from a GMO field. A neighboring field of wildflowers can receive it. Fertilization of some of those wildflowers is possible. Wild plants might then show traits that engineers built into the crop. More studies are needed. Ladybugs, bees, and butterflies help farmers, and the effects of GMOs on them are not settled. Some shoppers fear a second effect. A crop whose job is to destroy insect pests might destroy helpful insects too. Proof of that fear has not been shown. Pollination of crops, and of other plants, is work the monarch shares with many helpful insects. Monarch numbers have fallen by almost 90 percent across the past twenty years. Scientists do not agree about Bt. Do Bt toxins hurt monarch young after they hatch and start eating GMO plants? That is the unsettled question. One group of experts blames heavy spraying. Weed killer on crops that resist herbicides is wiping out other plants monarchs need in order to live. Another group says the reason is different. Open land the monarchs can call home is scarcer than in the past. GMOs might not be the cause. Who gains from GMO crops is its own question. Small-scale farmers have seen mixed results from a wide shift toward an industry built on GMO crops.

6Drift can carry pollen off a GMO farm and onto a next-door farm that did not use those seeds. A farmer may end up raising a crop that was never planted on purpose. Organic farms that do not buy GMO seeds can be hurt by that. Ownership of the seeds stays with the company that developed them. Farmers do not own them. Holding seed back to plant the following year breaks the law. Milkweed is the main food of monarch butterflies. Herbicides sprayed on neighboring GMO fields are cutting the amount of milkweed down. Health is the next debate. Supporters of growing these foods say serious human health problems can be eased by them. Poorer regions of the world could receive more food. Some GMO crops have been built to fight disease. Rice is one example. Vitamin A is what scientists are trying to make that rice produce. The rice itself has been changed. In some places, diets lack vitamin A, and blindness is widespread. The new rice might help. Other people say more study of long-term health must come before humans eat genetically modified food. Crops made to kill insects worry them. So do crops sprayed heavily with herbicides. Diseases such as cancer are the fear. New food allergies are another fear. GMO foods can carry proteins people have never eaten. Common food allergens include soy. Eggs belong on that list.

7Milk and peanuts belong on it too. Across twenty years, studies have asked how risky these foods are for health. Whether the answers are good enough is still debated. Proponents point to one review of nearly eighteen hundred published papers. Those papers, the review concluded, did not show harm to human health from GMOs. Oregon, despite protests, passed a law in 2013. The law stops any ban on GMO crops inside the state. Almost three hundred people signed a statement in that same year. Scientists were among them. Other experts were among them. Their claim was that science has not shown GMO safety. Opponents point to several hundred studies of their own. Harm to human health and to the environment is what they say those studies show. Charts in some studies track rises in depression, in weight gain, and in Alzheimer's disease after GMO foods reached the market. Agreement on the conclusion fails because agreement on the evidence fails. Each side asks whether the other side's research is fair and accurate. Safety studies are not reliable, opponents say, because the companies that profit from the crops are the ones that run them. Industry advocates call the studies favored by anti-GMO activists flawed. They also call those studies biased. Patents on most genetically engineered seeds belong to private companies. Some independent researchers report trouble. Unbiased studies of those seeds are hard for them to do.

8Any new technology hides its full good effects and its full bad effects until study has lasted a long time. Nations do not answer the label fight in one shared way. This country answers differently from many nations abroad. More than sixty countries have taken one of two paths. Some ban GMOs until later study can prove them safe. Others require a label on foods that contain GMOs. The United States allows GMO foods on the market unless harm can be proved. Special labels are not required by the government. Opinion polls still show a wish held by most shoppers here. They want labels when ingredients were genetically modified. In the United Kingdom, an item that contains GMO foods must carry a label. In the United States, some foods that are not GMO carry labels of their own. Clear labels, many people believe, would let them choose whether to eat GMO foods. New laws are being sought in the states where some of those people live. Most of the efforts so far have failed. No state had required GMO labels earlier than Vermont. In 2014 that state demanded labels on GMO foods sold inside its borders. Some businesses across the country have made a pledge. Specialty grocery stores are among them. Any GMO food they sell will be labeled. An environmental meeting in Paris ran for two days. The year was 2012. France's prime minister, Jean-Marc Ayrault, is shown standing.

9He voted to keep a temporary ban on growing GMO foods in his country. Laptops in a lab record temperature and light. Scientists want to learn how those variables change the way plants grow. Companies that develop genetically modified foods, grow them, and sell them say a label rule would hurt their business in an unfair way. Facts about GMOs will not reach the public through labels, their spokespeople argue. Fear is already widespread. Any label that says GMO, some of them say, will stop people from buying. Mandatory labels, many insiders fear, will push every GMO product into one lump. More fear would follow. New GMO products that might help people later would be hindered. Labeling every product, they add, would be expensive. It would be complicated. Only about two decades have passed since people began eating food grown from genetically engineered seeds. Hundreds of published reports have looked at benefits and at risks. Many people still believe the question of safety is unsettled. Seed saving is one reply to a related loss. More than three hundred unique kinds of corn were sold as seed to farmers a hundred years ago. Commercial corn today mostly comes from hybrid seed, and from only a few varieties. Historic and traditional foods have disappeared in many cases. Historic varieties of fruit in the United States, and of vegetables, have lost 90 percent of their number. Seed banks have been started around the world.

10They save seed from traditional crops, also called heirloom crops. A wide set of crops can be kept. Growers' know-how can be saved along with the seed. The hope is more food choices for generations still to come. Words from this book have set meanings. Agriculture means farming as a science or as daily work, including the raising of livestock. Something altered has been made different. To assess a thing is to judge it or measure it. A beneficial effect is useful, favorable, or simply good. A biased view gives unfair weight to one opinion, one group, or one cluster of beliefs. Consumers buy goods or services, or they rent them, and then they use what they got. Genetically refers to heredity and to how living things vary. Herbicides are agents, biological or chemical, whose job is to kill plants that are not wanted. Hinder means to slow a process, hold it up, block it, or bring it to a stop. Ingest means to take food in, or to take in some other substance. A mandatory rule is one a person is required to follow. Pesticides are substances, chemical or biological, that kill animals or plants seen as harmful. Processed food or material has been treated so it lasts longer or works better. Proponents speak in favor of an idea. Another word for them is advocates. A vulnerable thing can be hurt with ease.

19. China's Northern Dragon Wall

1One stretch of the wall stands near the border with North Korea. A World Heritage Site title went to the Great Wall of China in 1987. The naming body was UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Picture a wall longer than the gap between the North Pole and the South Pole. Line up every piece of this wall in one straight path. The path would reach about that far. The work is an amazing act of engineering. It is an amazing act of design as well. Few building jobs in history have been so ambitious. It is also one of the most famous landmarks people have made on Earth. It stands as proof of the long, rich story of China. Voters placed it on a list called New Seven Wonders of the World. For visitors to China, it is the largest attraction. It is also the most popular one. Builders raised the Great Wall along the northern edge of China. The work lasted many centuries. The aim was protection from invaders. Another aim was to shield Chinese culture from ideas coming in from outside. The wall did not always stop those invaders. Even so, a person who meant China harm, or meant its civilization harm, still had to get past a huge barrier. The route of the wall stays near the south side of Inner Mongolia. Inner Mongolia is a region of China that governs itself. When the wall was built, peoples who were not Chinese usually controlled that region. The Hushan Great Wall marks the eastern end. The map also shows Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, Beijing, and the Yellow Sea.

2Jaiyu Mountain Pass marks the western end. A map key notes important stretches and the Inner Mongolia border. A scale bar shows 150 km (93 mi.). Mountain passes far to the west are where the wall starts its path across China. The farthest eastern piece runs out into the Yellow Sea. Planners followed feng shui (FUNG SHWAY). That old Chinese art and science sets rules for space. The rules say how things should sit in relation to energy moving over the land. In feng shui, the land itself is a living dragon. Chinese builders shaped the wall so it would move with the land in a harmonious way. People often call the Great Wall a sleeping dragon. Gansu (GAHN-soo) Province holds the tail, and that end is the western one. Liaoning (lee-OW-ning) Province holds the head. That province sits in the east, near the Yellow Sea. Moving from the western tail toward the eastern head, the body crosses deserts. It crosses steppes. It crosses rugged mountains. It crosses lakes and rivers. It crosses fertile lowlands. It crosses beaches. The wall is not one unbroken line. Many separate pieces were built across the centuries. A truer name might be the Great Walls of China. Badaling is one piece visitors know well. It stands north of Beijing, the capital, by about 70 kilometers (43 mi.). Nine sections lie parallel to one another. From Beijing (bay-ZHING), several main sections can be reached by going no farther than 121 kilometers (75 mi.). In 2007, a vote placed this wall on the list called the New Seven Wonders of the World.

3Preservation is strongest at Badaling (BAH-dah-ling). Crews have restored it in a deep way. Its path bends through steep mountains to the northwest of Beijing. The path covers about 12 kilometers (7.5 mi.). Watchtowers there number forty-three. Huanghuacheng (hwong-HWAH-chung) sits still farther toward the east, up in the mountains. That piece is about 10.8 kilometers (6.7 mi.) long. The land around it holds lakes. In summer, yellow flowers cover the ground, and the section is named for those flowers. Two large Chinese characters are cut into an enormous rock that sits under the wall. The characters mean firm and strong. High mountains on the east side of Huanghuacheng carry an especially scenic portion. The stretch after that is Mutianyu (MOO-tyen-yoo), and it extends 2.25 kilometers (1.4 mi.). Parapets appear again and again along it. Watchtowers number twenty-two. Three of them guard a platform at a gateway. Simatai (SU-mah-tie) is northeast of Beijing. Roughly 5 kilometers (3 mi.) is the length there. Major restoration has taken place there as well. Visitors remember how steep it is. Thirty-four watchtowers rise along it. Mandarin Duck Lake splits them, with about half on each side. A short distance south of Simatai is Juyongguan (JOO-yoonggwahn). It occupies a valley that mountains encircle. Soldiers used it as a stronghold. Fierce battles happened there many times. One feature is a platform made of white marble. Sacred statues and writings fill an arched doorway in that platform. High peaks are the route of the Mutianyu section. Some of that section is granite. Officials celebrated after a 2009 survey at the Badaling Great Wall.

4The wall, they found, stretched farther than earlier belief. The government of China has carried out many surveys of this kind. Inside China, people call the wall Wan Li Chang Cheng. Those words point to a long wall measured as ten thousand li. One li is a Chinese unit. It equals about half a kilometer, which is one-third of a mile. Ten thousand of those units come to about 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage, as late as 2009, reported that the real length was not much past that older figure. A five-year survey finished in 2012. Workers combined GPS with 3-D modeling. They also used pictures from satellites, maps made from the air, and drones. The new total was larger. Count every section, and the length is about 21,196 kilometers (13,171 mi.). Long ago, small nomadic tribes of hunter-gatherers lived on land that is China today. Season by season, they moved. Wild animals and plants gave them food, clothing, and other necessities. Near 4000 bc, tribes on more fertile ground started growing crops. They started domesticating animals too. Villages of small size appeared. Farming groups ringed those villages with walls. Raids by northern nomads were what the walls were meant to discourage. By 500 bc, many independent states made up China. A king ruled each state. War set state against state. States in the north also fought enemies beyond them. Some kings hoped to unite every state and rule the whole set. The years from 475 to 221 bc are the Warring States Period.

5Fighting then was intense. Builders added many more walls so each state could protect itself. Qin (CHIN) was the most powerful state by 221 bc. It seized control over the whole of China. Zheng (ZHUNG), a ruthless fighter, became emperor. His title was First Sovereign Emperor of China. His power was extreme. Historians record a confident line of his. The dynasty, he said, would endure for ten thousand generations. Thousands of warriors shaped from clay were made on Zheng's order. Horses of clay were made too. At his death, they were buried beside him. He also ordered a border wall so enemies could not easily harm China. The planned length was almost 4,828 kilometers (3,000 mi.). Conditions for the workers were extremely harsh. Rumor says the construction killed four hundred thousand people. The year of Zheng's death was 210 bc. Afterward, the Great Wall was left to decay. Emperor Wu Di lived from 151 to 87 bc. He was sixth among the Han emperors. He ordered a fresh western section. Its length was 483 kilometers (300 mi.). He also had a string of separate watchtowers placed beyond the wall. From ad 386 until 1279, one ruler after another repaired pieces of the wall. Some of them lengthened it. Up to the early twentieth century, Chinese history was a run of dynasties. In each dynasty, rule passed down inside one family. Keeping invaders out was the wall's main purpose. The Mongols still invaded in the middle of the 1200s. Their leader was Genghis Khan. They created the Yuan (yoo-WAHN) dynasty. During their control of China, they let the wall go unmaintained.

6Hongwu drove those Mongols out in 1368. He became the new ruler. The Ming dynasty was his creation. Rebuilding the wall was his answer to the Mongol threat. The task was massive, because disrepair was extreme. For roughly the next 275 years, Ming emperors kept rebuilding and expansion at the top of their plans. Most new lengths were placed a little to the south of the older line. After the Ming years, crews have mostly repaired and renovated. A hidden mortar ingredient turned up in recent research. That ingredient is sticky rice. Experiments found the ideal mix. The rice should be 3 percent of the blend with lime. The result is stronger than mortar made in modern times. Today's reconstruction follows that old, tested recipe. The Great Wall rose in stages that covered thousands of years. The builders included soldiers. They included convicts. They included prisoners of war. They included peasants. Others joined as well. Force sent some of these people to the work. The conditions they faced were brutal. Early pieces used hang-tu, a rammed-earth method. Packed earth was pounded down inside a frame. Wood or bamboo formed that frame. Some desert spots had no soil. There, packed sand and shrubs from the desert were used instead. Three steps explain hang-tu. Workers first stood up a frame of wood and packed it with earth, or with sand plus shrubs. They next kept building until the height matched their plan. They last took the frame off. Hang-tu first showed up more than two thousand years ago.

7Those early walls stood apart around villages. They did not form a single long barrier. Growth in China brought change in its walls. A dynasty sited new work by looking at where enemies stood at the time. From 770 to 476 bc, the Zhou (JOH) dynasty used hang-tu walls to surround small states. The Warring States Period came next, from 475 to 221 bc. Walls then shielded large states that battled one another. The Qin dynasty, from 221 to 206 bc, produced large sections that ran without a break. Wall built in that era passed 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). Many people call that Qin wall the original Great Wall. Towers used wood and brick that the sun had baked. Inside, a ladder climbed to a top platform. A parapet with crenellations ringed that platform. Crossbow archers were stationed in the towers. Spacing put any enemy between two towers inside shooting range. Hang-tu walls joined the towers. Four horses could travel abreast on the top. Outposts on the wall's north side housed several hundred soldiers each. A sighting of the enemy brought a signal to the other towers. A section measuring 483 kilometers (300 mi.) was added under the Han dynasty. That dynasty ran from 206 bc to ad 220. The Sui dynasty, from 581 to 618, carried out extensive rebuilding. The Song dynasty, from 960 to 1279, added still more building. The Ming dynasty, from 1368 to 1620, took on major repairs and major rebuilding. Some hang-tu stretches were clad in brick or in stone by order of Ming emperors. The crews included architects, stonecutters, and bricklayers.

8Wooden molds shaped large bricks. Kilns baked them. Mortar then filled the spaces once the bricks sat in position. Where extra fortification was required, stone was chosen, because stone outlasts brick. A drawing of a Ming wall shows the parts from top to bottom. Crenellations and a parapet crown it. A paved surface lies under them. Brick or stone forms the wall. Earth and stones pack the inside. A base of stone supports everything. At Simatai, the section is 5.4 kilometers (3.3 mi.) long. Beacon towers there number thirty-five. More than ten million visitors enter China each year with this wall as their goal. Watchtowers along the sections reach an amazing 25,000. Outposts reach 15,000. All sections together measure about 21,196 kilometers (13,170 mi.). No longer chain of structures has ever been built. Width at the widest place is about 9 meters (30 ft.). About 8 meters (26 ft.) is the height of the tallest place. Sea level is the lowest point. The highest point rises more than 500 meters (1,600 ft.). Over many years, heads of state on the Badaling guest list have numbered more than 370. Famous people of other kinds have come as well. Sightseers reach China from around the globe because they want to see this wall. Separate sections offer different days out. Millions make the trip every year. Nearly all of them share one piece of advice. Build your fitness before the visit. Sections seen most often lie close to Beijing and are simple to reach. Badaling leads that group. It was restored and opened to the public before any other section.

9The year was 1955. People have described it as the grandest stretch. Renovation upon renovation also makes the walk there the safest. The Great Wall Museum is on that site. Its nine exhibition halls cover history. They cover construction. They cover art. They cover culture. Crowds are thinner on sections other than Badaling. Slopes on many of those sections are much steeper. Anyone fortunate enough to explore should expect long walks. Climbs will fill the day. Cameras will come out often. A guide can teach the wall's past and the way it was built. Cable cars run at some sections. Hikers can leave one section and walk to another. Overnight camping is possible. Mutianyu offers a toboggan run. Simatai offers paragliding. The Great Wall Marathon serves people who want an extreme sport. Few marathons anywhere are more challenging. The first race was in 1999. Runners number 2,500. Their home countries number more than 60. One runner called the event beautiful. He called it the harshest race of his life. Jinshanling (JEENshahn-ling) lies a little more than two hours north from Beijing. The section runs about 10 kilometers (6 mi.). Some rumors claim this wall shows up from space. The claim is false. The wall can still amaze a visitor. Its length is nearly half of a full loop around Earth's equator. A fresh section came to light in 2011. The place was Mongolia's Gobi Desert. William Lindesay, a British explorer, led the expedition. What turned up was a length of 100 kilometers (62 mi.). Blocks of volcanic rock form one part.

10Mud and shrubs form the other. Carbon dating let scientists place the find. The link is the Western Xia (SHEE-yuh), a dynasty whose years were 1038 to 1227. Before the find, historians had not credited that dynasty with wall building. Work began over two thousand years ago, and this landmark still draws wonder. Further study, and further sections, will open new views of China's colorful past. These words belong with the story. Brutal describes something extremely hard to endure. Kilns are ovens with a special job. They burn, bake, or dry clay. They do the same for brick and for glass. A test called carbon dating measures age by reading certain carbon left in a very old object that once was alive. A nomadic life means shifting from place to place and keeping no permanent home. A crenellated top has openings in its low wall so defenders can aim weapons outward. Parapets are low walls that guard the upper edges of roofs, bridges, and other structures. Restoration means returning a thing to the condition it had at the start. Domesticating is the raising of an animal or a plant until living with people is easy, or until people gain from it. Spatial refers to space and to the way objects fit inside that space. A fortification is a defense work that makes a place tougher and harder to attack. A fort is one kind. To traverse is to move across an area or through it. Heritage is a custom, a way of living, or a trait passed along by older generations.

20. City on a Peak in the Clouds

1A map places Machu Picchu in Peru, in South America, near the Urubamba River, with Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, and the Pacific Ocean around it. The site is high enough that clouds often come to visit. In the Inca language, machu means old. Picchu means peak. Machu Picchu stands in the Andes Mountains of Peru. It is known as the City in the Clouds. It sits 2,350 meters (7,710 ft.) above sea level. Dense fog often surrounds it. This mysterious and haunting city of the Inca was unknown to most of the modern world for more than four hundred years. In 1911 it was found again. It was recognized as a priceless treasure of the Inca Empire. The account moves from this mysterious city to an explorer, to who the Inca were, to why they built, to what they built, to the Spanish, and to Machu Picchu today. American explorer and archaeologist Hiram Bingham had studied old charts and texts. He became convinced of a hidden place in the Andes. He believed an Incan capital city was there, one the Spanish invaders had never found. Bingham traveled to Peru in hope of finding that city. A local Peruvian farmer told him where a long-abandoned city stood. Bingham made a steep and difficult climb up a long path grown over with plants. What he saw at the top amazed him. Through tangled vines and trees, he looked at a remarkable ruin of Incan architecture. The ruin included stone walls, terraces, and sacred temples. Bingham is credited with making Machu Picchu known to the world.

2He may not have been the first outsider to visit it. Missionaries and other explorers seem, from the evidence, to have reached the site decades earlier. They were less vocal about what they found. Hiram Bingham lived from 1875 to 1956. No one has discovered a written Inca language. Archaeologists and historians therefore try to understand the history by making educated guesses. In the more than one hundred years since the city was found again, they have built theories. The theories concern who the Inca were, and why and how they may have built the city. Some historians think the Inca began as a small clan of cave dwellers in the Andes Mountains. By 1400 ce, the Inca began to conquer other groups in the area. As they brought more people into their society, their army grew. Inca warriors threw bola stones at the legs of enemies. The stones were meant to trip those enemies and catch them. A statue of Pachacuti stands tall beside the road that leads up to Machu Picchu. Between 1438 and 1471, during the reign of the emperor Pachacuti, the Inca had some of their most prosperous years. His name is pronounced pah-chah-KOO-tee. He was a fierce and mighty warrior. He commanded a strong army. He defeated many neighboring kingdoms. Under his leadership, the empire stretched past the borders of present-day Peru. It came to include present-day Ecuador. Pachacuti is the ruler for whom Machu Picchu was most likely built.

3No one knows why the Inca built it. Archaeologists do have theories, and the theories differ. At first, Bingham believed Inca society had begun at Machu Picchu. He later changed his mind. He came to think it was the legendary last refuge of the Inca. He thought Inca rulers had battled Spanish conquistadors there. Today, archaeologists know that refuge was actually in the jungle. It lay many kilometers from Machu Picchu. Archaeologists were digging at part of the site in 2016. Another theory has been debunked. It said Machu Picchu was a temple for chosen women. Those women were a holy order dedicated to Inti, the Inca Sun god. Bingham's team found dozens of skeletons buried at the site. They thought nearly all of the skeletons were women. In 2000, another archaeologist from Yale found a different result. Only half of the skeletons were women. Some were infants and children. Today, archaeologists largely agree on one point. The skeletons were not those of priestesses. Dozens of other hypotheses have been offered about Machu Picchu. Various scholars thought it was a prison. Others thought it was a trade hub, a retreat for women, or a city devoted to the crowning of kings. Still others thought it was a station for testing new crops. Today, many archaeologists think it served as a royal estate. Emperors and nobles of the Inca would have used it. Whatever its purpose, experts think building began in the fifteenth century. The Inca chose the spot because of its strategic location.

4They could watch people moving in the valley below. People below could not see that a city stood on top. Even if they had seen it, the place would have been easy to defend. Steep mountains rise up to the city. Those slopes would have made an attack hard. The location had another advantage. Natural resources in the area were abundant. The Urubamba River flows far below Machu Picchu. A spring fed by rain supplies the area. A stone foundation still stands where the water comes out of the ground. The Inca built a system that collected spring water into the hillside. A canal carried river water to fountains. The fountains were a source of water for drinking and for bathing. The canal also crossed the farming terraces. Experts are not sure whether it was a source of irrigation. Water still flows from the fountains at Machu Picchu. Hiram Bingham thought a nearby granite quarry may have guided the choice of site. He theorized that workers did not have to carry heavy boulders from far away. In fact, most of the stones used in the construction are fairly small. The Inca are famous for the polygonal stones in their buildings. They were skilled carvers of stone. They may have used the wooden wedge technique. Workers drilled holes into rocks. They put wet wooden wedges into the holes. They waited until the wedges froze. Ice has greater volume than water. The ice would have forced the rock apart. That technique cannot explain the smoothness of the bricks.

5It also cannot explain their perfect straightness. How the Inca shaped the enormous blocks of granite remains a mystery. Carving granite is difficult even with the technology of today. The builders then joined the stones so tightly that mortar was unnecessary. If you tried to slip a knife between these stones today, the knife would not fit. The walls are that sturdy. The walls are in remarkably good shape. They have stood on the mountaintop for centuries. The Inca divided the city into two sections. An urban sector held the main buildings. An agricultural sector was where crops were grown. The urban sector included a district where workers and their families lived. It also included living quarters for the king and for important officials. It included the Temple of the Sun. That temple might have been used as a solar observatory. The Inca built windows with great care. The windows would receive light at certain times of the year. At the Temple of the Sun, direct sunlight enters a window on the east wall. It shines on a large rock in the center of the room. This happens on the summer solstice and on the winter solstice. Those dates fall in late December and in June. Only priests, in the view of some historians, were allowed to enter. On the winter solstice, the Temple of the Sun receives a beam of sunlight. The features of Machu Picchu include the Royal Palace and the Temple of the Three Windows.

6They include the Main Temple and the Temple of the Sun. They also include farming areas, homes, and open space. Archaeologists think the city was built for rich and powerful Inca in the 1450s. It was a royal spot. The ruler could relax there and entertain important visitors. About 150 homes were built at Machu Picchu. They housed about 750 residents. The homes were all about the same size. The royal palace, home of the emperor Pachacuti, was perhaps the grandest of all. In the western part of the site is the temple district. It is also known as the Acropolis. Here sits the Temple of the Three Windows. It is a large hall. Three trapezoidal windows stand in one wall. They are the largest-known windows in Incan architecture. Nearby is the Hitching Post of the Sun. It is also known as the Intihuatana Stone. The name is pronounced een-tee-wah-TAH-nah. It is a sundial. It consists of a wide pillar and a pedestal. The two were carved as a single unit. The stone stands 1.8 meters (6 ft.) tall. The agricultural sector lies at the southern end of the site. It was made of dozens of leveled terraces. Each terrace was designed to support the ones around it on the steep mountainside. Without terraces, the Inca would have found it hard to grow crops on those slopes. The Hitching Post of the Sun was carved from a single piece of rock. At midday on the vernal equinox and the autumnal equinox, the Sun stands directly over the pillar.

7Those dates mark the start of spring and the start of autumn. Because the Sun is directly overhead, the pillar does not cast a shadow. A rough translation of Intihuatana comes from Quechua, pronounced KECH-wah. Quechua is the language of the Inca. The rough meaning is to tie up the Sun. Those farming terraces were designed so well that they remain standing. When the Inca built the city, about 200 centimeters (79 in.) of rain fell every year. That much rainwater could have worn the soil away. Inca engineers designed the farming sector with a solution. Rainwater would seep through the soil. It would reach a layer of rocks and gravel placed underneath. From there, the water flowed to aqueducts along the sides of the terraces. It then flowed into the forest below. This system drained the water safely and efficiently. It helped keep the terraces and the other structures from collapsing. The city has stood for hundreds of years. Experts think people lived there only until the early or middle 1500s. Events elsewhere in the Inca Empire finally led people to leave Machu Picchu. Huayna Capac, pronounced WY-nah, became the new ruler in 1493. He extended the empire farther than ever before. By the time he died in 1527, the Inca ruled more than twelve million people. Those people spoke at least twenty different languages. After he died, his two sons ruled separate sections of the empire. The sons were Huascar, pronounced WAHSS-kar, and Atahualpa, pronounced ah-tah-WAHL-pah.

8They ruled peacefully for a couple of years. Then they fought for control of the whole empire. Civil war began in 1529. Atahualpa gained control from his brother in 1532. He held that control for only a short time. A few years later, the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro arrived. He came with 180 soldiers and 37 horses. The arrival of Pizarro caught the Inca unprepared. They had never seen guns in battle. They had never seen horses in battle. They were quickly overwhelmed. Thousands of Inca warriors died. Pizarro took Atahualpa hostage. The Inca offered more than 22 metric tons (24 t.) of gold and silver to free their ruler. They had collected that treasure throughout the empire. Pizarro still ordered him killed. The death of Atahualpa led to the downfall of the empire. A painting called Pizarro Spurned the Friendship of the King of the Incas shows one idea of a first meeting. It suggests how the meeting between the conquistador and the Inca ruler might have begun. People lived at Machu Picchu for only a few decades more. There is no evidence that the conquistadors ever attacked the mountaintop citadel. There is no evidence that they even reached it. Desertion, not an attack, ended life in this mysterious city. Historians think two forces had weakened the empire by the time the city was abandoned. One force was the years of fighting in the civil war. The other was the spread of smallpox. European explorers brought smallpox to Mexico in the 1520s.

9Experts estimate a terrible loss. Over several decades, the Inca population declined by 95 percent. Food supplies to the city may have stopped. The site was most likely too remote for people to stay without support. As a result, time and nature hid Machu Picchu from the modern world. Trees and vines began to cover the city. It stayed hidden for centuries. Only local people who farmed in the area knew of it. Hikers look out over the ruins today. The people of Peru are very proud of Machu Picchu. In 1983, the ancient city was named a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization. That organization seeks to preserve important historical places. The places have special cultural or physical significance. Machu Picchu is recognized as a place that can teach future generations a great deal about Inca culture. When Hiram Bingham left, he took thousands of artifacts with him. The objects went to Yale University so he could study them during his years of research. When Bingham died, the artifacts stayed there. For almost a century, the government of Peru asked that they be given back. In 2007, an agreement was reached. Security cameras, timed visits, and certified guides have added another layer of protection to the famous city.

10Historians continue to study Machu Picchu. They hope to discover new information about the Inca. A great deal has been learned about their history and their customs. 22. Colorful Seabirds of the North

1A horned puffin is shown trying to land on a rock at Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. This book opens with the sea clowns. A closer meeting with the birds comes next. Habits follow. 2Steering is the job of the feet. Speed and grace carry them along. A dive may reach 100 feet (30 m) or deeper. About half a minute is as long as they stay under while they hunt fish. Wingbeats in the air can hit 400 in a single minute. Under water, the motion looks like flight. Canada is near one of the biggest colonies of Atlantic puffins, in the Labrador Sea. Nesting colonies are home from mid-spring through summer. Some colonies sit on islands. Others sit on cliffs along the coast. The oceans are the North Atlantic and the North Pacific. Breeding season brings a large beak full of color, patches of bright white feathers, and feathery ornaments of several kinds. A mate is the point of that display. 3Rafts is the name for the large groups that ride the waves together. Four species each carry traits that set them apart. Even in breeding dress, their looks are the most modest. Orange colors the beak tip. A blue-gray section sits there too, ringed by a yellow line. Legs are orange. Face, chest, and belly are white, and they stand out against a black back and black feathers on the upper wing.

4Height for an adult horned puffin averages 15 inches (38 cm). Home waters are the northern Pacific, for the most part below the Arctic Circle. Tufted puffins use the northern Pacific on the Asian side and on the American side. Alaska is as far north as they go. Japan is as far south as they go, and so is central California. A black chest and a black belly set them apart from Atlantic puffins and from horned puffins. Winter dress is black, with a large beak of red-orange.

5Summer breeding brings striking changes. A white mask appears on the face. An olive-yellow section appears on the beak. Long golden plumes, feathery in texture, grow above the eyes. Feet turn orange. Rings around the eyes turn orange too. Height for an adult rhinoceros auklet averages 13.8 to 15 inches (35 to 38 cm). This puffin species is less widely known. One home is North America's shore on the Pacific. The Asian coast near Japan is another. In the breeding season a short horn stands upright where the upper bill begins. The bill itself is thin and yellow-orange. That horn is why the name exists. Feathers are mostly brown. The back is the darker brown. Chest and belly are paler. White feathers form two thin stripes on the left side of the head and two on the right. Birds are usually back from the ocean by the end of March or the start of April.

6Colonies in the breeding season can hold as many as several thousand birds. The same mate is usually kept. The same nesting site is used year after year. Each pair then prepares a burrow. Depth is about 3 to 6 feet (1 to 2 m). One egg is what the female lays there. Soft soil is the usual burrow site for tufted puffins, for European Atlantic puffins, and for rhinoceros auklets. Rock crevices on coastal cliffs are the usual site for horned puffins and for North American Atlantic puffins. Puffling is the name for a chick just hatched. Thick down makes the chick look like a small round puffball. Some sources say, wrongly, that parents abandon the chicks at some point. The truth is that chicks leave by themselves when they are ready. Full maturity comes around age five. Life can last twenty years or longer.

7Every puffin species prefers small fish. Sand eels are favorites. Herring and hake are favorites too. Colony, place, and time of year change which fish are taken. Winter brings fewer fish, so the diet adds squid, crustaceans, and marine worms. Eating by adults happens under the water. Fish are also gathered to carry home to chicks. Stacking is a famous skill. Meat, eggs, and feathers have drawn human hunters for centuries. Some places still allow that hunting. Newer dangers have appeared. A drop in food fish is among the most serious. Some fish now found in large numbers are too big for a chick to swallow.

8Other fish offer less nutrition. Either problem limits what puffins can eat. Nets set for fishing also catch the birds. Pollution harms them. People have disturbed many nesting sites. 9The seabirds returned to Eastern Egg Rock. By 2014, breeding pairs on the island numbered 148. A sponsor stands behind Project Puffin. That sponsor is the National Audubon Society. Birds are what the society works to protect, along with other wildlife and their habitats. A cliff by the sea holds a den, and an Atlantic puffin stands at the entrance. The country is Iceland. Much of each year is spent at sea, so a viewer has to plan for that. Land time is the breeding season only. Remote cliffs are the main places to look. Islands are the other main places. A hike of many miles may still yield only a distant look at one bird, or at two. A boat tour can make the sighting easier, often from closer range. People can watch those answers and turn them toward human difficulties that look similar. One aim of hers is to teach more people about the field. Her work has received several awards. Many gains come from fitting natural answers to human problems. One gain is plain. Long ages of trial stand behind nature's strategies. They succeed in real life. Survival of the organisms that depend on them would fail otherwise. Elegance is another surprise, and it often comes with simplicity. See how a burr is built, and the build is not terribly complex. Chemical antifreeze is the usual way to stop parts from freezing. It works. Living tissue, though, finds it highly toxic. Careful handling is required. A second kind of antifreeze is not toxic. Life in the Antarctic depends on it, and so does life on the cold floor of the ocean. Extreme cold is no barrier for some fish. A natural protein in the bloodstream stops ice crystals from forming. Similar proteins are a hope of researchers. Organs saved for human transplant might be preserved by them. An inset photo, taken through a microscope, shows silk being made for a web. The larger photo is a funnel spider.

9Stickiness and strength are obvious to anyone who has blundered into a web. Compare a silk strand with a thread of steel. The silk is three times stronger. Webs stay flexible and also sturdy because of that strength and because of their unusual design. Scientists want to study both the silk and the design. A material might then copy what arachnid builders achieve in strength and in flexibility. Fences beside highways could be made from it. A speeding vehicle's blow could be absorbed. Injuries in a crash could be reduced. Two microscopic views show microorganisms that make natural plastics. Plastic seems to be everywhere. People produce this long-lasting material by the millions of tons. Medical devices use it. Toys use it. Everything between those uses it too. Durability turns into a problem after the items are thrown away. Huge piles of waste remain and do not disappear. Natural plastics made by microorganisms may be an alternative to artificial ones. Bacteria help make the natural kind. They also help dispose of it. Soil holds different microbes, and those microbes eat the natural plastic that was thrown away. Carbon dioxide and water are what remain. A chimpanzee is shown eating medicinal plants. Wild animals get sick, just as humans do. Some species seem to know a treatment. Chimpanzees are one example. Monkeys are another. Native plants or minerals are the remedy. People in many places have also used natural remedies for illness and for injury. That practice has lasted thousands of years. Nature still has important lessons for humans.

10A great deal remains to be learned. Scientists who study the living things around us can find inspiration. Important problems can gain solutions. More sustainable living can be learned.
