The best answers may sit right under our noses. Biomimicry is the science that can uncover them. Words here carry set meanings. An adaptation is a change, in an organism or in a species, that improves survival in its home. To contaminate is to add a harmful or unwanted substance until something is unsafe or useless. Dispersal is how organisms or objects are moved and spread across a wide area. Ecological describes links among organisms, and links between organisms and where they live. An ecosystem joins a community of living things with the habitat around them. Exploit means to take profit or advantage from someone or from something. People who live in a place, and other animals who live there, are its inhabitants. Microbes are living things so small that ordinary sight cannot catch them. Microscopic means visible only when a microscope is used. Color in a substance can come from pigment. Europe's fourteenth through sixteenth centuries saw a sudden flowering of science, of culture, and of art. That flowering is the Renaissance. Resources are stores of things that are valuable or highly useful. Quartz and sand hold a hard compound called silica. Glassmakers often use it. Spew means to force a large amount out fast, as if spitting it. Sustainable use does not finish a resource and does not harm it permanently.

24. Elizabeth Tudor Rules England

1A map from the 1500s shows three kingdoms at once. Scotland's kingdom is the northern label. The North Sea is named on the eastern side. England's kingdom is the southern label. London is marked with a star. Wales has its own label. Ireland's kingdom sits to the west. The Atlantic Ocean is the water named there. France is labeled across from England. Asia, Europe, and Africa appear on the wider view. The first topic is the Tudor family. The next topic is how a queen was made. Battles come after that, both near and far. One battle story is France's civil war. Another is Mary, Queen of Scots. Another is the Spanish Armada. The last topics are Elizabeth's older years, the close of her time, the ruler who followed, and the mark she left. A word list finishes the book. The opening picture is Elizabeth as a girl. A great many people rank Elizabeth Tudor as England's finest monarch. The family behind her was full of knots. Her father already ruled England long before she was born. People called him King Henry VIII. Catherine of Aragon was his wife. Mary was their daughter. Mary stood at the front of the line for his throne. A boy to rule after him was Henry's wish. The boys Catherine bore did not live. Henry felt deep disappointment. Anne Boleyn came into his life a few years later. Her place at court was lady-in-waiting. He wanted Anne for his wife. Ending the match with Catherine was his firm aim. He carried that plea to Pope Clement VII. Clement stood at the head of the Roman Catholic Church. Henry asked Clement to wipe out the marriage in law. Clement said no. Rage took hold of Henry. He cut England free from that church.

2He put himself at the top of a church he had just formed. Its name was the Church of England. A secret wedding then joined him to Anne Boleyn. Canterbury's archbishop was the religious leader of the new church. That archbishop ended the marriage to Catherine in law. England was already pulled in two directions. Catholicism was one side. Protestantism was the other. A picture shows Anne Boleyn. When Elizabeth later wore the crown, her father's choices would test her. During the 1500s, people all over Europe began to doubt how the Roman Catholic Church did things. Historians call that period the Reformation. A different kind of Christianity grew out of it. Protestant churches were founded then. Henry VIII's Church of England still used Catholic ways of worship. It refused the pope's right to command it. One painting lines up the Tudor family from the left. The faces are Lady Mary, then Prince Edward, then Henry VIII, then Jane Seymour, then Lady Elizabeth. September 7, 1533, was Elizabeth's day of birth. Her mother was Anne Boleyn, newly crowned as queen. Her father was Henry. Almost nobody pictured this baby as a future ruler of England. Once she was born, Henry blamed Anne. He had wanted a boy, and she had not provided one. The year 1536 brought a charge of treason against Anne. Henry had her put to death. He also said Elizabeth was illegitimate. He and her mother were husband and wife on the day Elizabeth arrived. Officials still said the wedding had never been valid. That decision dropped Elizabeth from the path to the throne. Jane Seymour became Henry's next wife. She gave birth to Prince Edward. Edward was the male heir Henry had longed for. Jane's death came soon after that birth.

3Henry went looking for a wife once more. This search was for wife number four. New wives did not mean Elizabeth was left without care. Her schooling was broad and serious. Math was one subject. History, geography, architecture, and needlework were others. She learned to speak French and to write it. Italian, Greek, and Latin were part of her studies too. She could use each of those tongues with real skill. Tutors saw an outstanding pupil. They thought very well of her. Horseback riding filled some of her free hours. Dancing was another pleasure. So was playing the lute. Visits with her father were rare. Now and then she shared a household with her sister and her brother. Three further weddings followed for Henry. No child came from any of them. The last of his six marriages took place in 1543. Catherine Parr was the bride. She pushed Henry to write down a clear order of succession. Mary and Elizabeth were put back into that order. Mary was placed second. Elizabeth was placed third. Edward, their brother, stayed first. The year 1547 was the year Henry VIII died. The crown passed to Prince Edward. He was nine. While he ruled, England's church moved further toward Protestant ways. Death came for Edward only six years after the crowning. Mary took the throne next. Catholic faith had been her mother's faith. Mary held that faith with great strength. She aimed to stop every Protestant practice. Anyone who would not follow Catholic teaching was, in her view, a heretic. She sent hundreds of those people to their deaths. The nickname Bloody Mary grew from that. Elizabeth still prized the Protestant faith. She went to mass anyway. She studied Catholic teaching as well. She hoped those choices would keep her alive.

4She also hoped Mary would look on her with favor. Mary guessed that Elizabeth still worshiped as a Protestant in secret. Mary also guessed at a plot. Rebels tried to pull Mary off the throne. Mary blamed Elizabeth for the rising. Arrest followed. The prison was the Tower of London. Elizabeth insisted she had done nothing wrong. Two months in that tower was Mary's order. House arrest then lasted close to a year. Illness killed Mary in 1558. The throne passed to Elizabeth, who stood next. Her crowning day was January 15, 1559. Her age was twenty-five. Rejection and prison were behind her at last. She soon showed herself as a Protestant monarch. People who disagreed with her faith were treated with tolerance. Advisors from the Catholic side worked for her. Protestant advisors worked for her too. She hunted for a path between the two camps. Success did not always come. Critics spoke from both camps. Some Protestants said she went too easy on Catholics. Some Catholics answered with the word heretic. They said she had left the faith behind. Hard days did not stop her from working with energy. Charm was another of her strengths. Music returned to the court because of her. Art returned as well. The change felt sharp after Mary's brutal, violent years. Intelligence earned respect from the people near her. Wit earned respect too. A picture shows her greeting a visitor. That visitor may have been royalty who hoped to wed her. Marriage talk started as soon as her reign did. Courtiers cared about the question. Ordinary people cared too. A strong match could tie England to other lands in new alliances. An heir was the other hope. Elizabeth saw a danger in marriage. Her power as queen might shrink.

5A king from abroad carried a second danger. Another country might end up ruling England. Proposals arrived in large numbers. Every proposal met a no. By then she was a firm ruler of a Protestant England. Sixteenth-century France was different. Catholics were the larger share of its people. Protestants there were known as Huguenots. They started to believe they could beat the Catholic rulers. Those rulers had turned into steady foes. The year 1561 was when Elizabeth sent an ambassador into France. His task was to urge the French crown toward the Protestant faith. Fighting began in 1562. Catholics and Huguenots were the two sides. Six thousand soldiers went from England to join the fight. Catholic forces proved stronger. Elizabeth pulled out the English troops still there. She admitted the loss. Across Europe, Protestants lost heart. While France stayed unsettled, Elizabeth watched Scotland. She wanted to stop France from joining Scotland as an ally. Scotland bordered England on the north. It was an old foe as well. A picture names Mary, Queen of Scots. Scotland's Catholic queen was Mary, Queen of Scots. Elizabeth's father was Mary's great-uncle. The two women were cousins because of that tie. Mary would not accept Elizabeth as the true heir. Many Catholics agreed with Mary. They refused to treat Anne Boleyn's wedding to Henry VIII as real. In their eyes, Elizabeth was illegitimate. Year after year, Catholic groups made plots. The aim was to depose Elizabeth and to kill her. They wanted the crown for Mary. Mary was tied to some of those plots. Strain marked the two queens' dealings from the start. Later, Mary had to abdicate. Her son received the crown. Political trouble drove her out of Scotland. She came into England. Nineteen years of prison followed, on Elizabeth's order.

6Another murder plot reached Elizabeth in 1586. She understood that waiting would only invite more danger to her rule. Arrest came for Mary. A court found Mary guilty of treason. Elizabeth put her name on the death warrant, though she did not want to. February 8, 1587, was the day Mary was put to death. Spain became the next threat. King Philip II followed the Catholic faith. Plans to invade England were already in his mind before Mary died. The execution made him ready to strike. Sir Francis Drake explored for England with Elizabeth behind him. His raids had been stirring Philip's anger. Spanish ships were plundered on the voyage home from the Americas. Those American lands were territories people had only lately found. Drake told his sailors to attack the Spanish vessels. Gold filled those vessels. Silver did too. Both metals were bound for Spain. In 1587 Drake entered Cadiz Harbor, on the Spanish coast. Ships sitting at anchor were wrecked in large numbers. The blow came before Spain could sail. Loot was one goal. Breaking Spanish spirit was the other. Philip decided he would spend all his strength to pull Elizabeth down. England prepared for battle. The Spanish Armada left port. Philip meant to sail as far as the Netherlands. Spanish control already covered the Netherlands. About seventeen thousand Spanish soldiers waited on that shore. Their job was to invade England. English crews were skilled at sea. Their ships were better and quicker. Their weapons were strong. Storms made the weather terrible. The water turned rough. Heavy harm hit the Armada in the fight. A retreat toward the north was forced on the fleet. The ships then faced a brutal sail around Scotland and around Ireland. A map traces the Spanish Armada's path in 1588.

7One hundred thirty ships made up the fleet. The course ran north. It then bent around Scotland's coast and Ireland's coast. Spain lay at the end of that long way home. Rocky shores wrecked many of the Spanish vessels. Sailors died in the thousands. Half the ships were gone by the time the rest reached Spain. Half the seamen were gone as well. England cheered the Armada's defeat. Elizabeth had come through one more test of her rule. War bills weighed on England after that win. Debt spread among the people. Crops failed. Epidemics broke out. An unmarried queen left people asking who would rule next. Elizabeth pushed for journeys of discovery across the world. She hired explorers for the New World and for lands past it. Goods from distant places arrived in Europe in greater amounts. She used that flow to lift England's commerce. Trade was also her way to ease the debt. Silk was one cargo she wanted bought and sold worldwide. Food was another. Spices were another. Poverty still held some families. A merchant class was rising at the same time. Its members were growing rich. Presses for printing got better in these years. Literature was a love of Elizabeth's. She cheered on that kind of work. Schooling expanded at a huge pace. The number of readers climbed in a big way. A late portrait shows Elizabeth I. Readers now included the middle classes. The lower classes gained readers too. Pride in the nation kept growing. Most of Elizabeth's subjects felt love for her. Respect was just as common. A strong education stood behind her. Support for the arts was a belief she held firmly. Music kept growing while she ruled. Art and literature grew as well. Court doors stayed open to painters.

8Poets, writers, and other artists were welcome too. The year 1590 found England's arts in full bloom. William Shakespeare is widely treated as the finest playwright who ever lived. Fame came to him in a huge way during her reign. His plays often reached her court. His company of actors came with them. Some plays mirrored what was happening in England. Other plays were comedies. Those comedies pleased her most. His sonnets pleased her too. She became a warm patron from the throne. Admiration for his writing ran deep. A 1590 picture shows her watching a play at Christmas. Her final years saw England out in front of global exploration. The empire kept spreading. Arts stayed strong. Winter of 1603 brought a turn in her health. She still tried to look powerful. Courtiers could tell she was slipping. Favorite sweets sat untouched. Swallowing grew hard. Tonsillitis was one illness people suspected. Ulcers in her throat were the other guess. Speech left her on March 21, 1603. Three days after that, March 24, she died. Sleep was quiet when death came. Sixty-nine was her age. Forty-four years was the length of her rule. April 28 was the funeral day. Grieving subjects came in the thousands. Westminster Abbey is where she was interred. Queen Mary I, her half-sister, shares that tomb. The coffin lies in a chapel. King James I, the next ruler, built the monument above it. Six marriages by Henry VIII shook the kingdom and left it unstable. Who would follow Elizabeth became a widespread worry. In public, she would not give the name. Advisors felt the weight of that silence. Subjects felt it too. The name was spoken only in private. Nobody fought over the person she had picked.

9The future king was James VI. He was her nearest living relative. Mary, Queen of Scots, was his mother. Henry VII was a direct ancestor of both Mary and James. Henry VII had been the first Tudor king. James took the crown once Elizabeth was gone. In England he was known as James I. The new king shared the Protestant faith. Power changed hands without a war. Her private choice joined England's throne with Scotland's. The year 1707 made the two lands one country. A bitter European rivalry ended with that union. James inherited a solid government from her. A strong navy came with it. Foreign trade had been something she pushed. Money from her had paid for New World exploration. A worldwide empire was now within England's reach. People later called the Elizabethan Age England's Golden Age. Calming religious strife was among her greatest works. That strife had ripped England open. Protestantism, under her, became England's official faith. Women gained a freedom they had not had before. She fed a new thought. A woman could aim at any work a man could aim at. Love of country showed in her life. Enemies and allies both saw her proof. A woman could lead with intelligence. She could match a man in results and in success. Monarchs of her size are rare. She ranks among history's most popular women rulers. She also ranks among the best known. Strong leadership brought her praise. High regard also came from the way she backed the arts. Few people who rose to England's throne were loved so widely. Few were so compelling. She was the Tudor line's final monarch. Tudor rule in England had begun in 1485. A timeline gathers the main dates of Queen Elizabeth I. Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn became her parents in 1533.

10The year 1536 was Anne Boleyn's execution. The year 1544 fixed the order of succession. The year 1547 brought Henry VIII's death, and Edward became king. July 6, 1553, was the death of King Edward VI. October 1, 1553, was Mary's crowning. The year 1554 was when Mary ordered Elizabeth locked up. The year 1558 brought Mary's death and Elizabeth's rise as queen. The year 1563 was Elizabeth's defeat in France's civil war. The year 1587 was the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots. The year 1588 was the defeat of the Spanish Armada. The year 1590 was when the arts began to thrive, largely from Elizabeth's backing. March 24, 1603, was Elizabeth's death. James I then ruled both England and Scotland, so the two countries stood as one. The word list gives plain meanings. Abdicate means a king or queen gives up that role. Conspired means people secretly planned an act that was illegal or that would cause harm. Alleviate means pain, suffering, or trouble is made smaller. Depose means a leader is pulled from power all at once. An ambassador is an official sent to live in a place, or to travel there, and speak for a country or its people. Heretics are people who reject beliefs or practices that officials accept. Annul means something is ended by an official act, or is declared to have no legal force. Illegitimate describes someone whose parents were unmarried at the birth. Plundering is theft of every valuable thing, done by force. An armada is a big group of boats, most often warships. Succession is the line, or the process, by which a powerful job passes to the next person. Commerce is goods being bought and sold, which is trade.

25. False Hair Across the Ages

1A reader can start with a welcome to wigs. What a wig is comes next. What goes into one follows. The earliest examples come after that. Greece and Rome, and the wish to hide a bald head, have a part of their own. Fashionable hair in France comes later. Styles that grew extreme follow. A question about hair now, and hair still to come, closes the story. Special words sit at the end. Human hair makes the longest-lasting wigs. Cutting and styling are also easier than with synthetic fiber. Recorded history shows a deep obsession with hair. The story runs from the culture of ancient Egypt into modern life. Wigs have mattered inside that obsession. Vanity of a personal kind is one reason people wore them. Showing one's place in society is another reason. Styles vary a great deal. A full wig is one choice. A toupee is another. An extension is a third. Periwig is another name for a full wig. Peruke is a name too, said puh-RUKES. Coverage runs over the whole top of the head and both sides, reaching the neck. A toupee covers less. It reaches from the forehead to the crown, and from ear to ear. Hair of the wearer's own still shows in back.

2An extension is a section of hair, or of fiber. Pins can attach it. Clips can attach it. Glue sometimes does the job. The base may be a wig already made, or it may be natural hair. A fuller look is the goal, or a longer one. Tape that sticks on both faces can hold a toupee against the scalp. Materials vary too. Wool has been used. Hair from a goat has been used. Horsehair has been used. Straw and grasses have been used. Plastic of certain kinds has been used, nylon among them. Any color in the rainbow is possible. For centuries, hair from people was often the material people wanted most. It looked the most natural. Hair from six people might go into one wig. Sometimes the number of heads was ten. Cost was higher than for other choices. Only the very wealthy could pay. Nylon is the choice for many people today. The price is lower. Care is simpler. The look can still pass for real hair. Before the 1700s, a wig was often built for one person alone. Most people could not pay a price that high. Makers usually started with a mesh cap that fit tightly, plus a base of fabric shaped to the head.

3Hair, or some other material, was looped across the mesh. It was tied off. Beeswax held it to the fabric. Resin could do that job. Glue could too. Styling then followed whatever fashion the time demanded. The 1700s made a different wig popular, one that could suit anybody. A ribbon sat at the cap's edge. Pulling it tight held the wig on. Many head sizes could use the same wig, so the price fell. More people could buy one. Weaving uses a tool called a ventilating needle. Hair is drawn through holes in the base. Knots then lock the strands. Tomb paintings from ancient Egypt show complex wigs. Sculpture from that land shows them too. The oldest wigs anyone knows date to 1400 bc, and the place is Egypt. Looking like the gods was one reason to wear them. Covering a bald spot was another. A bald spot was judged unattractive. Strength and health were what a full head of hair was thought to mean. Egyptians believed their gods wore hair that was fancy, thick, and braided. Wigs copied that look. Length was already uneven in that early time. Some stopped at the neck. Some stopped at the shoulders. Others reached the waist.

4Thickness was shared by all of them, along with curls and braids. Extra fullness sometimes came from extensions. A light coat of beeswax often set the hair so the shape would hold, much as hairspray does now. The film Cleopatra put many hairstyles on Elizabeth Taylor. Three wigs were needed for each style. Egyptian society did not limit wigs to one class. Ivory ornaments decorated the human-hair wigs of the royal household. Silver ornaments did too. Hairstylists kept those royal wigs in good shape. Wool or goat hair was what the wealthy classes could pay for. Straw was all that poor people could afford. Daily wear of wigs has been rare in Asian cultures. Theater is a different story. Costumes in Japanese theater have used wigs for many centuries. Chinese theater has done the same. Greek goddesses, Aphrodite among them, wore hairstyles that may have shaped the fancy wigs of Greek women in those times. Two later world empires also put false hair on wealthy people. Noblewomen of ancient Greece wore complicated wigs. Noblewomen of ancient Rome did too. Braids and curls, many of them, were pinned above the head. Larger curls stayed put with hairpins. Social status rose with the number of braids and with how ornate the style became.

5Volume came from wigs of human hair. Still more volume, for some women, came from extensions. Blond was a favored color. Red was favored too. Some of the Roman elite kept Germanic slaves whose hair was blond or red. A supply of hair for wigs and extensions was always ready that way. Bald spots were hidden, by wealthy men and wealthy women alike, because those spots were judged unattractive. A few Roman emperors, on rare days, used wigs as disguise. They could leave the palace and mix in the street without being known. What ordinary people truly thought of them became clearer that way. Julius Caesar ruled Rome as emperor from 100 to 44 bc. His hair was thinning, and he was unhappy about it. A first attempt grew the back hair longer and combed it forward over the scalp. Failure followed. Cleopatra, his girlfriend and the last pharaoh of Egypt, then offered a hair-loss recipe. Ground-up mice went into the mix. Horse teeth went in. Bear grease went in. The potion failed Caesar as well. A laurel wreath seemed easier, and it worked better. Victory in battle was what the wreath stood for. His bald head was covered nicely at the same time.

6Fashion dropped wigs after the Roman Empire ended. Several centuries passed that way. The early seventeenth century brought wigs back. France's ruler, King Louis XIII, started wearing them as his hair thinned. He was only twenty-three. Respect from the royal court, he feared, would fade if people thought baldness was coming. His wigs copied the look of his natural hair. A part ran down the middle. The hair was smooth and carefully groomed. It lay flat on the scalp, then fell in gentle waves as far as the shoulders. Looking like the king was a way for many noblemen to count as fashionable. Similar wig styles spread among them. Full wigs in this period belonged mostly to men. Extra fullness and thickness, for some of those men, came from extensions. Women who were losing hair sometimes wore wigs too. Women who still had plenty of hair used extensions to decorate their styles. Coiffure was the name for such a style, said kwah-FYURS. Clothing at the royal courts grew more elaborate, so hairstyles had to grow fancier. Demand for wigs rose. Demand for extensions rose too. Real hair and false hair were both shaped over a frame, or over a pillow, to build a form. Lard, which is fat from a pig, then set the style.

7Powdered starch finished the set. Lavender sometimes scented that starch. Orange blossom sometimes did. Height could reach three feet (0.91 m) before any hat or ornament was added. Model ships, built in careful detail, sat inside some women's styles. Creation was so hard that the hair stayed in place for as long as three months. Combing stopped. Washing stopped. A cartoon dated 1778 shows one of these wild wigs from women's fashion in France. Time turned the lard rancid. Cockroaches came to it. Mice came to it. Rats, in some cases, built nests in the hair. Scratching without ruin to the style took a special tool. It was a long stick tipped with a claw. By the eighteenth century, a wig was worn by nearly everyone in Western Europe who belonged to a royal court or to certain jobs. The wig became a central piece of a uniform. It marked a doctor. It marked a barrister, meaning a lawyer. It marked a judge. Clergy members were marked by it. Members of the nobility were marked by it too. Horsehair was a frequent material. Stiffness and thickness came with it, and the cost was lower than human hair.

8Large curled wigs, heavy with powder, later left fashion. People in these jobs still wore them in public. Judges in the United Kingdom still wear them in court today. Barristers there do too. The wig is part of the uniform. Pictures make the link from then to now. One picture is an eighteenth-century view of a court in England. Another shows judges meeting at Westminster Abbey. Toupees entered fashion in that same century. Curls and powder still made them ornate. One large gain set them apart. They felt cooler. They felt lighter. A full wig was extremely hot to wear. It was quite heavy too. The year 1795 brought an English government tax on wigs and on the powder used with them. Only a few years passed before the tax ended. A great deal of money reached the government while it lasted. Britain's fashion for wigs died out as a result of the tax. By the 1850s, wigs had been dropped by many people in Europe. Common people often judged them a needless luxury. Only the aristocracy, in that view, could pay. Some clever sellers collected used wigs. Street buyers could get them for little money. Buyers turned them into floor mops. Buyers turned them into rags for polishing.

9Bigwig, meaning an important person, is first known from 1703. The source is an English journal called English Spy. The people with the most money, and the most influence, were the ones in the largest and showiest wigs. Sir Edward Willes judged cases in eighteenth-century Britain. A person might call him a bigwig. The twentieth century brought better technology, and nylon threads became a wig material. Real human hair was what the threads resembled, at a much lower cost. Color choices grew wider too. Any hue in the rainbow was possible, so looks multiplied. Reasons for wearing a wig are still many. Fashion is one. Style is one. A simple change of appearance is one. Self-esteem is the aim for people who are bald or whose hair is thinning. A costume may include a wig for a clown or an actor. Fashion of each age has shifted the styles. Length has changed. So has the amount of decoration. Across human history, wigs have still mattered. The next great fashionable hairstyle is anyone's guess. Hair can fall out because of some illnesses. Treatments can cause the same loss. Wigs are prescribed by many doctors for these patients. A more positive feeling is one possible result. A better response to treatment is another.

10Long hair is given today by some people to nonprofit groups. Those groups make wigs for children whose hair is gone. Special words can be set out plainly. An obsession is an extreme interest that fills the mind far more often than usual. The aristocracy is a society's highest class, usually rich and powerful. Ornate means covered with a great amount of detail. Elaborate means full of parts and details, or complicated. Rancid is the word for spoiled oils or fats, when the taste or the smell turns sour and unpleasant. Elite names the people in a society who stand at the top in success, wealth, or power. To embellish is to add details that make something more appealing. Resin is a sticky, fragrant substance taken from the sap of trees. Toupees are false hair pieces that cover part of the head, usually where hair has been lost. Extensions are lengths of hair or fiber fixed to a wig, or to natural hair, by pins, clips, or glue. Wigs are coverings for the head, built from hair or from materials that look like hair. Fashion means the styles or customs of looks and behavior that are popular at a given time.

26. Farms Across America: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow

1A grower shows a younger person how plants are raised inside a greenhouse. The book has these parts, in this order. First comes a look at one farm. Next comes the older American custom of farming. Then comes the story of family farms that now operate as large businesses. After that comes farming that reaches other countries and farming that stays nearby. Then comes a way of living that does not stay fixed. Last comes a list of useful words. Homesteaders pose in a Nebraska celery field. The photo dates to 1904. Picture a Farm John and Magreta Hoefer began their family farm during 1901. The place was close to Elgin, a town in Nebraska. Their land covered 160 acres. That area equals 0.65 square kilometers. The children were five girls and two boys. Before school, those children rose for chores. Opening the henhouse was one job. Milking the cows was another. The hogs received their slop. The horses received their feed. When the school day ended, work outdoors began again. The heavy seasons were spring, summer, and fall. People pulled their suspenders up and got ready. Gardens still needed care, and so did the fields. Hands and muscle did almost every task. Wagons moved only when horses pulled them. A large household had to be fed from what the farm grew. The animals needed feed of their own. Some extra crops were raised so the family could sell them. Doing all of that work took a huge effort. The farm John and Magreta started would shock them if they could see it now. Later generations made the holding much bigger. Children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren all took part in that growth. Great-great-grandchildren share in running it today. The land they manage is more than 1,000 acres. That is the same as 4 square kilometers. Seven separate Hoefer farms share that land. The people farming now do not call on every relative to work the soil. Machines do a large share of the jobs. The fleet includes large tractors. Combines are part of the fleet too. Irrigation can run on its own. Computers watch the operation and help direct it. Cattle are part of what the family raises. Corn is grown because it brings in cash. Soybeans are a cash crop as well. Popcorn is one specialty crop. Organic vegetables are another. Over the last two hundred years, farming in this country changed in a deep way.

2The wider U.S. economy changed along with it. Those changes altered the jobs people hold. They also altered how families get food on the table. There was a time when a farm was home for nearly every family. Working the land is now the job of only a small share of people in America. The nation still gets its food from those farms. Tons of food also leave the country on ships. Agribusiness, as a worldwide system, counts these farms as an important piece. When conditions shift, farmers here have proved they can adjust. Changes still coming will call for that same kind of strength. A photo from about 1900 shows a Montana farmer steering a plow. Farming as an Older American Custom Farmers once made up most of the United States. In 1790, small farms were home and workplace for 90 percent of American families. Each family tried to grow food and put enough aside. The stored food had to carry them through winter. Plans had to be made with care. Drought could ruin a growing year. Flood could ruin it too. So could disease in the crops or in the animals. A ruined year was not only a letdown. Hunger could follow, and so could the loss of money. The pulling power came from draft animals. Horses stood in front of wagons. Mules and oxen did that work as well. A plow that opened the ground needed the same kind of pull. People also had to labor all the time. On a smaller family farm, chores belonged to everyone in the house. Grandparents took part. Young children took part too. The jobs ran from first light until dark, because the home and the farm both had to function. Some families lived on bigger places known as plantations. Enslaved people were made to work those fields. Cotton was one crop raised for sale. Tobacco was another. Even hard labor left the result unsure. The weather could decide whether a year succeeded. The price of farm goods could decide it too. A large change in society was already underway by the early 1900s. The Industrial Revolution had its start in the late 1700s. By the early 1900s it was moving faster. Rural people kept leaving farms for factory jobs in cities. Farming itself was changing, and that change helped the move.

3Slavery was gone by 1900. Family farmers were down to 38 percent of the labor force. The share kept getting smaller. City populations in the millions still had food, because farmers could grow enough. Farm communities fed themselves at the same time. Three developments let farmers produce more. A growing country could then get the food it needed. Mechanization was the first development. New technology was the direct cause. One person with a powered machine could finish work that once needed dozens of people. Better methods were the second development. Less land could then yield more crops. Seeds were improved. Chemical fertilizers came into use. Weed killers came into use. So did technology that brings water to fields. Modern transport was the third development. Farm goods could travel very far. A farmer was no longer stuck selling only nearby or only in one region. Trucks could carry crops to a train or a ship. Buyers across the nation could be reached. Buyers in other countries could be reached too. The country was also growing in size, and that growth helped farming. From the 1860s on, the United States took control of the Great Plains. Prairies and other grasslands fill this wide region. It runs west from the Mississippi River. The Rocky Mountains mark the far side. Trees were scarce on most of that land. The soil was rich, so farmers and ranchers could cultivate it and make heavy use of it. Rocky, wooded country back east was harder to work. People still speak of the Great Plains as America’s breadbasket. The same name is sometimes used for the whole world. Huge amounts of food can come from this region. Family Farms Run as Big Business Fewer people on farms keep turning out more food. That pattern has not stopped. Farmers and the people who labor for them are about 2 percent of U.S. workers today. The amount of agricultural products is still higher than it has ever been. Size is one way to understand farming in America now. A federal agriculture department, called the USDA, supplies the figures. Only 9 percent of the farms are midsize or large-scale. Those farms turn out 65.2 percent of the food. The share is close to two-thirds. A number of these farms are very big. Families still own and run nearly every one of them. “Nonfamily farms” are less than 2 percent of the farms in the United States.

4Corporations from outside the family are the owners of that small group. How Size Compares with What Farms Produce One chart groups U.S. farms by the income they earn. Another chart groups food production by the size of the farm. Readers see 2.9 percent beside 1.3 percent. They also see 6.1 percent beside 10.6 percent. Other marks are 24.2 percent and 42.4 percent. The last marks are 22.8 percent and 89.7 percent. Labels in the key are small, midsize, large-scale, nonfamily, and family. Income is how the USDA decides which size a farm is. In a year, a small farm brings in no more than 350,000 dollars. A midsize farm’s yearly earnings run from 350,000 dollars up to 999,000 dollars. A large-scale farm’s yearly income is 1 million dollars or more. The USDA released these figures in a 2015 survey of how farm resources are managed. Sorghum is one crop in that picture. Soybeans show up as well. Incorporation is the legal form of most family farms. Important business gains can come from that form. The tax bill may be lower. A bank loan may be easier to get. If money trouble hits, the owners may have more protection. Retirement or death of an owner is another time that protection can matter. Lon Frahm’s operation, Frahm Farmland Inc., shows what a large-scale farm can be. He is the chief executive officer. People shorten that title to CEO. He is the top boss. Six generations of his family have farmed in Kansas. The year he took over was 1986. Cropland then totaled 5,000 acres. That equals 20 square kilometers. About ten employees now do the farming. The cropland is almost 27,000 acres. That equals 109 square kilometers. Corn is one crop. Soybeans, wheat, and sorghum are the others. Sorghum is a grain rich in protein. It is fed to livestock. Frahm Farmland followed a path common on American farms. Production grew a great deal, because the farm needed to succeed and to earn a profit. Corn, and Then a Still Bigger Crop Bushels of corn per acre are what one chart measures. The USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service gathered the numbers. The chart follows those numbers across years. More Food from the Same Land Every business that aims at profit is driven by productivity. Farming is that kind of business.

5Year after year, farms in America have produced more. From the 1960s onward, the count of U.S. farms has held fairly steady. About 2.1 million is the figure. Farmland acres have held about steady too. Over those same years, output of agricultural products more than doubled. Foodstuffs in America come mainly from big operations such as Frahm Farmland. Managed well, they often beat smaller farms on productivity. They often beat them on efficiency too. More agricultural products can come from each acre. Spending on land is lower on average. Spending is also lower for equipment, supplies, and buildings. Other costs of running the place are lower as well. To cut the cost of human labor, larger farms have been first to adopt new tools. A machine can milk a cow without a person at its side. A drone can watch the livestock. A tractor with no driver can cross a field. It finds its path with GPS, the global positioning system. Ground moisture is read by sensors. Those sensors turn irrigation on and turn it off. Seeds developed for this purpose push yields higher. Fertilizers do the same. So do pesticides and herbicides. Yield is the amount of crop the land gives. In a milking parlor, many cows are milked together. Red bell peppers are sorted and packed by migrant farm workers. The scene is in Southern California. Big farms often hire immigrants because costs stay low and profits stay high. Some of those workers lack official papers. Others are guests who are allowed to work. Wages for them are often much lower than wages paid to American workers. Monoculture is a method many large farms use when they want peak efficiency. It means one farm product is grown in a very intense way. The product might be a single crop. It might be one breed of livestock. Equipment and buildings can then be limited to what that product needs. The owner can also become highly skilled at that one product. Danger sits inside the plan. One violent storm can destroy the only crop. An outbreak of disease can destroy it too. Soil loses quality when variety is missing. Fertilizer then has to be used heavily. A sharp fall in the market price can hit the farmer hard. Whatever is grown or raised is the thing whose price can collapse. What People Ask About Factory Farms Some livestock sites are built to send as many animals to slaughter as quickly as they can.

6CAFO is one name for them. The full name is concentrated animal feeding operation. “Factory farm” is the other common name. Small pens indoors are where the animals often stay. Natural light is missing. Room to move is scarce. This style of care is used most often for dairy cattle, hogs, and chickens. Three complaints are heard most often. Manure leaves these sites by the ton, and the environment is harmed. The way animals are raised, and the way they are killed, is often cruel. Disease can spread because the animals are packed close together. Antibiotics are given at high levels to fight that risk. Germs can learn to survive the drugs. Those same drugs enter people who eat the meat. Health can be put in danger because of that. A factory-farm photo shows hens packed tightly together. Production contracts with huge agribusiness firms are signed by about one farmer in three. The aim is to reduce risk. The farmer agrees to raise crops the company provides. Sometimes the farmer agrees to plant the company’s seed. A set price is what the company promises to pay. Pricing is still largely in the company’s hands. The farmer may be told to upgrade buildings and equipment at a high cost. The farmer, not the company, pays that bill. Speaking in public about poor treatment can cost a farmer the business. Each farmer has to compare what the contract gives and what it takes. Some pay is guaranteed. That promise supports the work and the money already spent. The farmer can also end up with little power against a giant firm. Bargaining power stays limited even for a very large farm. These corporations hold a growing share of agriculture. They hold a growing share of the wider food business too. Shoppers feel the efficiency of big farms in a simple way. Prices tend to be lower. If milk is cheaper to produce, some of that saving can show up at the store. Corn and wheat work the same way. Chickens and pigs work the same way. The Share of Income Spent on Food A chart includes the figures 28 percent and 24 percent. The USDA Economic Research Service is where the chart comes from. Other marks on the income scale are 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, and 0 percent.

7Years run along the bottom. Since 1930, the price of food has climbed a great deal. By 1997, food took a smaller slice of what Americans earned. Early in that century the slice was more than twice as large. Farms Ahead: Far from Home and Close to Home Looking forward is a habit for many farmers. They spend money on crops or animals because they hope for income later. They ask whether extra land would help them produce more. They ask the same question about a tractor full of new technology. Forecasts tell them what the weather may do. Clouds in the sky tell them too. Hay may need cutting right away. A coming storm may be a reason to wait. Life on a farm is built around plans for what comes next. Nobody can name one future for every American farm. The answer changes with the place you study. Two strong trends are forming the next chapter of U.S. agriculture. One reaches across the world. One stays in the local area. Farming is a global business now. Economists, for the most part, say globalization is changing how farms are run. The United States is part of that change. So are other countries. Goods cross borders, and money crosses borders. Banks and companies in different nations take part in that flow. What people buy is already shaped by it. What they eat is shaped by it. How they earn a living is shaped by it too. A soybean crop from Nebraska may be sent to China. A crop from Iowa may go the same way. Money from China, called capital, comes back to the United States. Avocados leave Mexico on trucks. U.S. food distributors receive them. Dollars from the United States pay for the fruit. Growers here can sell more of what they raise in other countries. The same links create risk. Trouble in a distant country can reach a farm in America. A trade fight between the United States and China is one case. China can cut back on soybeans and corn bought from America. Huge agribusiness firms are crossing oceans and borders more than they ever did. They purchase resources, or they rent them. They go to the place where the resource is found. Shuanghui International, a Chinese conglomerate, bought Smithfield Foods Inc. in 2013. The price was 4.7 billion dollars.

8Virginia is where Smithfield is based. No U.S. company processes more pork. Once the sale was done, more than four hundred farms were under Chinese control. Thirty-three processing plants were part of that control. One hog in every four in the United States was part of it too. The USDA is the source of those counts. More deals among processors and distributors in different countries are likely. The reach of globalization is still growing. Some large farms look outward to the world. Some smaller farms in America look the other way. They focus on buyers close to home. Nearly 90 percent of U.S. farms are small. The products they turn out are just 24.2 percent of the total. For about half of the owners, the main paycheck comes from work away from the farm. “Hobby farm” is the name some of these places earn. Enjoyment, more than profit, is why the owner keeps going. Even so, “local food” is showing up in more towns and cities. More of these farmers are dropping an old aim. Shoppers at a Los Angeles farmer’s market can buy vegetables grown nearby. Some of those vegetables are organic. These growers are stepping away from mass production. What they raise is sold at markets close to the farm. Restaurants nearby are another customer. Older methods are a choice for many of them. Chemical fertilizers are limited or not used. Pesticides and herbicides are treated the same way. Owners of future farms, large and small, will have to deal with damage to the environment. Experts on agriculture fear that today’s methods cannot keep going. Valuable resources are being used up. In some places, research shows, wells underground are pumped too hard. The water source can run dry. Some big animal sites create pollution in huge amounts. Streams and rivers are poisoned. The air gets worse. Soil is harmed when fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides are used too much. Soil, a Resource Worth Protecting People walking past a field rarely think about the ground. A farmer cannot ignore it. Healthy land is what keeps a farm alive. Yields tend to drop when land is in poor shape. Food from that land tends to be less nourishing. Soil is not just dirt. Organic matter is part of it. Most of that matter is plants breaking down, plus tiny living things. New growth gets nutrients from them. Trying to swap in chemical fertilizers does not fully replace those nutrients.

9Research says the chemicals also hurt soil over many years. A small group of farmers is changing methods, and the group is growing. Their aim is to guard the soil and improve it. No-till farming is spreading. The plow is left unused. Stems and leaves from the last crop are allowed to rot where they fell. Crops that put nutrients back may be rotated in. Cattle may graze a field after the harvest. Both habits help soil stay in good health. A child is shown putting vegetable plants into rich soil. A method can fill the barn this year and still scar the land for a long time. More farmers see that their future is threatened. They are starting methods that can be kept up. They know the land sets the limit on how long a farm can last. One photo shows floodwater. The other shows land turning to desert. Climate change is behind both scenes. Farmers lose either way. Another environmental danger is larger still. It is climate change. Around the world, average temperatures are going up. Patterns of weather are not what they were. Some places that once counted on steady rain now get less of it. Other places get far more. Researchers see cropland disappearing at a faster pace. Deserts are spreading, above all in dry regions. Climate change is one reason. U.S. studies say farm output could fall by a large amount. Corn yields in the Midwest could be down by as much as 25 percent by the year 2050. Soybean yields could fall by that same amount. Food supplies could feel a serious effect. North America would be touched. The rest of the world would be touched too. Farming is not built to adjust in a hurry when change is large and fast. Like most businesses, it does better when tomorrow looks like today. Careful plans need that kind of steadiness. Economics ahead may swing more wildly than farmers here have known for a long time. Climate may swing that way too. The swings may be unlike any these farmers have seen. Life on the Farm Does Not Stay the Same From the founding of the country, farm business in America has kept growing. Farms got bigger. The methods got more advanced. A nation with more people each year was fed by that output.

10The world was helped too. Since 1970 the number of people on Earth has doubled. The total is almost eight billion. Daily farm work goes on. Seeds go into the ground. Crops are tended. Animals are raised. The result is food for the rest of us. People who have farmed for many years treat the work as a way of life. Earning a living is only part of it. Caring for land, crops, and animals gives them satisfaction. Across the last hundred years, that feeling has stayed much the same. Who holds the farm is starting to change from one generation to the next. The typical farmer in America is 58 years old. Many workers in America retire around that age. Young people are choosing other work. Some of them grew up on farms and still leave. The labor is hard. The hours are long. A good result is never sure. Income is never sure either. Decades from now, people will still farm. They will adjust to the changes that show up. The look of those farms at the century’s end is much harder to guess. So is the question of who sits on the tractor. Corn will still need picking. Cows will still need milking. One photo shows a farmer letting a grandchild take the wheel of a tractor. The open question is whether that child will still be driving one as an adult. Words to Know agribusiness (n.): the industries that grow farm goods, prepare them, and move them to buyers. mechanization (n.): bringing in machines for work that people or animals used to do. optimize (v.): to bring something to its best or most effective state. degrades (v.): makes something poorer in quality, or wears it away. fertilizers (n.): substances, natural or chemical, that help plants grow. productivity (n.): the pace at which work gets done or goods get made. incorporated (v.): turned into a company that the law treats as a real organization. surplus (n.): the extra amount after what is needed has been supplied. unsustainable (adj.): not able to continue at today’s pace, or based on uses that drain a resource or wreck it for good. irrigation (n.): bringing water to fields or crops so they will grow. vulnerable (adj.): open to being hurt. mass production (n.): turning out huge quantities of a product with machines inside a factory.

27. Feet, Goals, and a Worldwide Game

1The sections of this book are a remarkable sport, play at every level, how a match works, how the sport was born, famous players, a game open to all, and words to know. The day is the seventh of July in 2019. A full stadium in Paris is waiting. Paris is in France. The crowd is impatient for the U.S. Women's National Team. The short name is USWNT. People wonder whether the team can match what it did in 2015. The first half ends. Nobody has scored. The strain grows. Megan Rapinoe is a cocaptain of the USWNT. At the half she takes deep breaths. She settles herself again. That reset helps. In minute 61 she scores the opening goal. The crowd turns wild. Teammates cheer her. The moment enters history. The picture shows Rapinoe taking a penalty. The match is the women's World Cup final of 2019. FIFA runs that World Cup. The setting is France. Moments like this one have pulled millions of fans toward a ball of their own. Watchers have become eager spectators. They follow matches on television. Those watchers also pack stadiums, and the stadium count reaches the thousands. The sport is spectacular. It fits every age. It fits every country. This is the most popular sport on Earth. Another name for it is association football. About 240 million people play. Club totals stand above 300,000.

2Fan estimates reach 3.5 billion. That is half the people on Earth. Pro play is run by FIFA. In French the first words are Fédération Internationale. The rest is de Football Association. FIFA was founded in 1904. Its base is Switzerland. Late in 2021, membership stood at 211 countries. Each member has a national team. FIFA sets up international contests. Teams in those contests hope to reach the World Cup. The men's World Cup comes every four years. The women's World Cup comes every four years. Thirty-two men's teams are chosen. Twenty-four women's teams are chosen. Millions watch the final matches. One photo shows Alistair-Patric Heselton on the left. He is from Great Britain. Rene Renteria is on the right. He is from the United States. The two battle for the ball. Another photo shows a Colorado team in blue. They face the Yuwa Supergoats in red. The Yuwa Supergoats are a girls' team from India. Many youth teams play across national lines. The United States Soccer Federation is a FIFA member. People usually call it U.S. Soccer. It governs every soccer league in the United States. Those leagues include amateur teams. They include professional teams. They include men's teams and women's teams. They include youth teams. They include Paralympic teams. Students play at every stage of school. Elementary school has players. College has players. A person does not need a team membership to enjoy the sport.

3Two people are enough. They can take a ball to a park. They can use almost any open ground. That freedom is part of the sport's wide appeal. Nearly every country plays this sport. It crosses national borders. It crosses differences of culture. It crosses differences of income. That is true in industrial countries. It is true in developing countries. Most people picture an outdoor field. Some players use a gymnasium. A rink made for ice hockey can wear a layer of artificial turf. Men's soccer has been in the Summer Olympic Games since 1900. It missed only one of those Games. Women's soccer joined the Games in 1996. The Paralympics have included soccer since the Paralympics began in 1984. Blind soccer was added in 2004. The map names Australia and Africa, then Europe and Asia, then South America and North America. Some places call the game football. Some call it soccer. Some use another name. North America says soccer. Several other places say soccer too. Italy says calcio. South Korea says chukku. Football is the name in most of the world. A match sets two sides against each other on the pitch. Pitch means field. Each team tries to put the ball in the other team's net. Each team also tries to stop the other from scoring. A team has eleven players.

4One is the goalkeeper, or goalie. Ten are field players. Each spot on the team watches its own area of the pitch. Defenders mainly play defense. They try to keep the other team from scoring. Midfielders move often between attack and defense. Forwards mainly play offense. The center forward is also called the striker. That player is usually the team's top scorer. That player is usually the strongest attacker. Every player, in any position, must be ready to switch fast between attack and defense. Field players may touch the ball with the feet. They may use the legs, the chest, or the head. Hands are not allowed for them. The goalkeeper may use hands inside the penalty area. A kickoff starts the match. The ball sits on the center spot. A player from the starting team kicks it. The kick may be a pass to a teammate. That opening side works the ball toward the far end of the pitch. A goal means the ball goes past the other goalkeeper and into the net. The field diagram names the main lines and the player spots. The goal line is also the endline. A ball that crosses it can bring a goal kick. It can bring a corner kick. The score counts when the ball passes the posts and finishes in the net. The penalty area is called the box.

5The goalkeeper may use hands only inside that area. A corner kick must come from the corner arc. The sideline is also the touchline. If the ball leaves there, play restarts with a throw-in. The width runs from 49 to 100 yards. That is 45 to 90 meters. The length runs from 100 to 131 yards. That is 90 to 120 meters. The center spot is also the center mark. Kickoffs happen there. The halfway line is the midfield line. At a kickoff, only the kicking side may stand inside the center circle. The penalty arc may hold only the player taking the penalty. The penalty spot is a circle. It lies 12 yards from the goal line. That distance is 11 meters. The ball is set there for a penalty kick. On the diagram, G means goalie. D means defender. M means midfielder. F means forward. A striker is marked among the forwards. Each end of the diagram shows one goalie, four defenders, three midfielders, and forwards. Only the goal box is the legal place for a goal kick. If the starting team knocks the ball out of bounds, the other team throws it in. The throw comes from the spot where the ball left. When a ball exits over the goal line, the goalkeeper kicks it back in. Opponents receive a corner kick after a side puts the ball beyond its own goal line.

6A foul inside a team's own penalty box against an opponent brings a free kick. That kick is taken from the penalty spot. It is called a penalty kick. Many penalty kicks become goals for the team that was fouled. The sport is demanding. Playing it well takes training. It takes conditioning. Pitch size changes with the kind of field. An international field has its own size range. An Olympic field has its own range. A youth field has its own range. A high school field has its own range. Any of those pitches is large next to the fields of most other sports. A match has two halves. Each half lasts 45 minutes. The only break is 15 minutes. Before the whistle ends the match, one player may run as far as 7 miles. That distance is 12 kilometers. Most of the running is fast. Training builds stamina. It builds endurance. It builds flexibility, which helps players avoid injury. It builds muscle strength, which helps a player hold off someone trying to take the ball. Players keep polishing skills. They keep working to master the game. A goalkeeper must stop balls that pass the defenders. Goalkeepers need to be strong. They need to be tough. They need to be fast. They need to accept the chance of getting hurt. Field players must master kicking.

7They must master dribbling, passing, and heading. They must master shooting at the goal. They must master tackles that take the ball from an opponent. Dribbling means moving the ball a short way with the feet. A tackle wins possession by knocking the ball free of the other side. Heading means moving the ball with the head. Passing means sending the ball to another player. Shooting means kicking the ball in order to score. A photo shows a crowd of about 65,000. The place is Crystal Palace. The year is 1897. The match is the English FA Cup Final. Aston Villa plays Everton. Across the British Isles, this game was already known from the eighth century through the nineteenth. The count of players was not fixed. Sometimes a whole village played. The old game was less organized. It was more violent. Kicking an opponent was allowed. Other physical attacks brought no penalty. These rough early forms were popular. Authorities still opposed them. Those leaders wanted the violent pastime stopped. A large change came at the start of the nineteenth century. Educators carried the game into public schools. Schools wrote different rules. Their fields differed widely too. A paved school yard needed less rough play. It needed more skill at dribbling. Schools chose different styles. Some wanted only the feet, which is soccer. Others wanted the hands as well, which is rugby.

8School leaders saw the teamwork the sport encouraged. They saw the cooperation it encouraged. Soccer then became a regular part of school. In 1863, Cambridge University wrote rules so schools would play in one way. Those rules banned hands. Because hands were banned, football split away from rugby football. In this split, football means soccer. The first soccer organization was the Football Association. The founding date is October 26, 1863. By 1871 it had fifty member clubs. Its first contest was the FA Cup. That cup came the next year. Outside Great Britain, the sport picked up speed in the last ten years of the 1800s. It kept growing after that. FIFA was founded in 1904. National associations numbered twenty-one in 1912. It had thirty-six by 1925. It had forty-one by 1930. Play for the opening World Cup came in 1930. In the late 1930s, rules from the 1800s were brought up to date. They were also reorganized. A similar revision came in 1997. Today the sport is a worldwide phenomenon. Its appeal keeps growing. Some women's teams are better than men's teams. Some are more successful. Pay for women is often lower than pay for men. In 2022, several USWNT players protested. Because of those protests, U.S. Soccer agreed to pay men and women the same. The sport has had many gifted players. Pelé is widely seen as the greatest player in the sport's history.

9Say the name PAY-lay. No other player has been on three World Cup winning teams. He played striker for Brazil's national team. His playing years ran from 1956 to 1977. He scored 1,281 goals. Those goals came in 1,363 matches. That total is a world record. The record still stands. One of his gifts was a rare skill for reading where players would move. In 1994, Briana Scurry's role with the USWNT was in goal. She went on to make history. A save she made during the 1999 championship locked her place in the sport's story. That championship was the FIFA World Cup. In her career she won or earned every trophy in her field. She earned every award in her field too. In 2017, soccer's national hall of fame added her name. On the field she is a strong role model. Off the field she is a strong role model for people everywhere. The World Cup is only one way to play. Some players choose futsal. Futsal is a fast indoor form of the game. Others choose the shore and play beach soccer. Most players want something more traditional. They choose old-fashioned soccer. Students have many ways to join. A city or a town may have a soccer organization. Those groups field teams for different ages. Young players learn how to handle the ball from their coaches.

10They teach attacking plans. They teach defending plans. The game teaches sportsmanship. It teaches teamwork. Those ideals matter on the field. They matter off the field. Millions of cheering fans cannot be wrong. Millions of players cannot be wrong. This spectacular sport offers excitement for everyone. Youth leagues are popular in many countries. One photo shows a girls' match already underway. Words to know. Administrators are the people who run a group, such as a company, a school, or a hospital. Anticipating means looking ahead to what will happen, often with excitement. Avid describes a strong interest or a strong wish, and it means eager. Conditioning is training and exercise that make a person better or stronger. Endurance is the power to handle strain or suffering across a stretch of time. Enticed means drawn in, or tempted, by something pleasant. Formidable describes someone very impressive or very powerful. Size, strength, or skill can make that person inspire respect or fear. Fostered means helped something grow. A phenomenon is a remarkable event. It can also be a person or thing that is hugely popular because of an unusual quality. Stamina is the strength or energy to keep going for a long time. Standardized means brought into line with a set of rules. Transcends means goes past a limit or past what people expected.

28. Fighter Pilots from Tuskegee

1Contents. Today's Target: Berlin. A Flying Unit Made of Black Airmen. Opening Battles. Voices Against Them. Red Tails. Home Again. Word List. A small photo shows Dr. Roscoe Brown, one of the earliest men trained as a Tuskegee Airman. He is telling about a fight in the air with enemy planes that attacked. Guarding big bomber groups, by flying along with them, was the pilots' chief task. Today's Target: Berlin. Lieutenant Roscoe Brown Jr. flew high above Germany and kept a careful watch. His fighter was a P-51 Mustang. March 25, 1945, fell in the last year of World War II. Mustangs of the 332nd Fighter Group flew under his lead. Guard duty covered two hundred American bombers. Berlin, Germany's capital, held the day's target, a plant that made tanks. Enemy planes were the threat. Brown's duty was to hold them off the bombers. Sleek, fast, and heavy with weapons, the Me-262 was a first. No earlier fighter had been driven by a turbine. This one was a jet. Skilled German hands made it lethal. Bombers drew near the target, and Brown searched the sky. A big formation showed up all at once, quick, from in front and from higher up. Messerschmitt jets, the Me-262, had been launched to shield the capital. Nothing flying then was more advanced. Speed was extreme. Armament was heavy. Pilots among Germany's finest were at the controls. Famous work of the Tuskegee squadron was to stay with bomber groups and shield them. Aircraft with no guns, sent to photograph possible ground targets in detail, also received Red Tail protection. On the radio Brown shouted Bogeys!

2Bogeys! Other pilots understood. Planes were in view, and they might not be friends. German jets swung to the back of the bomber group. A wolf pack closing on prey is the picture. Then four of those jets dropped into a dive. Fire opened from all four as they shot past the American bombers. The shots, for the most part, went wide. Behind him, Brown searched again. Four more Me-262s were rushing at the bombers, low and from the rear. Over the radio he ordered the tanks dropped. A handle released the fuel tanks hung beneath each wing of the Mustang. Reaching this deep into Germany had required that extra fuel. Leaving the tanks on during a fight was a very poor plan. Action could start. The plane rolled. A dive aimed straight at the enemy jets, and speed built on the way down. Level with the Me-262s, he came out of the dive and fired on the closest one. Aim held. Flames burst from an engine on that jet. The German pilot left the aircraft a moment afterward. A confirmed victory belonged to Lt. Brown. A picture shows four pilots. They were in the first set of men trained for the 332nd, a fighter group that was entirely Black. The trainer was the flying branch of the U.S. Army. Two further Americans from that group also brought down Me-262s in the same battle. Five more jets were damaged by Brown's fellow pilots. No plane of theirs was lost. No bomber was lost. What the 332nd did that day earned a Presidential Unit Citation. During the war, few group honors for airmen ranked higher.

3The incredible part sits underneath. Service as pilots was almost denied to these American heroes. Being Black was the cause. Borders and names of the European countries pulled into World War II appear on a map. Italy held Ramitelli Airbase. From there, Tuskegee pilots covered hundreds of bombing missions that were strategic. Germany lay under those routes. So did Czechoslovakia, Austria, Hungary, and Poland. Virginia, 1947: Black students attend a school kept segregated. A Flying Unit Made of Black Airmen. Across many states in the America of the 1930s, laws treated Black people unfairly. Segregation kept them apart from white people. Different schools were required. Separate restaurants were required. Drinking fountains had to be separate. Public restrooms had to be separate. The color of skin decided it. Segregation shaped the military as well. Units for Black soldiers stayed apart from other races, for living and for training. Command always sat with white officers. Training a Black pilot was something the Army Air Corps would not do. War in Europe looked likely to many U.S. leaders near the end of the 1930s. Nazi Germany and the nations allied with it would be the foe. The flying arm of the U.S. Army realized something. Pilots were too few. An answer seemed clear to leaders in the Black community. Let Black people learn to fly as pilots, they asked the government. Opposition came from some military leaders. Good pilots in combat, they thought, were beyond what Black people could be. Congress of the U.S., in 1941, at last compelled the Army Air Corps to stand up a flying unit whose airmen were all Black.

4An experiment was the army's word for it. Could Black pilots match white pilots at the work? That was the test. Success was not what everyone hoped for. January 23, 1942, Tuskegee Institute, Tuskegee, Alabama: Major James A. Ellison offers a salute to Mac Ross, who came from Dayton, Ohio. Cadets of the Black Air Corps stand for review. Fame later gathered around the Tuskegee Airmen, yet a Black American had flown as a military fighter pilot before them. Eugene Bullard volunteered with the French Air Force in World War I. Two German aircraft are thought to have fallen to him on those flights. August 1917 brought the United States into the war. Volunteers from America who were already flying for France could move into American service with the Army. Bullard alone was refused. His race was the reason. March 1941 created the 99th Pursuit Squadron. No earlier unit in the air forces of the Army had been entirely Black. Black trainees learned aircraft mechanics. Other support work was taught too. June brought a move to airfields near Tuskegee, Alabama. Forty-seven officers began the group, with 429 enlisted men. Growth, once the name Tuskegee Airmen took hold, reached 996 pilots. Supporting military staff passed 15,000. Command of the 99th Pursuit Squadron belonged to Captain Benjamin O. Davis Jr. West Point Military Academy had graduated him. The U.S. Air Force later made him its first Black general. Combat was still ahead, and already the obstacles were many. Alabama training brought discrimination inside the bases and outside them. White officers stood over the Black airmen, and the treatment was sometimes unjust.

5Parts of a base open to white people stayed shut to these airmen. Townspeople nearby caused trouble. Police caused trouble. Until 1948, military branches stayed segregated, and military police were among them. Colored was a word often turned on Black people then, and the use was discriminatory. Civil rights gained an early protest from within this same force. B-25 bombers were the aircraft of the 477th Bombardment Group. White officers had a club on base. In 1945 the officers of the 477th were told they could not use it. A peaceful protest followed. The civil rights movement counts that protest as an early milestone. Opening Battles. Upset was real. Capt. Davis gave them a path. Fly as well as any white unit. Fight as well, or fight better. That showing would be the reply. April 1943 sent the 99th into the fighting in North Africa. A German base on a little island near Sicily's coast was the first mission. Gun positions on that island were knocked out by the squadron's P-40 Warhawk fighters. Escort for friendly bomber squadrons started too, the mission type that would bring the widest fame later. German soldiers on the island quit in under two weeks, helped along by this work. Capt. Benjamin O. Davis Jr. became the Air Force's first Black general. The Army's first Black general was his father. Electronic aviation gear of the modern kind did not exist for World War II pilots. Old trainer planes were the school. Navigation used maps and photographs taken from the air. Sharp eyes and fast reflexes carried them.

6Voices Against Them. Success on that first operation failed to please certain officials who ran the war effort. A complaint said pilots from one 99th group had peeled away to chase enemy fighters. Friendly bombers then had scant cover. Another complaint said no enemy plane had been shot down on the missions. Pull the 99th out of combat, said several white officers of high rank in the Army Air Forces. Gen. George Marshall, chief of staff for the army, would not abandon the experiment so quickly. An official review was ordered, to study the 99th's record. Fighting could continue, he also decided. The review, once published, found the island attack well done. Critics had already been answered in another way. Summer of 1943 gave Lt. Charles B. Hall the unit's first victory. A Focke-Wulf 190 went down under his guns, and that type ranked with Germany's finest fighters. No Black pilot in American military service had brought down an enemy aircraft before. Italy's invasion then saw twelve German planes fall in two days to pilots of the 99th. Experience in combat built a record of excellence. Challenging it grew steadily harder. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt stood among the earliest backers. A 1941 visit included a request to fly beside one of the Tuskegee pilots. More than an hour aloft followed. The plane was a Waco biplane. Beside her flew C. Alfred Anderson, known as Chief and shown in the picture. Landing left her pleased. Her words: he certainly could fly. Red Tails. September 1943 placed Benjamin O. Davis Jr. in command of the 332nd Fighter Group. His rank by then was lieutenant colonel.

7Three new squadrons of Black fighter pilots belonged to it: the 100th, the 301st, and the 302nd. Operations in Italy later folded the 99th Fighter Squadron into that same group. Aircraft grew more advanced. One step was the P-47 Thunderbolt. The lasting aircraft came after: the P-51 Mustang. Long-range escort, deep inside enemy land, suited this amazing fighter. Red paint covered the tails of both the P-47 and the P-51. Pride in the unit was the message. A motto of equality was the reminder. All blood runs red. Red Tails became the name the 332nd pilots used for themselves. A restored P-51 of the World War II years now teaches the public about these airmen. Identification was easy, for friends and for enemies, because the tails were red. Friendly bomber crews saw the skill and started a nickname, the Red-Tailed Angels. Black pilots in the 332nd were unknown to most of those American crews. One of them called the fact a secret the Army had kept better than any other in the war. Fear of the red-tailed Mustangs grew among German pilots. Black Bird Men was their name for the men who flew them. Damaged bombers, easy prey for determined German Air Force pilots, often called the Red Tails in to guard the trip home. A drawing records a day when the bomber Jeze Belle sent a call for help. Two Tuskegee planes answered. The attacker was shot down. Guarding bombers and wrecking the aircraft that struck them did not limit the Red Tails. Swift hits on vital ground targets broke enemy supply lines and the roads and rails that moved goods.

8Final war years included two hundred escort missions by the 332nd. Across all of them, enemy aircraft destroyed fewer than twenty-five bombers. A loss count that small was astonishing. Other escort groups sometimes lost as many bombers as that on one mission alone, all to enemy fighters. June 1944 brought a rarer feat. Machine guns on P-47 Thunderbolts, flown by 332nd pilots, sank a destroyer belonging to the Italian navy. No other moment in the war saw a major navy ship sunk by aircraft that used machine guns alone. War's end left courage, skill, and fighting power proved in front of everyone. Aircraft destroyed in the air came to 112. Aircraft destroyed on the ground came to 150. Hundreds beyond those were damaged. Railroad cars, trucks, and further vehicles destroyed passed 950. Medals for the work numbered in the hundreds. Respect and thanks from the white bomber crews, protected on mission after mission, mattered just as much. Cost was real. Enemy action and accidents took sixty-six pilots. Capture took thirty-two. Heavy damage from air raids struck Berlin, the capital, in World War II. Britain flew those raids. America flew them. Russia flew them. Before the war, a top photo shows the Reichstag, a piece of Germany's parliament, standing in Berlin. After bombing upon bombing, a lower photo shows what remained. A signing on July 26, 1948, shows President Harry S. Truman. His order stops segregation inside the military. Home Again. Europe had been fought free of the Nazis. Home still ranked these airmen as citizens of a second class.

9Parades to welcome the heroes did not happen. Achievement, though, was noted by the military. An unfair system had been exposed. Segregation by race could not pretend that ability truly differed. In 1948 he chose to stop separating the races inside the armed forces, and this success was one reason. Full civil rights for every American were a fight that had only started. A later remark came from retired airman Harold Brown. Failure by the Tuskegee Airmen, he observed, would likely have left President Truman unwilling to desegregate the armed forces. Experiment was the label on their training. Brown treated that label as proof. Belief from the military had been absent. Skill was shown anyway. An important share of America's long push for civil rights belongs to them. Impressive achievements are what memory keeps. A 2007 ceremony awarded the Congressional Gold Medal for those achievements. Dr. Roscoe Brown is the one speaking. Retired Lt. Col. Alexander Jefferson stands at the left. Survivors in attendance numbered over three hundred. The room was the U.S. Capitol Rotunda. A Red Tail F-15 stands beside retired Lt. Col. Harold Brown. His tour takes in the Alabama Air National Guard, including the fighter wing numbered 187. A Pilot's Life.
