Childhood gave Harold Brown, later a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel, a dream of piloting. Seventeen was his age when training began. Nineteen, in 1944, brought graduation from Alabama's Tuskegee Institute and a second lieutenant's rank with these airmen. A pioneer was not how he saw himself. Flying was the whole wish. And the flying came. World War II missions for the Airmen totaled thirty.

10A 1945 crash in Austria led to capture by Nazi forces. Rescue came. Service continued through the Cold War. Military retirement arrived in 1965, after twenty-three years. Ohio University then granted him a degree in mathematics. College teaching followed. Awards for the service have been many. The year 2020 placed him among Minnesota's honorees for aviation, in that state's hall of fame. Age ninety-five made him one of the oldest Tuskegee Airmen still alive. Word List. Civil rights are rights in law, in social life, and in economic life. They promise that every citizen will have freedom and will stand equal. A fighter is a military airplane, fast and armed, made to fight other airplanes. A formation is the pattern a group holds. Combat concerns fighting that military forces do against each other. A mission is an assigned task of a special kind. Discrimination means treating a person or a group unfairly because of gender, race, age, religion, or some other difference. Segregated means held apart over a group difference, race among them. Equality means a state where rights match for everyone. A squadron is a military unit. It holds more than a single small group, whether of soldiers, of airplanes, or of ships. To escort is to accompany someone or something, often as a guard. World War II was a war of the whole globe, from 1939 until 1945. Germany, Italy, and Japan stood on one side. Britain and France stood on the other, with the United States, with Russia, and with further nations. An experiment is a test, a trial set up in a scientific way.

29. Fire Mountains of Our Planet

1Readers meet the topics of this book one after another. The blast at Vesuvius comes first. Reasons that people stay near volcanoes come next. Then the book turns to the places where volcanoes appear. It also turns to the causes of those volcanoes. Steep composite mountains have a section of their own. Wide shield mountains have a section of their own. Small cinder cones have a section of their own. Lava domes have a section of their own. A closing section follows those parts. A list of special words ends the book. In one picture, a volcano gives signs that it is active. The year 79 CE brought earthquakes to the region around Pompeii. That city belonged to Rome. Alarm stayed low among the people who lived there. Shaking of this seismic kind had visited the region in earlier times. Serious damage did not make them abandon the city. They built it again after the harm. Minor quakes were the usual kind. Familiarity with those quakes grew over the years. Love for their beautiful city kept the residents in place. Occasional shaking of the ground was not a reason they would go. A fallen building was not a reason they would go. Steady hissing smoke rose in a plume from Mount Vesuvius. The mountain stood close to the city. No resident tied that smoke to the trembling underfoot. Life in Pompeii had already lasted for centuries. Not one person there had watched this volcano erupt. Living things teemed across the slopes of Mount Vesuvius. Those slopes wore a cover of trees. They wore a cover of flowers. They wore a cover of grass. The last eruption lay a thousand years in the past. Dormant was the word most people chose for the mountain. Extinct was the word some people chose instead. August 24 broke the long quiet. The hour was about one in the afternoon. A blast of tremendous force shook the land around the mountain. Molten rock left the summit. Ash left the summit. Dust left the summit. Darkness filled the sky. Together, dust and ash and stone have the name tephra. Tephra dropped onto the city. Ground 16 kilometers from the mountain lay under that fall.

2Ten miles is the same distance. Three o'clock brought a gush of lava from the volcano's mouth. The speed of that gush was alarming. Whatever stood in the way was ruined. By six o'clock the dust-and-ash cloud had climbed 32 kilometers. Twenty miles is the same height. Lightning formed inside the cloud because energy there was swirling. Ash did not stop falling. On the ground the layer reached 1 meter deep. The same depth is 3.3 feet. Debris piled so heavily that buildings fell. One picture sets Mount Vesuvius above the ruins that diggers have opened at Pompeii. Families in the cities round the mountain tried to get away. Homes were coming down under the volcano's attack. Farms were coming down as well. People gathered things of value. They gathered treasures light enough to carry. Then they rushed off. Some tried to cross the ash on foot. That ash lay deep. That ash was hot. Death came to many of them. Other people died when stones hit them. Those stones dropped out of the black sky. Air thick with ash and dust choked still others. Midnight made the danger worse. Ash filled the giant cloud. Poisonous gas filled it too. Dust hot enough to glow filled it. Smoke filled it. Density and weight grew too great for the cloud to stay aloft. What followed was a pyroclastic flow. Down the slopes it raced. Top speed reached 500 kilometers in an hour. The same speed is 310 miles in an hour. A further picture shows lava so hot it glows, bubbling upward inside a volcano. A plaster cast of one Pompeii resident appears in a picture. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius killed that person. Pompeii, not far from the mountain, disappeared under a surge cloud. Many people perished under that cloud. Later their bodies decayed. Holes of air remained in ash and mud that had turned hard. Each hole kept the shape of the body that had been inside. Workers who study ancient sites poured plaster into those holes. The finished casts show the look of the dead at the last moment. Only moments were needed for the first surge cloud to pass.

3People in Pompeii were scorched. People in Pompeii were buried. Herculaneum suffered the same fate. The cloud moved over both cities the way a wave moves. Fresh dust kept rolling out of the volcano. Fresh ash kept rolling out too. Further surge clouds came after the first. At the end, burial was total for two cities of Rome's empire. Nothing of them remained on the face of the Earth. Discovery did not come until more than a thousand years later. What you have just followed is the record of something that truly happened. One question is how a blast that large can occur. Another question is what can set off an explosion so catastrophic. A third question is why anyone would still choose a home near a volcano. More than one reason keeps people near these mountains. Farmers use the rich soil that volcanoes leave. Other people bathe in the wonderful hot springs. Respect for volcanoes has grown as years have passed. In early times, science could not say when a volcano would erupt. Science could not explain volcanoes either. Beliefs took volcanoes in. Traditions took them in. Lore took them in. Indigenous stories in Hawai'i tell of a goddess named Pele. Say her name as PAY-lay. Those stories blame eruptions on her anger. Her name was given to some kinds of volcanic glass. One kind is Pele's hair. Another kind is Pele's tears. A tear of that sort begins as a small drop of lava. The drop cools during its flight through the air. By the end of the flight it is solid. Wyoming holds an extinct volcano called Devil's Tower. Across the Great Plains, many Indigenous tribes give the place deep spiritual weight. Bear Lodge is the Lakota name. Tree Rock is the Kiowa name. A picture caption also uses Bear's Lodge. Creation and renewal are what the sacred place stands for. Offerings are part of a pilgrim's visit. Prayer is part of a visit. Ceremony is part of a visit. Ancient Romans believed in a god named Vulcan. They placed his blacksmith forge beneath the surface of Earth. Volcanoes, in that picture, were the chimneys of the forge below. Lightning bolts for Jupiter came from Vulcan's work.

4Jupiter ruled as king of the gods. Weapons for Mars came from the same forge. Armor for Mars came from it too. Mars was the war god. Vulcan's own name is the source of the word volcano. Volcanologists still compare the smell of a volcano to a blacksmith forge. Mount Fuji carries great spiritual weight in Japan's Shinto tradition. Buddhist tradition in Japan gives the mountain that weight as well. People treat the peak as a stairway into another world. They honor it as the spirit home of Kono-hana. Kono-hana is a deity of Shinto. Pilgrimage in Japan has a sacred center at Mount Fuji. Art in Japan has a sacred center there too. Spiritual meaning has not left volcanoes. Symbolic meaning has not left them either. Scientists now add tools and instruments to that older respect. The tools reveal how a volcano grows. The tools reveal how a volcano behaves. A coming eruption is something scientists can now predict. About 3.5 billion years ago, the earliest volcanoes appeared. Lava, hot and from deep inside Earth, spread across vast areas. The hard outside of Earth is the crust. Continent-sized sheets of rock make up that crust. The name for those sheets is tectonic plates. Continents themselves are made of some of the plates. Ocean floors are made of others. Heat just under the plates is extreme. About 1,200 degrees Celsius is the figure. The same heat is 2,192 degrees Fahrenheit. Rock at that heat melts. The liquid is called magma. At times magma forces a path upward. Cracks in the crust let it seep out. A volcano forms at that seep. A diagram of the inside marks vents and a magma chamber. One diagram shows plates on the move. Labels on it include a volcanic arc and a trench. Further labels name continental crust, oceanic crust, and the mantle. An ocean plate that rams a continental plate is forced downward. An active volcanic region is the result. Scientific estimates put the number of different erupting volcanoes, across the past ten thousand years, above fifteen hundred. Each year, the world sees about thirty-five eruptions, or about forty. A thin thread of smoke can be the only clue.

5A thin thread of steam can be the only clue. Slow eruption, with no real pause, is the habit of some volcanoes. Vesuvius belongs to the other habit. Quiet can last hundreds of years. Quiet can last thousands of years before the next explosive blast. Plate edges are the usual home of volcanoes. Thick liquid magma carries the plates, which drift slowly. Direction is not the same for every plate. A crash into a neighbor is one possible motion. A pull away from a neighbor is another. A sideways grind past a neighbor is a third. Rubbing and sliding on that scale open wide cracks in the crust. Magma can break through those cracks. A volcano can begin at that breakthrough. A map of the pattern marks the Pacific Ocean. The same map marks the equator. Along the Ring of Fire lie more than half of all active volcanoes. The world holds at least five hundred volcanoes that are active. Plate edges are where most of them stand. Volcanoes crowd the rim of the Pacific Ocean plate in particular. Ring of Fire is the name of that rim. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is another region of strong activity. That ridge is a chain of mountains under the Atlantic Ocean. There, a pair of plates drifts apart. Magma seeps through the ocean floor between them. Piles of magma grow as time passes. Some piles become mountains high enough to leave the water. Iceland rests on the tops of large volcanoes that belong to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Distance from a plate edge does not stop every volcano. Hawai'i is the example. Those islands sit in the middle of the Pacific plate, far from its rim. A hot spot lies beneath them. At a hot spot, magma stays very near the top of the crust. The magma there is hot. Island-building is one result. The work is slow. Tens of thousands of years may pass. Hundreds of thousands of years may pass. Yellowstone National Park sits inland on the North American plate, far from the plate edge. Under its buried lakes and waterways, a hot spot waits. Ground there is heated by the magma.

6Water there is heated by the magma. Think of a giant teapot. Geysers appear because of that heat. Hot springs appear because of that heat. Wyoming is where a visitor can watch Yellowstone water leap from the ground. Old Faithful is one geyser that does this. A diagram of the island chain marks Kauai. It marks Hawai'i. It marks the hot spot. It marks the way the plate moves. Eruption style is not the same for every volcano. Place of formation changes the style. Cause of formation changes the style. A gentle, gradual eruption is one style. Another style is a sudden blast as powerful as many atomic bombs. Mount Vesuvius, already described, is a composite volcano. Southern Italy's west coast is where it stands. Explosive behavior defines this type. Violence in an eruption can be extreme. Destruction in an eruption can be extreme. Stratovolcano is the other name. No other type is more common. Size is usually very large. Sides are steep. Peaks are even in shape. A crater like a bowl often crowns the top. That crater is a hollow. Magma exits there. Hot gas exits there. Ash exits there. One picture shows how striking a composite volcano's shape can be. Two pictures compare Mount St. Helens before 1980 and after the eruption. Washington State is the home of that mountain. The date of the eruption was May 18, 1980. Deaths numbered sixty-three. Hot wind roared down the slope. Forest across 311 square kilometers was flattened. The same area is 193 square miles. Viscous magma near the surface is typical for most composite volcanoes. Thickness is what viscous means. Slow movement, like syrup, is the other part of that meaning. Vents are the tubes that carry magma upward. Unusual thickness lets magma cool inside a vent. Hardening follows the cooling. A plug then blocks the vent. Magma underneath cannot get out. Heat underneath cannot get out. Gas underneath cannot get out. Pressure starts a slow climb. A critical threshold is the end of that climb. Explosion comes next. Violence can be great enough to ruin the whole mountain. In 1980, obliteration took the whole north face of Mount St. Helens.

7An eruption of this type throws up an enormous cloud. Ash rides in that cloud. Dust rides in it. Smoke rides in it. Hot gas rides in it. Rock rides in it. The climb of the cloud covers many kilometers. Blackness takes the sky. Ash then falls back to the ground. Too much density brings the debris cloud down. The fall becomes a violent surge cloud. Great height is common among composite volcanoes. Ice often caps them. Snow often caps them. One explosion can melt the entire icy cap at once. Water then rushes down. Mud rushes down. Rock rushes down. Speed can hit 100 kilometers an hour. The same speed is 62 miles an hour. Lahar is the name for a mudslide that a volcano sets off. One picture shows a huge lahar on a slope where ice and snow had melted. Oregon's Crater Lake is a famous caldera. Collapse of the volcano into itself made that huge basin. Southern Oregon's Klamath people pass down a story of how the lake began. In the story, the first coyote loved a star. He discovered a path up to her. A fall brought him back to Earth. The strike of that fall dug a hole. Crater Lake is that hole. Giant size is possible for a cloud of volcanic ash. Dust and ash from such a cloud can circle the planet. Sunlight can be shut out. The whole planet can grow cooler. The year 1815 brought the eruption of Tambora. Indonesia is where that volcano stands. People in far-off North America then lived through a cold summer. Snow fell during that summer. A composite volcano can empty an entire buried lake of magma. A great hollow is left underground. Support for the surface is gone. Land drops into the vacant chamber. Caldera is the name of the wide bowl that remains. Side-to-side width can reach 100 kilometers. The same width is 62 miles. Water often gathers in a caldera as years pass. A large lake is the result. Oregon's Crater Lake formed in that way. Huge forests can be wrecked by a composite volcano. Whole cities can be buried. Human deaths can follow. Another danger sits in the long quiet.

8Hundreds of years may pass with no eruption. Memory fades. Homes go up much too close to the mountain. Video sometimes shows lava of a bright orange color leaving a volcano's top. The lava may flow. The lava may spray. Runny texture marks this lava. The movement is smooth. The movement is quick, in the manner of stream water. Land receives the spreading lava. Hardening is slow, and the rock builds upward. Shield volcanoes supply lava of this runny kind. Gentle slopes are usual on a shield volcano. Smooth slopes are usual too. The outline resembles a shield. One picture shows Hawai'i's Mauna Loa, a volcano of the shield type. Mars carries a volcano named Olympus Mons on its surface. Among known volcanoes in the solar system, none is larger. The whole of Arizona could fit beneath it. Gentle behavior, not explosive behavior, is the usual shield eruption. Roads can still be lost under the lava. Homes can still be lost. Forests can still be lost. Hot gas sometimes sprays from a shield volcano's crater. Steam sometimes sprays from that crater. A bright fountain of lava can be the result. Stable paths make these flows easier to follow. Predictable paths do the same. Scientists can often stand very near the lava and study it. Quiet activity can continue for a long stretch of time. Extreme size can grow during that stretch. On Hawai'i, Mauna Loa ranks as the world's tallest volcano. From a base on the seafloor it climbs 9,170 meters. The same climb is 30,080 feet. Mount Everest does not reach as high. Another eruption could add still more height to Mauna Loa. Set beside Olympus Mons, even Mauna Loa looks small. Height on that Martian shield volcano is 27 kilometers. The same height is 17 miles. A short active life will not build a large mountain. Some volcanoes only toss small bits of lava upward. The tossing lasts a brief time. Those bits harden. Ash bits harden with them. The result is black rock that weighs little. Cinders is the name for that rock. Around the vent, cinders stack into a hill. The hill has the shape of a cone.

9A crater crowns it. Cinder cone is the name for such a hill. A volcano that appears suddenly, and is brand new, often takes this form. Older, larger volcanoes sometimes grow extra cinder cones inside a crater. They grow them inside a caldera as well. A single eruption is all that most cinder cones ever have. Loose rock is what they are made of. Wind wears them down quickly. Rain wears them down quickly. One picture shows cinder cones on Mauna Kea, a volcano in Hawai'i. A diagram gives the label lava dome. One picture places a lava dome above the vent called Novarupta. Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve is the setting. A second picture shows a scientist checking a lava dome that sits inside a crater. Small, short eruptions also build lava domes. Pasty, thick liquid is the lava they use. The liquid oozes from the vent. Hardening comes quickly. Later lava may push up through the dome's center. The dome swells. Cracks open on the outside. Other volcanic activity is often nearby when a dome forms. Larger volcanoes often hold these domes in a crater. They often hold them in a caldera. Violent explosion is common, as it is for composite volcanoes. Nothing shows more clearly that Earth keeps changing than a volcano does. New rock is born where lava leaves a vent. New land is born there too. Ash from volcanoes turns into soil of extreme fertility. Farming makes use of that soil. Geothermal energy is drawn from volcanoes in some places. Power plants run on that energy. Electricity is what those plants make. A life inside a volcano is possible for some people. Papua New Guinea has a port city named Rabaul. An active volcano stands close to that city. Eruptions there come again and again. Fame and beauty mark certain volcanic mountains. Mount Fuji in Japan is one. Mount Rainier in Washington is one. Mauna Loa in Hawai'i is one. People choose homes near volcanoes for reasons that are easy to see. Danger should stay in mind all the same. Some of the strongest forces on Earth live in volcanoes. One picture shows Japan's Mount Fuji in its beauty.

10The word list below collects terms from this book. Something airborne is being carried along by the air. Quiet that lasts many hundreds of years is what dormant describes. Billowed means the thing swelled and bulged because wind pushed it. Leaving a dangerous place is what it means to evacuate. Caldera names a basin with the shape of a wide bowl. The land there has fallen into a magma chamber that is empty. Thousands of years without an eruption, and no hint of one ahead, is what extinct means for a volcano. Cinders are pebbles or rocks, black in color and light in weight. Flying scraps of lava and of ash harden into them. A forge is the fierce fire a blacksmith uses. Metal is melted there so the smith can form it. Heat made naturally inside Earth is what geothermal refers to. Crater names the hollow, shaped like a bowl, in a volcano. From that hollow come gases. From it come ash and lava as well. Debris means leftover bits after everything else is gone or ruined. A geyser is a spring that, every so often, hurls heated water and steam in a jet. Earth's crust is built from tectonic plates, and each plate is a huge sheet of rock. A lahar is the big slide of mud that follows a volcanic eruption. Teeming means swarming, or packed full. The moment an effect starts to happen is a threshold. Melted rock in liquid form, lying under the surface of Earth, is magma. To be obliterated is to be destroyed with nothing left. To traverse a place is to go across it or through it. Rocks, water, and gases mixed together and still hot make a pyroclastic flow. Gravity is what sends that mixture racing. Size, amount, strength, or excitement can all be tremendous when they are very great. Shaking of the ground, including the shaking of an earthquake, is seismic. A viscous material has the thick feel of syrup. Scientists who make volcanoes their study are volcanologists. A surge cloud is superheated, and it travels fast. Ash, gas, dust, and rock are what it carries. Its path runs along the ground.

30. Five Great Works of Nature

1A world map marks five famous places. North America holds the Grand Canyon. Asia holds Mount Everest. Africa holds Victoria Falls. Mexico, in the Americas, holds Paricutin. Australia holds the Great Barrier Reef. Oceans and continents frame those sites. Europe, the Pacific, and the lands around them sit on the same map. Arizona's Barringer Meteorite Crater shows another kind of wonder. Space rocks hit Earth there and left an amazing landform. A place earns the name natural wonder when the structure is amazing. Beauty belongs to it too. People then ask how nature built it. Humans did not build these landforms. Nature did. Some wonders appear within one person's lifetime. Others need millions of years. Our planet holds many of them. This book looks at five. One is a canyon of many layers, cut by a river. One is a young volcano that buried a village. One is a waterfall that takes your breath. One is a coral reef of immense size. One is a mountain that towers over the land around it. The Colorado River once wound across a large plateau. That was five to six million years in the past. The word plateau is said pla-TOE. As the river flowed toward the sea, it carried off small pieces of that high flat land. The process is water erosion, said e-RO-zhun. Two factors decide how much soil and rock the water takes. One factor is the speed of the water. The other is the volume. Rock type matters too. Limestone is soft and breaks easily. Sandstone is soft. Shale is soft. Granite is hard and resists breaking. Slate is hard. Schist is hard. Softer rock in this canyon broke into pieces, and the Colorado River carried those pieces downstream. Harder rock stayed behind. Over millions of years the cutting made deep canyons. A map places the canyon in Arizona, inside the United States. The river slowly shaped the rock into the structure visitors see now. A side view shows the plateau and the Colorado River.

2Wall layers tell a geologic story. The story covers about two billion years. The top of the canyon is the youngest layer. Most visitors get their first view there. That top layer is called the Kaibab Formation. Nearest the river, the lowest layer is the oldest one. Rocks lying scattered on the canyon floor reach back as far as two billion years. Scientists call that age Precambrian time. No geologic age on Earth is older. The canyon is a fine place to study geology and the history of Earth. The layers are easy to see. They are easy to reach. Geologists visit often. John Newberry was one of the first scientists to come. His visit was in 1858. Writing down those layers was a scientific first, and he was the one who did it. His drawing was also a first. It showed the canyon as if a slice had cut through it. He identified the stratigraphy, which means the rock layers. He was not the first person to see the canyon. Reptile kinds in this canyon number more than forty-seven. Most of them are harmless. Visitors should still watch for snakes. Bites on humans are rare. Two snakes are venomous. One is the Grand Canyon rattlesnake. The other is the diamondback rattlesnake. In winter, rattlesnakes hibernate in dens. A single den may hold hundreds. These snakes rarely share a home. A winter den is nearly their only shared time. Warm spring days bring them outside. Each snake then travels alone. Births come late in the summer, and the mothers are females. The babies are born live. The birth place holds the newborns only briefly. The stay lasts about seven days, or it may last ten. After that, the first baby skin comes off. They add a first rattle. They move on to look for food. A growing rattlesnake sheds at least once a year. Each shed adds a new rattle to the tail. A mature diamondback may reach 2 meters in length.

3That is about 6.5 feet. Weight can reach 6.8 kilograms, or 15 pounds. Rattlers can live twenty-five years. Long before explorers from Europe arrived, Native Americans made homes in this canyon and beside it. That span was more than four thousand years. Those early groups hunted local animals. They gathered plants that could be eaten. Centuries of that life came before they settled and built villages in the canyon and around it. The year 1150 found most of those first tribes gone. The Havasupai people stayed. Some of them still live in the canyon. Some still work there. Every year, millions of people come to Grand Canyon National Park. They hike. They raft. They come to see this majestic wonder. Havasu Falls sits on the Havasupai Reservation. The falls show that water is still cutting the western part of the canyon. A great many natural creations took millions of years. Humans were not yet on Earth when some of them began. Other creations belong to recent times. Mexico's Paricutin volcano is one recent formation. The name is said pah-ree-koo-TEEN. Growth took slightly longer than nine years. The year 1943 was the beginning. The place was a field. Dionisio Pulido farmed that ground and found a fissure in the corn. A fissure, said FISH-ur, is an opening in the ground. That crack's length was about 1.8 meters, which is 6 feet. More cracks soon appeared. Black smoke rose from the holes. Ash piled on the ground and built a cone. About twelve hours later the cone stood 10 meters high, or 33 feet. After a day it stood 50 meters, or 164 feet. Growth continued. In just a week the height was 100 meters, or 328 feet. News groups all over the world paid attention. Film makers from Hollywood even shot a movie in Mexico. The volcano was their backdrop. Some villagers got short-term work. A map shows Mexico, the Gulf of Mexico, Paricutin, and the Pacific Ocean. A picture shows a church steeple. Volcanic debris buried the town, and the steeple is all that still shows.

4People in Paricutin hoped the village would be spared. Only a few months passed before the cone had become huge. Slow lava began to reach the town. People from Paricutin had to leave. People from four other towns had to leave. The move was permanent. Homes were left behind. Farms were left behind. Across nine years, lava and ash covered the whole village of Paricutin. San Juan, the town close by, was mostly buried as well. In the end, Paricutin was gone except for the church steeple. It rises out of black rock. It reminds viewers of nature's power. Volcanoes like Paricutin are called cinder cones. Another name is scoria. They are the simplest kind of volcano. They appear suddenly. They erupt. Then they go dormant for decades or for centuries. Pressure inside Earth pushes lava out. Exit is a vent at the center, cut into the ground. An explosion throws the lava up into open air. Cooling comes next. It breaks into small pieces. Those pieces harden. They fall as rocks and as ash, also called cinders, around the vent. The pile becomes a cone. A longer eruption builds a taller cone. Most cinder cones have a crater at the top. The crater is shaped like a bowl. Because Paricutin is young, scientists have watched it grow from the first day. Today it stands about 424 meters tall, or 1,391 feet. It covers 26 square kilometers, or 10 square miles. Watching the growth has helped scientists understand the strong forces shaping this planet. A diagram labels the cinder cone, the crater, rock fragments, and the central vent. Water carved Victoria Falls. Water also carved the Grand Canyon. A map places the falls in Africa, between Zambia and Zimbabwe, near the Indian Ocean. No falling water on the planet has a greater mass. The drop is 108 meters, or 354 feet, into a deep pool. People in Zambia call it Mosi-oa-Tunya. The name is said MOH-see wah TOON-yah.

5It means the smoke that thunders. Thunder names the booming sound. Water crashes over basalt gorges into the pool below. Smoke names the water vapor that rises from the bottom. That vapor shines with changing color. People can see it from as far as 20 kilometers, or 12 miles. Victoria Falls stands on the Zambezi River. Zambia stands on one bank. Zimbabwe stands on the other. The river marks the border, and the continent is Africa. Formation began millions of years ago. A small crack appeared in the rock, straight across the river's path. About 150 million years in the past, parts of the earth moved. That movement opened the crack. Over the years, water wore away the soft sandstone. A cliff formed. The river now falls over that cliff. The pool below is called a plunge pool. A Scottish explorer named David Livingstone came to the falls. The year was 1855. People from outside Africa had probably never viewed these formations before him. He named the falls for Queen Victoria of England. Many people prefer Mosi-oa-Tunya. That name fits what visitors actually see and hear. Two national parks now include the falls. One park is in Zambia. One park is in Zimbabwe. Close to two million visitors come each year. A diagram labels the cliff, the hard rock, the soft rock, and the plunge pool. A few details are easy to remember. The falls is really six waterfalls. Their names are Devil's Cataract, Armchair Falls, and Horseshoe Falls. The list continues with Main Falls. Rainbow Falls belongs on it. So does the Eastern Cataract. Bungee jumping draws people to a bridge here, and that bridge is a popular site. A full moon keeps the park open into the night. Moonlight through the vapor makes a rainbow, and people come to see it. Below the falls, people raft and kayak. Surfing those rapids is possible too. A map places Mount Everest on the border region of China and Nepal, with the Pacific Ocean to the east.

6The mountain is named for Sir George Everest. He was a Welsh surveyor and a geologist. No mountain on Earth stands taller. Few sites anywhere look this spectacular. Nepali people call it Forehead in the Sky. Tibetan people call it Goddess of the Valley. The landform sits in the Himalaya mountain range. Its height is 8,850 meters, or 29,035 feet. Nepal lies on one side of the peak. Tibetan China lies on the other. It looks over the Plateau of Tibet. Snow covers the Himalayas, so they can look old. For mountains, they are actually quite young. That formation began twenty-five to thirty million years in the past. Two parts of Earth's crust collided. Over time, the two parts rubbed. Pressure made the ground crumble. The ground rose above the sea. Because the mountain is young, the peaks are still jagged. They are still steep. Endless years of weathering have not yet smoothed them. Beauty from a distance hides harsh conditions. The average temperature is about minus 36 degrees Celsius, or minus 33 degrees Fahrenheit. In January it can fall to minus 60 degrees Celsius, or minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit. July is the warmest month. Even then the temperature only reaches minus 19 degrees Celsius, or minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit. The air never rises above freezing. Glaciers therefore sit at the top. Permafrost sits there too. Height also means storms can arrive without warning. Temperatures then plummet. Every year, storms drop still more snow on the summit. Animals and plants struggle in those extreme conditions. Animal life on this mountain is rare. The wild yak is one of the few that manage it. High slopes offer only a little grass, and that grass is its food. Weight for this big mammal can pass 454 kilograms, or 1,000 pounds. Height can reach 1.8 meters, or 6 feet. Survival has a reason in the blood. Oxygen enters yak blood more readily than it enters the blood of other animals.

7That adaptation saves lives where the air holds little oxygen. Soft hair grows thick and close against the skin. A shaggy outer coat reaches almost to the ground. The two layers help the animal stay warm. A picture shows wild yak at graze. Early settlers in the Himalayas believed gods made homes in the peaks. They believed demons lived there too. They held the mountain sacred. They built monasteries at its base. Because of that belief, nobody tried to climb Mount Everest until outsiders arrived. British explorers came in the early 1900s. Other European explorers came too. The earliest climbers quickly learned how harsh the mountain is. Temperatures freeze. Winds are powerful. Weather changes. The terrain is rough. A picture shows the mountaineers Hillary and Norgay accepting awards for what they achieved. A legend clings to this mountain and to the Himalayas. People call it the yeti, said YEH-tee, or the Abominable Snowman. The long word is said a-BOM-in-a-bal. Sherpas tell of large footprints in the mountains. They tell of yak bones that look gnawed. Hillary's team carried a supposed yeti scalp to Europe. They carried skins to the United States as well. Scientists agreed the scalp came from a goat. The skins, they said, were bear skins. Proof of a living yeti is still missing. Climbers still came, both skilled and unskilled. Each hoped to be first to the top. Nobody succeeded until 1953. Sir Edmund Hillary was a beekeeper from New Zealand. Tenzing Norgay was a Sherpa from Nepal. Those two men were the first to climb the mountain successfully. It was Hillary's second try at the summit. Later climbers arrived from every part of the world. Reaching the top meant risking death. They still chase the peak called Forehead in the Sky. A map places the Great Barrier Reef along Australia. A diver in a picture moves among coral shapes on that reef. The reef is really more than three thousand reefs together. The stretch measures beyond 2,300 kilometers, or 1,429 miles.

8Queensland's coast is the line it follows. That coast lies in Australia's northeast. Sea life there is enchanting. Sea turtles live there. Sea slugs live there. Urchins live there. Dolphins, whales, and sharks live there. Birds and reptiles together include more than two hundred species on this reef system. Picture a reef as rocks lined up in a chain. A range is another way to see it. Those rocks lie at the water's surface or near it. This is the largest coral-reef system in the world. More than four hundred kinds of coral make it up. Coral polyps live and die, and that cycle builds reefs like this one. Coral reefs grow in every tropical ocean. None of the others is as large. Age for most coral reefs that are already established falls in a band from five thousand years up to ten thousand. Experts in large numbers share a date for the latest growth here. It began between six thousand and eight thousand years ago. The last ice age was close to finished then. A first glance may say the reef is rock. It is not. Millions of animals called polyps built it from their outer skeletons. Polyps are related to anemones. They are related to jellyfish. When polyps die, new polyps grow on the old skeletons. Many layers of skeletons become the limestone base of a reef. Other living things help too. Algae help. Sponges help. Shellfish help. Different kinds of algae supply the beautiful colors. The tiny polyp, though, builds most of the structure of this wonder. A reef is a living thing built from certain animals. It gives food to other animals. It gives them shelter. Ocean temperature changes bother reefs. Thousands of species live here. Fish alone number 1,625 kinds. Marine mammals number more than 30 kinds. Seaweed numbers 500 kinds. Marine turtles number 6 kinds. Breeding is another major use of this reef. Birds breed there. Sea turtles breed there. Several endangered species breed there. The humpback whale is one.

9The large green sea turtle is one. The dugong, or sea cow, is one. Scientists come because the reef is fascinating and beautiful. Scuba divers come. Tourists come. A World Heritage Site listing arrived in 1981. The listing came from UNESCO. UNESCO is part of the United Nations. Education is one focus. Science is another. So are cultures around the world. All of these groups now have environmentalists beside them. Protection is the goal. Later generations should still be able to study the reef and enjoy how beautiful it is. Many institutions are also doing research there. Universities are doing research there. They want to learn how to help protect it. Wonders do not stop at these five. From east to west, and from north to south, natural wonders appear. They appear in the highest places and in the lowest. Some formed millions of years ago. Some formed within one lifetime. Each one is unique. Earth has few sights that steal the breath the way these landforms do. Visits by travelers will continue. Scientists will keep visiting. People who seek adventure will keep visiting. Study is one reason. Recreation is another. The Grand Canyon is only one wonder among many. Paricutin is only one. Mount Everest is only one. Victoria Falls is only one. The Great Barrier Reef is only one. Other famous wonders include the Northern Lights, also called the aurora borealis. That light show brightens skies in the Northern Hemisphere. Arizona's desert holds Barringer Meteorite Crater, and the crater is a massive hole. It is almost a mile wide. It is 174 meters deep, or 570 feet. Ayers Rock is the world's largest solid rock. It rises 862.5 meters above sea level, or 2,830 feet, in Australia. Ha Long Bay lies in the Gulf of Tonkin, in Vietnam. Limestone islands fill that large bay. The count is higher than 1,600. Austria is home to Eisriesenwelt Cave, said ICE-reez-on-veldt. No ice cave anywhere is larger. It runs 42 kilometers, or 26 miles, inside a mountain.

10A few words help with these places. A cross section is a picture of the inside of something, as if a straight cut went all the way through. Iridescent describes shining colors that change when the light or the angle changes. Landforms are natural shapes on the face of Earth. Valleys count. So do plateaus, mountains, plains, and hills as well. The word dormant means quiet for now, yet able to wake and act again. A fissure is a long, narrow crack or opening. Monasteries are clusters of buildings. Monks live in them. Nuns live in them. Worship happens there too. A glacier is a huge body of piled ice together with packed snow. They last all year, and they creep downhill. In a cold region, permafrost is soil that never thaws. A plateau can be pictured as flat ground lifted high and spread wide. A gorge is a long deep valley wrapped by higher ground. A polyp is a small ocean animal without a backbone. Coral is one kind. They have tube-like bodies and mouths with tentacles. Sherpa names a people whose home culture lies in the Himalayas. Sherpas often guide mountain climbers. Stratigraphy is the way rock and earth layers are arranged in a geologic formation. Terrain is what the ground is like, its natural shape and surface. Living things that share a body plan and can have young together form a species. Topics in this book include Australia and the cinder cone. They include coral, erosion, and the Grand Canyon. They include the Great Barrier Reef, Havasu Falls, and the Havasupai. They include Sir Edmund Hillary and the Himalayas. They include David Livingstone and Mexico. They include Mount Everest and national parks. They include Native Americans, John Newberry, and Tenzing Norgay. They include Paricutin, the plateau, and the plunge pool. They include polyps, rattlesnakes, and reefs. They include Sherpas, Victoria Falls, and volcanoes. They include the yak, the yeti, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and the Zambezi River.

31. Four Mysteries, Fact or Trick

1A 1952 photograph, taken by someone who was not a professional, opens the book. Plenty of viewers believed the object was a spacecraft from another world. Was the picture genuine, or was it a fake? Four puzzles come next. One is a huge figure said to walk the woods. One is patterns flattened into farm crops. One is a curse tied to a royal burial. One is a patch of sea where vessels and aircraft disappear. You are asked to judge at the end. Difficult words are explained last. Imagine hearing that smelly, hairy giants live in wilderness. Imagine hearing that visitors from space lay complex drawings in fields of wheat. A friend might say people die because they disturbed a sacred grave and triggered an old curse. Someone else might say an Atlantic force makes planes and ships vanish. What test would show whether any of this is true? A picture of a young king's tomb asks if a curse guarded it. Evidence in these pages lets you call each tale genuine or a hoax. Acres of field carry designs so detailed that another picture asks who, or what, made them. Losses of ships and of planes remain hard to explain, and a further picture presses that question. Sightings of Bigfoot are marked on a map. The key says each mark equals one report. Oregon is labeled. So is Washington, inside the United States. Remote country in the Pacific Northwest has carried these accounts for hundreds of years. Native peoples there describe meetings with creatures that keep to themselves. The creatures are huge, look like apes, and walk on two feet. Salish communities in Canada used the name Sasquatch. It means a wild man who belongs to the woods.

2Lofa, Omah, and Shampe are names from other tribes. The shared idea is a being with a human shape, bigger than most humans. English speakers, from the 1950s onward, have mostly chosen the name Bigfoot. A 1967 photograph is Roger Patterson's. People still argue over it. A bear is one guess. A human inside a gorilla suit is another. A real Bigfoot is the third. Native storytellers are not the only witnesses. People who build railways have spoken up. So have people who work in forests. Hikers have spoken up, and travelers, and residents of lonely places. Alberta, Canada, holds a report dated 1811. That is as early as the written sightings go. Most reporters had never come across the older Native accounts. Nothing in those accounts had a chance to steer their words. Size is the first detail people give. A Bigfoot may stand 8 feet high, which is 2.4 meters. Hair lies in tangles over the whole body. Prints left behind are huge. They run longer than 14 inches, or 35.5 centimeters. They press 3 inches into the ground, or 7.6 centimeters. Estimates of weight, drawn from that length and that depth, fall between 350 and 800 pounds. The metric range is 160 to 360 kilograms. A scream at a high pitch is what witnesses usually hear. A foul smell is what they usually notice. Animals that might be real and might be imaginary are the subject of cryptozoology. Those researchers, along with other curious people, have poured time into the search. They have poured money into it too. Websites exist to log sightings and to check them. Follow-up has covered thousands of eyewitness accounts. Proof is still missing. Heights on a chart put a grizzly at 9 feet, or 2.74 meters.

3The Bigfoot mark sits at 8 feet, or 2.44 meters. A human mark sits at 6 feet, or 1.83 meters. Further marks show 4 feet, or 1.22 meters, and 2 feet, or 0.61 meters. On that chart, Bigfoot comes out shorter than the bear and taller than a typical person. Dr. John Bindernagel, in 1998, examined a pit set among very large rocks. A nest, he thought, had been made there by a Bigfoot. Albert Ostman was a lumberjack. The year 1924 found him alone in the mountains, looking for gold. A construction job had kept him busy for over a year. His plan was a vacation lasting three weeks. Night number three brought a kidnapping. He was still in his sleeping bag. The thing that took him was huge, and it stank. Hours passed. He was dropped in a clearing. Hairy creatures, huge and apelike, stood around him. There were four. The group looked like parents plus two children. Nearly a week passed before he escaped. Shock was severe. Injury was not. Other reports exist. Some of those meetings included violence. Northwestern forests and glaciers hold few people. A dead body does not last. Decay takes it. Insects take it. Scavengers take it. One belief says Bigfoot slips between dimensions and stays in ours only briefly, which is why no corpse has turned up. Science expects something else. A real animal should leave a corpse, or bones, or fossils, for someone to find. None of those remains has ever appeared. Northern Washington, in 1977, produced a sighting that was planned as a trick. Three young men were behind it. Gorilla suits were their costume. Walkie-talkies were their tool. After that exposure, some listeners assume further reports were staged as well.

4On some websites, the share of sightings confirmed as hoaxes is said to reach 80 percent. You are asked to choose. A man's foot looks small in one picture next to a cast taken from a much bigger print. Circles in crops are the next puzzle, and many of them are enormous. Stonehenge once had a design of 149 circles. It showed up in daylight, and the whole event took 20 minutes. Tall crops with flattened circles inside them were noted as far back as the year 1590. Most examples sit in England. A further twenty-nine countries have them. Wind was the farmers' old explanation. Counts jumped sharply in the 1980s, and the jump was worldwide. Circles that began as simple shapes became complex pictures. Math ideas appear in them. Fractals are part of that math. Forming usually happens at night, and the process stays unexplained. Spaceships are what a few witnesses say they saw. Whirlwinds are the other claim. A full moon is almost always overhead when those claims are made. Sky lights sometimes appear. A hum may join them, or something like music. Inside the circles, radiation is sometimes measured. Crushing is not what happens to the plants. The bend sits at the stalk's lowest node. Growth inside the circle is often stronger than growth in plants that were never bent. Soil inside shows changes, both chemical and physical, and research ties those changes to the better growth. Lab work hints that microwave beams of high power could push crops down in this pattern. Nobody has shown where the beams would start, or who would aim them. A message from extraterrestrials is the reading some people prefer. Stonehenge stands in Wiltshire, England, and that county is full of circles.

5Overnight watchers there say a detailed pattern can finish in only a few minutes. A picture shows stalks bent so they form a spiral. People create a large share of the designs, and their motives differ. Ropes, long planks, and barrels can press plants down to one matched height. The goal for some is only to show that human hands can do it. A trick or a hoax is the goal for others. Artists of these fields say a divine spark gives them the design. Doug Bower and David Chorley, both from England, spoke in 1991. Their claim was bold. Every circle from 1978 on, they said, was their work. They had wanted to watch the public react to odd shapes. A giant hoax was enough of an answer for some hearers. Others could not believe two men could lay out patterns that large and that complex, at night, and stay unseen. Doug later withdrew what he had admitted. Seven years had passed. Unknown forces, he declared, were the real makers. He demonstrates a field method in one picture. The caption adds that faking the design takes heavy labor. Tornado damage and a crop circle do not look alike, and a diagram sets the two paths side by side. A tornado spreads across a broad stretch and leaves a messy pattern. A crop circle looks planned, and the detail is fine. Weather is still offered as a cause. The tidy shapes make that offer weak. A second weather idea names a plasma vortex, a whirlwind that carries electric charge. Microwaves from it, the theory says, heat the water in a plant so quickly that the plant falls. Witnesses who report odd lights, or a hum, could be hearing and seeing that vortex.

6It might stay hovering. It might travel as though someone were steering it from far away, which would make it resemble a UFO. A weapons idea has also been raised. Researchers suggest that militaries in Britain and in the United States are building a weapon of very high energy. Focused microwave radiation would be what it sends out. Test shots of that secret weapon, in this account, are what flatten the crops. Again the question is yours. Real event, or hoax? Treasures of great value filled the Egyptian tomb of King Tut, and a picture shows that wealth. Discovery day was November 4, 1922. The pharaoh was Tutankhamun. Today most people say King Tut. Howard Carter found the tomb. Workers from Egypt, hired locally, helped. London papers, including the Daily Mail, started a curse story. A wall, they wrote, carried a painted threat. Enter the sacred tomb, it warned, and death's wings would arrive quickly. Papers elsewhere copied the tale and spread it worldwide. Pharaohs, early Egyptians believed, had cobras as protectors. On the opening day, a cobra ate the canary Carter kept. A bad omen is how many readers took it. Onlookers, curious, watch him open a tomb door in a 1922 picture. Money for the search came from George E. S. M. Herbert. He was the fifth Earl of Carnarvon. Death came in Cairo in 1923. A mosquito bite had become infected. Curse of a pharaoh, the papers said, was what killed Lord Carnarvon. His dog in England, they added, howled and fell dead at that same minute. Cairo's lights, they added, all flickered. Subscriptions rose on sensational copy, and the papers knew it. Twenty-six people linked to the find, they reported, died during the first ten years.

7Suspicion hung over many of those deaths. The mystery has themed movies. It has themed books and games. Excitement sometimes mattered more than truth. In the early years of the 1900s, a reporter might invent a detail to spice a story. Illness had already gripped Lord Carnarvon for twenty years when the infected bite ended his life. Coincidence could explain the date. A lower death count comes from research. Six people connected with the find died during those first ten years, not twenty-six. Long lives were common among the workers. Carter's own work on the tomb lasted a minimum of ten years. Seventeen further years of life followed the discovery. He would not accept a curse. Tommy rot was the phrase he used. Words said to be painted inside were never on the walls. Carter walks beside Lord Carnarvon in one picture. The earl had funded the hunt in Egypt. That ground is known as the Valley of the Kings. Biology is the explanation some people prefer, a rational one. Decay in a body can grow molds. It can grow bacteria. Illness and death can follow. Did that process help cause Carnarvon's death? Gloves of rubber, plus special clothes, protect archaeologists now. Earlier diggers, and people who stole from tombs, may have fallen ill without that protection. A curse story could have grown from those illnesses. Burial of a king was a huge effort in ancient Egypt. Riches were supposed to travel with him into the next life. Danger legends may have been invented so robbers would stay away. Real curse, or hoax? The book leaves the choice open. Tall pyramids of stone in the desert are where the picture shows pharaohs buried.

8Canada, the United States, Mexico, and Puerto Rico share a map with Bermuda, the Bahamas, Miami, and San Juan. Strange Atlantic reports are sometimes drawn on a wider map than this one. The reports are sporadic, and they reach as far back as 1780. Three points frame the famous zone: Miami in Florida, the island of Bermuda, and San Juan in Puerto Rico. Vincent Gaddis, in 1965, wrote about the events in a book titled Invisible Horizons. Naming rights for Bermuda Triangle belong to him. Triangle of Death was his other label. Devil's Triangle was a third. Aircraft and vessels go missing there in numbers, and no trace remains. Fair weather does not prevent it. A simple reason is hard to give. A crew can vanish and leave the mystery intact. Fog can turn dense, then clear, with little warning. A compass can fail. So can the rest of the navigation gear. Flight 19 was a training flight for the U.S. Navy. The day in 1945 looked clear. Five bombers of the Avenger type lost their sense of direction. They were trying to stay out of weather that was turning worse. An airship sent to rescue them vanished too. Ellen Austin, a merchant ship, was bound from London to New York in 1881. A ship with nobody aboard was found floating. Nothing suggested a fight had happened. Men from the Austin boarded, aiming to sail the empty vessel onward to New York. Fog thickened around both ships in a squall. By morning, contact had been gone all night. The empty ship was located again. Its second crew had vanished as well. Bringing a deserted ship into port could win the crew a reward. The USS Cyclops is an early case linked to this triangle.

9March 1918 was the month. The route was Barbados toward Baltimore, in Maryland. People aboard numbered 306. A picture shows the ship. Captain Donald Henry, in 1966, commanded a tug named the Good News. A cargo barge was under tow. Puerto Rico was the start. Fort Lauderdale, in Florida, was the goal. Clarity marked the day. Fog then thickened fast around the barge. Instruments on the tug all quit. Part of the power quit too. Five minutes felt like a pulling contest against the fog. The tug finally dragged itself out, barge included. Water inside the fog seemed to bubble and turn choppy. Water outside stayed calm. A hidden power, some people insist, lies behind the lost ships and the lost crews. White lights, strange ones, stood on the horizon when Christopher Columbus looked. His compass went wrong. Lights of that odd kind lead some thinkers to UFOs that seize people and leave with them. Weather is the rival explanation, the hard weather natural to these waters. A hurricane can rise without warning. A violent waterspout can rise too. Tidal waves are ordinary here. Violent shifts in the air are a known effect of the Gulf Stream, and that current runs through the Triangle. Wreckage would be carried off. No trace would remain. Crews found later sometimes say a storm ruined the ship and forced them off it. A calmer view says the region is simply busy. Few stretches of ocean carry more traffic, so odd accidents pile up. Distance is another correction. Some losses pinned on the Triangle took place hundreds of miles from it. Ships once listed as lost have reappeared. A few of the lost ships were never real.

10Storytellers had invented them. Real zone of danger, or hoax? You decide. A ship in this huge ocean can be wiped out fast by violent weather, and the sea can keep every clue. Rapa Nui, known also as Easter Island, leaves a question about its moai. Who carved those statues, and who moved them? Stonehenge leaves a question about purpose and about method. Mysteries, meaning events we cannot yet understand, are not going away. Nonsense is what some listeners will hear. Reality is what others will claim. Trust is higher for some sources than for others. A claim still needs evidence first, ordinary claims and extraordinary ones alike. Four cases now sit beside part of the evidence. Weigh it, and decide what you believe. More puzzles wait if you want to research them. Words in this book can be read as follows. A conundrum is a riddle or a situation that confuses. To decompose is to rot or to fall apart into small pieces. A fractal repeats a curve or a geometric shape many times, changing the size while the proportions stay alike. A hoax is built to trick or to mislead. Intricate work is complex and full of detail. Microwave names a wave of electromagnetic energy. Radio waves are longer. Infrared radiation is shorter. Radar and heating often rely on it. A node is the spot on a stem that sends out a leaf or a branch. Pharaoh was the title of an ancient Egyptian ruler. Plasma is a gas of charged particles, able to carry electricity. A reclusive person stays apart and solitary. To have retracted a statement is to have withdrawn it. Sporadic events come at odd intervals, not on a steady beat.

32. From a Loose League to One Nation

1A picture shows the Liberty Bell. Delegates put their names on the Declaration of Independence. The year was 1776. North America was home to the colonies they represented. There were thirteen of them, and Britain ruled them. They announced that they were free. They announced that Great Britain no longer ruled them. At the same moment they called themselves a confederation. The states were joined for one shared cause. The new union took the name the United States of America. A working government had to be designed. Delegates of those original colonies, now called states, started shaping a plan. The plan was for a central government that could actually work. Five years passed before the plan sat firmly in place. The war against Great Britain was still going, and that delay explains the wait. Feeling truly united took much longer. Another forty years had to pass. Another war with Great Britain had to be fought. A note belongs with this opening. The original thirteen states pushed Indigenous peoples off ancestral lands. Westward expansion in the 1800s repeated that pattern. Native peoples resisted European colonization with diplomacy. They also resisted with warfare. Widespread epidemics badly hampered those efforts. The diseases had arrived with Europeans. The year was 1777. Each state had appointed delegates to the Second Continental Congress. Those delegates agreed to send a new plan of government out for review. Every state would see it. The plan could work only if all thirteen states ratified it. The document was the Articles of Confederation. A nation is not the word the document used for the United States. It described a firm league of friendship. Thirteen sovereign states shared that league. The federal government in the plan was weak. State governments were strong. States liked the authority they kept. They liked the freedom too. Each state wrote its own constitution. Each state printed its own money. A map places many Indigenous peoples around those first states. The names include Algonquins, Abenaki, Ottawas, and Chippewas. They include Iroquois, Hurons, Illinois, and Miamis. They include Pottawatomies, Delaware, Powhatan, and Shawnee. The Mississippi River is marked. Farther south the map names Cherokee, Chickasaws, Creek, Choctaws, and Seminole.

2Founding of the original thirteen states happened on ground those peoples already occupied. The states also bordered that ground. Under the Articles, the federal government received no authority. It could not act on its own. No single leader spoke for the union. War had left the United States in debt. Congress was the only federal branch the Articles created. That Congress could not tax people. Revenue to pay the debts required a tax, and Congress had none. Only the states could tax their own citizens. The missing power to tax became one fatal flaw. A second flaw was the empty executive chair. Nobody held sole command. Congress did elect a president, but only to watch over its meetings. That president could not make decisions. Congress also could not repair the Articles when something failed. Nine states out of thirteen had to agree before a change was legal. The states did approve the plan. Several years passed after that approval before the flaws grew obvious. Nearly five years passed before all thirteen states settled their differences and approved the Articles. Maryland ratified last. Major fighting in the Revolutionary War came to a stop. The year was 1781. U.S. General George Washington beat British General Charles Cornwallis. The place was Yorktown, in Virginia. Official peace still waited two more years. Representatives of the United States and of Great Britain talked in Paris, France. The talks began in the middle of 1782. They ended when the Treaty of Paris was signed. People also call that treaty the Peace of Paris. The date was September 3, 1783. Only then was the war officially finished. The treaty set down two important ideas. The first idea named the United States a sovereign country. Independence from Great Britain was part of that recognition. Second, it drew the country's borders. One edge was the Atlantic Ocean. The opposite edge, to the west, was the Mississippi River. New Orleans was an exception. The Floridas were an exception. Spain controlled both. The northern line followed the Great Lakes. It also followed the borders of Quebec and of Nova Scotia. Both of those places were part of Canada, and Britain controlled Canada.

3A map of the settlement shows British-controlled Canada. Some ground on the map is marked as a claim of Great Britain and of Spain together. It shows the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. U.S. states and territories appear on it. New Spain appears. So do New Orleans and the Atlantic Ocean. A wider story sits behind that map. Desire for wealth drove much of Europe's colonization of North America. Routes that carried trade from Europe to Asia broke down badly. The century was the 1500s. Ottoman Turks were battling various groups. Profitable trade was lost. Many European powers then looked for new sea routes west, hoping to reach Asia. Between 1565 and 1625, four countries planted colonies in North America. Spain was one of those colonizers. Britain was another. France was another. The Netherlands was another. Land was divided by the treaty of 1783. The United States received a share. Great Britain received a share. It paid no attention to the rights of Indigenous peoples. Those peoples had lived on the land since before recorded history. Fighting in the Revolutionary War had finished. The treaty had been signed. Severe money trouble came next. Soldiers went home poor. They went home exhausted. Money was missing from the government. Power to tax was missing too. Pay for service never reached many of those veterans. An even larger money problem loomed. The nation had borrowed to fight the war. The sum was more than $76 million. Lenders included foreign countries. They included individual Americans. They included state banks. In Massachusetts, money trouble sparked a rebellion. Independence had been their fight. Some of those farmers still lost their farms. Some were jailed because debts went unpaid. In 1786 Daniel Shays acted. He had been a captain in the Revolutionary War. Farmers joined him. Other workers joined him. The crowd numbered about a thousand. They marched on Springfield, in Massachusetts. They then went on toward Boston. The U.S. Army met them there. Guns were fired on both sides. Trials followed for some workers. The sentence for those workers was hanging.

4Others received no punishment. Shays' Rebellion stirred similar conflicts. Connecticut saw them. New York saw them. Pennsylvania saw them. Many citizens and leaders drew a lesson. Handling trouble like this, many concluded, required a federal government with more strength. To face the country's many problems, fifty-five men came to Philadelphia. The month was May 1787. The building was Independence Hall. At first they meant only to modify the Articles. A stronger federal government was the aim. They did not stop at expanding the old plan. They agreed to draft a constitution. An executive would lead the union under the new document. It would let Congress tax. It would include a way to amend the rules. A picture shows Independence Hall. Twelve states sent delegates. Rhode Island was the one that declined. Every delegate was an influential leader at home. The men most involved in building the union are sometimes called the founders. All of them were wealthy. All of them were educated. All of them were white men. That fact reflected the voting rules of the time. In most states, only white men who owned property could vote. The delegates chose George Washington to preside. People remember the meeting by a name. It is the Constitutional Convention. It lasted several weeks. Arguments about changing the Articles grew hot. Two questions of power caused the heat. The first question was representation. Under the Articles, every state had one vote. Population did not matter. Some delegates called that unfair. More seats in Congress would mean more power. Two plans were offered. One gave seats according to population. States with more people would get more representatives. The other plan gave every state the same representation. Population would not count. The second question was slavery. Black people taken from Africa were held as enslaved people. So were their descendants. They were treated as property. Freedom was denied to them. Force kept them in that life. Conditions were often terrible. They were forced to work, and they were not paid. Keeping slavery as an institution mattered to the Southern states. Counting enslaved people for representation was another Southern goal. Enslaved people had no rights.

5They could not vote. Southern delegates still believed the count would help. Their states would stand closer to equal with Northern states. Northern states had larger populations. A compromise covered both questions. Congress would have two houses. The upper house was the Senate. Each state would send two senators, so representation there was equal. The lower house was the House of Representatives. Seats there would follow population. On slavery, Congress was barred from any change to the institution for twenty years. Delegates also agreed to a fraction. The count used a fraction. One enslaved person equaled three-fifths of a person. That fraction decided how many representatives a state received. George Washington, like many founders, profited from enslaved labor. That labor happened on his estate. Delegates also argued about the president's power. They built a system called checks and balances. A power given to one branch would be matched by equal power in the other two. Three branches were proposed. The legislative branch would hold two houses of Congress. The executive branch would hold a president. The judicial branch would hold courts. Those courts would enforce the laws. The document itself explains how a later change, an amendment, can be made. On September 17, 1787, delegates signed. Thirty-nine of them put down their names. States received the Constitution next. They would vote on it. People everywhere argued about whether the plan was a good one. Support came from a group. People called that group the Federalists. Their work was winning a yes from the states. That yes is called ratification. They believed a large republic could protect the rights of individuals better. Another group, the Antifederalists, attacked the plan. They thought states would lose influence. They thought states would lose power. They did not want this plan to stand as the country's law. The Antifederalists wanted a list of citizens' unalienable rights. Government would never be allowed to take those rights away. In time, all thirteen states voted yes. The deal between the two groups added ten amendments. Together those amendments are the Bill of Rights. They guarantee freedom of speech. They guarantee freedom to practice religion.

6They guarantee freedom from a state religion. Other rights are listed too. A picture and a note remember Abigail Adams. She was an early supporter of women's rights in America. Another note looks at who could vote. In the first presidential election, in 1789, the vote in most states belonged only to white men who owned land. Since the Civil War, amendments have widened that right more than once. The vote has been extended to people of all ethnicities. It has been extended to women. It has been extended to any citizen older than eighteen. Many people still argue that voting-rights laws discriminate. They say the harm falls unfairly on people of color. In their view the harm is still serious. Even now, the harm appears across a wide stretch of the country. George Washington became president once the new Constitution was in force. The Electoral College chose him in a unanimous vote. April 30, 1789, was the day he took office. A great leader is what many people believed him to be. He served two terms. Each term lasted four years. His years as president were 1789 to 1797. During the first term he named Alexander Hamilton secretary of the treasury. Hamilton offered a plan for the nation's money troubles. One part was a policy that taxed imports. Another part created the first national bank. Faith in the government seemed to return because of the plan. The national debt was paid down. Economic growth picked up as a result. After Washington's second term, John Adams won the election of 1796. Adams served as president from 1797 to 1801. Thomas Jefferson came next. He took office in 1801 and served until 1809. Another problem waited. The Treaty of Paris had granted extra land after the Revolutionary War. What should the country do with it? Lands farther west were claimed by state governments. Indigenous peoples had lived there since before recorded history. A single area sometimes had several states claiming it together. The Land Ordinance of 1785 explained how to divide the property. The pieces were townships and sections. Sections would be sold to settlers.

7Some sections were kept for the government. Some were kept for public schools. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson, a Virginia delegate, designed the Northwest Ordinance. It gave rules for making states in the Northwest Territory. In the end it would create six new states. Slavery would be illegal inside those new states. Growth of a certain kind was what the ordinance promised. The United States would expand by adding states. It would not expand by planting colonies the way Britain had. Together, the two ordinances prepared a huge move. Settlers would head west in great numbers in the early 1800s. Government projects supported that growth. New roads were built. Canals were built. Railroads were built. The country seemed able to keep up with how fast it was spreading. Debts were being paid. Power in the new government had been divided, and that division was set. The grim mood that followed the war had lifted. Leaders then made larger plans. The story of those plans is the Louisiana Purchase. France and Spain signed a treaty. The year was 1800. The new French land had the Mississippi River as its eastern edge. The Rocky Mountains formed the western edge. The port of New Orleans came with it. Westerners in the United States lost a route. They could not use the Mississippi. They could not use New Orleans. Both had carried their crop shipments for trade. Napoleon Bonaparte was the person the United States approached. He was France's emperor. The hope was to buy New Orleans. A picture shows Tecumseh. He led the Shawnee people. They fought American settlers who were moving into the Northwest Territory. Many Indigenous peoples had their homeland in that territory. Bonaparte had suffered major setbacks. A war in Europe was going badly for him. He needed troops. He needed money. To pay for the war, he surprised the American representatives. He offered more than New Orleans. He offered the entire Louisiana Territory. The price was $15 million. France named a price. The United States paid it. The month was October, and the year was 1803. Overnight, the nation was twice as large. It added 800,000 square miles.

8That is 2.07 million square kilometers. It also added 200,000 new citizens. Indigenous nations living on the land did not agree to give it up. Nobody even asked them. A map shows the Louisiana Territory beside the older United States and beside New Spain. The purchase nearly doubled the country's land area. It also pushed settlement farther west. In many cases that push destroyed Indigenous peoples or drove them from their homes. An exploring party left on Jefferson's orders. He was president. The month was May, and the year was 1804. Two army officers led it. One was Meriwether Lewis. The other was William Clark. A group of 45 people went with them. Their jobs were clear. A water route from one side of the continent to the other was one task. They were to map it. They were to explore the Louisiana Territory. They were to report back. Sacagawea traveled with them. She was a Lemhi Shoshone girl. She worked as an interpreter. Success for the expedition depended on her. That fact became clear as they traveled. The journey lasted more than two years. The group came home with journals. They came home with drawings. Hundreds of plant samples came home with them. Animal samples came home too. The trip laid groundwork for taking land in the West. Indigenous peoples already lived there. The impact on them was severe. A picture shows Lewis and Clark's group moving through the Louisiana Territory. During those same years, an old ally was at war. France fought Great Britain in a raging struggle over who would dominate Europe. Neutrality for the United States was Jefferson's aim while he was president. He wanted the country out of that war. The presidency passed to James Madison. The year was 1808. He hoped for the same neutrality. Neutrality did not hold. British ships began seizing U.S. ships. French ships did too. They searched the ships. The aim was to stop supplies from reaching their enemies. Britain also seized sailors who had been born British and were now American. Those sailors were forced to serve Britain. Citizens of the United States had won independence from Great Britain.

9Tyranny from that country had returned. Madison sent a warning in 1812, during his presidency. Britain must stop searching U.S. ships. Britain must stop seizing them. Otherwise there would be war. The reply did not satisfy him. He declared war on June 18, 1812. The United States had no navy fit to fight Great Britain at sea. An invasion aimed at conquering British-controlled Canada failed. Facing that powerful nation again was beyond what the army could do. War then continued for two years plus half a year. Both countries' agreement is the heart of the Treaty of Ghent. The day was December 24, in the year 1814. They agreed to end the war. A picture shows a sea fight on August 19, 1812. Victory in the picture goes to a U.S. ship named Constitution. The beaten ship is the British Guerriere. One more battle still followed, even though peace was official. On January 8, 1815, Americans won a decisive fight. It was the Battle of New Orleans. General Andrew Jackson led them. He did not know a peace treaty had already been signed. British dead in that battle came to almost three hundred. The loss ranks among the worst defeats Britain suffered. Fewer than twenty men died on the U.S. side. The win sent a clear message. The western part of the country was truly under the United States, not under Great Britain. A winning feeling spread among citizens. They believed the War of 1812 had gone their way. The honest result is different. Victory belonged to neither country. Perhaps the most important result was a feeling. Because the win came late, the United States of America finally felt like one nation. A timeline gathers the larger story. From 1754 to 1763 came the French and Indian War, also called the Seven Years' War. From 1764 to 1765 came the Sugar Act, the Quartering Act, and the Stamp Act. The year 1767 brought the Townshend Acts. The year 1770 brought the Boston Massacre. The year 1774 brought the Coercive Acts, also called the Intolerable Acts, and the First Continental Congress.

10The year 1775 started the Revolutionary War and brought the Second Continental Congress. July 4, 1776, was the day the Declaration of Independence was signed. The year 1781 ended the Revolutionary War, and all thirteen states approved the Articles of Confederation. The year 1786 brought Shays' Rebellion. The year 1787 brought the Constitutional Convention. The year 1791 saw every state ratify the Constitution, and it saw the Bill of Rights ratified. The year 1812 opened another war with Britain. The year 1814 brought the Treaty of Ghent, which ended the War of 1812. These words belong with the story of the new government. Amend means to make a change that improves something. Authority is the power to govern, to give orders, or to decide, and it can also mean the people who hold that power. Checks and balances divide power. Each branch of government holds some. No one branch is supposed to dominate. A compromise is a decision in an argument where each side gives something up in order to agree. A constitution is the basic set of laws that tells how a state or a nation is run. When people or groups discuss a question they do not agree on, that talk is a debate. The executive branch is the one that leads. It also carries out the laws. Incurred means brought upon oneself, especially a negative or unwanted result. The judicial branch tests laws against the constitution. Lawmaking belongs to the legislative branch. Prosperity can mean success. It can mean wealth. It can mean good fortune. Official approval is what ratified means. Fighting authority, or fighting power, is what a rebellion means. A representative is chosen to stand in for others. Speaking can be the job. Voting can be the job. Acting for a group can be the job. Citizens elect the leaders in a republic. They elect the representatives too. Revenue is money received from selling something, from taxing it, or from investments, goods, or services. Sovereign means independent and able to govern itself.
