They also hold millions of viewers to their televisions in football season. The game is spectacular. Its competitors are fierce. Its fans are devoted. Inside the United States, this sport sits at the top. It has held that place for about thirty years.

2Pro games draw huge interest. College games do too. The National Football League runs the pro game. The short name is NFL. A typical game draws around seventy thousand people. The playoff weeks lead to the Super Bowl. That championship is among the biggest sports events on Earth. College play is governed by the NCAA. Those letters stand for National Collegiate Athletic Association. In the United States, college football ranks third in popularity. The NFL is ahead of it. Major League Baseball is ahead of it too. Most women who play do so as amateurs or as semipros. Fewer young people are taking up the sport. For children younger than fourteen, many adults judge the contact too hard. A photo shows the Denver Broncos against the St. Louis Rams. The crowd at Mile High Stadium has no empty seats. A map marks IFAF nations across six land areas. The long name is International Federation of American Football. Those areas are North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, South America, and Australia. The map also shows the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, and the equator. The short name of that federation is IFAF. Many countries play the American game. It is not yet as global as some other sports.

3Interest is still growing. Membership in IFAF tops seventy nations. Those nations sit on six continents. Canada has had its own form of the game since the late 1800s. Canadian play is similar. The field size differs. The number of players differs. Some rules differ. Most people picture an outdoor field. Indoor play is possible too. The 1980s brought an indoor version named arena football. Its rules fit a smaller field. The result is a faster game. A field diagram gives the main measures. College posts and pro posts measure 18.5 feet from side to side. That width is 5.6 meters. The goalpost is 10 feet tall. That height is 3 meters. A score can come from a kick that clears the bar while staying inside the uprights. Depth of the scoring area is 10 yards. That depth is 9.1 meters. A touchdown requires the ball to be carried into that area. A pass that is caught there also counts. One marked distance on the diagram is 160 feet, or 48.8 meters. Another is 360 feet, or 109.7 meters. Hash marks appear at each yard. Markers appear every 5 yards. The 50-yard line marks the middle. It sits 50 yards from either end zone. That distance is 45.7 meters. An arrow on the 10-yard line points toward the nearer end zone.

4Markers also show an end line, and they show a goal line. The sideline borders the field. People nickname the sport the gridiron. Yard lines plus hash marks make a grid, and that grid earned the nickname. In a game, two teams try to move the ball toward the other end zone. They try to get it in, which scores a touchdown. One method is to run with the ball. The second method is a throw toward a teammate nearer the scoring area. A completed pass means the teammate catches it. After the catch, a further advance is allowed. An interception means an opponent catches the throw. The catching team then owns the ball. An incomplete pass stops play. Nobody caught it, and it fell to the ground. Attackers form a line that is also called a platoon. That group's job is to score. A defensive platoon tries to stop the other team from scoring. A 2014 photo shows a New Mexico running back diving for the end zone. The opponent is Arizona State. Early balls were probably oval rugby balls. An inflated pig bladder sat inside a casing of pig hide. Those balls were hard to throw. Later the bladder was dropped.

5The shape was made smoother. Today's balls are cowhide. Some people still call them pigskins. At any moment, each club has just one platoon on the grass. Which platoon depends on who controls the ball. Each platoon has eleven players. Six points is the value of a touchdown. The offense usually scores it by running the ball into the other end zone. A pass into that end zone can score it too. A touchdown is not limited to the offense. One way is to recover a fumble. A fumble is a ball an opponent loses control of. Another way is to intercept and reach the other end zone. After a touchdown, a kick through the goalposts adds one point. A run or a pass into the end zone adds two points. A field goal is worth three points. It is a kick between the goalposts. If tacklers down the ball carrier inside the carrier's own scoring area, the play is a safety. The defense then receives two points. A 2014 photo shows Team Germany, which has the ball. Their stance faces Team Sweden along the scrimmage line. The game is in Austria. Play starts with a kickoff to the offense. That team advances in stages. Each stage must be at least 10 yards.

6That distance is 9.1 meters. The offense has four chances, called downs. Those chances must produce the needed 10 yards, or a score past the goal line. If it gains at least 10 yards inside the four downs, it keeps the ball. It earns a new first down. It may then try for another 10 yards. Every play starts at the line of scrimmage. That line is imaginary. It crosses the field. Its place comes from where the last play ended. Penalty yards, if any were given, also move it. Teams use many specialized plays. A play is a plan for moving the ball. If the offense cannot gain 10 yards in four downs, it gives the ball up. Defense uses two main plans to stop a score. Bringing down the runner is a defender's aim. They also try to force fumbles and interceptions so they can take the ball. A tackle is complete when one knee touches the ground. It is also complete when both knees touch. That contact ends the play. Running out of bounds ends the play too. In pro games, true playing time is sixty minutes. College games use the same sixty minutes. That clock divides into four quarters, and those quarters make two halves. High school games are shorter.

7They last forty-eight minutes. A tie at the end of sixty minutes adds overtime. That extra period is fifteen minutes. A full game usually lasts about three hours. The extra time comes from stoppages. A player may go out of bounds. A penalty may be called. A pass may fall incomplete. Players wear a helmet and a chin strap. They wear shoulder pads, a jersey, and gloves. They wear hip pads, pants, and thigh pads. They wear socks, knee pads, and shoes called cleats. Pads under the uniform help prevent injury. A diagram places both platoons at the line of scrimmage. On defense the marks are S for safety, CB for cornerback, and LB for linebacker. DT means defensive tackle. DE means defensive end. On offense, C means center and G means guard. T means tackle. TE means tight end. WR means wide receiver. QB means quarterback. RB means running back. Jobs on the field are specialized. The quarterback leads the offense. In the huddle, that player calls the play. From his spot, the center shoves the ball back through his own legs. The ball goes to the quarterback. That move is the snap. It is also called hiking the ball. The quarterback may then run. The quarterback may pass.

8The quarterback may hand the ball off. The same diagram shows where attackers and defenders stand. A referee watches the rules. Six other officials watch with the referee. Birth of the sport came late in the nineteenth century. Several universities in North America played it. It grew out of two English games. One was soccer, also called association football. The other was rugby, short for rugby football. Rugby is somewhat like soccer. Rugby uses the hands as well as the feet. Two universities in New Jersey played a game like soccer. Princeton was one of them, under the older name College of New Jersey. The other was Rutgers. Other universities in the Northeast began to play that game too. Harvard University preferred a style closer to rugby. Yale University picked up that style, and other schools followed. Walter Camp studied at Yale from 1876 to 1881. People call him the Father of American Football. He was Yale's captain. Inside the Intercollegiate Football Association, he held an important place. He pushed for rule changes. Those changes turned the old game into the American game played now. At first, the same players handled both attack and defense. Separate units for attack and defense arrived in the 1940s. It later became the usual way.

9A picture shows Walter Camp. Jerry Rice is the best wide receiver the sport has known. He played twenty seasons, starting in 1985. He won three Super Bowls with the San Francisco 49ers. NFL marks under his name number nearly forty. Joe Montana may be the most gifted quarterback the sport has had. His NFL career began in 1979 with the 49ers. Jerry Rice joined that team in 1985. Together they made the 49ers a dominant NFL force for several years. Four Super Bowl titles for the 49ers came with Montana leading. He retired after the 1994 season. He left with many playoff records. Walter Payton was a running back for the Chicago Bears. He played thirteen seasons, beginning in 1975. All-star selection for the Pro Bowl came his way nine times. He helped his team win the Super Bowl in 1986. For a time he held the NFL record for career touchdowns. He held the record for rushing yards. He held records in many other categories too. Students can play in several ways. Towns and schools often run youth leagues. Those leagues use tackle football. Touch football is another form. Flag football is another form. Those two forms are less rough than tackle. Many lovers of the sport would rather watch.

10Fans show their love in many ways. Some wrap up warm and sit through temperatures below freezing. Others wear wild clothes. Others paint their faces in team colors. Some wear gear that matches a team theme. A cowboy hat fits the Dallas Cowboys. A yellow beak and a feathery red crest fit the Arizona Cardinals. A fan can find great fun in this beloved American sport. A player can find great fun too. There is plenty of excitement for everyone. A photo shows fans proving their loyalty to a favorite team. Words to know. Advocated means supported or recommended. Amateur means not professional, and done as a hobby. Dominates means keeps strong power over something or someone. The end zone is the area past the goal line and before the end line. Blockers up front clear a path, and that help lets the runner score. A platoon is a group of teammates who share one job, such as attack or defense. Possession means control or ownership. Specialized means built to do one particular task. Spectators are people who watch and do not take part. Strategies are thought-out plans for a problem or a goal. Ultimate means the best or the greatest, or the thing that comes at the end. Vying means competing.

39. Helping Wild Animals Heal

1This book walks through wildlife rescue in order. An introduction opens it. Wildlife rehabilitators come next. Rescue comes after that. Rehabilitation follows. Release follows rehabilitation. Disaster rescue has its own part. A closing, a word list, and a topic list finish the book. A header names the Tucson Wildlife Center. A wild animal in trouble is a reason to tell an adult immediately. If no trusted adult is near, a phone book can help. Look under the words Wildlife Rescue. Look under the words Animal Rescue too. A baby bird may hop on the ground with no parent in sight. You might wonder what to do if that bird seems orphaned. You might find a rabbit that cannot seem to hop. You might see a raccoon that wobbles and sways as it walks. Many people are unsure which actions help. They are also unsure which actions harm. People with special training know the right response. The raccoon is one animal they know should be left alone. A raccoon that walks that way is probably sick. They know whether the rabbit can be helped. They know whether that rabbit can go back to the wild. They can judge a baby bird and decide what care, if any, it needs. They can also teach other people how to help. One picture shows Topsy. Topsy is a female great horned owl. She is three months old. A windstorm blew her from the nest. Rescuers took her in after the fall. Neck injuries are healing. Back injuries are healing too. Wildlife rehabilitators are the people who give aid when wildlife is sick, hurt, or orphaned. Rehabbers is the short name. Rehabilitate means to bring an animal back to good health. Rehabbers rescue wild animals. They care for those animals while healing goes on. When recovery allows it, they release the animals into the wild. Their training covers many fields. Some are nutritionists. A nutritionist knows what each species should eat. A nutritionist also knows how much food is right. Others are behaviorists. A behaviorist has studied how wild animals act. That study helps the person understand one animal.

2It also helps the person predict what that animal will do. Some rehabbers are animal-housing specialists. They know which cage, pen, or other enclosure fits each species. An injured animal may need one special kind of shelter so it can heal safely. One picture shows caretakers treating a sea turtle. The injury is in the turtle's right flipper. Rehabber Lisa treats a young javelina named Tripod. A car hit Tripod. One back leg was lost in that crash. Common causes of injury include being hit by vehicles. Hitting other objects is another cause. Poisoning is another. Illegal hunting is another. Litter and pollution are another. Animal attacks are another. Many rehabbers can treat illness in wild animals. They can treat injuries too, in the way veterinarians do. Not every rehabber is a veterinarian. Not every veterinarian knows wild-animal care. Most rehabbers focus on capture and transport. Safe handling of wildlife is a skill they have. That skill protects the animal. It also protects the rehabber. More people now live where wild animals live. Rehabbers are needed more often because of that. Farming takes land. Houses take land. Businesses take land. Natural habitats are destroyed. Natural foods are destroyed. Animals then face a higher chance of being orphaned. They face a higher chance of injury. They face a higher chance of death. People and human activity cause most wildlife injuries. Some rehabbers are generalists. They work with many mammals. They work with many birds. They work with many reptiles. Other rehabbers are specialists. A specialist may focus only on owls. Another may focus only on bats. Another may focus only on ocean animals. Urban wildlife is a common patient. Those animals live in cities or towns. Squirrels are one example. Raccoons are another. Foxes are another. Some brave rehabbers work with dangerous animals. Bears are among them. Mountain lions are among them. Bobcats are among them. Most rehabbers treat animals that are indigenous. Indigenous means the animal already belongs to the rehabber's home region. Special permits allow that work. Special licenses allow it too. Exotic animals are different. They are not native.

3They migrated to the region, or people brought them. A rehabber needs extra training for those animals. Extra licenses are required. Extra permits are required. One picture shows a Florida state wildlife worker. The worker is examining a panther kitten. Many centers focus on particular species. They still talk with colleagues who know other species. A different kind of animal may arrive and need help. People often ask how someone becomes a rehabber. Many begin as volunteers. They learn inside the homes of trained rehabbers. They learn in those rehabbers' backyards. Volunteers are not paid. Most rehabbers are not paid either. Rehabbers often buy food with their own money. They buy medicine with their own money. They buy shelters with their own money. Donations sometimes help. The gifts come from people. They come from businesses. They come from other organizations that care about wildlife. Helpers act because they care about animals. They want the animals to get healthy. Good care of wild animals also supports healthy habitats. It can prevent illness in people. It can prevent injury to people. One picture shows a volunteer holding a baby red-tailed hawk. A rehabber removes a bandage from the hawk's leg. The leg broke when the hawk fell from its nest. Two rules come first if you meet an animal that may need rescue. Do not touch the animal. Call an adult right away. The adult can phone a wildlife rehabber. That rehabber is trained for rescue. Watching, while you stay in a safe spot, is a way you can help. Note where the animal hides. Rescuers can then find it when they arrive. Small holes in a cardboard box let you cover a small animal that is hurt. A laundry basket can do the same job. The cover shields the animal from predators until help comes. One picture shows a rescuer giving water to a koala. He had saved that koala from a wildfire. Some behaviors mean you should stay away. They can mean the animal is sick and dangerous. A bat on the ground is one warning. A wild animal that seems tame is another.

4Extra drool is another. Foam around the mouth is another. An animal that cannot move is another. Extreme anger in the animal's look is another warning. A nocturnal animal is normally active at night. Daytime activity in that animal is a warning. The warning is strongest for a raccoon. It is strong for a skunk. It is strong for an opossum. It is strong for a fox. It is strong for a bat. Hurt, frightened animals can be injured further if they are held the wrong way. They can die from that handling. The wrong enclosure can injure them. It can kill them. Wild birds may break bones while trying to escape a wire cage. They may damage feathers in that struggle. Parents may abandon a baby if they smell a human on it. This risk is greater for mammals than for birds. Mammals have a sharper sense of smell. Injured wild animals are often scared because they are in pain. They may bite to defend themselves. They may kick. They may scratch. They may peck. They may stab. Help from people is something these animals do not recognize. Diseases in wild animals can pass to humans. They can pass to pets. Among wild animals, bats rank higher as carriers of rabies. Coyotes are more likely. Raccoons are more likely. Foxes are more likely. Skunks are more likely. Rabies is a deadly disease. Every warm-blooded animal can catch it. Humans can catch it. Possible exposure means treatment must start without delay. People sometimes take baby animals from home when no danger exists. The result can be tragic. A hopping baby bird may not be an orphan. It may be a fledgling. A fledgling is a young bird learning to fly. Before they can fly, fledglings practice by hopping along the ground. Parents usually watch them. People may not be able to see those parents. Baby rabbits are sometimes taken by mistake. Baby seals are sometimes taken by mistake. Baby deer are sometimes taken by mistake. None of those babies may be in trouble. It is normal for them to rest quietly.

5A beach can be the resting place. Grass can be the resting place. The mother may be eating nearby. Judgment belongs only to people who have learned how these animals normally live. They can tell whether human help is needed. If help is not needed, removal from the mother hurts the baby's chance to survive. A baby that is not wounded does not need rescue. Some people think taking a wild animal home is a kindness. Love of wildlife is not the same as skill to care for it. Wild animals need far more training than dogs and cats need. Taking a wild animal home is also against the law. Think of yourself hurt in an accident. You would not want a random person to take you home and treat you. You would want a trained helper, such as a doctor. A nurse would also fit that need. You would want a clean place. You would want the right equipment. You would want the right medicine. Wild animals deserve that same high level of care. One picture shows veterinarians examining a red panda. They are using medical equipment. Spring is the busiest season for wildlife rescue. Wild animals give birth in spring. Babies are weaker then. They often cannot survive alone. A car that hits the mother can leave the baby an orphan. A hunter can kill the parents. A predator can kill the parents. A checkup is the first step at a rehabilitation center. First aid is part of that step. New arrivals are quarantined. Each one stays in its own cage. The goal is to stop a possible infection from reaching the other animals. Rehabbers write detailed notes on every animal. The notes show whether the animal is improving. They show when medicine is due. They show when feeding is due. Problems at these centers vary widely. Broken bones must be treated by veterinarians first. Diseases must be treated by veterinarians first. After that treatment, the animal can rest at the center and get well. Igor is a black vulture. He had been fed birdseed.

6Meat was the food he needed for good health. His bones grew fragile. They broke during his rescue. Healing may happen in one place. Recovery may happen in another. A small dark cage may be the first room for a hawk whose wing is broken. The dark cage lets it stay calm while healing begins. Once the bone has healed, an outdoor flight cage may be next. There the hawk can exercise. There it can learn to fly again. Young injured animals often need extra care while they heal. As they grow stronger, an adult animal may share their space. The young animal can learn from that adult. Hunting for food in the right way is one lesson adults give. One picture shows birds that have been rehabilitated. They practice flight inside a flight cage. Release waits until they have healed enough. Infant animals must stay warm. An incubator can provide that warmth. Hot-water bottles in the cage can do it. Heating pads can do it. Lightbulbs in the cage can do it. Most wild animals fear people. Life away from home adds stress. A wild animal can die if stress rises too high. Workers limit contact with people for that reason. They keep noise low. They cover cages with towels. Other techniques are used as well. They also avoid staring. In the wild, a stare means an animal is being hunted. One picture shows a puppet standing in as a mother. The young condor then does not imprint on the humans who feed it. Early in life, a baby animal imprints on its mother. Daily watching of its mother teaches a baby duck what kind of bird it is. Rehabbers work hard so baby birds do not imprint on people. If they do, they grow up believing they are human. Humans, not their own kind, become the company they seek. Raptors are birds of prey. A raptor that imprinted on people can be dangerous once it is outdoors. Other birds can become dangerous in the same way. A hiker may draw that bird's wish for attention.

7The hiker may not know the bird is used to people. The meeting can hurt the hiker. It can hurt the bird. Because of that risk, these birds often cannot return to the wild. Meat-eaters at a center need meat if they are to heal. They need meat if they are to grow strong. Rehabbers collect roadkill for that food. Roadkill is the name for animals that cars or trucks have just hit beside a road. Freezers hold mouse-cicles. A mouse-cicle is a frozen mouse used as food. Some centers raise their own animal food to save money. Quail are raised that way. Mice are raised that way. Rats are raised that way. Rabbits are raised that way. One picture shows a volunteer feeding a mouse by hand. The patient is an adult red-tailed hawk. The hawk is almost completely blind. Each animal must get its natural foods, or something close to them. Some foods make wild animals sick. Some foods hinder normal growth. For many baby animals, milk from cows does extreme harm. It can even kill them. Natural foods prepare a rescued animal to live in the wild later. Orphans that grew up at a center need those foods most. A taste for human food can be a problem after release. Failure to learn hunting can be a problem. Failure to learn how to forage can be a problem. The animal might starve. Release begins with a choice of place. Rehabbers start that search long before the animal is ready. Natural history of the species is essential knowledge. A possible habitat is judged against what that animal needs. The qualities of the place are judged too. The chosen area must offer plenty of food. It must offer water. It must offer shelter. It must be safe from contact with humans. The animal itself must be healthy enough to go. Running, climbing, swimming, or flying has to come easily. It must be able to see. It must be able to hear. It must be able to locate food. It must be able to avoid predators. It must be able to be social with its own kind.

8A wildlife biologist is often asked to help with the release. An ornithologist is often asked too. Their help keeps the process smooth. One picture shows a Tasmanian devil. It will be examined before release. The first release step moves the animal outdoors. Animals of the same species share that outdoor space. The space may be a pen. It may be a cage. Outdoors, the animal adjusts to weather. It also adjusts to seeing humans less often. Slow release is common for young animals. Orphans are the clearest case. A pen is set in a safe wild place. The door stays open so the animal can come back. Food continues until it is clear the animal can feed itself. Fast release is common for animals that were rescued as adults. Life in nature is already familiar to those adult animals. A release site is where those adults are carried. The best site is near the place they were found. Then they are let go. One picture shows a group of onlookers. A rehabber opens a carrier door. A bald eagle flies free. Return to the wild is impossible for about half the animals in these centers. They are too sick, or the injuries are too severe. Many have lost limbs. Many have lost beaks. Many have lost wings. Many have lost eyesight. A bird whose injured wing heals badly could not fly in the wild. A bird with only one eye could not hunt there. Sometimes it is clear the animal will never survive outdoors. Sometimes it will not survive at the center either. Rehabbers then face a hard choice. Pain can make euthanasia the kindest choice. Euthanasia means a quick killing without pain. It can end the suffering. One picture shows an adult female great horned owl. A wing injury keeps her from flying quietly. The noise warns the prey she hunts. Release is impossible for her. Human activity is not the only source of wildlife injury. Natural disasters injure animals too. Wildfires are one kind. Tsunamis are another. Hurricanes are another. Terri Crisp gives much of her time to animals hurt by natural disasters.

9In 1986 a wildfire raged in California and trapped a Shetland pony. She coaxed the pony into a car and rescued it. Alaska in 1989 was where she worked during the oil spill known as Exxon Valdez. Sea otters were among the animals she tried to save. Loons were among them too. In 1992 she worked after Hurricane Andrew. Hundreds of hurt animals were part of that rescue. She founded Noah's Wish. The group trains volunteers. Those volunteers rescue animals put at risk by natural disasters. One picture shows Terri Crisp holding an animal she rescued. Her rescues have followed earthquakes. They have followed fires. They have followed floods. They have followed hurricanes. They have followed oil spills. They have followed tornadoes. They have followed other disasters. Before the Asian tsunami of 2004 reached land, many wild animals ran inland. That knowledge was remarkable. Pets did not fare so well. Farm animals came through the disaster poorly. Some people in the struck areas depended on working farm animals. Many of those animals were killed. Many were injured. Many were left in devastated places with no food. The Humane Society International joined other organizations. Volunteers joined them. Together they helped the animals. They also helped the people who cared for those animals. The aim was to get lives back on track. One picture shows a man in high water after the tsunami. The month was December 2004. He carries his daughter. He carries their dog. They are moving toward safety. A role remains for animals whose return to the wild will never happen. Rehabbers use them as ambassadors. The animals help teach respect for wildlife. Children learn about wild animals that live nearby. Adults learn that too. They learn to respect habitats. Respect lets wild animals keep finding food. It lets them keep finding shelter. Rehabbers do important work. They care for injured wild animals. They return many of those animals to the wild. You can help by respecting wildlife. Seeing an animal in distress is a reason to phone a rehabber.

10One phone call may give that animal a chance. The chance is to grow up. The chance is to live free and healthy. One picture shows a bird of prey used as an ambassador. Children learn from it about animals that live near them. These meanings belong to words in the book. An ambassador represents a country, a species, or a cause. Coaxing means winning agreement by gentle persuasion. Colleagues are people who do similar work. Devastated means destroyed by violent force. Exotic means the animal comes from another place, and that place is often distant. A fledgling is young, and flight is the skill it is still learning. To forage is to search for food or to gather it. An incubator is a warm enclosure for a baby animal. Indigenous means native to one particular place. An ornithologist is a scientist whose study is birds. Quarantined means kept apart so disease will not spread. Veterinarians are doctors for animals other than humans. They treat illness. They treat injury. The topic list names subjects in this book, without page numbers. Animal housing is one topic. Natural history is one. Babies are one. Animals that cannot be released are one. A behaviorist is one. A nutritionist is one. Capture and transport are one. An ornithologist is one. Care is one. Orphans are one. Causes of injury are one. Predators are one. Contact with humans is one. Rabies is one. Terri Crisp is one. Rehabbers are one. Dangerous animals are one. Release is one. Disease is one. Recovery is one. Exotic animals are one. Respecting wildlife is one. The Exxon Valdez oil spill is one. Rules for children are one. Fast release is one. Slow release is one. A flight cage is one. Spring is one. Food is one. Substitute parents are one. The Humane Society International is one. Training is one. Hurricane Andrew is one. A tsunami is one. Imprinting is one. Urban wildlife is one. Indigenous animals are one. Veterinarians are one. Licenses and permits are one. Volunteers are one. Money is one. A wildlife biologist is one.

40. Holding Back the Colorado

1This book begins with a wild river. It then shows the dry region around the site. It explains a dam unlike any other. It follows the work of preparing the ground. It follows the building itself. It describes a visit. A final look treats the dam as an engineering marvel. Word meanings come last. A watershed map places Nevada, Utah, and Colorado around the Colorado River. Lake Mead is marked. So are California, New Mexico, and Arizona. The Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of California frame the wider picture. Through the southwestern United States, the Colorado bends and keeps moving. Desert country would be parched and lifeless without the water it carries. Farmers have used the banks for centuries. Irrigation from this river kept their fields alive. Spring snowmelt was the hard part. The river swelled and often drowned farmland. Later it fell away until only a trickle remained, and crops died. That unreliable supply turned some early settlers away. It pushed others to seek control of the flow. Hoover Dam came out of those efforts. Americans treat it as an iconic landmark. Visitors still feel awe. More than seventy-five years have passed since the concrete was set. Las Vegas, Nevada, lies about 30 miles to the northwest. That distance is 48 kilometers. The dam itself sits on the line between Arizona and Nevada. Black Canyon is where it spans the Colorado. The surrounding country belongs to the Mojave Desert. Say that name moh-HAH-vee. Heat and dryness rule there.

2Plants are so scarce that large stretches resemble a moonscape. North of the wall, Lake Mead breaks that dryness. The lake is the reservoir held by the dam. It did not exist until construction made it. People made this lake. Inside the United States, no lake of that kind is larger. Shoreline runs for 550 miles, which equals 885 kilometers. Plants and animals of fourteen hundred species live in and around it. One view pairs the lake with the river. Another shows people out boating, skiing, and fishing. Measurements help explain the size. Thickness at the crest is 45 feet, or 13.7 meters. Each of four intake towers stands 395 feet tall, or 120.4 meters. Water for the power plant is controlled by those towers. Height from foundation rock up to the crest is 726.4 feet, or 221.4 meters. The top width, measured across Black Canyon, is 1,244 feet, or 379 meters. Weight passes 6,600,000 tons. In metric tons that is 5,987,419. Down at the base, thickness reaches 660 feet, or 201 meters. No taller dam existed anywhere when this one was new. Engineers treated the job as a remarkable feat. Two older ideas share the design. One is the gravity dam, which fights the push of stored water by sheer weight. The other is the arch dam. Its curve faces upstream. Water mostly meets the steep canyon walls, and those walls squeeze the arch. The squeeze makes the structure stronger and shoves it into the ground.

3A sketch labels the downstream side, the gravity portion, the arch, and the upstream side. People class Hoover Dam as an arch-gravity dam. Electricity is made in its power plant from the river's energy. Seventeen turbine generators sit inside. The current serves roughly 1.3 million people. Interest in controlling the Colorado rose as the twentieth century opened. In earlier years the river emptied into the Gulf of California. A canal changed that. The year was 1901, and the builder was a private company. The canal's name was the Alamo Canal. It turned water aside so California's Imperial Valley could be irrigated. Crops then flourished on land that had been dry. Livestock flourished with them. Floods in 1905 were severe enough to wreck the gates that controlled the canal. Imperial Valley was left devastated. People living there wanted a bigger canal, one the government would keep up, so irrigation could return. Arthur Powell Davis argued that a dam would spread the benefit to more people. His post was chief engineer. He later became the first person to direct the Reclamation Service. The office belonged to a federal department, the one called Interior. A later name for the service was the Bureau of Reclamation. Dams in the western states are the work most often linked to this agency. Canals in those states are linked to it as well. Davis gave Congress a report on the Colorado in 1918. A decade passed. Then the Boulder Canyon Project Act went through Congress.

4Hoover Dam was approved in that law. So was the All-American Canal, meant to bring Imperial Valley its water. An appropriation bill followed in 1930. President Hoover's signature on that bill let building begin. Black Canyon, pictured before any work, was the real construction site. The Boulder Dam name still stuck until 1947. Renaming that year honored Herbert Hoover. He had been the thirty-first president. Choosing ground was step one. Planners wanted a place that could store the most water safely, with the least effort and the least cost. Two canyons led the list. One was Boulder Canyon. The other was Black Canyon. A gap of 20 miles, or 32 kilometers, separated them on the border of Arizona and Nevada. Surveyors from the Bureau of Reclamation checked both. Mapmakers went with them. Granite in the walls made Boulder Canyon the first pick. Faults, which are cracks, later showed up in that granite. Black Canyon replaced it. Andesite breccia formed the bedrock there and formed the walls. That kind of rock had no cracks. Housing was poor at the start. Tents held some workers and their families. Baths happened in the river. The start date was March 11, 1931. Around them the Great Depression had brought staggering hardship to the economy of the United States. Work drew 21,000 unemployed men into southern Nevada from across the country. A large share came in the summer of 1930. Actual building was still far off. Blame for the Depression fell widely on President Hoover.

5His answer was jobs. He wanted the largest number of workers he could hire. He told crews to survey and begin other early tasks even though lodging was missing. Drinking water was missing. A hospital was missing. Camps ran without electricity. They ran without running water. Rough as it was, the men needed wages badly. Six Companies won the contract. Behind that name stood six construction firms. Dams, bridges, tunnels, and roads were work they already knew well. Charge of engineering fell to Frank Crowe. Innovative methods had marked the many western dams he had built. Moving the Colorado off the site was phase one. Blasting opened four tunnels. The Arizona bank got two of them. The Nevada bank got two. Above the future dam, a cofferdam formed a watertight barrier and steered the current into those tunnels. A matching cofferdam closed the lower end. A barrier of rock stood there too. Water downstream could not creep back, so the site stayed dry. Labels on a diversion map point out the Arizona tunnels, the Nevada tunnels, both cofferdams, and the rock barrier. Heat was extreme, and the tunnel crews worked all seven days of every week. May 1931 opened this enormous task. Rocks fell on the crews daily. Blasts shook the canyon. Diesel trucks poured out fumes. Pace had to stay fast. Until the tunnels existed, no one could start the dam wall. Overhead, high scalers knocked loose stone off the walls.

6They also cut the grooves that would grip each side of the future dam. Jackhammers were their tools. Dynamite was another. Wooden swings held them 800 feet over the river, a drop of 244 meters. Temperatures climbed as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, or 49 degrees Celsius. Dozens died when rocks or tools fell. Deaths tied to the building totaled ninety-six. More than the wall was rising. For roughly five thousand workers and the families with them, the U.S. government built Boulder City. Houses were part of it. A hospital was part of it. So were plumbing and systems for sewage. Night recovery got easier once the town was ready. Injuries could be treated. Heat exhaustion could be treated. A photograph presents Boulder City as suburban housing the government put up for these crews. Supply trains needed tracks, and those tracks were laid. A road joined the town to the dam site. Power had to come from far away. A line 222 miles long, equal to 357 kilometers, ran from San Bernardino in California and ended at Black Canyon. January 29, 1932, was the day crews broke out at the upriver mouth of Nevada's first diversion tunnel. Three more openings followed not long after. Concrete then lined every tunnel. November 1932 was when they could take the river. Cofferdams came next, one upriver of the future wall and one downriver. Diversion of the water, once those barriers stood, beat the schedule by nearly a year.

7Pumps emptied the site after the river had been shifted. Solid bedrock had to carry the dam. Silt and stones buried that rock under 135 feet, or 41 meters. Thousands of years of Colorado flow had laid the cover down. June 6, 1933, marked the end of that enormous dig. Building the dam could finally start. Concrete in all the structures totals 4,360,000 cubic yards. The metric figure is 3,333,459 cubic meters. Picture a highway 16 feet wide, or 4.9 meters, running from San Francisco until it reached New York City. This concrete could pave that road. Rock, earth, and sand dug from the project passed 5,500,000 cubic yards, or 4,205,052 cubic meters. A road made from that spoil would be even larger. One picture shows crews excavating where the foundation would sit. Columns of stacked blocks form the dam. It was never poured as one single mass. Wet concrete rode down in huge buckets. Each bucket emptied into its own wooden form, a mold waiting below. Puddlers smoothed what had been poured. Air bubbles had to go, or the hardened concrete would be weaker. Heat was the next danger. A chemical reaction inside the pour could crack it. Steel pipes were laid in the forms first, a maze 582 miles long, or 937 kilometers. Each pipe measured 1 inch across, which is 2.54 centimeters. Cold water kept moving through them. Grout replaced that water after cooling. A finished form was taken apart once its concrete had set.

8Workers stood the same form up again on the new top and poured another lift. That is how each column grew. Spaces left between columns received grout too. Spillways were added after the columns stood and the grout was in. Floodwater from the Colorado would have somewhere to go. It would drop through the spillways and never reach the crest. A crest overflow would wreck the power plant. Two of the old diversion tunnels, converted for the new job, would carry spillway water away. Last came the power plant and the four intake towers that would meter water toward it. Plugs closed the two inner diversion tunnels along roughly a third of each tunnel. Penstocks, which are steel pipes, went inside. Flow from each intake tower to the power plant is what those penstocks govern. Falling water carries energy. A hydroelectric plant turns that energy into electricity by way of turbine generators. Spread of cities was one result of Hoover Dam. Natural habitats changed as well. Look at the desert tortoise in the Mohave Desert. Before 1950, about two hundred of them might live in one square mile. That area equals 2.5 square kilometers. A square mile now holds only five or six. Groups are trying to guard what habitat the tortoise has left. A picture shows the animal. Completion arrived on February 1, 1935. Tunnels that had carried the Colorado around the site were plugged. Behind the wall, the river climbed. It spilled over the cofferdam.

9Lake Mead was the result. The full project had used about 21,000 men. A typical day saw 3,500 of them. The peak day saw 5,218. Spending reached about $165 million. Today's economy would put that at $3 billion or more. Dedication day was September 30, 1935. President Roosevelt spoke while the structure was still known as Boulder Dam. In his words it stood as the world's greatest dam. He ranked the work as an engineering win of the highest kind. American resourcefulness, American skill, and American determination were the qualities he named. Tourists inside the visitor center get a view straight down, like a bird over the wall. Guides lead tours that show details the public does not usually see, both in the dam and in the power plant. Visits have been welcome since 1937, and millions come every year. Displays explain how nature shaped this region over time. They tell the dam's own history. They tell how the Bureau of Reclamation worked to settle the West and to support irrigation. Highway 93 lets drivers cross the crest. An overlook gives broad views. Dam tours and power-plant tours are both offered. Those tours draw close to one million people a year. All year, Lake Mead is a place for fishing. Boating and picnics fill the calendar too. Plants and animals of the area can be watched and photographed. Taller dams exist now. By 2014, the count of higher dams was twenty-six. Fame still keeps Hoover Dam near the front of the list.

10Remote country was among the hardest problems, though not the only one. Roads, electric power, and houses had to appear before the main work was possible. Size alone counted as a technical achievement. Dam design everywhere learned from it. So did dam construction. Labor by the original builders still benefits millions. Water reached California because of the dam. It reached Arizona and southern Nevada. Power did too. The Southwest could flourish after that change. Building the landmark, and living with its impact, remains an unforgettable piece of United States history. Sunset light on the dam, seen from the Mike O'Callaghan-Pat Tillman Memorial Bridge, fills one last picture. A short list explains difficult words. Money set aside in a formal way for one use is an appropriation. Solid rock under the soil is bedrock. When substances turn into different substances, that process is a chemical reaction. Divert means to send something onto a new path. Digging out or uncovering material is excavating. A new and original idea can be called innovative. Something parched is extremely dry and short of moisture. Recovering or restoring a thing is reclamation. A reservoir stores a large body of water for drinking or for farms. Finding a way past problems is resourcefulness. Spillways give water a path around an obstacle, and a dam is one such obstacle. A turbine has a fan-like shape and takes energy from moving water, from wind, or from steam.

41. Homes in Dry Lands

1Friends who are Bedouin embrace in the Sahara. The place is Morocco. Contents. Deserts That Demand Much. Desert People of the Sonoran. The Bedouin and the Sahara. Nomads of Mongolia and the Gobi. A Way to Live. Word List. Four scenes sit together. Egypt's Sahara holds an oasis, and palm trees stand near it. Flowers grow in sand dunes in Australia. Water runs in the Sonoran Desert. Bolivia holds the largest salt flat on Earth. Deserts That Demand Much. A dictionary usually calls a desert a dry land. The wording may add that the place is inhospitable and that life there is scarce or absent. Some desert regions match that wording. Other desert landscapes are full of life. Trees can grow there, and shrubs, and cacti, on the sides of mountains where many kinds of creatures thrive. A different desert can look like a sea of sand without end, dunes rolling like waves. Streams and rivers cross some desert regions. Those waters may go dry at certain times of year, or stay dry for a long stretch. Shared traits do exist. A desert is arid. Precipitation in a year is usually under 25.4 centimeters, which is 10 inches.

2Soil tends to be dry. Plants are fewer than in other places. Great cold is possible in some deserts. Sun and heat are what most of them have. Close to one-fifth of the land on Earth is desert. Hot deserts stand on five of the seven continents. Europe is an exception. Antarctica is the other. Size varies too. A desert can be small. A desert can be huge. A trip around the world can show more of these lands, and more of the first peoples of these lands. Their history there runs for thousands of years. In India's Thar Desert, children run as a group. Mali's Sahara is where a woman of the Tuareg people cooks a meal outside her home. Survival in the desert works as survival works anywhere. People adapt to what surrounds them. Food must be found. Water must be found. Shelter must be found. Any hard place on Earth asks the same. Basic needs have to be met, or life fails. For the people who live there, though, a desert is more than a struggle to last.

3It is home. It is a way of living. Libya is where a man of the Tuareg people rides a camel among a crowd. Desert People of the Sonoran. Heat and dryness mark the Sonoran Desert. It covers 310,800 square kilometers, or 120,000 square miles, from the southwestern United States into northern Mexico. Rain can stay away for months. A summer day can hit 49 degrees Celsius, or 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Winter nights can fall below freezing. Set beside other deserts, this one is relatively lush. It is relatively bountiful. Nearness to the ocean is why more rain falls here than in any other desert. Summer monsoons often soak the whole of it. Shade trees grow. So do large cacti, among them the saguaro, pronounced suh-WAR-oh. Summer flowers grow as well. The Tohono O'odham, pronounced toe-HOE-noh OH-eh-dom, are Indigenous people of this desert. They are one of three main groups inside the wider O'odham people. Their name means desert people. A map of the region marks California, New Mexico, and Arizona. It marks the Pacific Ocean and Mexico, within North America. Native plants in the Sonoran Desert number more than 2,500.

4No other desert in the world has more. Across thousands of years, water came from the desert, and so did food and a place to shelter. During the last few hundred years, newcomers from Europe arrived. Newcomers from the United States arrived too. They moved onto that land. Bit by bit they took ground where O'odham life had already lasted for thousands of years. Four tribes now divide the ground that holds many of the O'odham. One tribe is the nation called Tohono O'odham. The O'odham language is also spoken by people of the Gila River community. It is spoken at Ak-Chin. It is spoken at Salt River, a community also called Pima Maricopa. Each of those is an Indian community. Differences in the language show up from tribe to tribe. Sells, Arizona, is the largest community. The nation called Tohono O'odham has its capital there. Life today is on reservations and also off them, in towns and in cities. Francine Jose displays baskets. Relatives made them long ago. Floodwater was their irrigation, including the diverting of water, and planting sites were chosen with care.

5Dryland farming became a mastery. Corn grew. Squash grew. Beans grew. Modern life drew more O'odham people as time passed. Further ground was lost to others. The government of the United States pressed them to take up the ways of that country. Traditions were still defended across the years. Many O'odham fold pieces of those traditions into lives of the twenty-first century. Farming is one piece. Cooking old recipes is another. Making baskets is another. Saguaro fruit, and the harvest of it, matters deeply to the culture of the Tohono O'odham. Spring brings beautiful flowers. They open on the cactus. Large red fruit follows, ripe in the middle of June. The fruit is taken from the tops of these giant cacti. Height can reach 22 meters and more, which is 75 feet. Tools made for the job are used. Wine is made from the fruit. That wine has an important place in the New Year celebration, held early in July. Around 1907 an O'odham woman gathers the fruit, in the upper photo. The lower photo shows the same traditional tools still in use. A map of the Sahara marks Morocco and Tunisia.

6It marks Western Sahara, Algeria, and Libya. Egypt is there, with Mauritania, Mali, and Sudan. Niger and Chad are there. The Atlantic Ocean borders Africa. Yearly rain in certain stretches of this desert stays under 25 millimeters, which is 1 inch. The Bedouin and the Sahara. Northern Africa holds the Sahara, from rocky ground to dunes of sand, across 8.6 million square kilometers, or 3.3 million square miles. Heat is extreme. Dryness is extreme. A storm there is most likely to be sand, or dust. So little rain falls that few plants flourish, and few animals do. Bedouin people, pronounced BED-oo-in, live across the Sahara in North Africa. The Middle East is home to them as well. Their name comes from Badw, an Arabic word for the people of the desert. Children of the Bedouin get ready to race camels. Dry vegetation is what these houses are built from. The village is Bedouin, inside Egypt's Sahara. The upper photo shows them. Rugs and pillows, bright with color, fill a Bedouin tent in Oman. The lower photo shows the inside. Nomadic life was the old pattern for the Bedouin of the Sahara.

7Rainy winters were for roaming. Dry summer months sent them back, with herds of camels, of sheep, or of goats, to land that had been cultivated. Water came from oasis to oasis, or from wells they dug. Home was a low black tent called a bayt, woven from goat hair or from the wool of sheep. Sun, wind, and blowing sand were kept out. Air could still move, which mattered in the intense heat. Bayts are still home for some Bedouin. A camp can be taken apart quickly, packed, and set up somewhere else. More than a hundred years have seen other countries take over land the Bedouin had long used. Nomadic life is gone for many. What remains is seminomadic. Others have settled. Towns and cities hold their houses. Apartments hold them too. Ancestors' ways are still followed by some. Even a nomadic family can now buy supplies at a market or from another seller. Herding animals is no longer the only usual work. Many other jobs are held. Inside a home in Oman, a mother who is Bedouin smiles. Her son is with her.

8Near Petra, in Jordan, a Bedouin village is called Umm Sayhoun. A map places the Gobi in Asia, between Mongolia and China, with the Indian Ocean marked nearby. Mountains blocked the rainy weather that would have let plants flourish, and the Gobi formed as a rain shadow desert. Nomads of Mongolia and the Gobi. Southern Mongolia reaches into northern China across 1.3 million square kilometers, or 500,000 square miles. Rock covers most of that Asian desert. People there are very few. Mongolia's first people have a language in which Gobi means large and dry. A place with no water is another meaning. Horses, sheep, goats, and cattle were the old herds of the Mongolian nomads who call this cold, windy desert home. Two-humped camels, the Bactrian kind, were herded too. A woman of Mongolia moves her animals through the Gobi. Outside the family ger, a boy from that same land is running. A ger is a yurt: a round tent that can be carried, built on a wooden frame and covered in felt. Harsh heat, cold, and wind are what the felt holds off. People are sheltered well.

9Animals can still suffer in that weather. Recent decades have seen families leave nomadic life by the thousands upon thousands. Several causes drove the move from desert to city. Winters of unusual harshness, and summers of unusual dryness, cost thousands of families their animals. Some lost every animal they had. Shifts in government hit herders as well, and earning a living grew hard. Since 1989, Mongolian nomads moving to the capital of Mongolia, looking for food and for work, have numbered more than half a million. Most brought the ger along. Districts of these tents grew up inside the city. A Way to Live. Thousands of years have passed with people calling deserts home. Challenges differ from one desert to the next. Solutions have always been found by the first peoples of each desert, so the place would serve them. In earlier times, homes, food, and water came almost only from what the local land offered. Much is different now. Modern lives are what many desert dwellers lead. Traditional lives, the lives of ancestors, still continue for some. Traditions of the desert community are still celebrated by many.

10Demand and reward sit together in desert life. Deep respect for the environment has always marked the peoples who make a desert home. Ample gifts are honored and used. Great power is acknowledged, and so is beauty. The United Arab Emirates has a crowded road. A man leads a camel along it. Word List. Ample describes a supply that meets the need, or passes it. Arid describes a place that is very dry. Bountiful means giving in a generous way. Cultivated describes land prepared for farming or for gardening. Dismantle means to take something apart. Dwellers are the people who live in one set place. Other animals that live there count too. Incorporate means to join something in, or to include it as a piece of a larger whole. Indigenous describes a people's tie to being the earliest to inhabit a place. Irrigation is the practice of bringing water to land or to crops so growth is helped. Monsoons are storms of a season. They bring heavy rain. Teeming means filled with. Tribes are groups. The people in one group share culture. They also share land.

42. How Animal Parks Changed

1Contents Opening Wild Animals Held Long Ago The Earliest Public Zoos A Change in Purpose Zoos That Work to Save Species Zoos in Our Time Closing Thoughts Word List Topic List. Modern zoo grounds are planned with the animals' surroundings in mind. Visitors can study the animals. They can also study natural habitats. Opening A trip to a zoo can start a question. How did people begin to hold other animals captive? Some animals stay in small cages. Others have more ground on which to roam. Someone who has seen more than one zoo may notice a further difference. Some parks are larger. Some look more up to date. Care can look different from park to park as well. Practices have shifted across the centuries. The shift is still going on. Parks differ a great deal in size. They also differ in the money they can spend on expansions and upgrades. This book follows how zoos began. It follows how their purpose changed. It tells the story of keeping captive animals and putting them on display. Wild Animals Held Long Ago Nearly every great civilization put wild animals where people could see them. In earlier centuries, a king or another ruler was the only person who could pay for that privilege. A collection of animals came to stand for wealth and power. The animals were lavish gifts. Gold and gemstones were gifts of the same kind. Rulers kept the animals so they themselves could enjoy them. Cages were built so viewing would be easy. Comfort for the animals got little thought. Care got little thought too. Explorers who traveled the world met animals they had never seen. They carried those animals home. Spices, jewels, and silk traveled with them.

2Alexander the Great lived from 356 to 323 BC. This famous conqueror kept many kinds of animals. Bears were among them. So were monkeys and elephants. At his death the collection passed to Egypt's King Ptolemy I. The Greek thinker Aristotle watched how the animals behaved. Curiosity drove that watching. His book, History of Animals, describes several hundred vertebrate species. Crowds in ancient Rome treated deadly fights as sport. The fighters might be captive animals. They might be people. Romans used animals for entertainment that drew big crowds. Animal-rights activists today would call that use incredible cruelty. Roman leaders arranged fights between wild animals. Lions fought bears. Gladiators also fought these animals. Animals died in numbers too large to count. People now see those shows as torture and cruelty. Many of the animals were taken from the wild. Others were bred while captive. Breeding kept a steady supply ready for displays of ferocity and strength. Through the Middle Ages, most people gave nature little attention. By the 1200s, interest in animal collections had returned. Rulers often traded animals as gifts. Frederick II was king of Germany from 1212 to 1220. He was Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 to 1250. His collection included cheetahs trained to hunt. He took his animals with him when he traveled. The trip to Germany, made for his wedding, included lions. Elephants came along. Camels and further creatures came too. Ornaments, gems, and costly cloth decorated the animals. They were treated as honored guests at an important event. Animals shown to the public were still seen only as objects of curiosity. They lived in small cages barred with metal. They could not hide from view. They could not keep their natural behaviors. The Earliest Public Zoos From the 1700s onward, kings and queens lost power and privilege.

3Ordinary people moved into posts where decisions were made. Rights once held only by royalty began to change. One of those rights was the sole right to keep wild animals and study them. The 1790s brought the French Revolution. In those years a collection that had belonged to royalty was moved. Its new home was a botanical garden in Paris. The garden is the Jardin des Plantes, said zhar-DAN day PLAHNT, meaning Garden of Plants. That collection became the first public zoological garden known to history. People call such a garden a zoo. In the same era, circuses and traveling shows carried exotic animals. They were popular across the land that would later be the United States. Crowds came to see touring groups of North American animals. Mixed displays of minerals, fossils, and plants drew crowds as well. In the 1700s, people in London could visit the animals kept at the Tower of London. Admission could be a small sum of money. A visitor could instead give a cat or a dog. Those animals became food for the bears or the big cats. In 1816, London's Royal Menagerie used small cages and tight viewing spaces. The early 1800s brought larger cities. People also began to set natural land aside as parkland for recreation. Open space was growing. Interest in the natural world was growing too. Parks and gardens built for living animals multiplied. Visitors could see many kinds of animals. Plants were on view as well. In 1828 a zoo opened in Regent's Park. The city was London. Its purpose was to study animals in captivity. Keepers hoped to use that knowledge for the animals' wild relatives.

4Through the rest of the century, new zoos followed that example. Europe saw many of them. The United States saw many as well. Popularity rose quickly. The cities of the time were dirty and ugly. A zoo offered a break from them. It also offered a close look at how wild animals live. An animal shut in a small, empty space grows unhappy. It also grows unhealthy. Opening a zoo did not, by itself, guarantee decent care. By today's standards, care often fell short. People knew little then about what the animals needed to eat. They knew little about the surroundings the animals needed. Health often failed. Animals that normally live in family groups were shut in alone. Separation caused stress. Bare cages of concrete were easy to hose clean. Most animals had nothing to climb except a shelf for sleep. Big cats had those shelves. Boredom had nothing to break it. Nothing offered stimulation. Early zoos seldom posted facts about where an animal came from. Natural habits were seldom explained. A curious visitor usually learned only a name and a feeding time. A Change in Purpose As time passed, wild animals grew harder to obtain. Governments abroad began to treat wildlife as a natural resource that had real worth. They expected those animals to be purchased. Trapping had already pushed some wanted animals near extinction. Hunting had done the same. Zoos felt pressure to care for the animals they had. Replacements were no longer easy. The old focus was entertainment alone. The new focus included the health of the residents. Captive breeding programs became part of that focus. Research showed a pattern. Animals in zoos bred more readily when they were healthy. They also bred more readily when their space felt like a natural home.

5At the San Francisco Zoo, a new compound for tigers gives more room. The cats can roam, run, and climb, and they can do so in safety. The 1960s brought many shifts. Thought changed. Values changed too. The setting was the United States. One welcome shift gave the natural world greater importance. In the 1970s, groups pressed zoo managers to improve care. Some people wanted every zoo closed. They wanted captive animals set free. In those years a group called the AZA stated why collections of wild animals still mattered. The letters stand for Association of Zoos and Aquariums. They educate the public. They advance scientific knowledge. Zoos also began to work with one another. Care improved. Homes grew less stressful and more natural. Breeding succeeded more often. Breeding giant pandas in captivity is always hard. A zoo in San Diego runs that program. Continual success has been maintained there. The scimitar-horned oryx is a kind of antelope. It lives only in zoos now. It once lived in northern Africa. In the wild, it is extinct. Zoos That Work to Save Species In recent years a fresh role has fallen to zoos. Human numbers keep rising. To get food, building materials, and land for homes and farms, people destroy more and more natural habitat. Some species have vanished from their own wild homes. They survive only inside zoos. Captive breeding offers the strongest hope that some of these animals, already threatened, will go on. When it is possible, the young are returned to wild places that are protected. The AZA now stresses education, conservation, and scientific study more than the entertainment a zoo can sell. Attitudes change.

6Technology changes. The environment changes. Zoos must keep pace with those changes if they are to meet their mission. Species Survival Plans, or SSPs, are among the most important jobs many zoos do today. The AZA built this captive-breeding program. It centers on species that may vanish from the wild. Zoo professionals coordinate the work. Many zoos take part together. The first aim is a population that stays healthy. The population of an endangered species should also stay genetically diverse. Genetics is the science of similar traits and how they are handed on. A new generation receives them from the one before. Look inside any cell of an animal's body. Genetic material is there. That material works like a blueprint. It guides body structures. It also guides many natural behaviors that are distinct to the animal. Inside the dog family, no member is rarer than the red wolf. They nearly vanished before biologists started breeding them in captivity. Releases began in the late 1980s. The place was Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge. That refuge is in North Carolina. Captive breeding centers held red wolves as well. By June 2007 the count of those wolves was above 200. The centers numbered 39. The work of many people has put red wolves on the road to recovery. An animal carries genetic material shared by its whole species. It also carries genetic material that differs from one animal to the next. Hawks offer an example. In some individuals, what they inherit gives a bit more speed than the rest of the hawks have. Extra speed raises the chance of catching extra food. It is more likely to stay healthier. It is more likely to reproduce more. Variations of this inherited kind, inside one species, are called genetic diversity.

7Diversity of that sort helps a species adjust when conditions change. It also leaves the species less open to dying out in the end. SSPs work as hard as they can to keep that diversity, for this exact reason. Most of the animals have already died, so an SSP usually begins with extremely few. The black-footed ferret is native to the Great Plains. Its SSP began with only seven founders. A founder is an animal from the starting group. Only fourteen founders stood behind the red wolf SSP. The animals live at many different zoos. An illness at one zoo, or a disaster there, will not erase the whole breeding population. For mating, animals are moved from one facility to another. A zoo professional records which animals have already mated. The record helps keep genetic diversity as wide as possible. Washington, D.C., is home to the National Zoo. That zoo began an SSP. The animal was the golden lion tamarin. This small monkey is native to Brazil. Putting tamarins back into the wild has raised their numbers. That work has succeeded. The zoo is also working with Brazil to protect the habitats where tamarins live. A species is chosen for an SSP for two reasons. One is its conservation status, either endangered or threatened. The other is whether professionals can give time to its care and study. Giant pandas were chosen for a further reason. Lowland gorillas were chosen for the same reason. People know them well. They inspire the public to join conservation work. The count of SSPs now stands above one hundred. Through these plans, zoos stand at the front of wildlife conservation. For many species, an SSP is the best hope of escaping extinction.

8Each plan also keeps a goal of education. It works to show the public why that species has declined. Zoos in Our Time For most zoos, conservation now sits at the center of the work. Public opinion, to a large extent, has not caught up with that shift. Zoos spend enormous effort teaching visitors about their role as centers for conservation. At the same time, most visitors come at least partly to be entertained. Interest has to be held. Zoos therefore keep building new programs and new exhibits. Tucson, Arizona, has the Reid Park Zoo. A platform was added there so visitors can feed giraffes. Success has been wild. Earnings from the program mostly support conservation projects. Those projects are spread around the world. Feeding a giraffe by hand is a visit people do not forget. Staff labor hard on devices and on tasks that stir the animals. Proof exists that habitat enrichment helps captive animals. Animals that receive it do much better than animals that do not. The aim is to keep an animal stimulated for as long a stretch as possible. Much of the work is trying, missing, and trying again. Keepers may spend months on a new form of enrichment. They may then find that the animal wants nothing to do with it. Hiding food inside an enclosure is a common method. The animal must search and must reach. Natural behavior is stirred that way. Other enrichment speaks to the senses. Some zoos freeze taste treats. Ratsicles are one kind. Fishsicles are another. For polar bears, ice is simple. It is also a pleasure. A keeper is teaching this lion a touch. The object of the touch is a target.

9Smell can be stirred as well. Cooking spices are one tool. Keepers sometimes place dung in an enclosure. Giraffe dung in a lion exhibit is one example. The dung itself is a kind of enrichment. Many zoos train behavior to some degree. The training often lets staff give better care. A lion or a tiger can learn to touch a target. It can learn to put its tail through a fence. Later it will take an injection in that same way. A baboon can learn to offer a shoulder so the injection can be given. Veterinarians can then give care that is better. The care is often less intrusive. Money is a constant worry at every zoo. Keeping the animals and caring for them costs a huge sum. Exhibits must be maintained. Staff must be paid. Zoos must always hunt for ways to cover those expenses. Every zoo keeps a wish list of projects. Updating old exhibits is on it. Building new ones is on it too. Spending at a zoo, by one set of estimates, breaks down this way. Staff salaries take 60 percent. Pay goes to keepers and to groundskeepers. Educators are paid too. So are cashiers, curators, and the director. Maintenance and supplies take 23.9 percent. That share covers buildings, exhibits, equipment, and vehicles. Electricity takes 7.2 percent. Food for the animals takes 6.7 percent. Medicines for the animals take 1.2 percent. Getting new animals takes 1 percent. Expansions and improvements sit outside these shares. One new exhibit may be priced at 1 million dollars. The price can climb as high as 10 million dollars. All of these figures are estimates. The figures come from the Reid Park Zoo. That zoo is in Tucson, Arizona.

10What it costs to feed zoo animals, by estimate, looks like this. Lions and tigers are carnivores. Meat, at 5 pounds a day, costs 50 dollars a week for each animal. Treats of bones and oxtails cost another 50 dollars a week for each animal. Elephants and rhinos are herbivores. Hay costs 50 dollars a week for each animal. Pellets of vitamins and minerals cost 50 dollars a week for each animal. Giraffes are herbivores too. Hay for one giraffe costs 25 dollars a week. Pellets of vitamins and minerals cost 25 dollars a week. Zebras are herbivores as well. Hay for one zebra costs 12 dollars and 50 cents a week. Pellets cost the same amount. Polar bears are omnivores. Meat, fish, fruit, and vegetables together cost 200 dollars a week for each bear. Tortoises of many species eat dark leafy green vegetables. Fifty tortoises together cost 200 dollars a week. For 500 animals, the year adds up to 168,000 dollars. All of these figures are estimates. The figures come from the Reid Park Zoo. That zoo is in Tucson, Arizona. Closing Thoughts Zoos today stand far from the private collections that rulers kept long ago. Across the centuries, growing knowledge brought enormous gains. Care of captive animals improved. Enclosures improved. The enrichment animals receive improved. Most zoos now take steps that are informed, positive, and active. They work to save animals from extinction. They teach the public why wild habitats should be preserved. On a future visit, remember this. The animals are not there only to entertain. They also point to how varied the natural world is, and how striking that variety can be. Our own involvement can help protect that world and keep it.

43. How Hip-Hop Grew

1Cheryl James stands in the center of a photo. Sandra Denton stands on the right. Together they are known as Salt-N-Pepa. On the left is their DJ, Dierda Roper, known as DJ Spinderella. The parts of this book come in this order. The opening looks at the 1970s, in the city of New York. After that, the book tells how hip-hop started. Then come the four pillars. The DJ is one pillar. Breaking is one pillar. Graffiti art is one pillar. The MC is one pillar. Then come women in hip-hop. Then comes controversy. Then comes a golden age. Then comes the spread that did not stop. A word list comes last. The City in the 1970s During those years, the city’s economy was coming apart. Manufacturing in the city was in decline. Unemployment rose because of that decline. Poverty followed. Homelessness followed. Crime rose. Roads, buildings, and other public works were crumbling. Even so, officials cut money for schools. They cut money for community services. They cut money for job programs people needed in order to face these problems. A photo shows boys standing before painted graffiti. New York is the city in the picture. The decade is the 1970s. Racism over many decades had built economic walls. People of color hit those walls. Black people hit them in particular. Most could not afford to leave the city. Many white residents did leave. Neighborhoods that were already poorly served got worse. Those neighborhoods were home to many people of color. Still more businesses shut their doors. Jobs disappeared. Clubs disappeared. Movie theaters disappeared. With those losses, youth here needed fresh ways to have fun and to express themselves. What they invented was not limited to a fresh musical style. They started a whole cultural movement. How Hip-Hop Was Born Cindy Campbell was a teenager with a plan. The afternoon was hot.

2The season was summer. The year was 1973. Clive, her older brother, was the person she asked to spin records. The event was a party before school started again. DJ means disc jockey. Home for the party was the South Bronx. That neighborhood sits inside New York City. Most people there were Black or Puerto Rican. Jamaica was the country the Campbell family left. Their new home was the United States. Five years had passed since that move. Local parties were part of Clive’s childhood back in Jamaica. The person at the decks spoke while the songs played. The music played on sound systems that could be carried. His nickname was Hercules. On stage he used the name DJ Kool Herc. Fancy equipment was out of reach. He chose records from his own collection. Two turntables were hooked to an amplifier made for a guitar. The same record played on both turntables. He moved between them so the percussion breaks would last longer. Those breaks were the best part for dancing. A photo shows DJ Kool Herc performing in England. The year is 2000. The party was a huge success. Fame across the whole Bronx arrived before another day had passed. He did not know what the coming decades would bring. Music from that South Bronx afternoon would later inspire listeners nationwide and overseas. He later said the people in the room had no sense that history was happening. Nobody knew a cultural revolution was starting. The title people later gave him was Father of Hip-Hop. Griots and the Path to Rap During those performances he drew on a Jamaican practice called toasting. In toasting, a voice talks. Sometimes the voice chants. A rhythm runs underneath. The 1950s are when this practice caught on. An older West African tradition stands behind it. That tradition belongs to griots.

3Say the word GREE-ohz. A griot is a storyteller. A griot is a poet. A griot is a singer. A griot is a historian. Many people who love hip-hop treat rappers as griots of the present day. A rapper, like a griot, tells the community’s story. Struggles are recorded. Triumphs are recorded. The telling entertains, and it also informs. In that way, history and culture of the community are shaped and kept. A griot from Mauritania is shown performing in New York City. Four Main Parts This culture is larger than its music. It is not only music. At the start, the community had no clubs for shows. It had no stages for dance. It had no galleries for art. Artists carried their creativity into the streets instead. The street was the stage. The city was the audience. Four pillars, or key elements, hold the culture up. One pillar is the DJ. Another is breaking. Another is graffiti art. The last is the MC. The DJ A DJ’s job is to keep music going without a gap. One turntable is ending a song. The second turntable brings the next song in. The change from song to song feels smooth. Few sounds mark hip-hop as clearly as scratching. Pioneering DJs in New York City developed it. Grand Wizzard Theodore was one of them. The scratch comes from a hand moving a vinyl record back and forth. The record is playing on the turntable while the hand moves it. Grandmaster Flash appears in a 2002 photo, working the decks at an event. What those early DJs noticed was a favorite part of each song. They loved the break beat. That is the stretch of a song when every sound drops out except the drums. DJ Kool Herc repeated that stretch. So did other early DJs, including Grandmaster Flash.

4Both turntables carried one identical record. With these methods, DJs built new music out of older music. The idea reached far beyond hip-hop. It shaped music makers for years afterward. The influence was profound. Breaking Break dancing is a name some people use. Dancers who started this in the street wanted a different word. Breaking was the word they kept. The names they chose included b-boys. They also chose b-girls. Breakers was another name. The year 1984 is the date of a photo. B-boys are shown competing. While a break beat played, breakers showed skills they made up in the moment. Six kinds of movement were typical. Top-rock is fast, skilled work with the feet. The breaker is standing. Down-rock is footwork too. The floor holds both hands and feet. Acrobatics are what power moves demand. They demand speed, agility, and strength. A freeze is a sudden stop of every motion. The breaker holds a pose. The pose is often unusual or difficult. Balance on one hand is one example. Balance on the head is another. Popping is a flowing motion of arms and of legs. Locking snaps a limb into a held spot. The angles are often sharp. Dance battles were common. Two breakers took turns, or two crews did. Each side showed its best moves. People stood in a circle and judged creativity and skill. The style was easy to recognize, and that fame spread. Fans of hip-hop all over the world took the dance up and loved it.
