Graffiti as Art Graffiti is writing, or it is drawings, painted on property that belongs to the public. It existed long before hip-hop rose. In the early 1970s it became an important part of hip-hop culture. A canvas was not the surface. Artists painted buildings. They painted subway cars, trains, and bridges. Part of the thrill was simple.

5Thousands of people would see the work every day. Marking public property is against the law. Outlaw artist was an identity many of them claimed. Beyond this culture, vandalism was the label people used. Inside the culture, it was art. In time, artists were asked to show work in major galleries around the world. Museums have kept famous pieces from hip-hop’s graffiti years. Art books have kept them too. Lady Pink is shown working on a painting. The painting honors women who took part in hip-hop. Several of the first artists are named here, along with several of the best known. Sandra Fabara is one. The name Lady Pink is hers. Next on the list is Fred Brathwaite. Fab 5 Freddy is the name he uses. Another artist on the list is Jean-Michel Basquiat. Donald Joseph White is one. He is known as Dondi. The MC Early on, the word for a rapper was MC. The letters expand into the phrase master of ceremonies. Beside the DJ, the MC worked as a partner of sorts. The DJ mixed dance music so the party would continue. The MC took the microphone. Call-and-response was used to lift the crowd and pull people in. Soon the talk turned into rhymes that locked to the music. Rappers are judged on content. They are judged on flow. They are judged on delivery. Content can cover many subjects. Clever lines about self-confidence are one kind. Comment on society and on politics is another. Good flow means the lyrics stay on the beat. Good delivery means a voice people can tell apart from others. Words are spoken clearly. Breathing does not break the flow. Knowledge, a Fifth Pillar Many fans count knowledge as a fifth pillar. KRS-One, and other legendary MCs, say the other four elements are bound together by knowledge. Greatness requires knowledge of one’s own history and identity.

6It requires knowledge of the community’s history. It also requires knowledge of hip-hop’s history, its values, and its ideas. That knowledge lets artists grow and find fresh ways to express themselves. Social change can then be pushed forward by the art. Women Who Shaped Hip-Hop Women have helped shape this culture from the start. Sharon Green was one of the earliest. She is MC Sha Rock. She is considered the first woman to rap. Breaking, as a b-girl, was how she started. The neighborhood was the South Bronx. Her age was fourteen. MC skills developed quickly after that. A record deal in 1979 made her the first woman rapper to get one. Funky 4 + 1, her group, shared that deal. National television came two years after that. No hip-hop group had performed there before them. Sylvia Robinson is sometimes called the Queen of Rap. She is sometimes called the Mother of Hip-Hop. She ranks among the most influential music producers ever. In 1979 she founded Sugar Hill Records. No hip-hop label had come before it. Early records that many people still know passed through her production. “Rapper’s Delight” was one of them. The Sugarhill Gang performed it. It was the first hip-hop hit across the nation. At the time, hip-hop was mostly unknown outside New York City. Listeners elsewhere in the country met hip-hop through this record. Men dominate the hip-hop industry. Men dominate the music industry in general. Women in hip-hop have faced sexism from the start. Later popular styles, made by male artists, often used lyrics that showed no respect for women. Those lyrics became a staple. Several rappers changed the music and pushed it forward. MC Lyte was one. Queen Latifah was one. Salt-N-Pepa was one. Lady B was one. Lauryn Hill was one. They used hip-hop to strengthen themselves and to strengthen other women.

7Rap became a platform. They talked about treatment of women inside hip-hop. They talked about treatment of women in the wider culture. Roxanne Strikes Back Lolita Shante Gooden was fourteen and already among the strongest rappers of her time. Most people know her as Roxanne Shante. The year 1984 brought a release from her. The song’s title was “Roxanne’s Revenge.” The subject was the sexism women go through. Success for the song was huge. Finals of a freestyle MC contest came the following year. She was the clear winner of the last rap battle. A low mark from one judge kept the win from her. The reason came out years afterward, when that judge explained it. He was a well-known MC himself. He believed a young girl winning would make people take hip-hop less seriously as art. She lost the battle. She still went on to make two rap albums. Younger women in hip-hop later had her as a mentor. Wrapped in Argument Hip-hop started as music for parties. Even the earliest artists still spoke about serious social problems and political ones. They were honest about racism they had lived through. They were honest about poverty, violence, and injustice. Grandmaster Flash, together with the Furious Five, was among the first. Their song “The Message” came out in 1982. It was a blistering picture of urban poverty. Street misery in New York City was part of that picture. Public Enemy, in the later 1980s, turned music into a voice for Black pride. Racism faced by Black people in this country was in the songs too. Lana Michelle Moorer is the name MC Lyte was given. She broke barriers in the industry. Her music took up racism. It took up sexism. Drug use, and the harm it did in her community, was in the music.

8She is shown on stage in 1993. The city is New York. Few hip-hop groups of that era carried more influence than Public Enemy. The years were the late 1980s and the early 1990s. Argument followed the group as well. In the 1990s a style called gangsta rap began to dominate hip-hop. Lyrics in that style often struck some listeners as offensive. As the style grew more popular, the music industry pushed it ahead of other styles. Many Black artists could not get a record deal unless their music fit this genre. With that rise, many people outside the culture started to treat all rap as offensive. Poetry is how many other listeners have understood rap. Older poetry and rap share a great deal. Both use rhythm with skill. Both use rhyme. Both tell stories. Maya Angelou, among the most celebrated poets, saw the link too. Famous rap artists worked with her. She was a source of inspiration for them. A photo shows her speaking a poem aloud. President Bill Clinton is being sworn in. Roots in Spoken Poetry Poetry spoken aloud during the 1960s made rap’s later rise possible. The Last Poets were one performing group. New York City was their home. The Watts Prophets came from California. They spoke poems over a bongo beat, or over jazz. The poems carried weighty messages. Black pride was one. Racism, poverty, and justice were others. People often treat these poets as the step that came before. Hip-hop of recent times followed their work. A Golden Age Hip-hop music spread across the country in the mid-1980s and the early 1990s. The culture changed because of that spread. New artists brought new musical influences. Diversity grew. Styles innovated. Local radio stations wanted new hip-hop. Club DJs wanted it too. Mainstream popularity and success shot upward. Record companies began spending large sums to produce new albums.

9Different cities grew different styles. New York City produced hardcore rap. It also produced boom-bap. Los Angeles, California, produced G-Funk. It also produced gangsta rap. Run DMC was among newer artists who mixed hip-hop with music of other kinds. De La Soul used pieces of jazz and of blues. A Tribe Called Quest did that too. The result was called jazz rap. Salt-N-Pepa built a brighter, upbeat style. People called it pop rap, or hip pop. Sampling was one defining habit of this era. A sample is a piece of one song reused inside a different song. Artists pulled samples from many genres. Jazz was one. Blues, soul, and rock were others. Movie sound was sampled by some artists as well. Across an Ocean Almost 9,000 miles lie between the Bronx and New Zealand. That distance is about 14,484 kilometers. Hip-hop made that crossing early in the 1980s. The Maori were ready to listen. New Zealand’s Indigenous Polynesian people go by that name. Black communities in the South Bronx had faced a similar squeeze at the start of the 1970s. Disadvantage was the setting for large numbers of Maori. Money was harder to come by. Crime was higher. Health care and education were hard to reach. They felt mainstream culture in New Zealand did not show them. Hip-hop spoke strongly to that feeling. Maori bands took it up as their own music. Upper Hutt Posse was one band. Third3ye was another. The Music Does Not Stop As rap grew more popular around the world, the culture became a global phenomenon. It took root in France. It took root in Mexico. It took root in New Zealand and in South Africa. Break dancing seized imaginations when films arrived. Wild Style came out in 1982. Breakin’ came out in 1984. The dance became popular in the United Kingdom.

10Japan took up the dance. Germany did too. So did Russia. So did South Korea. Today, striking graffiti can be seen on city streets in many places. Brazil is one. Morocco is one. China is one. Graffiti covers a building in Brazil. That image sits at the top. Hungary is the site of a dance contest. The dancer is a b-girl, and she is from Japan. That contest is the left-hand picture. England is where one member of a Muslim duo performs. The music is hip-hop. That image sits at the right. The start was a street party. A young girl hosted it. The year was 1973. The place was the South Bronx. It became a sensation across the globe. Few resources were on hand. That shortage produced musical inventions that rank among the century’s most creative. New forms of artistic expression came out of it too. Hip-hop still shapes many parts of popular culture around the world. The mark has lasted. Words to Know sensation (n.): a person or a thing that stirs great excitement. transition (n.): a passing into a new stage, a new place, or a new condition. portable (adj.): easy to carry or to move. pioneering (adj.): bringing in ideas or methods that are new. profoundly (adv.): in a strong or intense way. innovation (n.): the act of bringing in something new, or of inventing it. genre (n.): a group of literature or art that shares a style, a form, or a kind of content. economic (adj.): related to how goods and services are bought and sold. distinctive (adj.): having a quality that stands out and is worth noticing. culture (n.): the ideas and customs that mark one society as its own. ceremonies (n.): formal gatherings saved for days that matter. phenomenon (n.): an event or an occurrence that is remarkable.

44. How School Buses Move a Nation

1A school bus can lower carbon emissions because one bus takes the place of many private vehicles. The average school bus carries fifty-four students. Those riders would otherwise need about thirty-six private vehicles for the trip to school. Newer, greener technology works with that change. Together they can help keep the air cleaner. A bus is bigger than a car. A bigger vehicle burns more fuel to cover the same distance. The number of people on board changes the comparison. Shared rides make buses far more fuel efficient than the cars they replace. Shared rides also make buses far less polluting. A fuel chart uses a trip of 10 miles (16 km). The chart measures gallons of fuel. Thirty-six family vehicles use 14.4 gallons (54.5 L) on that trip. A regular bus that burns diesel fuel uses 1.4 gallons (5.3 L). A hybrid bus runs on diesel fuel plus electric power. That hybrid uses 0.8 gallons (3 L) on the same trip. In 1943, children at an army base rode to school in a horse-drawn bus. That older kind of travel helped the country conserve gasoline during World War II. It also helped the country conserve tires during the war.

2The account that follows looks at a daily ride people trust. It looks at taxes that pay for transportation. It looks at mass transit on a huge scale. It looks at history, at safety, and at yellow buses that are turning green. A closing word list comes at the end. Sarah walks outside on a freezing winter day. The air is so frigid that her hair starts to stick while she pulls her hood up. She pauses for that hood. Strands of hair cling together. The hair is not fully dry. Water from her morning shower has frozen at once on her head. She shivers. Then she gets moving again. The bus stop is one block from her family's apartment. She is not worried about standing in the cold. She knows the wait will be short. The bus arrives right on time. She greets the driver as she steps on. In her mind she is reviewing material for a science test. She barely notices the bus leave the stop. The bus rumbles down the road and takes her to school. This part of the day is something she simply takes for granted. A school bus is such a common sight that few people ask how the system works.

3The Houston Independent School District added 44 new buses at the start of the 2016 school year. Those buses joined a fleet of 1,100 vehicles. Each new bus has a full three-point safety belt for every passenger. Seat belts make riders in private cars much safer. People still debate whether that same gain is true on school buses. School buses are built to much stricter safety standards. A driver also has trouble checking that every belt is used correctly. A bus often holds more than fifty students at one time. That number limits how well the belts work. Some districts are beginning upgrades that are kinder to the environment. A district in New York introduced a fully electric school bus in 2016. The bus has zero carbon emissions. Its electric engine does not put pollutants into the air. It can travel about 120 miles (190 km) before it needs a recharge. Propane fuel is another green trend. Propane costs much less than traditional diesel fuel. Propane also helps reduce emissions. Hybrid buses use both electric power and diesel fuel. In 2007, drivers of hybrid buses reported better mileage. That mileage was almost twice the mileage of regular school buses.

4School transportation coordinators work closely with drivers and with mechanics. Their job is to keep school bus travel safe. The American public school bus system is the safest transportation choice for students. The National Safety Council gives a strong comparison. School buses are forty times safer than private cars. Districts require drivers to go through intensive safety training. Buses are examined often for mechanical problems. Emergency exits are built into the vehicles. Roofs are reinforced. The way the seats are laid out helps protect students in a crash. Seats are spaced close together. Seat backs are made to absorb an impact. This design places passengers in a kind of protective box. In most states, safety belts are not required on school buses. A few states have passed laws that do require them. Texas is one of those states. New York is another. California is another. Flashing stop signs warn drivers that students are getting on or off. Cameras help the driver see what is happening inside the bus. Cameras also show what is happening outside. More safety upgrades can be expected as technology advances. The school bus system is one of the most important mass transit systems in the United States.

5It is also one of the most complex. Moving students takes a small army of people. That group includes bus drivers, mechanics, and school transportation coordinators. The system depends on a well-built network of roads. Those roads connect remote rural areas with larger towns and cities. School buses travel on every kind of roadway. They use interstate highways. They also use unpaved rural lanes. Individual school districts control the vehicles. They control the drivers, the mechanics, and even the fuel. No single central authority runs every school bus. Each district works out its own busing plan. Taxpayer money pays for the buses. That money often comes from local property taxes. The same taxes pay for police departments. They pay for fire departments. They pay for libraries and for schools. Some states also give schools transportation funds. Those funds are used for busing. Buses are essential to the American public school system. That system is based on a principle. Everybody is entitled to an education. Planning the buses that take students to school and back home is an enormous job. The public school bus fleet in the United States uses more vehicles than any other mass transit in the nation.

6It also moves more people than any other form of mass transit. In 2013, about 480,000 buses did this daily work. They carried slightly more than half of all public school students. The American school bus fleet has more than twice as many vehicles as every other mass transit system in the country combined. Hong Kong, across the Pacific Ocean, offers a comparison. There, 90 percent of all travel is done by mass transit. Seven million people ride each day. In 2013, twenty-six million students across the United States rode school buses daily. Several reasons make the American system so large. The country covers a huge area. The population is large. In many places, students have no other public transit. This is especially true in rural areas. Those areas often have no public transit at all. Rural American school bus routes tend to be very complex. They also spread over wide areas. The rural system in Kingman, Arizona, covers an area larger than the entire state of Delaware. A 1973 scene shows white children riding a bus. They traveled from a North Carolina suburb into the inner city of Charlotte.

7A 1979 scene shows black children and their mothers on a bus. They crossed Cleveland, Ohio, as part of a desegregation plan. In recent years, coordinators have met new problems while planning routes. Some districts have consolidated schools. Consolidation is a process in which several smaller schools combine inside one larger building. Many students can share resources in that larger school. Sharing can cut education costs. Consolidation also means some students must travel much farther. In those districts the bus system becomes extremely important. Routes grow larger and more complex. One of the country's longest routes was in rural Texas. In the mid-1990s it carried some students roughly 100 miles (160 km) each way. Those students spent more time on the bus than they spent in school. During the second half of the twentieth century, school districts tried to aim the bus system at a new goal. That goal was school integration. School integration is the process of bringing African American students and white students together in schools. Before 1954, many American schools were segregated. Black students and white students were sent to separate schools. Those separate schools were not equal. White students usually received better educational opportunities.

8They also received more resources than black students did. Then, in 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court made a landmark decision. The case is called Brown v. Board of Education. The Court declared that school segregation discriminated against African American students. Integration began after that ruling. In the South, integration met fierce resistance. In Northern states and Western states, segregation was de facto. Black families and white families already lived in separate neighborhoods. As a result, their children went to different schools. School buses took on an important role at this point. In the 1970s and 1980s, schools worked together on a practice called desegregation busing. Black students were bused to white schools. White students were bused in the other direction. The practice was controversial. By the 1990s, most school districts had stopped it. A size comparison helps explain wide rural routes. At 1,954 square miles (5,060 sq km), Delaware is the second smallest of the fifty states. In Arizona, the Kingman Unified School District covers more than 3,000 square miles (7,779 sq km). If that district is counted as 3,000 square miles, a difference can be found. The district is 1,046 square miles (2,709 sq km) larger than Delaware.

9Coordinators must study several factors so these wide routes work well. They try to keep students from spending too much time commuting every day. They place bus stops that are not too far from students' homes. Each district decides what walk range to the stop is acceptable. Many districts offer a bus to any student who lives more than 2 miles (3.2 km) from school. A bus is also often offered when walking would put a student in danger. Crossing a highway is one example. The work of setting routes is done before each school year begins. Around 1910, a horse-drawn stagecoach used as a school bus waited in front of a high school in Colorado. American public schools organized mass transportation for students long before the modern school bus existed. In the nineteenth century, many students attended one-room schoolhouses. Those schools stood in rural districts where few people lived. Some students walked. Others used horse-drawn wagons or sleds. Over time, districts learned that a system of horse-drawn wagons was efficient. The wagons traveled between collection points that had been arranged ahead of time. They picked up students and carried them to school. Populations grew, and technology advanced.

10Transit systems then changed over to motor vehicles. The basic idea of public transportation for students stayed the same. Districts used large passenger vehicles. They designed routes and sent vehicles around them. They fetched students before school. At the end of the day they delivered students home, or near home. The big yellow school bus that students know today developed over time. The first motorized vehicles that carried students did not look much like modern buses. A school bus from the 1920s resembled an extra-long Model T. Buses gradually grew larger so they could hold more and more students. The yellow color was adopted because it is highly visible. Educators wanted school buses to stand out on the road. Parents wanted the same thing. Motorists could then see a bus easily and stop in time for students to board safely. Today, federal law requires American school buses to be painted a color called National School Bus Glossy Yellow. The law also requires the label School Bus. Those letters must be at least 8 inches (20 cm) high. These rules are meant to make school buses instantly recognizable. A picture from 1925 shows one of those early motor buses.

45. How the Colonies Broke with the Crown

1A map of North America in 1750 shows who claimed which land. New France covers a wide northern stretch. British Canada sits nearby. British colonies line the Atlantic coast. Louisiana is marked. So is a disputed zone. Florida appears. New Spain appears. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean frame the continent. More than 200 years ago, colonists began a war against an empire. They came out of that war as the winners. Their homes were in the land now called the United States. The empire they fought was Great Britain. Britain was already old, rich, and strong. It wanted a larger empire. It wanted firm control of land in the place Europeans then named the New World. That name covered the Americas. North America was part of it. Central America was part of it. South America was part of it. Britain was not alone in that desire. Other countries in Europe wanted American land too. Europeans saw raw materials in the New World. They also saw room for populations that were growing at home. Indigenous peoples were already there. They had lived on that land for thousands of years. Spain began colonizing in the 1400s. Spanish colonizers enslaved Indigenous people. They also killed Indigenous people whose families had lived there across thousands of years. Deaths by the 1700s stood in the millions. Violent fighting caused many of those deaths. Disease brought by Europeans caused many more. In eastern North America, Great Britain seized Indigenous land by force. On that land Britain set up thirteen colonies. People who crossed the Atlantic to live in those colonies were called colonists. The ocean distance let them form their own ideas. It also let them form their own habits. Each colony held a charter from the British king. Each colony also had a legislature. Property owners in the colony elected that legislature. A strong independent spirit grew from this life. That spirit later fed the Revolutionary War. The break is striking because the two sides had once been partners. France and Great Britain spent the 1700s fighting several wars. North American land was the prize. Colonists stood with Britain in those fights. Their shared foe was France. The 1750s brought the same hunger for land.

2France wanted it. England wanted it too. For hundreds of years the two kingdoms had competed in Europe for power and territory. The same rivalry crossed the ocean. French explorers had traveled a long route. The route started at Newfoundland. It followed the St. Lawrence River downstream. The Great Lakes were on it. The valley of the Ohio River was on it too. Trading posts along that route were the work of French fur trappers. England claimed those same regions. England urged colonists to settle them. Indigenous nations nearby usually had a warmer tie with the French. Relations with the British were harder. Years of trade explain that bond. British settlers kept pushing west and leaving the East Coast behind. They claimed ground where Indigenous people had lived for centuries. They claimed hunting ground too. Indigenous people wanted those ancestral lands back. A painting shows the Battle of Fort Duquesne. The year of that battle is 1756. Many Indigenous nations joined France. They hoped to protect trade. They hoped to protect their lands. They hoped to protect their independence. Other nations joined Great Britain. They were promised some land in return. The Cherokee were among them. The Catawba were among them. So were nations of the Iroquois Confederacy. France had partners too. The Delaware sided with France. The Shawnee sided with France. The Ottawa sided with France. Forts rose across the valley of the Ohio River. Both European powers built them. Each fort was meant to guard a claim. Early in 1754 the French raised Fort Duquesne. The name is said doo-KAYN. Today the city of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, stands on that spot. Britain had started a fort in a place that could control the whole valley. French forces drove the British workers off. The French then finished the fort themselves. A map of the fort labels the Ohio River. It labels the Allegheny River. It labels the Monongahela River. Britain sent a young surveyor to tell the French to go. His name was George Washington. Eight other men went with him. The French would not leave. Washington, his men, and Seneca allies then struck a party of French scouts. Ten of the scouts were killed. Twenty-one others were captured. Washington's group next built Fort Necessity.

3It stood about 60 miles from Fort Duquesne. That distance is 96.5 kilometers. In the summer of 1754 the French took Fort Necessity. Washington and his men gave up. After the surrender, they got away. Washington later served as a volunteer aide. He worked beside Britain's General Edward Braddock. Braddock meant to push the French out of the Ohio River Valley. Fort Duquesne was the place to start. French soldiers hid in the woods. Indigenous allies hid with them. They waited beside the marching British columns. Then they sprang an ambush. General Braddock was killed. More than half his men were killed too. The British who lived panicked. They ran. Many people call this clash the opening true battle in a conflict named the French and Indian War. A wider struggle contained it. People know that wider struggle as the Seven Years' War. Colonists remembered the surprise style of fighting. In the American Revolution they later used the same guerrilla warfare against British soldiers. A later map shows land claims once the war had ended. British Canada remains in the north. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean still frame the land. Thirteen colonies sit along the east. Some inland ground is marked British but reserved for Indigenous peoples. New Spain and Florida appear as well. In 1756 Great Britain officially declared war on France. Formal fighting started that year. Battles had already been fought in the two years before. Those earlier battles took place in North America. They also took place in Europe. Britain sent more soldiers to the colonies. France sent more soldiers too. Early on, France looked likely to win. Indigenous allies helped the French. The French also understood frontier fighting better than the British or the colonists. The balance changed by 1758. Britain's force on the continent had grown to almost 42,000. Those troops hit key points. Fort Niagara was one. Lake Champlain was one. Quebec was one. France lost its link to the Ohio River Valley. It lost its link to the Mississippi River. It lost the port at New Orleans. France had claimed all of that land. Supplies from those places had kept the French alive in North America.

4The winner of the war was Great Britain. A peace called the Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763. East of the Mississippi, French claims across North America were wiped away. British colonists could now move into land France had controlled. Florida stood at one end of the newly open land. Canada stood at the other. For Indigenous nations the change was a disaster. Colonists took still more of their land. For a short time after the French defeat, colonists were glad to belong to Great Britain. Many of them had fought next to British troops. They had shared an enemy. Once France was beaten, that feeling changed. British protection no longer seemed necessary to many colonists. They no longer wanted British oversight either. Several British moves after the war made them angry. King George III and Parliament raised colonial taxes. The goal was to shrink the huge debt the war had created. Britain also posted soldiers in the colonies to guard the bigger empire. Colonists were told to house those soldiers. They were told to feed them. Britain tried to slow American settlement farther west. Leaders hoped that limit would mend ties with Indigenous nations. A year had passed since the peace signed in Paris. The new year was 1764. Parliament passed the Sugar Act. An older law was being widened. People called that older law the Sugar and Molasses Act. It dated from 1733. Colonists who bought Spanish molasses now paid a tax. French molasses was taxed too. Spanish sugar was taxed. French sugar was taxed. Coffee gained a tax. Some textiles gained a tax. The law also tightened rules on lumber leaving the colonies. Iron exports were regulated further. Markets where colonists could sell their goods were limited. Cheap sugar from Spain and from France became too costly. Colonists had to buy British sugar instead. The money helped the British government pay war debts. The colonial economy was thrown off by the change. In 1765 Parliament passed the Quartering Act. The Seven Years' War had ended. About 10,000 British troops were still in America. The act told colonists to lodge those troops in private homes. The soldiers lived with families. They did not have to pay rent. No duty required them to help around the house.

5Every colony refused except Pennsylvania. What New York would not give was billeting. Billeting means food and a place to stay. Parliament answered by suspending New York's governor. It also suspended the colony's legislature. The punishment was meant to force obedience. The tax that truly enraged people was the Stamp Act. Parliament passed it that same year. It was Britain's first serious try to press authority over the North American colonies. Printed paper now required a stamp. The stamp was British, and colonists had to pay for it. Books were taxed. Newspapers were taxed. Calendars were taxed. Playing cards were taxed. Other paper goods were taxed. Hidden in the details was an income tax. It was the first tax aimed only at the American colonies. Colonists did not want an outside power taking their money. British leaders felt they had carried the colonies for too long. In Britain's view, colonists owed support to the government. That government had been their protector. That government had also fought France beside them. The loudest colonial complaint was about voice. The government that taxed them gave them no say. People cried out that tax without representation was wrong. They wanted Parliament to hold a voice that belonged to them. Other English subjects had that kind of voice. King George disliked being told what to do by colonists. He believed the American colonies should pay to support his empire. The king considered how to strike back at the rebellious colonists. At the same time, the colonists began to act together against the taxes. Over the years they had built ways to govern themselves. Virginia's elected assembly was the House of Burgesses. It made laws for that colony. It was founded in 1619. No earlier elected assembly existed in a North American colony. Other colonies treated it as a model. Among the British colonies, the Virginia Assembly was the earliest body voters had elected. In 1765 its members debated whether the Stamp Act was fair. Patrick Henry was a young lawyer. He stood and made a claim. Only people of Virginia, he said, could place a tax on Virginians. The assembly accepted his stand. Some people still called him a traitor.

6They said he was arguing against the Crown. Women in the 1700s were mostly shut out of politics. They still served the patriotic cause. A group called the Daughters of Liberty organized boycotts. Members joined the boycotts themselves. Many women bought the goods a household needed. Some ran small shops. Because of that, refusing British goods hit British merchants hard. Women also formed sewing circles to aid the revolutionary cause. Newspapers printed Henry's position. Soon protest against the Stamp Act spread through all 13 colonies. Samuel Adams added his voice. He was a tax collector. He was also a politician from Massachusetts. Adams, Henry, and others who stood with them gained a name. People called them Patriots. They stood with their colonies and against the king. Support for King George earned a different name. Those colonists were called Loyalists. Their loyalty was to the Crown. Some Patriots formed the Sons of Liberty. The Daughters of Liberty were already organizing. Both groups urged people not to trade with Britain. They urged people not to buy British goods. Some colonists even attacked British stamp agents. Parliament had more acts still to pass. More attacks were still to come. In October 1765, representatives from nine colonies traveled to New York. Thirteen colonies existed, so four stayed away. People call that meeting the Stamp Act Congress. Its request to Parliament was a repeal of the Stamp Act. Repeal means to cancel it. King George said yes to canceling it. The year of that yes was 1766. The calm did not last. In 1767 the Townshend Acts became law. They taxed glass. They taxed paint. They taxed lead. They taxed paper. They taxed tea. The money was supposed to pay for running the colonies. Anger rose again, just as it had against earlier taxes. Colonists boycotted British goods. To boycott is to refuse to buy. In 1770 Britain withdrew every Townshend tax except one. British merchants were losing income. Tea was the one tax that remained. Strain between Patriots and Great Britain kept growing. British soldiers spread through the colonies to make people pay. Each new tax added resentment. One night in Boston, resentment turned into violence. The French and Indian War was over.

7In the years that followed, many British soldiers lived in Boston. Open trouble stayed rare for a time. Colonists hated having soldiers in their houses. Years passed with both groups sharing the same streets. The date was March 5, 1770. That night a rowdy Boston crowd picked a fight. The fight was with some British soldiers. The soldiers fired into the crowd. Five colonists died. Those colonists had been armed only with snowballs. They also had sticks. They also had stones. Samuel Adams, a Patriot, saw a chance. He wanted more colonists to favor independence. Paul Revere was his friend. Adams asked him to make a picture. Revere was a silversmith. Revere engraved the scene. He printed it. He sold it as a poster. Adams named the fight the Boston Massacre. The printed image showed soldiers firing. The crowd in the picture looked peaceful and finely dressed. Newspapers printed the image too. The picture did not tell the night truthfully. It still did what Adams wanted. Many colonists became enraged. The picture people remember is that engraving of British force used on colonists who looked peaceful. Many people believe Crispus Attucks was the first to die in that Boston crowd. He lived in the city. His ships worked out of Boston Harbor. Freedom from Great Britain was a belief he held strongly. Speakers at his memorial praised his bravery again and again. A picture records his face. Tea was all that remained of the Townshend taxes. The tea tax itself was not new. In 1773 the Tea Act was revised. Colonists were required to buy tea from only one seller. That seller was Great Britain's East India Company. The company was failing with money. Colonists still had no seats in Parliament. They were angry that some taxes had never been canceled. In December 1773 a frustrated group acted. They climbed onto a British ship. They dumped tea into Boston Harbor. The load was 342 chests. Their clothing copied the dress of the Mohawk Nation. The disguise was meant to keep blame off them. Britain was not fooled. Britain was not amused. Leaders decided the time for goodwill had ended. People later called the night the Boston Tea Party. Summer of 1774 brought the reply.

8King George and Parliament passed the Coercive Acts. Colonists renamed them the Intolerable Acts. The laws were written to punish rebels. Punishment would last at least until Britain was paid back for the tea. One law shut Boston Harbor to every ship. Many workers in Boston lost their jobs. Families feared they would starve. Colonists elsewhere felt sorry for Boston. They were furious at Great Britain. Colonial assemblies spoke up for the city. British governors in those colonies often did not want that support declared. Britain named General Thomas Gage governor of Massachusetts. He was sent to Boston to take the city in hand. He brought 4,000 troops. Colonists had to house that army. They had to feed it. The Intolerable Acts pulled the colonies together against Britain. The Stamp Act had done something similar before. In September 1774, delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia. The meeting was the First Continental Congress. Every colony sent people except one. The missing colony was Georgia. A picture shows Patrick Henry speaking. The listeners look fully absorbed. The delegates demanded a repeal of the Intolerable Acts. They also demanded a colonial voice in every tax law. Parliament refused both demands. Mutiny was the word Parliament used for the colonies. Wider boycotts were the delegates' answer. This time the refusal covered all British goods. They knew their choices might bring war with Great Britain. They agreed to gather again in 1775. Meanwhile they told colonists in Massachusetts to store weapons. Massachusetts looked like the right place to start. General Gage and his soldiers were already in Boston. The Continental Congress began training fighters. People called them militiamen. People also called them minutemen. Colonists were getting ready to fight for independence. Many of them no longer believed the old country. Many no longer trusted it. Patriot soldiers earned the nickname minutemen for their speed. They could seize their weapons and be outside within a minute. Most of them did not even have uniforms. In Boston, General Gage grew alarmed. Reports said colonists were storing weapons at Concord. Concord lies about 20 miles west of Boston. That is 32 kilometers. The date was April 18, 1775. That night he sent out 700 British soldiers.

9The mission was secret. They were to seize the weapons. Gage also hoped to arrest two rebel leaders. One was Samuel Adams. The other was John Hancock. Both were in Lexington, a town near Concord. A picture shows General Thomas Gage. The plan leaked through a Patriot doctor. His name was Samuel Prescott. He warned the militia that British troops were on the way. Before the soldiers reached Concord, they met a waiting group. Lexington's village green held seventy waiting militiamen. The British tried to walk past them. Then a shot rang out. Nobody had ordered it. Nobody knows which side fired it. That shot began the Revolutionary War. A later poem by Ralph Waldo Emerson gave the moment a famous name. The poem is called Concord Hymn. In the fight that followed, eight militiamen died. Ten more were wounded. British losses were heavy. The soldiers still marched on toward Concord. Boston still tells a famous tale about Paul Revere. The tale says he warned the fighters at Lexington and at Concord that British troops were approaching. The tale is taller than the truth. Something else is true. What Revere did do was send someone to observe the soldiers. The spy was to hang lanterns in a church tower. The number of lanterns would show the route. One lantern meant the soldiers were coming by land. Two lanterns meant they would cross the Charles River. That night Revere saw two lanterns. He left Boston on horseback. William Dawes rode with him. They headed toward Concord to spread the warning. Samuel Prescott joined them on the road. British officers stopped Revere. They stopped Dawes too. Prescott got away. He was the rider who actually reached the militiamen with the warning. A picture shows the famous midnight ride that stories still give to Revere. In Concord the British wrecked some supplies. Most of the weapons were already gone. Americans had hidden them before the troops arrived. Hancock escaped arrest. Adams escaped too. Massachusetts militia reached Concord with nearly 500 men. At the North Bridge they attacked British soldiers who were worn out. The next day the British began marching back to Boston. The attack continued along that road. Militiamen hid behind trees.

10They hid behind stone walls. From there they fired into the British lines. That same style had shown up before. French fighters used it in the war that also involved Indigenous nations. So did those Indigenous fighters. Trained British professionals felt humiliated. They had lost to colonists who were quickly trained and poorly matched in equipment. The dead numbered 273 on the British side. The dead numbered 93 among the militiamen. The Revolutionary War was underway. A picture shows Patriot troops facing British soldiers. Lexington, Massachusetts, is the town in the scene. The ground under them is the village green. These words help a reader follow the story. Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. A colonist is a person living in a colony. The word also fits a person who helps found one. Delegates are chosen or elected people who speak and act for others. Economy means how money circulates. It moves through industry. It moves through trade. It moves through finance. The setting may be a country or a smaller region. Export means sending materials or products away so they can be sold somewhere else. To found something is to create it or set it up, as with a group or an organization. Guerrilla warfare is irregular fighting, often a surprise attack, by small independent bands of soldiers. Imposed means forced on people by power or by authority. A legislature is an elected group. Its work is writing laws and changing laws. Levied means collected by a government, as a tax is collected. Migrated means moved on purpose from one region to another to live or to work. Mutiny is a refusal to obey a government or another authority, a rebellion. Parliament is the lawmaking body of the United Kingdom. Two houses form it. One is the House of Commons. The second house is the House of Lords. Basic substances used to make other things are called raw materials. Regulated means controlled in amount, rate, speed, or behavior so that something worked properly or followed rules. Reimbursed means paid back for money already spent. Stationed means assigned to a place. Stockpile means to keep a large supply for a later need.

46. How the Piano Took Shape

1A major maker of fine pianos keeps a factory in New York, shown here. Another factory stands in Germany. The parts of this book come in this order. Keyboards from long ago come first. Then comes the earliest piano of the modern kind. Then comes the spread of pianos. Then come later designs. A word list comes last. Keyboards from Long Ago Few instruments are as widely known as the piano. Listeners can pick out its sound in almost any style of music. The sound was not always the one people hear now. Earlier relatives of the piano made very different tones. The clavichord was the first keyboard to be used widely. Players in Europe were using it by the 1400s. Nobody knows who invented it. That is true of many early instruments. It was a long box made of wood. Wire strings of uneven lengths were stretched inside. A soundboard lay under those strings.

2When the strings moved, the board moved with them. That movement helped the tones carry. Length ran from 122 centimeters to 213 centimeters. In feet, that is about 4 to 7. People set the box on a table before they played. Homes in the fifteenth century were one place it was heard. The First Piano of the Modern Kind In the opening years of the 1700s, Bartolomeo Cristofori built instruments that had keyboards. His first name is said bar-toh-loh-MEH-oh. His family name is said kree-STAW-foh-ree. He wanted a harpsichord whose loudness a player could control. To get that control, the instrument had to behave more like a clavichord. Strings had to be struck. Plucking them would not do. He rebuilt the mechanism, the set of parts that make the instrument work. A quill gave way to a hammer. Leather covered the hammer so the tone would be better.

3A pressed key sent the hammer up into the string from underneath. Letting go of the key brought down a piece called a damper. The damper rested on the string. Vibration stopped, and the note ended. How the Parts Move The main pieces are the string, the damper, the key, and the hammer. Pressing a key sends a small hammer upward. It strikes the string that sits above it. Letting go lets the damper drop back onto that string. The note stops. A grand piano Cristofori built in 1720 still exists. It is the oldest one anywhere that has survived. Players could now strike hard or touch the keys lightly. Both loud notes and soft notes were possible. He named the instrument the pianoforte. Italian supplies both halves of that name. One half means soft. The other half means loud. Later the name shortened to piano. Other builders added to what he had designed.

4A German builder named Silbermann took his version to Johann Sebastian Bach. Bach had already written a great deal of music for the harpsichord. He was not impressed by Silbermann’s piano. Silbermann was so angry that he broke the instrument apart with an ax. Pianos in Many Places European musicians did not welcome the piano quickly. Bach’s opinion of it warmed later. Haydn wrote many pieces for it. Mozart did too. By the late 1700s, listeners in Europe wanted more music written for piano. Builders changed the instrument so it would sound better in large halls. Felt replaced leather on the hammers. The softer cloth gave a tone that was rich and warm. Keyboards grew as well. A keyboard once held fifty-four keys. Later models held eighty-eight. Grand pianos, shaped like a wing, were made longer and bigger. The extra length made room for more strings.

5Soundboards of metal took the place of wooden ones. Tones came out purer. Some pieces keep a crowd of hammers in motion. Fine Playing and a Heavy Cost An old compliment said a fine player could “tickle the ivories.” The saying came from the keys. Wood keys were once faced with ivory cut from elephant tusks. Elephants died in huge numbers because of that use. Using ivory is against the law today. Plastic now covers the keys. Louis Pratt, shown in 1955, was a master at cutting ivory. African elephant tusks supplied the keys his company made. Every early piano was a grand piano. By the nineteenth century, demand in Europe was very high. Demand in North America was very high too. Makers answered the demand with pianos that were smaller and cost less. Buyers could then choose an instrument that fit inside a house. Women at the Keyboard In the nineteenth century, girls and women were urged to learn the piano.

6The aim was not a life on stage. The aim was to prepare them to be wives. Skill at music was treated as a sign of grace and charm. Playing also opened a path to teaching. A woman who taught piano could earn her own pay. Chances to earn money were scarce for women then. A postcard from long ago pictures a duet. A woman and a child share the bench. As sales rose, players tried more kinds of piano music. African Americans sang gospel at the piano and played it there too. They also tested new styles. Ragtime was one result. It is a jazzy music written only for this instrument. Players Who Became Famous Many pianists known around the world have built a name in a certain genre, or type, of music. A few of them are listed here.

7Scott Joplin was the son of a man who worked on the railway. People called Joplin the “King of Ragtime.” His piece “Maple Leaf Rag” came out in 1899. It is the ragtime hit more people know than any other. Sergei Rachmaninoff was a Russian composer of the early twentieth century. His first name is said syihr-GYAY. His family name is said ruhk-MAH-nyi-nuhf. He was a highly skilled pianist as well. He wrote classical pieces for piano and played them himself. Many of those pieces are beautiful. Billy Joel is known as the “Piano Man.” From the 1970s on, he wrote rock songs built around the piano and performed them. An electric motor drives the player piano in this picture. The instrument dates to the late 1800s. Later Designs Recorded music arrived in the early twentieth century. Sales of pianos fell. A family could hear piano music at home without owning an instrument or learning to play.

8Builders looked for a way to draw buyers back. They made pianos that played themselves. A mechanical device sat inside. Foot pedals at the bottom pumped it. Rolls of paper were held in the device. Holes punched in the paper told the piano which notes to sound. Pumping the pedals set those notes off. Lessons were no longer required. Anyone could have music from the instrument. Digital forms of these self-playing pianos showed up in the 1980s. A player picked an electronic file and pressed a button. The keys moved by themselves while the music sounded. A person could also play this piano by hand. Weight was built into all eighty-eight keys. Fingers met a feel close to an older instrument. Tone and touch on a digital model both stay close to that. It is lighter, and it costs less. Many families today own a piano that is electronic, also called digital.

9A band in Australia includes someone playing a digital keyboard. Digital keyboards are different in one important way. Their keys are not weighted. The size people buy most often has only sixty-one keys. These keyboards are light. They are sturdy. They are easy to carry from one place to another. Some bands that travel use them. Many of them can copy other instruments. A trumpet sound is possible. A flute sound is possible. Some can make effects, such as a bird’s chirp, from a single key. Cristofori would be astonished by the noises coming from the newest forms of what he invented. A digital keyboard is one end of the range. A concert grand is the other. Either way, the piano is still among the instruments people love most. Words to Know plucked (v.): pulled at something, or picked at it, and then let it go.

10project (v.): to make a sound louder, or to cause it to carry. soundboard (n.): a thin board under the strings of an instrument, placed there so the sound is louder. vibrated (v.): shifted back and forth at high speed. ancestors (n.): relatives who lived a long time before now. attractive (adj.): having a quality that pleases someone or draws that person closer. digital (adj.): related to computers or to electronics. composer (n.): someone whose work is writing music. felt (n.): a cloth that is firm and soft, made by pressing fibers together with heat. lever (n.): a flat bar, or a handle, pressed so that a machine, an instrument, or another device will work. mechanism (n.): one piece of a machine, or several pieces working as a set. pedals (n.): flat levers pushed by the feet in order to play certain instruments.

47. Hunger Close to Home

1State cards called Electronic Benefit Transfer cards look like credit cards. They took the place of food stamps. The topics move from a hidden epidemic to the reasons food costs too much. Next comes how help with food works, then the politics of hunger. After that, the book shows how gaps get filled, how kids can help, and how anyone can help. A word list comes last. School's final day has arrived. A long summer break thrills almost everyone. A boy named Aaron is the exception. He sinks in his chair. His head rests on the desk. His stomach growls. School lunch was his only meal today. He knows the cupboards at home hold nothing. His mother holds two jobs. Even so, food money is gone by the month's end. He lets out a sigh. A long summer stretches ahead of him. Aaron is not alone. Millions of children in America are hungry each day. You might be one of those children. United States Department of Agriculture is the long name behind the USDA. That agency counted households in 2019. It found 35.2 million Americans in homes it called food-insecure. People in those homes could not always get enough food for everyone who lived there. Children made up 10.7 million of that count. About one child in seven in the United States was food insecure. Hunger causes pain. It also causes stress. A health agency called the CDC studied children who eat too little. Its long name is the Centers for Disease Control. Prevention is part of that name too. Those children have more health troubles than children who eat enough. They also miss more school.

2Once they are in class, focusing is harder. Learning is harder too. Tiredness from hunger keeps them from enough exercise. The harm lasts. Young bodies grow quickly. Young brains develop quickly too. Too little food can slow the body. It can slow the mind as well. The United States raises food in huge amounts. It sends millions of pounds of food to other countries. The government runs programs for people who cannot pay for meals. Hunger in the United States is still an epidemic. The question is why. Trouble can strike any family. A factory shuts, and a parent loses work. A guardian falls ill and cannot work. One parent, raising children alone, has to remain at home. The reason may be an aging relative. The reason may be a sick child. Lost pay, or pay that was never enough, forces hard choices. Sometimes the choice is bills or meals. Millions of Americans hold full-time jobs and are still food insecure. Since the 1950s, housing has cost more. Medical care has cost more. Food has cost more. Those rises have outstripped the wages of most people. The lowest legal pay was fixed in 2009 by the federal government. It was $7.25 for each hour. A full-time year at that rate is $15,080. Many jobs at that pay hire people only part of the time. The aim is to skip benefits. Health insurance is one benefit they skip. Taxes and insurance can squeeze people who earn more than that too. USDA numbers say women are more than 60 percent of the adults who get food help. The National Women's Law Center reports another gap. Low-paying jobs are where women land more than twice as often as men.

3Even in matching work, a woman is still likely to be paid less than a man. In 2019 the Institute for Women's Policy Research measured full-time pay. Women earned 81.5 cents for each dollar a man earned. The U.S. Census counts single parents who care for children. Women are more than 80 percent of that group. They are twice as likely as single fathers to live in poverty. A mother in poverty often means her children live in poverty too. Help with food from the federal government started as help for farmers. The time was the Great Depression. From 1933, the USDA bought crops farmers could not sell. Those surplus crops went to people who needed them. In 1939 the government printed real stamps. People used the stamps to buy leftover food. By 1964, buyers could choose any kind of food. Surplus food was no longer the only choice. A new name arrived for the Food Stamp Program in 2008. It became the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. The new name showed a fresh focus on nutrition. A picture from the Great Depression shows the government handing out extra food. The goal was to feed hungry Americans. A chart asks who gets SNAP. The chart's source is a research group. Its name joins the Center on Budget with Policy Priorities. People who are elderly, along with people who have disabilities, are 23 percent. Children are 44 percent. Other adults are 33 percent. Nearly two-thirds of SNAP users in 2018 were children. Elderly people and people who have disabilities filled out that share.

4Income is what the federal government checks before it grants food stamps. In 2020, a two-person family earning $17,240 in a year sat at the poverty level. That is the government's name for that line. A single parent at the minimum wage, working full time, earns $15,080 a year. That parent and that child both live in poverty. SNAP served Americans in 2019. The number was above thirty-five million. A month of food-stamp help averages under $5 for each day. A second federal program has a long name. WIC stands for a long federal title. It begins with Special Supplemental Nutrition Program. The program serves women. It also serves infants and children. People call it WIC. It helps women who are pregnant. It helps children younger than five. The foods are chosen for nutrition. Milk is one. Baby formula is another. Baby food is another. The National School Lunch Program, or NSLP, reaches more than thirty million children. It serves free lunches at public schools. It also serves lunches at a lower price. Family income does not decide who may eat. First Lady Michelle Obama pressed for a new law. Congress approved a 2010 law. Its name begins Healthy, Hunger-Free. The ending is Kids Act. Funding for NSLP went up. New rules for nutrition were set. That was the first such reset in thirty years. A picture shows children eating a free lunch at a school in Oregon. Some schools with low incomes get federal money for breakfast. The same money covers lunch. Every student at those schools can eat free. The government does spread a safety net under many hungry Americans. The money set aside for federal food programs still changes from year to year.

5Politics shifted, and the program was cut hard in 1980 and 1981. Some of that money was put back by 1990. In some years Congress removes billions from SNAP. In some years it adds money for school lunches. People argue about the size of the federal food budget. They argue about who should be fed. They argue about the test for who qualifies. One example is the poverty measure still in use. It was first built in the 1960s. The formula does count inflation. It does not count other costs that keep rising. It does not count the way family budgets have shifted. Childcare has climbed faster than food. Housing, transportation, and education have climbed faster too. More families now strain to pay what they owe. Qualifying is not the same as receiving help. Plenty of people never learn that they qualify. Plenty do not know the steps to apply for SNAP. Shame stops others from asking. An application often means leaving work for part of a day. It also means finding a ride to a government office. Missing work is a cost that hungry people cannot pay. A chart titled A Spike in SNAP counts participants in the millions. The Great Recession hit the United States at the close of 2007. It lasted several years. The 1930s Great Depression was the last time the economy had dropped this far. Jobs vanished for millions. In time, millions of those jobless Americans used SNAP to help buy food. Month by month, more people met the rules. More of the people who met the rules joined.

6By 2012, SNAP reached more than 46 million people. That was a rise of 76 percent from the start of the Great Recession. The U.S. Department of Agriculture is the source of those figures. High-poverty places are often food deserts. A food desert is a place large grocery stores do not serve. Some are city centers where shops have shut. Others are country places with few people. A trip of ten miles for groceries is more than many can pay. Fifteen miles is too far as well. They buy simple food at small shops nearby. Prices there are usually higher. Quality meat is often missing. Fresh produce is often missing too. Minority communities suffer in a special way. Many of them cannot reach the big chain supermarkets. When federal money cannot cover every hungry American, local programs step in. Food banks exist in every state. They gather food from growers. They gather it from restaurants and from grocery stores. Charities then give it out. Food pantries are one kind of charity. Soup kitchens are another. Both serve the public. Cans and other foods that do not spoil quickly are common. Fresh produce is hard to store, so banks often skip it. Community gardens can close part of the nutrition gap for people with less money. Neighbors plant the food. They tend it. They pick it for home use or to share. The United States and Canada together have more than eighteen thousand of these gardens. Many of them grow vegetables for a nearby food bank. A picture shows a mother and her children in Colorado. They plant tomatoes in a garden at a middle school.

7The harvest is meant for a local food bank. Feeding America is the biggest nonprofit that helps families in America. Food banks in its network number more than two hundred. It has sixty thousand food pantries. About twelve million kids get meals from them each year. Charities still supply less than 6 percent of food help in the United States. Costs go up. Pay stays flat. Federal food programs get cut. These groups then find they cannot cover the need. Food runs out. Families are turned away. A nonprofit called AmpleHarvest links gardens that have extra produce with food charities. The link covers more than 7,500 charities. Washington, D.C., is home to the Central Kitchen, where volunteers cook. That kitchen turns out 4,500 meals each day. The meals go to shelters for people without homes. They go to soup kitchens. They go to other programs too. Kids themselves can act, beyond stamps and banks. Students in Concord, New Hampshire, held a hunger banquet for parents. The price of a seat was canned food for the pantry. In Bellingham, Massachusetts, a class of sixth graders filmed a video about hunger. The video won an award. It was meant to build awareness in town. Other students have raised cash for food banks. Bake sales were one way. Selling art was another path. So were washing cars, walk-a-thons, and read-a-thons. More kinds of fundraising have been used as well. Sam Adamo took his cello to a local farmers' market. He gathered $700 for the food bank near him in Rhode Island. Carson Pazdan loved to cook. He made a cookbook written for kids and by kids.

8Sales brought in more than $20,000. The money went to the Northern Illinois Food Bank. Macy Stewart was nine. She handed out empty bags at school. She asked classmates to fill the bags for St. Mary's Food Bank. The bags held 844 pounds of food. That weight is 383 kilograms. St. Mary's Food Bank stands in Surprise, Arizona. It was the first food bank in the world. The year it opened was 1967. William Winslow was seven when he saw a problem. Wake County, in North Carolina, had children who would lack food over spring break. A Mexican restaurant in town was the partner he requested. Customers who brought food got free cheese dip. The food was for BackPack Buddies. That program sends weekend meals home with students who need them. Next he asked a local grocery store for a spot outside the door. He wanted to tell shoppers about the program. One weekend produced 1,400 pounds of food. That is 635 kilograms. Cash gifts added $305. The gift meant extra food went home over spring break. Some states have lifted the lowest legal pay to between $10 and $15 an hour. Hunger rates in those states have dropped. William is in fourth grade now. He still runs a fundraiser every year. In 2016 he signed up 171 volunteers and organized them. They collected gifts at ten grocery stores. The gifts became eleven thousand meals for children in the region. In 2017 he hoped to spread the work across North Carolina. He swims. He is a Cub Scout. He says he is only a regular kid who gets involved. Any child can help, he says, if that child decides to try.

9In 2016 he gathered 8,100 pounds for BackPack Buddies. That weight is 3,674 kilograms. A map called Map the Meal Gap shows how common food insecurity is. One band is 4 to 14 percent. The next is 15 to 19 percent. Then comes 20 to 24 percent. Then 25 to 29 percent. The highest band is 30 percent or more. The map lets you compare hunger inside your own state. You can then set your state and your region beside other places. Ask where the share of food insecurity is highest. Ask where it is lowest. A household garden can send extra produce to a nearby pantry. You can also plant one more patch just to give away. Kids can give part of an allowance. They can ask others to give too. Children in Loudoun County, Virginia, made a simple plan. Each lunch they bought included a dime for the food bank. A school can run a drive to buy goods that food banks need. A nearby business can join the school in collecting funds. Learn what the nearby bank and the charities are short of. Learn which season brings the greatest need. Tell friends what you learn. Tell family and neighbors. Hunger in one's own town is something most people know little about. A letter to the local newspaper can teach them. You can study hunger where you live and read that report aloud in class. Letters can go to your representatives in Congress. Letters can go to state government and to local government. Ask them to back programs that keep every child fed. A letter-writing drive at school can tell officials what you think.

10The resources exist to keep children like Aaron from going hungry again. What is still needed is the will to do it. A phone line is there if you need food, or if somebody close to you does. Call 1-866-3-HUNGRY. Spanish speakers can call 1-877-8-HAMBRE. The National Hunger Hotline links callers to places that give emergency food. It also links them to government help and to other social services. The word list gives plain meanings. Access is a way to get near something, to enter it, or to be able to use it. Awareness is knowing that something is real. Benefits are money or services a government or a company gives someone. A campaign is a set of planned actions aimed at one goal. A census is an official count of the people in an area. An epidemic is something harmful or unwelcome that shows up suddenly in a community and spreads fast. Federal means the central government. That government shares power with states or with regions. Food assistance is help from federal programs for people who need food. Food banks are groups or centers that gather food and pass it to people who need it. A food stamp is a coupon, or another paper, that the government gives so people can buy food. Minimum wage is the smallest hourly pay the law allows. Nonprofit means the work is not done in order to make a profit. Outstripped means one thing passed another by being bigger, quicker, or stronger. Poverty is the condition of being poor. Surplus means more than needed, or what is left over.

48. Japan's Path to Anime

1Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki does many other jobs. He directs. He produces. He writes scripts. He writes books. He draws manga. A 2014 picture shows him speaking to the press at Studio Ghibli. He helped found that studio. Topics run from an introduction to art for everyone, then from curious sketches to comics. Later topics are cartoons that begin to move, the grief and lessons of war, anime now, and a word list. A picture pairs cave paintings at Lascaux, in France, with clay tablets from Mesopotamia. Both tell stories from long ago. Pictures existed long before written words. Many ancient cultures told stories with images. Some images were prehistoric paintings on cave walls. Some were fine figures cut into clay. The style showed how those artists saw themselves. It also showed how they saw the world they lived in. As language grew, people more often recorded ideas with written symbols. Words did that job too. Art stayed important to storytelling anyway. Today, images are not only paintings and drawings. They also move, in movies, in animated cartoons, and in video games. One widespread style of moving art comes from Japan. Japan is an island nation in Asia. People call the style anime. It is hugely popular all over the world. The story of this art goes back over two centuries.

2Earlier than the nineteenth century, large scrolls held most traditional art from Japan. The methods were exact. They took a long time. One method used a single long brushstroke for each image. Another method cut a reversed picture into a woodblock. Artists then spread a thick coat of ink and pressed the block onto a surface. That press made a print. The slow, difficult work made art costly. Only rich people in Japan could buy scroll art and enjoy it. Color prints needed a separate block for every color. Some finished pictures used twenty blocks. In 1814 a new art appeared. People called it manga. The sketches were drawn freehand on paper. Katsushika Hokusai was the artist who taught with these sketches. He urged students to draw pictures of their own. The students sketched and shared the work. Funny pictures caught on with the public. Because they were quick and easy to make, more people could afford them. Traditional scrolls had been out of reach for most. Manga was open to all Japanese people, not only affluent buyers of art. Japanese manga found its own strength in the late 1800s. Until the middle of that century, Japan stayed secluded. Contact with other nations was small. An 1853 naval trip from the United States changed that. Japan was pushed to unlock its ports.

3Trade with other countries was the demand. By 1858, trading ships regularly crossed the Pacific. They carried goods to six Japanese ports and back out again. British merchants rode those ships to the insular island nation. American merchants did too. Newspapers and magazines from home came with them. The word manga joins two Japanese words. Man means curious. Ga means sketches. Together they match the English word cartoon. Katsushika Hokusai was the first to use the term. He used it for the funny drawings in his own sketchbooks. Artists of Japanese manga were intrigued by what they saw in those papers. Political cartoons were one style. Comics were another. They began to use Western forms in their own work. Sequenced panels that tell a story were one of those forms. Soon, manga faces showed some of the strong feelings seen in Western drawings. By the start of the twentieth century, manga showed up often in Japanese newspapers. Political cartoons in that style made fun of the news of the day. Comic strips gave children and adults simple, funny stories. More and more readers loved these lively pictures. Strips in the papers look much like the Western strips they echo. The new century also brought a new entertainment: motion pictures. Studios in the United States started making movies.

4Other Western nations did too. Crowds flocked to theaters. The medium spread to more countries. Japan was one of them. The earliest movies were short. They were black and white. They were silent. Recorded talk was missing because the machines of the time could not match sound to the picture with accuracy. Musicians in the theater played as the film ran. Words on the screen explained the action. They also explained what the characters said. With no way to record voices, actors needed other tools for feeling. The acting was silent and still very dramatic. Faces and gestures were exaggerated. A picture from the 1917 silent film Patria shows actors. They use overly dramatic gestures in place of spoken lines, so viewers can read the feeling. Cartoonists everywhere were fascinated by movies. In the United States, illustrators found a way to make still sketches move. Walt Disney was one. Max Fleischer was another. Popular comic characters came alive on the big screen. Like live-action films, those cartoons had no sound. Music played while they ran. Characters in the cartoons told the story with movement. Gestures and expressions did the same work. People called the films shorts. A short ran for less than ten minutes. Children loved them. Adults loved them too. Theaters showed them before a full-length feature. In Japan, manga artists started making animated shorts of their own.

5Seitaro Kitayama was one of them. Bold manga faces suited the big action and the big expressions that silent stories needed. The Japanese name for these cartoons was animeshon. It came from the English word animation. In time the name shrank to anime. Better machines brought color to Western cartoons. Recorded talk arrived too. In the 1930s, cartoonists in America were pushed toward figures that looked more real. They were also pushed to make the motion more real. A process called rotoscoping helped. A movie projector threw a live actor's image onto a clear drawing board. The artist traced the outline onto a plastic sheet called a cel. A small action, such as sitting down, needed many cels. The result was impressive. Disney's first full-length animated film used this look. Snow White is the start of the title. The Seven Dwarfs completes it. It also used a new method called multiplane animation. The goal was a realistic background and realistic action. Different background pictures were painted on glass panels. The panels were stacked. During filming, the layers slid back and forth. That motion added depth and a sense of movement. Japanese anime later added sound. It did not copy Western tricks for a realistic look or for realistic motion. Animators kept treating the work as real art.

6The camera style matched other long Japanese films. A shot would hold still for a long time, then jump to a close-up for drama. Body movement was not casual. It was deliberate and carefully planned. Each small motion mattered to the plot. Artists also kept drawing in the black-and-white style that marked the work as truly Japanese. Walter Lantz Productions used rotoscoping to give characters motion that looked more natural. The artist traces the drawn figure over film of live actors. Anime has a look of its own. Backgrounds carry a great deal of detail. Characters are often full of energy. Expressions and gestures are exaggerated. Action is shown from angles that Western cartoons rarely use. Some of those angles are extreme. Eyes matter most of all. Large eyes mark a character as childlike and trustworthy. Smaller eyes, pulled into a squint, mark sneakiness. Tiny eyes mark evil. Shape and size do not stay fixed. Embarrassment shows as a blush across the nose. Scratching behind the head makes that embarrassment look stronger. Anger can show as blue lines across the face. It can show as narrowed eyes, as bulging veins, or as drops of sweat. Hair has its own style too. It is often brightly colored. It is styled in striking ways. It changes shape to show movement and feeling.

7Pictures label faces as embarrassed, happy, sad, and angry. Cost is one reason the look stayed put. Backgrounds are essential. Methods such as multiplane animation, with layers that shift, cost a lot. World War II began in 1939, and that start was a second reason. Japan's leaders wanted citizens on their side. To build pride in the nation, they banned films from other countries. Cartoons from those countries were banned too. They also ordered art that praised certain Japanese values. That art was supposed to attack Japan's enemies. Some animators refused the censorship and left Japan. Others kept releasing work in secret. Capture meant punishment. Posters of the time urged people in Japan to back their government against those enemies. The war's end was terrible for Japan. Nearly two million people in Japan were dead by the 1945 surrender. Atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima. They destroyed Nagasaki too. The ruin changed the people deeply. It changed their art. Light fun gave way to heavier themes. Artists in manga and in anime began to argue for peace. They argued for justice and for freedom. Television, a technology of the 1950s, often carried those messages. Home viewing was now possible, and the audience grew because of it. One of the most popular shows came from a manga comic called Mighty Atom.

8Osamu Tezuka drew it. Mighty Atom was the hero. He was a boy built as a robot. Rockets took the place of feet. His endurance was beyond a human's. The program sent him across the world. His task was to rescue it from danger. The program became one of the best-loved television shows in Japan. American viewers made it a hit in the early 1960s. They knew it by another title. The title was Astro Boy. The first Astro Boy series ran for two years. Reruns of those episodes played into the early 1970s. Other cartoon shows followed. People called them mecha. The heroes were teens and giant robots. Monsters were the threat they fought. During the 1970s, Japan loved a mecha show called Mazinger Z. Its hero was a super robot. A special metal found on Japan's Mount Fuji was what the robot was made from. Astro Boy first reached viewers on New Year's Day in 1963. Anime today, like manga, has grown more specialized. Characters and plots aim at particular audiences. Shonen is Japanese for young boy. Its plots stress action and comedy. Dragon Ball Z is one example. It first played in Japan in 1989. Television stations around the world still show it. That run lasted from 1989 to 2003. Shojo is Japanese for young girl.

9Early stories centered on feelings and on relationships. Later stories added more active heroines. Those heroines take part in romance and in adventure. A 1990s series called Sailor Moon is a classic shojo example. The artist is Naoko Takeuchi. It follows a girl in middle school. A magical brooch gives her power.
