In 1796 the Directory gave him the French forces in Italy and told him the job of pushing Italian armies, and Austrian armies, off the peninsula. A series of battles did it. He claimed Italy for France and came home a hero. A picture shows him leading troops in the Piedmont, a region of northern Italy. That Italian fight opened a pair of wars, and it came first, as France tried to grow an empire by spreading revolution. European nations joined to stop France and to hold their monarchies together. Historians call them the French Revolutionary Wars, running from 1792 until 1802.

4During 1798 a small army under Napoleon entered Egypt. The aims were to guard French trade routes and to cut Britain's commerce linking it to the Middle East. Several land battles in that campaign went his way. At sea he lost. A British fleet beat a French one off Egypt's coast. People call that fight the Battle of the Nile. It set aside any scheme for invading England. A portrait shows Admiral Horatio Nelson. On Europe's mainland Napoleon won battles. At sea, hope died against Britain's own seagoing master, Admiral Horatio Nelson. Nelson commanded at the Nile, and again at a still larger naval fight in 1805. That October, his tactics crushed a fleet of France and Spain, Spain then being France's ally. The place was Trafalgar, off Spain's southwest coast. The battle opened a century of British supremacy on the sea. In 1799 Napoleon used his military skill to stage a coup and overthrow the Directory. He made himself first consul of the republic and took a dictator's powers. He was then leading the Revolution's second war, against an alliance headed by Austria and Britain. A peace treaty followed in 1801, but peace rarely lasted long in the Napoleonic years. A picture shows him in crown and robes at the 1804 coronation in Paris. In May 1804 he took the title Emperor of the French. December 2 brought a ceremony inside Paris, at Notre-Dame Cathedral, he set that imperial crown onto his head by himself. The country of France had just rid itself of kings.

5An emperor now ruled. Rule from the desk Inside France he launched sweeping reforms. He built a central government that was strong and orderly, created a national bank, and reorganized the police. Relations with the Catholic Church were repaired, and Catholicism returned as the national religion. His most noted domestic policy may be the French Civil Code, later called the Napoleonic Code. It standardized the law. Before it, each town and each province kept its own customs. The code took rights from women and gave authority to fathers and to husbands. Family wealth sat in their control, and so did property and children. Male citizens gained rights that were equal, plus liberty in religion. Colonial enslavement, earlier abolished in France, was brought back. People of every social standing felt the code's effects. Women and children lost ground. Men gained freedom. A picture suggests that wide effect. He also reformed the economy, the law courts, and higher education. Tax collection had relied on elected collectors. He replaced them with collectors he appointed and paid a salary, so the money reached the government and could fund his endless wars. He watched the yearly spending of ministries to be sure the funds were used as he wished. Income tax was limited as a way to raise money. Goods carried the taxes, wine among them and tobacco among them, carried more of the load. The national debt disappeared. Poverty fell in a significant way. Energy and attention to detail marked both his governing and his military work. He dictated, on average, fifteen letters a day, on every matter of state.

6A picture shows citizens shopping at a market in the Napoleonic Era. Wars across Europe Ambition grew. He wanted other European nations conquered so the empire would expand. The conflicts that followed are the Napoleonic Wars, twelve years long, from 1803 to 1815. France was put on a total-war footing. Mass conscription filled the ranks, and most national resources went to fighting. At its height the Grande Armée, the Great Army, held about 680,000 men, including men conscripted from conquered lands. Enemies formed alliance after alliance to bring him down. He beat many of them, and each win enlarged the empire. Friends and close relatives were installed as rulers so the conquered nations would stand as allies. Unable to invade England, he tried to weaken it by economics. The Continental System sent French ships to blockade any European port that traded with Britain. He hoped Britain would then accept peace on French terms. The plan fell short of the success he wished. December 1805 brought one of his greatest victories, at Austerlitz. The region was Moravia, today inside the Czech Republic. French soldiers numbering sixty-eight thousand beat ninety thousand Russians and Austrians. Austria had to sign a peace with France, and Prussia was discouraged from joining a pact against him. The year 1810 saw the empire at the widest it would ever be, taking much of present-day Germany, and Holland as well. He began to worry about the empire after his death. He and Joséphine had no children together.

7With no heir, he divorced her and, in 1810, married Archduchess Marie Louise of Austria, who was eighteen. In 1811 she bore a boy who received the name Napoleon too. One painting shows Marie Louise with husband and son, both carrying that name. The collapse Land battles went his way. Sea battles did not. During 1812 came the choice many people call his career's greatest military blunder. Russia was the target of that invasion. Most nations in Europe had tried to slip past the limits France put on trade. Russia had ignored his orders again and again. Czar Alexander I had also begun an alliance with Britain. Napoleon felt he had to step in. June 1812 saw him march across the Russian border. Behind him marched a force of over 600,000. He wanted a quick win. Russian forces refused battle and burned crops as they withdrew. French columns often ran far ahead of their supply wagons, and hunger and disease wore them down. September 7 brought a turn. Near Borodino, the Russian army stood and fought. The French win was narrow. Deaths made a terrible casualty list. Russian soldiers lost numbered about 45,000, and about 30,000 French soldiers died. It was the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars. A picture shows Napoleon leading cold, hungry troops as they retreat from Moscow. He assumed Czar Alexander would sue for peace. By then the czar had signed a peace with Britain, yet he did not ask Napoleon for one. Wanting to conquer Russia, Napoleon chased the Russian army deeper into the country.

8Mid-September brought him to Moscow, almost empty and stripped of food. Czar Alexander I would not fight him. The army had been told to strip the city of supplies and, after the French arrived, to set much of Moscow on fire. By mid-October, food was scarce and the Russian winter was near. Napoleon turned the army back toward France. Russian forces harassed the staggering columns. Of that once-mighty force, the men who recrossed numbered only about ten thousand crossed into France again. After Russia, he tried to replace what he had lost, but time had run out. In 1814 Paris was ringed by nations joined in alliance and forced him off the throne. Exile took him to Elba, an Italian island. Early in 1815 he escaped, came back onto French soil. A fresh army was raised. Final defeat came at a Belgian field called Waterloo. The date was June 18, 1815, against forces drawn from Russia, Prussia, Britain, and Austria together. Fighting that day became a rout. Usually French troops, usually held in tight discipline, dropped weapons and fled. That humiliating loss closed those wars of Napoleon, and the era carrying his name. Many in France were glad. Endless war had sickened them, and so had the heavy taxes raised to pay for it. The monarchy returned in 1815. Until 1871, aside from one brief gap, kings ruled France, and so did another emperor, his nephew Napoleon III. Napoleon I played no part in those later years. Exile sent him to St.

9Helena, a remote British island in the South Atlantic. Guards watched him for the rest of his life while he dictated memoirs. Death came in 1821. His body later returned to France and was buried in Paris. What he left behind Ideas from his civil code became a base for legal systems in many nations of Europe, of Latin America, and of the Middle East. Through that path he pushed governments toward greater order, and he helped fix male supremacy in place. Total war is another part of the legacy: every part of a nation is pulled into the fight, whether people support it or not. His constant wars killed people across Europe whose estimated number is six million. Military schools around the world have studied his tactics and his campaign plans, and other wars have used them. Britain's Wellington, the British duke who commanded the allies against him at Waterloo, was asked to name which general stood above every other, in any time. With no pausing, he named Napoleon, for this age, for past ages, and for any age. A portrait shows the 1st Duke of Wellington, Arthur Wellesley. Dates from his life run as follows. Corsica was his birthplace in 1769. Military school in 1785 ended with the rank of second lieutenant. In 1793 he put down a revolt inside France and rose to brigadier general. Marriage to Joséphine de Beauharnais came in 1796. He crowned himself emperor of France in 1804. In 1810 he divorced Joséphine and married Austria's Archduchess Marie Louise.

10The Battle of Austerlitz, a defeat of Russian and Austrian forces, came in 1805. The Russian invasion and its terrible defeat came in 1812. In 1814 he gave up the throne and went into exile on Elba. Escape from Elba, a new army, and defeat at Waterloo all fell in 1815. A further exile, to remote St. Helena, also fell in 1815. Death on St. Helena came in 1821, and the body later returned to France. Words from the book An alliance is a bond between countries, or groups, agreeing that they will work and fight on one side. An empire is a set of nations or peoples ruled by one person or one government. The Enlightenment was a movement in Europe in the eighteenth century that favored reason and science over tradition and religion. Ambitions are strong desires a person means to reach. Blockaded, a verb, means passage through an area was obstructed. Exiled, a verb, means forced out of one's home country, often because of politics, or as a penalty. People counted as casualties are people hurt, killed, or missing in a war, an accident, or a disaster. A monarchy is rule by one person who is not elected, such as a king or a queen. Conscription is the forcing of people into a country's armed forces. Reforms are changes made in order to improve something. A czar was a male ruler of Russia before the Russian Revolution of 1917. A revolution is the forceful removal of a government and its replacement by another.

55. Nations Joined for Peace

1The topics start with a charter meant for peace, then the United Nations as it is now. Next come the Secretariat, the General Assembly, and the Security Council. The Economic and Social Council follows, then the International Court of Justice. Later topics are the World Health Organization and UNESCO. Another is the refugee office led by a high commissioner. The book ends with how complex and disputed the UN can be, plus a word list. A picture shows delegates from every part of the world. They are meeting to talk about founding the United Nations. The gathering was among the largest international meetings ever held. About 850 delegates came. They represented about 50 countries. The place was San Francisco, in the United States. Reporters and observers numbered more than 2,500. The month was June 1945. World War II was nearing its end. The month before, Nazi Germany had been defeated. Japan kept fighting into the next August. The Allies were closing in. The United States was one Ally. Russia, Great Britain, and China were Allies too, along with others. In San Francisco the delegates met, debated, and argued. The subject was what should follow the war. They made promises. They sketched plans. They struck deals. Their great hope was an organization able to handle the huge changes ahead. June 25, 1945, brought the full group together for a last meeting. The room was the San Francisco Opera House. Lord Halifax of Great Britain chaired the meeting. He told them the question they were about to decide mattered as much as any vote they would cast while they lived. A yes vote meant standing. The document was the charter that would create this new body. That charter was the plan for an international body. Diplomats had been shaping it for years. Every delegate rose. The audience, three thousand strong, rose as well.

2Applause filled the hall. From 1939 to 1945, that war destroyed more than any other fight people had known. Countries had now joined to build a body they hoped could guard the peace. Official work opened the following October. A picture shows the charter being signed by someone sent from the United States. Another picture shows a center run by the United Nations. It hands out food at a camp for refugees in the Gaza Strip. Today the United Nations is often in the news. Where people are starving, white trucks may appear. Big black letters spell UN on them as they bring food. Where countries are tense, or where a civil war burns, you may see peacekeepers. Their helmets are sky blue, marked UN, and they try to keep order. Where an earthquake has flattened a town, workers may hurry to put up tents. The tents are temporary shelter. More than seventy years after it was created, the UN still pushes countries to cooperate. Membership has grown to nearly four times the start. There are now 193 member countries. The main offices stand in New York City. About 44,000 people work for it around the world. It also joins with governments. It joins with nongovernmental organizations, called NGOs. Together they carry skill and aid to places that need them. Since the founding, the world's population has more than tripled. Missions have grown larger and more complex. At the center, the aims stay the same. Help people who are in trouble. Promote human rights and freedoms. Face global problems that countries can face only if they work as one. The missions do not always succeed. The UN is still often willing to walk into disasters others will not touch. Six main divisions, called organs, make up the UN. They are the Secretariat and the General Assembly.

3They are the Security Council and the Economic and Social Council. They are the Trusteeship Council and the International Court of Justice. Each one has a different job in a world that keeps growing more complicated. The notion of a world body was not new. After World War I, fought from 1914 to 1918, countries formed the League of Nations. Its main purpose was to keep peace in the world. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson could not persuade Congress to approve the treaty. That treaty would have made the United States a member. Congress voted to stay out. It feared membership would make the country give up control of its own affairs. The League had some successes. It still came apart slowly. The year 1946 brought an end to the League. By then the newer body was already at work. Day-to-day leadership sits in the Secretariat. It works as the executive branch. The building is a well-known landmark of New York City. People call that tower the Secretariat Building. It stands on the East River. From there, executives watch the daily work of the global body. The secretary-general is the top executive of the Secretariat. This person guides the work and the efforts. This person is often the main voice speaking for the organization. Commanding power, like that of a country's leader or a company boss, is not part of the job. The role is closer to a master communicator and a top diplomat. Persuasion is the tool. The aim is to move others into talks. Another aim is to win help when a crisis hits. The work is very hard. It takes determination, composure, and a gift for communication. UN members elect the secretary-general. The term is five years. A second appointment is allowed. So far, nobody has held the post for more than two terms.

4Eight people have served in the UN's history. They came from eight different countries. Those countries sit on five continents. The General Assembly is the UN's main body for decisions. It is made up of the 193 member countries. Members discuss there. They debate. Sometimes they vote on important questions. They may also meet to hear speeches by world leaders. Six languages are official. English is one. French, Spanish, and Russian are others. Arabic and Chinese complete the set. Members often wear headphones. An interpreter's voice comes through them. In some cases members vote yes or no on recommendations. Those recommendations are called resolutions. One example is agreeing to send humanitarian help after a natural disaster. Haiti, a Caribbean country, received money in 2010. Technical support came with it, after a huge earthquake. The help was for rebuilding after a huge earthquake. If a resolution is not about the UN's own internal business, the UN cannot force a country to obey it. Smaller committees sit inside the General Assembly. They study particular subjects and give advice. One committee works on disarmament and on international security. It builds programs that try to cut violence between countries. The Security Council's main job is peace and security in the world. Fifteen countries sit on it. Five seats never change hands. The permanent members are China, France, and the Russian Federation. The United Kingdom holds one of those seats. The United States holds another. These five were the main Allied victors of World War II. Any one of them can veto a resolution. A veto means a rejection. It stands even if the other countries disagree. The General Assembly elects the other ten members. Those terms last two years. A rights statement was adopted in 1948. People call that 1948 statement the Universal Declaration. Human Rights completes the title.

5It lists rights that every person deserves. Race does not change the list. Religion does not. Social standing and economic standing do not. The list includes a right to life, to liberty, and to security. It includes a right to privacy. It includes a right to an education. It includes a right to hold an opinion and to express it. It includes a right to own property. A picture shows peacekeepers from Lebanon and from Italy. They are getting ready for the International Day of Peace. The day honors people whose work is ending conflict. It also honors people who spread peace. News coverage often finds this council once fighting starts. Other kinds of conflict draw the same attention. Members must be able to meet quickly if the world faces a crisis. Sometimes the council sends armed peacekeepers from many countries. Their job is to guard a truce. Their powers are limited. The usual rule lets them fight only to defend themselves. If violence starts again, they must not pick a side. Rwanda, in Africa, received about 2,500 peacekeepers during the 1990s. The hope was to stop killing between two ethnic groups. One group was the Hutu. The other was the Tutsi. They could not stop Hutus from killing more than 800,000 Tutsis. Many people call this the worst failure the Security Council has ever had. The Economic and Social Council handles economic issues and social issues. Those issues touch cultures, countries, and the whole globe. People shorten the name to ECOSOC. Fifty-four members serve. Their three-year terms overlap. One lasting job is to notice vulnerable groups and to support them. A commission on the standing of women works to advance women's rights worldwide. A permanent forum on indigenous issues tries to protect smaller local cultures. Aboriginal groups in Australia are one example.

6In some places, pressure from outside puts these cultures at risk of vanishing. Another major task is to watch a balance. One side is economic growth. The other is keeping the environment whole. Growth matters for human needs. It makes new jobs. It sparks new technologies. It can also use up natural resources, or damage them. Clean air matters if the planet is to stay healthy. Clean water and clean land matter too. Holding both needs in balance is important. It is not always easy. Repair of Earth's ozone layer is a clear UN success. High in the atmosphere, that layer works like a filter. It shields all life from harmful radiation. In the 1980s, scientists found holes growing in the layer. The holes put people at a much higher risk of skin cancer. The UN answered with the Montreal Protocol in 1987. Nations had to cut, by a large amount, the release of certain chemicals. Those chemicals were opening the holes. The holes have grown smaller in the years after that pact. The layer has been healing. Former secretary-general Kofi Annan spoke about that protocol. He called it maybe the most successful agreement among nations up to that time. It showed that countries could work together on a worldwide problem in the environment. For ECOSOC, and for the UN as a whole, climate change may be the next great test. Global temperatures are warming. Sea levels are rising. Weather patterns are shifting. More communities feel the effects. More nations feel them too. A picture uses a purple spot for the largest ozone hole on Earth. It lies over Antarctica, drawn at its biggest size. The Trusteeship Council is an organ that stopped its regular work in 1994. The plan is to meet again if a need appears. Its job had been to help colonies ruled by other countries move toward independence.

7It guided African lands, including Rwanda and Burundi. It also guided Tanganyika, now called Tanzania, and other places, toward governing themselves. In 1994 the council paused. Palau, its last trust territory, had become independent. Palau lies in the Pacific Ocean. The International Court of Justice sits in the Peace Palace. The palace is in The Hague, in the Netherlands. Fifteen judges serve. They wear black robes and white scarves. A term lasts nine years. Each of the five permanent Security Council members always has a judge there. No two judges may come from the same country. Member states bring legal questions. The court offers opinions and rulings. It decides fights over borders. Rights to resources from nature are another subject. Fishing grounds are one example. It decides clashes between countries. People also call this court the World Court. A picture shows a health worker in Nigeria. The worker gives a child a shot against polio. The World Health Organization, or WHO, works to spread better health habits around the world. It offers advice and teaching. Topics include sanitation, hygiene, and nutrition. Other topics are factors that can stop disease. In 1967, WHO led a worldwide push to end smallpox. Smallpox was a deadly disease. Where it was common, UN workers taught people how to stop it from spreading. Vaccination programs were started across the world. In 1980, WHO said smallpox was officially extinct. Public health had won a victory that covered the planet. WHO also gathers important data. It warns members where a health crisis is underway. Plans from this agency aimed to slow COVID-19. A virus is what causes that illness. That deadly virus spreads in droplets from the breath. It caused a pandemic across the world. A picture sets two famous Egyptian monuments side by side. One is the Sphinx.

8The other is the set of pyramids at Giza. They are among the oldest and largest structures on Earth. UNESCO is a shortened name. In full it is the education, science, and culture arm of this world body. Its broad aim is cooperation among nations. The fields are education, science, communication, and culture. One of its best-known jobs is finding World Heritage Sites and keeping them safe. Some sites are prized for natural beauty. Others matter deeply to a culture. The UN's help preserves them. Few monuments are easier to recognize than the Sphinx. The pyramids at Giza belong in that same group. In 1995, Egypt planned a new highway close to those ancient structures. A UNESCO mission persuaded the government of Egypt to shift the road. The new line would sit farther from the sites, which would help preserve them. About sixty-five million refugees are in the world today. War drives them from home. So do violence and natural disasters. Some look for safety inside their own country. Others flee, or are moved, to a different country. Around the mid-2010s, Syrians leaving a war-torn homeland numbered close to five million. Many live in camps the UN runs in Turkey, in Jordan, and in Lebanon. A report comes from the refugee office inside the UN. Its short name is UNHCR. A high commissioner leads it. The report says today's refugee count is the highest since the Second World War. A crisis must get a fast answer. Teams bring emergency aid. Food is part of that aid. Clean water is included. Shelter is included. Health care is included. The final hope is a safe return home. When that cannot happen, the office looks for host countries willing to take these exiles in. A chart counts registered Syrian refugees. The scale runs from zero up to 6,000,000.

9Figures printed on it include 8,000, shown twice. They include 493,423, shown twice. They include 2,581,767, shown twice. Later marks read 3,977,504, then 4,595,198, then 4,850,957. Further marks read 5,116,057, then 5,479,998, then 5,556,192, then 5,667,026. UNHCR registrations in Egypt are included. So are those in Iraq, in Jordan, and in Lebanon. It covers people the government of Turkey registered. It covers people registered in North Africa. The UNHCR is the source. Almost no corner of the globe sits outside its programs and projects. It works to promote peace and to calm conflicts when they start. It holds big goals for the world's young people. It wants them educated, healthy, and able to live full, productive lives. It seeks human rights for everyone. Race does not limit that aim. Religion, income, and gender do not either. The body is still controversial. Some critics say the work costs too much and wastes money. Others point to times the Security Council failed to stop war. They also point to failures against genocide. Genocide means civilians killed in huge numbers. A further complaint says too much power sits with the nations named in the charter. Their choices can set aside what is best for some countries and favor others. In the same years, more than seventy of them, the organization has done much good. More than ninety million people get food from it. Without that food, many of them might starve. It vaccinates over half the world's children. That helps stop epidemics from crossing borders. It gives leaders a place to talk through differences instead of fighting over them. A picture from 2007 shows children in Lebanon. They play with a Spanish peacekeeper. The place is Marjayoun, in the south of Lebanon. The news people hear is usually bad. It is war, violence, and other conflicts. The wider view holds a lot of good news since the UN was founded.

10For the first time, under 10 percent of the world lives in extreme poverty. The World Bank is the source of that finding. A study from the Human Security Report says deaths in war have dropped steeply. The drop has been fairly steady since World War II. WHO says the average life span has grown. Fewer children die before they turn five. Many factors feed these good changes. This world body has been part of that change. The decades ahead hold many challenges. Climate change is among them. So are other worries about the environment. No simple path will settle these problems, or other problems, for all time. Whether the United Nations can meet what is coming is still a large question. The word list gives plain meanings. Human rights are what most societies say every person has from the start. Justice is one example. Freedom and equality are others. Climate change means lasting shifts in weather patterns on Earth, or in one region. Committees are groups that consider a course of action or decide on one. Humanitarian describes someone, or a group, devoted to helping people. Easing pain and suffering is the heart of that help. Composure is control over one's emotions, a calm mind or a calm look. International means having to do with two or more nations. Controversial means causing a great deal of disagreement. Negotiate means trying to reach a formal agreement by talking. A diplomat speaks for one government when dealing with a different government. An organization is a group or a system acting for a set purpose. Disarmament is the cutting down of armed forces and of weapons. Sanitation means keeping a place clean. It also means the steps and the tools that carry waste away.

56. Nellie Bly and the Stories She Chased

1Elizabeth Cochran was born rich. She did not stay rich. Her father was a judge and a businessman. He was so wealthy and powerful that their hometown was named for him. The town was Cochran's Mills, Pennsylvania. Elizabeth was born there in 1864. She was the thirteenth of fifteen children. Michael Cochran had ten children with his first wife. When that wife died, he married again and had five more children. As the wealthiest man in town, he had no trouble providing for his large family. When Elizabeth was six, her father died. He had failed to leave a will. The children from his first marriage inherited all of his money. Elizabeth's mother inherited nothing. After a year, she had to sell her late husband's mansion. The sale was needed to keep the family afloat. Many women had a hard time finding work in the 1800s. The task was even more daunting while raising five children. Elizabeth's mother quickly married again. She hoped the new marriage would give the family some financial security. Her new husband ended up treating them badly. Divorce was rare in that era. Even so, Elizabeth's mother managed to separate from her second husband. Young Elizabeth herself spoke at the divorce hearing. She said that her stepfather had generally been drunk ever since the marriage to her mother. The story begins with this fall from riches. It follows a quiet girl who watched the world. It includes a note that told people to watch for her. It includes ten days inside an asylum.

2It includes investigative reporting. It includes a trip around the world in seventy-two days. It includes a factory called Iron Clad. It ends with a return to the front page. Teaching was one of the few careers open to women at the time. Elizabeth went to a teacher's college when she was only fifteen. She changed her last name to Cochrane when she enrolled. Unfortunately, the family ran out of money for her schooling after only one semester. She was forced to drop out. Elizabeth and her mother moved to Pittsburgh. They ran a boarding house. She started to read a local newspaper called the Pittsburgh Dispatch. One day she read a popular column in the paper. The writer called himself Quiet Observer. He wrote that women belonged in the home. He said their place was cooking and looking after children. He called working women a monstrosity. Elizabeth was incensed. She knew from experience how hard poor women had to work to make ends meet. She wrote an angry letter in reply. As a girl, Elizabeth Cochran was nicknamed Pink. Her mother often dressed her in pink clothing. In the letter, she attacked Quiet Observer for being out of touch with ordinary people. She asked whether people who already have plenty can understand the life of a poor working woman. She pointed out a limit of that era. Girls were rarely given the same opportunities as boys. She described a boy who starts as an errand boy. He can work his way up until he is one of the firm.

3She meant he could end up as one of the people running the company. She wrote that girls are just as smart. She wrote that they are a great deal quicker to learn. She asked why they cannot do the same. She added a hope. If women were given opportunities, their lives would be brighter. Their health would be better. Their pocketbooks would be fuller. That would fail only if employers kept doing what they did then. Employers gave women half wages because they were women. Elizabeth argued that the world would be a better place if society followed her advice. She said society should stop gathering only the truly smart young men. It should gather the truly smart girls, pull them out of the mire, and give them a push up the ladder of life. Her letter impressed the editor of the newspaper enough that he offered her a job. He gave her the pen name Nellie Bly. The name came from a popular song of the day. Before that pen name, Elizabeth Cochrane signed her articles Orphan Girl. Writing as Nellie Bly, Cochrane continued to stand up for women. Her first story was about how hard women in poverty had to work. Her next article attacked the divorce laws of the state. She said those laws unfairly favored husbands over wives. She also wrote a series of articles about women who worked in factories in Pittsburgh. She took on weighty subjects. Even so, her editors were dismissive of her work.

4They placed her on the women's page of the newspaper. When Bly chose her own subjects, she wrote about social justice. When her editors assigned an article, they sent her to garden shows. They also sent her to write about fashion. She was frustrated by what she saw as lightweight assignments. She somehow convinced her editors to let her travel to Mexico. She would go as a foreign correspondent. While she was in Mexico, she wrote articles about the everyday lives of Mexicans. She showed the struggles of people living in poverty. Then she traced that poverty back to political corruption. She started writing in a negative way about Mexican politicians. The country's government threw her out. She returned to Pittsburgh. Bly had proved many times that she was a serious journalist. Even so, her editors still assigned her frivolous pieces. She worried that the respect she had earned would never come from them. One day, when she was twenty-three years old, she decided she had had enough. She left a note for her employers. The note said she was leaving for New York and that they should watch for her. She signed it Bly. Nellie Bly did not take New York by storm. She spent six months going from one newspaper to another with her hat in her hand. She was looking for work as a writer. In the 1880s, New York had more than a dozen daily papers. Her application was rejected again and again. Finally, she slipped into the offices of the New York World.

5She cornered John Cockerill, one of the paper's editors. She promoted her experience as a foreign correspondent. She offered to sail to Europe for the paper. She would come back in steerage, the cheap and cramped quarters used by all but the wealthiest passengers. She would report on the conditions aboard. Cockerill answered with an assignment he thought could not be done. He asked her to get inside one of the city's biggest madhouses and write about the conditions there. Madhouse was the name then for an institution that held mentally ill patients. It is not clear what Cockerill intended. He may have been impressed by her ambition. He may only have wanted to get rid of her. Bly rose to the challenge. Entering Blackwell's Island Insane Asylum was only one of many risks she took as a journalist. The asylum sat on a thin piece of land between Manhattan and Queens. That land is known today as Roosevelt Island. It was an isolated spot, across the East River and out of sight of most New Yorkers. There, the staff were abusing the people in their care. Bly pretended to be mentally ill. She was convincing enough to be committed to the asylum. During the ten days she lived there, she saw how the staff mistreated the other patients. Most of those patients were recent immigrants. Staff beat them. Staff gave them ice-cold baths. Staff forced them to eat spoiled food. Many prisons treated the people inside them better. Bly wrote an article about what she had seen.

6It became a sensation across the city. She tried to give a plain account, without polish, of how the patients were treated. She gave a frank report of the mistreatment they suffered. People across New York were outraged by what she wrote. Readers were horrified. Far from helping mentally ill people, the asylum was doing them serious harm. Bly asked what, other than torture, would drive a person to insanity faster than this treatment. Because of the article, the city promised more money for its mental institutions. It promised better care. The facilities also took steps so that a healthy woman like Bly could not be admitted. At age twenty-three, Nellie Bly had become famous for a new kind of reporting. It was undercover journalism. At the time, people called it stunt reporting. She did not only report the dry facts of a story. She pioneered a style in which reporters hide who they are. They get inside a particular community. They write about what they experience as part of the group. She spent the next few years as an undercover reporter. She went to jail to report on how female inmates were treated. She worked in a sweatshop to write about the poor conditions there. Throughout her career, Bly stood up for the least powerful people in society. She stood up for the most vulnerable. Her readers loved her for it. In 1887, she turned her time at the asylum into a book called Ten Days in a Mad-House.

7The next year, she published Six Months in Mexico. That book was a collection of articles about her work as a foreign correspondent. By the early 1900s, a whole new type of journalism had appeared. Its reporters were called muckrakers. They dug through dirty business such as corruption, crime, and the exploitation of vulnerable people. The trend started with Nellie Bly. Her exploits usually served to call attention to a great wrong. In 1889, she set out on a story that was pure adventure. Sixteen years earlier, the novelist Jules Verne had published Around the World in Eighty Days. The book described a speed of travel that people thought was impossible in the days before airplanes. Bly declared that she would prove such a trip was not only fiction. With only two days of preparation, she began a trek around the globe. She took only one suitcase and some money. Until this trip, Bly had not traveled overseas. In that era, only the richest Americans traveled abroad. Few women traveled alone anywhere. At twenty-five, Nellie crossed land, air, and sea. She went all the way around the globe. She traveled by steamship, by train, and even by donkey. She sent reports back to New York by telegraph as she went. Eager readers were fascinated by every detail of the journey. Subscriptions to the New York World boomed. Cosmopolitan magazine even sent a rival reporter around the world. That reporter went in the opposite direction. The magazine hoped she could beat Bly's speed. Her route took her to England, then to Egypt, China, and Singapore.

8She even made a brief stay in France so she could meet Jules Verne. History does not record whether he was jealous. She was living out a journey he had only written about. Several days of delay had built up when she arrived on America's west coast. Joseph Pulitzer owned the New York World. Later, the most prestigious award in U.S. journalism was named after him. He hired a private train to bring Bly back to New York in a hurry. Nellie Bly sparked a craze. The craze included a board game from 1890. She finished the journey of 24,899 miles (40,071 km) in 72 days, 6 hours, and 11 minutes. She finished well ahead of the fictional characters in Verne's story. She also finished 4 days ahead of the rival reporter. She set a real-life world record. The issue of the World that announced her return sold more than 280,000 copies. Someone even made a board game called Round the World with Nellie Bly. She described the trip as a maze of happy greetings. She said she was welcomed and congratulated everywhere she went. She called the journey glorious. She said the ride was worthy of a queen. When she was thirty, Elizabeth married Robert Seaman. He was a man more than forty years older than she was. Seaman was a millionaire who owned several factories. Elizabeth retired from journalism to run one of them. The company was Iron Clad Manufacturing Co. She took to industry just as quickly as she had taken to journalism.

9The country was starting to change how it stored and moved goods. Wooden barrels were giving way to the metal drums her new company made. Sales were brisk. While she ran the prosperous business, Elizabeth also created several inventions. One was a new kind of milk can. Another was a stackable garbage can. Her husband died after nine years of marriage. She then took over his businesses. As a journalist, she had seen firsthand how badly factory workers were often treated. She made sure to do the opposite. She paid her workers well. She provided health care. She even installed a gym and a library in her factories for her employees. Her success did not last forever. She was generous to her employees. Even so, some of them were embezzling. They were secretly stealing money from her businesses. Iron Clad Manufacturing went bankrupt. Her work as an owner of industry had come to an end. After her businesses failed, Elizabeth took up her Nellie Bly persona again. She went back to reporting. Writing for the New York Journal, she continued to give a voice to people who were beaten down. She wrote the story of the women's suffrage movement. Years ahead of time, she correctly predicted a date. Women would not gain the right to vote until at least 1920. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified on August 18 of that year. She moved to Austria just before the First World War broke out. She spent several years there as a war correspondent.

10She wrote for readers back home in America. She returned to New York after the war. She kept writing for the Journal until 1922. That year she got pneumonia. She died soon after. She was only fifty-seven when she died. In her lifetime, Nellie Bly made a tremendous impact. She was a pioneer and a role model for adventurous women. Her investigative style of journalism is still widely used today. When she died, the Evening Journal ran a tribute. The paper called her the best reporter in America. Ambition is a strong desire to reach a goal. Exploitation is the act of using someone or something unfairly for profit or personal advantage. Bankrupt means legally declared unable to pay debts, or left impoverished or ruined. A foreign correspondent is a journalist who reports news from a foreign country. Circumnavigated means traveled completely around, especially by sailing. Incensed means extremely angry. A column is a portion of a magazine or newspaper. It is devoted to a particular subject, or to the opinions of a particular writer. A journalist is a person who writes or prepares news for newspapers, television, or other media. A persona is a role or character that an author or actor takes on in the work. It is also an image or personality that someone shows to others. Corruption is dishonest or criminal behavior by those in power. Dismissive means having or showing a lack of interest or respect. Suffrage is the right to vote.

57. New York's Record-Setting Tower

1Visitors like the wide sight they get from the outdoor viewing floor of the Empire State Building. Five states can pass before the eyes in five minutes. Pick a day with clear air. Begin in New York City. One minute in the elevator is enough to reach the 86th floor. After that, walk the outside edge of the floor. Let your gaze run to the horizon. The observatory gives a high vantage point. Sight from there can stretch 80 miles (129 km). Each direction offers that same reach. The city of New York fills part of the scene. A share of New Jersey appears as well. A share of Pennsylvania appears too. A share of Connecticut is visible from the same spot. A share of Massachusetts finishes the group of five states. An evening trip may add stars in the dark sky. Travelers arrive from around the world. This historic landmark is what they come to see. High on this tower, five states can fill a single look. The tower stands 1,454 feet (443 m) tall. For forty-one years it held the world record for the tallest building. Each year, four million people visit. The modern design has won awards. The offices cover 2.7 million square feet, equal to 250,838 sq m. For decades this was the tallest building on Earth. Sunrise arrives about a half hour sooner on the roof than down at the street. The tower is beautiful. It is so large that it has its own zip code. A visit here is exciting. Fame pulls in tourists from every nation. Athletes come for a hard challenge. They race up 1,576 steps. The finish is the 86th floor. The race is the yearly Run-Up. Couples who are in love also seek this place. Hopeful people pick it when they want to propose marriage. No wonder people call it the most famous office building in the world.

2The men who created it had a great deal to offer as well. The plan began with two friends. One friend was Alfred E. Smith. The other friend was John J. Raskob. They set out to raise a tower known around the world. Each man had spent his childhood in New York. Immigrant parents raised them, and money was scarce. Each boy lost his father while he was still young. Each boy left school. Each boy took a job so the family could get by. Raskob had wealth by 1929. Smith had become famous. He had campaigned to be president of the United States. He lost that election. Side by side, the two men formed a winning team. Friends of Raskob put money into the project. Smith worked with Belle Moskowitz. She was his mentor in politics and his publicist. They fed the press stories about every part of the project. The stories gave special attention to a height no one had tried before. In 1929 and again in 1930, powerful New York real estate moguls raced one another. Each man wanted to raise the tallest skyscraper. The Empire State Building was in that race. The Chrysler Building was in it too. Floors kept being added to both towers. Each side wanted the honor of standing tallest. A surprise spire went onto the Chrysler Building in 1930. That spire made the Chrysler Building the tallest. In 1931 this tower received a spire of its own. That last piece let it win the race. The Waldorf-Astoria opened in 1893. At that time no hotel in New York City was bigger. None was more luxurious either. Smith and Raskob wanted the new tower to stand in central Manhattan. That area is called midtown. They chose the crossing of Fifth Avenue and 34th Street.

3One problem blocked them. The luxurious Waldorf-Astoria Hotel already occupied that ground. Smith and Raskob bought the hotel. The huge building had been made to last for many decades. Pulling it down would be backbreaking labor. The work also had to finish quickly. Investors could not earn a return until the new tower was open for business. Its offices had to be rented. A crew of six hundred worked through days and nights. Their task was to pull the grand hotel apart. Crews then set off dynamite. They dug down to hard bedrock. The rock lies 40 feet (12.2 m) under the street. A large fleet of dump trucks moved 28,529 loads across the city. Barges on the East River received those loads. Tugboats pushed the rubble out into the Atlantic. There the debris was dumped into the ocean. Five months later, nothing of the hotel was left. Only a wide pit remained where it had stood. Workers were still razing the hotel when the stock market crashed. The crash opened the way to the Great Depression. Before twelve months had passed, nearly a quarter of workers in America were without jobs. New York City faced hard times. Even so, work at good pay went on at the Empire State Building site. Al Smith found a way to help people in the cold winter months. Used lumber was not thrown away. Carpenters cut it into pieces. They left the pieces in an empty lot. People without jobs could gather the wood. They burned the wood so their houses would stay warm. The Great Depression meant that only 25 percent of the offices were rented on opening day. Until 1950, New Yorkers called the tower the Empty State Building. It was not full of tenants. During the Great Depression, unemployed New Yorkers stood in lines at soup kitchens. People could get soup at no cost.

4They could also get coffee, doughnuts, or bread. On April 7, 1930, work started on a skyscraper meant to stand tallest in the world. Giant steel columns and beams were the first supplies to arrive. The greatest weight sits at the bottom. There, crews set 210 columns upright. Each of those columns weighed 44 tons (39 mt). Workers riveted horizontal beams to the columns. The pieces formed a strong steel grid. A skeleton carries the weight of a person. In a similar way, a steel grid carries the weight of a skyscraper. This building weighs 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). It needed tremendous support. Concrete floors followed the grid as it climbed. The outside wall followed close behind as well. That outside wall is the curtain wall. Steelwork set the speed of the job. The speed was extreme. The grid climbed at four and one-half floors every week. Starrett Brothers and Eken was the contractor. That firm had to bring supplies and workers when they were needed. Supplies that showed up too soon created extra work. Crews had to unload them. Crews had to move them. Crews had to store them. Crews then had to move them once more to the spot where they were needed. Time and labor were wasted. A late shipment was a contractor's worst nightmare. Late goods brought construction to a stop. A complex schedule was written to prevent that halt. Every detail sat on the schedule. Materials came from close by and from very far away. Cement and mortar from New York traveled 149.5 miles (240 km). Steel girders from Pennsylvania traveled 369.3 miles (594 km). Limestone from Indiana traveled 707.9 miles (1,139 km). Those loads came from the United States. Marble came from Europe. Marble from Belgium traveled 3,670 miles (5,906 km). Marble from France traveled 3,689 miles (5,936 km).

5Marble from Germany traveled 3,892 miles (6,263 km). Marble from Italy traveled 4,283 miles (6,892 km). Trained crews faced deadly danger. They carried materials up to floors that were still open to the sky while the tower rose. One contractor was Paul Starrett. He believed no earlier plan had ever been shaped so well for speed. William F. Lamb was the architect. He selected art deco for the tower. That style was popular in the 1920s and the 1930s. The look matched the machine age. It was modern. It was geometric. Squares, rectangles, and simple curves shaped the design. Art deco skyscrapers showed daring in imagination. They showed daring in engineering too. Builders often used materials that factories had just learned to mass-produce. Because of that, the towers went up quickly. Limestone, a column, a mullion, a window, and a spandrel are pieces of the outer face. The rising look of the curtain wall is exciting to behold. That wall is a clear case of art deco put to work for speed. Windows and stone went into it. Decorative aluminum plates called spandrels went into it. Long steel strips called mullions went into it. Every piece was delivered ready to use. Crews attached the mullion strips to the steel grid first. A spandrel then slid in behind. A window came after that. Another spandrel followed. The sequence repeated. Next to that stack of windows and spandrels, workers slid a column of limestone into the space behind the mullions. The finished curtain wall looked bold. It looked proud. It looked as if it were soaring. On the upper floors it climbed at one floor each day. Work on the Empire State Building started on March 17, 1930. The first steel beams were set in place that day. Only a few months later, the steel grid stood at the 40th floor.

6The outer curtain wall was catching up. By fall, the steel grid had reached eighty-eight stories. The curtain wall was not far behind it. The outside rose, and the inside trades followed. Electricians, plumbers, and carpenters finished interior work close behind the shell. The official opening came after slightly more than twelve months of work. The day was May 1, 1931. President Hoover joined the opening-day event. Alfred E. Smith joined it. His grandchildren joined it. Those grandchildren were five years old. Governor Roosevelt joined it. Other guests joined it as well. A building of this size had never been tried. The new size created many new problems. Those problems called for new solutions and fresh innovations. Cranes that lifted supplies over crowded sidewalks worked slowly. They also put people on the sidewalk in danger. The fix used elevator cars saved from the hotel that had been torn down. Those cars carried supplies to the high floors in a safe and quick way. Builders still use that idea on construction jobs today. Wheelbarrows moved supplies slowly. To speed that task, crews laid tracks like the rails of a small train. Tracks circled each floor. Tracks also ran inside the elevators. Workers could then push bigger carts that held heavier loads. One cart carried as much as eight wheelbarrows. A movie moment still startles people who look at this tower. King Kong climbed the side in 1933. He clung to the mast. Airplanes shot him down. He made that climb twice. The first climb was in the 1933 film. The second was in 1983. The later event marked fifty years since the first movie. A huge King Kong balloon was fixed to the mast. The balloon measured 82 feet (24.9 m). In 1931, thousands of people watched from the street below. They saw the dirigible Columbia fail at its task. The airship had tried to collect mail from the mooring mast.

7So much planning and so many new ideas might make a person think every plan worked. One plan did not. The spire had been added so the tower would stand taller than the Chrysler Building. Al Smith invented a use for that spire. The idea failed completely. He wanted the spire to do useful work. He pictured a great mooring mast for dirigibles. In those years, people treated dirigibles as the modern way to travel. He said a passenger could walk down a plank from an airship. The plank would lead to the 102nd floor. The first dirigibles approached the mast. Gusts held the airships back from the mast. Docking was impossible. No real use for the mast appeared until 1950. Then the mast became a base for an antenna. The antenna served something brand new. That something was television. Crowds packed the sidewalks and stared upward. Workers strolled along a thin edge with empty air beside them. Reporters said the city had no finer show beneath the open sky. Those workers were the steelworkers. The job was dangerous. Timing inside a team was critical. Trust inside a team was critical. The bond was so important that a four-man crew acted as one. If one man got sick, the other three went home too. Each member had to be brave. Each member had to be skilled. Each member had to know the others completely. Each member had to trust the others completely. People called these steelworkers sky boys. Every man had one set role. The heater made a rivet red hot. He heated it in a bucket of glowing coals. Then he tossed the rivet. The catcher caught it. He set it into its hole. The bucker-up pressed one end of the rivet. He pressed with a metal bar.

8The riveter worked the opposite end. An air hammer was his tool. All of this happened on narrow beams. Nothing waited below to catch a man who fell. Two Indigenous Mohawk communities provided many of the best steelworkers. One is Akwesasne (ahg-weh-SAHSS-neh). The other is Kahnawake (gah-nah-WAH-geh). The men traveled from Canada. They also traveled from upstate New York. Weekdays were spent in Brooklyn. Home was the place for weekends. Downtown Kahnawake was a neighborhood where more than 800 Mohawk people lived. A restaurant sign there honored the ironworkers who passed through its doors. The sign named them the greatest in the world. Their skill stood out. A fast worker in the group set a rivet once each minute. Other crews worked just behind the sky boys. They stood on scaffolds high over the streets. Those men built the curtain wall. Interior workers came behind them. Plumbers were in that group. Carpenters were in it. Electricians were in it. Bricklayers were in it. Still more trades joined them. Seven million hours of labor went into a long list of tasks. Crews installed 6,700 radiators. They installed 2,500 sinks and toilets. Pipe runs totaled 51 miles, or 82 km. Steel that was set and riveted came to 57,000 tons, or 51,709 mt. They placed 6,400 windows. Limestone placed on the job came to 200,000 cubic feet, or 5,663 cu m. They installed 67 elevators. Shafts for those elevators stretched 7 miles, or 11 km. They laid 10 million bricks. They raised a building of 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). Plaster on the walls came to 10,000 tons, or 9,072 mt. The project cost five workers their lives. At the busiest moments, about 3,500 people rushed around the site together. Keeping so many workers safe was a large task. Keeping them healthy on a dangerous site was a large task too. The site ran its own hospital.

9A nurse stayed on duty full time. A doctor came several times each day. He treated anyone who needed care. August is a hot month in New York City. Cool drinking water was piped up to every floor. Water boys carried buckets to the crews. Many of those boys were only sixteen years old. They climbed to spots that were precarious. Some water boys felt a thrill when they stepped onto the beams. They soon learned a safer way to look. They stopped looking down. They looked toward the end of the beam. Some people feared the finished tower would fail. They thought a lightning strike would destroy it. They thought wind would batter the highest floors. They thought those floors would sway. They thought people would fall. One summer, a scientist counted lightning hits on the mast. The count reached forty-eight. The mast took no damage. A hurricane later struck the city. Wind speed climbed to 120 miles per hour, or 193.1 kmph. Only the crown moved, and the shift measured just a few inches. No person fell. Real disaster came during World War II. The day was a Saturday. Fog confused the pilot of a bomber from the U.S. Army Air Force. The aircraft struck the tower. The impact and the fire afterward took fourteen lives. The tower remained upright. The U.S. bomber weighed 10 tons (9.1 mt). It struck the floors from the 78th to the 80th. The plane tore a hole 18 feet (5.5 m) wide. One engine passed straight through the building. On special holidays the tower uses a new LED lighting system. That system can show sixteen million colors. The lights put on shows in the sky. When work finished in 1931, this skyscraper was the tallest in the world. It kept that rank for more years than any other building has.

10In 1971 the World Trade Center became the tallest instead. People have named the Empire State Building America's favorite building. It is also listed among the Seven Wonders of the Modern World. The tower turned fifty in 1981. Soon after that birthday, it was declared a landmark. A landmark has to be kept so it still looks as it always has. Updates are still allowed. Air conditioning is one modern change. Today the city's best-known office tower remains a strong mark on the New York City skyline. Al Smith had said the tower was made for the generations still to come. The years have shown that his words were accurate. A few special words belong with this story. Art deco is a bold style used in decoration, design, and buildings during the 1920s and the 1930s. Strong lines and shapes drawn from geometry define it. When pieces are riveted, metal pins or bolts hold them. Workers beat or bend those pins while they are hot so the joint stays tight. Scaffolds are platforms put up for a short time. Workers stand on them to build, repair, or decorate. Barges are freight boats with flat bottoms. They usually travel a canal or a river. A spire is the sharp point at the top of a tower or another building. Dirigibles are big airships, often with a stiff frame and with no wings. Gas inside them lets them float. Steel is a tough metal formed from iron and carbon. Something iconic stands for an important symbol. People recognize it at once. Something unprecedented has never taken place before. Something mass-produced is turned out in very large numbers. A vantage point is the spot from which a person looks at a thing or thinks about it. Moguls are people with power and importance inside a profession or an industry.

58. Newcomers Who Changed Many Lives

1Three lives fill this book, and they appear in a set order. Gloria Estefan is the first life. Dikembe Mutombo is the second. Albert Einstein is the third. A later page names ways to read further. A word list finishes the book. Each of the three moved to the United States from another country. The push that sent each person away was not the same push. The work that made each person influential was not the same work. Even so, two threads run through all three stories. Remarkable success is one thread. A strong wish to improve human life is the other. A picture catches Gloria Estefan in performance on October 10, 2002. Women Rock! Girls & Guitars was the concert in the picture. That night was the event's third year. That concert was a benefit. Breast cancer awareness was the cause it hoped to lift. Gloria Maria Milagrosa Fajardo was the name given at her birth. Havana, in Cuba, was the city of that birth. September 1, 1957, was the day. Flight came at the age of sixteen months. The family was escaping a Communist government. Fidel Castro, a dictator, led that government. Miami, in Florida, was where they settled. A ghetto in Miami was home for Gloria and her mother. Before the move, her father had been a soldier for Cuba. The year 1961 pulled him into the Bay of Pigs invasion. Cuban exiles carried out that landing. The government of the United States stood behind them. Overthrow of Cuba's government was the aim. Success did not come. Capture was the father's fate. Eighteen months in a Cuban prison followed. Release finally let him shift the family to Texas. Military service in Vietnam came later and lasted two years. Miami saw the family again in 1968. A caretaker's load sat on Gloria while she was still growing up. Rebecca was her younger sister. Care of Rebecca fell to Gloria. Daytime hours sent their mother to work. Night hours sent their mother to school. Care of her father fell to Gloria as well. Doctors had found multiple sclerosis in him. Doctors suspected a link to Agent Orange. That substance is a toxic chemical. Military service in the Vietnam War was when he met that chemical.

2Trees were what the chemical was meant to destroy. Shrubs were a target too. Enemy soldiers had used that cover to hide. Exposure reached American soldiers at the same time. After-school hours were Gloria's time to tend her father. She kept that watch until the age of sixteen. A veterans' hospital took him in then. Guitar playing in her own room became a refuge during those years. Singing in that room became a refuge too. The University of Miami accepted her in 1975. Only part of the cost was covered by a scholarship. Psychology was the subject she chose. A bachelor's degree was complete in 1978. Love of music was already strong. Shyness was just as strong. Performing where strangers could see her did not seem possible. A Cuban wedding was the place her mother once took her. Emilio Estefan was there. He would later become her husband. His band was there too. The Miami Latin Boys was the band's name. Cuban-American players made up that band. Before much time passed, she was playing along as an accompanist. Now and then she took the lead vocal. Leadership of the group belonged to Emilio. Keyboards were his instrument. His help is what let Gloria push through the shyness. More and more of the singing became hers. Pop songs she had written entered the group's repertoire. Miami Sound Machine was the name the group took on. Albums began to come out. The year 1984 is when that success shot upward. Hispanic listeners alone held up the early fame. A much more mixed audience recognized them soon after. Pop was one style those listeners enjoyed. Dance music was another. Soul was another. Latin music was another. A billing that put her name first showed how important she was. That billing was Gloria Estefan and the Miami Sound Machine. Later the name on the bill was only Gloria Estefan. Cuts Both Ways, her first album on her own, came out in 1989. One year after that, a semitruck hit the bus that carried her tour. The crash was very serious. Her back was broken. A full recovery was not what doctors expected.

3Determination pulled her through physical therapy. Hard work in that therapy pulled her through as well. Recovery did come. Fans sent a flood of loving support. That support held her spirit up. Into the Light was the album that marked the recovery. A tour lasting a year marked it too. She wanted to return care to the people who had cared after the crash. A benefit concert in 1992 was her way. Three million dollars was the sum raised. Victims of Hurricane Andrew received that money. A picture shows her with her son Nayib after the 1990 recovery. Nayib stands on the right in that picture. Honors piled up in the years that followed. Awards piled up too. Other successes piled up with them. Today she stands among the world's most successful people in entertainment. Tickets for her concerts sell out. Her records sell in the millions. The year 2010 found her helping to organize a march in Miami. The Ladies In White were the people the march supported. Those women were protesting. The protest targeted Cuba's government for its treatment of people who speak against it. Exile from Cuba, in her family's story, has shaped her life with great force. Castro's government, in her view, rules by tyranny. She still speaks against that rule. Many exiles elsewhere in the world take a similar stand. They guard the traditions of their culture with fierce loyalty. They also condemn the oppression that forced the family out of the homeland. Cuban roots show in her music. Cuban roots show in her life. An American upbringing shows there too. Millions of listeners from both cultures still come to her work. A picture from 2001 shows Dikembe Mutombo on the left and Tyrone Hill on the right. They hold a trophy given to the Philadelphia 76ers. That year the 76ers beat the Milwaukee Bucks. The win took the NBA Eastern Conference Finals. Mutombo's birth country is Democratic Republic of the Congo. Zaire is the older name of that country. His neighborhood in the capital, Kinshasa, was among the poorest. Poverty was something he knew by living inside it. Talent and good fortune then carried him into basketball. That career unfolded in the United States.

4The career was an amazing success. He made a promise about that success. Children growing up poor, in many parts of the world, would share in the help he could give. A scholarship brought him to Georgetown University. A medical doctor's life was his plan. Basketball was a love as well. Height of 7 feet 2 inches made a professional future seem possible. During his second year, the coach asked him onto the university team. He changed his academic plan. Playing ball became the new aim. Graduation came in 1991. One degree was in linguistics. Linguistics means the study of language. Another degree was in diplomacy, the study of how nations deal with one another. Four European languages were his, spoken fluently. Five African dialects were his as well. His NBA career opened in 1991. The Denver Nuggets picked him once college was done. Those Nuggets were ranked eighth. The Seattle Sonics were ranked first. The Nuggets defeated them. The playoff upset ranks among the most surprising ever. A later contract took him to the Atlanta Hawks. With the Hawks, he grew into the league's standout defender. Blocked shots were a category he led again and again. Rebounding became another of his great strengths. The honor Defensive Player of the Year was his on three occasions. What he wanted most was a championship. A trade in 2001 sent him from Atlanta to the Philadelphia 76ers. The championship chance he had wanted was finally real. In that same year the honor Defensive Player of the Year came to him a fourth time. The NBA finals were the round his team entered. The Los Angeles Lakers were the opponent. His team played well. The title still went to the Lakers. He kept shining as a player whose high level rarely dipped. Fans loved him. In his sport, his stardom was real. A knee injury in 2009 led him to leave professional play. Full attention could then go to humanitarian projects. He did not settle for enjoying sports glory. Star power, in his hands, lit support for health projects. It lit support for education projects too. The United States was one place that work reached. Congo was another.

5Lands beyond those two were another. Inside the United States, he joined an NBA effort named Strong STARTS. The short name points to strong schools that act so troubled students can be reached. Teens with emotional problems got help succeeding in school. During his Hawks years he joined their Team Up program. That program pushes students toward community service. Soup kitchens are one kind of service. Homes for senior citizens are another. The year 1997 is when he set up the Dikembe Mutombo Foundation. Better conditions in his native country are its purpose. Every day in Congo, children die of illnesses that immunization stops in other countries. Those other countries run immunization widely. Mutombo taught people in Congo why immunization matters. He taught them why routine health care matters. His own gift of 22 million dollars started the building work. The foundation then raised a research center and a hospital. The cost of that project was 30 million dollars. The hospital holds 300 beds. Kinshasa is the city. His mother Biamba Marie Mutombo gave the hospital its name. About one hundred patients is a day's average there. Hundreds of jobs for the local area come from the hospital. Hillary Clinton, then U.S. Secretary of State, visited in 2009. Afterward she spoke to university students. She held up his public service as a model. Democratic Republic of the Congo could learn from it. All of Africa could learn from it. A picture shows him taking cheers beside President Joseph Kabila of Congo. Kabila stands on the right. The moment is the opening of the Biamba Marie Mutombo Hospital. July 2007 was the month. Kinshasa, his hometown, was the place. His reach traveled far. Free basketball clinics took him all over Africa. Uniforms for teams were part of what he gave. Equipment for teams was part of it too. His money and uniforms sent the women who play basketball for Congo to the Olympic Games of 1996. Atlanta was the host city that year. A picture from June 2001 shows Kofi Annan greeting him. Annan was secretary general of the United Nations. Sport had earned him awards. Later awards honored a different gift. He could draw people together for a shared good.

6The United Nations saw the reach of his ties around the world. It named him its first Youth Emissary. Young people in many countries worked with him. He spoke for CARE, a group that fights poverty. The year 2010 brought him the Sports For Good award. Congo was the place that work had served. Death came in September 2024. He was fifty-eight. His life remains a clear model of an immigrant's choice. Good fortune and open doors became a way to give back. The gift went to his own country. It went to the wider world as well. Albert Einstein raises a question you can ask yourself. Would you want the word genius to point at you? That is what happened with him. Intelligence made him famous in exactly that way. Dislike was the attitude of many teachers at his schools. They saw no potential in him. Fame still spread around the globe. His ideas changed the human picture of physics. Physics is the science of matter. It is the science of energy. It is the science of motion. It is the science of force. Wild hair made him famous too. Passionate beliefs about world peace made him more famous still. Germany was his birth country. March 14, 1879, was his birth date. His Jewish family owned a small shop. The shop made electrical equipment. Most children are talking by age two. Albert did not start talking until age three. School, once he entered it, went poorly. German schools laid a strict structure on students. They laid a strict routine on students. He disliked both. Schoolwork felt dull. It felt boring. Classroom learning drew little of his interest. Mathematics came to him quickly all the same. Hard math ideas were ones he taught himself. He did that even before secondary school. Several failures in business came first. Then the family left Germany for Italy. Albert was fifteen. He did not leave with them. He stayed in Germany. An entrance exam stood between him and a technical school. He failed that exam. Electrical engineering was the study he had wanted there. A year in Italy with his family came next. Secondary school was finished later in Switzerland.

7A Swiss college followed. The program there certified him to teach math. It certified him to teach physics. Professors did not warm to him. They would not recommend him for a teaching job. A picture of his passport includes a map. Yellow areas on that map mark European countries where he lived. Those years came before he moved. The new country was the United States. Harsh prejudices against Jewish people were widespread in the late 1800s. Harsh feelings against them were common. Harsh actions against them were common. Anti-Semitism is the name for those attitudes. Germany held them with special strength. Religious oppression drives many people to emigrate. Einstein left Germany for that reason. Anti-Semitism's heavy climate was the reason. Switzerland made him a citizen in 1900. A Swiss patent office hired him in 1902. Seven years of work followed. Spare hours went to physics. Spare hours also went to the violin. The year 1905 brought a Ph.D. in physics. The University of Zürich granted it. Those same years produced many professional papers on physics. Colleagues rejected the unpopular ideas at first. Later experiments showed the ideas were right. The ideas sat ahead of their time. Few people understood them then. Few people understand them now. Fame as a physicist came anyway. New thinking about matter was part of what he built. New thinking about energy was part of it. Physics topics of many kinds drew his study. Before him, talk of atoms rested mainly on speculation. Mathematics was the tool he used to prove that atoms exist. He also showed a change that light can cause. Light's energy becomes electrical energy when it strikes certain metals. For centuries, scientists had argued about what light is. His work let them step forward. They could grasp more of how these principles behave. One famous theory concerns an observer's rate of motion. That rate changes how time is measured. Picture a train moving at 60 miles an hour. A ball leaves your hand toward your brother. The speed of that toss is 15 miles an hour. Inside the train, both of you read the ball's speed as 15 miles an hour. Your mother and father stand on the station platform.

8For them the ball's speed adds the toss to the train. Fifteen miles an hour plus 60 miles an hour makes 75 miles an hour. A drawing shows the difference. The difference depends on whether the watcher is inside the train or outside it. Light, speed, and motion then opened many further ideas for him. Those ideas are too many for this book. They are too complicated for this book. A later page points toward more reading. Older ideas of motion were revised by his work. Older ideas of time were revised too. Those older ideas had lasted for centuries. He introduced a further claim. He also proved it. Motion can be relative. Time can be relative. Relative means they do not stay constant in every situation. The equation E = mc2 is what many people know best. E stands for energy. M stands for mass, which is matter. C stands for the speed of light. C2 means c squared. Squared means c is multiplied by itself. A tiny bit of matter, the equation says, can become a huge amount of energy. Nuclear power rests on that idea. Uranium is one radioactive fuel used this way. Only a tiny amount of that fuel is used. The heat energy that comes from it is huge. Fame in science followed these ideas and others. The year 1909 started the first of several teaching posts. Universities in Europe were the places. Honors came in large number. Awards came too. One prize was the Nobel Prize. It was given for physics. The year was 1922. Lecture tours took him to the United States. They took him to the Far East. They took him to Spain. They took him to South America. He was teaching in Germany again. A key election gave victory to the Nazi Party. The year of that vote was 1925. He rejected the Nazis' social beliefs. He rejected their political beliefs. The year 1932 followed his third tour of lectures. That tour had crossed the United States. A university in New Jersey made an offer next. Princeton University was the school. The offer was part-time teaching. The post would take turns with the work he still had.

9That work was in Germany. He accepted the offer. The family moved to New Jersey as that year ended. January 1933 made Adolf Hitler chancellor of Germany. Einstein did not go back to Germany. Citizenship in the United States came in 1940. A picture shows him taking the oath of that citizenship. His secretary, Helen Dukas, stands at the left. His daughter, Margaret Einstein, is there as well. He often argued for Israel as a Jewish state of its own. He argued for peaceful answers to tension between nations. He argued for nuclear disarmament by every nation. Peace had his passionate support. Disarmament had it too. World War I was underway when he took a rare stand. Few German scholars would speak against Germany's part in that war. He was one of those few. After the war, people attacked his pacifist values with harsh words. Pacifist means peaceful. After World War II, his call for disarmament among nations grew louder. He had helped build the first atomic bomb. Even so, he spoke against any further making of nuclear weapons. He spoke against any nation's use of them. April 18, 1955, was the day he died. Princeton, New Jersey, was the place. He was seventy-six. One legacy was the lesson of his own life. Genius in every part of life is not required. A person can still give something important. Speech did not come until he was three. A school entrance exam was a test he failed. College was not a place where he excelled. Absentmindedness was so strong that his own address was hard to remember. Shortcomings of that kind did not block him. His contributions to knowing how the physical world works were enormous. A peaceful world was part of his vision. Recognition is due for both of those gifts.
