The respect he has received is of a kind few others get. A picture shows him talking with the physicist Robert Oppenheimer. Oppenheimer directed the secret Manhattan Project. That project was to design an atom bomb. It was also to build one. Einstein's first years after he emigrated to the United States included help starting that project. He worked with Oppenheimer.

10Later he protested against every nuclear weapon. Readers who want more can look up the people and events in this book. Gloria Estefan is one name to seek. Dikembe Mutombo is another. Albert Einstein is another. Disarmament is another topic. CARE is another. The Bay of Pigs invasion is another. Three books about Albert Einstein go further than this one. Joyce Goldenstern wrote Albert Einstein: Physicist and Genius in 1995. Stephanie Sammartino McPherson wrote Ordinary Genius: The Story of Albert Einstein in 1995. Steve Parker wrote Albert Einstein and Relativity in 1994. The word list below gives meanings used in this book. Anti-Semitism means prejudice against Jews. It also means discrimination against them. Humanitarian describes work aimed at human welfare. Ending pain and suffering is a large part of that aim. A dictator is a ruler who holds absolute power. Tyranny is often how that rule is carried out. Immunization means protecting a person from a disease by inoculation or vaccination. Disarmament means cutting down armed forces and weapons. A legacy is anything passed on when someone dies. Money can be a legacy. Property can be a legacy. A message to humanity can be a legacy. To emigrate is to leave one country in order to settle in another. A refuge is a place that offers safety. It can offer comfort. It can offer protection. Exiles are people forced out of the country where they began. Horrible conditions can be the cause. A government order can be the cause. Religious oppression is unjust treatment aimed at one religious group. Fluently describes language use that is easy, smooth, and expressive, in speech or in writing. A repertoire is what a group is ready to perform. Songs can belong to it. Roles can belong to it. Plays can belong to it. Operas can belong to it. A ghetto is one section of a city. Many people from a minority group make their homes there. Poverty is the usual condition there. Speculation rests on ideas and theories. Proof is what speculation does not yet have. Tyranny means government that is oppressive and unjust. Cruel use of power is another meaning. Unjust use of authority belongs to that meaning too.

59. Nine Innings and a Diamond

1A 2013 photo from the Japan Series shows a runner just escaping a tag. The city is Tokyo. An umpire watches closely. This book asks what the game is, how the rules work, and how American play looked in earlier years. It visits famous ballparks, famous players, a sport that does not age, and words to know. The United States did not yet exist when early English settlers shaped the game we know. They carried different versions into the British colonies. Eighteenth-century America played stool ball. It played trap ball. It played rounders. Each of those games used batting. Each used throwing. Each used running. Each demanded quick choices. Independence from the British was nearly seventy years old when 1845 arrived. New York City was the meeting place of a club named the Knickerbockers. The rules they wrote became the base of the game. Millions around the world enjoy that game now. Artist George H. Hastings showed spectators at a Boston club game in the 1880s. That club was also called the Boston Beaneaters. The sport is major in Canada. Japan treats it as a major sport. Taiwan does too. So do South Korea, Argentina, and the United States. A map marks countries where the game is played.

2North America now has 30 teams in Major League Baseball. The short name is MLB. Those teams compete for the World Series, the championship of North America. Minor league clubs number 240. Minor leagues give players a place to sharpen skills. Only a small share of them reach the majors. People call the sport the great American pastime. It is played in more than one hundred countries. Fans number in the millions. The World Baseball Softball Confederation directs contests between countries. That body organizes the World Baseball Classic. The tournament comes every four years. It was created to spread the sport worldwide. Young players flock to Little League, and that program is hugely popular. About 2.4 million children play. They live in more than one hundred countries. Every year since 1947, Little League has staged a World Series for youngsters. A field diagram labels the outfield. It labels center field, left field, and right field. It labels the center fielder, the left fielder, and the right fielder. The infield holds a second baseman, a shortstop, a first baseman, and a third baseman. The diagram also marks the pitcher, the catcher, and the coach's box. It marks the pitcher's mound, foul territory, home plate, and the on-deck circle.

3People sometimes call the infield a diamond. The name comes from the shape made by the bases. A game uses two opposing teams. Each team has nine players. The teams take turns on offense. Offense means batting and running the bases. They take turns on defense. Defense means pitching and fielding. The pitcher throws to a catcher on the same team. Then a batter on the opposing side takes a swing. If the bat hits the ball, the batter runs. The run goes counter-clockwise. The runner must touch each base in order on the way to home plate. A pitch inside the strike zone can be a strike even if the batter does not swing. A swing that misses is also a strike. The umpire makes that call. A foul ball can be a strike too, if the batter has fewer than two strikes already. Foul territory is the place where a foul ball lands. Three strikes make the batter out. A pitch outside the strike zone is a ball if the batter does not swing. Four balls send the batter walking to first base. A home run can be a ball hit past the outfield. A home run can also be a full run to home plate right after the hit.

4Otherwise the runner may stay safe on a base. When a teammate hits, that runner may sprint to the next base. Only one runner may stand on a base. A run goes on the board when a runner reaches home plate. The team with more runs wins. After a hit, the batter runs toward first base. Fielders rush to catch a fly. They rush to field a ground ball. The aim is to stop the runner from moving on. A catch before the ball touches the ground makes the batter out. If the ball hits the ground first, the defense fields it. The defense tries to get the ball to a base player. That player can force an out by tagging the runner. The player can also touch the base the runner must reach. Three outs end the turn at bat. The teams then switch roles. Earned run average is called ERA. The formula is runs allowed, divided by innings pitched, then multiplied by 9. Here is a question. Picture 20 runs charged to a pitcher across 63 innings. What is that pitcher's ERA? Batting average is called AVG. The formula is hits divided by at-bats. Here is another question.

5Picture 25 hits spread across 103 trips to the plate. What is that batter's AVG? One photo shows a runner sliding safely into home. A game has nine innings. In one inning, each team plays once in the field. Each team also bats once. First at bat is always the team that traveled in. The home team bats second. A tie after nine innings brings extra innings. Play continues until someone wins. The sport uses many statistics to judge players. Stats is the short name. ERA starts with runs a pitcher has allowed. That number is divided by innings pitched. The result is multiplied by nine, because a regular game has nine innings. The product is the average. Batters are judged by AVG. They are also judged by runs batted in, or RBI. AVG sets a batter's hits against that batter's times at bat. RBI counts runners who scored because of the batter's success at the plate. In the nineteenth century, race-based unfairness marked life in the United States. It marked the twentieth century too. African American players once had separate leagues. From 1890 to 1947, the major leagues shut out African Americans. They shut out Latinos as well. Discrimination did not stop those players from playing.

6By 1870, African American teams were already forming. People called them the Negro Leagues. Some of the game's most talented players were in those leagues. The sport changed over time. The color barrier broke. The Negro Leagues faded. A 1936 photo shows a Newark player at bat. Hundreds of teams took part in the Negro Leagues. Women practiced their skills at many pro games in the 1940s. They did so in the 1950s as well. More than six hundred women competed. They filled fifteen professional women's teams. Women have never been allowed into a major league game. Even so, they have given a great deal to the sport. Millions of men entered military service in 1943 during World War II. Professional players were among them. The pool of major league talent shrank. Philip Wrigley owned the Chicago Cubs. That shortage moved him to start a professional league for women. Spelled out, the name starts with All-American and continues Girls Professional Baseball League. The short name is AAGPBL. In the early days, as many as twenty thousand fans came to cheer one game. Major league men returned once the fighting ended. Pro baseball became mostly a man's game again. The women's league played its final season in 1954.

7Rising popularity changed the map of the sport. For years the East Coast held the focus. In 1957 the Brooklyn Dodgers chose to move. Their new city was Los Angeles. The New York Giants soon followed. Their new home was San Francisco. The move west brought new teams. It brought new divisions. Old parks were torn down. New stadiums went up. Fenway Park in Boston is home to the Red Sox. It is the oldest major league park in the United States. It opened on April 20, 1912. Today it is still much like the park that first opened. Boston fans keep a special feeling for their field. Fans in many other cities feel that way about their own fields. Fenway can seat as many as 37,673 people. Wrigley Field can seat 41,072 devoted fans. Wrigley is the second-oldest park. It stands in Chicago. It is home to the Cubs. It was built in 1914. Both parks show their age. Fans still find something very special in them. History soaks Wrigley and Fenway. Many things change. These two old parks stay the same, and fans take that as a reminder. Major league play once used only sixteen stadiums. It now uses thirty arenas across the country.

8Long ago, games came only in daylight. Now they often come at night. They often come inside domed stadiums. Players were rarely traded. Many stayed with one club for season after season. Today players move constantly. Trades come often during a season. George Herman Ruth is better known as Babe. He is the most famous player in the sport's history. Many people call him the best who ever played. As a Yankee he was also called the Sultan of Swat. He spent twenty-two seasons in the majors. He broke every home-run record. He helped set attendance records no one had heard of. He helped the Yankees win seven pennants. He helped them win four World Series titles. For many Americans, hope took the shape of Jackie Robinson. The date was April 15, 1947. He broke the color barrier. He was the first African American player in the majors. People called him Number 42. He played ten seasons with the Dodgers. He reached six World Series with that team. The Dodgers won the championship in 1955. Each year the sport marks Jackie Robinson Day on April 15. Puerto Rico's pride is the nickname people give Roberto Clemente. The Pittsburgh Pirates used him in right field.

9His years ran from 1955 to 1972. A homer he hit in the seventh game in 1971 turned the series. The Pirates beat the Orioles by 2 to 1. That win took the championship. In 1972 he died in a plane crash. The next summer he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame. He was the first Latin American player inducted there. Derek Jeter is a modern hero. Many regard him as one of the game's greatest competitors. He played shortstop. He led the American League in hits. He led it in runs. He was a World Series champion five times. He retired in October 2014. He said a Yankee memory was the honor he wanted most. A 2013 photo shows a player sliding past the catcher to score. The event is the Little League World Series. The place is Williamsport, Pennsylvania. The sport is a wonderful pastime. It is also more than a pastime. Players need sharp thinking. They need bodily strength. Some people say the game is like life itself. On a team, each person has a position. Life works that way too. Success takes cooperation. Every year, spring arrives. Warmer weather arrives. A new season starts with them.

10The game is for players. It is also a pastime for millions around the world. It carries fans back to warm childhood memories. Those memories include T-ball. They include stickball. They include softball. Great traits of the human spirit live inside the game. One quality is patience. One is perseverance. One is grabbing a chance that comes only once. Words to know. A barrier is a rule, a block, or a problem that stops progress. Coveted means wanted very strongly. Discrimination means treating a person or a group in an unfair way. The reason can be religion, age, race, gender, or some other difference. Fielding means playing in the field during a game. Foul describes a play that breaks the rules and brings a penalty. Inducted means chosen to join a group. Pennants are yearly prizes for the winners of the American League and the National League. Perseverance means staying determined and committed through challenge or delay. Statistics are numbers that are gathered, arranged, and studied. A strike is a negative call. It comes when a batter swings and misses, lets a good pitch go, or hits a foul that is not caught. Plays are judged by an official called an umpire. Vying means competing.

60. One Hour Inside a Great Art Museum

1Thousands of famous works fill this museum. One of them is a painting by Vincent van Gogh. The picture's title is Self Portrait. A straw hat is part of that title, and the painter shows his own face. Vincent van Gogh painted his own face in it. More than six million people walk through the doors each year. A huge staircase rises in front of me. Those stairs climb to the main entrance. The building is the Metropolitan Museum of Art. New York City is the city around it. Ms. Kessler, my English teacher, gave us a job. We must join a guided tour. Afterward we write an essay. The essay sets three artworks next to each other. It must show how they are alike. It must also show how they are different. At first the assignment sounds useless. I wonder if art is nothing but paintings hung on a wall. I climb slowly. Still, I reach the top and step inside. The entrance room is called the Great Hall. People of every age stand around me. Their backgrounds are not all alike. Many different languages fill the air. Some adults draw their own versions of the art. Some children draw too. A young woman stands in the middle of a group, and I join them. She introduces herself as Jada. Art history is her subject at a college close by. The museum also employs her as a docent, a person who leads visitors. She shares background before we walk. Opening day was in 1870. The building covers the length of four city blocks. Inside are more than two million objects. The oldest come from ancient times. The newest come from the present. Our route will cross the whole museum. It will take one hour. Jada calls it a highlights tour. We will study only a few pieces. Millions of others remain in storage and on the walls. Her talk keeps going, and my interest grows with it. Jada strikes me as someone easy to like.

2Now I truly want to know why she cares so deeply about art. Pretty pictures may not be the whole story. A scene of the Great Hall shows the first room visitors enter. Signs there explain the collection. They also explain the exhibitions. Another scene shows Egyptian galleries. Mummies are on view. So are other objects taken from tombs. Those Egyptian rooms are where our walk begins. Enormous glass cases line the way. Mummies fill them. Other amazing artifacts fill them too. I wish we could linger. The schedule will not allow it. This place is huge. Falling behind the group is not an option. Then we reach a vast room. The ceiling is high. A real temple of stone stands on a raised base. Shallow water in a pool rings that base. Light pours in through a giant window wall. Jada gives the temple a name. It is the Temple of Dendur. Jada tells us about the Aswan Dam on the Nile River. In 1933 workers made that dam taller. Massive floods followed. During part of every year the water covered this temple. Other historic sites went under as well. Destruction was a real threat. A further rebuild of the dam came in the 1960s. After that, the danger to the sites was permanent. Fifty countries joined a rescue. The United States took part. Together they shifted twenty-two historic temples to safer ground. Egypt then handed this saved temple over as a gift. The receiver was the United States. The gift was a way to say thank you. Jada describes how this gallery copies the temple's original setting. The pool plays the role of the Nile. The windows play the role of outdoor sunlight. Construction happened around 15 BCE. Egypt then belonged to the Roman Empire. A chieftain from Nubia dedicated the building. One dedication was to Isis, a goddess of Egypt. Another was to his sons, Pihor and Pedesi. The Nile had drowned both sons.

3Picture writing covers the front face of the temple. Jada asks us to notice it. Princes appear in those pictures. The pharaoh appears too. They bring offerings to gods and to goddesses. The picture writing, called hieroglyphs, takes two forms. Outside, carvers cut the images down into the wall. That cut-in style is sunken relief. Inside, the images stand out from the wall. That raised style is raised relief. Electric lights are what we depend on now. Long ago, light came only from the sun. Candles gave light too. So did oil lamps. In a dark inner room, pictures that stick out were easier to see. A person could feel them as well. English names are scratched on the stone. Visitors did that carving from the seventeenth century through the nineteenth century. Spray paint did not exist yet. A dim hallway is our next path. Jada leads, and the hall opens into the American art wing. We step into a huge room. Stained glass, three stories tall, lights the space. A handsome staircase takes us up toward American paintings. Furniture galleries wait up there too. The number of objects stuns me. Even these stairs have a past, Jada says. Their first home was a Chicago building called the Stock Exchange. That structure was among the earliest skyscrapers in America. Builders finished it in 1894. My hand follows the banister as I go up. Copper forms a detailed geometric pattern there. I stop and look down into the wide gallery. Colored glass sparkles along the walls. The next room holds a painting I recognize at once. It is enormous. The title is Washington Crossing the Delaware. The painter was Emanuel Leutze. The year was 1851. George Washington appears with his troops. They are out in harsh weather. Their boat is on the Delaware River, and the river is icy. The date in the scene is Christmas night. The year of that night is 1776. American history class is where I first met this image.

4Washington's men struck a British loyalist camp without warning. Jada warns us that the scene does not tell the past cleanly. Several details are historically wrong. The clearest mistake is the flag. The American flag is painted in, yet the country had not adopted it by the time of that fight. She adds a second problem. The boat was not big enough for Washington to stand. Standing would have flipped it. Leutze still made those choices. He wanted a stronger feeling from anyone who looked. Jada asks us to look with careful doubt. She names that habit a critical eye. Question the content. Learn the history behind it. In this canvas, Washington is meant to represent ideas. America, in those ideas, is powerful. It is unique. It is righteous. Other paintings in this same museum reply to Leutze's scene. Jada tells us to look for them. Some were made by Black painters. Some were made by Indigenous painters. Their aim was a picture of America with more complexity. The canvas size is 12.4 by 21.5 feet. That equals 3.78 by 6.47 meters. Down we go again. Rooms along the way hold furniture. Lamps fill some of them. Other objects help each room rebuild one specific time. The walk feels endless. At last a long hall opens. Knights in full armor sit on horses that are armored too. They seem about to charge straight at us. A glass case is Jada's next stop. The case holds French armor for a whole body. The date is about 1600. Steel is the main material. Gilded decoration makes it beautiful. Preservation looks almost perfect. Silk the color of yellow still lines the helmet. Straps of red leather barely look worn. Fancy as it is, this suit saw real battle. Jada is clear about that. A saddle was made to match. So was a headpiece for the horse. Walking around in it is hard to picture. Fighting in it is harder still.

5The weight shows, and the number confirms it. Altogether the suit comes to 77 pounds. That is 34.9 kilograms. On battlefields, kings wore suits like this. Other noblemen did too. Tournaments were another place for such armor. A side room comes next. More armor waits there, but these are helmets. They come from Japan. Samurai warriors once wore them. Those warriors were a military elite. From the twelfth century to the nineteenth, they gained power in Japan. The power was political. It was social. It was economic. Outside Japan, few arms-and-armor collections are this large. The helmets in front of us do not match one another. Materials change from one to the next. Size changes. Shape changes. One of them holds my attention. A bright red flame decorates it. A tiny figurine grips a sword. The century is the sixteenth. Makers shaped it to echo hats that older men wore in that era. The figurine stands for a Buddhist guardian. Wisdom is what that guardian protects. Once I know a hidden history, an object such as this helmet makes more sense. I understand its purpose better. More than 17,000 works sit in the Greek and Roman rooms. A statue at one side shows an Amazon warrior who has been wounded. It dates to the first century CE or the second. Our path is a long hallway. White marble statues gleam along both sides. Jada explains that Romans made almost every statue here. Each one copies a Greek sculpture. The Greek versions were several hundred years older. Metal, not marble, was the Greek material. Bronze formed the bodies. Copper picked out small parts. Silver did too. Lips were among those parts. Eyelashes were too. Later people melted many of the metal works. They needed weapons. They needed coins. Surviving metal sculpture is therefore rare. The white we see today is also misleading. Jada says ancient marble was not left bare. Statues received bright paint. Temples did too. A small room is our next stop.

6Its name is cubiculum. Painters covered its walls, and those walls traveled here. Their first home was the Italian village of Boscoreale. The name is said boh-skoh-re-AH-le. New York City is where they stand now. Brilliant color fills the paintings. The scenes show a sanctuary in the open air. Jada retells the day of August 24 in the year 79 CE. A famous volcano, Mount Vesuvius, blew apart. Deadly ash fell in enormous amounts. Villages all around were hit. People were busy with everyday life. Nothing had warned them. Ash buried them in layers. Deaths were many. Damage was huge. The same ash saved things as well. It sealed cities the way a time capsule would. Architecture survived inside that seal. Artwork survived too, including the walls of this room. The paintings themselves are older than the eruption. They go back to 70 BCE. More than a hundred years separate the art from the disaster. The method on these walls is fresco. Painters spread water-based color directly on the plaster. Up on the roof, the Roof Garden offers one of the museum's strangest exhibit spaces. Every spring, work by an artist of our own time goes on view. The backdrop is stunning. New York City's famous skyline rises behind it. Green trees of Central Park do too. One installation on view is by Hector Zamora. He is an artist from Mexico. A gallery sign explains art from Oceania. Those are Pacific islands. Melanesia is one group. Micronesia is another. Polynesia is a third. We leave the small painted room behind. The next rooms focus on Africa. Oceania has rooms too. So do the Americas. Nothing looks the same. Lighting has changed. Sound has changed. The design of the exhibits has changed. Wooden boats of giant size hang overhead. We pass beneath them. Masks line the route. They are elaborate. Shapes vary. Colors vary. Materials vary. No two are the same. Jada pauses. She asks what we ourselves count as ordinary beauty.

7A specific job stood behind many objects in this museum. Being pleasant to look at was not the chief aim. Beauty is still there, but each object has its own kind. Learn the maker's intention, she adds, and the link can grow stronger. The link is to the object. It is also to the maker. One African gallery stops me. A male figure stands there. Impressive is the word that fits. Height is only about 3.5 feet. That is 1.1 meters. Jada identifies a power figure from Africa. Nails cover the wood. He looks as if he is in command. His open mouth could belong to a leader shouting urgent orders. The eyes seem full of wisdom. They seem perceptive too. Makers from the Kongo peoples created him. His role was to hold particular forces of power. His role was also to display authority. A round cavity sits in a prominent place on the stomach. Ritual medicine once filled it. A beard was there at the start. Organic matter formed it. Palm extract was one ingredient. Fibers were another. The organic parts decayed. Nails that once fixed the beard did not. Old age is what the beard represented, Jada says. Wisdom is the other meaning. People turned to this sculpture for legal agreements. They turned to it to stop conflicts. They turned to it for healing the sick. Another name for these Central African figures is minkisi. Special sculptors did not work alone. Ritual leaders worked with them. A new nail went into the body whenever people sealed an important agreement. That nail was the record. I stop and sort through the day. Cultures I had never studied are now in front of me. Time periods I had never pictured are here too. Skip this visit, and I would have missed them. Another thought follows. Only a few hours back, any other plan would have sounded better. Jewelry in this gallery includes an ear ornament from Peru.

8Turquoise is one material. Gold is another. Further materials are mixed in. Visitors in a nearby scene study paintings of very large size. The room belongs to modern and contemporary art. That is our next stop with Jada. Dates on these works run from 1900 to now. Paintings of every size fill the rooms. I struggle to name what they depict. Upstairs, one big canvas stops us. My first thought is a child in a rage, flinging paint. Jada names the artist. He is Jackson Pollock, from America. He helped found a movement. The movement is abstract expressionism. Autumn Rhythm is the title on the canvas, with Number 30 beside it. Pollock finished it in 1950. Jada says he and other artists in that movement refused familiar subjects. Familiar techniques were refused too. Feeling, and a personal bond with the work, mattered more. They painted without a fixed plan. Gesture was a focus. Color was a focus. An image a viewer could recognize was not. Pollock did not stay with a brush. His choice was action painting. Paint was poured. It was splattered. It was thrown. Canvases rested on the floor. A standard easel was not part of the process. Tradition lost its hold on these artists. The later direction of art changed because of them. Our next stop is a painting of vivid red. Arrows run across it. Circles do too. Shapes like stick figures appear as well. A head similar to a mask sits at the top and seems to stare. The maker is Jean-Michel Basquiat. One parent was Haitian. The other was Puerto Rican. Brooklyn is where he grew up. Brooklyn is my home too. His first art was graffiti. The years were the 1970s. They continued into the 1980s. Graffiti is exactly what this canvas brings to mind. Detail is everywhere. Color is everywhere. Lines cross and recross. Some spots look sprayed. New York itself comes to mind. The city is exciting. It is busy.

9Possibility seems to fill it. We finish at a cloth work titled Street Story Quilt. Colorful fabric carries another view of New York life. Apartment blocks in the quilt match the kind of building I live in. Figures tell part of the tale. Written text tells the rest. The main character is a boy. His age sits below mine. The difference is only a few years. Harlem is his neighborhood. Faith Ringgold is the artist, Jada tells us. Art is only part of her work. She campaigns for the rights of women. She campaigns for civil rights as well. Museum doors were often closed fifty years ago. A Black artist could be shut out. A woman could be shut out. A Black woman, and Ringgold is one, could face both exclusions. She became known for speaking out against that unfairness. Splashed paint would not have counted as art in my old view. Graffiti would not have counted. A quilt would not have counted. Jada's account of where artists find ideas has shifted that view. I also hold on to something else she said. A lovely landscape is not, by itself, the test of good art. A person painted to look real is not the test either. Context helps us judge why a work matters. Inspiration helps. The mark a work leaves on a culture helps too. From those clues we decide what we ourselves think. I still have thinking to do. Even so, her meaning is starting to land. One visitor strolls by two abstract canvases. Barnett Newman painted the one on the left. Mark Rothko painted the one on the right. Both hang among modern and contemporary works. Outside, the front steps draw crowds. Visitors like to gather there. My legs are tired by the time the walk winds down. Hundreds of European paintings pass beside us. I only glimpse some famous ones. Van Gogh is among them. Monet is among them. The giant staircase takes us down.

10The Great Hall is the end of the tour. So much has passed in front of me that I feel overwhelmed. The learning feels just as large. Awe is the right word for the Met. One hour felt like a trip around the world. It also felt like a trip backward through time. I have to confess a mistake. I had not understood why art is important. The city meets me at the exit. Sights rush in. Sounds rush in. Smells rush in. I sit down for a rest. The seat is the great steps outside the entrance. Ideas for the essay are still fresh, so I want them on paper. Choosing will be the hard part. Which pieces can I compare when every piece seemed wonderful? I am certain of a return visit. The next one will last longer. The next one will be for me, not only for class. A few words help with a visit like this. Abstract expressionism is a way of painting that shows emotion through shapes and patterns instead of only through people or objects. Artifacts are things humans made or used in the distant past. Conventional describes what is common, what is traditional, or what most people accept. Cultures are the customs and ideas of particular groups of people. A docent guides visitors, most often in a museum or a similar cultural site. A facade is the front face of a building. Galleries are rooms or whole buildings where the public comes to see art. Highlights are the parts of an event that stay most memorable, important, or exciting. Illuminated means lit. Intentions are plans, goals, or the purposes behind an action. Intricate describes something very detailed, complicated, or complex. Organic describes what comes from a living thing. Replicate means to reproduce something or to imitate it exactly. A sanctuary is a place of safety, and it can also mean the protection that place gives. Statuesque describes someone tall, beautiful, and dignified.

61. Paris and Its Iron Tower

1Contents. A Symbol of Paris. A Tower of Strength. The City Called the City of Light. A Bold Plan. People Who Doubted. Walking the Tower. A Place People Must See. Words to Know. A Symbol of Paris. No other structure in Paris comes close to the Eiffel Tower in height. If you travel to France and visit its capital, Paris, you cannot miss the tower. You may never take a tour of this world-famous landmark. You will still see it from practically every part of the city. The structure is made of wrought iron. It towers over the city people call the City of Light. It has fascinated people from around the world since it first opened to the public in 1889. More than 250 million people have come to the Eiffel Tower since that year. Visitors frequently use one word for it. They call it breathtaking. Facts in Brief. The tower's height, before the antenna, is 300 meters, or 984 feet. The antenna is 24 meters, or 79 feet. The total height is 324 meters, or 1,063 feet. The tower has 108 stories and three platforms. The platforms stand 57 meters, 115 meters, and 276 meters above the ground. Those heights are 187 feet, 377 feet, and 906 feet. The weight is 10,100 metric tons, or 11,133 tons. The iron structure alone weighs 7,300 metric tons, or 8,046 tons. More than 250 million people have visited. Among monuments that charge a fee, this one gets the most visits in the world. It was completed in 1889. It was constructed for the 1889 World's Fair.

2The base measures 100 meters, or 328 feet, on each side. A Tower of Strength. The Eiffel Tower is a huge iron structure with a bronze color. Four slightly curved girders form it. Enormous decorative arches sit beneath the lowest of three platforms. Those arches give an appealing balance to the gentle curve of the rising girders. The original height of this unmistakable landmark was 312 meters from the ground to the top of the flagpole. That height is 1,024 feet. Through its first forty-one years, no built structure stood taller than the Eiffel Tower. New York's Chrysler Building, built in 1930, ended that record. An antenna was installed at the top in 1957. It brings the tower's total height to 324 meters, or 1,063 feet. The iron tower's design looks light. It looks airy. People of its time considered that design a major architectural achievement. A map can place the tower in Paris beside Avenue Gustave Eiffel and the Seine River. France can be shown between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. The Champ de Mars is the ground beside the tower. The City Called the City of Light. Builders put up the Eiffel Tower for the World's Fair of 1889. The fair marked the hundredth anniversary of the French Revolution. The tower honors what citizens can do when they join together. The structure stands along the south bank of the Seine (SEN) River. It stands on the Champ de Mars (shawm duh MARS). That ground is a large public greenspace. People gather there by day.

3They gather there at night. They come to marvel at the famous landmark. Paris has a French nickname, La Ville-Lumière. People often translate it as City of Light. It actually means City of Enlightenment. The name refers to the value that people of the city place on culture. It also refers to the value they place on knowledge. The area around the Eiffel Tower has many attractions. They include museums, gardens, and fountains. They include ornamental ponds and cultural centers. A Bold Plan. Credit for the design of the Eiffel Tower usually goes to a French civil engineer. His name was Gustave Eiffel (eh-FEL in French). He had helped design the Statue of Liberty. Maurice Koechlin (mor-EES kay-KLAHN) and Emile Nouguier (ay-MEEL NOO-gee-ay) were the people who made the first drawings. They were the chief engineers for Eiffel's company. In 1884, they developed the tower's design. They intended to enter it in a contest. The contest's organizers wanted designs for the centerpiece of the 1889 World's Fair. Koechlin and Nouguier designed a tall tower. It would be a latticework of iron beams. At the base, the beams would act as four legs. They would curve inward as they rose. They would meet at the top. The four main beams would be tied together by horizontal metal beams. Those joins would come at regular intervals along the four sides. Gustave Eiffel (1832–1923) had already designed hundreds of metal structures before this tower. They included a railway station. They included an observatory. They included many bridges. A construction diagram can show elevators at the upper right, among the detailed plans.

4Building supports for bridges was a skill Eiffel's engineering firm already had. Using that skill on a structure 300 meters tall was a daring idea. That height is 984 feet. A French architect named Stephen Sauvestre was brought onto the team. He was to make sure the finished tower would be beautiful. It also had to be structurally sound. Sauvestre recommended enormous curved arches. The arches would connect the tower's columns. He also recommended large halls on each level. The hall walls would be made of glass. The contest received 107 proposed projects in all. After this design was declared the winner, Eiffel's team began construction. Ground was broken on January 26, 1887. The supports began to be assembled on July 1 of that same year. March 31, 1889, was the completion date, a little more than two years after the start. Builders used 18,038 pieces to construct the tower. Those pieces weigh 7,300 metric tons, or 8,046 tons. Eiffel used latticework wrought iron. His goal was to show metal matching stone in strength. He also wanted to show that metal did not weigh as much as stone. The pieces were first prepared at Eiffel's factory. The factory stood on the outskirts of Paris. A total of 150 workers assembled individual pieces into sections. Each section measured about 5 meters in length. That length is 16 feet. A picture from March 1888 can show the tower at the first level. Huge horizontal girders joined the four legs. One picture from July 1888 can show the second horizontal section in place.

5Another, from late November, can show the tower nearing completion. At the factory, bolts joined the pieces that formed each section. At the site, rivets replaced the bolts. Workers heated the rivets before installing them. After cooling, the rivets shrank. The shaft of each rivet became shorter. The two heads were pulled together. That shrinkage guaranteed an extremely tight fit. Workers used 2.5 million rivets in all. A team of four workers installed each one. The foundation is made of stone and cement. It rests on a layer of gravel. It was positioned to resist wind. Sandboxes held the four legs while the tower was being built. They also sat on hydraulic jacks. The jacks kept the first platform level. A level platform was required so the rest of the tower above it would be properly balanced. The crew that assembled the tower numbered as many as three hundred. They used wooden scaffolds. They used small steam cranes. People considered the tower an engineering marvel. The work took two years, two months, and five days. That speed, together with the precision at every stage, was remarkable at the time. The elevators were remarkable too. People considered them an important technical feat. Elevators had never been used in a structure this tall. After construction was complete, workers coated the tower with 60 metric tons of paint. That weight is 66 tons. The paint protects the iron from rust. Since 1899, workers have repainted the tower every seven years. The color has changed over the years. It went from dark red to dark yellow.

6It then went to brown. Most recently it became bronze. Two extra notes belong with the tower. It sways a little because of wind. It moves more because of heat. On hot days, the sunlit part expands. The tower can lean up to 18 centimeters, or 7 inches. A single elevator travels about 103,000 kilometers each year. That distance is 64,000 miles. It equals two and a half trips around Earth's circumference. People Who Doubted. When Gustave Eiffel and his team were drawing their plans, not everyone favored the ambitious project. Hard structures were already part of Eiffel's strong design record. Some people still doubted that he could build a tall tower able to withstand the wind. One math professor predicted a collapse. He said a tower even three-fourths the height of the planned one would fall. Not everyone was thrilled about how the tower would change Paris. After construction began, a group of three hundred people asked the Paris Exposition to halt the project. The group included artists, writers, and architects. The petition called the tower ridiculous. It claimed the tower would be an eyesore. The writers compared that eyesore to a gigantic black smokestack. Construction proceeded despite the objections. The tower was completed just over a month before the World's Fair began. People were awed by the architectural sensation. Their awe lasted through the six months or so of the fair. It lasted afterward as well. The tower had been built as a temporary exhibit. It was scheduled to be torn down after twenty years.

7Eiffel did not want the tower dismantled. He worked to give it lasting value for the scientific community. He described his vision in his own words. Science, he said, could use the tower as an observatory. It could also use the tower as a laboratory of a kind it had never been given. The day after the tower first opened to the public at the fair, Eiffel equipped the third floor. He put a meteorology laboratory there. The lab contained barometers. It contained lightning conductors. It contained wind gauges. It contained other instruments. Eiffel opened the lab to scientists studying a wide range of topics. He also conducted thousands of experiments of his own. The Paris Exposition celebrated French achievements. It ran from May 6 to October 31, 1889. Over eighty structures on the Champ de Mars held exhibits. The exhibits came from Europe. They also came from North America and South America. The Tower in Two World Wars. During World War I, the French military used the tower for wireless communication with ships. They also used it to intercept enemy messages. Hitler gave an order in World War II that the Eiffel Tower be torn down. The demolition never took place. French resistance fighters cut the elevator cables after Germany occupied Paris. They wanted the Nazis to have to use the stairs. A July 1941 picture can show Adolf Hitler with a group of German Nazis while they toured Paris. In the end, being so tall is what saved the tower. The first radio transmissions started using the tower in 1909.

8Later, in 1925, it was used for the first public radio program. In that same year, it began to be used for television experiments. The year 1935 marked the start of the first regular broadcasts. Radio and television antennas on the Eiffel Tower now number 120. Walking the Tower. One thrilling way to experience the tower is to ride a glass elevator to the top. On the way up, visitors see the landmark's architecture at a range of heights. At the top, they get an exquisite view of Paris. They see many places of interest. The top includes two levels. One level is covered. The other is in the open air. Visitors can enjoy the view by day or by night. They can enjoy it in any weather. Gustave Eiffel's office, now restored, is also on the top floor. It includes maps. The maps give directions and distances to various other major cities. A picture at the top can show that restored office. Wax figures can show Gustave Eiffel on the right, in conversation with Thomas Edison on the left. The first floor and the second floor offer many attractions. Visitors can shop for souvenirs. They can dine. An ice-skating rink sits 57 meters, or 187 feet, above Paris. The second floor has souvenir shops. It has restaurants. It has displays about the tower's construction. It also has a glass window. The window gives a plunging view down to ground level. A see-through floor is the main draw on the first level. The floor creates the illusion that you are walking on air.

9You look down 57 meters, or 187 feet, to the ground. Interactive displays about the tower are on the first floor as well. There is a video show. There are restaurants and shops. There is a piece of the original spiral staircase that led to Eiffel's office. Since 2004, the first floor has also had an ice-skating rink every winter. Behind-the-scenes tours offer extras. One extra is a visit to the original engine room. That room still controls the elevators. A visitor in Paris during a special event gets an additional treat. The tower may present a light show. It may present a fireworks show. To celebrate the Chinese New Year in January 2004, the structure was bathed in red lighting. Europe Day in May 2006 dressed the tower in blue. Europe Day is a celebration of peace and unity in Europe. When France hosted the Rugby World Cup in 2007, the tower wore an enormous rugby ball. Green lighting stood for the playing field. Beams of light stood for the goal. A spectacular light and fireworks show took place at the tower to usher in the year 2000. To celebrate that year, over a million people gathered on the streets. They came to see a New Year's Eve display of LED lights and fireworks. At night, sensors turn on 336 projectors by themselves. The projectors are furnished with yellow-orange lamps. A Place People Must See. People all over the planet recognize this tourist attraction more easily than most others. It has been an important part of the plot in dozens of novels.

10It has appeared in dozens of movies. Many of those stories destroy the tower. It has inspired over thirty replicas. The copies include ones in Guatemala, Japan, Pakistan, Romania, and Belgium. They include ones in Mexico, China, Russia, and Las Vegas, Nevada. Paris, Texas, has a replica, and so does Paris, Tennessee. The tower has inspired many people to sketch it. It has inspired people to write about their impressions of it. Some people see history when they look at the tower. Other people see love and romance in it. Whatever draws them, people know this iconic structure. They dream of visiting it. A trip to Paris should include a visit to the Eiffel Tower. Words to Know. assembled (v.) put together from parts, or gathered together. landmark (n.) an important historical building or site, or an object on land that marks a place. engineer (n.) a person who plans, builds, or fixes machines, buildings, bridges, or similar structures. latticework (n.) a framework formed from overlapping strips of wood or metal. eyesore (n.) something that is especially unattractive. plunging (adj.) related to a rapid fall or a steep slope. feat (n.) an amazing action or accomplishment. precision (n.) the quality of being exact or accurate. girders (n.) large beams made of steel or iron. replicas (n.) copies or reproductions of something. hydraulic (adj.) operated by the pressure of a liquid, such as water, or by its movement. transmissions (n.) messages or other items sent from one person or place to another person or place.

62. Peach Baskets and the Orange Ball

1This book moves from a last-second finish to peach baskets, then to a sport that grew. It covers dribbling, running, passing, and shooting. It covers court rulers, a game bigger than its start, and words to know. In Burkina Faso, in West Africa, wheelchair players wait under the hoop for a rebound. In 2013 the Philadelphia 76ers answered a game-winning point. The other side was the Brooklyn Nets. The 76ers won 121 to 120. The win came in overtime. Only a few tight seconds remain on the clock. The score is level. A player bounces the ball toward the far end and hunts for a gap. The pass comes suddenly. A teammate is waiting near the other team's hoop. That teammate leaps and slams the ball through the hoop. The buzzer sounds at the same moment. Time is gone. A standing crowd, fully charged, roars. This game is finished. The setting may be a pro arena. It may be a game with neighborhood friends. Either way, the sport is thrilling. It asks players to be lightning fast in the mind. It asks them to be lightning fast in the body. Every arena shares one joyful aim. Send an orange ball through a hoop. The sport began in 1891.

2The inventor was Dr. James Naismith, born in Canada. He taught physical education at Springfield College. That college is in Massachusetts. He wanted restless students busy indoors. Rainy days were a problem. Cold winter days were a problem. He wrote the rules himself. Peach baskets were fastened by him onto the rail of a balcony. One basket stood at each end of the gymnasium. Those baskets still had bottoms, unlike hoops now. A ball that dropped in had to be lifted out by hand. Later the bottoms came off. Metal hoops took the place of the baskets. Early play had no dribbling. Players moved the ball with a bounce pass. The first college game came in 1892. Inside the United States the sport caught on fast. Schools took to it in particular. A ball was enough to start. A basket was enough. A court was enough. Naismith was born in Canada. He studied physical education in Montreal. Teaching then carried him out of Montreal and into the United States. Many Native peoples name their style rez ball. Rez is short for reservation. College play among Black schools held its opening conference in 1916. From then on, the sport was more than a game for Black communities.

3It was woven deep into Black culture. The sport matters to Native peoples as well. From 1870 until 1978, U.S. officials removed many Native children from home. The children lived at schools. They played this sport there. Over time it became part of Native culture. Native players usually use a style that is unusually fast. The sport's popularity widened after World War II ended. Wounded servicemen came home. Wheelchair play grew popular with them. The ball was not always orange. Before the 1950s the color was brown. Lots of people play today. Men play. Women play. Boys play. Girls play. Almost every nation has players. The American National Basketball Association began in 1949. The short name is NBA. That league was central to the huge growth of pro play. It is the biggest pro basketball organization. It is also the most famous. It has thirty teams. College play fields more than three hundred teams across the nation. The largest college body is the NCAA. Those letters stand for National Collegiate Athletic Association. Nearly every high school has a team. Women were already active in 1892. That was only one year after Naismith invented the game. Lisa Leslie is a WNBA superstar.

4Diana Taurasi is a WNBA superstar. Maya Moore is a WNBA superstar. The letters WNBA stand for Women's National Basketball Association. Women's play has gained a much bigger group of fans. A 2015 college photo shows Jackie Young on the left. She shoots over Caylie Young. France's women's team stands with silver medals. The medals are from the 2012 Olympics. Fan numbers keep rising around the world. Player numbers keep rising too. The rise covers women and men. It covers amateur play and pro play. FIBA counts at least 450 million players worldwide. FIBA is French. The first words are Fédération Internationale. Then comes de Basketball. Leagues exist all over the world. A global championship is the FIBA Basketball World Cup. It is held every four years. The Olympic Games have featured the sport since 1936. There it is a highly competitive event. China has loved the sport for about one hundred years. India has loved it for about that long. Australia has too. The Philippines has loved it especially. The Philippine Arena is the largest basketball building in the world. It can hold fifty-five thousand fans. The next-largest buildings are in the United States. Serbia has one of them. Canada has one of them.

5A game is split into four quarters. In the NBA each quarter lasts twelve minutes. Each team puts five players on the floor. The court is a rectangle. A hoop hangs on a backboard at each end. The hoop is 10 feet above the floor. That height is 3 meters. The aim is the higher score. Points come from shots through the other team's hoop. A made shot is usually worth two points. Beyond the arc that marks three points, a made basket counts as three. Foul shots can add points too. After a foul, the referee may award the fouled player some free throws. A foul happens when another player breaks the rules. The break can be an accident. It can be on purpose. Unfair body contact is a foul as well. The referee blows a whistle. Hand signals show which foul occurred. The award may be one free throw. It may be two. It may be three. The number depends on the kind of foul. Each of those shots is worth one point. The shooter stands behind the free-throw line. The defending team may not interfere. Free throws often decide a win or a loss. Players keep shifting into spots where they can shoot.

6They also shift into spots for a pass to a teammate who has a good look. The other side tries to block shots. It tries to steal the ball. The ball may move only by a dribble. It may also move by a pass. As play runs up and down the court, a team flips to defense or to offense. The flip depends on who has the ball. Zone defense is one common plan. In a zone, each player guards a section of the court. Person-to-person defense is the other common plan. In that plan, each player guards one opponent. Attacking plans vary. Often a player without the ball dashes or changes direction. That move is called a cut. The cut is made so the player can catch a pass and shoot. A court diagram labels the midcourt line. It labels the baseline, the sideline, and the three-point line. It labels the free-throw line, the center circle, the top of the key, and the basket. It labels the key. The spots are center, small forward, shooting guard, point guard, and power forward. The short marks are SG, PF, PG, C, and SF. The other team is marked as the opposing side. A missed shot can bounce off the hoop.

7It can bounce off the backboard. Players from both teams jump for that rebound. A strong rebounder helps the team keep the ball. Coaches assign roles, which are the positions. Ball handling is usually sharpest in the point guard. That player sets up the attack. The point guard controls the ball. The job is to get it to the right teammate at the right moment. The shooting guard takes many long shots on offense. On defense, that guard faces the other team's best player on the perimeter. The small forward uses speed. On offense the small forward scores close to the basket. On defense the small forward steals. The power forward attacks with the back toward the basket. On defense the power forward plays under the basket. That player may instead guard the other power forward. The center uses height to score. The center uses height to protect the basket. Manute Bol shares the NBA height record with Gheorghe Muresan. Each stood 7 feet 7 inches. That height is 231 centimeters. History's shortest NBA player was Muggsy Bogues. He stood 5 feet 3 inches. That height is 160 centimeters. The court has had many outstanding players. Their personalities were vivid.

8Their feats broke records. George Mikan stood 6 feet 10 inches. That height is 208 centimeters. The 1950s made him an early example of a big man. He changed what the sport was. Before him, people thought the game belonged to small, quick players. Wilt Chamberlain played in the 1960s and the 1970s. He stood 7 feet 1 inch. That height is 216 centimeters. He held the top marks for scoring. He held the top marks for rebounding. He held the top marks for durability. Many rank him among the finest players in NBA history. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar kept changing games for his teams. His high school team won seventy-one games in a row. It was little surprise that he became the NBA's all-time leader in points. People call Lisa Leslie a mother of the WNBA. Her skills were phenomenal. She ruled the court through the 1990s. She ruled it through the 2000s. Four Olympic golds came with the American squad. Voters named her WNBA MVP three times. MVP means Most Valuable Player. She won two WNBA championships. Earvin Johnson is known as Magic. He became famous with the Los Angeles Lakers. He became famous with the Olympic Dream Team. Fans were amazed by his command of every part of the game.

9His passes were surprising. They were skillful. They looked almost like magic. Michael Jordan is often called the greatest player the sport has had. He holds an impressive stack of records. People nicknamed him Air Jordan. They nicknamed him His Airness. The names came from his leaps and his famous slam dunks. Three Ohio state titles came while LeBron James was still in high school. Right after graduation, the Cleveland Cavaliers picked him. No younger NBA player had ever been named Rookie of the Year. He also became the youngest to reach ten thousand career points. Maya Moore starred in high school. She starred in college. Her college team won ninety games in a row. That streak broke records. Soon after joining the WNBA, she ranked among the top scorers. Wide praise placed her among the sport's finest women athletes. Four championships came with her help. Two Olympic gold medals were hers. The sport has traveled far from a simple start. News coverage keeps fans interested all year. Courts sit in neighborhood parks. They sit at schools. They even sit in some driveways around the world. A person who wants to learn can do so with ease.

10Schools offer ways to practice. Community clubs offer ways to practice. They offer ways to join a team. Nobody knows where the next great stars will appear. The Cage is a famous court. It stands on West 4th Street in New York City. Words to know. Acclaim means strong, eager praise. Competitive describes a rivalry among people, teams, or businesses. Defense is the effort to stop the other team from scoring. It also names the players who do that work. Dribbles means moving a ball ahead with repeated bounces. In this sport the bounces come from the hands. The same word can cover taps in soccer or field hockey, by feet or by a stick. Durability means a person or thing can stay strong for a long while. Interference means blocking something from going forward or from being finished. Leagues are groups of teams that play one another. Offense is the effort to score on the other team. It also names the players who try to score. Opposing describes a clash or a contest with someone or something. Phenomenal means amazing or impressive. A rebound is the bounce back off a hard surface. Strategies are thought-out plans aimed at a problem or a goal.

63. Rights Set Down Beside the Highest Law

1Lorena, the mother of Mary Beth Tinker, appears with her and with Paul, the younger brother. Mary Beth is reacting to court news from 1969. A black armband had gotten her suspended at junior high. The pages after this one take up the country's highest law. They tell how a written list of rights was joined to that law. They spell out what the list guards. Later changes come after that, along with people who still had to struggle. A last look and a word list close the book. During 1965, five students in Iowa's city of Des Moines wore black armbands inside school. Punishment came from the school district. The bands were a protest, and the protest stayed peaceful. The target was the Vietnam War, fought from 1955 until 1975. Leaders of the district ordered the bands taken off. The students would not obey. Suspension from school followed. Three of them, together with their parents, sued the district. America's highest court, the United States Supreme Court, heard that lawsuit in 1969. Judges on the U.S. Supreme Court said the armbands could stay. No disturbance had come from the students. Other students' rights had not been blocked. An amendment inside the U.S. Constitution was the basis of the ruling. Judges treated the black bands as speech. Protection for that speech sits in the First Amendment. That amendment is one piece of the Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights names the opening ten amendments. Citizen liberties are what those amendments guard. A large building for the United States Supreme Court stands in Washington, D.C. The Bill of Rights belongs inside the U.S. Constitution. When the United States formed, that Constitution became its earliest law and its highest one.

2Government work takes its framework from it. Any further law has to follow the principles written there. Earlier, the land was not yet one country. Great Britain had planted thirteen colonies on ground seized by force, ground Native peoples had held. Rule came from the British Parliament and from King George III. Colonists in America had nobody speaking for them in Parliament. A widespread feeling grew that their rights were ignored. Revolution began among the colonists in 1775. Independence from Great Britain was declared in 1776, one year later, and the United States was established. Britain refused to accept those steps. Fighting lasted seven further years and stopped at last in 1783. Visitors in the city of Washington, D.C., can see the original U.S. Constitution. Men who helped set up the United States of America are known as the Founders. Their communities treated them as respected leaders. Wealth was common among them. So was a strong education. Law or politics was the background of most. While the war with Great Britain went on, these men built a confederation of states. Power at the center of that confederation was weak. A congress was created to watch over ordinary government business. The congress had a president. Kingly power was something the Founders refused to hand their leaders. Most powers went to the states instead. Once the war was over, the system looked unsuccessful. Change was the decision. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the meeting place in 1787. A constitution was the writing job. Rules and guidelines for a fresh system of government were the aim. Debate over the Constitution happened at Independence Hall in that same Pennsylvania city. More strength for the central government was wanted.

3People call that central government the federal government. The Founders still refused to allow enough strength to strip citizens of rights and freedoms. Their goal was a democracy. In that form of government, citizens hold power. Choosing leaders is their right, and elections are the method. Native nations supplied ideas the Founders borrowed. The strongest inspiration was the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Several Native nations belonged to it. Together they ran a government that covered many states. Each nation also kept a government of its own. September 1787 was the finish of the new constitution. By the middle of 1788, approval had come from every state except two. The Constitution was now the law of the land. Election made George Washington the earliest president. Opening words of the U.S. Constitution are We the People. Protection still did not cover every person in the original document. Enslaved people were left out of the rights it outlined. Native peoples were left out. Most women of that time were left out too. Later amendments, and later laws, widened those rights to reach these groups. Creation of the Constitution left women out. Many women still helped build the new nation. Essays by women took up politics. Other essays took up gender equality. Still others took up abolition. Political issues were discussed in gatherings the women hosted. Some women sat in on sessions of Congress. Political rallies included them. Abigail Adams stands among the most influential of these women. She was married to the Founder John Adams and served as his close advisor. One letter to her husband carried a famous request. Her request was that he remember the ladies while the new constitution was being written.

4North Carolina voted against the Constitution. Rhode Island did too. Approval was refused. Joining the new government was refused too, until rights were set down in a bill. Federalists, some of the Founders, warned that such a list could be dangerous. A written set of rights, they said, might teach people a false lesson. Anything missing from the list might look unprotected. James Madison, a leading Founder, shared that view. Thomas Jefferson, another important Founder, took the opposite side. A bill of rights, he said, was necessary. Jefferson and other Antifederalists wanted certain rights guaranteed. No government should be able to remove them. Both Madison and Jefferson came from Virginia. That state's constitution already held a Declaration of Rights. Bills of rights appeared in several state constitutions. Jefferson wanted citizen rights written out inside the U.S. Constitution. Agreement from Madison came at last. He began building a bill of rights. One model was the Declaration of Rights from Virginia. Another, dated 1215, was the Magna Carta. The English Bill of Rights, dated 1689, was a third model. A picture places James Madison above Thomas Jefferson. Both helped make the Bill of Rights. Madison read bills of rights from other states. Delegates offered suggestions, and he listened. His proposal to Congress was twenty amendments. Congress reduced the count to twelve. States received those amendments in 1789. North Carolina was now willing to ratify. Rhode Island was willing too. By the close of 1791, ten of the twelve had yes votes from three out of every four states, the share the rules demanded. Those ten became the Bill of Rights. Limiting a government's powers with a bill of rights did not begin in the United States.

5England's version passed in 1689. More than 100 years separated that law from the American one. Written documents that guard civil and political rights now exist in most democracies around the world. A written constitution with a bill of rights exists in Canada. New Zealand has one. South Africa has one. Germany has one, and so do India and Japan. Forty-seven nations in Europe and nearby have taken up a pact named European Convention on Human Rights. Five important rights of a person sit in the First Amendment. Speech is one of them. Sharing ideas in public cannot be answered with jail. Criticism of the government does not remove that shield. Citizens may also petition. They may ask for changes to laws they reject. Peaceful gatherings for protest are allowed as well. During the civil rights movement, large peaceful protests were among the strongest tools. In 2017, members of the Lakota nation protested in North Dakota. An oil pipeline was being built through lands they hold sacred. The press is another First Amendment protection. News may be shared by journalists. Opinions may be shared too. During the 1700s, the public got information only from newspapers and other printed materials. Radio now falls under press freedom as well. Television does too. So does the Internet. Religion is a further First Amendment right. One official religion is the pattern in many countries. It is not the pattern here. Special preference for one faith over another is blocked. Americans may follow any religion. They may follow none. Owning weapons is a citizen right under the Second Amendment. Using weapons is part of that right too. Some readers think the amendment was aimed only at militia groups.

6The National Guard is an example of such a group. Other readers think every U.S. citizen received the right to own weapons and to use them. British soldiers, before the Revolutionary War, could take over private homes. The Third Amendment stops officials from making citizens shelter soldiers in their homes. Under the Fourth Amendment, a search needs a solid reason. An arrest also needs a solid reason to think a crime was committed. A judge must be asked for a warrant. Without it, police cannot search someone's property. They cannot take that property either. People accused of crimes are covered by four amendments: the Fifth, then the Sixth, then the Seventh, and also the Eighth. The Fifth says nobody can be pushed into a criminal trial without good reason. The reason must support a belief that guilt is possible. A criminal offense means a crime against the public or against a state. Court must prove the charge before any punishment. The Sixth requires a trial as soon as possible. The trial has to be public. A jury must be present. A lawyer is a defendant's right. Knowing the accuser is a right as well. The Seventh deals with a civil crime, meaning a crime against a person or a company. A jury trial is a right in that setting too. The Eighth rejects punishments that are cruel and unusual. Fines that climb too high are rejected too. In the era of that amendment, burning with red-hot irons was a punishment some criminals faced. Others were locked in wooden stocks where the public could see them. Those punishments are forbidden now. A painting made in 1805 shows a crowd in Great Britain.

7People shout insults at men standing in wooden stocks. The stocks were the punishment for their crimes. Rights that the earlier amendments never named are covered by the last two parts of the Bill of Rights. The Ninth says that listing some rights does not cancel others. Citizens may hold further rights. The Tenth says government holds only powers the Constitution gives it. Any power left unlisted is held by the states, or else by the citizens. Dates that matter for the U.S. Constitution include these. Fighting in the American Revolutionary War starts in 1775. The Declaration of Independence wins approval from the Continental Congress in 1776. That war ends in 1781. Writing of the U.S. Constitution happens in 1787. Approval comes in 1788. The Bill of Rights, meaning those opening ten amendments, is added in 1791. Slavery is abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865. The 14th Amendment, in 1868, grants citizenship rights to everyone born in the United States. Naturalized people are included. The 15th Amendment, in 1870, gives every male citizen the vote. Color does not block it. Race does not block it. Women gain the vote through the 19th Amendment in 1920. The voting age drops to 18 under the 26th Amendment in 1971. More amendments arrived after 1791, the year those ten amendments were attached. A new amendment is hard to pass. Only Congress may propose one. A Constitutional Convention may propose one too, if two-thirds of all state governments call for it. After a proposal, three-fourths of all state governments must vote yes. Ratified is the word for an amendment that becomes law. Twenty-seven amendments stand in the Constitution today. After the Bill of Rights, two of the most important are the Thirteenth and the Fourteenth.

8They passed once the Civil War was over. That war ran from 1861 to 1865. Slavery inside the United States was made illegal by the Thirteenth Amendment. The picture is an illustration of a celebration. People who had lived in slavery mark the passage of that change. Citizenship in the U.S. reached formerly enslaved people through the Fourteenth Amendment. Children born to immigrant parents received it too. Equal protection of the laws was promised to every U.S. citizen. Race was not allowed to change that promise. Racial segregation of public schools in the U.S. ended largely because of this amendment. During the 1940s, Oliver Brown tried to place his daughter in a school close to home. He was a Black man in Topeka, Kansas. White students were the ones that nearby school served. The school said no. A school for Black students was the only option, and it sat farther from her home. Brown carried the dispute into court. By 1954 the dispute had reached the Supreme Court. Nine judges, the full bench, said public-school segregation by race broke the Fourteenth Amendment. Schools serving white children and schools serving Black children were not equal. Historians treat the ruling as one of the Court's most important. Suffragists march because they want women to gain the vote. Inside a democracy, voting ranks among a citizen's most important rights. Before the Constitution, land ownership was required. White men made up most of the owners. All white men received the vote in 1856. Most Black men still lacked a legal vote until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870. Women received the vote from the Nineteenth Amendment. Their organizing and their fight lasted more than seventy years.

9Passage came in 1920. Americans are now supposed to have their rights guaranteed by the Bill of Rights and by later amendments. Fights for those rights still happen often. Alondra Jones, in 2000, was an honor student living in California. Her high school sat in a low-income area. Black students and Latino students made up most of the enrollment. Textbooks were too few. Computers were absent. Upkeep of the buildings was poor. Rats infested them. Another high school showed her a sharp contrast. Books were there. Computers were there. Buildings were clean and safe. She understood that her own school got far less money than other schools in the state. A 2006 photo shows Alondra Jones speaking at an ACLU conference. Almost one hundred other students joined her lawsuit. A group known as the American Civil Liberties Union did the filing. That nonprofit legal group defends rights held by American citizens. Judges in the case said California had failed to give students equal protection. The Fourteenth Amendment demands that protection. A good education, the court said, was every student's right. Socioeconomic status could not erase it. Samantha Elauf was seventeen in 2008 when she asked a clothing store in Oklahoma for a job. A hijab was the reason for refusal. Many Muslim women wear that head covering. Store leaders said it broke the dress code for employees. A federal body, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, took the store to court on her behalf. The lawsuit climbed to the Supreme Court. A 2015 ruling favored Samantha. Judges said the store had discriminated against her on account of her religion. She stands with her mother before the Supreme Court building.

10Across history, different groups have kept struggling for rights. Peaceful protest has been one of their methods. Rights held by single persons have a United States story that opens with the Constitution. Perfection was not part of that document. When it was written, protection left out most people in the country. Later generations fought to gain what the Constitution promised citizens. They fought to keep those rights as well. Alondra Jones belongs in that line of people. Samantha Elauf does too. More than two hundred years have passed since people penned the Bill of Rights. Scores of later amendments, plus many laws, have widened the shield so every citizen is covered. Advocates still push for equality. They still push for protection under the law. Call a change, or an added piece, an amendment when it alters a document or a law. Someone who is excluded has been kept outside a group. The Bill of Rights names the opening ten amendments of the United States Constitution, and those amendments guarantee chosen rights. Federalists backed ratification of that Constitution. The same label also names the Federalist Party. A confederation joins states, provinces, or groups under one organization, while central authority stays limited. A petition is a formal request in writing, or a formal appeal, sent to authority. Official approval is what ratify means. Written rules and principles that United States laws rest on are the Constitution. Speaking or acting for another person, or for a group, is representation. Finding fault, or judging with disapproval, is criticizing. A warrant is an order in writing that allows an arrest or a search. Equality is the condition in which the same rights belong to everyone.

64. Shackleton's Ship in the Ice

1Beside the stuck ship, the crew of Endurance pose together for a photograph. Six sections shape this account. They cover the trap, the lost south, waiting on the ice, the run to Elephant Island, the deadliest water, the safe return, and a word list. Ice closed on Endurance before anyone in the crew could step onto the Antarctic mainland. Caught The ship was trapped. January 1915 found Endurance inside the Antarctic Circle, locked in pack ice. The crew felt sure the ice would break, as it had for earlier ships, and let them sail. They trusted Sir Ernest Shackleton, a veteran explorer of the Antarctic, to lead them out. Ice kept closing. The strong wooden hull stayed fast. Weeks became months. Shackleton and the men waited in hope the ice would set them free. That release never arrived. A daunting task remained. They sat in the most isolated region on Earth. Home did not know their fate or their position. Satellites did not exist, and neither did radios that could reach far. No call for help was possible. Survival meant saving themselves. Lost in the far south Sir Ernest Shackleton conceived the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. He and a team would land on the Antarctic coast, travel by dogsled, and try a crossing of the continent that no party had completed. Their mission sat in Britain's long custom of exploration, a custom that had mapped and recorded much of the globe. Antarctica was still among the least known places. Harsh conditions demanded huge supplies, careful plans, and real courage. Shackleton had that courage, and the Antarctic was not new to him.

2Two earlier expeditions there had made his name. He led in a way that was tough and fair. He never ordered a job he was unwilling to do with his own hands, and the men respected him for it. Bold years at the poles By the late eighteen hundreds, explorers from the West had walked nearly every land on Earth. Polar regions still hid mysteries that drew daring travelers. Teams that included Ernest Shackleton tried for the South Pole twice, in 1902 and again in 1909. Both times they were turned back. In 1911 the Norwegian Roald Amundsen and his team were first to stand at the globe's southernmost point. Only weeks later, Britain's Robert Falcon Scott reached that same point. On the way back, Scott died on the return, and so did the four men with him, from hunger and from cold. A photograph shows the Trans-Antarctic crew aboard Endurance. Shackleton picked that ship himself, impressed by a stout hull built to meet heavy ice and push through it. The crew he gathered was hardy and experienced. Captain Frank Worsley would prove a superb navigator under the worst conditions. Frank Wild, a close friend, was second-in-command. The rest were skilled and resourceful, qualities Antarctica's surprises required. Endurance left Great Britain in August 1914. On December 5, 1914, four months later, it cleared the final harbor. That harbor was South Georgia Island, lying in southern seas of the Atlantic. Pack ice, which ringed much of the continent, met the ship only two days out.
