That example fueled a wealth of research, as other scientists tested his ideas and asked questions of their own. His years run from 1942 to 2018. The science was remarkable. So was the unbridled zest for life that inspired people. Brilliance and a curiosity that would not stop sat in his mind. Severe limits from illness did not remove his drive to locate a purpose for life, and a meaning in it.

10Birth fell three centuries after the death of Galileo, the Italian astronomer. Death fell on Albert Einstein's birthday. It fits that those dates tie Hawking to two scientists who also changed how people think about the universe. Words from the book Acclaim, a noun, is strong or enthusiastic praise. Asserted, a verb, means stated something with force or confidence. Compressed, a verb, means squeezed tightly together. Conceivable, an adjective, means able to be imagined. Controversial, an adjective, describes a subject that stirs wide disagreement. Cosmology, a noun, is the study of how the universe began and what it is. Devastating, an adjective, means causing great harm to body or to feeling. A diagnosis is the naming of an illness or an injury. Eccentric, an adjective, means strange, or behaving unlike what people expect. A fellowship is money given for graduate study that includes teaching or who researches. Infinitely, an adverb, means without any limit. Inquiry, a noun, is the act of seeking information or of asking. A predicament is a fix that is hard, unpleasant, or confusing. Prestigious, an adjective, means highly honored or respected. Radiation, a noun, is energy sent out as waves or as particles. Rigorous, an adjective, means very strict or demanding, and also careful and exact. Staggering, an adjective, means shocking in its scale. A synthesizer is an electronic device that makes and shapes sound, often for music. A theoretical physicist explains and predicts nature by using mathematics and abstract ideas. Unbridled, an adjective, means free of restraint. Unceasingly, an adverb, means without a stop. Unintelligible, an adjective, means impossible to understand. Vigorously, an adverb, means with energy and force. Visualization, a noun, is the forming of a mental picture.

70. The Air War That Saved Britain

1Pilots from India reach London in 1940, ready to fly for the Royal Air Force. Six sections organize this account. They cover a refusal to quit, the buildup in the air, the sky battle, the long bombing of cities, Britain's proudest stretch, and a word list. On the beaches at Dunkirk, French soldiers and British soldiers wait, with no clear idea of what comes next. A refusal to quit June 1940 found the fighting on Europe's mainland nearly finished. Adolf Hitler led Nazi Germany. Only nine months had passed since that nation opened World War II. The opening blow was the invasion of Poland, dated September 1, 1939. Germany had grown into a formidable Axis power. Allied powers stood against it. Both Britain and France belonged to that Allied side. Their declaration of war on Germany came two days after Poland was invaded. In the months after that, Denmark fell, then Norway, then the Netherlands. May 1940 brought the German blow to Belgium and to France. Close to 400,000 troops from Britain crossed to the mainland to help. Germany's forces were too strong, and they were also too quick. Belgium was in German hands after a little more than a fortnight. The French army and the British army that had tried to hold Belgium were retreating at full speed. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers from Britain and France were trapped by May 27. The trap was Dunkirk, a port in France. Capture looked almost sure. Destruction looked almost sure. Then an astonishing rescue began. For the next week, craft shuttled across the English Channel. Navy ships of Britain took part. Fishing boats took part. Civilian boats took part. That Channel is the Atlantic stretch lying between the British Isles and Europe's mainland. June 4 saw about 338,000 troops brought off and set down where Britain could keep them safer. A German landing now seemed blocked by the Channel alone.

2Prime minister Winston Churchill spoke to the whole nation. His aim was to harden people for a fight that looked unavoidable. He called for every bit of strength. He called for confidence. He told them to guard the country no matter the cost. His last demand was that they never give up. Pictures of that Dunkirk rescue show the boats at work. An air war, the Battle of Britain, was about to open. Members of the Women's Auxiliary Australian Air Force are shown at work on an airplane. Getting ready to fly Back in 1938, two years before those events, many Britons feared a war with Nazi Germany was forming. Hitler had enlarged Germany's forces and looked ready to use them. Leaders in Britain started bracing for the worst. Their own forces were growing. Once war was declared, every eligible man had to register. Young men entered the army, the navy, and the air arm. Young women entered too. They signed on in Great Britain, and also in lands of the British Empire, among them Australia, Canada, India, and Kenya. Britain watched Germany's air arm, the Luftwaffe, with a wary eye. Leaders prepared for war fought mainly from the sky. New fighter planes were built and sent up by the Royal Air Force, the RAF. Air bases grew. Cities were ringed with antiaircraft guns. Ordinary people would fill crucial jobs, and the jobs would cover a wide range. Factories of war hired hands to build planes, and also tanks, ships, and guns. Children joined drives that gathered scrap metal and gathered paper. Officials urged families to plant gardens and to save food. Rationing of food began. Posters of propaganda were printed and hung, both to lift mood and to ready people for danger that might arrive. The public was told, above every other message, to stay calm and carry on. A service called Air Raid Precautions, or ARP, started work in 1937.

3Coordinating the answer to air attacks was its task. Firefighters and rescue crews were hired and trained for the wreckage bombing would leave. From 1939, ARP wardens enforced blackout rules. Streetlights had to go dark. Windows needed black curtains. The goal was to hide targets from German bomb crews overhead. A picture shows an ARP warden near London setting the hour of the blackout. In city blocks, some families built backyard shelters known as Anderson shelters. Part of each shelter sat underground, with iron sheets over the top. During 1939, local units called the Home Guard took shape. The volunteers, many of them past the usual age for enlistment, promised to fight if German troops landed. Six people could fit in an Anderson shelter. Leaving the cities Plans for civil defense moved children out of big cities, and also older people and patients from hospitals. The countryside of Britain was one destination. Far parts of the empire, Canada and Australia among them, were others. Evacuation's first wave began on the war's first day, September 1, 1939. Children left their families. Most stayed with people who were complete strangers. In time, some 3.5 million people, children in the majority, boarded trains or ships and were carried to safer ground. A picture shows children in London waiting to be sent away. A June 1940 map of Europe marks control of the land. Ireland sits apart from the fighting. Separate marks show Axis control, countries that stayed neutral, and Allied control. Named on the map are England, the Netherlands, the English Channel, Germany, Belgium, and Luxembourg. Also named are the Atlantic Ocean, Austria, Switzerland, France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain. Once France fell to Germany in June 1940, Britain had no ally left on the continent. Occupied ground sat just across the Channel. At the narrowest, that water was only 30 kilometers, which is 18 miles. Some figures in Britain's government thought giving up was the only sane path.

4Churchill was not among them. He was a forceful leader, newly risen to be prime minister. He had studied how Hitler worked, and he believed the dictator meant to occupy Britain. A growling voice and brilliant speeches let him persuade his ministers. Defense of the homeland, he argued, was the single option. An April 1940 picture shows Churchill speaking to sailors in London. Another shows British troops on the English coast, braced for a German landing. When Britain made plain that it would keep fighting, Nazi planners drafted an invasion. Planners code-named it Operation Sea Lion. German soldiers, counted in the tens of thousands, would cross aboard troop ships from the freshly taken coasts of France and of Belgium. Soldiers trained as paratroopers would drop from aircraft. No day was fixed. Planners on both sides assumed the landing had to come before winter, because after that the stormy Atlantic was as deadly as a weapon. Germany's first job, before any landing, was to destroy the Royal Air Force. While RAF planes remained a threat, a crossing could turn into a bloodbath, both for ships and for men trying to reach shore. July 1940 brought the first German war planes over Britain. During the Battle of Britain, a British Spitfire fighter is shown chasing a German bomber, the Heinkel He 111. The sky battle Raids from Germany opened early in July. The Luftwaffe tested what the RAF could do, learning all it could. Those first blows fell mostly on the Channel. Supply ships were sunk. Port cities were bombed. From August the attacks grew much heavier. Bombers and German fighters crossed in wave after wave and struck targets in Britain. Pilots of the RAF flew straight at those formations. They tried to knock the attackers from the sky or shove them off their path. Britain held two advantages the Germans never fully grasped.

5Radar came first. Spelled out, the name means finding direction and range by radio. The new gear sent radio signals that found incoming planes and warned the RAF an attack was near. Pilots then scrambled and tried to cut the raiders off. Because of radar, defenses could mass where they were needed. Towers for the system stood along the shore. German crews tried to wreck them and had only limited success. Women in the air arm Crucial help in the Battle of Britain came from the Women's Auxiliary Air Force, the WAAF. Women served at radar stations. As plotters in command rooms, they steered RAF fighters toward Luftwaffe squadrons. They also ran barrage balloons. Those huge balloons hung over cities and pushed enemy planes to higher altitudes, which made the bombing less accurate. Service in the WAAF passed 180,000 women by 1943. A picture shows WAAF plotters at their boards while aircraft fill the sky. Colossus, the computer that let Britain read Germany's coded military notes, is shown under the hands of a Women's Royal Naval Service member. Britain's second advantage was among the war's great secrets. By mid-1940, experts from Poland and from Britain had broken the secret codes German leaders used in sent messages. British chiefs could therefore read communications that were supposed to stay hidden, both on strategy and on tactics. In the Battle of Britain, those intercepted notes often told air commanders about a German raid before Luftwaffe planes had even left the ground. Through August, the steady raids ground the RAF down. Flyers and ground crews were worn out. Many flew several missions in a single day, each one a fight that could kill them. Planes, airfields, and other RAF sites were smashed faster than crews could mend them. A German strike on August 24, 1940, turned the battle onto a new path. Several German planes bombed civilian districts of London.

6Until then, Luftwaffe raids had aimed only at military sites and at factories. People today think the London hit was an accident. Churchill saw a chance to hit back at once and ordered a strike on Berlin. The next night, British bombers numbering more than seventy flew deep into enemy land. Damage from their bombs was small. British spirits still rose. German leaders were stunned and furious. The Luftwaffe's own air marshal had promised that no enemy bomb would ever land on Berlin. Early in September the Luftwaffe changed its method. Raids now hit factories and neighborhoods in London, and in other large British cities. What had been the Battle of Britain became a campaign against the people themselves. Britons came to call those raids the Blitz. A picture shows Hermann Göering, the Luftwaffe's air marshal, speaking with an official of that air arm. Planes of the fight Britain's Supermarine Spitfire was a fighter. Its speed could reach 594 kilometers an hour, or 370 miles an hour. Its climb could reach 11,000 meters, or 37,000 feet. Handling was easy, and speed was high. Eight machine guns rode on it, and each gun could fire 350 rounds. Germany's Messerschmitt Bf 109 was a fighter the Luftwaffe had already proved in battle. It outpaced the Spitfire and matched it in maneuver. Bf 109 planes guarded the German bomber fleets. The Messerschmitt Bf 110 used two engines and two crew. It was slow, and RAF fighter squadrons tore those planes apart. Britain's Hawker Hurricane was a fighter that could also bomb. It could meet German fighters and could bomb German ships. Top speed was 541 kilometers an hour, or 335 miles an hour. The Heinkel He 111, a German medium bomber, did the most destruction in the Battle of Britain and again in the Blitz. Five crew flew it. Its bomb load passed 2,268 kilograms, or 5,000 pounds. The Avro Lancaster was a heavy bomber and one of the war's best night bombers.

7Some were changed so they could carry a bomb of 6,250 kilograms, or 14,000 pounds. Cities under bombs Britain's press made the campaign's name famous. Blitzkrieg, a German word for a war like lightning, supplied that name. German leaders wanted to terrify Britain's people, drain their will to fight, and smash war factories. In a furious speech, Hitler promised to lay Britain's cities to waste. September 7, 1940, opened the Blitz. German bombers numbering more than three hundred hit major cities across Great Britain, with six hundred fighters alongside. Smoke trails marked dogfights as RAF fighters met the enemy. Bombs burst in neighborhoods and in streets. That day's raids killed 430 civilians and badly wounded about 1,600 more. Through later days, weeks, and months, bomber waves kept dropping explosive bombs and incendiary bombs, while German fighters tried to hold the RAF off. A picture shows London smoldering after that first mass raid on the city, dated September 7, 1940. German Heinkel He 111 bombers, flying as a squadron, are shown over the English Channel. September 15 brought raids of special severity. London suffered two huge Luftwaffe attacks, starting just past midnight and lasting until the following dusk. German aircraft in the assault numbered nearly 1,900, and the attack lasted nearly 24 hours. Crews were surprised again by how many Spitfires and Hurricanes came at them in a rush. A claim had reached those crews that Britain's fighter command would soon have no aircraft left. Once more the RAF stopped Germany from winning a decisive result. Each year, people remember the date as Battle of Britain Day. When raids were spotted, air-raid sirens roared and told city people to take cover. Some went under bridges. Some used church basements or warehouse basements. Others used shelters built at home. Few of those places were safe from a direct hit, or from a blast that landed close.

8A picture shows a bus in a crater left by a bomb that wrecked part of a London station on the underground railway. The raids forced Britain to face an ugly truth. Wealth or poverty could decide who lived. People with money could flee to country estates. Officials of means could hide in bunkers underground. An average family got little thought. Neighborhoods of working people were especially exposed, and German bombers hit them often. Many families watched homes burn or blow apart. Deep shelters underground were needed, but the government was slow. Officials feared that crowds in underground train stations would disrupt the stations' work. They also feared some citizens would hide below and refuse their jobs, to avoid being outdoors while bombs fell. Tickets were purchased all the same, and people slept on the platforms. Bombs kept falling, and the public grew angrier that leaders did so little for safety. Some staged protests to force attention onto the danger. At last those leaders admitted they must do more for the cities' most vulnerable people. Shelters in London's underground stations were approved and organized. A bunker system went up that could shield some 64,000 people. Residents of London at the time were estimated at 8.6 million. A picture shows Londoners waiting out a raid down in a train station. Bombing cities brought results Germany had not planned. Most British people drew together, defying Germany. They stood with Churchill. War bonds became one way they paid for the fight. The Home Guard gained more volunteers, and so did further groups. Neighbors took in family and friends whose houses were gone. Instead of breaking the will to fight, the raids often built camaraderie and a harder resolve. Ideas of surrender faded. The switch also gave the Royal Air Force a break it badly needed. Attacks on airfields, hangars, and plane factories had nearly cracked the force.

9Skilled pilots were few and exhausted. Without meaning to, the German High Command let the RAF recover and regroup. British bombers flew missions of their own to keep Germany off balance. They hit factories, and they hit bases and ports where an invasion was being prepared. Landing craft and other ships were destroyed. Rail lines that fed the staging areas were blown up. Mid-September brought welcome news from Britain's intelligence service. Hitler had chosen to put the invasion off. Winter was close, Atlantic storms would soon rise, and the RAF was still just as hard to beat. City bombing, though, was nowhere near finished. As September closed, more Luftwaffe attacks shifted to night. Darkness made German planes very hard for the RAF and for other defenses to find. Industrial cities took the worst of it along with London. Regular targets included Manchester, Glasgow, Belfast, Birmingham, and Bristol. Port cities suffered too, because the Luftwaffe hoped to sever relief that came in convoys of ships from Canada and from the United States. On May 10, 1941, after eight months of bombing, those huge raids flew for the last time. June brought a surprise German drive into Russia and into the wider Soviet Union. With that, the Blitz ended. Across both the sky battle and the bombing of cities, Britain was battered and burned. Civilian deaths reached some 40,000. Homes destroyed or badly damaged passed a million. Hitler's grand plan had been blocked, and the country lived to fight on. The proudest hour Britain had stood up under everything Nazi Germany could drop. Its forces could now regroup, rebuild, and rearm. By early 1942 a formidable alliance tied Britain to the Soviet Union and to the United States. That second partner had joined the fighting in December 1941. Bombers and fighters from the United States joined the RAF against targets Germany held on the mainland. By outlasting the Luftwaffe's overwhelming campaign, Britain kept a base that Allied air operations could not spare.

10British and American air power together pounded Germany's forces, its industry, and its cities. A sharp irony followed. In June 1944, several years afterward, Britain was the ground from which the Allies invaded France while Germany still held it. A 1944 picture shows American troops training for that invasion. Ruin stood all around, yet people in Britain tried to keep ordinary life going. On June 18, 1940, still before the Battle of Britain opened, Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a speech. He urged citizens to meet their duty to the country. Future generations, he said, should look back and call the time Britain's finest hour. For many British people, the country's conduct in World War II, and its courage, still stand for that finest hour. Words from the book Propaganda, a noun, means stories or claims that are false or stretched, spread to sway people or to push one view. Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. Blitzkrieg, a noun, is a sudden, intense military blow meant to win quickly. Radar, a noun, is a device that locates or tracks objects by sending radio waves and catching them after they bounce back. Camaraderie, a noun, is the friendship or warm feeling shared by companions who pass their days side by side. Civilian, an adjective, concerns people outside the military and the police. Rationing, a noun, is the controlled sharing of goods and services when supplies run short. Luftwaffe, a noun, is the name of Germany's air force. Royal Air Force, a noun, is Britain's air force, shortened to RAF. Paratroopers are soldiers trained to leap from planes and fight behind the lines of an enemy. Vulnerable, an adjective, describes someone who can be hurt with ease. Prime minister, a noun, is the government leader in most countries that use a parliament.

71. The Ancient Stone Ring on Salisbury Plain

1A monument from before writing comes first, then a Stone Age site and a landscape crowded with monuments. A project lasting 1,500 years follows, with questions about purpose, the site in our time, a story still unfolding, and a word list. Among prehistoric places, Stonehenge ranks with the most visited in the world. Long ago, people in the south of England spent enormous effort. They stood a ring of huge stones upright. The name of that monument today is Stonehenge. Centuries later, many of the great megaliths lie fallen. Fascination remains. It remains even though the original purpose was forgotten. Roughly nine hundred years ago, Geoffrey of Monmouth, a historian in England, tried to explain the mystery. His tale was fanciful and concerned Merlin, wizard of the legends about King Arthur. Merlin, he wrote, told another king to build a memorial meant to last forever. Stonehenge was the outcome. Magic from Merlin, Monmouth claimed, helped the building, and he set the date about sixteen hundred years ago. People long ago spent huge effort in the south of England so a ring of great stones could stand. Many of those megaliths later fell, yet the place still draws wonder. Geoffrey of Monmouth, about nine hundred years ago, offered Merlin and magic as the explanation, and he set the building about sixteen hundred years in the past. Investigators have studied Stonehenge for hundreds of years. Archaeologists are among them, along with historians and scientists. They want explanations from science, not from the supernatural.

2Digging at the site has searched for clues. History, builders, and purpose are the targets. What has been learned matches any legend for wonder. Kings, wizards, and magic fill those legends. An age of about two thousand years was once the scholarly guess. Shock followed when research pushed the start much earlier. Work had begun three thousand years before that guess. The time was the Neolithic period, from 10,000 to 2500 bc. People in Britain still lacked metalworking. The wheel had not been invented. Archaeologists are tracing where the bluestones began. Those stones are a rare kind used at the monument. A locator map sets the site inside the United Kingdom. Waters shown are the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. Scotland is marked, with the cities Edinburgh and Glasgow. Northern Ireland is marked, with Belfast. Ireland is marked, with Dublin. England is marked, with London. Wales appears as well. Wider labels reach Europe, then Asia, then Africa. Earth and huge rocks are the building materials. The Washington Monument towers more. Egypt's great pyramids are more enormous. Majesty here comes mostly from how old and how mysterious the place is. Visitors cross a grassy plain in England's south. Standing stones, massive ones, slowly enter view. Circles sit inside other circles. A ditch forms the outer ring. Raised soil, an embankment, is surrounded by that ditch. Diameter is about 110 meters, which is 360 feet. The famous stone ring stands at the center.

3Many of its stones are gone. More than one kind of stone appears at Stonehenge. Sandstone slabs that stand and form the outer ring are known as sarsen stones. About 36,000 kilograms, or 79,366 pounds, is the weight of the largest. Lintels of stone lie across the tops. Once, those lintels linked every standing stone. Inside the sarsen circle lie smaller boulders, the bluestones. Their rock is dolerite, a coarse kind of basalt. About 2,994 kilograms, or 6,600 pounds, is the weight of the largest bluestone. Another set of standing stones sits inside the sarsen ring, arranged like a horseshoe. Together they make trilithons. Each trilithon is a square arch: two upright stones and one lintel across them. Width is about 6.7 meters, or 22 feet. Height is 9 meters, or 29.5 feet. An artist has drawn the monument as it may have looked when finished. Labels point to a trilithon, a lintel, the bluestones, and a sarsen stone. Seventeen sarsen stones still trace the Sarsen Circle. Thirty, archaeologists believe, stood there once. Average weight of the large blocks is 22,680 kilograms, or 50,000 pounds, heavier than a school bus. Height is more than 5 meters, or 16.4 feet. Stones that stand alone also belong to the monument. The Heel Stone is one. The Slaughter Stone is another. Both lie outside the Sarsen Circle. During the thousands of years since, people may have hauled some stones off. Others likely sank. Rituals of importance were probably held here.

4Crowning a ruler may have been one. Celebrating a harvest may have been another. Honoring dead ancestors may have been a third. Some experts think entry was limited to high priests or to other religious leaders. Ordinary people stayed outside the sacred stone circle. Rolling hills and grasslands make up Salisbury Plain, and Stonehenge stands there. Life on that plain seems to reach back past ten thousand years. Woodland covered it in the Neolithic period, and animals were plentiful. Hunter-gatherers found a place of plenty. Ancient pits dug up by archaeologists hold flint tools, flint weapons, and animal bones. The abundance of food, experts speculate, may have made the area feel sacred to those Neolithic people. Around 7500 bc a slow change began to shake the culture. Hunting and gathering gave way, little by little, to farming. Food could be produced more reliably. Larger groups could be fed. Big social projects became possible. Enough food meant less time spent farming and hunting. More time remained for monuments such as Stonehenge. Sheep graze the lush grass of the plain beside the stones. Evidence from archaeology puts the start of building near 3000 bc. Work continued across generations, past a span of one thousand years. Moving the giant stones, and setting them, is viewed as one of early humanity's great engineering feats. Distant quarries, archaeologists believe, supplied the sarsen stones. Distance was about 32 to 48 kilometers, or 20 to 30 miles. Wheels and wagons did not exist yet.

5How, then, were the stones hauled? Far-fetched answers have included giants, magic, and even aliens from space. Realistic options are what archaeologists have chased. Experiments have tested Stone Age methods for moving sarsen-sized stones. Replica stones of similar weight were loaded onto wooden sledges. Those sled-like platforms slid on wooden rails slicked with animal fat. Dozens of volunteers pulled. The trials showed the trip to the site was possible. That method is now a leading theory. Bluestones were a harder puzzle for many years. Nowhere near Stonehenge is a source for them. Research eventually reached Wales. A quarry there lies northward by more than 241 kilometers, or 150 miles. Some unknown reason made the builders believe those heavy stones were worth a staggering journey. Rafts may have carried them, some experts speculate, floating along the ocean coast until the stones were nearer the site. Volunteers in London, during May 2016, tested whether people could pull a heavy stone block like the ones at Stonehenge. No machinery was used. Standing the stones up was a separate engineering problem. One possible method began with a pit under every long stone, right at its foot. Wooden wedges could be pushed, bit by bit, under the top end, lifting it slowly. Once the upper end had risen far enough, the lower end fell down into that pit. Ropes then pulled the stone upright. Other researchers picture a different lift. Wooden platforms were built beneath the stones.

6Setting lintels onto the trilithons may have demanded the most planning and the most skill. Ramps of dirt and wood, high enough to meet each pair of uprights at the crown, are one possibility. A sledge could carry the lintel. Teams with ropes would ease the lintel upward along that ramp until it sat where it belonged. No nearby rock matches the bluestones, so the search ran north into Wales, past 241 kilometers, or 150 miles. Rafts along the coast are one idea for that haul. In London, in May 2016, volunteers pulled a heavy block with no machines, to test what human teams could do. Raising a slab could start with a pit at its foot, wedges under the high end, and ropes once the foot dropped in. Lintels may have ridden sledges up ramps of dirt and wood. Innovative engineering came from these master builders. Their languages are nearly impossible to recover. So are the religions they followed. Writing was not used. Little of their art survives. Archaeology is the only source of modern understanding. Skeletons of people found near the site, and animal bones, have been tested. The tests offer striking clues about origins. Some builders seem to have come from Wales. Others came from lands nearby. A quarry in Pembrokeshire, Wales, is under excavation. The bluestones may have started there. Newer finds say a few people migrated from still farther off, from mainland Europe. The size of Stonehenge suggests separate groups joined forces.

7Knowledge, skill, and muscle were shared. A skeleton was found in 2002 near the town of Amesbury, about 3.2 kilometers, or 2 miles, from the stones. Death came about 4,300 years ago, while building was still underway. Importance is clear from the grave. Gold jewelry was inside, along with arrowheads and stone wrist guards. Archers of that time commonly wore such guards. Chemicals in the teeth were tested. Growth happened in mainland Europe, near the lands that are Germany and Switzerland today. The reason for the move is still unknown. Distance was more than 1,126 kilometers, or 700 miles. Death came far from home. Burial was with honor. Many objects surround this Amesbury Archer's skeleton. A knife is there, along with pots, rings, and earrings. Mystery surrounds the purpose, yet the design holds clues. A practical use, such as shelter or a market, does not seem to have existed. Experts are therefore convinced the place was an open-air temple. Visits were for spiritual reasons. Religious uses, researchers believe, shifted across the long history. Ceremonial uses shifted too. A burial ground was likely the beginning. As many as 240 burials have been unearthed nearby. No Neolithic burial ground in England is larger. Cremation was common. Weapons and jewelry went into some graves. A skeleton of a Neolithic man found at the site is displayed with a reconstructed face. The visitor center near Stonehenge holds them. Astronomy supplies another popular theory. Some giant stones line up with the sun's motion.

8Summer and winter solstices make this especially clear. About June 21 each year is the summer solstice, the longest day. At dawn, sunlight reaches straight to the monument's center. About December 22 is the winter solstice, the shortest day. At sunset, sunlight passes straight through the gap in the biggest sarsen pair. The layout works, in a sense, like a giant clock for the seasons. Farmers needed that information to plan planting. A further theory has appeared in recent years. Some experts think the project was huge because it was meant to unite people nearby. Tribes from far away, the evidence suggests, traveled to Stonehenge, and many stayed for good. Trade may have drawn them. Shared protection may have drawn them. Plenty of food in the region may have drawn them too. Sunrise on June 21, 2014, sends light through the stones. That date is the year's longest day. Europe's prehistoric landmarks include this one among the most famous. What the public sees now is not the view from 1900. By then, most giant stones had tilted or fallen. During the last century, heritage groups put parts back, guided by archaeological evidence. Cranes lifted some stones in 1958. Concrete anchored some of the uprights. Restorers believed the public would then see the original look more clearly. Watchers in 1958 saw England's largest crane set a lintel across two upright stones. Study of the monument and the land around it continues.

9The newest technology maps what lies underfoot. Magnetometers detect magnetic fields. Laser scanners measure possible archaeological sites with precision. Radar that penetrates the ground can scan down to 9 meters, or 29.5 feet. Tourists can use the visitor center and handle its exhibits. Houses of the Neolithic have been rebuilt with authentic materials and methods, including thatch on the roofs, based on finds nearby. Volunteers show old rope weaving, pottery making, and the grinding of grain. Yearly visits top nine hundred thousand. Two children try to drag a sarsen stone. Other visitors step into reconstructed huts of the kind the builders might have lived in. By 1900 most of the giant stones leaned or had fallen. Cranes in 1958 lifted some, and concrete held some upright, so visitors could picture the older shape. England's largest crane that year set a lintel across two standing stones. Magnetometers, laser scanners, and radar that can reach 9 meters, or 29.5 feet, down now map what is buried. Rebuilt houses use old materials, including thatch. Volunteers show rope, pots, and grain. The yearly crowd passes nine hundred thousand. An ancient time and place left this amazing landmark. Visitors are struck by how cleverly the designers aimed the monument at the sun. Massive stones let people picture hundreds of workers moving them to the site together. Teamwork and muscle, visitors may realize, were required to raise the stones and to link them. For centuries the circle was a central sacred site for people of the surrounding lands.

10UNESCO, the United Nations body for education, science, and culture, gave it the title World Heritage Site. Special recognition and protection were the judgment. Imaginations around the world are stirred by it today. England has other stone circles. A larger one stands at Avebury, 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, to the north. A lintel is a piece of stone or of wood. It lies over an opening. A window is one such opening. A door is another. Scientists who study remains of ancient cultures are archaeologists. Ceremonial describes what relates to a formal event, or what is used for one on a special occasion. Large stones that prehistoric people built with, or set up as monuments, are megaliths. An embankment is dirt piled as a wall or as a mound. It may hold up a road. It may keep water back. Neolithic names the Stone Age's latest stretch. Polished stone tools and weapons mark that stretch. A way of life, a tradition, or a trait passed from one generation to the next is heritage. Quarries are dig sites for stone. Marble comes from them too. So does slate. Cleverness or skill used on a problem or a challenge is ingenuity. Returned to an earlier condition is what restored means. A solstice is one of two moments in a year. At those moments the Sun stands farthest from the equator. Creating something new and original is what innovative means.

72. The Boy King and a Death Unsolved

1A British archaeologist named Howard Carter found the tomb of King Tut. A photo shows him studying the golden sarcophagus while the dig was underway. This book follows the find, Tut's homeland, his family, the boy who ruled, the end of a ruling line, the tomb, the suspects, the body, the question of a solution, and words to know. The date of the find was November 4, 1922. The place was Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Egyptian workers helped him. The tomb belonged to Tutankhamun. Say that name toot-an-KAH-muhn. Most people say King Tut. His reign in ancient Egypt sits more than 3,300 years in the past. He became pharaoh at age nine. Say pharaoh FAIR-oh. His rule lasted under ten years. Death came suddenly when he was about nineteen. Ever since the burial was found, people have asked how the young king died. They have asked why. Archaeologists work a bit like detectives. Pronounce that job title in two beats: AR-kee, then OLL-oh-jist. They study evidence. They ask questions. Answers are often hard to reach. The work feels like a jigsaw that is missing many pieces. They study the tomb. They study the body. They study the person's belongings. They also study writing on papyrus. They study words cut into stone. Some of those texts lasted through the centuries. The questions include where Tut lived. They include what his health was like. They include who his family and friends were. They include whether he had enemies. Those answers may unlock the largest question. Why did this king die so young? Ruling families called dynasties governed ancient Egypt for about three thousand years. There were thirty of those families. Historians sort them into periods. The list runs from the Early Dynastic Period to the Old Kingdom. Then comes the First Intermediate Period. Then the Middle Kingdom. Then the Second Intermediate Period. Then the New Kingdom. Then the Third Intermediate Period. The Late Period closes the list. A kingdom was a time of strong central government. An intermediate period was a time of weaker central government. Tutankhamun belonged to the 18th Dynasty. That family was the first to rule in the New Kingdom. The New Kingdom began around 1550 BCE. Tut's birth came almost two hundred years after that beginning. In that Egypt, religion filled daily life.

2People worshipped hundreds of deities. A fuller picture of Tut's life, and maybe of his death, needs that religious history. One image shows how Tut may have looked, with his funeral mask behind him. At the opening of the New Kingdom, two gods stood above the rest. One was Ra. Say it RAH. The other was Amun. Say it AH-muhn. People believed Ra lived inside the Sun. Art often showed him as a falcon. It also showed him as a man with a falcon's head. A sun disk sat on his headdress. His main center of worship was Heliopolis. Heliopolis lies near today's Cairo. Art usually showed Amun as a man. His headdress was tall and carried two plumes. His main center of worship was Thebes. Thebes lies near today's Luxor. In the 18th Dynasty, Sun worship took a new form for some Egyptians. They took an old sun symbol, the Aten. Say it AH-tuhn. They treated the Aten as a new god who created the world. Art showed a large golden disk. Rays of light reached from the disk toward Earth. The rays often stopped close to royal faces. Each ray ended in a hand. The hand held an ankh. The ankh stood for life. A map shows ancient Egypt. As the Aten grew more important to nobles, other gods received less worship. For most people the Aten was simply one more god among many. Some household shrines included him. He was no threat to older beliefs until a young man became pharaoh. That man was Amenhotep IV. Say it ah-muhn-HO-tep. His rule began in 1352 BCE. Egyptian art gives him a long face. It gives him thin calves. It gives him a belly that sticks out. Many theories try to explain why his pictures differ from the usual Egyptian style. Various diseases are among those theories. Some experts think artists gave the Aten female features. They say the god had traits shared by men and by women. Amenhotep grew up inside the newer Aten faith. He saw the Aten as a god for every person in the world. The god was not for Egyptians alone. Aside from Cleopatra, no Egyptian queen is as famous as Nefertiti. Say it neh-fer-TEE-tee. Pharaoh Akhenaten favored her above his other wives.

3Once the prince's mother died, Nefertiti likely raised young Prince Tutankhaten as a stepmother. That prince later became Tutankhamun. Death came for Nefertiti while she was still in her early thirties. The pharaoh believed the Aten made the world at the start of time. He believed the Aten ruled it alone. He believed the bright rays kept giving the world life. Some experts give Amenhotep IV the title of first monotheist in the world. Others say that label does not fit. He admitted other gods existed. He simply chose to worship only the Aten. He expected Egyptians to worship him. He believed he stood equal to the god. The people did not accept that. At home they kept the old gods. Public worship was aimed at Amenhotep IV. Early in his fifth year he took a drastic step. He began a religious revolution. That means a sudden, total change in Egypt's official religion. He announced that public worship could honor only the Aten. He took a new name, Akhenaten. Say it ahk-eh-NAH-tuhn. The name means He Who Serves Aten. Akhenaten shut temples where people worshipped Egypt's other gods. He tried to destroy those temples. Public holidays tied to gods other than the Aten were banned. Religious festivals tied to those gods were banned too. His harsh acts upset a huge population used to many gods. The priests who served those gods were angered. People in several Egyptian regions tried to halt the wrecking of nearby temples. The pharaoh's army was able to control them. He also ordered a new capital. The chosen ground had never held a building. The site was north of Thebes. He called it Akhetaten. Say it ahk-eh-TAH-tuhn. The name means Horizon of Aten. Priests of Amun and followers of Amun called the move a heresy. It went against the religion most Egyptians accepted. Today the area is called Amarna. The upheaval is called the Amarna Revolution. A temple carving at Amarna shows Akhenaten and Nefertiti. Nefertiti may have been Tut's stepmother. Three of their children appear with them. King Tut was born in that new capital. The year was about 1345 BCE. His name was Tutankhaten. The name means the Living Image of Aten. Genetic tests in 2010 let researchers name the mummies of his parents.

4They identified mummies of his grandparents too. The tests used DNA taken from bones. Tut's father matched the mummy who may be Akhenaten. They built a family tree of five generations. The tests show Tut's mother as a full sister of Tut's father. The samples could not identify her any further. Royal families in Egypt often married close relatives. Other cultures of that time did the same. The marriages kept land inside the family. They kept the power that came with the land. Akhenaten died in 1336 BCE. He had ruled for seventeen years. The next events puzzle people as much as Tut's other mysteries do. At best, the old evidence does not go far. Scholars have offered several theories about who took the throne next. In the last century they found signs of two rulers with very short reigns after Akhenaten. One was Smenkhkara. Say it smen-kah-RAH. Akhenaten may have been his brother. Tutankhaten may have been his brother. The other short ruler may have been Nefertiti. The proof is still too thin for anyone to be certain. The throne stood empty again within three or four years of Akhenaten's death. Tutankhaten became pharaoh at age nine. Before his reign, and during it, Tut lived as a wealthy person. He wore jewelry of gold and of silver. He wore linen clothes. He used perfumed oils. He used makeup. Archaeologists found all of these kinds of things in his tomb. Court custom would have sent the pharaoh hunting beside his royal companions. The hunt often used a bow. It often used a moving chariot. Two chariots were placed in the tomb. Nearly fifty bows were placed there. Board games were placed there for the afterlife. The games included senet. They included hounds and jackals. During his reign he married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. Say it AHNK-eh-suhn-PAH-ah-tuhn. Nefertiti and Akhenaten's third daughter was this queen. She Lives Through Aten is the meaning of her name. At least two girls were born to Tut. Both daughters died. Several servants worked in his court. His personal attendant was Tutu. Years of service to the family were already behind Tutu, as with many house workers. The service went back to Tut's grandfather. That grandfather was King Amenhotep III. Other servants, some younger than the king, helped with even the smallest tasks.

5One servant was a cupbearer. The cupbearer's job was to keep drinking cups full. The young king's cup came first. Military decisions mostly fell to other people, since the pharaoh was only a boy. They did most of the political work. Two men mattered most. Ay was one of them, and he was old. His title was Commander of Chariotry. He had been a chief administrative adviser since Akhenaten's reign. Horemheb, the second man, was a general in the army. Say it HOR-ehm-heb. His titles included Great General of the Army. Both men had served Akhenaten. People think both strongly disliked Akhenaten's religious changes. They hoped the young king would restore the old gods. They hoped he would restore the old ways of worship. Horemheb appears in a wall painting as King Tut's general and adviser. Ruins remain from Akhenaten's city of Akhetaten. The city was built around 1348 BCE. Tut felt the pressure of Horemheb and of Ay. They persuaded him to end worship of the Aten. Above all they wanted Amun restored as chief god. The boy king followed their lead. Tutankhaten was set aside. The new name was Tutankhamun. The new name means the Living Image of Amun. The queen took a new name too. She became Ankhesenamun. Say it AHNK-eh-suhn-AH-muhn. By swapping Aten for Amun in their names, king and queen sent a message. Priests of the older faith could read those names as a sign that royalty was dropping Aten worship. Historians are sure Ay and Horemheb drove the changes of Tut's reign. Tut was very young. Historians believe he did what he was told. As part of the return to older ways, the court moved back to Thebes. Akhetaten, once thriving, was left to decay under the Egyptian sun. In 1327 BCE, King Tutankhamun died. He was about nineteen. Ancient texts never officially recorded how he died. That silence created a mystery. Workers mummified the young pharaoh. His grave was a tomb set inside the Valley of the Kings. Near Thebes, that valley served as a large cemetery for royalty. Other New Kingdom kings were buried in the same way. Tut had no surviving children. The throne was open to another person in the royal court.

6Ay had long experience there. That experience made him the new pharaoh. He married Tut's widow. Ankhesenamun never appears in the historical record after that. Ay ruled only four years. He died in 1323 BCE. Horemheb then became pharaoh. A pharaoh, like a person today, had more than one name. There was a name from birth. Other names came when the person became pharaoh. Those names often sat inside an oval. The oval is a cartouche. Say it car-TOOSH. Ancient Egyptians believed names held great power. They thought a name written on an object could harm that person if the object was broken. They thought it could even kill the person. After sixteen years on the throne, Horemheb ordered a destruction. Everything linked to the Aten religion was to be destroyed. Everything linked to Akhenaten was to be destroyed. He wanted a break from earlier leaders. He wanted to show devotion to Amun. He even counted his own reign as if it began when Amenhotep III's reign ended. He acted as if Amenhotep IV had never ruled. He acted as if Tut had never ruled. He acted as if Ay had never ruled. His men demolished the Aten's abandoned temples at Amarna and in other parts of Egypt. They smashed statues of Akhenaten and of his family. Statues of King Tut were smashed. Statues of Ay were smashed. They gouged names and faces out of wall art. Later, workers took away the stone blocks that carried that art. A digger there always hopes to meet a ruler's tomb that is still sealed. Twenty-seven years passed under Horemheb's rule. He died in 1295 BCE. His death ended the 18th Dynasty. Ramses II came afterward, a major ruler in the 19th Dynasty. Ramses II's grandfather had served in the army with Horemheb. Ramses II kept taking building stone from the site. That plunder finished the destruction of Amarna. Broken pieces of Akhenaten's once-splendid capital vanished under drifting sand. People forgot the city. In the 1800s, many archaeologists from Britain and from Europe went to Egypt. They wanted to read Egyptian writing called hieroglyphics. Say it hy-ur-uh-GLIF-iks. The writing covered many walls and monuments. It revealed a great deal about how pharaohs lived. Scholars had long been stuck on that ancient writing. In 1798 Napoleon brought an army to occupy Egypt.

7A soldier in that army found an object more lasting than the occupation itself. It was a flat black rock. Three languages were carved on its surface. Two were forms of ancient Egyptian. The third was Greek. Translation of the remaining languages took the following twenty-five years. They used the Greek text as a key. They used knowledge of Coptic, an Egyptian language, as a key. Progress jumped when a single scholar noticed a key difference. Ancient Egyptian was not simple picture writing. Its symbols stood for sounds, not for whole words. The Rosetta Stone, that same rock, still ranks among archaeology's greatest finds. Archaeologists learned that a pharaoh's tomb held whatever a person might need after death. They dug up many tombs in hope of money from those sacred objects. They were always disappointed. Robbers had already emptied those tombs many years earlier. Early in the 1900s, scholars still believed one royal tomb there had never been located. It was the tomb of Tutankhamun. They believed every other known pharaoh there had already been found. A determined British archaeologist, Howard Carter, hunted for Tut. More than five years brought no success. His patron agreed in 1922 to pay for a final season of digging. The patron was the fifth Earl of Carnarvon. Time was running out. Then his luck changed. Later that year he found the tomb. Almost nothing in it had been disturbed. The riches included thrones. They included jewelry, weapons, and statues. They even included food for the afterlife. Tutankhamun's mummy wore a large gold mask. It lay inside three coffins, one nested in the next. Those coffins sat in a sarcophagus of quartzite. Four shrines of wood covered with gilt were nested around the sarcophagus. They filled the room. The innermost coffin was pure gold. It weighed about 242 pounds. That weight is 110 kilograms. Carter's find caused a sensation. No pharaoh in history became better known than Tut. Carter could open the tomb only with permission from Egypt's government. In the late 1800s that government wrote rules for foreign archaeologists. One rule said that an intact tomb must keep every artifact in Egypt. Carter argued with the government. His claim was that the burial had already been opened.

8He claimed he could take half the treasure back to England. In the end, every artifact stayed in Egypt. The golden funeral mask stayed. The jewelry stayed. The statues stayed. Today Egypt's government works with researchers from other countries. It allows objects from the tomb to travel on tour. Egyptians have the last word on that treasure. Dying young was not rare in ancient times. In ancient Egypt the average life lasted about thirty years. Many people did not even reach that age. Even so, some historians had reasons to suspect foul play. They saw a teenage king already weak from disease. They saw genetic disabilities. Motives belonged to several figures around the throne and the ruling household. Ay and Horemheb guided many of Tut's decisions. Both became pharaohs after he died. Tut had no natural heir. If they wanted power, they had to move before any child of Tut survived. They also had to move before adulthood let him shove both advisers away. Ay showed a hunger for power by marrying Tut's widow. Horemheb may have drawn suspicion from some people of that time. A statue in his tomb carries an inscription. That carved text declares his innocence in any wrongful killing. The words might instead concern Ay's death. Horemheb's turn came after only a brief rule by Ay. If Tut was murdered, those two men were the likeliest suspects. Other people also fell under suspicion. Some researchers named two servants as possible killers. One was the cupbearer, who could reach the king's drink without limit. The other was Tutu, who could reach the king himself without limit. Few people were allowed into the king's bedroom. Those two were among them. Either man could have killed the pharaoh. A heavy object might have struck the king's head. A push might have sent him down stairs. Poison might have gone into his food or his drink. A wall painting of Ay was found in Tut's tomb. For years, people guessed that a blow to the head killed Tut. Pictures from X-ray work on the mummy supported that guess. One study came in 1968. Another came in 1978. Both came from the School of Dentistry at the University of Michigan. The pictures showed damage at the back of the skull. Experts called that damage strong proof.

9They said a heavy object had hit the back of his head. In 2005, researchers in Cairo decided to test that idea. An Egyptian archaeologist, Dr. Zahi Hawass, led the group. An advanced form of X-ray was the tool they used on the mummy. The method is CT scanning, also called CAT scanning. A CT scanner takes many X-rays. Each X-ray comes from a different angle. A computer turns that information into images. Those images are much more detailed than pictures from an ordinary X-ray machine. Hawass announced a clear result. A blow to the head was definitely not the cause of death. In his view the harm to the skull came after death, which is what postmortem means. That word means it happened after death. Tut was already dead. The damage probably came during mummification. A photo shows Dr. Zahi Hawass beside Tut. The mummy is about to go into the CT machine. The scans also showed several physical problems the young king lived with. He had a cleft palate. He had a club foot. Walking was extremely painful. He needed a cane. Walking sticks in the tomb, canes among them, numbered more than 130, and they were decorated. The scans showed something else that might explain the death. Shortly before he died, he suffered a broken leg. The leg had not healed properly. Hawass said an infection may have grown from that injury. Death may have come a few days later. A different group of experts finds no trace of infection. Between 2007 and 2010, the remains got another look from Hawass and fellow researchers. This time they used genetic tests. Two important conditions appeared that they had not seen before. One was repeated attacks of severe malaria. Malaria was common in Egypt. By itself the disease probably would not have killed him. Great weakness may have followed that illness. The other finding was bone necrosis. That is a breakdown of bone. It was in the bones of his left foot. The condition may have left him open to other infections. Those other infections have not yet been found. Does the mystery end there? Did the young king die from physical problems piled together? Did an accident play a part? Did a disease play a part?

10Did an infection from the broken leg play a part? Could the cause simply have been natural? Some members of the Hawass team, once the scans were read, suggested a different story. The leg may have broken while Tut was being embalmed. Other scholars still feel sure of a different cause. They think Howard Carter's team broke the leg. The break would have come years ago, when the team lifted the body from its coffin. Poison is still possible. A failed attack might also explain the broken leg. If any of those ideas is right, definite proof may never appear. More evidence keeps arriving. More pieces of the jigsaw keep turning up. Theories about how the young king lived become easier to test. Theories about how he died become easier to test. Different experts may still read the same clues in different ways. What is your reading? A photo shows Carter's team taking objects out of the tomb. Words to know. An archaeologist is a scientist who studies what ancient cultures left behind. Deities, in religions with one god, are the supreme beings and creators. In religions with many gods, deities are those gods or goddesses. Deterioration means becoming worse as time passes. Dynasties are lines of rulers from one family in a country. Embalmed means a dead body was treated so it would not decay. A headdress is fancy wear for the head, and ceremonies are a common time to use one. Hieroglyphics is a writing system of pictures or symbols. Those marks can stand for words, syllables, or sounds. Ancient Egyptians used it instead of an alphabet. An inscription is words cut into stone or metal. Belief in a single god is what makes a person a monotheist. Papyrus is a paper made from stalks of a grasslike plant. Ancient cultures used it. A pharaoh is a ruler of ancient Egypt. Postmortem means happening after death. Protruding means sticking out. Remnants are small parts left after the rest is gone. In ancient times, a sarcophagus was a coffin or a tomb cut from stone. It is often carved and richly decorated. Terminated means reached an end, or caused something to end. Unrestricted means having no limits. Vast means great in size, in number, or in amount.

73. The Branch Led by the President

1President Johnson signs the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stands just behind him and watches. The parts of this book come in this order. An opening scene comes first. Next is how the Constitution sets up the president’s branch. Then comes the way Americans pick a president. Then come the offices inside that branch. Then comes the work a president does. Then come famous actions by that branch. Then comes the system that limits each branch. A closing comes after that. A word list comes last. Opening Lyndon B. Johnson faced the television cameras. He began, “My fellow Americans.” He told the country he would now make the Civil Rights Act law. The year of that act was 1964. Johnson said people of every race must be treated the same. Classrooms were included. Hotels were included. Restaurants were included. The voting booth was included. Before this law, Black Americans were barred from the schools white Americans used. They were barred from the same restaurants. Voting was often blocked for Black Americans. The country is still working so that every person can vote. Johnson ended his speech and signed. Each letter got a new pen. Each period got a new pen. Each dash got a new pen. He used more than seventy-five pens before he finished. The pens became gifts for supporters standing in the room. King was one of the people who received a pen. That signing was a major day in the history of the country. A president’s ordinary day is still packed. Members of Congress may come in for a meeting. A speech may go out on television. A school or a hospital may get a visit.

2A bill may be signed into law. Leaders from other countries may be hosted. The president leads the U.S. government. No two days match. This is the executive branch doing its work. The Executive Branch Inside the Constitution American leaders adopted the Constitution in 1788. It set out laws and principles for governing a young country. The system has changed as it grew, but it is still in force. The document is a plan for the government. Three parts, called branches, divide the government. The president leads the executive branch. That branch runs most government work and most departments. The legislative branch is the House of Representatives together with the Senate. It speaks for citizens and writes laws. The judicial branch runs the justice system through courts. At times the branches work together and meet in the middle. At other times they stand against each other. Article II of the Constitution states what the executive branch may do. Its job is to carry out laws that Congress has written. To do that, it names the people who head federal agencies. The cabinet is part of that group. Writers of the Constitution argued about this branch. Who would be trusted to put laws into action? England’s king had just been defied in a rebellion. Some writers feared a single head of state with too much power. A return to rule by one king was what they feared. George Washington served first in the office. His service began in April 1789. It ended in March 1797. He also signed the Constitution, as one of 39 men. Once the Revolutionary War ended, leaders tried a different lesson.

3They tested a government in which nobody was assigned to enforce the laws. That government collapsed after eight years. The people who framed the Constitution then made a choice. What the country needed was a powerful office to lead the government. One person would lead it. That person is the president. They gave this office wide powers. At times this leader may decide without the others, when the nation needs that speed. This office is nothing like a throne. Voters choose who holds the office. Congress watches many of the president’s acts. Federal courts watch them too. Three basic tests are written into the Constitution. The president must be at least 35 years old. The president must be a citizen by birth. The president must have lived in the country for 14 years or longer. John F. Kennedy was 43 when he entered office. To this day he is the youngest person elected president. How Americans Pick a President Pure democracy is not the system used here. That system would give every citizen an equal say in each decision. It is a representative democracy instead. People elect officials, and those officials decide in the public’s name. A presidential election shows how this works. When citizens mark a choice for president, that vote is not the last word. Article II says electors from each state make the choice. Those electors form the Electoral College. The word college makes people think of a campus. No classes meet there. It is a group of voters whose job is to select the president. Victory in the nationwide vote of the people usually brings the presidency as well.

4That pattern does break. Population sets how many electoral votes each state receives. A small state gets more electors per person than a large state does. Small states then have a voice. States with more people cannot simply run the election. Many voters still dislike this college. They dislike it because one person’s vote does not count the same as another’s. In 2016, Hillary Clinton was the nominee on the left of a photo. Donald Trump was the nominee on the right. Nearly three million more people marked a ballot for Clinton. Trump still took the election, because he collected more electoral votes. A close nationwide count can let electoral votes decide the winner. The winner can be someone with fewer votes across the whole country. Winning the electoral votes that matter in certain states is enough. By 2020, five presidents had lost the popular vote and still won the electoral vote. Offices in the Executive Branch Many agencies and officials report to the president. They help carry out the laws. A vice president is part of the branch. Voters elect the vice president on the same ticket as the president. Several duties belong to the vice president. One is casting a vote that breaks a tie in the Senate. Another is stepping in if the president cannot keep serving. Sometimes a president dies. Sometimes a president must leave for another reason. The order of who comes next is fixed. The vice president is first. The Speaker who leads the House is second. Next is the Senate officer known as president pro tempore. After that come the heads of departments. The secretary of state is the first of those heads.

5More than once in U.S. history, a vice president has moved into the top office. Death of the person in office is one reason. Resignation is another. After John F. Kennedy was assassinated, Lyndon B. Johnson took his place. That happened in 1963. Richard Nixon later stepped down, and Gerald Ford replaced him. That happened in 1974. Laws from Congress are carried out through a wide net of federal agencies and departments. The Central Intelligence Agency is one agency. The Environmental Protection Agency is another. The Treasury Department is one department. The Education Department is another. The president appoints many of the people who lead these offices. Those leaders form the cabinet. Agencies have multiplied since those first years. Only four people sat in the cabinet Washington assembled. The cabinet now has more than a dozen. Work the President Does Article II gives the president wide powers. One example is command of the armed forces. Command of the military sits with the president. American forces can be sent anywhere in the world. The purpose may be to keep peace. The purpose may be to protect interests of the United States. The president may also pardon people guilty of federal crimes. State crimes are outside that power. Diplomacy means handling the nation’s ties with other countries. That work belongs to the president and to this branch. The president names ambassadors. The Senate must confirm them. Those ambassadors represent the country in other lands. In 2018, Elizabeth Richards spoke with Lebanon’s army chief of staff. Her post was ambassador in Lebanon. Peanuts brought in from other countries face a tax near 164 percent. The point is to help peanut farmers in this country.

6The president can make trade agreements with other countries. American companies are the ones these deals are meant to aid. Tariffs are another tool this office can set. A tariff is a special tax on goods the country imports. It can also apply to goods the country exports. A huge number of officials are appointed by the president. Supreme Court justices are among them. Cabinet members are among them. Heads of agencies are among them. The Senate must approve many of these choices. Nearly Seventy Thousand Decisions While one Congress serves its two years, this office names people for almost 70,000 jobs. Federal judges are in that group. U.S. attorneys are in that group. Cabinet members, ambassadors, and others are in it too. The Senate usually approves most names quickly. That is not always true. Nominees for the Supreme Court nearly always face a hard review before the Senate says yes. The president has a large part in how laws come to be. This branch does not write the laws. It can accept a law Congress has made, or it can refuse it. Both houses must pass a bill by a majority vote. The bill then goes to the president. A signature turns the bill into law. The president can say no by issuing a veto. A vetoed bill does not become law on its own. It becomes law only if Congress votes it through again. Two-thirds of the members in each house must vote yes. That second vote overrides the veto. The refusals by presidents now add up to more than 2,500 bills. In March 1985, Ronald Reagan vetoed a bill.

7The bill would have sent aid to farmers. Famous Actions by This Branch The president can also issue executive actions. They tell federal offices what this leader wants done. They direct what the government does. Some of these choices change daily life for citizens in a deep way. During the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. The year was 1863. It said that enslaved people in the rebel states of the South “shall be forever free.” In 1935, Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered a new agency into being. It was the Works Progress Administration, the WPA. It hired thousands of Americans. The jobs came when the Great Depression was at its worst. That depression filled the 1930s. WPA workers built roads. They planted trees. They even painted murals. In 1939, men from the Civilian Conservation Corps planted seedlings. The hillside in Oregon had been cut clear of trees. Like the WPA, the CCC was his project for putting people to work. An executive order in 1942 forced a Japanese American family from home. They were among 117,000 people sent to live in prison camps. Some executive orders have done harm. One infamous case followed a surprise attack. Japan struck Pearl Harbor, in Hawaiʻi. Because of that strike, this country entered the Second World War. That war ran from 1939 to 1945. After the attack, Roosevelt signed an order. It let officials order citizens of Japanese ancestry to leave the places they lived. They were placed in detention camps. Inside the camps, officials treated them as if they opposed their own country. Roosevelt’s Four Elections People call Franklin Delano Roosevelt FDR. He was president number thirty-two.

8He was the first president elected four times. He is still the only one. His years in office ran from 1933 to 1945. In that time he led the country through the Great Depression. He also guided the country for nearly the whole of that war. He died in 1945, just before the war ended. After his death, an amendment to the Constitution capped the presidency at two terms. Checks and Balances The Constitution makes each branch a check on the others. The three branches are executive, legislative, and judicial. No one branch is supposed to take too much power. The veto is a check on the lawmaking branch. In the normal path, a bill needs the president’s signature to become law. A fresh vote by two thirds of Congress can cancel a veto. That bar is hard to clear. One party seldom holds that large a share of the seats. Congress checks the president in return. It can override a veto. It can accept or reject people named to the Supreme Court. It can accept or reject cabinet appointees. Treaties also need the Senate’s approval. A treaty is a peace agreement between nations. The president commands the armed forces. A formal declaration of war belongs to Congress alone. Try, and Try Once More Overriding a veto is difficult. Congress has another path. It can revise the bill. Parts the president dislikes can be cut or changed. If the new version passes, the president may sign it the next time. Richard Nixon speaks a farewell to his staff. The day is the one after he resigned in 1974. Congress can also remove a president through impeachment.

9The House is where the charges are written down. The House votes on whether to send the case to the Senate. The Senate then holds a trial. A guilty finding removes the president from office. The House has voted to impeach a president four times. Andrew Johnson’s term was 1865 to 1869. Bill Clinton’s term was 1993 to 2001. Donald Trump faced impeachment two times between 2017 and 2021. The Senate cleared all three men. Steps toward impeachment also began against Richard Nixon. His term was 1969 to 1974. The formal vote never came, because he left office first. The executive branch checks the judicial branch as well. The president nominates justices. The Senate must approve them. The judicial branch checks the other two. It decides whether Congress’s laws follow the Constitution. It decides whether the president’s orders follow the Constitution. Courts halted immigration orders that Barack Obama had issued. In 2014 he tried to use such an action in two ways. Some immigrants without papers would get work permits. Deportation would be blocked for them. The Supreme Court stopped those actions. A photo shows Obama in 2014. The people who framed the Constitution first gave more power to the lawmaking branch than to the executive. Since then, executive power has grown. One old check was Congress’s power to declare war. In recent history that check has slipped into the background. The last time Congress declared war was 1942. Every military action since then has been led by the executive branch without that declaration. The Vietnam War is one example. The Iraq Wars are another. A painting from 1856 shows George Washington speaking. The scene is the Constitutional Convention of 1787.

10Closing So far, the government the framers set up in 1788 has bent without breaking. It has recovered from strain. What this branch is allowed to do tends to shift as years pass. The way people read the Constitution shifts too. Even so, this branch has been able to carry out the nation’s laws. The lawmaking branch still limits the president. The courts still limit the president. The three branches stay in balance. What ties the three together is the Constitution. What a president is able to do will probably keep shifting. New challenges in the years ahead will shape that change. Words to Know pardon (v.): to forgive a mistake or a wrong act. cabinet (n.): the circle of people who advise a president, or who advise another country’s leader. resilient (adj.): able to get past trouble, or to recover quickly. dominate (v.): to control something, or to overpower it. trade agreements (n.): deals between countries about how goods and services will be exchanged. executive (adj.): describing the part of government that heads the country and puts its laws into effect. veto (n.): a refusal to approve a bill, so the bill does not become law. federal (adj.): belonging to the national government that splits power with the states or with regions. acquitted (v.): cleared by an official finding that no crime or wrong was proved. impeachment (n.): a formal charge of wrongdoing brought against someone. ambassadors (n.): officials who travel to a place, or live there, to represent their country or its people. overriding (v.): taking over from something else, canceling it, or putting something in its place.

74. The Charter the Barons Demanded

1Contents. A King the People Hated. The Barons Make a Plan. Runnymede and a King Who Broke Faith. What Followed the Charter. Words to Know. A King the People Hated. England's people suffered greatly in the late twelfth century. Several kings seemed to care about no one but themselves. They seemed to care about nothing else either. The troubles started in the time of King Richard I. People knew him as Richard the Lionheart. England came close to bankruptcy while he reigned for ten years. The king taxed the English people heavily. He needed the money for his part in the Third Crusade. While Richard was away at war, his youngest brother tried to take the throne. That brother was John. The attempt failed. On the way home from the failed crusade, Richard was captured. His captors held him prisoner in Austria. They demanded an enormous ransom for his release. After Richard gained his freedom, he forgave his brother. He then imposed more taxes. The new taxes paid for a war in France. He wanted to defend his holdings there. He died in France in 1199. An arrow wound killed him. Before dying, he named John as the next king. John was the youngest of four boys. People had not expected him to become king of England. The people of England did not want more taxes when John became king. More taxes were exactly what they got. In almost every way, John proved to be a terrible king. He infuriated the barons through heavy taxation. He also seized their property. He insulted the honor of their wives. He insulted the honor of their daughters. John took many hostages from noble families so a rebellion would be harder to start.

2When he needed gold, he ransomed the hostages back to their families. Sometimes he killed the hostages. He did so even when the ransom had been paid. Who the Barons Were. In medieval England, a baron was a noble who had received land from a superior. The land was given in return for loyalty. It was also given in return for military service. Higher-ranking barons received their land from the king. They could then give parcels of that land to lesser barons. In 1214, the barons swore an oath. They swore to achieve fair treatment from the king. King Philip II changed France. Under him, France grew from a small feudal state into one of Europe's most powerful countries. John added a terrible family crime to his offenses in 1203. His nephew Arthur lived in France. Arthur was fifteen years old. King Philip II of France favored Arthur as the future ruler of England. Arthur was therefore a rival for the English throne. John could not tolerate that rivalry. John's forces captured the lad. Arthur then disappeared. People generally assumed that John ordered Arthur murdered. Rumors said that John committed the vile act himself. A major defeat in France struck John in 1204. That year, Philip defeated a mercenary army that belonged to John. Philip reclaimed most of the French territory that England's royal family had held. The loss of those French lands brought John scorn. It also brought him hate from many of his subjects. John kept stirring up trouble wherever he could. In 1205, the archbishop of Canterbury died. England needed a new archbishop. Pope Innocent III wanted an English cardinal to have the post. That cardinal was Stephen Langton. John had his own choice.

3His demand was that the English bishop John de Gray get the post. He was adamant. When he did not get his way, he began persecuting the English clergy. He confiscated church lands. John de Gray was one of the few men King John trusted throughout his life. Because of that trust, de Gray was given an elaborate tomb in York, England. John's rebuke of the pontiff brought a strong response. Pope Innocent placed an interdict on all of England in 1208. The doors of England's churches closed. No church clergy could perform masses. They could not marry anyone. They could not perform baptisms. They could not perform funerals. John still would not relent. The pope then excommunicated him. John continued to alienate Innocent anyway. He seized more property that belonged to the church. He seized more church revenue as well. In exasperation, the pope made an alliance with the French king, Philip. Their aim was to invade England. They meant to depose John. John realized that he was in a dire situation. In 1213, he finally agreed to let Cardinal Langton become archbishop. He did not stop there. To the amazement of everyone, he humbled himself before Innocent. He offered to make the pope the feudal overlord of England. Innocent was delighted and accepted the offer immediately. He pardoned the penitent king. John's bold move was a masterstroke. Overnight he went from a cornered outcast to a man with a powerful friend. That ally was the Roman Catholic Church. Eighteen years was the length of Innocent III's time as pope. The Barons Make a Plan. Archbishop Langton had been an ardent opponent of John from early on. He remained an opponent. The pope now felt affection for John.

4Langton himself had been raised to archbishop. Langton was still determined that John be removed from power. He became an advisor to a group of some two hundred barons. Those barons also wanted to get rid of the king. Not every baron stood against John. A few were committed to reconciliation between the nobility and the king.
