One of them was his advisor William Marshal. Marshal was, in the view of many people, England's most formidable knight. They respected him for his character. They respected him for his loyalty. He had served four kings, including John. He became a liaison between the barons and John during negotiations. The first earl of Pembroke was William Marshal's official title. A map of the barons' meetings from 1213 to 1215 can mark several places. They include Bury St. Edmunds, St. Albans, London, and Runnymede. England, the English Channel, and France can appear on the same map. July 1213 was the month of the barons' first meeting as a group. The town was St. Albans, near London. At this meeting, the barons considered killing John. They then rejected that idea. They chose quieter methods for reaching their goals. They pressed John to keep King Henry I's Coronation Charter. That charter had been approved more than one hundred years earlier. The Coronation Charter spelled out basic laws. The laws were the ones the king would follow with the nobles. They also covered church officials. They covered the common people of England. John said yes: he would keep Henry's Coronation Charter. He agreed to abide by the laws set forth in it. John did not keep his promise about the Coronation Charter. The barons met again in November 1214.

5The town was Bury St. Edmunds. They met to discuss their options. Archbishop Langton supported their cause by citing Bible passages that fit it. He also cited the Coronation Charter. The charter included some protections from royal tyranny. Langton argued that it gave a historical justification for the barons' challenge to John. Robert Fitzwalter was a baron on Langton's side. He became the leader of the barons. He was instrumental in guiding their plans. A picture can show Stephen Langton at the center, dressed in purple. He was the archbishop of Canterbury for almost twenty-two years. At the meeting in Bury St. Edmunds, the barons started to show their strength. They chose to stop paying any more scutage to John. The money would have supported his military campaigns in France. They went a step further. They drew up a list of demands to present to the king. The Coronation Charter was the base of their list. Extra rules said the king had to obey the same laws that bound everyone else. If John refused the demands, the barons would take up arms against him. A Tax the Barons Despised. One form of taxation was called scutage. King John used it to excess. The barons hated it. It was a payment made in place of military service. Barons who declined to join the king in a war could pay it. John used the funds from scutage to pay mercenaries. The hired fighters filled out his ranks. In January 1215, Fitzwalter met with John. A few other barons came with him. They meant to express their unhappiness with his reign. They meant to present their draft charter. A picture can show that the barons met King John several times to present their ideas and their needs.

6Those talks went badly. His promise was a reply to their grievances by Easter. He did not reply. The barons then went ahead with a formal list of demands. War preparations began in that same period. Runnymede and a King Who Broke Faith. Before they turned to war, the barons tried one last curb on John's excesses: the Magna Carta, or Great Charter. They wanted to try the charter before they resorted to war. The first Latin document was known as the Articles of the Barons. It listed sixty-three demands. Among the many clauses were provisions that shielded the barons from abusive royal power. Other provisions dealt with excessive taxation. Protection for the rights of the English Church was another demand in the document. It specified that no free citizens would be imprisoned without first being tried in a court of law. They would not be punished without that trial either. To make certain that John would honor the charter, the document provided for a committee. Twenty-five barons would be elected to it. They would be authorized to assure the king's compliance. They could use force if necessary. London was seized by a group of barons in May 1215. London was the most important city in England. The seizure further weakened John's position. Reluctantly, the king agreed to meet the barons and discuss their grievances. The meeting began on June 15, 1215. It took place in a large meadow at Runnymede. Runnymede is a town on the River Thames west of London. Archbishop Langton mediated. John stood on one side. Fitzwalter stood on the other, with about forty other barons. Several leading churchmen stood with the barons.

7A tent was set up for the king. A small throne stood in that tent. When John arrived, he wasted little time on formalities. He declared that he agreed with the entire contents of the charter. He affixed his royal seal to the document. He swore an oath that he would uphold it. In the days after the meeting, scribes copied the Great Charter. Those copies were also written in Latin. The copies were distributed. How the Charter Was Made Official. Most pictures of the Runnymede meeting show King John using a quill pen. That picture is inaccurate. The king's seal is what made the Magna Carta official. This was how almost every medieval document became official. An engraved design sat on a handheld seal or on a signet ring. The design was pressed into a blob of soft, warm wax. The wax then hardened. Someone could press the seal onto the document. More often it was placed on a ribbon or a cord. That ribbon or cord was attached to the bottom of the document. Few people believed the king would abide by his oath to uphold the charter. A solemn oath was no harder for John to break than a dry twig is to snap. The barons were afraid he would ignore the charter at the first moment it was safe to do so. The king proved just as faithless as everyone suspected. He wanted no part of the charter. Help was what he asked of his ally, Pope Innocent. Innocent took John's side. The pope made the charter void in August 1215. John was thereby freed from all its provisions. The barons could tolerate nothing further after that. Some barons, including Marshal, remained loyal to the crown.

8A large group did not. Led by Fitzwalter, they launched a civil war. They invited Philip's son, Prince Louis of France, to join the fight. They intended to put Louis on the throne once they were victorious. Louis raised an army. He invaded England. In 1216, developments came that no one expected. Pope Innocent died in July. A fever killed him. In October, John also died. Dysentery felled him while he was confronting Louis's forces. John's son, Henry III, then became king. Henry was nine years old. Marshal was now in service to his fifth king. He was seventy years old. He became regent to the young king. A list of charter events can be set out in order. In April 1199, John became king of England. In July 1205, the archbishop of Canterbury died. In March 1208, Pope Innocent III laid England under an interdict. In May 1213, King John bowed to the pope. He allowed Stephen Langton to become archbishop of Canterbury. In July 1213, the barons met as a group for the first time, in St. Albans. In November 1214, they met as a group for the second time, in Bury St. Edmunds. In January 1215, Robert Fitzwalter and a few other barons met with King John. In May 1215, the barons seized London. In June 1215, the record says that King John signs the Great Charter. In August 1215, Pope Innocent III nullified the charter. In July 1216, Pope Innocent III died. In October 1216, King John died, and his son Henry became king of England. In September 1217, William Marshal defeated the barons and ended the civil war. In November 1217, King Henry III reissued the charter.

9Henry was too young to understand the dangerous situation he was in. He relied on Marshal's experience. He relied on Marshal's guidance to bring the rebellion to an end. The civil war continued even so. Marshal, serving as regent, told Henry to issue the charter again. The reissue would prove to the barons that Henry was not like his father. Many paintings make Henry III look just like his father, John I. What Followed the Charter. The English throne gained proof of Marshal's worth. He forced the rebel barons to submit in 1217. He ejected Prince Louis from England. Henry reissued the Great Charter. The reissue pacified the barons who had doubted him. They had feared his reign would differ little from John's. Marshal's promise that the king would follow the charter was enough for their trust. Henry turned eighteen in 1225. He again reissued the Great Charter. The new issue reinforced his pledge to be a law-abiding ruler. Henry agreed: the law stood above every person. That included the king of England. One further reissue of the charter came in 1297. That reissue came during the reign of Henry's son, King Edward I. A picture can show the four remaining copies of the Magna Carta together in April 2015. It was the first time they had been together. The gathering celebrated the 800th anniversary of the charter. Liberty gained a powerful symbol in the Great Charter. It also stood for the principle that no one is above the law. English Common Law grew from it as a base. Its clauses say that everyone must be treated as innocent until proven guilty. They say that everyone is entitled to a trial by a jury of peers.

10Many ideas in the charter deeply influenced political thinking in Europe. More than five hundred years later, the American colonies broke away from British rule. They created the United States. Many of those same ideas found new expression in the United States Constitution. They also appeared in the Bill of Rights. Words to Know. abide (v.) to accept an agreement or a circumstance, or to conform to it. affixing (v.) sticking or fastening one thing to another. baptisms (n.) religious rituals in which people are doused with water, or submerged in it, to become Christian. barons (n.) men who held a low rank in the nobility of Europe. charter (n.) an official document that defines the rights and responsibilities of a person or a group. excommunicated (v.) expelled from a church community. feudal (adj.) related to a European system of government in the Middle Ages, based on rights and duties between landowners and the people who worked the land. grievances (n.) official complaints about something thought to be wrong or unjust. humbled (v.) brought down in power or prestige, or made to feel less proud. justification (n.) a good reason for doing something. mercenary (n.) a person hired to fight. nullified (v.) made to have no effect, no value, or no legal power. oath (n.) a formal promise. pacifying (v.) soothing anger or dissatisfaction, or calming it. penitent (adj.) feeling bad about wrongdoing, or showing regret for it. regent (n.) someone who rules a kingdom for a monarch who cannot rule. scutage (n.) a feudal tax that could be paid so a person did not have to perform military service. tyranny (n.) harsh or cruel acts by a person or a group in power.

75. The Control Center in Your Head

1Contents. The Brain. Three Brains in One. The Brain Stem. The Cerebellum. The Cerebrum. The Right Half and the Left Half. Studying the Brain. Making Maps of the Brain. Watching the Brain at Work. Control by Thought. Keep Your Brain in Shape. Training the Brain. Guard Your Brain. Words to Know. The Brain. One body part weighs only 2 percent of your total body weight. That same part uses more than 20 percent of your energy. The answer is your brain. It is your most complicated body part. Your brain needs plenty of energy. It must fuel about 86 billion neurons. These brain cells carry electrical signals. The signals are needed for thoughts. They are needed for memories and for feelings. Neurons are the reason you can ride a bike. They are the reason you can remember your teacher's name. Neurons form a network. The network has more than 125 trillion connections. The name for each connection is synapse. Stars in 1,500 Milky Way galaxies would still be fewer than the synapses in your brain. This complex wiring lets your brain act as the control center for your whole body. Signals travel through neurons. They go to different parts of the brain. They go to different parts of the body. Three Brains in One. The link from the brain to the rest of the body is made of neurons. They deliver instructions to muscles. They bring back information from your senses. Those same cells also link the brain's three main parts. Those parts are the brain stem, the cerebellum, and the cerebrum. Each part controls specific body activities. The parts have numerous connections. Each part can communicate with the others. The Brain Stem. People sometimes call the brain stem the lizard brain.

2It does pretty much the same job in lizards as in you. It controls body processes that are essential for survival. Day and night, your brain stem keeps you breathing. It keeps digestion going. It keeps your heartbeat going. It keeps other autonomic body processes running smoothly. Fight, flight, or freeze is another response under the lizard brain's control. That response is your immediate reaction to a difficult situation. The Cerebellum. Each time you move, your cerebellum is at work. It coordinates muscle movements. Other brain parts send signals that include your current speed. They include your current position. The cerebellum adds targeting instructions to those signals. With its guidance, you can touch your nose in one smooth motion. Without it, the movement would be jerky. You might even miss your nose completely. The cerebellum also regulates balance. It regulates motor control. It stores memories of muscle movement. Those memories are called procedural memory. Procedural memory is the unconscious memory of how to do something. Muscle memories become stronger with repetition. That is why practice helps some movements become automatic. Playing guitar is one example. Skateboarding is another. Some experts think muscle memories also strengthen routes inside the brain. They believe the memories can make the onset of diseases slower. Alzheimer's is one such disease. Other forms of dementia are others. The diseases may also become less intrusive in daily life. Physical exercise strengthens more than your body's muscles. It strengthens your brain. A diagram of the brain can label the cerebrum, the corpus callosum, and the cerebellum. It can label the brain stem. It can label the left hemisphere and the right hemisphere. The Cerebrum. No part of the brain is larger than the cerebrum. Nearly 75 percent of the brain's volume belongs to it.

3It is almost 85 percent of the brain's weight. Most high-level brain activity takes place here. That activity includes thought, speech, learning, and emotions. Information from the senses is also read by the cerebrum. What the senses report arrives in the brain as electrical signals. The cerebrum interprets those signals as sounds. It interprets them as images and as other sensations. Stored memories are what it uses for a comparison. It attaches meaning to each result. Those electrical impulses can turn into the sight of a purple bus. Another stream becomes a crowing rooster. You may be surprised to learn something about ignoring. Part of the cerebrum's important work is to ignore some things. To see why, notice everything your senses are telling you right now. Information from your senses pours into the brain without a stop. By screening some things out, the cerebrum helps you focus on what remains. It works like an adjustable filter. Only certain things pass through at certain times. Brain or Computer. Computers remember information more precisely. Brains learn better. Brains adapt to changes better. Brains are also better at making sense of information that is jumbled. They are better with information that seems unrelated. The Right Half and the Left Half. If you could look inside your head, you would see that the cerebrum is divided into two halves. The halves are called hemispheres. A bundle of nerves called the corpus callosum connects them. It carries messages between them. The messages let the two halves work together. Each hemisphere runs the opposite side of the body. The signal that lifts your right hand comes from your left hemisphere. Shaking your left foot is a job for your right brain.

4Either hemisphere can carry out some tasks. The two halves are still not identical. The right brain usually controls creativity. It usually controls artistic skills. It usually controls how you interpret what you see. The left brain generally controls speech. It generally controls writing. It generally controls math skills. The corpus callosum lets the left brain tell the right brain what it saw. The right brain can then decide what the vision meant. You could still see that purple bus if the corpus callosum were missing. You could not tell anyone what it was. Each hemisphere has four sections, called lobes. One section is the frontal lobe. Another is the parietal lobe. Another is the occipital lobe. The last is the temporal lobe. Each lobe processes specific information, or it has a special job. Scientists did not realize this until the 1800s. A doctor then recorded the strange story of Phineas Gage. A picture can show Phineas Gage holding the iron rod that went through his left eye and his frontal lobe. Studying the Brain. The Rutland and Burlington Railroad employed Phineas Gage as a foreman. He was injured in 1848. A three-foot iron rod was blasted straight through his head by an accidental explosion. Amazingly, Gage survived. The hole in his head did not affect his memory. It did not affect his ability to think. It drastically altered his personality. Gage became rude. He became thoughtless. He became stubborn. He was so different that his friends said he was no longer Gage. Part of Gage's frontal lobe was gone. That part of the cerebrum governs emotions. It governs attention. His injury gave scientists one of the first clues about brain regions. Specific regions control specific functions.

5The injury also showed that one damaged part does not stop the rest of the brain. The rest can keep working. The case was not a complete answer to every question about how the brain works. Jobs of the Lobes. The frontal lobe handles problem solving. It handles attention. It handles speaking. It handles emotional control. The parietal lobe handles movement. It handles recognition of objects. It handles categorization of objects. The temporal lobe handles hearing. It handles memory. It handles understanding speech. The occipital lobe handles vision. It handles shape recognition. Making Maps of the Brain. Doctors studied Gage's case for many years. His brain was not saved after his death. Then, in 1914, World War I began. Large numbers of soldiers suffered brain injuries. Injuries to certain regions consistently caused the same symptoms. With that information, doctors could begin creating maps. The maps linked brain regions to functions. Learning about the brain from injuries was like learning about cars from broken engines. Scientists could identify essential regions. They could not yet say what each region did. They could not yet say how the regions worked together. Mapping brain structure is very different from mapping brain function. A picture of an EEG screen can show normal brain activity for a four-year-old child. Watching the Brain at Work. Scientists needed a clearer understanding of brain function. They needed a way to study healthy brains without damaging them. A German scientist, Hans Berger, built a machine in the 1920s. The machine could measure electrical activity in the brain. It is called an electroencephalogram (il-LEK-troh-en-SEH-fuh-loh-GRAM). People also call it an EEG machine. It provided a partial solution. Everything you do begins with tiny electrical signals in your brain.

6Running begins that way. So do singing and thinking, and more. An EEG measures these signals through electrodes placed on the surface of the head. Researchers can then see brain activity when you walk. They can see it when you talk, when you read, and when you do more. Berger's wave is the name of the brain-wave rhythm an EEG measures. The name honors this scientist-inventor. One EEG picture can show the brain functions of a person in a light sleep. Unless electrodes are surgically implanted inside a person's skull, an EEG has a limit. It can detect only signals near the brain's surface. Watching activity deeper in the brain was difficult. It was potentially dangerous. A test called an fMRI became available in the 1990s and changed that limit. An EEG measures electrical activity. An fMRI does something else. It identifies active brain regions and maps them by measuring blood flow. The technique is noninvasive. It gives an indirect measurement of brain activity. Electrically active neurons require more oxygen. A picture can show two medical professionals reviewing an fMRI. Blood is your body's oxygen delivery system. Where blood flow is higher, neurons are generally more active electrically. Unlike electrical signals, changes in blood flow can be detected deep inside the brain. The detection does not require a cut. An fMRI lets scientists detect the precise regions you use when you sing. It can do the same when you laugh or when you startle. It gives far more detail than an EEG can provide. Control by Thought. Once brain signals could be detected, another question came up. Is it possible to decode these signals? If a computer could decipher a brain's electrical signals, people might control an artificial limb by thought.

7They might control a robot through a brain-computer interface. A Note on the Letters. fMRI stands for functional magnetic resonance imaging. This idea may sound like science fiction. Experimental mind-controlled devices already exist. Electrodes detect the brain signal. A computer decodes it. The information can then control a mechanical device. Researchers hope the technology can help people with disabilities. It may help them move more easily. It may help them communicate more easily. The technique could also send brain signals from one person to another. Early tests sent one person's finger-movement brain signal across the Internet. It went to another room. A special device in that room passed the signal on to a second person. His finger moved. It followed instructions from another brain. The University of Washington, in 2013, was the first place this human brain-to-brain link was made. It happened just three weeks after another experiment. Another kind of computer-brain interface was used by a Harvard Medical School team. They linked up with a rat's brain. The rat's tail moved because a scientist directed it with his brain. A picture from the University of Washington can show one researcher sending a brain signal over the Internet. Another researcher receives it. The signal makes his finger move on the keyboard. Keep Your Brain in Shape. Your brain is an amazing machine. Proper care lets it run at its best, as with a machine. How do you keep it in top condition? For starters, use it. Exercising your brain helps it grow. Muscles grow with physical exercise in a similar way. Take violin players. Complicated movements of the left-hand fingers are what they learn. The brain area that controls that hand is larger than in most people who have not practiced those movements.

8Puzzles and games that you do poorly are worth a try when the violin is not your instrument. It sounds odd, but a game you already do well will not push your brain to create new neural connections. If you are a language person, try number puzzles. Try logic puzzles such as sudoku. A person who does well with numbers can try drawing instead. Getting hands to look right is especially hard. These activities will keep your brain healthy. They will keep it strong. A picture of word games can remind you that word play makes the brain work harder. Give your brain the food it needs. Blueberries have lots of the right nutrients. Walnuts do too. Those foods help your brain work smoothly. Training the Brain. A change in the brain usually stays in the regions that your activity uses directly. Some kinds of mental training may change more of the brain, research suggests. Research at Harvard Medical School showed one example. People who practiced meditation for eight weeks had changes in certain regions. Those regions are used for learning. They are used for memory. They are used for emotional control. Physical exercise also has benefits across the brain. Exercise that raises your heart rate is especially helpful. Dr. Arthur Kramer directs the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology. The institute is at the University of Illinois. He studies how exercise affects the brain. Kramer says that exercising is good for your body and your brain. Research has shown a pattern in children who exercise regularly. They have better memories. They have better attention. They often do better on school tests. Dancing is good for your brain. Learning new steps and patterns encourages new neural connections.

9Dancing also calms the brain's stress response. That calm reduces pain. It lowers tension in the body. Sleep is another key to healthy brain function. Dr. Ken Paller directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Program at Northwestern University. During sleep, the brain appears to play memories again, according to the evidence. That replay may help skills stick in your memory. It may help information stick as well. However the process works, too little sleep decreases your ability to learn. It decreases your ability to think. Each night, experts say, people should sleep seven to nine hours. A picture of intense sports can show that hard physical exercise increases blood flow to the brain. Guard Your Brain. According to the research of Dr. Ann Mckee, protection is the most important key to brain health. Shock-absorbing fluid guards your brain against some injuries. The fluid is called cerebrospinal fluid. A hard skull guards the brain as well. A fall onto concrete from only two or three feet can crack your skull. It can bruise your brain. This kind of injury is called a concussion. It can come from a hard hit to your head. It can come from being violently shaken. Most concussions from sports are mild. Each one still causes damage to your brain. Most mild concussions finish healing if the person rests and waits. Swelling inside the skull can follow a more serious concussion. The swelling can cut off the brain's blood supply quickly. Only a few minutes without oxygen is all your brain can last. A properly fitted helmet gives extra protection during sports. It may save your brain. It may save your life. No other body part may matter more than your brain. Exercise helps it operate smoothly for years to come.

10So do brain foods, enough sleep, and protective headgear. Words to Know. autonomic (adj.) occurring or acting as an involuntary or unconscious process; related to the involuntary nervous system. brain stem (n.) the brain region at the top of the spinal cord, in charge of basic jobs such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure. cerebellum (n.) the lower back part of the brain; it coordinates sensory information with muscle movement so the body can keep its balance and move smoothly. cerebrum (n.) the largest part of the brain in many mammals; it controls thinking, feeling, communicating, emotions, and some of the senses. corpus callosum (n.) the group of nerve fibers in the middle of the brain in some mammals; it connects the two hemispheres and lets them communicate. decipher (v.) to make out the meaning of something that is hard to understand. electrodes (n.) points through which electricity flows into a device, or out of it, such as a battery. hemispheres (n.) halves of a sphere, or of a mostly round object such as a planet or a brain. lobes (n.) rounded or curved sections of a body or an organ, such as the ear, the brain, or the lungs. motor (adj.) related to muscle movement that the nervous system controls. network (n.) a group of things that are connected and that communicate with one another. neurons (n.) nerve cells that move information inside the brain and between the brain and the rest of the body. noninvasive (adj.) related to a medical procedure done without cutting into a body or inserting anything into it. onset (n.) the start of something. signals (n.) actions, sounds, or objects used to send a message.

76. The Creator's Fast Field Game

1This book asks why the sport dazzles, where it began, who can play, how the rules work, who the heroes are, and how an old game faces the future. A word list closes it. A photo shows a Cornell player carrying the ball against Syracuse. This thrilling game grew from a field contest that ranks among the oldest on Earth. Europeans who reached North America took the game from First Nations people. Those Native players had used various forms for centuries. It is the fastest game played on a field. It is also one of the hardest and most exciting to play. Watching it is exciting too. It shares a great deal with soccer. It shares a great deal with hockey and with basketball. Through most of the 1900s, athletes who played it were fairly few. They lived in only a few regions. Popularity is now booming. The sport is moving into the mainstream, above all as a youth sport. Experts think the game grew among the Algonquin tribes. Their home was the valley of the St. Lawrence River. That valley is in today's Canada and in today's New York. In time the game traveled far west.

2It traveled far south. Tribes used different names. The Algonquin name is baggataway. The old form was very unlike today's game. A field could stretch for miles. A side rarely had fewer than one hundred players. Sometimes a side had as many as one thousand. Most tribes still used a curved stick. The stick was 3 to 4 feet long. That length is 0.9 to 1.2 meters. A net on the stick passed the ball, carried it, and shot it. The ball was stuffed deerskin. Early contests were huge. They could last as long as three days. A sketch by the artist H.W. Hall shows First Nations players and other players. A large crowd in Canada is watching. First Nations people treated the game as a sacred rite. They believed the gods watched over it. Many tribes called it the Creator's game. They used it to toughen young men. They used it to strengthen them. They used it to settle large tribal disputes. They used it to strengthen tribal fellowship. A demonstration by a local tribe took place in 1834. The crowd was mostly white and Canadian. The place was a racecourse in Montreal, in Quebec.

3The game took hold in that region. Soon Canada had many clubs for white players. It had many clubs for First Nations players too. George Beers, a dentist in Montreal, set the rules on paper in 1860. Because today's rules rest on his, people call him the father of modern lacrosse. His rules set the size of the stick. They set the size of the ball and of the goal. They set how many players would take the field. They set the size of the field. The 1870s were the years when the sport surged inside the United States. Clubs appeared in New York City. They appeared in Baltimore, Boston, and Philadelphia. They appeared in Newport, Rhode Island. Boys in private schools played. Elite colleges in the Northeast played. Rosabelle Sinclair had been on the first international team from Scotland. She brought the women's game to Bryn Mawr School in Baltimore. Play was limited to the teams of these schools. People therefore treated it as a gentleman's sport. The joy of playing was the reason they took the field. They did not play for paying crowds. They did not play for advertisers. Gifted athletes who could have enlarged the sport chose not to join.

4They moved toward sports that offered fame and fortune. Another stall came from a lack of gear, including the sticks, called crosses. Before the 1970s, stick-making belonged to certain Mohawk artisans in Ontario, Canada. American demand was low, so factories had little cause to turn out sticks in bulk. They already mass-produced baseball gloves and basketballs. Cheaper sticks of light metal reached the market in the 1970s. From then on, American interest climbed sharply. Today men play all over the world. Women, boys, and girls play too. Some teams use an indoor form called box lacrosse. They play it in hockey rinks that have no ice. Outdoor tournaments often use football stadiums. Levels of play vary widely. Its name is Federation of International Lacrosse, and its nations come from around the globe. It holds a men's world championship every four years. It holds a women's world championship on the same cycle. North America has two leagues at the professional level. Major League Lacrosse is the outdoor league. It has eight teams. The National Lacrosse League is the indoor box league. It has nine teams.

5College teams for men and for women play hard in the United States and in Canada. Northeastern colleges have long treated the sport as huge and competitive. Interest is spreading fast. College programs now treat it as a major sport. The Summer Olympics included it twice, in 1904 and in 1908. A 1908 photo shows the Canadian winners. In the United States the fastest growth is at the youth level. High schools are growing fast too. As young people across the country take up the game, college play will surely grow. Pro play will grow as well. Outside North America, small devoted groups have long existed in Australia. They have long existed in England. Some of history's best players came out of northern England. Manchester, a large city, is the heart of that area. Over the last thirty years the sport has grown across Europe. It has grown across East Asia. It has grown across the globe. Someday it may be the next huge international sport. The game shares many traits with soccer, hockey, and basketball. It is still its own sport. The most distinctive tool is the crosse, the stick every player uses. Players cradle, catch, pass, and shoot with it.

6Cradling is a back-and-forth motion of the stick head. That motion keeps the ball in the pocket while the player runs. Hands on the ball are allowed for the goalie alone. In that limit, the rule matches soccer. Men wear more protective gear than women. The women's game allows less body contact, so their gear is lighter. Gear can include the crosse, an eye mask, a helmet, and a mouth guard. It can include shoulder pads, gloves, rib pads, and arm protectors. It can include cleats. Goalkeepers often add a throat guard and extra chest padding. Length of the stick's shaft runs from 2 feet to 5 feet. That length is 0.6 to 1.5 meters. A triangular head sits at the top. A net is fitted to the head. The goalkeeper's head is larger. The goal is 6 feet high. It is also 6 feet across. That height is 1.8 meters. The ball is rubber. Its circumference is about 8 inches, or 20 centimeters. A men's field is 110 yards long. That length is 101 meters. The field is 60 yards wide. That width is 55 meters. A midfield line crosses the field.

7An X marks the center. Every period opens with two rivals facing off on that mark. A whistle blows. Each player tries to win the ball. A men's team has ten players. Three attackers stay on the other team's half. Three defenders stay on their own half. Three midfielders cover the whole field. A goalkeeper guards the net. Women's fields carry fewer lines. Women's teams put twelve players on the field, not ten. The aim is the higher number of goals. A goal comes from hurling the ball into the other net. It can also come from bouncing the ball in. Whoever wins the face-off then sprints toward the opposite goal. That player may shoot. That player may pass to an attacker who is well placed to score. Defenders try to protect their goal. They try to take the ball. They may poke the carrier with their sticks. They may slap the carrier's stick so the ball pops free. The sport does not allow a tie. Sudden-death overtime settles a tied match. Playing time is one hour. Men split that hour into four quarters of fifteen minutes. Women split it into two halves.

8Women's play also zones the field differently. Body contact is much more limited in the women's game. Every form of the sport shares speed. The running is breathtaking. The maneuvering is breathtaking. The teamwork is complex and breathtaking. Shots at the goal can pass 100 miles per hour. That speed is 161 kilometers per hour. Oren R. Lyons is a legendary goalkeeper. The Onondaga Reservation was his childhood home. His most important work later happened away from the field. He played at Syracuse University. In 1957 that school named him an All-American. After sport, he became a spiritual leader. His title is Faithkeeper of the Onondaga. The Onondaga are one of six nations in the Iroquois Confederacy. Indigenous communities worldwide have gained from his humanitarian work. Jim Brown is remembered as one of football's all-time greats. In 1971, football's professional hall of fame added his name. His first love, though, was lacrosse. Many call him the greatest American player the sport has had. Manhasset, on Long Island in New York, was his hometown. That area has a long lacrosse culture. He excelled at Syracuse University. For him, no other game let his athletic gifts out so fully.

9Syracuse was also Gary Gait's school, just as it was for Jim Brown and for Oren Lyons Jr. Gary and his twin, Paul, broke nearly every college record there was to break. The twins changed the sport through speed. They changed it through trick handling of the ball. Gary later succeeded in the National Lacrosse League. He succeeded in Major League Lacrosse too. He remains Syracuse's all-time leader in goals. He now coaches the women's team there. Jen Adams leads the women of Loyola University, which is in Maryland. Earlier, the young player left Australia for America and shattered many marks in the women's game. She is famous for speed. She is famous for agility. She is famous for team play and for sportsmanship. Her 445 goal points for Maryland's Terrapins set a record. In 2009 she played for Australia at the Women's Lacrosse World Cup. Oregon High School Lacrosse Association is the group behind the high-school match in the photo. Popularity today is higher than at any earlier time. Across hundreds of years, the older form belonged to First Nations people, and later the name lacrosse stuck. For many tribes it was a deep spiritual tradition.

10It was a political tradition too. People on every continent play it today. It is growing fast. More and more people are taking it up. Speed draws young athletes. So do the unusual challenges. So does the way teammates must play together. Youth clubs are appearing across North America. No one knows where the next Jen Adams will appear. No one knows when the next Jim Brown will appear. Words to know. Inducted means formally admitted to a group. Adapted means changed to fit a new situation. Agility means being able to move quickly and easily. Mainstream means the leading ideas, habits, or trends of a group. Cradle means to hold or support something gently. Maneuvering means moving around, or guiding how something moves. Gravitated means moved toward something, or became interested in it. A rite is a ceremony for a religious or other solemn event. Humanitarian describes work that helps people, especially by easing pain and suffering. Spiritual concerns a divine being, the soul, or the spirit. Zoning means setting an area apart because its features or its rules are special. Indigenous means native to a particular place.

77. The Farmer Who Swore the First Presidential Oath

1A painting places Washington at Mount Vernon beside the rest of his family. The life that follows opens with a solemn oath and with the plantation. War comes next. Revolution comes after that. A plan of government follows, then the name Father of His Country, and a word list comes last. April 30, 1789, was the day George Washington swore the oath of office. New York was the city, and he was the earliest person to hold the presidency. A cheering crowd stood before him. The personal journey had been astonishing. His first military commission, years before, had not let him imagine this spot. He stood at Federal Hall, in the city of New York, ready for inauguration. He held himself straight. Robert Livingston approached, Bible in hand. Livingston was chancellor of New York. Washington needed only to set his hand on the book and speak the oath. He promised faithful execution of the president's office. He promised to carry out that office faithfully. As far as his ability reached, he would guard the nation's Constitution, shield it, and stand up for it. That act made him the nation's first president. February 22, 1732, was the birth date. Parents were Augustine Washington and Mary Ball Washington. The father made a modest living from the family's rural Virginia plantation, called Mount Vernon. Death took the father when George was only eleven. Lawrence was a half brother. Eight siblings shared the family, and Lawrence filled a father's place. Formal schooling was slight. Practical experience at the plantation filled his young manhood.

2Tuberculosis killed Lawrence in 1752. Control of the estate passed to George at age twenty. Farming was how he saw himself, though many enslaved people worked the fields under his oversight. Westmoreland County, Virginia, was the birthplace. At age three the family moved to the Virginia house called Mount Vernon. Military life drew him as strongly as the plantation did. Descriptions Lawrence gave of earlier service likely lit that interest. During 1752, thirteen separate British colonies were what later became the United States. A separate militia belonged to each colony. Lieutenant Robert Dinwiddie, in that same year, named Washington an assistant to officers in Virginia. The post was called adjutant. Events around him soon pushed heavier duty onto him. November 1753 brought British worry. Settlers from France, living in the valley of the Ohio, were the cause. Those settlers were enlarging the land they held. Dinwiddie sent Washington about three hundred miles, into Pennsylvania, to negotiate. The French rejected any idea of leaving. By 1754 an alliance joined them with Native peoples, and the British were the opponents. Tension rose. A British fort in what is now Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, fell in April 1754. The French renamed it Fort Duquesne. Washington, by then a lieutenant colonel, meant to take it back. A surprise attack on May 28, 1754, succeeded. The commander was killed, and twelve soldiers from France died as well. The rest were taken prisoner. Promotion to colonel came at once. Europe's Seven Year's War had a North American part, the French and Indian War, and it was now underway.

3France struck back in July at Fort Necessity, Washington's base in Pennsylvania. The fort had been built in haste, in the open, within bullet range of the woods. French fighters overwhelmed his men and won. Surrender was forced. Negotiations let him retreat, while France took the fort. Scant help from Virginia's government discouraged him. The army was small and poorly fed. Officials whose posts came through a commission from the king challenged his authority. To them he merely served the colonial governor. Loss of the fort did not erase a growing reputation. People saw a brave commander who demanded much. A fine officer's name would soon be his, even after that loss. A second British push on Fort Duquesne in 1758 succeeded. General John Forbes led it, with Washington's aid, and the fort was captured. Retirement followed, with the honorary rank of brigadier general. He believed soldiering was finished and went home to Mount Vernon. Early in 1759 he married Martha Dandridge Custis. She was a widow, and her family ranked among Virginia's richest. Thousands of acres of her land joined his already large estate, and so did more enslaved people. His view of slavery shifted across his life. Enslaved labor at Mount Vernon helped make the family rich. More than once he blocked paths those people might have used toward freedom. Near the end he began to doubt slavery. He ordered freedom, at Martha's death, for the 123 people he himself had enslaved. Once he had died, in the year 1799, Martha feared she herself might be killed.

4She felt forced to free them sooner. The 153 enslaved people tied to her estate stayed unfree. At her death in 1802 they were split among her grandchildren. Husbands, wives, and children were torn from one another. Political change around him stayed in view from Mount Vernon. By the 1760s Britain had passed laws taxing colonists on goods such as sugar and on tea. Punitive steps enforced the taxes. Boston Harbor was even closed. Opposition united the colonists. Washington was chosen, with representatives of other colonies, for a secret meeting. The meeting was the First Continental Congress. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the place, the month was September of 1774, and nearly two months passed before it ended. Formal independence was not yet his goal. Military action later, if Britain kept disrespecting colonial rights, did have his support. He wore his military uniform to the meeting. November put him in charge of Virginia's volunteer armies. The Second Continental Congress met in May 1775 and named him commander of the Continental Army. Tenure began on July 3, 1775. He refused pay. Early months brought more ammunition and early wins against the British. The next March he drove the British army from Boston into New York City, an important victory. Ready for freedom, Congress produced the Declaration of Independence, with delegate Thomas Jefferson in the lead. Approval came on July 4, 1776. Opposition at the city of New York was strong. British General William Howe held command. Britain's powerful navy controlled the waters around the city.

5A map covers fights of 1776 and 1777 around New Jersey and inside it. Places marked include New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Delaware. The Atlantic Ocean is marked too. Long Island is marked August 27, 1776, by New York City. White Plains is October 28, 1776. A route from Halifax is June 29, 1776. Trenton is December 26, 1776. Princeton is January 3, 1777. Brandywine is September 11, 1777, near Philadelphia. Germantown is October 4, 1777. Monmouth is June 28, 1778. Morristown and Valley Forge appear too. Colonial troops and British troops are both shown. British troops leaving New York City are dated August 25, 1777. The scale reads 50 miles. Summer of 1776 brought a humiliating American defeat on Long Island, in New York, at the hands of General Howe. Three hundred of Washington's men were killed. More than a thousand were captured. Another assault from Howe in September forced a retreat north to White Plains. Defeats continued. The army fell back into New Jersey, then west into Pennsylvania. Pursuit stopped at last in Trenton, New Jersey, where the enemy camped. Christmas night in 1776 was pitch-black when Washington led a crossing of the Delaware River into Trenton. Surprise caught the enemy. The British were driven back to New York. A series of fights at Saratoga in 1777 then handed Britain a resounding defeat. Saratoga lies about 180 miles, or 290 kilometers, north of New York City. For the colonists it was a turning point. France had watched the struggle.

6Revenge was wanted for an earlier loss during the Seven Years' War. French forces joined the Americans. Another test of leadership waited near Philadelphia. Colonial government had its seat there then. Combat filled both the summer of 1777 and the autumn that followed. Winter quarters were at nearby Valley Forge. The winter was harsh. Food and supplies ran scarce. Three thousand men deserted. Government support at Valley Forge was thin, so supplies failed and starvation came near. Early in 1781 the British opened fresh fighting across the colonies of the south. Washington saw a chance. French troops and the French navy backed him as he marched south into Virginia. The meeting place was Yorktown. October 19, 1781, brought British surrender. They were outnumbered and fully surrounded. Independence had been won, and Washington had led the victory. After the war he watched the United States struggle to stand. He supported building one government, federal in form, for the nation that was still young. His writing said the states needed a union that could not be dissolved, set under a federal head. Fellow Virginian James Madison urged a trip to Philadelphia. There, writers would set down an official design for government. The meeting was called the Constitutional Convention. Summer of 1787 was brutally hot. What to call the president was no small question. Blood had been spent to leave the British king behind. His Elective Majesty would not serve. His Mightiness would not serve. Madison was horrified by those titles and by others. He pushed leaders to use the title President, for the United States.

7Delegates worked, gave ground, and coaxed one another. A fresh Constitution was the result. Those delegates would soon be known as the nation's Founding Fathers. February 1789 brought a unanimous election. Washington, who had presided at the convention, became the first president. Fortitude and military success won the delegates. He himself lacked enthusiasm. His wish, he wrote, went no further than living and dying an honest man on his own farm. The presidency produced many firsts that remain. Congress heard him read the speech that opened his term. Presidents now deliver that address before a gathered crowd. In 1790 he delivered the earliest address on the state of the union. It is usually given each year in February now. He decided who would sit in the president's cabinet. He served only two terms. That custom held through 1940. Law made it binding in 1951. A picture shows President Barack Obama giving an inaugural address in 2013. April of that year still brought him out of Mount Vernon and into the city of New York. Inauguration happened before a jubilant crowd. He pledged allegiance to the Constitution. That document set three branches. The president led the executive one. Congress made up the legislative one. The Supreme Court made up the judicial one. Opinions of others were heard. Decisions, once made, were stood by. Thomas Jefferson said the mind of Washington was sure in conclusion. A major achievement of the first term was a bargain between two cabinet members, Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson.

8Hamilton, as Secretary of the Treasury, was building a strong national bank. He wanted the federal government to pay war debts owed by separate states. Jefferson's agreement was required. Jefferson was Secretary of State and led the political opposition. He agreed, but asked that the nation's capital sit in a southern state. The compromise is why Washington, D.C., lies sandwiched between Maryland and Virginia today. Reelection came in 1792. The second term was far harder. One trouble was the Whiskey Rebellion. A tax fell on people who made whiskey. Many believed the law treated them unfairly and hurt their rights in the economy. Some protesters physically threatened the tax inspectors. Growing unrest worried the president. State militiamen were ordered by him to put the revolt down. Other hard choices arrived too. France and England were at war again, and the United States risked being pulled in. He declared the country neutral. John Jay, a justice of the Supreme Court, traveled to Britain. His job was a treaty that would stop another war from starting. Many people judged the terms too friendly to Britain. Outrage followed. Public and press both criticized him severely. He kept his views, as always. Heat still came from the public, which had adored him for a long time. Two terms were enough. He set a precedent almost every later president followed, until the limit became law in 1951. A final message to the American people came before he left office. The Farewell Address named issues he thought would shape the nation for years.

9Alliances with European nations, he warned, could drag the country into later conflicts. He also cautioned that an army grown too big could turn sharply against liberty in a republic. From a military man the warning may surprise. Early 1797 brought retirement to beloved Mount Vernon. On December 12, 1799, a sore throat and exhaustion sent him to bed. Doctors treated him without success. Death came two days later. He was sixty-seven. Retirement gave him longer hours among his family. Life and presidency still shape the country. He was the first president and set many important precedents. Personal character also taught the world what an American president should be like, in style and in temperament. As an officer he had learned courage. He had learned confidence, discipline, and a lively energy that took charge. Those traits served him in office. Presidents who came later have hoped their own administrations would display the same qualities. Henry Lee was an officer and a congressman in Washington's own time. Lee ranked him ahead of others in war, ahead of others in peace, and first inside his countrymen's hearts. Admiration was strong then. Father of His Country remains a nickname in wide use. Labels like that often shrink famous figures to something too simple. While they lived, they were complex. They were imperfect. They were as real as anyone alive now. The dollar bill first carried his face in 1869. The Civil War was already over. The design shown now first appeared in 1963. Points on a life timeline include these.

10A move to the Virginia estate of Mount Vernon happens in 1735. Birth in Westmoreland County, Virginia, is 1732. The year 1754 finds him fighting. The conflict is the French and Indian War, a piece of the wider Seven Years' War. In 1775 he is named to lead the Continental Army as its top commander, during the American Revolution. Presiding over the Constitutional Convention is 1787. The Whiskey Rebellion is 1794. The year 1789 brings his election to the presidency, the first one the United States held. Retirement at Mount Vernon begins in 1797. Death on December 14 is 1799. Advisers gathered around a president, or around another leader of a nation, form a cabinet. A militia is an army of ordinary citizens rather than trained soldiers. Chancellor can name a country's leading official. It can also name an official who handles law for a government. Harsh, unfair, and meant as punishment is what punitive means. Delegates are people chosen or elected to represent others and to act for them. A seat is the central place of a given activity or authority. A front is a battlefield of direct fighting with an enemy. A surrogate takes the place of someone or something else. Inaugurated means brought into office by a formal ceremony. Tenure is how long an official post is held. Indissoluble describes something that ruin cannot finish, that destruction cannot finish, and that breaking cannot finish. Tuberculosis is a disease caused by bacteria, and it mostly affects the lungs.

78. The Games Then and Now

1Contents. To Be First in the World. The Games of Ancient Olympia. The Games Return. The Games Keep Changing. The Games of Our Time. Word List. In 1980 Maria Colon of Cuba won the women's final with the javelin. The distance was 68.4 meters. Both a world record and an Olympic record stood at that mark then. To Be First in the World. The motto reads Citius, Altius, Fortius. Those three Latin words are the Olympic motto. Faster, Higher, Stronger is what they mean. Doing well in a sport means trying to come out ahead of the others. Gold at these Games means something larger. It names the best athlete on Earth. Ancient Greece is where the Games began. Peaceful contest is what they have promoted across a long history. The cost of holding them is high. Cities still compete with one another for the honor. A host of the summer meeting becomes part of that rich tradition. A host of the winter meeting does too. The Games of Ancient Olympia Athletic meetings were already common across the regions of ancient Greece, and they had been so for centuries. Honoring important Greek deities was the aim of many events. Government belonged to each city-state on its own. Law did too. So did an army. Those city-states collided again and again. War was one field. Sport was another. In the myths of Greece, the sky belonged to Zeus. Writings that survive place one organized festival of contest at Olympia, in Greece, and they date it to 776 bce. A much earlier start is what many historians suspect. Four athletic festivals, not one, filled the Greek calendar, and a different god received the honor at each. Only one stop in that cycle was the Olympics. In our time the summer meeting and the winter meeting trade places, with two years between turns.

2Zeus, ruler of the gods, was the one these Games honored. Mount Olympus was his home. His place at the top of the Greek pantheon lifted this festival above the rest very quickly. A map from about the era of those first Games shows the Greek world. Italy is on it, and Mount Olympus is on it. Ancient Greece appears, with Asia Minor. The Aegean Sea is marked, and so is the Ionian Sea. Delphi, Eretria, and Thebes are named. Athens, Olympia, and Corinth are named. Argos is there, and Sparta is there. The Mediterranean Sea appears, and Rhodes appears. Greek areas are shaded, Crete is shown, and other lands sit beside the Greek city-states. Footraces were all the earliest Olympics contained. Growth came quickly, until fourteen separate contests were on the program. The list took in running and boxing. It took in the discus and the javelin. Wrestling was there, and so was jumping. A racetrack called a hippodrome held them. Freedom and violence both ran higher than in events now. Kicking was allowed in wrestling. Punching was allowed. Hair could be pulled, and bones could be broken. Chariots slammed together often. Pain and blood followed, above all on the turns. Grave injury showed up often. So did death. Spectators came by the thousand, traveling out of every part of Greece. Preparation for the athletes lasted months. For some it lasted years. Glory poured over anyone who won. An olive branch cut from a sacred tree was the single prize the officials gave. Money from a hometown often followed, so the win could be celebrated. Taxes never had to be paid again by a champion. Trade found an opening at the ancient Games. So did communication. Food was sold. Supplies were sold. Visitors were given places to stay.

3People arrived from every corner of Greece, so Olympia suited business meetings. Family reunions suited it too. Luxuries stood on the grounds: a hotel, a pool for swimming, a sauna, a place to buy and sell, and a bank. A stadium was there, a gymnasium was there, and an arena for horse racing was there. Religion had a share in the early Greek Olympics. Civic life had a share. Social life had a share. A temple rose on the grounds, holding a huge statue of Zeus built from gold and from ivory. Ceremonies opened with a procession, a formal parade of every athlete and every official. A sacrifice came next. White oxen were offered, and the number could reach one hundred. A feast closed the celebration. An artist drew the old grounds. The drawing shows a stadium beside a track for horse racing. It shows a gymnasium and the Temple of Hera. It shows a bank with a market, the quarters where athletes lived, a swimming pool, and the ground used for boxing and for wrestling. The Temple of Zeus is on that drawing too. Peace in Greece was the largest meaning of the Games. A truce was observed by the city-states at every Olympics, and it was enforced without slack. Peaceful terms replaced war as the way those states competed. Weapons were barred from the city of Olympia for the length of the Games. Travel across Greece could go on freely while the Games lasted. War among the city-states was not a fear on those roads. Inside the temple at Olympia, the giant figure of Zeus has a famous rank. It is counted among the Seven Wonders left by the ancient world. Clothing was rare among the athletes. Most went nude. A few wore nothing but small shorts. Nudity, to the Greeks, was socially acceptable.

4Loose cloth, they believed, might trip a runner. Women were shut out by a strict civil law. Taking part was forbidden. Even watching was forbidden. Death could be the penalty. Girls were the exception, and they could sit as spectators. A separate festival for women athletes was created in 470 bce. Hera, goddess and wife of Zeus, was the one it honored. Those contests are the Heraean Games, and women compete in them. Popularity of the ancient Olympics stayed wild for centuries. Greece fell to the Roman Empire in 146 bce, and the Games still went on. Near 393 ce they stopped. The Roman emperor Theodosius, pronounced thee-uh-DOH-shee-us, was a Christian, and he banned every pagan festival. This festival was included. Olympia was left empty. The grounds were left empty. Neglect lasted hundreds of years. War, earthquakes, and floods followed. Burial and forgetting were the end for the old grounds. The Games Return Time had swallowed the site. Historians still cared about the legends. Archaeologists started a search in the 1700s. By the 1890s the big buildings at Olympia were mostly found. Digging had uncovered them. Pierre de Coubertin, a Frenchman pronounced duh coo-bair-TAHN, could not let the ancient Olympics go. Sport, in his view, was a better way to compete than warfare. Good character, he thought, grew when a person took part in sport. He urged the world to bring the Olympics back as a contest among nations. The idea was loved. He gathered the International Olympic Committee, the IOC, in 1894. A ruined entrance to the stadium still stands in Olympia, Greece. Builders set it up around 200 bce. Organization of the Games mattered deeply to Coubertin. Peace was what he wanted the modern meeting to be. Politics would be laid down. Warfare would be laid down, the way the Greeks had managed for their own Games.

5Love of the sport, he insisted, had to be the reason an athlete entered. A hunger for prizes must not be the reason. A modern winner therefore gets a prize that only stands for honor, just as an ancient winner did. Neither money nor goods are handed over. Another IOC rule limited the field to amateurs. An amateur earned nothing from the sport. Amateurs were the whole field when the Olympics were new. Later the IOC loosened the ban that had kept professionals outside. Before that loosening, medals were taken from an American named Jim Thorpe. He belonged to the Sac and Fox Nation. The medals were gold, from 1912, in the pentathlon and in the decathlon. Fifteen events sit inside those two contests together. Word had reached the IOC of a short stretch when he played baseball for pay. Racism, some people believe, had a part in what was decided. The medals stayed taken. He is still ranked with the greatest athletes who ever lived. Greece, where the old Games were born, held the first modern ones in 1896. A rebuilt stadium filled with Greek citizens, proud and numbering in the thousands. Registration passed two hundred athletes, drawn from fourteen countries. Women were kept out of the contests, matching the ancient rule. Track and field was on the program, covering running, jumping, and throwing. Tennis was on it. Weightlifting was on it. Cycling, wrestling, swimming, and gymnastics were on it too. Each event's winner took an olive branch given as an honor, plus a certificate, plus a medal of silver. Runners in the men's marathon appear in a picture from the 2008 summer meeting. Beijing, China, was the host. A picture shows the Olympic flag coming down at the close of the 2008 summer meeting.

6Beijing, China, was the host. Success slipped at the two meetings that followed. Paris held one in 1900. St. Louis held one in 1904. No Olympic grounds were built by those hosts. No athlete villages were built. Housing was poor, and so was the equipment. Weather ruined many events held outdoors. Delay was common, and so was cancellation. Promotion was weak. Advertising was weak. Few people noticed, and few people came. World's fairs filled those same host cities in 1900 and again in 1904, and the Games had to fight the fairs for a crowd. Mistakes became lessons. Growth was slow, until the Games turned into the popular Olympics people know now. The Games Keep Changing A year off the regular schedule, 1906, brought back an old custom. Athletes marched in an opening procession. They circled the stadium before any contest, each group behind its national flag. Every Olympics since then has opened with a ceremony full of color and full of care. The Olympic flag was Coubertin's design. Flight came first in 1920. White cloth carries five rings, each a different color, locked with the others. Five settled continents, working as one in peace and in harmony, are what the locked rings mean. Look at any nation's flag and you will find at least one of those colors. Posters survive from the summer meeting of 1900, hosted by Paris, France. Posters survive from the summer meeting of 2004, hosted by Athens, Greece. France's Chamonix, pronounced sham-oh-NEE, held the first winter meeting of the Olympics in 1924. Athletes numbered more than 250, and they came from 16 nations. Women and girls made up 11 of them. Sixteen events filled that first winter program. Speed skating was among them. Cross-country skiing was among them. Ski jumping was among them.

7Ice hockey was among them. Popularity of the Winter Olympics grew large. Norway's Sonja Henie, pronounced SOHN-yuh HEN-ee, skated at the 1924 winter meeting. She was twelve. A fall left her last. Failure at that age did not turn her aside. Early Winter Olympics later counted her among their greatest competitors. Fame eventually placed her with the best-known athletes who ever lived. Gold was hers at the winter meetings of 1928, 1932, and 1936. Spectacular shows on ice came afterward, and so did films. A picture shows that Norwegian skater. Women athletes met a milestone in 1928. Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, was the city. Summer competition was officially open to women for the first time. The Olympic torch entered use that same year. A relay of runners was added in 1936. Honor for the Games' origin is the reason the flame is started at Olympia, with sunlight gathered by a lens. From Olympia the torch travels to whichever city is hosting. Runner hands it to runner. Countries lie on the route. Oceans lie on it too. Opening night gives the last runner a special guest to receive the torch. A past Olympic champion is often that guest. The guest sets the Olympic flame alight, and it keeps burning until the Games end. Cathy Freeman, a sprinter from Australia, lights the cauldron as the 2000 Olympics open. An individual gold medal later made her a first. No Aboriginal woman had won one before her. War and argument sometimes break into the Games. Cancellation took three Olympics because war was on. Other meetings went forward in years of sharp controversy across the globe. Athletes have used the Games to protest discrimination, both racial and tied to gender. Raven Saunders reached the podium at the 2020 Games for a silver medal and crossed her arms into an X.

8She is a Black woman, and she belongs to several communities that meet discrimination. The X was her symbol. Where people meet who suffer different kinds of unfair treatment, she said, is what those crossed lines show. Un Guk Kim, lifting for North Korea, sets a world record. The meeting is London in 2012. A pandemic that circled the globe touched some of these Games. Summer of 2020 was put off for a year. COVID-19, the virus behind the illness, kept moving. Winter of 2022 was not delayed. It kept its dates. A positive test for the COVID-19 virus, taken while the Olympics were on, ended the chance to compete for many athletes. Berlin, Germany, in 1936, drew argument from around the world. Germany's leader then was Adolf Hitler. The Nazi Party stood behind him. It was a group built on racism. World War II would later grow from what that group did. Racist ideas were what the Nazis hoped to spread by using the 1936 Games. Eighteen Black Americans on the Olympic team answered with performances that brought humiliation instead. Jesse Owens, a runner, was one of them. Shown at the far right, Owens set several records at world level. College track had already made him famous before any Olympic start. Athletes whose disabilities differ from one another compete at the Paralympic Games. Italy in 1960 held the first of them. Athletes numbered 400, from 23 nations. By 2021 the gathering had passed 4,400 athletes, and 162 nations sent them. Since the summer meeting of 1988, the Paralympics have run beside the Olympics. Shared cities and shared venues required a partnership. The International Paralympic Committee joined the International Olympic Committee. Bright yellow vests mark guides who help runners with little or no sight hold their lanes. A tether, a short rope, links each pair at the wrist.

9The Games of Our Time Since the return in 1896, the modern Olympics have shifted in many ways. A huge spectacle is what they became. Competition grew enormous. Reaching a level that can stand against the world is a full-time job, hard on the body and hard on feeling. Gold medalists from the early years would mostly fail to qualify now. Levels that would have stunned those earlier athletes are ordinary for competitors today. Skiing across country makes the change plain. In 1924 the men's race covered 50 kilometers, or 31 miles. The winning time was 3 hours plus 45 minutes. The same race in 2022 was won in a time just past 1 hour and 11 minutes. Halfpipe gold went to Chloe Kim at two winter meetings, 2018 and 2022. Harder training than ever is required of anyone who wants an Olympic place today. Latest gear is part of a real medal chance. So are the best coaches, and so are sponsors. An early age is when many athletes start, with coaches shaping what they can do. Hours upon hours go into sharpening skill. Special centers exist in many countries so Olympic hopefuls can train with support. Deanna Price appears in a college contest here. Seven days each week go into her preparation for the Olympic Games. Winning presses so hard that cheating appears. Some athletes decide training is not edge enough. Drugs that boost performance have been used in secret by some Olympic athletes in recent years. Trainers on the team have often taken part. Doctors have often taken part. Winning was the aim. Banned substances of that kind have stained how the Olympics look, and they have stained its name. Testing became routine in the middle of the 1970s. Officials look for substances that lift performance.

10A failed test can take a champion's medals away. Cycling star Lance Armstrong had to send his medals back. Steroids were in use. Growth hormones were in use. Better performance was the point. Judges have raised arguments too, in figure skating and in diving. Points may have gone to athletes from a judge's own country when the points were not earned. Judges may have promised to swap points. Honest Games, fair to all, are what the IOC must protect. Size and popularity climb every time the Olympics return. The best athletes in the world are there. A host country greets them. Surprises of a startling kind often show up. A world record falls at most of these meetings. Centuries of history sit inside the modern Olympic Games. Efforts by one person, and efforts by a team, can be breathtaking. An ideal still links these Games to the ancient ones. Sportsmanship is that ideal. Peaceful contest among nations is that ideal too. Word List. Ancient describes what comes from long ago, what is very old. Archaeologists are scientists who study leftovers of cultures from the distant past. Athletes train for sports, for games, or for other work that needs strength, speed, and skill. Character is a person's moral strength. Competitors are the people or the teams that enter a contest. Controversies are clashes of opinion about some issue. A motto is a short phrase that carries a guiding idea for a person or for a group. A procession is a parade done in formal order. Qualify means to prove skill high enough for entry into a hard event. Symbolic describes something that stands in for an idea. Tarnished describes what has been disgraced, or what has lost shine, polish, or purity. A truce is a promise that peace will be kept.

79. The Great Arena of Ancient Rome

1A map places Rome in Italy, between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Adriatic Sea, with the Mediterranean Sea, Europe, Asia, and Africa around it. The Colosseum is one of the most popular tourist sites in Rome. In the heart of the city stands this important ruin of ancient Rome. The Colosseum is an amphitheater. An amphitheater is a round or oval building. Tiers of seats rise in curved rows around an open space. The stage area is completely surrounded by the audience. That arrangement makes it easier to see the action in the performance space. The Colosseum is an impressive example of Roman architecture. When it was built, it was the world's largest amphitheater. It remains a testament to the power of the Roman Empire. It also remains a testament to the empire's lasting impact. The account moves from what the building is, to Rome then and now, to its history, its construction, its defining features, the games, and the Colosseum today. Today the city of Rome is a sprawling, cosmopolitan hub. It is known as the Eternal City. Visitors from across the globe come to enjoy its museums, its historic monuments, and its food. The Colosseum is one of many ruins in modern Rome. It stands like an ancient backdrop in the middle of the busy metropolis. In earlier times, the Roman Empire had its center in Rome. Western civilization still feels the lasting impact of ancient Rome and of the Romans who lived there.

2Many countries have modeled their laws on laws the Romans developed. Buildings put up during the empire still influence designs and materials today. Concrete is one example. The Romans perfected it, and they used it to build the Colosseum. It is still a popular material for structures that are strong and long-lasting. The Colosseum was completed in 80 ce. It is an enduring landmark. It is one of the most famous monuments in the world. This huge structure remains an impressive achievement, even as a ruin in modern times. It is a reminder of the wealth and power of ancient Rome. It is also a reminder of the fierce and grisly battles that took place inside its most famous structure. The Roman Empire began under Emperor Caesar Augustus in 27 bce. The empire that centered on Rome ended more than five hundred years later, in 476 ce. At its peak, the empire covered much of Europe. It also covered the Middle East and parts of North Africa. Its population was once about fifty to sixty million people. That was approximately one-fifth of the world's population at the time. A map of the empire in the first century ce marks Britain, Macedonia, the Atlantic Ocean, Gaul, Rome, Spain, Asia Minor, Greece, Syria, the Mediterranean Sea, Arabia, Egypt, Africa, and Asia. The original name of the Colosseum was the Flavian Amphitheater. The name honored the Flavian emperors who built it. The Flavians were a Roman imperial dynasty.

3They ruled the empire between 69 and 96 ce. The dynasty began under Emperor Vespasian. He started the building of the Colosseum. Before the Flavians, Emperor Nero had ruled. Nero was a cruel and unpopular leader. Vespasian decided to wipe out all memories of the ruler who came before him. He tore down Nero's palace. He built the Colosseum in its place. After Vespasian died of natural causes, his son Titus became emperor. The Colosseum was completed under Titus. A marble portrait bust shows Vespasian with a slight smile. That smile reveals the wit he was reported to have. The Colosseum was built to entertain Roman citizens. It was also built to show the power of Rome and its emperors to the rest of the world. Military conquests supplied the money needed for this impressive amphitheater. Historians estimate a huge quantity of stone for the exterior wall alone. More than 292,000 cartloads of travertine were taken from local quarries. Travertine is a heavy limestone rock. Much of the building work was done by Jewish people. They had been enslaved after the first Jewish-Roman war and set to hard labor. Workers used wooden cranes to lift the heavy stones. Enslaved people powered the cranes. An enslaved worker would climb inside a circular wheel and walk to set it turning. The wheel rotated a central shaft. The shaft pulled in or let out a connected pulley. The pulley ran out along a lifting bar.

4Heavy objects were attached to that bar. A reconstructed crane shows the kind of machine ancient Romans used to lift heavy stones. An aerial view of the Colosseum shows its massive size. The building measures 189 meters (620 ft.) long. It measures 156 meters (512 ft.) wide. That is about the size of a modern sports stadium. It was much larger than any other amphitheater built at the time. It could seat over fifty thousand spectators. Its floor was made of wooden planks. The planks were covered in sand brought from Egypt. The architects used the ingenuity of Roman engineering. The Colosseum had four main floors. Each of the first three floors had eighty arches. The fourth floor had rectangular windows. The arches were placed with care so they could support the weight of the stones above them. On the first floor, the arches also had a practical use. They were entrances and exits for the arena. Professional sailors were hired for a special job. They used their knowledge of sails and wind to make the velarium. The velarium gave spectators shade they badly needed from the Sun. This huge awning was made of canvas. Ropes held it in place. The ropes were attached to spokes at the top of the arena. The awning could be extended or pulled in, depending on where the Sun stood. It was more cost-efficient to build the stairs and seats in workshops away from the site.

5Workers then transported them to the Colosseum for installation. Travertine was the material for the stairs and for most of the seats. The ringside seats were an exception. Those seats were marble, and they were reserved for the most important Romans. Visitors can look up at the outer wall and see holes. Wooden beams were inserted in those holes. Ropes tied to the beams held the velarium in place. Below the floor was the hypogeum. It was a large network of rooms, cells, and tunnels. In Latin, the name means underground. Inside the hypogeum, people and animals waited for their time in the arena. They were scheduled to fight, and then they would come up onto the stadium floor. A system of lifts hoisted animals and men from the hypogeum to the floor. Sophisticated mechanics opened two things at the same moment. They opened the door of an animal's cage. They also opened a trapdoor in the floor. A labeled view of the building points out five features. The outer walls were filled with statues of famous Romans. Gladiators and animals were led out from cages under the arena. The wooden floor was covered with sand. Free women, and enslaved men and women, watched from the very top.
