People used eighty arches on the first floor to enter and leave the arena. Violence was an important part of ancient Roman culture. The myth of how Rome was founded tells of two brothers.

6Romulus killed his twin brother, Remus, after an argument about where to build the city. Artwork that celebrated violence appeared in many settings in Rome. It appeared on monuments and in public buildings. The scenes came from mythological stories, from gladiatorial combat, and from military conquest. They served as reminders of Roman might and of the power of the emperor. A Roman mosaic shows two gladiators fighting. What the Colosseum was used for reflected a culture that was often harsh and violent. The games began at dawn. Trumpets sounded. A chariot procession followed. The gladiators gave a salute. The games did not end until darkness fell. The morning games consisted of comic duels. The fighters, who were often women, used wooden weapons. Slavery in ancient Rome was not based on a person's skin color. It was not based on where a person was from. A majority of the people the Romans enslaved had been taken captive in wartime. Many Roman generals grew rich by selling conquered people into slavery. Julius Caesar was one of those generals. Animal events came next. Animals were brought from all over the Roman Empire. They stood for how far the empire's power reached. Most Romans had never seen these unfamiliar beasts. The animals included lions, tigers, elephants, hippos, and bears. Some animals were paraded for show. Many were killed in fights against one another. Others were hunted down as part of the show. Several pairs of gladiators fought at once during the later part of the afternoon.

7Romans often described gladiators as rough and frightening men. They said these men lived outside normal society. Some were condemned criminals. Some were prisoners of war. Some were enslaved people forced to fight. Others were freemen and retired soldiers who wanted fame and fortune. A gladiator who succeeded in a battle might be awarded money. If he was enslaved, he might even be awarded his freedom. Gladiators who lost stood for Roman ideals. Those ideals were the glory of warfare and the importance of dying a noble death. Training for these fighters took place at a special school known as a ludus. There were several types of gladiators. They used different kinds of weapons. The Equites, pronounced EK-wi-tayss, fought on horseback with spears. The Bestiarii, pronounced bes-tee-AH-rih-ee, fought wild animals with spears and knives. The Samnite gladiators, pronounced sahm-NEE-teh, carried shields and spears. The Retiarii, pronounced re-tee-AH-rih-ee, used nets and tridents. Romans wanted each fight to be different. They did not want the audience to grow bored. Gladiators fought under strict rules. The audience understood those rules as well. One important rule banned sneaky attacks from behind. Ancient records show a surprising survival rate. About 90 percent of gladiators lived to fight another battle. One gladiator did not have to kill the other. The fight only had to be entertaining enough for the audience. Gladiators used different weapons and armor to defend themselves.

8The gear included tridents, nets, helmets, swords, and shields of different shapes. An 1872 painting called Pollice Verso, meaning With a Turned Thumb, is by Jean-Léon Gérôme. It shows a gladiator looking toward the shouting crowd of Romans in the Colosseum. Emperors often took part in animal hunts. Animals used in the hunts included lions, elephants, bears, tigers, deer, goats, and dogs. They also included leopards, crocodiles, boars, hippopotamuses, and rabbits. Most of the animals were trained to fight. Some were trained to perform tricks for the crowd instead. Official referees oversaw the fighting. In Latin they were called summi rudii. When a gladiator was wounded, he would ask for mercy. Sometimes the crowd was asked whether he should be spared. People in the crowd could give a thumbs up or a thumbs down. That signal decided the gladiator's fate. Each year, the Colosseum draws somewhere from four million to six million tourists. The income of audience members decided where they sat. The seats fell into four separate sections. The richest and most powerful people in Rome sat closest to the action. That group included the emperor, the senators, and special priestesses. They occupied the marble seats. People of the noble class sat in the second tier. Free Roman men sat in the third tier. Women and enslaved people sat on wooden benches on the very top level. They also used standing-room sections at the top or in the aisles. Those places reflected their low social status.

9People of especially low standing were strictly banned from the Colosseum. Actors and gravediggers were among them. The stone seats with the best views of the floor were reserved for the most important people in ancient Rome. Gladiator games and animal hunts finally ended after four centuries. By 600 ce, the Colosseum had been badly damaged. Neglect, lightning, and earthquakes had harmed it. Around this time, Christianity was spreading across the empire. Leaders of the Christian faith judged the games to be immoral. Because of that, the importance of the Colosseum began to fade. Financial crises and military crises also helped end its era. Emperors were no longer willing to spend money on repairs the building needed. The public began to lose interest in the games. The Colosseum was eventually abandoned. It was used as a quarry for other building projects. The steps of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome are one example. Those steps are made from stones taken from the Colosseum and used again. John Warwick Smith painted a watercolor of the ruins in 1802. Over the centuries, natural disasters and vandalism have destroyed nearly two-thirds of the Colosseum. Since the early 1990s, several projects that are still going on have brought major renovations. A cleaning of the outer walls was finally finished in June 2016. The facade has had extensive restoration. The work removed dirt that had built up over the centuries. Much of the soot and grime came from automobile fumes.

10On weekdays, travel around the Colosseum is limited to cabs and buses. On weekends, only people on bicycles or on foot are permitted. The Colosseum is one of the most famous monuments to have survived from the ancient world. It is also one of the most recognizable. It is one of the most popular destinations in Italy. In 2007, it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. No greater symbol exists of the power and historical impact of Rome and the Roman Empire. Architecture is the design and construction of buildings. Quarries are places where marble, slate, or other kinds of stone are dug out. A dynasty is a series of rulers from the same family in a country. Renovations are repairs, or restorations of something to an earlier and better state. Gladiators were fighters in ancient Rome who fought in public to entertain other people. Spectators are people who watch an event without taking part. A hypogeum is the underground part of an ancient structure. It is often a room or a network of rooms. Utilitarian means useful or practical. Vandalism is the intentional destruction of property. Ingenuity is cleverness or skill in solving a problem or a challenge. A velarium is a cloth covering used to shade the audience at a Roman theater or amphitheater. A pulley is a circular lever, usually a wheel with a rope around it.

80. The Great Mud Mosque of Djenné

1People who live near the Great Mosque of Djenné pass it often. They are on their way to markets and to nearby rivers. The town of Djenné, pronounced je-NAY, is one of the oldest towns in sub-Saharan Africa. It is a small town. About thirteen thousand people live there. It is in the country of Mali, in West Africa. Djenné is home to a religious building found nowhere else in quite the same form. That building is the Great Mosque of Djenné. Mosques are places of worship for Muslims. Muslims follow the religion of Islam. Islam is one of the largest religions in the world. It has more than one billion followers. Islam is built on five pillars, or obligations. A person must meet them in order to live a virtuous life. The pillars are a declaration of faith, prayer, fasting, charity, and pilgrimage to Mecca. Mecca is the birthplace of Islam. Travelers visit the Great Mosque to study Islam. They also worship at the world's largest structure built of mud. Sub-Saharan Africa has few architectural achievements greater than this one. The story runs from this wonder of Africa to a stop on a trade route, a place of worship, three mosques in turn, building with mud, a role beyond worship, and the heritage of Djenné. Djenné is relatively hard to reach by ordinary travel.

2It lies on a floodplain between the Niger and Bani Rivers. A person can reach it only by ferryboat. During the thirteenth century, that location proved a perfect link to Timbuktu. Timbuktu lies 483 km (300 mi.) to the north. Traders traveled from the coast north toward Timbuktu. Timbuktu was a major stop on the trans-Saharan trade routes. Those traders passed through Djenné, and the town grew. Growth of the city meant more commerce. From the thirteenth century to the sixteenth century, the marketplace was the most important source of income for residents. Merchants came from north of the Sahara Desert. They brought salt from desert mines. They also brought cloth, copper, and silver. In Djenné they traded those goods for products from south of the desert. The southern goods included gold, kola nuts, and leather. The route did more than move goods. It also spread the Islamic religion into new regions of Africa. Islam had come to Mali in the ninth century. It began to have a greater influence under Mali's Muslim king, Mansa Musa, during the 1300s. As years passed, Djenné grew into a center where Islamic scholarship flourished. In Mali, religion and culture meet in a major way at the Great Mosque of Djenné. The second construction of the Great Mosque of Djenné appears in a drawing made in 1896.

3Followers of Islam needed a place to worship in the town. Construction of the Great Mosque began in the thirteenth century. The mosque people see today is not the original building on this site. Historians say the original mosque was likely built under the town's ruler, King Koi Konboro. He put up the mosque on the site of his palace. He used local materials and a traditional design. Under the rulers who followed Konboro, the mosque kept growing. Towers were added. Surrounding walls were added. Over time, rain took a toll. Exterior mud washed away and became unstable. Considerable disrepair had overtaken the Great Mosque of Djenné by the 1800s. During a holy war by the Tukulor Empire in the nineteenth century, a West African tribal leader named Seku Amadu conquered the town. Amadu let the original mosque fall into still worse disrepair. Islamic law did not allow its destruction. Then, in 1834, Amadu began a new and plainer mosque. The new mosque was built on a nearby site. The work took two years. It was completed in 1836. Amadu's mosque lacked any ornamentation. It was much larger than the original mosque. It featured minarets, which are towers. Low and squat, this second mosque made an impression through its massive size.

4French forces captured the city in 1893. They replaced the mosque, which had already fallen into ruin, with a school. Workers must repair the walls of the Great Mosque of Djenné every year. If they do not, the rain will cause the building to deteriorate. The mosque people see today was completed in 1907. It was built on the site of the original Great Mosque. People once believed it had been built under French supervision. New research supports a different idea. The masons' guild of Djenné built the current mosque without the French. Workers forced to labor were brought by the guild from villages nearby. Workers combined tons of sand, mud, rice husks, and water. They formed bricks for this third version of the Great Mosque. This was the last time the mosque was built completely from the ground up. Even so, it changes every year. Wind, rain, and shifts in temperature make the walls crack and degrade. Regular repairs are required. Today's mosque has been sculpted many times. It may look different from the original. The rounded outer walls take on a warm color in bright sunshine. Mosques in places such as Egypt, India, and Turkey are often carved and tiled in ornate ways. The Great Mosque of Djenné stands out because of its plainness.

5Its tall brown walls reach heights of 16 meters (52 ft.). They are made of mud that the Sun has baked hard. That gives the building its uniquely smooth, sculpted look. Bundles of palm-wood sticks jut out from the walls at regular intervals. Those sticks are called toron. The prayer wall is called the qibla wall, pronounced KIB-luh. It faces east toward Mecca. It overlooks the city's marketplace. Three boxlike minarets rise from the main wall. Each is topped with an ornate sculpted ostrich egg. The egg is a symbol of purity and fertility. Minarets are typical features of mosques. Five times a day, Muslims are called to prayer from these towers. People reach the minarets by climbing spiral staircases. A man chosen by the mosque stands near the minarets and calls Muslims to prayer. Visitors climb one of six sets of stairs before they enter the prayer hall. The hall can hold up to three thousand people. Mecca is the city that matters most in the Islamic religion. Western Saudi Arabia is where that city stands. During daily prayers, Muslims turn to face Mecca. The whole surface of the Great Mosque covers 5,625 square meters (60,547 sq. ft.). It is the largest mud-brick building in the world. It is considered one of the greatest architectural achievements in Africa.

6UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1988. The walls are 41 to 61 centimeters (16 to 24 in.) thick. They are built of smooth mud. The tallest minaret is 16 meters (52 ft.) high. There are three minarets. Eighteen decorative buttresses, or projections, stand on the main wall. The building sits on a raised platform 3 meters (9 ft.) high so it can avoid flooding. Inside, a roof covers half of the mosque. Ninety wooden pillars span the enclosed prayer hall. The roof contains vents so the inside can stay cool. Removable ceramic caps top the vents. When the caps are taken off, hot air can escape. The other half of the mosque is an open-air prayer hall. It sits behind the roofed hall. An arcade, or arched passageway, surrounds this courtyard. The large open courtyard is used for public prayer. A worker spreads mud on the outer wall to maintain the building. The mosque was built with traditional materials from the region. The mud was a mix of butter and clay. That mix was used to create the bricks, the mortar, and the plaster. Locals baked the mud in the sun to make bricks called ferey. They also used the mud as mortar to bond the bricks when they built the walls. The mud serves as a plaster that coats the walls.

7The coating gives the walls a smooth, sculpted look. At the base, the mud bricks are laid as thick as 61 centimeters (24 in.). That thickness supports the weight of the walls above. The mud walls insulate the building. They absorb the Sun's heat. They keep a cool temperature during the day. After dark, the absorbed heat is released. The interior stays warm through the night. West Africa often has drastic changes in humidity and in temperature. Because of that, the mosque includes bundles of toron. The bundles stick out from the walls at regular intervals. They help reduce cracking. The decorative toron also serve as built-in scaffolding during the yearly maintenance. The building had to withstand possible water damage. The whole mosque was built on a raised platform 3 meters (9 ft.) high. The platform helps it avoid flooding from the nearby Bani River. Ceramic gutters along the roof collect precipitation. They direct the water away from the walls so the exterior is not damaged. During repairs, workers climb on the outside of the mosque. They use the toron as scaffolding. Each year, thousands of people race to the mosque during the Crépissage de la Grande Mosquée. The name is pronounced kray-pee-SAZH DU LAH GRAHND MOSS-kay. It means Plastering of the Great Mosque.

8They replaster the walls. Today the Great Mosque is central to the community of Djenné. Residents take an active role in its preservation. Every year the whole community joins the festival. They replaster the exterior walls. Heat, humidity, and rain have damaged those walls over the previous year. During the festival, children carry baskets of mud to the mosque. In the days before the festival, citizens collect fine clay soil. They take it from the nearby Niger and Bani Rivers. They use it to form the mud plaster. The women of Djenné typically supply water for the mixture. They put the water in special pits. Young boys take on the job of mixing the plaster. At the start of the festival, a race is held. The race decides who will be first to carry plaster from the pits to the mosque walls. Then men climb ladders. They use the toron for scaffolding. They spread the muddy mixture on the cracking walls. The lively festival includes music and food as well as work. Musicians entertain the workers to encourage them. The town's elders sit in a place of honor. They watch the proceedings. They offer advice when it is needed. Young children sing, run, and play in the middle of the festival. The Great Mosque of Djenné allows only Muslims to go inside.

9People who are not Muslims may view the mosque only from the outside. The Great Mosque holds a significant place in the history and culture of Djenné. Because of that, its citizens have fought to preserve it. Constant repairs and plastering have gradually weakened the structure underneath. Architects said in 2006 that the mosque might collapse very soon. They began a large restoration program. They asked the community to pause its annual repair for a time. That pause took away an important tradition. It also took away a major tourist attraction that is essential to the economy of Djenné. The festival resumed in 2012. Today, many ancient mosques around the world have been modernized. Advances include electrical wiring and indoor plumbing. The Great Mosque of Djenné has been given a loudspeaker system. Locals have opposed further updates. They want to preserve the building. They see it as an important part of their culture and their religion. Foreign investors have offered to rebuild the mosque with concrete in place of the walls. They have also offered to tile over the sand floor. Those changes would improve the structure. They would also remove an important tradition that unites the community of Djenné. In 1988, the United Nations made Djenné a World Heritage Site.

10The town gained protections that help preserve its history. The Great Mosque is kept from undergoing significant modernizations. For the time being, the people of Djenné will keep maintaining their cultural heritage. They will also keep their annual festival. One of the few modern additions to the mosque is lighting on the outside. Architectural refers to the design and construction of buildings. Modernized means updated, or made to fit modern technology, ideas, or style. Disrepair is the state of being in bad condition or of needing repair. A mosque is a place of worship in the Islamic faith. Inaccessible means impossible or hard to reach or use. Muslims are people who follow the religion of Islam. Islam is the monotheistic faith of Muslims. It is based on the teachings of the prophet Muhammad. A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred or special place, such as a shrine. Preservation is the act of keeping something in its original condition, or of caring for it for the future. Mecca is a city in Saudi Arabia. It is a holy destination for people who practice Islam. Minarets are narrow towers near a mosque. Worshippers are called to prayer from them. Scaffolding is a system of temporary platforms. It supports workers while they build, repair, or decorate a structure.

81. The Landing on the Normandy Coast

1Contents. The Men in the Boats. How the War Reached 1944. The Plan Called Overlord. Five Named Beaches. Utah Beach. Omaha Beach. Gold Beach. Juno Beach. Sword Beach. After the Landings. Words to Know. The Men in the Boats. Dozens of small landing craft held hundreds of huddled men. They thought about families who were far away. The boats waited just off the coast of France. German forces occupied that coast. Most of these men were not highly trained soldiers. They had not spent their whole lives in the military. They were teachers. They were store clerks. They were housepainters. They were other ordinary citizens. They came from the United States. They came from the United Kingdom. They came from Canada. Their governments had drafted them to fight in World War II. The landing craft rocked in rough water. Many of the men were seasick because of that rocking. Every one of them was scared. To start the mission, they had to jump into cold water. Then they had to run across the beaches. Members of the German army shot at them during that run. Those German soldiers had also been ordinary citizens before the war. The world these men knew had changed. Failure was not a choice they could accept. The mission had a code name, Operation Overlord. It was a must-win for the Allies. This is the story of D-Day. The Letter D in the Name. In military terminology, the letter D in D-Day stands for day. Forces used this code for the day of any important military operation. The D-Day in this story was June 6, 1944. Days before it and days after it were marked with minus signs and plus signs. D minus 3 meant three days before D-Day. That date was June 3. D plus 3 meant three days after D-Day. That date was June 9. A map of Europe in 1942 can show who held which lands.

2Labels on that map include Ireland, Prussia, England, the Netherlands, Poland, and Germany. They also include Belgium, Luxembourg, Czechoslovakia, France, and Austria. They include Switzerland, Hungary, Romania, Portugal, and Yugoslavia. They include Italy, Spain, Bulgaria, and Albania. The Atlantic Ocean is marked as well. A key can show three kinds of land. One kind was under Axis control. One kind was a neutral country. One kind was under Allied control. How the War Reached 1944. German troops invaded Poland in September 1939. That invasion is how World War II began. They quickly captured Poland. They then successfully invaded France in June 1940. Over the next four years, Germany and the other Axis powers took over most of Europe. Those other Axis powers were Italy and Japan. They also took many islands in the Pacific. The Allied nations were trying desperately to stop the Axis powers. The Allies included the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada. They included the Soviet Union. They included many other nations. To win the war in Europe, the Allies first had to free France from German rule. Success in France would trap German troops. Allied-occupied France would stand on one side. The Soviet Union would stand on the other. The Plan Called Overlord. For Allied forces in World War II, few days mattered more than June 6, 1944. Allied landings on the Normandy beaches of France marked the start of a long mission. The mission was also brutal. Its aim was to free Europe and end the war. No earlier military operation had tried to do as much as the D-Day invasion. The Allies had to move more than 156,000 men across the English Channel. They also had to move the men's equipment, artillery, and tanks. They had to do this before the Axis powers discovered the plan. A discovered plan could let the Axis concentrate their forces.

3Those forces could then crush the invasion. A map of the crossing can mark ports and beaches. On the British side are Portland, Southampton, Portsmouth, Shoreham-by-Sea, and Dartmouth. Great Britain and the English Channel are labeled. On the French side are five beaches: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. Marks can show where United States forces, British forces, and Canadian forces were headed. Under the plan, Allied airborne forces would jump by parachute into zones across northern France. They would jump early on the morning of June 6. Other troops would come out of naval landing craft. They would storm five beaches. The beaches were Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. German troops guarded them. By the end of the day, the Allies hoped to hold a foothold along the French coast. From there they hoped to begin an advance into German-occupied France. A beach map can mark German positions and United States positions as of midnight. It can show Utah Beach beside Omaha Beach. Utah Beach in Figures. The number of United States troops landed was 20,000. The number of military vehicles landed was 1,700. The number of United States casualties was 589. Five Named Beaches. Utah Beach. The troops belonged to the United States 4th Infantry Division. Paratroopers came from the 82nd Airborne Division and the 101st Airborne Division. The 4th Infantry Division was scheduled to land on Utah Beach at 6:30 am. Utah was the westernmost of the D-Day beaches. Five hours earlier, paratroopers had been dropped inland. The drop points sat 2 to 5 miles from the shore. That distance is 3.2 to 8.0 kilometers. The paratroopers had one road to secure. That road ran from Valognes (vah-LOHN-yuh). It ran to Carentan (kah-rohn-TOHN). German soldiers could not be certain about the paratroopers. The jumpers might be the main attack force. They might be a decoy force. A decoy would distract the Germans from a larger assault.

4The troops who landed at 6:30 am were supposed to push inland. They were supposed to meet the paratroopers as soon as possible. The landing from the sea did not go as planned. Strong currents came from the poor weather. Those currents set the amphibious craft down 2,200 yards from the intended targets. That distance is 2 kilometers. The troops had to wade ashore. Brigadier General Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was there. He was the oldest son of former United States President Theodore Roosevelt. He told his men, "We'll start the war from here!" He ordered them to advance. The spot was not a heavily defended part of the beachfront. American casualties at Utah Beach were minimal next to the losses at the other beaches. By afternoon, the United States 4th Infantry had met the American paratroopers. The German defense was defeated quickly. The Americans' inland advance by the day's end was about 4 miles. That distance is 6.4 kilometers. They were roughly 1 mile from the 82nd Airborne paratroopers at Ste. Mère-Église (sahnt-MER-e-GLEEZ). That gap is 1.6 kilometers. Ste. Mère-Église lies some 6 miles north of Carentan. That distance is 9.7 kilometers. A map can mark German positions and United States positions as of midnight along Omaha Beach. Gold Beach can appear beside it. Omaha Beach in Figures. The number of United States troops landed was 34,000. The number of military vehicles lost was 136. The number of United States casualties was 3,686. Omaha Beach. The United States 1st Army fought at Omaha Beach. The beach was 6 miles long. That length is 9.7 kilometers. It was the largest of the five beaches. From the beginning, the 1st Army faced incredible odds. Lieutenant General Omar Bradley led those troops. Cliffs 100 feet high overlooked the beach. That height is 30.5 meters. The cliffs made an American attack very difficult.

5The Germans had also placed obstacles they called dragon's teeth. Each one was a toothlike block of concrete about 3 to 4 feet high. That height is 0.9 to 1.2 meters. The obstacles were meant to take out landing craft. They were heavily mined with explosives. Germans fired from the tops of the cliffs. They also fired from thirteen resistance nests. A resistance nest is a small defensive position that can fight on its own. Even before anyone fired, the Americans faced odds that were firmly against them. The attack was scheduled for 6:30 am. At that hour the tide was low. The dragon's teeth were visible. The plan was to land infantry beside twenty-nine amphibious Sherman tanks. Those tanks would give the Allied troops a huge advantage in firepower. Disaster struck when the tanks left their landing craft too far from the beach. Of the twenty-nine tanks, every one flooded except two. They sank. Storms That Moved the Invasion. The invasion date was first set for June 5. The Allies wanted good visibility for the landing. They wanted light winds from the northwest. They wanted low tides. Because of the tides, June 5 through June 7 were the best dates. If those days failed, the Allies would wait two more weeks for ideal conditions. Storms marked the weather on June 5. A landing from the sea would fail if winds were strong and waves were high. Low clouds would keep pilots from seeing targets. Pilots needed that view to drop paratroopers. They also needed it to attack enemy positions. Poor weather pushed the operation back to June 6. The weather on June 6 was not much better. The sunk tanks went to the bottom of the ocean. Nothing could save the tanks. Nothing could save their crews. Troops on the beach did not get the armored cover they had expected. The weather added to the Allies' difficulties.

6Powerful winds carried many landing craft far off target. The rising tide did the same. When the troops did land, units could not tell who stood where. They could not tell what each unit was meant to do. The confusion was widespread. German fire picked off American troops at a devastating rate. Lieutenant General Bradley thought about calling off the whole operation because the losses were so severe. The only way off the beach was a sprint toward the cliffs. The runners had to dodge heavy German gunfire. Americans who got that far then had to scale the towering cliffs. As troops climbed, United States Navy destroyers came as close as they could. The ships attacked the German fortifications. The destroyers mattered greatly. They distracted the Germans. They gave some relief from gunfire that had been aimed only at the Americans on the beach. By afternoon, the German battle effort was weakening. Night came with the Americans holding a place on Omaha Beach. Gold Beach. A map can mark German positions and British positions as of midnight. It can show Gold Beach beside Juno Beach. Gold Beach in Figures. The number of British troops landed was 24,970. The number of military vehicles landed was 2,100. The number of British casualties was 1,023. British troops of the 50th Infantry Division secured Gold Beach. It was one of two beaches taken by British troops. It sat in the middle of the five beaches. Landing time was 7:25 am. British forces immediately faced a major problem. The problem was the weather. Incredibly strong winds covered German mines with seawater earlier than expected. Other beach obstacles were covered early as well. A picture can show the Mulberry harbor at Gold Beach. It was about 6 miles long. That length is 10 kilometers. Flexible steel roadways formed it. Steel pontoons supported the roadways. Concrete pontoons supported them as well.

7British engineers could not disarm the mines and obstacles as planned. Twenty armored cars were damaged by them. British troops could have met disaster in that situation. It was not, because incredibly accurate naval attacks took out German defenders. Aerial attacks did the same. Most of Gold Beach was in British control by the afternoon. They quickly pushed inland. They also captured the fishing village of Arromanches (ar-roh-MAHNSH). That village later became the site of Mulberry harbor. The Allies used the harbor to unload supplies. As a strategic move, the Gold Beach invasion succeeded in a tremendous way. British troops were then able to link up with Canadian forces. Those Canadians had landed at Juno Beach. Juno Beach. A map can mark German positions and Canadian positions as of midnight. It can show Gold Beach, Juno Beach, and Sword Beach. Juno Beach in Figures. The number of Canadian troops landed was 21,400. The number of military vehicles landed was 3,200. The number of Canadian casualties was 961. The Canadian 3rd Infantry had the task of taking Juno Beach. The plan was to move inland. The Canadians were to form a link between Gold Beach and Sword Beach. Both of those beaches were in British hands, or were meant to be. A major challenge met the Canadians before they even reached the sand. They landed at 7:55 am. Bad weather and a rising tide left German mines partly underwater. The Canadian demolition teams then faced those hidden mines. A picture can show a bulldozer tank. The Americans used a tank like that one to get through the Germans' dragon's teeth. Demolition engineers could not destroy the mines. Canadian landing craft suffered extremely heavy losses from the mines. They left 30 percent destroyed or damaged. With landing craft damaged, many Canadian soldiers struggled to wade ashore. Troops who did reach the beach were hit by a powerful wave of German firepower.

8The first wave of Canadians had about a 50/50 chance of surviving. The Canadians were not ready to give up. Those who were not hit kept fighting. They worked their way off the beach. They pushed farther inland. Once they left the beach, German resistance died down. The Canadians took command quickly. Their losses were heavy. Their inland advance still went farther than the advance on each of the other four beaches. They captured a number of towns. They captured a critical bridge. They then linked up with the British at Gold Beach. Sword Beach. A map can mark German positions and British positions as of midnight. It can show Juno Beach beside Sword Beach. Sword Beach in Figures. The number of British troops landed was 29,000. The number of military vehicles landed was 2,603. The number of British casualties was 630. The British 3rd Army raided Sword Beach. It was the other beach attacked by British forces. The main goal was to capture the town of Caen (KAHN). Caen lay 9.3 miles inland. That distance is 15 kilometers. Caen was the town where every main road in the region passed. Control of those roads was crucial if the Allies were to advance successfully. The raid began at 7:25 am. Troops stormed the beaches. Paratroopers from the 3rd Parachute Brigade landed inland. Paratroopers from the 5th Parachute Brigade landed inland as well. They joined the British troops from the beach. German resistance at Sword was light for the British. The resistance was lighter than on the other beaches. The fighting did not stay light for the whole morning. After the invasion, tanks stood in the streets of Normandy towns such as Tour-La-Ville. By 8:00 am, most of the fighting was over. British commandos and paratroopers farther inland had joined together by 1:00 pm. The day was matching the plan in every detail.

9Sword Beach did not stay secure for long. The Germans launched a counterattack. By 8:00 pm, the beach had been reached by the German 192nd Panzer Grenadier Regiment. The German success proved temporary. Allied tanks could attack those German vehicles. Fighter planes that had already arrived at Sword could attack them too. The counterattack failed. Even so, it kept British troops from linking up with Canadian troops from Juno Beach on that day. The link had been part of the plan. The British were unable to reach Caen on the same day. People still counted the mission as a huge Allied victory. Allied forces managed to stabilize the beach. They advanced roughly 4 miles inland. That distance is 6.4 kilometers. They repelled the German counterattack. They met the Canadians on the following day. Allied troops would capture Caen six weeks later. The date was July 20, 1944. After the Landings. The cost in soldiers' lives was high on both the Allied side and the Axis side. Operation Overlord was still a tremendous success. Through great sacrifice, Allied forces gained a foothold. From that foothold they could begin to push German forces back. They could begin to liberate occupied France. The operation was a tremendous military victory for the Allies. It was also a day of mourning. So much happened on D-Day that accurate casualty numbers were hard to record. That was true for the Allies. It was also true for the Axis. The word casualties does not mean only deaths. It means all losses suffered by the armed forces. Those losses include people killed. They include people wounded. They include people missing in action. They include prisoners of war. Historians estimate German casualties between four thousand and nine thousand. They estimate more than six thousand Allied casualties on D-Day. About one more year passed before the war ended. Allied troops kept capturing territories in Europe that Germany occupied.

10Germany finally surrendered on May 8, 1945. Japan surrendered on August 15, 1945. Those surrenders officially ended the war. D-Day was a significant turning point in World War II. The later liberation of France was a turning point as well. Without the efforts of Allied soldiers on D-Day, the war's outcome would have been much different. Their sacrifices were part of that change. Words to Know. aerial (adj.) taking place in the air. Allies (n.) the countries that aided one another against Germany, Italy, and Japan in World War II, including Great Britain, the United States, France, and the Soviet Union. amphibious (adj.) related to military operations in which troops enter enemy territory from the water. artillery (n.) large guns that fire heavy shells over long distances. Axis powers (n.) the countries that fought the Allies in World War II, including Germany, Italy, and Japan. casualties (n.) people injured, killed, or missing during a war, an accident, or a disaster. commandos (n.) members of a military unit trained for quick raids inside enemy territory. decoy (adj.) describing a person or object used to trick someone away from a real target. drafted (v.) ordered into military service, especially during wartime. foothold (n.) a position from which a force can start moving toward a goal. fortifications (n.) defensive structures built so a place is stronger against attack; forts. infantry (n.) soldiers trained and equipped with weapons and gear to fight on foot. liberation (n.) the act of setting someone or some place free. mines (n.) bombs hidden underground or underwater that explode when touched or moved. mourning (v.) grieving, or feeling sad, especially for someone who has died. Panzer (n.) a type of German tank used in World War II. paratroopers (n.) soldiers trained to jump from airplanes and fight behind enemy lines. repel (v.) to force something back or away.

82. The Largest Hairy Rainforest Spiders

1Baby Goliath spiders look very much like the adults. They are only smaller. This book starts with a heavy giant. The biggest tarantula comes next. Life in hot, humid tropics follows. A powerful hunter fills another part. Hawks, owls, and wasps come after that. The life cycle is explained later. A last part asks what these spiders can teach people. A word list closes the book. A person who finds spiders unsettling will want to keep clear of the Goliath bird-eating spider. Early explorers gave it that name after they reported a Goliath spider eating a hummingbird. Few spiders anywhere grow larger than these fierce hunters. The fangs are 0.75 inches (2 cm) long. Venom from those fangs is strong enough to paralyze prey. A spider this large can make some people uneasy. People face far less danger from it. Mice face more. So do other small mammals and insects. Some people find it fascinating. Others find it completely horrifying. Either way, the Goliath bird-eating spider is a huge and unusual arachnid. A size chart puts the spider's diameter at 12 inches (30.48 cm). The weight is 6 ounces (0.17 kg). A human hand on the chart is 7.44 inches (18.89 cm) long and 3.3 inches (8.4 cm) wide.

2A golden tint shows up on some Goliaths. That color is why the scientific name is blondi. Tarantulas form a huge group of spiders. About nine hundred kinds have been identified. Rainforests hold some of them. Deserts, grasslands, and mountains hold others. Home regions include the United States and Central America. Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia are home regions too. Other names are Goliath bird-eating spiders and Goliath tarantulas. No tarantula grows larger. Eight eyes are part of the body plan, as in many other arachnids. Eight legs are part of it too. The body has two main sections. Head and neck join up front. That joined part is the cephalothorax. The mouth, the stomach, and the brain sit there. The legs connect to that same front section. The abdomen is the rear section. It holds the glands that make silk. Those glands are called spinnerets. A body diagram shows the legs attached to the cephalothorax. That front part holds the brain, the eyes, the fangs, the mouth, and the stomach. Pedipalps sit near the mouth. The abdomen holds the silk glands. Most spiders push venom into prey with their fangs. Every spider has eight legs. Every spider has jaws with fangs, and most spiders make venom.

3Every spider has glands that make silk. Every spider has a tough outer skeleton for protection. Every spider has eyes, and most have eight. Sensory hairs cover the body. Coffee-colored hairs cover most of a Goliath tarantula. Some body parts are light tan or reddish. Other parts are a darker brown. The long legs are covered mainly with dark brown hairs. Next to most other spiders, a Goliath is truly huge. No spider on the planet is heavier. Weight can reach 6 ounces (170 g). A large apple is a fair comparison. With the legs stretched out, the span is almost 1 foot (30 cm) across. That is nearly the width of a dinner plate. Each leg joint, also called a knee, carries hairs of a lighter color. Eight eyes do not add up to sharp sight. A Goliath can tell bright from dim. It cannot use vision to pick out fine details. Special hairs do the hunting work instead. Those hairs sense movement. The smallest shake of the ground, or of the air, is picked up. The spider can then locate prey. Goliath bird-eating spiders belong to a family called hairy mygalomorphs. Hairy is a fitting word for them. Mygalomorph is a science word for the way the fangs are set.

4This family has existed for millions of years. The jaws are more primitive than the jaws of most other spiders. They move up and down, not side to side. The fangs therefore stab downward into a victim. Mygalomorphs also have sensory parts near the mouth called pedipalps. Prey is seized with the pedipalps. Those parts then draw the prey toward the fangs and the mouth. A few extra facts stand out. A Goliath bird-eating spider has forty-eight knees, because each leg has six joints. Hunters in South America go after these spiders. They may keep them as pets, or they may eat them. A bite on a human is not deadly. Swelling follows, and so does pain. A wasp sting feels similar. A bee sting does too. A map of the range shows Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, French Guiana, and Brazil in South America. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean border that region. South American rainforests have hot, steamy, swampy sections. That is where these spiders live. Rainforests cover only about 6 to 7 percent of Earth. This biome still holds more than half of the world's plant and animal species, including many tropical spiders.

5Goliaths are active at night. Daylight hours are spent resting in the burrow. A night trip rarely goes more than a few feet from home. They live alone, except when they guard young or search for a mate. These spiders are skilled hunters. Crickets are prey. Frogs, beetles, and bats are prey too. Mice and other small animals can be prey as well. A small bird is eaten at times. Birds are not a usual meal, though. Home is an underground burrow, or a space under rocks. Unlike many spiders, they do not spin webs. They do spin silk. The silk may line the burrow. It may also form a mat placed on purpose at the entrance. A mouse or another small animal crawls past. Its steps shake the silk mat. Sensitive hairs on the spider read those shakes. The spider rushes out and makes the kill. Fangs are part of every spider, tarantulas included. Fangs on an extra-large Goliath reach nearly an inch. That is about half a human thumb. When prey comes close, the spider pounces. The legs grab the animal. The fangs inject venom. A toxin in that venom attacks the prey's nervous system. The prey is paralyzed and killed. The spider often drags the meal back to the burrow, or to some other safe spot, before eating.

6The mouth is a short opening shaped like a straw. It can only suck, so food must be liquid. Solid food cannot be eaten. Openings near the fangs spray strong digestive juices. The spray lands on tissue of an animal already bitten and paralyzed. Those juices break the tissue down. Give a large tarantula about thirty-six hours with a mouse. Hair and bones are what remain, heaped in a small pile. It breaks down the tissue and sucks up the liquid that remains. A hunting scene shows a Goliath spider attacking prey. These spiders are very aggressive hunters. Defense uses more than venom-filled fangs. A Goliath may rear up on its hind legs so it looks more threatening. It may also make a loud hiss by rubbing leg hairs together. That behavior is called stridulation. Stiff hairs can be shot in a cloud at an attacker. Tiny hooks, or barbs, cover those hairs. The barbs can enter the eyes and the throat of a predator. The irritation that follows is severe. Tiny hairs often end up all over the faces of scientists who study these spiders. The hairs sting the eyes, the skin, and the throat.

7Even a spider this large has enemies. A hawk may eat one. An owl may too. So may a skunk or a snake. One of the deadliest enemies is an insect called a spider wasp, or a tarantula hawk. A female wasp stings a tarantula when she finds one. Paralysis follows the sting. Death does not. The wasp digs a hole, puts the spider inside, and lays an egg on the abdomen. Hatching comes, and the larva bores a tiny hole into the abdomen. It crawls in and begins to feed. Organs are saved for last, so the Goliath stays alive as long as possible. One picture shows a Goliath spider raised in a defensive pose. A second picture shows a spider wasp dragging a smaller tarantula toward that tarantula's burrow. Pushing away the old skin is how a tarantula from Honduras finishes a molt. Molting for a Goliath tarantula follows a very similar pattern. Tarantulas molt when they outgrow the harder outer covering, called an exoskeleton. They leave the old skin behind. A new exoskeleton hardens underneath. During a molt, a Goliath is at its weakest. Predators are most dangerous then. A year brings one molt for an adult, or sometimes two.

8Spiderlings, the young spiders, molt more often because they grow quickly. Like many other spiders, Goliath tarantulas can regrow a lost or damaged limb. That skill helps if a predator grabs a leg. Off comes the leg. Escape follows, with seven legs left. The missing leg can grow back at the next molt. Timing matters. The new leg may be weaker than the others. The spider may be a little clumsier than before. Claws, sensory organs, and spinnerets can regrow too. Legs on a female Goliath are a bit shorter than legs on a male. Their bodies are larger. Females also live much longer. Life in captivity has stretched past twenty-five years for some females. Males live fewer than ten years. Scientists still do not fully know why, but females often kill males during mating. Mating is followed by egg-laying. About fifty eggs go into a sac made of silk. Her burrow is where the sac is kept. Waiting to hatch does not stop her hunting trips. The sac goes along. Guard duty lasts until hatching. That wait is about six to seven weeks. A few weeks of her watch follow. The first molt ends that watch. Then they are on their own.

9Blue and black are the real colors of the young. Color changes as they grow and molt. Goliaths have existed for millions of years. In all that time, they have not changed much. Sheer size has fascinated local people, scientists, and spider fans. Learning continues on two fronts. One is how these spiders regrow limbs. Another question is the effect of Goliath venom on a prey animal's nervous system. The idea of one crawling up an arm might be terrifying. Even so, Goliath spiders, like every living thing, have an important place in the living community around them. Rodent numbers stay in bounds partly because of them. Insect numbers do too, along with other species. A number of predators, in turn, feed on these spiders. Studying Goliath spiders, and other rainforest life, shows how species depend on one another. It also shows why they and their environment should be protected. A visitor in Goliath bird-eating spider country may want to watch these giants from a distance. They are huge and hairy, and they may be scary. Even so, the animal kingdom has few giants more interesting than these. A female Goliath can be seen in Guyana, South America. A word list explains the special terms.

10Arachnids belong with the arthropods. Two body segments are theirs, and so are eight legs. Spiders and scorpions are in that group. The nervous system gathers information from the senses and responds to it. It also affects thinking and behavior. Burrows are holes an animal digs in the ground to use as a home. To paralyze means to make one or more body parts unable to move. Digestive describes the action of breaking food down so the body can use it. To regenerate means to produce or create again. Silk is the name for strong threads a spider produces. A silkworm produces them too. Irritation can mean being annoyed, angry, or impatient. It can also mean discomfort in a body part. Venom is poison in fluid form. Some animals kill prey with it. Some defend themselves with it too. It is usually delivered by a bite or a sting. To molt is to drop an outer covering. The covering might be skin. It might be hair or feathers. A shell is possible too. A fresh layer then takes its place. Vibrations are small, rapid trembles. They may run forward and back. They may run from side to side. Vulnerable means able to be hurt easily.

83. The Muslim Commander Who Won Back Jerusalem

1A map of the Middle East from 1137 to 1193 marks the Caspian Sea and the Tigris River. Aleppo and the Euphrates River are shown. So are Tikrit and the Mediterranean Sea. Baalbek, Damascus, and Baghdad appear. Hattin, Jaffa, and Jerusalem appear. The Persian Gulf, the Arabian Desert, and Cairo appear, along with the Syrian Desert and the Red Sea. Asia, Europe, Egypt, and Africa are labeled. Countries of the Middle East today include Turkey and Cyprus. They include Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq. They include Iran, Israel, and Palestine. They include Jordan and Egypt. They include Sudan, Libya, and Saudi Arabia. They include Yemen, Oman, and Qatar. Kuwait is included. So is the country called the United Arab Emirates. Sections ahead cover his world, his youth, command, fights with the Crusaders, a formidable opponent, the return to Damascus, honor as a leader, and a word list. Jerusalem ranks among the oldest cities on earth. Yusuf was the boy's name. Home was the Middle East, close to nine centuries ago. Culture and history were abundant in that region. He grew into a Muslim commander whose fame may top every other. The name he carries is Salah al-Din. Three major religions were born in that complex region: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Followers share Jerusalem. Sacred buildings stand there, and so do other holy places. Passions about the region run deep. Shared heritage made many empires covet the city. Nearly forty years before his birth, in 1099, Christians from western Europe conquered Jerusalem. They were known as Franks. Muslim governance had lasted four hundred years.

2Safety was promised by a Christian leader, both to residents who were Muslim and to residents who were Jewish. Muslims, earlier, had shielded Jews and Christians. Crusaders refused the order. Thousands were slaughtered. Years afterward he was determined to take Jerusalem back for Muslims. He was born in 1137, or else in 1138. The family was Muslim. Tikrit, in Mesopotamia, was the place, a long way from Jerusalem. Mesopotamia today is mostly Iraq, plus parts of Syria, of Turkey, and of Iran. His father was a wealthy chief whose ethnicity was Kurdish. The family left Tikrit while he was an infant and moved west to Aleppo, part of a Turkic empire under Sultan Zengi. Soon the father was serving Zengi. After a few years the family shifted to Baalbek. Damascus came next. School at a mosque began by age seven. Studies took in science and math. Poetry and philosophy were included. So were religion and the history and culture of Muslims. Interests leaned toward the mind more than toward armies. He learned his religion. Islam's five pillars guided him. They are faith, prayer, fasting, gifts to the poor, and a sacred journey. Muslim society stressed a spiritual life, a personal link with God, called Allah in Arabic, and cleaning the life inside a person. Faith was not something worn only on the surface. It was a reality people lived. Justice showed in it. Mercy showed in it, and so did nobility. Love showed in it, and so did generosity. Humility showed in it too. The pillars can be listed.

3Faith is a spoken declaration. Muslims say Allah alone is God. They say Muhammad carries his message. Prayer means facing Mecca five times daily, at dawn, at noon, in the afternoon, in the evening, and at night. During Ramadan, the holy month, fasting bars food and drink from dawn until dusk. Giving alms makes it a duty to share part of what one earns with people who lack enough. A pilgrimage, when a person is able, is a single trip to Mecca during a life. Life changed after Zengi died in 1146. His son Nur al-Din took control of part of the kingdom. The father of Salah al-Din became governor of Damascus. An uncle, Shirkuh, rose to general in the army. Army service under Nur al-Din began at age fourteen. A few years later the young man became the sultan's chief aide. Nur al-Din was the model. Rich and powerful, the sultan still lived simply and honorably, spending wealth for his people's benefit. Every man, he believed, was equal. Fairness and generosity marked his rule. The same kind of man was the vow. Salah al-Din works as a nickname given to honor him. Its sense is a person who honors the faith. Western writers sometimes cut it down to Saladin. On his orders, a citadel carrying his name rose in Cairo, Egypt. Work ran from 1176 to 1184. The aim was a shield against the Crusaders. Learning continued, and military leadership grew. In his late twenties, several expeditions took him to Egypt under Uncle Shirkuh. The aim was to keep Egypt from Frankish control.

4Political turmoil gripped Egypt. Shawar, the ruler, was also called a vizier. He fought on the Crusader side against the Turks. Later he changed sides and fought with Muslims, against those same Crusaders. After Shirkuh's forces drove the Franks out again and again, Shirkuh decided to take Egypt. The vizier planned an assassination. Egypt's religious leader treated Shirkuh as the man who had set the land free, and handed him the vizier's post. Illness killed Shirkuh only nine weeks later. At thirty-one, in 1169, Salah al-Din became the new vizier and the commander of Egypt's troops. He then founded the Ayyubid dynasty, said eye-YOO-bid, named for his father Ayyub. Jerusalem and the land around it would be freed from Frankish control. That was the vow. A new Muslim era had started. Egypt's economy improved. Many schools were built and drew scholars from Europe and from Asia. Egypt grew into an even stronger center of learning. The old ruler's palace, with four thousand rooms, could have been his home. A small plain house was his choice. Most riches from the palace were given away. Flattery was not demanded. Loyalty came from character and from a gentle, generous nature. During the 1180s the Franks fought one another. They had taken Jerusalem eighty years before, and now they argued about rule of that holy city. Raymond of Tripoli respected Muslim ways. Raynald of Chatillon, said sha-tee-YOHN, was treacherous. Hostility toward Muslims marked him. Raynald came out on top along the routes where Muslim traders passed.

5A French knight, Guy of Lusignan, said loo-zee-NYON, gained Jerusalem's crown. Before Raynald's rise, Arab traders and Frankish traders had crossed the lands in peace. Open war was avoided, though clashes happened sporadically. Popes ordered the wars called Crusades. Each one was a military campaign. Catholics were urged into battle. The aims were capture of Jerusalem and of the region beside it, an end to Muslim rule, and a return of the holy city to Christendom. Fighters believed guilt for their sins would be wiped away. The opening Crusade was ordered in 1095 by Pope Urban II. Treaties with Salah al-Din were broken by Raynald. Muslim trade caravans were attacked. Coastal towns were raided. War against the Franks followed, with a vow to kill Raynald. He aimed to push the Franks from the region. He aimed to take the holy city back. He aimed to strengthen Islam. Early in July 1187, Tiberias was captured and its castle, belonging to Raymond of Tripoli, was besieged. Raymond urged giving the town up rather than fighting. Guy chose a rescue attempt, hoping to reach the castle in time. A Crusader force of twenty thousand was gathered under King Guy. Forward movement of those Crusaders crossed a hot, barren plain toward Tiberias and stopped when water ran out. Harassment from Salah al-Din's forces was constant. Morning brought the march onward. Hattin, a village, was ahead, and there his soldiers struck. Determination marked the Frankish fight. Defeat was still complete, with many killed on the field. King Guy was captured. Raynald was captured. Many of Guy's knights were captured.

6Many ordinary soldiers lived, but bondage was their fate. Raymond got away. Death still took him within a few weeks. After Hattin, Guy's life was spared, but the threat against Raynald was carried out. Men held in Raymond's castle at Tiberias were released, and the castle was taken. For the Franks, Hattin was a devastating defeat. A battle map for 1187 to 1192 marks the Mediterranean Sea and the Syrian Desert. Tyre, Acre, and the Sea of Galilee are shown. Hattin and Tiberias are shown. The Arabian Desert, Jerusalem, and the Dead Sea are shown. Siege was laid to Jerusalem. Two weeks after the siege began, the holy city was his. The date was October 2, 1187. Crusaders felt a crushing blow. In 1099 the Christian takeover had killed thousands of Muslims. His armies, by contrast, did not kill many Christians. Christian holy shrines were not desecrated, and followers could visit them. Prisoners who were Christian could purchase release. They had to pledge that Muslims would not be attacked. His brother arranged freedom for a thousand captives who had no money. All older prisoners were freed by Salah al-Din. Christians who were left received their lives, but they were forced into slavery. Jerusalem was back under Muslim control, the goal at last achieved. Tyre, on the coast, was next, the strongest Christian fortress still standing. If that fortress fell, his hope would be complete: one Muslim empire, at peace and joined together. The task was harder than the wish. Frankish refugees packed the fortress at Tyre.

7Christian resistance took its center there. He had delayed Tyre in favor of Jerusalem. The delay cost him. Defenses there were strengthened, and surrender was refused. Around the same time he freed King Guy. Guy took his supporters to Acre. Muslims held that city. A siege was begun. The effort was not taken seriously. Soldiers of the Muslim side had strengthened Acre. Frankish numbers were far smaller. Reinforcements from Europe, however, were on the way, and he had not accounted for them. By the time his army reached Acre, Christian numbers had grown so much that he could not dislodge them. A siege of 638 days followed. Muslims held the fortress. Guy's Christian supporters surrounded them. His own army, in turn, surrounded those supporters. News that Jerusalem had fallen was slow to reach Europe. When it arrived, Europe launched the Third Crusade. England's King Richard I was one of the kings who gathered armies. People often call him Richard the Lionheart. Their aim was to seize the holy city again. In the end he led the effort, backed by English and French armies and by others. Spring of 1191 brought the leaders. Philip Augustus of France arrived first. Richard the Lionheart arrived weeks later. Richard commanded with brilliance. Muslim soldiers holding Acre gave up. Barely a month had passed since his landing. Surrender terms required the Muslims inside to pay for release. Funds could not be raised quickly enough. The prisoners in Richard's hands numbered three thousand. He had them slaughtered. Pictures show both leaders: France's Philip Augustus, and the English king called the Lionheart.

8August 1191 saw Richard march Frankish troops about 130 kilometers, or 80 miles, south, determined to take Jaffa. Archers under Salah al-Din attacked without pause on the trek. The hope was that Richard's army would weaken. Richard kept his men strong. The Muslim army, instead, grew weaker. Long years of combat lay behind the Muslim troops. Europe's army was rested, and a brilliant commander led it. Jaffa and other coastal cities could not be kept from Richard. The Muslim army went to Jerusalem to fortify it. Troops of the Franks came after him when January 1192 arrived. Brutal weather stopped them short of the city, and they turned back. News then reached Richard. John, his brother, was home in England and was reaching for Richard's lands. Home was the decision. Before leaving he tried once more for Jerusalem. The story says he saw the city from outside, realized the army was too small, and turned away. A truce was negotiated by Salah al-Din's brother. The two leaders never actually met. Signed on September 2, 1192, the truce lasted three years. Terms were generous. Franks could keep the coast from Tyre to Jaffa. Everything else would stay Muslim land. Jerusalem was part of that. Christians could still visit holy places freely. The Third Crusade ended with that truce. Because he behaved with honor, the Christian world kept a lasting respect for him and a lasting gratitude. Builders raised a mausoleum over the tomb in 1193. Restoration came in 1898. After the truce he went home to Damascus.

9Only six months passed before death. The day was March 4, 1193. He was fifty-five, or possibly fifty-six. Money and lavish living had never mattered much. He gave everything away, so no money remained for a proper burial. A son later built a mausoleum in Damascus and buried him there. Family rule over Egypt and the lands beside it lasted to 1250. Then a different group seized power. Jerusalem stayed under Muslim rule up to the First World War. Today Damascus, in Syria's south, has a statue of him mounted on a horse. Large parts of the Muslim world revered him, and the reverence continues. Union was one cause. Winning Jerusalem back for Islam was the other. Christians had lost the city to him. Many still held him in high esteem. People of every religion saw a leader of noble character. Battle showed his fierceness. Friend and foe alike received his compassion. Europe and the Middle East regarded him highly for integrity, intellect, and military skill. Enemies received generosity from him. Everyone who met him came away respectful. As death neared, the oldest son heard where that greatness had come from. He had won men's hearts by gentleness and by kindness. An example of honorable leadership was set in his lifetime, and the example continues today. Life dates include these. Birth in Tikrit, Mesopotamia, is 1137 or 1138. In 1174 Nur al-Din dies, and an effort begins to unite the Muslim states. Service under Nur al-Din, ruler in Syria, runs from 1152 to 1169.

10Success in uniting those states comes in 1185. Rule of Egypt, and command of Egypt's Syrian troops, begins in 1169. Jerusalem is recaptured on October 2, 1187, after a battle of two weeks. The Battle of Hattin is July 4, 1187. The Third Crusade begins in 1189. The Battle of Jaffa ends on August 4, 1192. The battle at Acre ends on July 12, 1191. The truce with Richard the Lionheart is September 2, 1192. Death in Damascus is March 4, 1193. Being fair, honest, and moral is integrity. Supported or recommended is what advocated means. Related to serious study or to logical thought, or scholarly, is what intellectual means. Antagonistic describes a hard dislike. It can also mean opposition, or hostility, aimed at a person or at a group. A mausoleum may be one large tomb. It may instead be a building that holds several tombs. A place is besieged when armed forces ring it, hoping to attack or to take it. Pilgrimage means travel toward a place that is sacred or otherwise special. A shrine is one example. Disrespected, damaged, or destroyed, when the target is sacred or respected, is what desecrated means. Reinforcements are added supplies, or added people, sent so a military force grows stronger. Belonging to a people who share cultural heritage or nationality, marked by customs, traits, language, and shared history, is ethnicity. Sporadically means now and then, without a steady pattern, or with gaps that come by chance. Bothered or annoyed without stop, often by pressure or fear, is what harassed means.

84. The Mystery of the Missing Honeybees

1Contents. Who Took the Strawberries? Busy Bees. Gone from the Hives. On the Case. Only One Crop. Bees on Trucks. Ways to Help the Bees. Words to Know. A picture can show a healthy honeybee colony moving into a new hive. Who Took the Strawberries? Think of your favorite fruit. Now imagine a world where that fruit is extremely rare. Many other fruits, nuts, vegetables, and flowers might be just as rare. They might not exist at all. That is the world people would have without honeybees. Honeybees do more than make honey. Plant blossoms get pollinated by them. One in three bites of the food people enjoy comes from honeybees' hard labor. Honeybee numbers then started falling fast in 2007. Scientists have been puzzled by the cause for years. The problem slowed over time. What set it off at the start is still a mystery. Work to help save honeybees is still going on today. Busy Bees. Honeybees live in colonies. A colony is a busy place. Each bee performs a specialized task. Every bee in a colony needs the other bees. They must work together to keep the hive humming. Outside the colony, a lone honeybee is not likely to survive for more than twenty-four hours. Activity outside the hive has a single purpose. The bees look for flowers in bloom. They collect pollen from those flowers for food. They collect nectar to make honey. In one day, bees from one healthy hive can visit more than 100,000 flowers. While they visit, they perform one of the most critical processes in nature. That process is pollination. When a bee brushes against the anthers inside a flower, pollen grains stick to the bee's body. Other flowers receive that pollen on their pistils.

2The bee carries it from blossom to blossom. Pollination is this continuing move of pollen from anthers onto pistils. Pollination leads to fertilization. Fertilization will eventually result in seed formation. A diagram can label anthers, pollen, and a pistil while a bee pollinates a flower. Without pollination, plants do not reproduce. They eventually die off without being replaced. That loss is a serious problem for animals that rely on those plants for food. Gone from the Hives. The problem of disappearing honeybees became clear in October 2006. One of his Florida apiaries was the place an American commercial beekeeper came to. He had come to retrieve four hundred hives. Only three weeks earlier, the hives had looked busy. They had appeared healthy. Food, baby bees, and a few queens were all that remained inside. The beekeeper looked around. He expected piles of dead insects on the ground. The twenty million missing bees had left no trace. A picture can show a frame from a honeybee colony before the bees vanished and after they vanished. This beekeeper's experience was not unique. News of further losses started to appear across the United States. They surfaced across Europe, China, and other regions. The numbers were shocking. During the winter of 2006 to 2007, a huge share of colonies vanished. The United States had an estimated 2.4 million bee colonies. Roughly 750,000 of them were gone. On average, United States beekeepers lost 38 percent of their colonies. The largest known disappearance came in 2008. It happened in the almond tree groves of California. Two billion bees vanished there. Farmers and beekeepers faced an emerging crisis. They were desperate for science to shed light on the mystery. On the Case.

3The name scientists gave the problem was colony collapse disorder. They shortened the name to CCD. They began documenting its symptoms. CCD happens in a matter of weeks. Most of the occupants of a hive that seems healthy suddenly vanish. Few dead bees from the colony can be found. Sometimes none can be found. Only the queen and the very young bees stay behind. Those members would normally never be left alone by the rest of the bees. Once the symptoms were identified, the real detective work began. Scientists from around the country set out to find the cause. They also hoped to propose a solution. CCD scientists surveyed beekeepers. They collected samples of wax. They collected pollen. They collected live bees and dead bees when those bees could be found. When scientists dissected the bees, they found multiple diseases. The diseases suggested that the bees had compromised immune systems. Scientists then looked at germs already known to harm a bee's immune system. They found fungal bacteria that made it difficult for bees to eat. The bees were left too weak to forage. Scientists also detected a virus in a large number of CCD hives. It was a variation of a well-known fatal pathogen. The pathogen is called acute bee paralysis virus, or ABPV. Efforts to pinpoint a single germ as the root cause led nowhere. Everything the scientists had examined seemed to be a result of CCD. It did not seem to be the cause. The scientists next turned to several parasites. One mite has an ominous name, Varroa destructor. People also call it the vampire mite. It clings to adult bees. It sucks their blood. It leaves open wounds. Those wounds make the bees susceptible to infection.

4A picture can show a scientist taking samples from a hive with CCD. A chart can show average yearly hive loss by state for 2020 to 2021. The scale marks include 100 percent, 70 percent, 60 percent, 50 percent, 40 percent, and 30 percent. The source of the chart is the Bee Informed Partnership. Another parasite is called Nosema apis. It has an equally gruesome effect on honeybee health. This parasite produces spores. The spores infect the bees' intestines. They essentially eat the bee from the inside out. These parasites had been observed in hives before CCD. Whatever was triggering CCD seemed to come from another source. Only One Crop. Bees and hives were not the only place researchers decided to look. Their next look was at the ways farming itself had changed. Years ago, most farms were small. Families ran them. They grew and harvested a variety of crops. Today, many farms are massive corporate operations. They practice monoculture. Monoculture means a farm grows only one crop, for example wheat, corn, or soybeans. Monoculture is simple for farmers. It is efficient. It is not good for bees. Growing a single crop produces a single blooming season. Once those flowers fade, bees in that area have no source of pollen. They have no source of nectar. Bees must also face chemical pesticides. The chemicals are meant to rid fields of other insects that might destroy a whole harvest. Pesticides used correctly can save crops. They can also spell trouble for bees. Bees use their bodies to filter toxins out of the honey they produce. Farmers find it challenging to choose chemicals that kill harmful insects. They want those chemicals to leave beneficial insects alone. In the United States, farmers try to spray when plants are not blooming.

5They hope to keep bees safe. Even with these precautions, scientists still found pesticides in samples from hives with CCD. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, a huge amount of chemicals is used on crops each year. The amount is more than a billion pounds. Scientists have long known how toxic many pesticides are to bees. A new class of pesticides worries some scientists in particular. The chemicals are called neonicotinoids, or neonics. These pesticides are systemic. Plant seeds are treated with the chemicals. The chemicals then spread to every part of the plant as it grows. A single neonics treatment lasts a long time. It kills various crop pests, as it should. Researchers discovered what looked like an unintended consequence. CCD rose rapidly where these treatments were used. Life without Birds and Bees. In 1958, Mao Zedong started the Great Sparrow Campaign. He was the founding father of the People's Republic of China. People across China killed hundreds of millions of sparrows. The sparrows ate grain. Zedong thought that grain could feed Chinese people instead. The birds also ate insects. Locusts ate the crops people needed once the sparrows were gone. Starvation hit as many as 45 million people. China turned to heavier pesticide use because of this. Parts of China now use so many chemicals that the bees have all disappeared. Farm workers must do the bees' job. Fruit trees get their pollen from cotton swabs held in workers' hands. They work bloom by bloom. Scientists wonder whether systemic pesticides weaken the bees' immune systems. A weaker system could let pathogens such as the paralysis virus take hold. The pesticides affect the nervous system.

6Learning might become harder for bees because of them. They might interfere with memory. They might interfere with navigation. That interference could explain why bees fail to return to the hive after foraging. These conclusions seem logical. The new pesticides arrived around the same time as CCD. Overlap in timing is not enough to show that the pesticides actually cause CCD. Recent research says otherwise. Researchers are becoming even more convinced that CCD does not have a single cause. It may result from a combination of factors. Bees on Trucks. Scientists kept exploring other factors that could contribute to CCD. One factor is a form of job stress. For 150 million years, bees have flown around the world. Bees and humans have a very different relationship now than they did 10,000 years ago. Humans once foraged for food that was pollinated naturally. They later used bees for monoculture farming. People can control where honeybees work. They can control when the bees work. A note from long ago sits beside modern trucks. Rafts on the Nile River carried beehives for the ancient Egyptians. They followed the bloom. Today, trucks transport hives all over the country. Honeybees are excellent pollinators. Moving them into a field while crops are blooming helps farmers ensure a plentiful harvest. Today in the United States, semi-trailer trucks carry hives from one farm to another. They travel all over the country. The honeybees they haul pollinate 15 billion dollars' worth of food each year. That figure is for the United States alone. A highway trip for a million bees can sound odd. It helps production under modern monoculture farming. Farmers might need bees for one crop in February. They might need bees for another crop in a different part of the country in April.

7Almond trees, for example, depend completely on honeybees for pollination. Trucks bring bees to the groves in California around Valentine's Day. Work starts for them when almond blossoms open. For two weeks, those 600,000 acres are a bustling sight. They are a beautiful sight. That area is 242,811 hectares. More and more farmers asked for pollination services. Managed honeybee colonies declined rapidly. Their numbers became very low. Bees are loaded again after the blossoms fall. They are shipped to a new location. Transport is tough on the bees. They are shut inside trucks. They have no way to obtain flower nectar. Beekeepers feed them sugar water instead. That food is comparable to junk food. The stress of moving from one job to the next kills millions of bees. A chart can ask which crops need bees most. The crops are almond, apple, broccoli, blueberry, cherry, and cucumber. They also include watermelon, tangerine, lemon, cotton, peanut, and grape. The chart measures percent of harvest. Its scale runs from 0 to 100. Migrant bees face another problem. The problem is contagion. When bees arrive at their next pollination job, they meet millions of other migrant-worker bees. One estimate says these huge farms are where two-thirds of all bees in the United States meet. Bringing bees from different parts of the country spreads parasites. Bees from other parts of the world do the same. Disease spreads at a rapid rate. Parasites and disease travel cross-country with the honeybees. In the United States, beekeepers have tried to fend off disease. They add antibiotics to the sugar water that the bees feed on while they travel. Using antibiotics as a preventive measure creates a problem of its own.

8Overuse of antibiotics may have weakened the honeybees. They may be less able to fight other diseases. They may be less able to resist the effects of pesticides. The drugs also kill beneficial bacteria. Those bacteria help the honeybees process food. An additional concern grows over time. Bacteria can build up resistance to antibiotics. The drugs then become ineffective. The hazards of migratory beekeeping are one more piece of the CCD puzzle. Every piece counts, as in any puzzle. CCD looked more and more like a complicated mix. The mix includes biological stresses. It includes chemical stresses. It includes physical stresses. Ways to Help the Bees. CCD is complex. An exact cause is still beyond what scientists can point to. They have yet to find a complete cure. They have improved prevention measures. They have discovered some promising treatments. CCD has therefore become less common as time has passed. The drop is not as large as scientists would like. More research will be needed before the case of the missing honeybees is fully solved. In the meantime, people can use the knowledge they already have. They can use available resources. They can foster environments that are friendly to bees. Those environments benefit plants. They benefit bees. They benefit people. Stronger Bees That Survived. In some places, bee species seem to be breeding into stronger strains. They seem to be evolving that way. The Africanized honeybee is one example. It is a hybrid of the European honeybee and the African honeybee. A lab in Brazil lost some of these bees in 1957 when they got out. They spread north.
