They reached the United States in 1990. People were horrified. European honeybees are less aggressive than Africanized bees.

9Rumors spread that they did not make honey. Rumors said they did not pollinate plants. In fact, they do both of those things. The bees are more defensive. They are also healthier. Some beekeepers began to welcome them. They saw the bees as nature's answer to CCD. Honeybees benefit from access to many kinds of plants. Honeybees can forage longer when many kinds of native wildflowers are available. A yard can become a sanctuary that people make for honeybees. A sanctuary can be full of blooming native plants. There, bees can reduce their contact with pesticides. They can thrive in a natural environment. Rooftop pollinator gardens are gaining popularity. Backyard gardens are gaining popularity too. They appear in many rural neighborhoods. They appear in many urban neighborhoods. The bees visit parks and gardens. They produce honey. They pollinate native fruit trees and plants. What Lawns Do Not Offer. Colony collapse disease is in decline. Another bee crisis is on the rise. Many species of native bees are endangered. They are at risk of extinction. Manicured lawns have contributed to the decline of wild bees. Some bees can survive only if particular plants are present. There are fewer native plants now. There are more honeybees, which farmers bring in to pollinate crops. Wild bees are having trouble finding food. They are having trouble finding shelter. Anyone with a bit of outdoor space can help local bees. They can keep the kinds of plants the bees need. Small kinds of help are possible even for commercial farmers who grow one crop. They can help without sacrificing a productive harvest. They can set aside a small portion of their land for native plants. Those plants would sustain bees all year.

10A couple of weeks of bloom each year would not be the only food. The native plants would help create a population of homegrown pollinators. Farmers could also investigate more organic means of pest control. Those methods would let them avoid toxic chemicals. Bees are small. They are still important contributors to the health of many other species. Humans are among those species. Taking action to protect bees helps the bees. It helps us as well. Words to Know. apiaries (n.) places where collections of hives are kept for raising bees. bustling (adj.) moving in a rushed, noisy manner. compromised (adj.) damaged or impaired in some way. contagion (n.) a sickness passed by direct or indirect contact, or the way that sickness spreads. demise (n.) the end or failure of something; death. disorder (n.) a physical or mental condition that is unhealthy or not normal. fertilization (n.) the joining of male and female cells so a new animal or plant can begin. forage (v.) to search for food or other supplies, or to gather them. gruesome (adj.) causing fear, shock, or disgust. migratory (adj.) describing a regular move from one habitat or region to another at set times of the year. onset (n.) the start of something. parasites (n.) plants or animals that grow on others or feed off them. pathogen (n.) a tiny living thing, such as a virus or a bacterium, that makes a creature sick. pesticides (n.) chemical or biological substances that kill harmful animals or plants. pollinate (v.) to put pollen in a flower in order to fertilize it. sanctuaries (n.) safe places. susceptible (adj.) easily affected or influenced; vulnerable. systemic (adj.) of, relating to, or affecting an entire system or an entire body.

85. The Pharaoh Who Ruled for Sixty-Six Years

1Queen Nefertari, first wife of Ramses II, appears in a colorful image. Ahead are a famous pharaoh, a royal surprise, growing up, the young warrior and king, battles, the close of the New Kingdom, the title Ramses the Great, and a word list. A colossal statue of him weighs 6.58 metric tons, or 7.25 tons. The British Museum holds it now. It was found first in his temple, the Ramesseum, at Thebes in Egypt. Power came during Egypt's golden age to the pharaoh whose name is written Ramses II and also Ramesses II. About five hundred years, from 1550 to 1080 bc, are called the New Kingdom. The Eighteenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth Dynasties rose and fell in that age. Inside the Nineteenth Dynasty, he was the king who came third. The reign sat near the middle of the period. About sixty-six years passed, from 1279 until 1213 bc. Length like that was astonishing. Most people then died before forty-five. Fame grew until he was among Egypt's best-known pharaohs, earning the title Ramses the Great. Nefertari, his first wife, is shown in color. The statue now in the British Museum weighs 6.58 metric tons, or 7.25 tons, and it once stood at the Ramesseum in Thebes. That long reign sat inside the New Kingdom, the age running from about 1550 until 1080 bc, when the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Nineteenth, and the Twentieth each rose and fell. He was that nineteenth line's third king. Most people then died before forty-five, so the length of his rule astonished people. Ramses the Great became his title.

2Birth was around 1303 bc. The father was Seti I, a military commander. The mother was Mut-Tuy, said MOOT TOO-ee. An older sister may have been named Tia. A younger sister may have been named Henutmire, said he-nuht-MEE-ray. Pharaoh was an unlikely future. The parents were not even royal. King Tutankhamun, pharaoh then, died with no heir. Ay, his vizier, briefly became pharaoh. Horemheb took Ay's place after only a few years. Horemheb had commanded Tutankhamun's army. The grandfather, a general called Paramessu, had served in that army beside Horemheb. As pharaoh, Horemheb named Paramessu heir. Several years later Paramessu took the throne. He renamed himself Ramses. The family became royalty, starting the line called the Nineteenth Dynasty. Grandfather likely became ruler near the boy's tenth birthday. A few years after that, Seti I reached the throne, and the son stood next. A map of the reign, 1279 to 1213 bc, marks the Orontes River and Kadesh. It marks the Mediterranean Sea, Pi-Ramesse, and the delta of the Nile. The Nile itself, Abydos, Karnak, and Thebes are shown. So are the Ramesseum, the Red Sea, the Egyptian Empire, Abu Simbel, the Hittite Empire, and Nubia. Early life is poorly known. Artwork and carvings in buildings he later raised supply what is known. Home was probably in the family's house in the Nile delta. Lessons would have included reading and writing. Mathematics would have been taught. Science would have been taught. Geography, history, and medicine would have been taught as well. He would have learned from texts called the Books of Instruction.

3Those texts taught children how to live well. Later he may have entered the Prince's School, for children of royalty, of nobles, and of officials. He was named successor to Seti I and made crown prince while still young. Much of the schooling was training beside his father at a pharaoh's work. Someday the army would be his to lead in battle. Strength and endurance had to be built, likely from early childhood. Challenges meant to ready him for fighting included catching bulls with rope and mounting horses that were still wild. At Abydos, carved pictures in Seti I's temple show two scenes. One scene gives a gift to Amun, a god. The other is the prince roping a bull. A captain's title in the army came early, perhaps in name only. Titles and authority given young prepared the nation for his later rule. As a teenager he counted as an adult in many ways. Military campaigns with his father taught diplomacy and war, preparation for being pharaoh. He kept his own household. Marriage came too, probably at only fifteen. Nefertari was the first wife and the favorite. A rich tomb built for her shows a deeper care than he gave the rest. Words cut there dedicate the tomb to Nefertari, called the chief queen, the woman for whom sunlight shines. Many wives were common for rulers. He was no exception. Historians think eight or more royal wives came over the decades, plus several minor wives. Nefertari stayed chief wife until she died. At least five children were theirs.

4Amen-her-khepeshef was the oldest son and the heir. Say the name as ah-muhn, then hair, then KE-pe-shef. Thirteen years was the length of Seti I's rule. Ramses was probably co-ruler in the final years. Either way, his role in that rule was important. Military campaigns were his charge. Courage in war became his reputation. One campaign is shown in artwork at the Beit el-Wali temple, said BAYT EL WAH-lee, in southern Egypt, then called Nubia. He charges in a chariot. Two oldest sons follow in smaller chariots: Amen-her-khepeshef and Khaemwaset, said kahm-WAH-set. Historians place the fight during a Nubian rebellion. Nubia lay south of Egypt. Gold was there, and other riches too. Control of it often set Egyptians and Nubians against each other. Kings in Egyptian art are usually drawn larger than everyone else, so viewers see who is in charge. Seti I died when Ramses was about twenty-five. The son became pharaoh, leader of the military, of religion, and of justice. Because a pharaoh led religion as well as politics, the reign opened with a year of festivals and coronation ceremonies. Four new names joined his birth name. Symbols showed their religious weight. The Horus name was Kanakht Merymaat. Horus, shown as a falcon, rests above the palace. Kingship was the domain of that god. The Nebty name was Mekkemetwafkhasut. A cobra stood for Lower Egypt and a vulture for Upper Egypt. With the palace, Nebty stood for the goddesses of both lands. The Golden Horus name was Userrenput-aanehktu. A bee meant Lower Egypt and grass meant Upper Egypt.

5Horus on gold meant the king's life would not end. The prenomen was Usermaatre-setepenre. It stood for rule over both Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt. New names, Egyptians believed, showed the gods' protection and showed that the pharaoh himself was divine. Early on, he restarted architectural jobs his father had ordered. Stoneworkers and artisans had been told by Seti I to raise a huge religious hall at Karnak. Columns numbered 134, each at least 21 meters, or 69 feet, high. Walls received slow, careful raised relief, also called bas-relief. Background is cut away so the pictures stand up. Ramses soon ordered a faster method, sunk relief. Pictures are cut straight into the stone instead of by clearing the background. Temple building moved at double the old rate. No other ancient Egyptian pharaoh raised more temples. Visitors look tiny beside the columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall. Floor space of the hall is 5,000 square meters. That is 53,820 square feet. The Ramesseum was meant to honor him and to keep his memory alive forever. A temple for Nefertari was cut into a solid mountain of rock. Important building filled his life. The mortuary temple called the Ramesseum, at Thebes, is among the most impressive works. Another is the lovely temple raised at Abu Simbel for Nefertari, whom he loved. A new capital was ordered, replacing Memphis, capital in the Old Kingdom from 2649 to 2150 bc, and replacing Thebes. During New Kingdom Egypt, from 1550 to 1070 bc, Thebes was the capital and the center of religion.

6The city was named Pi-Ramesse, loosely translated Ramsesopolis. It sat in Egypt's far north and covered 18 square kilometers, or 7 square miles. From there he could watch the Hittites more closely. Those long-standing enemies lived eastward. The region is the one now called Syria. Before the Nineteenth Dynasty, Hittite forces east of Egypt had seized some Egyptian territory. Seti I had started to rebuild Egyptian power and planned to retake land. When the new king took the throne, the Hittites tested his mettle. They attacked and took Kadesh back. The city mattered because the main route for trade ran there, following the Orontes River. Early on, Ramses defeated those Hittite forces. Many small provinces came back, including some his father had failed to regain. During the reign's fifth year he led a huge force toward Kadesh, hoping to take it back. Soldiers numbered about 20,000. Chariots numbered about 2,000. That battle became one of the reign's most famous events. The Hittite attack was the earliest recorded military ambush. Their force included 2,500 chariots. Together the sides fielded about 4,500 chariots. No chariot battle on record has been larger. The story was carved on pylons and on temple walls across Egypt and Nubia. The Egyptian telling is therefore among the best-documented events of ancient Egypt. Art shows him larger than every other figure, clearly beating the enemy. His account goes further and suggests he faced the enemy alone. Some Kadesh scenes are unusual. Most battle art shows a pharaoh's enemies collapsing in fear or in death. These pictures surround him with a powerful Hittite army of soldiers, weapons, horses, and chariots.

7The Hittites look like equal adversaries. Why use so different a style? Because the result was not the victory he wanted believed. He was nearly killed. Neither side could claim a clean win. Egypt's result was closer to a draw. Records from both Egypt and the Hittites, pieced together, make the true story more complex than his official version. Scholars think the army split while nearing the city. His group was the lead division, known as the Army of Amun. Another division trailed by about one day's march. Another, experts think, swung around to strike the city from the far side. Spies likely convinced him the Hittites were many miles off. He soon learned they were dangerously near and preparing to attack. Word went to the other divisions. The ambush overran the reinforcements that might have reached him. The Hittites then charged his much smaller force. His own telling says he held the enemy off by himself while the rest of the army fled. Other records say an elite division called the Ne'arin arrived just in time and saved him. Heavy losses on both sides brought a truce. He pulled his forces back to Egypt. A detail from battle art, also using the name Qadesh, shows Hittites surrounding him. Across the following year he ordered writings cut in stone. Bulletins numbered at least seven. Poems numbered eight. Every one of them made him the hero. Some experts say this was history's first known propaganda campaign. Hostilities did not end.

8About fifteen years later the nations again neared war. Battle so far from home was hard, so talk looked wiser than fighting. During year twenty-one of the reign, he and the Hittite king settled on a treaty of peace. Two copies survive. One uses Egyptian hieroglyphs. The other uses Akkadian, the Hittite language. An elite unit called the Ne'arin reached him in time, other records say, after he had sent for the rest of his army. Both sides lost heavily, then agreed to stop fighting, and he went back to Egypt. Art of the fight, sometimes named Qadesh, shows Hittites all around him. Bulletins followed, seven or more of them. So did eight poems. Each one cast him as the hero. Some experts call that the earliest propaganda campaign anyone knows. About fifteen years later war nearly returned. Distance made talk wiser. In the reign's twenty-first year the two kings made peace. One treaty text uses Egyptian hieroglyphs. The other uses Akkadian. Egypt gave up any right to Kadesh and to the land around it. War ended, and a clear boundary stood between the nations. Clauses of a kind still used in modern peace treaties were included. One provided alliance if foreigners attacked. Another was a mutual promise not to strike each other's territory. Visitors can see a copy hanging inside the building where the United Nations General Assembly meets. A Hittite princess became his wife thirteen years afterward, and the marriage sealed the deal. Rule lasted until 1213 bc, sixty-six or sixty-seven years, and ended in natural death at age ninety-one.

9Arthritis, dental trouble, and arterial disease marked his last years and may have helped cause death. Amen-her-khepeshef, oldest son and first heir, died before him. So did the eleven sons who stood next. Merneptah, the thirteenth son, became pharaoh and ruled for a decade. Decline of the Nineteenth Dynasty had already begun. Control of Nubia was lost. Magnificent temples were left to desert sand. Only 150 years after the death, the New Kingdom ended. Fame in ancient Egypt was so great that at least nine later pharaohs took his name. Ramses the Great is the modern title, partly from military success. Territories lost under earlier pharaohs were taken back, and Egypt controlled more land than ever. Monuments and temples beyond any other pharaoh's count were his doing. People still admire them and study them. Statues, elaborate pictures, and hieroglyphs hand historians a deep store of facts. Ancient Egyptian life is what those facts describe. From a modern view, those are the real grounds of his greatness. Art, architecture, and historical records were left behind, and they let us understand the people and the culture of his time more clearly. At Abu Simbel, two temples are cut from sandstone. The bigger one's doorway has giant sculptures of him on both sides. Dates on a timeline include these. Birth is 1303 bc. A scale mark sits at 1310 bc. Ramses I becomes pharaoh in 1298 bc. Seti I becomes pharaoh in 1291 bc. Ramses II becomes pharaoh in 1279 bc, and work on the Ramesseum starts around then. Marriage to his first two wives is 1289 bc.

10A Nubian revolt is put down in 1281 bc, with his two oldest sons taken into battle. The fight at Kadesh is 1274 bc. The Ramesseum is finished in 1259 bc. Work at Abu Simbel begins around 1264 bc. Nefertari dies in 1252 bc. Peace with the Hittites is 1258 bc. In 1244 bc Isetnofret, the second wife, dies. He marries a first Hittite princess, and Abu Simbel is finished around then. A second Hittite princess is married in 1231 bc. Death at age ninety-one is 1213 bc. A scale mark sits at 1210 bc. Campaigns are planned strings of actions aimed at chosen goals. Pharaohs are the rulers of ancient Egypt. Propaganda is news, art, or other media that often uses false or stretched information to sway people. Diplomacy means the skill of bargaining. It is also the practice of that bargaining, carried on by people who speak for different countries. Pylons are towers of great height, or other structures that stand upright. Supports are a common use. A dynasty is a run of rulers who share a family. A successor follows another person in a job or in an elected post. Hieroglyphs are pictures and symbols that work as writing. Ancient Egypt is where they are best known. A truce is an agreement to stop fighting. A legacy is something passed from past to present. Vizier names an official of high rank. Ancient Egypt used the title. Some Muslim countries have used it too. Mortuary means related to burial.

86. The Prince from Pella Who Marched Across Asia

1A map of the empire at its peak in 323 bce also marks the route of exploration. Labels include Macedonia, the Caspian Sea, and the Black Sea. Taxila is marked. So are Asia Minor, the Hydaspes River, and Persia. Babylon, the Mediterranean Sea, and Alexandria appear. India, the Persian Gulf, and the Euphrates River appear. Egypt, the Arabian Sea, the Nile River, and the Red Sea appear as well. Sections ahead cover the beginning, years as a prince, the rise to king, conquest, a Persian view, the legacy, and a word list. Alexander III was born a prince. The time was more than twenty-three centuries ago. The city was Pella. Macedonia was the kingdom around it. Nations and kingdoms, near and far, would fall to him in a short life. Violent oppression marked the journey. Legend has rarely produced a leader so famous, or a conqueror so famous. Land and power were not his only drives. He deeply wanted to pass beyond anywhere people had traveled. Aristotle, among the most learned men of the age, was his teacher. New ideas appealed to Alexander. A thirst for knowledge pushed him farther, so he could learn more. The map's date is 323 bce, when the empire was at its largest, and it also traces where he explored. Macedonia and Egypt are on it, with Persia, India, Babylon, and Alexandria. Seas on it include the Black Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Mediterranean Sea, the Arabian Sea, and the Red Sea. Rivers include the Hydaspes, the Euphrates, and the Nile.

2Aristotle's teaching fed a hunger to learn, and that hunger pushed the marches. Birth was in 356 bce. Philip II, the ambitious father, had studied military strategy while captive as a young man in neighboring Greece. Strong armies there were his classroom. Home again, he seized Macedonia's throne from his nephew Amyntas. A superior, well-trained army secured his rule over Macedonia and the Greek states around it. Callisthenes, said kuh-LIS-thuh-neez, was a writer who recorded the life. Much of that writing vanished over time. Later authors kept pieces of the stories. Because so much finally rests on one source, the biases coloring it matter. Across more than two thousand years, a writer on Alexander's payroll cannot be treated as pure fact. Ask how enemies might have told the same events. Conquests and the costs of war were smoothed over. The writer did not always paint Alexander in the best light. Disagreement with Alexander ended in the writer's early death. Today a statue in Pella, Greece, shows Alexander on the horse Bucephalus. Olympias, the mother, was not born a Macedonian. She feared the throne might skip her son for that reason, and that her own place would vanish. She raised him to be king and would accept nothing less. Ambition from both parents passed to him. At twelve he showed a strong will. Philip refused to buy a superb horse that was also nervous. The name was Bucephalus, said byoo-SEF-uh-luhs. Alexander saw that the unbroken animal feared its own shadow. He took charge.

3Turning the head, by the reins, away from the shadow would calm it. He was sure of that. He leaped onto the back and rode off easily. The horse stayed his constant companion. Philip was often gone, taking control of other Greek lands. Experts received the job of educating and training the son for kingship. Greek youths learned riding and hunting first, so they could fight well. Sword, javelin, and bow joined those skills for success in brutal battle. Tests of manhood demanded two killings: a wild boar, and a man during battle. Alexander managed both. History, politics, and ethics were studied too. At thirteen, Aristotle was brought to Macedonia. The well-known Greek philosopher became the teacher. Intelligence and knowledge earned Aristotle respect. Literature, science, medicine, and philosophy caught Alexander's interest through him. A lifelong love of culture and of art began there. A statue of Aristotle stands at Stagira, Greece, his birthplace. In 340 bce Philip left for battle and made Alexander regent. At sixteen, during that absence, Alexander stopped a small revolution. Still in his teens, he commanded a section of troops in some of Philip's battles. Military skill was honed for kingship. Change came in 337 bce. Philip married a woman born in Macedonia, threatening Alexander's claim. Philip also began thinking about a larger empire. Persia was the strongest empire in Asia, and Greece counted it an enemy. Lands Greeks claimed had been seized by Darius I and by his son Xerxes, said ZURK-seez. That seizure sat more than a century in the past.

4Philip wanted some of those lands back. Growth of empire and of wealth, through an Asian conquest, was also his plan. Newly won Greek allies would help. Those allies formed the League of Corinth, which joined city-state armies to free Greek cities from Persian control. In 336 bce the feared birth happened. Philip's wife had a daughter. King Philip was assassinated before that year ended. The new wife and the baby were killed on Olympias's orders. Kingship arrived at age twenty. First he called for support from his father's army. Trust had been earned while he served under Philip. Persia, now ruled by Darius III, required a strong army. Philip's plan to rule Persia would be carried through. A map of Macedonia and the city-states marks the Black Sea, Macedonia, and Pella. The map treats Asia Minor as a piece of Persia's empire. The Aegean Sea, Delphi, Thebes, Corinth, and Athens appear. Some of the strongest capitals of Greek city-states are on that map. The father's army would not be enough. Membership in the League of Corinth brought support from most other Greek city-states. Leaders in Thebes and in other states had disliked Philip's growing power. More and more refused Alexander's ambitious plans. Revolution might end Macedonian control of Greece and block the move into Asia. He met opposition directly, determined not to lose Greece. Speech could persuade. Intimidation and force were also acceptable tools of control. Thebes and other League city-states began to oppose him. Territories around Macedonia did too.

5His army crushed the rebellion. Thebes was the warning he left for everyone else. Six thousand citizens were killed. Thirty thousand more were sold into slavery. The severity left no doubt. Merciless and ferocious methods would be used until every Greek city-state submitted. One year after becoming king, he was ready. New lands, new cultures, and the Persian Empire were the plan. At twenty he needed the army that had trusted him under Philip, because Darius III now ruled Persia. Greek city-states on the map include Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Delphi, with Pella in Macedonia. Thebes lost six thousand people to death and thirty thousand to sale as slaves when it resisted. A year after the crown was his, the march toward Persia could begin. Spring of 334 bce opened the march into Asia. Botanists, zoologists, and surveyors came along to study the lands ahead. Boats carried him along the Hellespont. That tight channel joins two seas, the Aegean and the one called Marmara. Landing in Asia Minor, now Turkey, he threw a spear into the ground. The claim was staked with dramatic flair, a tribute to warriors and heroes of earlier times. Soon the armies met at the Granicus River. Foot soldiers and riders filled both sides. A route map through Asia Minor shows the Black Sea and Macedonia. It shows the Sea of Marmara, Gordium, and the Hellespont. The Granicus River is marked. Asia Minor appears as part of the Persian Empire, with the Aegean Sea, Issus, and the Mediterranean Sea.

6That region, Turkey today, was the Persian Empire's northernmost part. Darius III stayed out of the fight. Historians say Persia's soldiers were less ready than Macedonia's, and no strong plan guided them. Speed and better weapons overwhelmed it. Victory followed. The fight probably lasted about an hour. An ax nearly killed Alexander. A companion from childhood is said to have saved him. After the cavalry, foot soldiers in a phalanx formation moved in against anyone still standing. Thousands of well-trained Greeks faced Persia. Masterful archers were there, with cavalry and infantry. A tight formation called a phalanx was used. Soldiers marched shoulder to shoulder in helmets and body armor, carrying shields, daggers, and spears. Vision and leadership from Alexander were what made the rest matter. Example was his method. He went ahead of the armies. If they lacked water, he lacked it too. If dead horses forced soldiers to walk, he walked. Weapons experts and engineers were employed. Strategies were communicated deftly. Speed and flexibility marked the fighting. Cities along the Aegean Sea were reclaimed. Fall of 333 bce brought Darius III and his army against Alexander at the Battle of Issus. Persia had the larger numbers. Infantry went in with cavalry on the flanks. The bloody fight still went to Alexander. Darius fled to Babylon and abandoned his army. The win was decisive. Rule of the Persian Empire was a step closer. An ancient mosaic shows the two men fighting in that battle. Next came a move south, to beat the Persian fleet by taking cities on the Mediterranean shore in Syria and in Phoenicia, Lebanon today.

7Refusal to surrender meant bloodshed. Tyre resisted seven months. Many of its citizens were killed before defeat. The coast brought them to Egypt during autumn of 332 bce. Persia's leader in that land gave up quickly. Greece and Macedonia respected Egypt's history as a civilization. Egyptian governors were appointed. Egyptian religion was encouraged. Weary of Persian rule and of many wars, Egypt welcomed him. Alexandria was founded where the Nile meets the Mediterranean. It was the first of twenty cities to carry his name. With the city underway, further Persian lands were the next goal. Departure from Egypt came in summer 331 bce. Babylon, in Mesopotamia, now Iraq, came next. Then he crossed the Euphrates, a river that runs toward the Persian Gulf. Darius, the old enemy, was near. After Issus, Darius rebuilt and prepared another meeting. October 331 bce brought the Battle of Gaugamela. Persia again had more soldiers. Even so, the Macedonian king, the officers with him, and the soldiers still crushed the Persian side. One thousand Macedonians died. Persian dead were far more numerous, about fifty thousand. Darius fled again. After Gaugamela, rule over Persia's empire sat nearer to his grasp. He hurried on through Asia. Before he could kill Darius, a local ruler named Bessus did it and made himself king. Focus shifted to Bessus. Capture came, then death, as punishment for murdering Darius. More land and more people fell under Alexander. The year 324 bce brought two marriages.

8One wife was a princess of the local land. The other was Stateira, whose father was Darius III. Many officers married Persian women. Persian ways entered his life. He dressed in Persian clothing. He expected low bows, the Persian form of honor. Not every Macedonian agreed. Men who had followed him across a decade were weary. Home was what they wanted. He wanted the empire pushed on, toward the east. During 327 bce he talked them into a region they named India. Afghanistan and Pakistan occupy that region today. Where local tribes resisted, the invasion left thousands dead. An arrow punctured his lung in one fight. The injury was severe, but he recovered. Soldiers burned the palace of Darius at Persepolis, in present-day Iran. Until Alexander destroyed it, the Persian Empire was among the widest super powers of the ancient world. Cities were razed on the eastward quest. Symbols of Zoroastrianism, the ancient religion of Iran, were destroyed. Deep respect for Persian culture later made him regret the destruction he had wreaked. Soldiers wrecked the tomb of Cyrus the Great, a famous Persian leader. Alexander afterward paid to repair it. Spring of 326 bce brought him to Taxila. Taxiles, the ruler, did not resist. Troops were given, and elephants, an important battle resource of the region. In return, Alexander was asked to fight Porus, an enemy who ruled nearby Indian lands. June found the army at the Hydaspes River, said hy-DAS-peez. Whether Alexander used elephants is unclear. Elephants of Porus did damage the Greeks, then panicked from the fight's intensity and retreated.

9Porus surrendered. It was the last big battle. Efforts to push farther east failed. Weary troops mutinied and persuaded him to turn toward home. Fever struck after he reached Babylon. Death came in June 323 bce. The body was taken to Alexandria, in Egypt, and placed in a golden casket. Honors followed there and in Greece. The reign lasted twelve years and eight months. Age at death was thirty-three. Brutality and widespread destruction were his. Armies under him killed a number estimated near 750,000. History has mostly smoothed over the horrific tactics and treated him as an excellent leader and commander. A shared vision unified followers. Battle was led with superb understanding. Greek cities under Persian rule were taken back. The empire then reached Egypt and a large share of central Asia, regions Europeans had never explored, let alone conquered. Generals of later ages copied him. Those generals killed Indigenous people and stole from their land. People he met were introduced to Greek culture. That prepared the way for later rulers who forced their own cultures and religions onto the conquered. Fifteen years of conquest brought no lost battle. Ambition without restraint, a turn toward violence, and genius in war combined. The result was a kind of conqueror new to the world. A conquest timeline runs from a mark at 360 bce to a mark at 320 bce. Birth in Macedonia is 356 bce. Aristotle becomes the teacher in 343 bce. Philip is killed in 336 bce, and Alexander becomes Macedonia's king.

10Bucephalus becomes his horse in 344 bce. A revolt on the eastern border of Macedonia is stopped in 340 bce. The advance into Persia and the win at the Battle of Granicus fall in 334 bce. Tyre is captured in 332 bce, then Egypt is invaded and welcomes him. Darius and the Persian army lose the Battle of Issus in 333 bce. Darius is killed in 330 bce. Darius and the Persians lose the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 bce. Conquest of central Asia continues in 327 bce, with a push into India. Porus loses the Battle of Hydaspes in 326 bce. Death in Babylon is 323 bce. Someone ambitious wants badly to succeed, or to reach a hard goal. Ships or other vehicles under one commander or owner form a fleet. Assassinated means slain by an attack that was planned, and politics is often the motive. Soldiers trained and equipped to fight on foot are infantry. People who study plants are botanists. A person seeking knowledge and truth about life, or studying philosophy, is a philosopher. Soldiers who fight from horseback, or troops who fight from armored vehicles, are cavalry. A regent reigns when the monarch cannot. A city-state is a city, or a built-up district, behaving as a country of its own. Surveyors measure land and name the physical features they find. Moral principles that guide behavior are ethics. Positioned at one side or at both sides is what flanked means.

87. The Researcher Who Won Two Science Prizes

1Ahead lie her early years, a long wait, arrival in Paris, two kinds of rays, public honors, darker days, work at the front, later years, gifts she left, and a word list. She is introduced as a trailblazer. Scientific instruments crowded the laboratory of Marie Curie. Some tools there were inventions of her husband, Pierre. Others came from Jacques, Pierre's brother. Few women worked as scientists then. Even so, research by one woman, and the discoveries that followed, altered the world. She departed her homeland for science and for math. A leading university was the place. Obstacle after obstacle seemed to stand in her path. She kept going. No woman before her had received a Nobel Prize. No other person has ever taken Nobel Prizes in two separate fields of science. That scientist was Marie Curie. The picture of that laboratory shows instruments packed into the room. Pierre built some of them. Jacques, the brother of Pierre, built others. Science was rarely a woman's work then. She still left home for math and for science at a major university. Barriers kept appearing. She did not quit. A Nobel Prize reached her ahead of any other woman. The prizes sit in two sciences, not in a single field. Nobody else has been honored that way. A photograph seats Marie Curie in the center, with her brother and her sisters. Left to right, the others are Zosia, Hela, Joseph, and Bronya. Birth came on November 7, 1867. The baby was Maria Sklodowska, later called Marie Curie.

2Warsaw, Poland, was the city. Childhood used the name Manya. Five children shared the family, and Manya was the youngest. Their mother had led a school as headmistress. She left that post when Manya arrived. Math and physics were the father's subjects at a high school for boys. Poland was not a country of its own in the year of her birth. Wars had ended in a division of the land in 1815. Russia held part. Prussia held part. Austria held part. Rule over the family's region belonged to the Russian Empire. Wiping out a Polish national identity was the empire's aim. Fear shaped Manya's childhood. Loyalty to Poland could put lives in danger. Speaking the Polish language could do the same. A family picture from the 1880s shows her beside her father, with Bronya and Hela. Teaching work ended for the father in 1873. Support for Polish independence was the cause. Money grew scarce. Boarders had to be taken in. Typhus, a deadly infection caused by bacteria, killed Zosia, the oldest sister, in 1876. Two years after that, the mother died. Manya was ten. What the father offered was care for the mind and care for the feelings. Classic literature was read aloud. Physics lessons used equipment from his old teaching post. Curiosity and brightness marked the child. Schoolwork was outstanding. Physics came easily, and math did too. Graduation from high school arrived in 1883, at age fifteen, with the top honors. Further schooling was the wish of Manya and of her sister Bronya.

3The University of Warsaw would not admit women. Leaving Poland was required, and money was short. Their answer was Warsaw's floating university. Teachers and thinkers from Poland offered it free, though the classes were illegal. Attics held some lessons. Basements held others. Europe's finest universities were far stronger. The classes still kept Manya up to date on new science. Both sisters aimed at the Sorbonne in Paris. Tuition money was missing. A bargain was struck. Earnings from Manya would pay for Bronya. After the degree, Bronya would repay the help. Five years of work as a tutor and as a governess followed. Spare hours went to math, to chemistry, to physics, to sociology, and to literature. That labor showed her the right path. Math and physics were it. Once Bronya's schooling was paid, Manya's turn arrived. Then and now, the Sorbonne ranks among the world's finest universities. Paris became her home in 1891. She was twenty-four. Enrollment at the Sorbonne came with a new name, Marie, the French form of Maria. Two years of hard study put her first in the class. The degree was a master's in physics. One year later, a second master's arrived, this time in math. Before the math degree was done, a commission asked her to study steel. The question was how different kinds of steel behave around magnets. Large equipment meant she needed a laboratory. Spring of 1894 brought an introduction. A colleague presented Pierre Curie, a professor of physics whose magnetism research had broken new ground.

4He directed the laboratory at a Paris school called the Municipal School. Industrial physics and chemistry were its subjects. Space in that lab was arranged for her. A photograph shows the newly married couple, Marie Sklodowska Curie beside Pierre Curie. The wedding itself was simple. Honeymoon travel was a bicycle trip. At the start they were only two scientists, each admiring the other's mind. Love grew from that respect. July 1895 was the marriage month. Research filled her days, yet she also earned a certificate for teaching. Young women were the students she hoped to teach in science. Once that research ended, a doctorate at the Sorbonne became the next aim. A daughter, Irene, was born to Marie and Pierre in 1897. Mothers of that era were expected to remain home with children. Marie stayed with her science. Pierre's father moved into the home and cared for Irene, so the couple could keep working. A topic was still needed for the doctoral study. Physics had just produced two major discoveries. Late in 1895, X-rays were found by Wilhelm Roentgen, a physicist from Germany. Early the next year, rays from the element uranium were found by Henri Becquerel, a physicist from France. Those rays were weaker than X-rays. Fascination with X-rays pulled many scientists into deep study. Marie chose the uranium rays instead. She wanted to know what those rays did to air. An electrometer was her tool. Air blasted by uranium rays carried electric currents almost too faint to notice, and she measured them.

5Becquerel's observations held up. Every form of uranium gave off electricity. A larger amount of uranium meant stronger rays. She formed a hypothesis and later proved it. The rays belonged to the structure of uranium itself. They were not produced by its physical condition. They were not produced by its chemical condition either. A new question followed. Was uranium alone in making air carry electricity more easily? Every element known at the time was tested. Thorium, she found, sent out rays as well. A new word, radioactivity, was hers. It names rays leaving the nucleus, the center of an atom. Tests continued on many materials. Pitchblende, a mineral that holds uranium, was one of them. The rays from it were stronger than the uranium inside could explain. A second radioactive element, still unknown, had to be in the pitchblende. That was her conclusion. Until then, Pierre Curie had studied crystals on his own. The year 1898 brought a change. As her work advanced, he paused his own project and joined the radioactivity study. Hunting a new element gripped them both. Long research produced two elements nobody had known. Polonium took its name from her homeland. Latin supplied radium's name, from that language's word meaning ray. Understanding in science shifted in a deep way because of what she learned about uranium rays. Atomic physics rests on that shift. Scientists then believed an atom could not be split into smaller pieces. Electrons were found by someone else around the same time.

6The person who showed that atoms hold a huge store of energy was Marie. Her research led toward machines such as the linear accelerator. A radioactive energy beam from that device is used to kill cancer cells. People in industry were fascinated. Radium produced light and also heat. New inventions seemed possible. Scientific breakthroughs seemed possible too. Pierre showed that living flesh could be harmed by radium's radioactivity. Treatment of cancer, and of other illnesses, became imaginable. Companies offered laboratory space. Raw materials and staff were offered too. Radioactive material was pulled from ore and used in medicine and in other work. Experiments on atoms confirmed her suspicion. Powerful energy sat inside atoms. Illness was common for Marie and Pierre during the research. Hard work might have been the cause. Radiation might have been the cause. Blame on radiation was an idea Marie rejected. Today it is known that radiation can sicken people and can kill. Years of close shared labor bound Marie and Pierre. June 1903 brought her Doctor of Science degree. Inside France, no woman had received a doctorate before her. Across Europe, no woman had received a doctorate in science before her. She had led much of the new physics work done with Pierre. A Nobel Prize, among the most honored awards on earth, nearly passed her by because she was a woman. The 1903 prize in physics was first aimed at Pierre Curie and at Henri Becquerel. A mathematician who sat on the nominating committee, and who championed women in science, warned Pierre.

7Leaving Marie off, Pierre answered, would be a grave injustice. Her name was added. December 1903 gave the prize jointly to her, to Pierre, and to Becquerel. Pioneering radiation work was the reason. No woman had won a Nobel Prize before. Fame around the world arrived at once. Pierre was promoted to professor at the Sorbonne. Pay was granted to Marie, and leadership of the laboratory as well. Attention and new duties gave her energy. Research and teaching continued. Explaining the discoveries to the public pleased her. A second daughter, Eve, arrived in 1904. Around then, the Sorbonne provided a fresh laboratory. That 1904 laboratory finally gave the Curies more room. Success was high when disaster came. Pierre crossed a street in 1906. A wagon pulled by a horse ran him down. Death was instant. Word of it traveled the world. Shock left Marie numb. In time she found the will to continue. His teaching post was offered to her. The post's title was Professor of General Physics. The school was the Sorbonne. No woman had been a professor there before. A modern laboratory, she hoped, would honor his memory. Publication of her textbook, A Treatise on Radioactivity, came in 1910. She set an international standard for how much radiation radium gives off. Scientists worldwide named the unit the Curie, recognizing what she had done. A life timeline runs this way. Birth in Warsaw, Poland, falls on November 7, 1867. High school graduation is 1883. The move to Paris is 1891.

8A physics master's is 1893. A math master's is 1894. Marriage to Pierre Curie is 1895. Study of Becquerel rays, and the birth of daughter Irene, fall in 1897. Discovery of polonium and radium is 1898. A physics doctorate and the Nobel Prize in Physics fall in 1903. Eve's birth is 1904. Pierre's death, and her rise as the Sorbonne's first female professor, fall in 1906. A Nobel Prize in Chemistry arrives in 1911. Portable X-ray machines enter her World War I work in 1914. The war ends in 1918, and the Radium Institute opens. Death comes on July 4, 1934. Late in 1910 she sought an empty physicist seat at the French Academy of Sciences. Edouard Branly was the only serious rival. His work had advanced wireless telegraphy. Supporters of Branly spread rumors about Marie that were false, hoping to shrink her chances. Defenders spoke for her. Branly still won the seat. A second Nobel Prize reached her in 1911, this time for chemistry. Radioactivity research was honored, along with finding radium and polonium. No scientist before her had two Nobel Prizes. No one else, even now, has won in two different sciences. On October 31, 1914, French soldiers cluster at a truck that carries X-ray gear. The equipment is hers, and it can move. During World War I those machines surely saved many wounded men. War began in the last part of July 1914. Days later, Germany entered France. Most of her staff left to fight.

9Supplies for research ran short. She searched for a way her science could serve the war. Portable X-ray machines, usable in the field, became her cause, so wounded soldiers could be treated. She poured herself into the project. Wealthy owners were persuaded to give cars. Twenty stations that could travel were set up. Two hundred fixed installations were set up as well. Coordinating help was not enough for her. She learned the X-ray equipment. She taught herself driving, so she could run the portable machines in person. A 1921 ship took her to New York. Daughters Irene and Eve toured the United States with her. She stands at the center of that group. After the war she worked without rest, and with success, to make the Sorbonne's Radium Institute a world-class place for radioactivity research. Chemistry's Nobel Prize reached Irene and her husband during 1935. Marie did not live to celebrate it. Extreme danger from radioactive substances is clear now. It was not clear in her lifetime. Death came on July 4, 1934, at age sixty-six. The illness was a kind of anemia often linked to long exposure to radiation. Burial placed her beside Pierre. Paris holds the Panthéon, resting place of France's most brilliant citizens, and the remains were moved there in 1995. For her own achievements she was the first woman buried there, and the only one. Atoms were understood differently after her work. Medicine gained new frontiers. Radiocarbon dating, a method for judging the age of old organic material, grew from that work as well.

10She showed that careful science, done on purpose, can produce extraordinary breakthroughs. The science mattered. The legacy reached further. Discrimination kept pressing on her. Certainty about her purpose stayed clear, and determination never wavered. The world received a model that inspires. She said life is hard for every person. She asked why that should stop anyone. What she demanded was perseverance, and confidence in oneself above everything. People, she said, should trust that a gift points them toward a task, and that the task can be reached. Staying determined and committed, even through challenge or delay, is perseverance. Too few red blood cells is the blood condition called anemia. Discrimination means treating a person or a group unfairly. Gender can be the basis. So can race, age, religion, or some other difference. Matter, motion, and energy are the subjects of physics. Prestigious describes something people honor, respect, and place in high standing. Detecting differences in electric currents is the job of an electrometer. Making enormous changes is what revolutionized means. A substance that cannot be split into simpler substances, and that contains only one kind of atom, is an element. Paris, France, is home to the university called the Sorbonne. Invisible energy that can pass through many solid substances is what X-rays are. Forming a hypothesis, an informed guess, is what hypothesized means. Each year, six Nobel Prizes are given. The fields are chemistry, economics, literature, medicine, and physics, with one prize also for advancing world peace.

88. The Roman Who Seized Power and Remade the Calendar

1Ahead are the shaping of a Roman empire, the world of his time, early life, military strategy, political strategy, the return to Rome, a legacy, and a word list. Gaius Julius Caesar was a military commander, a politician, and an acclaimed orator, and he was a complex man. Love came from the people and from his soldiers. Dealings with enemy combatants and with political foes were ruthless. Negotiation was a skill, and politics was cunning. Many in the Roman Senate still judged him lawless, hungry for power, and dangerous to Rome. Charm was part of him. Humor appeared at times. Above all he was an achiever. Energy and drive had no limit. A lifetime held many accomplishments. The world map changed under his leadership. Language changed. Government changed. Even the calendar changed. Soldiers and ordinary people loved him, yet enemies and political rivals met a ruthless man. The Senate's fear was that he was lawless, mad for power, and a danger to Rome. Charm and jokes sat beside that drive. Energy seemed to have no edge. Maps, languages, governments, and even the calendar shifted because of what he did. At the start, Rome was a city-state. That means a city joined with the countryside that supplied its food, acting as one political body. Neighboring city-states on the Italian Peninsula mostly shared language, culture, and religion with Rome. Fighting happened. Alliances happened too. Rome, in time, became the dominant city-state. Legend says kings once ruled it. Six of those kings were kind. The seventh spread terror.

2In 509 bce, legend says, the people rose and expelled that seventh king, Superbus. Citizens of the new Roman Republic deeply distrusted rule by one monarch alone. A legislative body, the Senate, was the reliance. Men in it were chosen by two consuls, magistrates elected every year. Consuls, not a king, oversaw government. If war created an emergency, a dictator could outrank the consuls. The post could not last. Two classes filled the Republic. Wealthy aristocrats were patricians. Plebeians included landowners of smaller means. Everyone outside the aristocracy was counted with them. Tension between the classes never left. A map of the Republic from 200 to 100 bce shows the Atlantic Ocean and Gaul, meaning France. Macedonia and the Black Sea are marked. Rome, Spain, and Asia, meaning Turkey, are marked. Greece, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa are marked. One shade is the Republic in 200 bce. Another is the Republic in 100 bce. Birth came during rapid expansion, and that growth would stir turmoil among Romans. The system let the Republic flourish. By 250 bce most of the Italian Peninsula was under Rome. Spain was taken to the west. Gaul, today's France, was taken to the north. Macedonia and Asia, today's Turkey, were taken to the east. Northern Africa was taken to the south. Conquered regions became provinces under governors. Governors were eager for the post because it paid well. Huge sums could be made by shipping grain to Rome, and by shipping enslaved people there too. Corruption in those governments was rampant. Ordinary citizens back in Rome gained nothing from the provinces.

3The local economy was poor. The split between upper and lower classes grew so unbearable that the Social War followed, from 91 to 89 bce. At his birth, two men competed for power. Lucius Cornelius Sulla had the patricians. The plebeian side was the one Gaius Marius represented. Birth fell on July 12 or 13, in 100 bce. The family was patrician, yet not especially rich or influential, and it sympathized with plebeian causes. Women in his world held little power. Formal entry into politics or government was closed to them. Marriage was a key route to power and influence for them and for their families. The family was not prominent until an aunt married Marius, the leader opposed to Sulla. That marriage lifted the family's political and social standing. Little is known of the early years. Parents gave him a strong education. At sixteen the father died suddenly, and the son was pushed to the head of the family. He married Cornelia, daughter of an ally of Marius and tied to Rome's most influential families. Soon Sulla rose to power and ordered the young husband to divorce her. By refusing, he stood openly beside Marius. The plebeian cause became his own. Danger was great. Property could be stripped away, and life itself was at risk. The army was his escape from Rome. Patrician rank made him an officer. Planning battles and fighting them pleased him. Legionnaires, the soldiers, liked him. Sulla's death in 78 bce brought a return to Rome and a political career.

4Law work came first. Oratory, meaning public speaking, was the next study. Pirates kidnapped him while he sailed to Greece to begin it. His own accounts say he befriended the captors. As a joke he insisted the ransom be set higher, and they raised it. After paying, he joked that payback would come. A small naval force was later raised. The pirates were captured and crucified. Political triumphs then strung together in Rome. He moved skillfully through the city's many intrigues. Cornelia's death in 69 bce led to a political marriage with Pompeia, daughter of the powerful ally Pompey. With Pompey mentoring him, important offices followed. Divorce from Pompeia came later. In 61 bce he was made governor of Farther Spain, today's western Spain and Portugal. Age and a balding head led him to wear laurel leaves as a crown. After that governorship he returned and, in 59 bce, won election as consul, a prestigious office. Patrician senators opposed him vehemently. He still got himself named governor of Cisalpine Gaul, today's northern Italy, and of Transalpine Gaul, today's France. Recruitment and expansion had ample ground there. Lands north of Rome counted as frontier. Those lands are now the north of France, plus Germany and Belgium. Earlier ambitious governors had crossed it with little success. People in Rome knew little of the northern tribes. Soldiers feared them and respected them. Advantages still belonged to Caesar's men, though the northerners were bigger, stronger, and tougher. Opponents usually had far greater numbers.

5Roman legions were much better organized. Their chain of command let them maneuver quickly and well. Equipment was more advanced. Most of all, they had Caesar. Keen military instincts and brilliant tactics were his. Infectious energy motivated people. Battle found him physically tough and utterly without fear. He led on foot and required officers to do the same. Siege engines, machines for attacking fortified forces, were built on his orders and saved countless Roman lives. Soldiers gave respect and loyalty. Others gave criticism. Ruthlessness in battle was notorious. Women could be killed or starved. Children could be too. So could other people who were not fighting. None of that troubled him. Harsh tactics brought great victories, yet even his own age found them extreme. One device that worked was the battering ram. Soldiers stood under a shed for protection. Chains held a heavy ram, and they swung it until fortified gates broke. In Gaul the soldiers started nervous, then defeated adversaries again and again. Setbacks came at times. Many scholars still rank him among history's greatest generals. The Rhine River was bridged. Armies entered Germany. The English Channel was crossed into Britain. In 52 bce a last united stand by the Gallic tribes was faced and beaten. Gaul was finally one. Exploits and looting there built a large personal fortune and great glory. Rome's future, and the future of Gaul and of what became modern Europe, felt the impact. Readers who want more on the campaigns can read the man himself.

6He wrote about what he lived. What he wrote about fighting in Gaul still survives, which is remarkable. Writings on his other conflicts survive too. Historians agree he likely cast his own actions in a positive light. Readers who look past that find gripping accounts of famous events. Students of Latin are often required to read the writings. Lionel Royer painted the scene in 1899. Vercingetorix yields. The moment follows the fighting at Alesia. Political agents and allies worked for him in Rome while he stayed in Gaul. General and politician both, he had to stay sharp amid Rome's political perils. The alliance with Pompey was cemented in 59 bce, the consul year, when Pompey married Julia, Caesar's daughter. Caesar then joined Pompey to Crassus, one of Rome's wealthiest men. The pair had been political opponents. Uniting them was a brilliant stroke. Together, Pompey, Caesar, and Crassus, called the First Triumvirate, held massive political sway. One coin, struck in 44 bce, carries Julius Caesar's face. The back of the coin carries Venus. The family traced its origins to that goddess. As his star rose, the other two grew resentful. Julia's death in 54 bce cut the marriage tie between Pompey and Caesar. Crassus died in battle the next year. Bitter rivalry replaced the old alliance. Triumphs in Gaul, as news of them reached Rome, pushed Pompey closer to the patrician faction, which saw Caesar as a threat. In 50 bce he wanted to come home. Senators insisted the legions leave his command. Pompey was not told to relinquish his armies.

7Patrician Senate leaders, Caesar knew, feared him. Without the army, he suspected, return would mean arrest. He might be killed as well. So in 49 bce he set out with his army. He brought them to the Rubicon River. The river marked the border between Cisalpine Gaul and Italy. He knew the crossing would count as war. His aim was to seize Rome's corrupt government. Reform of that government was his aim as well. Civil war with Pompey's men was ignited. Caesar's troops were seasoned. They quickly beat Pompey's men. Pompey fled into Egypt. Assassins there killed him. Ptolemy ruled Egypt. He had given the order. Caesar followed Pompey to Egypt. There he met Cleopatra. She was Ptolemy's sister. A relationship began. She and Ptolemy were rivals for Egypt's rule. She saw a strong ally. A son was born to them. With his help she took Egypt's throne back. Return to Rome came in 46 bce. The title he took for himself was dictator, over the Senate.

8Concentrated power enraged and frightened opponents. Romans had sworn never again to accept one monarch. He seemed to be aiming at exactly that. A picture shows the legion led across the Rubicon into Italy. He led the state only briefly, yet many reforms appeared. Taxation was updated. Great public works began. The Senate was expanded, and for the first time it included people from cities other than Rome. Many were his allies. He was surprisingly lenient and also gave important posts to some of Pompey's supporters. Reform of the republic had been his intent. A group of senators still conspired. The date was March 15, 44 bce, called the Ides of March. Attackers struck him and left him dead. A map of the Republic in 45 bce shows Cisalpine Gaul and the Atlantic Ocean. Transalpine Gaul, meaning France, is marked, with Macedonia and the Black Sea. Rome, Spain, and Asia, meaning Turkey, are marked, with Greece, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa. The map is the Republic at the time of his death. In 1865 a painter from Germany, Karl Theodor von Piloty, made a picture of the killing. Murder made Caesar a martyr at once. Romans declared him divine in 42 bce. The killing also opened chaos, and a war inside Rome followed. Conflict ran for years. Then a great-nephew, Octavian, rose. He became Augustus Caesar and Rome's earliest emperor. The judicious reign of Augustus let the empire steady itself. Brutal and cunning as Caesar was, military victories widened Roman influence and laid foundations for the Roman Empire.

9Greek and Roman knowledge spread into new territories, including Roman ideas of governance, of military organization, and of law. Gaul, which he had conquered, was among those lands. Reforming the Roman calendar ranks among his greatest achievements. The old one was lunar, based on the moon's monthly cycles, and it counted 355 days. A year in most calendars used now has 365 days. Leaders before him picked where those extra ten days would sit. That power let them shift elections and holidays to suit themselves. Astronomers helped him build a new calendar based on Earth's movement around the Sun, a solar calendar. Extra days were placed in specific months. The leap year was introduced. July is named for him. Inside the empire, newly conquered peoples took on parts of Roman culture. Greek stayed dominant in the eastern Mediterranean. Elsewhere, Latin became the main language of commerce and of society. His leadership therefore shaped the future of lands that would be joined, in politics and in society, under the Roman Empire. Life dates include these. Birth is 100 bce. The father dies, and marriage to Cornelia comes, in 84 bce. During 83 and 82 bce, Sulla takes charge in Rome. Sulla dies, and Caesar returns to Rome, in 78 bce. Election as Pontifex is 73 bce. Kidnapping by pirates is 75 bce. Marriage to Pompeia, daughter of ally Pompey, is 67 bce. Cornelia's death is 69 bce. Election as Pontifex Maximus is 63 bce.

10Divorce from Pompeia is 62 bce. From 60 to 59 bce he returns to Rome, is elected consul, marries Calpurnia, and forms the First Triumvirate. Appointment as governor of Farther Spain is 61 bce. In 58 bce he becomes governor of Cisalpine Gaul and of Transalpine Gaul, and he defeats Germanic tribes. The year 55 bce brings a defeat of Germanic tribes who had entered Gaul. Legions cross the Rhine. Britain is invaded. In 52 bce Vercingetorix unites rebel tribes in Gaul, and the uprising is suppressed. Julia, the daughter married to Pompey, dies in 54 bce. Crassus is defeated and killed in 53 bce. The Rubicon is crossed, and civil war begins, in 49 bce. The Ides of March assassination is 44 bce. Members of a society's highest class, usually wealthy and powerful, are the aristocracy. Martyr names someone whose beliefs, or whose deeds, bring suffering or death. An orator speaks in public. Eloquence is what marks the best of them. Generous or kind is what benevolent means. When a city or a built-up district behaves as its own country, it is a city-state. Pitiless, cruel, and wholly without morals is what ruthless means. Secret plans, or the making of them, are intrigues. Someone skilled at careful planning toward a goal is a tactician. Good sense or wise judgment is what judicious means. Strongly and with great emotion is what vehemently means. Very forgiving or tolerant is what lenient means. Producing a lot of money, or profitable, is what lucrative means.

89. The Stone City Called Great Zimbabwe

1Every wall at Great Zimbabwe was put up without mortar. That includes the ruins of the Hill Complex. Sculptures of birds, including one that is damaged, suggest a belief. Birds were important symbols to the people of Great Zimbabwe. In southern Zimbabwe, a striking complex of towering stone ruins sits in the landscape. The ruins are all that remains of a once-magnificent city called Great Zimbabwe. The mighty walls have intrigued Western scholars since the late 1800s. That is when Europeans began to study them. The site offers a fascinating glimpse of life in a thriving African civilization. That life belonged to the years between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Many parts of this history remain a mystery. One mystery is why the prosperous city was abandoned. The pages move from these mysterious ruins to a nation's namesake, a city of stone, the building of the great city, a thriving civilization, the work of protection, and secrets still held in the stones. The ruins of this ancient city are in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe is a landlocked country. It sits just north of South Africa. It sits west of Mozambique, in the southern region of Africa. Zambia and Botswana are among the neighbors that share its inland borders. The ruins lie in the southeastern part of Zimbabwe. They are not far from Lake Mutirikwi and the town of Masvingo. The word Zimbabwe is thought to come from a phrase in Shona. The phrase means stone houses.

2Shona is one of the three primary languages of Zimbabwe. Great Zimbabwe is such an important source of pride that the new nation borrowed its name. When Zimbabwe gained independence from Britain in 1980, the country took the name of the famous ancient city. A map of the region marks Zambia, the Mozambique Channel, Harare, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Masvingo, Botswana, and South Africa, with Africa labeled as well. The view from the Hill Complex takes in the other sections of the ruins. The vast ruins stretch over nearly 728.4 hectares (1,800 acres) of countryside. They include three main sections. The sections are the Hill Complex, the Great Enclosure, and the Valley Ruins. The Hill Complex and the Great Enclosure are made of stone buildings. They also include buildings of daga. Daga is a reddish mixture of clay and gravel. The Valley Ruins lie between the Hill Complex and the Great Enclosure. They hold the remains of a large number of daga dwellings. Those dwellings are scattered through the valley. The Hill Complex was probably the religious hub of the city. It was also probably the place where the kings lived. The Valley Ruins were likely home to the people who lived in Great Zimbabwe. Experts think the wealthy residents lived inside the Great Enclosure. In some places the walls rise 11 meters (36 ft.). That is as tall as a three-story building. In some places the walls are up to 6 meters (20 ft.) thick.

3The walls curve continuously. In some places they are quite smooth and decorative. The Hill Complex is the oldest section of Great Zimbabwe. It stands on a steep hillside in the northern part of the site. From there, the view of the rest of the city and the land around it is stunning. The Hill Complex ruins are about 100 meters (328 ft.) long. They are about 45 meters (148 ft.) wide. Massive stone walls reach up to 6 meters (20 ft.) thick and 11 meters (36 ft.) high. In one part of the Hill Complex, six upright posts are topped with birds. Those posts lead experts to a conclusion. This section was the spiritual center of the city. It may have been used for religious rituals. The Hill Complex stood at what is thought to have been the center of the city. It was also likely the home of the chiefs. The view south from the top of a stone wall in the Hill Complex is spectacular. The curving wall of the Great Enclosure shows a preference. The builders liked rounded shapes more than straight ones. The Great Enclosure lies in the southern area of the Hill Complex. It is the largest ancient structure in Africa south of the Sahara Desert. This oval ring of stone spans 250 meters (820 ft.) around. Like the Hill Complex, it rises as high as 11 meters (36 ft.) in some places.

4Researchers estimate that the builders used about one million stones. A second wall runs just inside part of the outer wall. It runs for about 55 meters (180 ft.). It forms a narrow passage. The passage leads to a conical tower. The purpose of that tower remains a mystery. Remains of daga houses can be found inside the walls. Smaller walls divide the area into compounds for different families. Scientific dating shows when the Great Enclosure was built. It was built in the 1300s, at the height of Great Zimbabwe's power. Archaeologists do not know why people built it. It may also have been a royal palace. The conical tower inside the Great Enclosure is completely solid. Rumors of a magnificent city south of the Sahara began to spread among Europeans in the sixteenth century. Portuguese explorers told of stone walls they had seen on their travels. In the late nineteenth century, Europeans came upon Great Zimbabwe again. They began to explore its history. They doubted that local African builders could have made work of such fine craft. The most famous works of art recovered from the site are eight soapstone bird statues. The birds sat atop columns in the Hill Complex. They measure about 41 centimeters (16 in.) tall. They have some humanlike features, such as lips. They may have stood for royal authority or for ancestry. People likely thought of the soapstone birds as protectors guarding the city.

5The bird statues inspired the design of Zimbabwe's national symbol. That symbol appears on the flag and on coins. Builders stacked stones to make curving walls of incredible height. Some Europeans thought wood samples found at the site came from the north. They became convinced that Phoenicians had built the city. Phoenicians, pronounced fi-NEE-shunz, lived near the eastern Mediterranean. Over the years, several amateur researchers tried to prove that theory. They ignored a large body of evidence. Pottery, spearheads, and tools indicated an African origin. In their search for a link to another culture, they even damaged or destroyed parts of the site. British archaeologist David Randall-MacIver finally studied the site in 1905. He studied the artifacts he found. He also studied how the daga buildings around the site were made. He concluded that Africans built Great Zimbabwe. A few different African tribes claim that their ancestors built it. Most scholars today think the Shona people built the city. The Shona have lived in the area since prehistoric times. The evidence indicates that people began the construction about one thousand years ago. The city was under construction for more than three hundred years. The construction is unique for many reasons. The walls were not built in straight lines. They were built in curves across the rolling land. Sometimes the builders worked enormous boulders into their plan. The Hill Complex is a stunning example of that method.

6Later investigations confirmed what Randall-MacIver had found. Local people built Great Zimbabwe. Some artifacts, such as tools, resemble items used by Shona people who lived near the site in the 1800s. The curving stone walls also point to a local design. They are unlike the more geometric designs favored by Arab cultures. Those cultures were once thought to have built the city. The builders mainly used smaller stones. They cut those stones into shapes like bricks. Stonemasons cut the stones from the large granite boulders that are common around the site. They needed millions of stone bricks for the walls. To make them, they used fire to heat the large stones to high temperatures. Cold water was poured onto the stones while they were still red-hot. The change in temperature made the stones split along lines that were naturally straight. The builders stacked the stones one on top of another to make the walls. Amazingly, they used no mortar to hold the stones together. This particular way of building is found in only a few other areas in Africa. Many people consider Great Zimbabwe the most impressive example. Workers used both boulders and cut stones for the walls of the Hill Complex. Inside the Great Enclosure, moss covers parts of the walls. The workers made the base of each wall a little thicker than its top. The walls therefore taper slightly as they rise toward the sky. This plan kept the towering three-story walls of stacked stones from toppling.

7The craft is quite impressive. Some of the earlier walls are a bit coarse. Building methods improved as time went on. Some of the more carefully built walls are very smooth. They look similar to a modern brick wall. The purpose of these massive walls is not fully understood. The walls were not designed to hold up weight. Evidence suggests that people built the walls as part of the city's defenses. Other evidence suggests another purpose. The walls may have protected the privacy of the city's elite. They may also have served as a symbol of royal authority. The Shona people have lived in the area around Great Zimbabwe since the Iron Age. That age began there in the third century ce. The land was ideal for farming and for raising livestock. Underground deposits held valuable materials. Those materials included gold, iron, copper, and tin. The people mined these resources for trade and for crafting. Over time, a simple society of farmers and cattle herders developed more complex social arrangements. Evidence suggests a change after about 1000 ce. The Shona began forming settlements with centralized states. That date matches the time when the Shona were likely building the city of Great Zimbabwe. In the fourteenth century, a powerful empire had Great Zimbabwe as the trading city at its heart. Traditional clothing is still worn by a Shona healer in modern times.

8Drawings made in 1892 show the floor plan of the Great Enclosure. They also show artifacts found near the site. At the height of the empire's power, the population was large. Counting the surrounding valley, it was likely over ten thousand people. Some estimates put it as high as twenty thousand. The empire's elite class owned the resources. That class took the leadership roles. This elite group most likely lived in the stone buildings, such as the Great Enclosure. Around the valley, the more modest dwellings of daga were probably where peasants lived. Cattle, crops, and trade were the backbone of a booming economy. The city stood along a busy trade route. The route connected other regions of Africa with ports along the Indian Ocean. The people traded gold that they mined from the surrounding hills. They traded it for goods from nations far away. Archaeologists have found metal ornaments made in a West African style. They have found glass from the Middle East. They have even found porcelain from China. These artifacts prove that the empire traded widely with other cultures. Works of art that local artists likely made have also been discovered. Those works show that the people had artistic traditions of their own. Great Zimbabwe was also likely a major religious center. Archaeologists have found several stone altars among the ruins. The religion was probably similar to the monotheistic religion that modern Shona people still practice. Despite clear signs of wealth and power, the city was largely abandoned by the middle of the fifteenth century.

9The reason is still unknown to scholars. One leading theory points to the land. Grazing cattle and farming may have overused the ground around the city. If the land lost the nutrients crops need, it would have been hard to grow enough food. A population that large could not have been fed. Another theory says the people may have moved. They may have sought more lucrative trade as other regions grew richer. Great Zimbabwe is no longer the busy metropolis it once was. It still has a role in modern Zimbabwe. Some Zimbabweans use the site for religious practices even today. It is also one of the country's tourist attractions. Contact with tourists has caused damage. The ruins need protection if they are to last another millennium. Environmental factors, such as climate, are wearing the ruins down. Invasive plants threaten the strength of the structures that remain. Legal protections have existed since 1893. More government funding is urgently needed if the site is to be fully preserved and studied. In 1986, the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization named the ruins a World Heritage Site. That choice means nearly every country in the world recognizes the site as worthy of admiration and preservation. Preserving the ruins is complicated. It means studying the factors that contributed to the decline. It means respecting the history of the structures and the land.

10It means carefully considering the beliefs of the people of the region. Stars light the beautiful ruins of Great Zimbabwe at night. The site has historical significance. It reveals fascinating and important information about life and global trade. That life belonged to a thriving empire in medieval southern Africa. The ruins have given captivating glimpses of the past. They still keep many secrets. One question asks what the conical tower inside the Great Enclosure was for. Perhaps the most intriguing question of all asks why the great city was deserted after centuries of prosperity. With proper care and study, the walls may yet reveal the answers to these mysteries. Conical means shaped like a cone. The elite are the most successful, wealthy, or powerful members of a society. Intrigued means that something drew out the interest or curiosity of others, or captivated them. Landlocked means surrounded on all sides by land. Lucrative means producing a lot of money, or profitable. A metropolis is a very large or important city. Monotheistic relates to belief in only one god. Mortar is a liquid mixture of materials. It hardens as it dries, and it is used to hold bricks or stones together. Prosperous means having success, or being well-off. Rituals are ceremonies with standard steps or actions. To taper is to become gradually smaller toward one end of an object. Thriving means growing and healthy.

90. The War That Made a Country

1A timeline of the quarrel runs through several famous events. The French and Indian War was one part of Europe's Seven Years' War. Parliament later passed the Sugar Act. The Quartering Act and the Stamp Act followed. So did the Townshend Acts. Violence in Boston became known as the Boston Massacre. Colonists dumped tea in what people call the Boston Tea Party. The Coercive Acts, renamed the Intolerable Acts, came next. The First Continental Congress met. On April 19, 1775, war began at Lexington and at Concord. The United States did not start as its own country. It started as thirteen colonies. Great Britain ruled them. So did the English king, George III. Britain placed taxes on the colonists. It also enforced new laws that people disliked. Colonists objected. They said a tax was unacceptable when they had no representative speaking for them in Parliament. Parliament seemed unwilling to honor the Bill of Rights of 1689. That bill covered every citizen of the British realm. Colonists were included. As time passed, bad feeling grew. Violence grew with it. King George III tried to tighten his grip. He used harder taxes. He used threats of military force. A chain of events pushed the two sides into open fighting. The Boston Tea Party was part of that chain. The clash came on April 19, 1775. British soldiers met colonists in two Massachusetts towns. One town was Lexington. The other was Concord.
