Shots were fired. A separate note explains a famous cry. King George would not cancel the taxes. A fight for independence began to look unavoidable for the colonies. Patrick Henry went home to Virginia after the First Continental Congress. In a speech there he said he would take liberty even if the other choice was death. During the war, Patriots shouted a short form of that idea. Their battle cry was Liberty or Death. The first shots came on Lexington's village green. Which side fired the opening shot is still unknown. Ralph Waldo Emerson later wrote a poem called Concord Hymn. Because of that poem, people remember the opening shot as one the whole world heard. War had started. Britain stood on one side. The thirteen colonies stood on the other.

2The ground they fought on already had owners. For thousands of years, Native peoples had made that region their home. By 1775, the coming of Europeans had killed millions of Native people. The next century would bring millions more deaths. Land from one coast to the other would be taken from them. A new meeting gathered on May 10, 1775. It was the Second Continental Congress. The place was Independence Hall. The city was Philadelphia, in Pennsylvania. Fifty-six delegates were there. With one shared vote they picked a commander. George Washington got the job. He was a Virginia delegate. He had once been an officer in the British army. Until then, people knew those troops by another name. They were the New England militia. Congress chose a new name, the Continental Army. The new name was meant to build unity among the colonies. Volunteers from all thirteen colonies would fill the ranks. Easy is not a word for Washington's task. His soldiers were a mixed, poorly prepared group. Farmers were among them. Carpenters were among them. Blacksmiths were among them. Weapons were few. Training was thin or missing. His orders said to capture every armed enemy. Destroying those enemies was the other allowed choice. Across the field stood Britain. That army was powerful. It was trained. It was well supplied. Washington expected to fail. He said so to Patrick Henry, a Virginia lawyer. From the moment he took command, Washington believed, his fall would begin. He also believed his good name would be ruined. He still trusted American independence as a cause. Command was the duty he accepted. He insisted on serving without pay. Independence was not every colonist's wish. His new troops were near Boston. Washington went to meet them around Concord and Lexington. Congress kept trying to repair the break with Parliament. A petition left the delegates' hands. King George III was the person they addressed. They asked again for colonists' rights. They asked him to call the colonists loyal English subjects. The king would not even receive the petition. His answer was a hard judgment. He said the colonists had moved into open rebellion. He said that rebellion was openly declared.

3In short, wanting independence made a colonist a traitor to the crown. Native peoples felt the war deeply. Separation was King George III's aim. He wanted Native peoples on one side and colonists on the other. He hoped the gap would stop violence between the two groups. Some lands had been set aside by Great Britain for Native peoples. Colonists disliked that decision. When the fighting came, Native peoples did not all choose one side. Some joined the Patriots. Others joined the British. At times a nation split. At times an alliance split. Britain's loss handed the United States a huge stretch of land. Native peoples had lived on that land for centuries. They lost more than ground. Cultures were lost. Countless lives were lost. Native resistance to Britain came before the American fight. A picture shows the Ottawa leader Pontiac visiting the British. The year is 1763. Soon afterward he tried to drive the British out. Support came from the Great Lakes region. Almost all the tribes there backed him. The struggle called Pontiac's War carries his name. It lasted from 1763 to 1766. While Congress sat in Philadelphia, colonial soldiers won a fort. The place was Fort Ticonderoga, in New York. Ethan Allen was a rough, tough farmer from New Hampshire. He and other local farmers had formed the Green Mountain Boys. A British fort stood on Lake Champlain. Congress asked Allen's group to capture it. Another soldier received orders too. His name was Benedict Arnold. Connecticut had given him an official commission to seize the fort. Both men wanted to lead. They argued for the whole journey. On May 10, 1775, they still took the fort together. The next day a second fort fell. It stood at Crown Point. Allen and Arnold captured it. Colonial spirits rose. The northern border was now safer from British attack. The wins also announced a plain fact. War had truly started. Colonists had to choose. Loyalists wanted to stay part of Britain. Patriots wanted independence from Britain. No middle choice remained. Lexington's opening battle had sent British soldiers back toward Boston. Major John Pitcairn led that retreat. Colonial soldiers camped outside the city and kept gathering.

4In time about 16,000 Patriot troops ringed Boston. The British supply line into the city was cut. General Thomas Gage saw a danger. Patriot troops might fortify hills across the Charles River. One hill was Bunker Hill. The other was Breed's Hill. Both stand in Charlestown. A map shows the British path. After losing at Lexington and at Concord, they fell back to Charlestown. They then crossed the river into Boston. Labels on that map include Lexington, Concord, Boston, and the Atlantic Ocean. The date was June 16 in the year 1775. Orders that night came from General Artemis Ward. He told Patriot soldiers to dig trenches. The hill he named was Bunker Hill. The soldiers misunderstood. They went instead to Breed's Hill. That hill sat closer to the British. Morning showed the slope covered with soldiers. Trenches covered it too. General William Howe brought the British response. Ships carried them over the Charles River. Cannons fired as they came. Patriots stood at a disadvantage. Their training was weak. They faced professional soldiers. Gunpowder was very scarce. Officers told them to save every shot. Fire, they said, only when the enemy was near enough that the whites of their eyes showed. The plan worked. British soldiers rushed uphill. Americans held their shots until the last moment that was still safe. Many attackers died. More British troops landed and charged again. Americans again waited, then fired. A third wave finally broke the defense. Gunpowder was gone. The Americans had to retreat. Britain took Breed's Hill. Britain also took Bunker Hill. A map of the fight marks the Mystic River and the Charles River. It marks Breed's Hill, Bunker Hill, Charlestown, Boston, and Copp's Hill. Patriot soldiers held one set of positions. British soldiers held another. Control of the two hills went to Britain. The price was high. British losses passed a thousand. The count includes both the wounded and the dead. Patriot losses were 441 men. Even in defeat, Patriot spirits rose. They had shown they could stand in a fight against a larger body of professional soldiers. Most of the action happened on Breed's Hill. People still name the fight for Bunker Hill.

5July 1775 is when General George Washington reached the army. His troops kept the British shut inside Boston. The shut-in lasted nearly a year. Canada was the next worry, so he sent men to invade it. He did not want Britain landing there and then marching south into New York. General Richard Montgomery led Patriots who took Montreal. The month was November 1775. Quebec was Arnold's target. He led the assault there. Severe December weather made that attack fail. Through the winter, Patriots turned captured British cannons on the soldiers inside Boston. The British left the city on a March day in 1776. The day of the month was the 17th. Thousands of Loyalists left with them. Washington's troops marched in as winners. A picture shows cannons the Continental Army used against the British. A saying still heard today is an invitation to sign a paper in a bold way, using the words John Hancock. The saying reaches back to 1776. That year Hancock signed the Declaration of Independence in a large, fearless hand. Fifty-three other people still needed to sign. His large name encouraged them. Thomas Paine, a Patriot, wrote a pamphlet called Common Sense. In it he said independence was the only right choice for the colonists. He challenged British authority. Most readers could follow him because the language stayed plain. About 150,000 copies sold within a few months. Many Loyalists shifted toward independence because of it. In June 1776 Congress picked a committee. The committee would write a statement. The subject was the colonists' right to govern themselves. Thomas Jefferson was the youngest member of Congress. He became the actual writer. People knew his skill with words. July 4, 1776, was the day Congress said yes. The document was the Declaration of Independence. Each of the thirteen colonies then passed it. With that yes, a new country existed. People called the new country the United States of America. Colony, the old name, no longer fit. The colonies were now called states. Hard days came next. Patriots lost fight after fight. A month after the Declaration was signed, General William Howe moved a huge force by ship.

6British soldiers entered New York Harbor. Their number was 30,000. The Battle of Long Island ran for three days. Outnumbered Patriots finally retreated. They went south across New Jersey. Philadelphia was the direction of that retreat. Britain occupied New York City. In another fight, Patriots surrendered Fort Washington. Patriot losses in that stretch passed 2,000. Some were dead. Others were prisoners. Three days was the length of that stretch. Nathan Hale is honored by a statue. He was a teacher, 21 years old. New York City held British troops. Hale volunteered to spy on them. He was caught. He was hanged. His final words said he was sorry to have only a single life to offer his country. Benedict Arnold had been a brave general. He believed Congress had treated him badly. He believed the Continental Army had too. In 1779 Washington gave him a fort. The fort was West Point, on the lower Hudson River. Arnold planned to sell that fort to the British. The plan came to light. The exposed plot made him a traitor. He then entered Britain's army. Earlier, in October 1776, his gunboats lost a fight. The place was Lake Champlain, in Canada. The Patriots still fought so hard that Britain grew worried. Beating the rebels might be harder than expected. The date of a bolder strike was December 24 in 1776. Boats carried George Washington and his men over the Delaware River. The target was Trenton, in New Jersey. Hessian mercenaries were the enemy there. Those hired soldiers came from Germany. They were allied with the British. The crossing took one night. Patriots got 2,400 men to the far bank. The river was icy. Sleet fell. Snow fell. The battle that followed lasted less than an hour. The Patriots won. It was the war's first major victory. A few days later Washington beat the British again. That fight was at Princeton, also in New Jersey. The two wins lifted Patriot spirits. A picture shows Washington accepting a surrender. The place is Trenton, and the year is 1776. Britain struck back in June 1777. General John Burgoyne led a large army south out of Canada. His plan aimed at the Hudson River around Albany, New York.

7Taking that area would cut New England and New York off from every other colony. During the march he took Fort Ticonderoga back. Patriot soldiers stopped his push at the Battle of Saratoga. The month was October. Burgoyne surrendered about 6,000 men. A map of his march south from Canada shows Lake Champlain twice. It shows Fort Ticonderoga. It names Riedesel, St. Clair, and Phillips. It marks British troops and British military leaders. People look back on Saratoga as a major turn in the war. France and other countries in Europe could now see that the Patriots might win. In 1778 France entered the fight. Great Britain was its old enemy. France sent supplies to the Continental Army. Spain soon declared war on Britain. The Netherlands did too. Shortage still haunted the Continental Army. Food was often missing. Clothing was often missing. Shelter was often missing. At Valley Forge, in Pennsylvania, Washington's troops lived through a freezing, hungry winter. Supplies arrived only after that suffering. June 1778 brought the next big fight. The terrible winter was behind them. Washington attacked the British army at the Battle of Monmouth. General Henry Clinton now commanded the British. Neither side won. No later battle in the northern colonies matched it in size. It did show something important. Patriots could meet Britain's soldiers on equal footing. Valley Forge has a National Memorial Arch. Washington's words are cut into it. He said the soldiers were naked and starving, yet their patience and loyalty were beyond enough praise. Women could not serve in the army. They still served the war in other ways. One way was making homespun cloth at home. The Stamp Act had passed in 1765. After that, many women boycotted British goods. They made replacements themselves. That home labor was an act of protest and of rebellion. The Daughters of Liberty even spun thread in public demonstrations. Women made bullets. They sewed blankets. They sewed uniforms. They raised money. At the camps they cooked. They cleaned. They nursed the injured and the sick. They searched for food. Carrying water out to soldiers under fire put some women's lives in danger.

8Mary Ludwick Hays stepped in for her husband, William Hays, after he was wounded. History remembers her as Molly Pitcher. At the Battle of Monmouth she carried water for the soldiers. She also carried water for the cannon. That work earned her the nickname Molly Pitcher. British forces took Savannah, in Georgia, in December 1778. They next attacked Charleston, in South Carolina, and captured it in May 1780. Another win came at Camden, also in South Carolina, in August 1780. Those three battles had the war's highest casualty rates. Loyalty to Britain was common among colonists who lived in the South. Britain was winning the South. Patriots refused to quit. The turn began in October. Patriots won at King's Mountain, in South Carolina. The fight lasted a quick sixty-five minutes. Few battles in the war left British soldiers out entirely. This one did. Patriots fought Loyalists. More Patriot wins followed in 1781. January brought a win at Cowpens. April brought a win at Camden. Those victories pushed General Charles Cornwallis north. Virginia was where he was forced to go. He had helped Britain win at Long Island in 1776. The year 1780 put him at the head of Britain's southern troops. The French alliance began to repay the Patriots. French soldiers helped hold the British back. They also fought beside colonists in the force Washington led into Virginia. The war's fighters included thousands of Black people. They did not all choose the same army. Most were enslaved. Most joined the side that seemed more likely to offer freedom. Great Britain's side included Black fighters. The number was more than 20,000. The Patriot side drew Black fighters too. Estimates run from 5,000 up to 8,000. Freedom was still decades away for many enslaved Black people. James Armistead stands as one American hero of that fight. Before the war he was enslaved in Virginia. His role was to serve as a double agent. He was good at it. The story he acted out was simple. He seemed to be a runaway loyal to Britain. Before long, Britain trusted him with a spy job aimed at the Patriots. The secret ran the other way too. Patriots were using him to watch the British.

9General Lafayette received battle plans from him. Those plans belonged to the British. Those details were ones the Patriots needed at Yorktown. Winning the wider war depended on Yorktown. After the fighting, a law called the Act of 1783 came into force. It freed enslaved soldiers of the Revolution. Armistead's work as a spy kept him out of that freedom. He went back to life as a slave. Freedom arrived years afterward. The help came from the French officer who had commanded him. Armistead added Lafayette to his own name. The added name showed thanks. It also showed the bond they shared. A painting from 1824 shows James Armistead Lafayette. A picture shows Cornwallis giving up to Washington at Yorktown. The war's most important battle was about to start. Twenty-four French ships met nineteen British ships. Cornwallis and his troops needed rescue. Britain had sent those ships for that job. Yorktown sits on the Virginia coast. The French fleet drove the rescue away. It also brought more soldiers for the land fight. French troops and Patriot troops moved in. They laid a siege around the British army. Three weeks passed. The British surrendered on October 19, 1781. That surrender ended the Revolutionary War. Victory belonged to the Patriots. The Peace of Paris arrived in 1783. Only then was independence from Great Britain official. The treaty gave the United States all the North American land west to the Mississippi River. Neither government truly owned that ground. The rightful holders were Native peoples. Colonies that had leaned on another country now had to join together. They had to build a nation from the start. Several people shaped the war. George Washington commanded the Continental Army. He later became the country's first president. Thomas Gage commanded British troops in the colonies. After Lexington and Concord, his army was trapped in Boston. John Burgoyne commanded the British northern army. He captured Fort Ticonderoga. He was later beaten at Saratoga. King George III was twenty-two when he became king of Great Britain. Keeping the colonies was his fixed goal. Cost did not change his mind. The Declaration of Independence came from Thomas Jefferson's pen.

10Thomas Paine wrote the booklet Common Sense. It moved many colonists to choose independence. From 1775 until 1778, William Howe was Britain's top commander on the North American mainland. The year 1778 brought a change of command. Henry Clinton took Howe's place. Pictures show George Washington and King George III. A few words unlock this history. Abandoned means left behind. A Loyalist lived in the thirteen colonies and stayed with Great Britain while the American Revolution was fought. Amends are acts meant to make up for a harm or a loss. Mercenaries are soldiers who will fight for any army that pays them. A casualty is a person hurt, killed, or missing in a war, an accident, or a disaster. Momentum is staying power. It is what keeps a movement going, or keeps it growing, as time passes. A commission is an official order, usually military, that requires someone to do a duty. Morale is the confidence or enthusiasm a person or a group feels while working toward a goal. A conflict is a clash of ideas, principles, or opinions. The word also means a fight, a battle, or a war. A Patriot backed independence. The people in question lived in the thirteen colonies, and the time was the American Revolution. Delegates are people chosen or elected to represent others and act for them. A petition is a formal written request. A large number of citizens often sign it. Independence is freedom from another power's control, influence, support, or help. Retaliated means struck back after being attacked. Nations use a treaty when they want a formal deal. Groups can use one too. The deal may promise peace or friendship. Self-governing means having the right to make and enforce laws without outside control. Unity is the quality of being joined in one group, one purpose, or one identity. In a siege, attackers ring an enemy and stay there. The stay is long. Attacks may continue. Food and other supplies are cut off. A map of important sites names Quebec, Ticonderoga, Boston, Concord, and Long Island. It also names Valley Forge, Yorktown, King's Mountain, Camden, Charleston, and Savannah. The Atlantic Ocean borders that map.

91. Tombs of Egypt's Golden Age

1A map of Egypt marks the Mediterranean Sea, Cairo, Memphis, and the Nile. Luxor, once called Thebes, appears beside the Red Sea. This book opens with a famous treasure. It then explains this royal burial ground. It explains how kings prepared for the afterlife, and what a tomb held. It follows how a royal tomb was cut and how its art was made. It looks at the valley now, and at treasure still to be found. Word meanings come last. November 1922 brought a staircase into the light. Howard Carter, a British archaeologist, uncovered the steps down to King Tutankhamen. Say that name toot-an-KAH-muhn. Explorers had thought Egypt's Valley of the Kings had no finds left. This tomb proved them wrong. Its royal seal was still whole. No earlier royal tomb in the valley had been found that way. Tutankhamen was among the least important pharaohs buried there. Four chambers made his tomb one of the smallest. Even so, the packed objects numbered more than five thousand. Many of those objects were solid gold. His golden funeral mask is inlaid with colored glass and with semiprecious stones. It ranks among Egypt's most famous treasures. Workers had laid the mask over the mummy, covering both the head and the shoulders. Few burial grounds on Earth match the Valley of the Kings for magnificence.

2Almost every pharaoh of Egypt's golden age lies here. That age is the New Kingdom. Three dynasties ruled it: the Eighteenth, the Nineteenth, and the Twentieth. The dates run from 1550 until 1080 bc. The length of that age is about five hundred years. Sixty-three tombs are known. A map marks KV 62 as Tutankhamen, KV 9 as Ramses IV, KV 57 as Horemheb, and KV 17 as Seti I. Some tombs are missing from the map. A few lie farther west. The key shows a discovered tomb and the label KV for Kings' Valley. During this age, Thebes was Egypt's capital and its religious center. Today that city is Luxor. Temples there honored the empire's pharaohs. Ancient Egyptians believed those rulers joined the gods after death. A mummified king needed a place where his body could rest undisturbed. His spirit still had to journey toward the afterlife. Al Qurn, pronounced el GOORN, is a mountain shaped like a pyramid above the valley. The pyramid stood for Ra, pronounced RAH, the Sun god. Across the Nile, a vast desert wadi offered a practical site. Say wadi as WAH-dee. It is a valley with steep sides. Soft limestone was plentiful, and tombs could be chiseled from it. Steep cliffs and a single way in made guarding easier. Thebes lay several hours' walk away, which helped keep robbers off.

3Ancient Egyptians ranked a pharaoh's tomb nearly as high as the palace he had lived in. The tomb guarded the body. People believed that body could live again after burial. Mummification took seventy days so the body would not start decomposing. Priests took out the internal organs, mummified them, and set them in a stone box. That box is a canopic chest. Nested coffins then held the body. A stone sarcophagus held the coffins. Granite or quartzite was carved for it. Weight could reach 9 metric tons, or 10 tons. The spirit needed protection too, while it moved through the underworld. Amulets went into the mummy's wrappings. Statues of protective gods went into the sarcophagus. One picture shows Howard Carter lifting a cover from Tutankhamen's third coffin, the innermost one. At many tomb entrances, Ra's names and prayers appear with pictures and hieroglyphs. Spells and prayers called funerary compositions covered walls and ceilings. Sometimes they covered the sarcophagus. Hieroglyphs and images ran down those surfaces in tall columns. Some spells were meant to bring the body back to life. A second group of spells sat within the sarcophagus. Their aim was to frighten demons. Those demons might try to sabotage the soul's journey. The writings had a third job.

4They guided the soul through trials on the way to the afterlife. Egyptians believed the pharaoh's soul had to travel west. It went through the underworld beside Ra. Obstacles and dangers waited along that road. A king was expected to want things in the afterlife, so royal tombs stored a wide supply. Wooden models filled storerooms, including boats and chariots. Cosmetics, clothing, and board games counted as personal goods. Furniture and lamps counted as everyday goods. Gems of high value were stored as treasure. Jewelry made of gold was stored too. So was artwork. Fruit sat in baskets. Preserved meat sat in boxes. Juice and other drinks sat in pots. Servants would be needed too. Servant figures filled that role, and they numbered in the hundreds. Each figure is a shabti, said SHAB-teez. The word means answerer. A spell on each figure was meant to animate it when the master called. Tutankhamen went into the tomb with 413 of these figures. Whether wood or stone, the small statues teach a great deal about beliefs and customs. Murals cover the burial chamber of Ramses VI, a king of the Twentieth Dynasty. Tombs in the valley share many features. Elaborate paintings and hieroglyphs decorate most of them. Halls and rooms often follow the same series. An entryway opens into a hall.

5Egyptians gave it this name: the passage of Ra. Images there often show the Sun god's many forms and names. Farther in, the hall of hindering often has a deep well cut into the floor. Experts think the pit may have slowed robbers. It may also have guarded against floods. Every plan ends in the burial chamber. Egyptians sometimes called that room the House of Gold. Storerooms opening off most of these chambers held furniture and supplies. Shared features did not make the tombs copies of one another. No pair in the valley is identical. Taste of the ruler decided the build and the decoration. Cutting started while the king still lived. Death left the builders only seventy days. By then mummification would be done, and the burial could not wait. An unfinished tomb might be rushed. Paintings or rooms could be left half done. Death came for Ramses IV while his tomb was still unfinished. Workers recut a chamber that already existed and used it for the burial. Other kings were buried in a tomb that was not the one begun for them. In the tomb of Ramses IX, experts think only two corridors had plaster before he died. The workmanship looks hurried. Layouts changed from early tombs to later ones. Early plans turned left once, or more than once.

6Later plans ran without turns. Experts think a straight line kept crews from cutting into older tombs by accident. A shared set of rooms can be labeled this way. A is the entrance. B is the passage of Ra. C is the hall of hindering, and it holds the deep well. D is the chariot hall, with sets of pillars. Chariots, though, have never turned up in that hall. E is the burial chamber. Time changed how the tombs looked and how they were laid out. Early New Kingdom work, in the Eighteenth Dynasty, is more than three thousand years old. Those tombs tended to be smaller than later ones. Their floor plans usually bent left in one or two turns of ninety degrees. Even now, workers raise walls above tombs. Falling debris would otherwise clutter the entrances. Placement shifted as well. Early in the New Kingdom, royal tombs sat at the bottoms of cliffs. Rain then washed water and debris down over an entrance. Later rulers more often put entrances on lower slopes. One reason may be that later tombs were meant to be opened again after burial. Another may be crowding in the valley. A tomb in a straight line was also less likely to strike another tomb. Experts think cutting began very early in a reign, close to the day power passed to a king.

7The first critical choice was the spot. The vizier, pronounced vi-ZEER, made it with senior workmen. He was the highest official of the court. A bad spot could force a new plan or a move. More than once, crews had already begun cutting when the first choice was abandoned. A workers' village explains much of this. Most digging at Dier al-Medina took place from 1922 to 1951. About four hundred tomb workers lived there with their families. The village sits about 1 kilometer, or 0.6 miles, south of the valley. Writings left in that village are a main source for knowledge of this royal burial ground. Limestone bedrock had to be cut for every tomb. Copper or bronze chisels started the rough passages. Wooden mallets drove them. Hand axes with stone blades helped. At the beginning, the passage was so tight that only one or two men could cut at once. A basket brigade of other workers carried debris out. A line painted by the foreman ran along the ceiling. That line was the reference for measuring, while walls, ceiling, and floor were refined. Simple tools still produced turns of ninety degrees. They also produced vertical walls that stayed parallel. The accuracy was remarkable. Decoration began once the cutting had gone far enough.

8Plasterers spread white gypsum plaster over the surfaces. Scribes drew vertical lines and horizontal lines. Those lines boxed in scenes and texts. Hieroglyphs and figures were sketched next. A supervisor came behind the scribes and corrected the work. Artists then painted blocks of color and filled in details. Sometimes they carved a relief. Parts of a scene were cut away so other parts stood out. Cutting away the background left raised figures, and that result is a raised relief. Details were carved into the figures before any paint. Horemheb's unfinished tomb still shows the first sketches and the corrections. Red ink marks the scribe's outlines. Black ink marks the supervisor's corrections. Because Horemheb died before the tomb was fully done, the steps remain visible. Scribes first outlined text and scenes in red. A supervisor checked those outlines and corrected them in black. He might fix a figure's proportions. He might note a missing image. Artists then traced the corrected images in black ink. Finishing work could include cutting the background away so figures stood up from the wall. Paint came last. Treasure hunters crowded the valley in the early 1800s. Like the robbers of ancient times, they took whatever could be sold to rich collectors. The year 1857 changed that pattern. Egypt's government set up the Antiquities Service.

9Its job was to protect ancient monuments and artifacts. Explorers today use methods meant to protect tombs and to preserve what is inside them. The year 1979 put the valley on an early World Heritage list. A special department inside the United Nations made that choice. Yearly visits pass one million. Tissue taken from mummies found here lets scientists study diet. It lets them study disease. It can even suggest how someone died. On a typical day, four to five thousand tourists come. Eighteen tombs open to the public, but not all at once. They rotate. One ticket lets a visitor choose three tombs from those open that day. One tomb is the exception. Tutankhamen's tomb needs an extra ticket. Objects first found in his tomb are kept at the Cairo Museum of Antiquities. A careless touch can discolor ancient paint. It can damage carvings. Rotation gives each tomb regular time away from crowds. Planned closures also leave time for restoration and for maintenance. Experts hope those breaks will offset the harm of staying open to the public. Decades after Carter's famous find, the valley gave up few fresh secrets. The year 1989 changed that. Egyptologist Kent Weeks studied a tomb called KV 5 more closely. Earlier labels had dismissed it as dull. Flood debris was cleared away.

10A corridor nobody had known about led to at least 150 chambers. The valley ranks among the richest archaeological sites anywhere. If the experts are right, more history is still buried. Scientists are excavating a tomb made for sons of the king Ramses II. That tomb is KV 5, and it is the largest in the valley. They are studying it as they dig. Difficult words in this book can be read as follows. To animate something is to bring it to life, or to make it lively. Hieroglyphs are picture-symbols used as writing, above all in ancient Egypt. To culminate is to arrive at the high point or the end. A mummified body has been embalmed and wrapped in burial cloth. Debris is the scattered leftover after the rest of something is gone or destroyed. Parallel lines or paths run the same way and stay an equal distance apart. Decomposing means rotting or breaking into smaller parts. Pharaohs is the title ancient Egypt gave its kings. Stone that has been quarried has been dug out for building, such as slate or marble. Dynasties are lines of rulers who share a family. A sarcophagus is a stone coffin from ancient times, often carved and richly decorated. Gypsum is a soft white mineral that plaster is made from.

92. Trains Built for Great Speed

1An ICE train, the Inter City Express, takes a bend in Germany. Contents. Racing Across Open Country. Where These Fast Trains Began. What Makes Them Go. Three Ways to Be Fast. The Shinkansen. The TGV. Maglev. Worries About Safety. Why These Trains Help. What Success Requires. The Years Ahead. Word List. A TGV rolls past sunflowers in a French field. Racing Across Open Country. Friday morning in Paris. A very fast train is leaving for Avignon, pronounced ah-veen-YONE, far to the south in France. The train is sleek and modern. You sit in comfort while it carries you into open country. Speed on the tracks can reach 186 miles per hour, which is 299 kph. A car would need seven hours for this trip. The train needs 2 hours plus 36 minutes. Science fiction seems to describe it. Scenes like this are ordinary, though, in countries around the world, because these trains exist. Millions of riders, spread through more than a dozen countries, already use them. Further countries are planning systems of this kind, or building them, so transport in this century, the twenty-first, can keep up. Where These Fast Trains Began. Speed on rails is old news. Some trains of the 1930s already reached about 100 mph, or 161 kph. Airplanes were not yet a common way to travel, so a long trip usually meant a train. Diesel fuel ran the engines on most of those early fast trains. An electrical generator took power from the diesel engine.

2Electricity from that generator turned the axles at the front of the train. Japan showed the world the first modern design when it hosted the Olympic Games in 1964. The train was the Shinkansen. People also call it the bullet train. Its first run linked Tokyo with Osaka. Average speed sat near 135 mph, or 217 kph. A chief breakthrough was the power source. Electricity did all the work. Fossil fuels did none of it. An early bullet train from Japan rushes past the city of Kyoto. London is where a Eurostar train sits waiting in a station. The 1970s saw Italy and Germany send out fast trains of their own. France built a large network for its fast trains in the 1980s. Spain opened service in the 1990s, on a system that is now the longest of its kind in Europe. A tunnel under the English Channel, sometimes called the Chunnel, was finished in 1994. A fast train can now go from London to Paris in two hours and fifteen minutes. Across Western Europe these trains race at 150 mph or more, which is 241 kph or more. Today, no fast-rail system on Earth runs longer than the one in China. Work began in 2004. The network grew with great speed. More than 3,728 miles of line, or 6,000 km, went in before six years had passed. Use of these trains spread widely across China. No country has more people. The count is above 1.3 billion, about 20 percent of everyone on Earth.

3Large cities are many, and the capital, Beijing, is one of them. Cars are still missing from many households. A fast train gives those people a needed way to move quickly from city to city. What Makes Them Go. Designs differ, yet some traits are shared. The shape is streamlined, like the nose of a jet airplane. Air slips smoothly over that shape. Drag, which means air resistance, stays small. Less energy is then needed to reach a high speed and to hold it. A Japanese train is shown above a Russian one. The look is not the same. Many features still match. A drawing labels the pantograph. Electricity from wires overhead runs most of these trains. A device called a pantograph joins the train to those wires. The link can break, as it does inside a tunnel. Battery power then carries the train until the pantograph joins the wires again. Some places skip the overhead wires. Current then travels in the tracks under the train. The tracks themselves are a vital part of the system. Welding joins them, so the whole length is smooth and the joints are gone. Builders keep the line as straight as they can. Curves would force a slowdown. A tunnel or a viaduct lets the line pass under an obstacle or over it, instead of bending around. A curve, when one is required, stays as gentle as possible, so speed can hold.

4A bend that is too tight means a slower train, or a train that might leave the rails. Computers at a central control keep the traffic safe. At top speed the engineer cannot read a sign the train flashes past. Every signal, including when to stop and when to switch tracks, must reach the engineer by electronics. Some of these trains lean as they take a corner. Not Fully in the Fast Class. In 2011 the nearest thing the United States had was Amtrak's Acela Express. One end was Washington, D.C. The other end was Boston, Massachusetts. New York City lay on the way. Top speed is 150 mph, or 241 kph. For most of the route the pace is only about half of that. Slower ordinary trains share the same tracks, and that sharing caps the speed. Three Ways to Be Fast. Popularity grew, and newer technology pushed the pace higher still. Many trains now in service average from about 150 mph, or 241 kph, up past 200 mph, or 322 kph. A few can exceed 300 mph, or 483 kph. Speeds that high are not the usual choice when passengers are aboard. Fast is true of all of them. The way they work is not the same. Three chief kinds stand out: the Shinkansen, the TGV, and the maglev. The Shinkansen. What sets a Japanese Shinkansen apart is the job of each car. Every car acts as a small electric locomotive.

5Forward push comes from each one. Extra cars may join the set, or cars may leave it, and performance stays the same. A motor in every car also means a very quick gain of speed and a very quick loss of it. Stops can come more often, and the schedule can still be kept. A Shinkansen passes Mount Fuji in Japan. Success for the TGV in France has been strong. TGV is short for train a grande vitesse. Those French words name what English calls a high-speed train. France was where these trains were used first. Gas turbines, similar to jet engines, supplied the power at the start. Electricity came later, as it had for the Shinkansen. Axles are handled differently. Each TGV car shares axles with the car ahead and the car behind. Neighboring cars rest on one base of two axles. That base is a bogie. Power is different too. Only two power cars drive a TGV set. One pulls from the front. One pushes from the rear. That push-and-pull plan costs less than the Shinkansen plan, in which every car makes its own power. The cheaper plan has a limit. Railcars cannot be added or removed with ease. Maglev. The Shinkansen and the TGV are mostly better versions of older train ideas. Maglev rests on a technology that is wholly new. The name is short for magnetic levitation. Magnets supply the power, and the train flies along the track without touching the ground.

6An electromagnet is a device of steel or of iron. It turns into a magnet only while electric current runs through a coil nearby. A maglev travels a test track in Germany. Special tracks called guideways carry a maglev. Coils sit in those guideways, and electric current runs through the coils. A household magnet can pull an object or push it away. The maglev and its guideway push and pull on each other with forces of that same kind. The train levitates. It floats above the guideway and never touches it. Friction is gone. Vibration is gone. Nothing of that sort cuts the speed or makes a noise. Quiet and pace are therefore usually better than on other fast trains. Forward motion also comes from magnetic force. An ocean wave shoving a surfer is the picture. Guideways for maglev stand in China. Building a maglev system costs more than building other fast trains. Japan runs maglev trains that riders board on ordinary scheduled trips. China does too. South Korea does too. Other countries are testing systems, or planning to build them, for later years. How a maglev stays on its path: matching magnets shove one another and hold the train in the center of the guideway. A pair of unlike magnets raises the train clear. Worries About Safety. High speed makes safety a major worry. Several protections are built into the design. A crash with a car is less likely because these lines usually do not cross a road on the same level.

7The train goes over the road or under it. Fences line many of the railways so animals stay out. Sensors warn the operators if something may be blocking the rails. On March 11, 2011, a powerful quake struck Sendai in Japan. Warning came early. Power was cut. Twenty-seven Shinkansen trains were in the struck area, and they lost that power. Emergency brakes came on by themselves. The trains stopped safely. Passengers were not injured. Protections do not erase every accident. Lightning struck nearby during China's summer in the year 2011. A fast train lost its power. A second train hit it from behind. Many lives were lost. The crash was a tragic reminder. Travel on the ground at high speed always carries some risk. Why These Trains Help. Set beside other ways of moving crowds, these trains offer many gains. A short hop can be quicker and easier by bus. A very long hop is a better job for an airplane. Trips from one hundred miles to five hundred miles suit the fast train perfectly. On those distances a bus is much slower. An airplane is no faster once you count the hours spent at the airport before the flight and after it. Comfort can be greater. Booths or tables are often there to sit at. Electrical outlets are plentiful, ready for gadgets. Around takeoff and landing, an airline passenger may not use a cell phone or another personal electronic device.

8A train passenger may use them at any moment. Reporters test the seats of a new fast train in China. Power for these trains can be drawn from many sources. Carry a normal load of passengers and the fast train uses fuel far more efficiently than a car, a bus, or an airplane. Electricity runs them, not fossil fuels, so they do not themselves let out the greenhouse gases that feed climate change. Coal still makes much of the world's electric power. That share is expected to fall as the world turns to sources that can last, such as the sun and the wind. The trains should therefore grow even kinder to the environment as years pass. A further major gain is relief for other transport systems. A road can hold only so many travelers at one moment. An airport has the same kind of limit. Capacity is the name for how many travelers a system can handle in an hour. Fill a highway or a freeway to that limit and huge jams follow. Movement can drop to a crawl. It can stop for hours at a stretch. Airports can overload in a similar way. Adding roads or airports to raise capacity is not a choice in many places. A railroad takes less land than a highway. A fast line can often be laid into those tight places, and the strain on the other ways of travel can ease. Jams on freeways can shrink because of these trains.

9Flying Across Spain. Spain's fast-train system is named Alta Velocidad Espanola. In Spanish the words mean Spanish high speed. The initials, AVE, are a Spanish word for bird. What Success Requires. Gains do not make fast rail the right answer for every region's transport needs. Building the systems can be very costly. Each mile of new track can cost many millions of dollars. Some countries treat that building cost as an investment in years ahead. Other countries ask whether an investment so large is worth making. A wonderful train still fails if too few people ride it. Economic sense, and environmental sense, both ask that each train carry as many passengers as it can. Building therefore fits only where crowds make the trip again and again. High population density means many people packed into a limited space. Europe has had success with these trains. Japan has had it. China has had it. One reason is that all three contain many areas where population density is high. In Germany, riders wait to board a fast train. An artist's drawing shows how fast rail could change travel in California. The Years Ahead. Growth is rushing forward. Fresh lines appear in countries that did not have them, and on continents that did not have them. Europe means to join its many separate systems into one gigantic network across the continent by 2025. Morocco is building the first system of this kind in Africa.

10In the United States, California is where the first true network is being developed. Finish it as planned and Los Angeles can be linked with San Francisco. The ride would take less than 2 hours plus 20 minutes. Speed can reach 220 mph, or 354 kph. World population is rising. Worry about energy sources is rising. Worry about the environment is rising. Fast trains will matter greatly as the world tries to meet its need to move people. Word List. An axle is a bar. Wheels turn around it. Greenhouse gases sit in the atmosphere of Earth. They trap heat. Global warming grows because of them. Economic describes what has to do with buying and selling goods and services. A network is a set of things, or of computers, joined to one another. An engineer is the person charged with running a train safely. An obstacle is something in the way, blocking progress or movement. Fossil fuels are energy sources dug from the ground. Coal is one. Oil is one. Natural gas is one. A sensor notices a signal. It also notices when conditions shift. Then it reacts. Fuel efficient describes fuel used well. Miles traveled for each gallon are the measure. Sustainable describes a use that does not use a resource up completely or damage it for good. A generator is a machine. Motion goes in. Electricity comes out. A viaduct is a low bridge over dry land or over a long valley.

93. Trains That Carried Children to Safety

1Europe in 1939 fills the opening map. A girl leaving home is the first story. A British banker arriving in Prague is the next. Hitler's plans come after that, then a call for help sent around the world. Trains full of children follow. A secret comes to light years afterward. The book ends in his own words, then explains harder vocabulary. Soldiers from Germany entered the Czech capital on military motorcycles. People stood silent and watched. Vera Gissing still remembers that invasion. March 15, 1939, was the day. She was young, and she was Jewish. Tanks woke her. Soldiers from the German army were marching. The streets were those of Prague, capital of Czechoslovakia. Rooms in the family house were taken over. German was the only language the soldiers would allow. Her father would not obey. A soldier spat. She saw the spit hit his face. The day was bad. Worse days were coming. Girls from the Eberstark family left the station in Prague on a day like that. Their parents were never seen by them again. Gissing's own departure is just as clear in her memory. Dozens of other Prague children shared the train her parents chose for her. Her eleventh birthday had not yet arrived. Best clothes were what she wore. A tag with a number hung from her neck. Steam from the engines rose at the main railroad station. It wrapped around parents and children waiting to say goodbye. Children were held close. Love was whispered. Hope was whispered. Speaking in 2002, she said the anguished look on her parents' faces that morning would stay with her forever. The memory was already sixty-three years old. England in 1938 is the setting of one picture. A German Jewish girl has arrived. In her hands are a doll and a little bag. Children climbed aboard one after another. England was where the train was bound. Gissing kept trying to hold her parents' faces in sight as the cars pulled out.

2She did not yet know those faces were gone from her life. She also could not foresee the fate waiting for them, or for most of the other parents standing there. They would be sent off to die. A man from Great Britain was unknown to her then. He chose to save her. For nearly fifty years he told nobody what he had done. London in 1938 was home to a banker named Nicholas Winton. He was twenty-nine. A ski trip in the Alps was the Christmas plan he shared with Martin Blake, a close friend. The Alps never happened. Blake, just before the departure, asked Winton to join him in Prague instead. Humanitarian work was already Blake's task there. Jewish families by the thousands had been forced out of the Sudetenland. That region lies in the north of Czechoslovakia. Food was needed. Other help was needed. Jewish organizations and Christian organizations worked side by side. Among the Jewish groups were Youth Aliyah and the Children's Aid Society. The Kindertransport was another. Winton once explained the trip. Europe's crisis had been their topic again and again, close to daily. He had not imagined that he himself would start working. The job turned personal because of his background. The family line was German and Jewish. Christianity was the faith his parents took up when they moved to England as immigrants. Stay in Germany, and the desperate case might have been theirs. Adolf Hitler, Germany's leader, was behind a sinister plot, and the Sudetenland takeover was one piece of it. Anger still burned from his years as a soldier. Germany's defeat in World War I, in 1918, was the wound. He laid part of the blame for that loss on Jewish people. He laid part of the blame for the depression that followed on them too.

3Black people were blamed. Disabled people were blamed. LGBTQ+ people were blamed. Roma people were blamed. In his view Jewish people formed an inferior race. Murder, he believed, was required if society was to be rid of them entirely. He helped start the German Worker's Party once the war had ended. The Nazi Party grew out of it. Restoring Germany's power in the world was the goal. Crowds responded when he spoke. He could stir them. He could push them toward action. Popularity followed, and then the title of chancellor. Control of the government was seized. Every rival political party was banned. The military began to grow. A secret plan aimed at land Germany had been compelled to surrender. The Treaty of Versailles, signed when World War I ended, was the document that had taken that land. A 1938 picture shows him shouting before a crowd. The country is Austria. Some residents of the Sudetenland raised a salute when German troops came in. Fear drove others out. Motion on the plan began in 1936. France had been given certain land, and by 1940 Hitler had taken that land back. Austria fell to him earlier, by two years. He had been born there. Objection came from leaders in other European countries. Intervention did not. Stopping him was left undone. The Sudetenland was the next target after Austria. Germany and Czechoslovakia share a border there, and German was the language of many local people. France, Great Britain, and Italy sent leaders to meet him in 1938. The Czechs counted those three as allies. War was the outcome they refused. His demands were signed into the Munich Agreement. German rule received the Sudetenland. Citizens across Europe already doubted him. Further conquests, they believed, were his real intention. Fear ran especially deep among Jewish people. Law after law in Hitler's Germany had been aimed at them. A lawyer's work was closed.

4A doctor's work was closed. A journalist's work was closed. Public hospitals could not be used. After age 14, public schools could not be attended. A marriage was banned if the other person was not Jewish. One belief fed every rule. Greatness, Hitler thought, would return only after Germany was cleansed of races he judged inferior. Wartime photographs often show Jewish men, women, and children wearing a star with six points. Two triangles fitted together are a common way to draw it. Another name is the Star of David. For thousands of years it has stood as a symbol of Judaism. Nazi orders during the war put that star on every Jewish person. Identification by non-Jewish people became easy. Shame was the point of the badge. Discrimination was the result the badge was meant to stir. The order covered every Jewish person older than six, in each country under German control. Steps grew harsher. Jewish people born in Poland, and Jewish people born in Russia, were to be collected by the army and taken out of Germany. Only what a person could carry was allowed. Homes were left behind. Trucks took some of them. Wagons took others. The border was where they were dumped. Being forced out was still not the worst. Nazi concentration camps soon held 30,000 Jewish people from Germany, seized and hauled there by the army. Think of a camp as a prison. Life there meant work under torturous strain that broke bodies. Execution was what Hitler ordered next. Terror pushed Jewish people all across Europe to flee Nazi persecution. Prague's Jewish citizens, who were citizens of Czechoslovakia, were already packed into filthy camps. Those camps were meant only as brief shelters. A visit from Winton showed him how bad the conditions were. New homes were the aim of some aid groups. He saw that elderly people and sick people got the attention.

5Czechoslovakia's Jewish children seemed to have no plan at all. Saving them became his decision. His words appear in a film made in 2002 about his life. Bad is how he described the situation. Refugees and helpers alike felt time was running out. Germans would reach the rest of Czechoslovakia soon. Escape looked impossible. No destination was obvious. They were stuck. A hotel on Wenceslas Square became his base in Prague. The dining room held his table, and he sat there day after day. Parents arrived hoping to place children where Hitler could not reach them. Families outside Czechoslovakia were the shelter he wanted to find. Trains were already moving thousands of Jewish children out of Germany and out of Austria toward safety in Great Britain. That program's name was the Kindertransport. A similar effort, he believed, could rescue thousands of children from the Czech lands. News traveled quickly. Families learned that an Englishman was working from Wenceslas Square. Hundreds of desperate families crowded the hotel. Two assistants were hired so the families could be helped. England was his next stop. Homes had to be found. Money for the rescue had to be raised. Refugee families from the Sudetenland were housed in a Czechoslovak school. Youngsters and adults lay crowded together. Straw mattresses on the floor were the beds, and people slept side by side. Letters went out from London to governments in many countries. Winton asked each one to accept the children. Refusal was common. A child without parents was against the law in those places. Help came from only two: Sweden, and Great Britain. Strict rules still governed entry to England. Every child needed a family waiting. A fee was also required. It was meant to pay, later, for sending the children back to Czechoslovakia when safety returned. Each child cost fifty pounds. People treated that price as a small fortune. Donors were asked for whatever they could give.

6The gap was filled by Winton himself. Ads in papers all over Great Britain sought families. Religious organizations were asked as well. Photographs of the children were sent or posted nationwide. He hoped a human face would move strangers to act. Paperwork was the other battle. Contacts in the German government and in the British government were pressed for permits. Children had to cross Europe. They had to be allowed into England. Delay sometimes led Winton, with a few helpers, to create permits that were not genuine. His comment was that the group had only made a slow system move faster. Currency in Great Britain is the pound. Fifty pounds in 1939 equaled a small fortune. The same sum was worth over 3,400 dollars in U.S. money. Look at the route of 1939. Children rode out of Prague, crossed the whole of Germany, and reached Holland's coast. A ferry carried them over the English Channel. Another train finished the trip in London. Seven trainloads made that journey. The first success came by air, not by rail. March 14, 1939, sent the earliest group, fifteen children, from Prague toward Great Britain. Six further months brought seven trains out of Wilson Railway Station. Holland waited, then the coast, then the boat across the Channel. New families took the children in their arms at a London station. Winton watched, smiling. He is photographed in 1939 with one small child he had brought out of Czechoslovakia. Safety was reached by 669 children in all. Keepsakes from home traveled with some of them. Letters of thanks, written by parents to the new British families, traveled too. Family houses took most of the children. A boarding school for Czech pupils in Wales took others. Plans existed for train number eight. The date was to be September 3, 1939. Another 250 children would have been aboard. Poland was invaded by Hitler's army that same day.

7Borders under German control all slammed shut. Nobody ever saw that train or those children again. Nearly six years of horrible fighting followed. Lives lost passed six million. Countries around the globe were pulled in. People came to call that war World War II. Male prisoners stand on one side of a barbed-wire fence in a picture. Female prisoners stand on the other. The place is a German concentration camp, and a guard keeps watch. Hitler's decision in 1941 was that every Jewish person must be killed. The decision belonged to his war plans. Concentration camps swallowed millions. Work continued until people grew too weak to live. Dying that way still seemed too slow to the regime, which was brutal. Murder replaced waiting. The name Holocaust is given to this attempt to wipe out the Jewish population. Shoah is a Hebrew word some Jewish people use instead. A whirlwind of destruction is what it means. Murder during the war took six million Jewish people. Children were more than a million of that number. People who were not Jewish were murdered in the millions as well. Human history holds few crimes judged more atrocious. Rescue work ended when the war closed in. Other help was what Winton looked for next. Relief work with the Red Cross occupied him. The Royal Air Force came later, and he learned to fly as a pilot. Peace returned him to banking. Marriage and a family followed. Silence about the children lasted until 1988. Grete, his wife, found the secret without meaning to. An attic hid a leather briefcase gone dusty. A worn scrapbook inside held the children's pictures. Each photo sat beside a name, plus notes about that child's family back in Czechoslovakia. The British family that had offered to guard the child in wartime was recorded too. Papers and letters spelled the work out in detail.

8She pressed him to speak. An article appeared in a newspaper. A British television program, That's Life, told his story in that same year. The audience held a surprise. Rescued children, more than two dozen of them, had come to thank him. The reunion was emotional, and the author Vera Gissing was there. A biography of Winton is one book she has written since. Another book tells her own war childhood. In her words, he got most of the Jewish children of her Czech generation out. Meeting a parent again was rare. Concentration camps were where those parents perished. Stay behind, and the children would have been killed next to them. She says they had been spirited away, and that was the difference. One generation is not the end of the story. Descendants of the 669 children now number as many as 5,000. A London station picture shows some of Winton's Children coming to meet the man who rescued them. They were marking seventy years since the evacuation. Old age has replaced the childhood flight. The name Winton's Children is one many of them still use. Research science, religious leadership, and film are fields where some of them later did remarkable work. Honors have come from the government of Great Britain and from the government of the Czech Republic. Queen Elizabeth II made him a knight in 2002. Bravery, service, or success is what that award marks. The Czech Republic's highest honor reached him in 2014. The award is titled Order of the White Lion. A far-off planet carries his name, given by two astronomers from the Czech lands. Kneeling was how he received knighthood in 2002, one of the highest honors his country gives. Soldiers once stood almost alone in that title. Artists can be knighted now. Athletes can. Politicians, humanitarians, inventors, and scientists can. Others can too. Great Britain's monarch performs the ceremony, or some other member of the Royal Family.

9Kneeling comes first. Each shoulder is tapped with a sword. A medal follows, and a title. A man who is a British citizen becomes sir. A woman who is a British citizen becomes dame. One picture places Winton next to a train. The journey copied the final portion of the old ride linking Prague with London, and in that way it honored the past. Seventy years after his last train, the year 2009 brought a railroad trip along the same path his children had ridden. People he had saved rode again. Liverpool Street station in London is where he waited, arms wide, to greet them. His 100th birthday celebration had happened only a few months before. Gissing grew up thinking of a savior and not knowing the man's name. Winton, for a long stretch of years, believed he had done nothing worth special praise. Meeting her, and meeting others he had saved, was what finally let him see the scale of what he had made possible. She helped write a book whose title names Nicholas Winton and also names the Rescued Generation. The year of that book was 2002. She writes of parental courage as war clouds gathered. Strangers in another country had to receive their only children. Families in Britain had to agree to take them. Strip Winton out of the story, she says, and every hope and every offer of help would have failed. She can sit in a garden now because of him. Grandchildren play. Laughter reaches her. Her daughter's voice calls the family inside for tea. The scene is ordinary. She says she can never treat it as something she was owed. A candid photo shows the two of them together. Laughter in one picture belongs to Winton and to a grandson. The boy's grandmother was a girl saved seventy years before. After the secret surfaced, Winton talked often about why he had acted for the Czech children.

10Heroic is a word he refused. Special is a word he refused. Silence, he said, fit a deed he did not see as grand. He had noticed events unfolding, and he had given whatever help he could. A ring was the thanks some saved people offered. Its inscription comes from the Talmud, a book of Jewish law. Save a single life, the line teaches, and the world is saved with it. Death came for Sir Nicholas Winton on July 1, 2015. He was 106. The day matched an anniversary, the 76th, of one departure from Prague. That journey had taken the biggest group of children, a count of 241. Words in this book can be read as follows. Anguished describes a person full of pain or of grief. Jewish can refer to a people's culture, to a religion, or to a group identity. Atrocious describes what is cruel, evil, or extremely bad. A keepsake is kept, or given, so a person, a place, or an event will not be forgotten. People held in a concentration camp are kept there against their will. Conditions are usually harsh. The reason is membership in an ethnic group, a minority, or a political group. If a law or a rule forbids something, that thing has been prohibited. Refugees run from famine, from war, from persecution, or from a natural disaster. Often they have nowhere definite to land. Hebrew points to the ancestors of today's Jewish people, those who lived around Jerusalem. A regime is government in a form that is rigid and that controls tightly. Systematic killing by the Nazis in World War II, above all of Jewish people, is the Holocaust. To be spirited away is to be carried off in secret. Humanitarian work is help for people, above all help that lessens pain and suffering.

94. True Bandits of the Frontier West

1The parts of this book come in this order. A deadly day in Coffeyville comes first. Then comes the James-Younger Gang. Then comes the Kid. Then comes the Buck Gang. Then comes the Wild Bunch, led by Butch Cassidy. Then comes why these stories became legend. A word list comes last. A group called the Dalton Gang had three brothers at its head. Bob Dalton was one. Emmett Dalton was another. Gratton Dalton was the third. A Deadly Day in Coffeyville The same three brothers were the outlaws people followed under the Dalton name. The frontier inside the Oklahoma Territory was the ground they crossed. That land is the state of Oklahoma today. Banks were robbed. Trains were held up. The crimes came in the early 1890s. They wanted a bolder act of banditry. They were sure it would bring fame. They were sure it would bring fortune too. The plan was to rob two banks at one time. The town was Coffeyville, Kansas, the place they came from. The date was October 5, 1892. Coffeyville is where the brothers rode in. Two accomplices rode with them. Fake mustaches and goatees were part of the disguise. The plan came apart fast. Street construction forced them to tie the getaway horses a block from the banks. Old neighbors were not fooled by the fake hair. Word spread through town that the gang had arrived and meant trouble. When the robbers stepped out carrying the loot, townspeople were already armed. The guns had been borrowed from a hardware store nearby. Until 1890 the Dalton brothers had worked as lawmen. They turned to crime after they were not paid for a job. The shooting lasted twelve minutes. Four people from town were dead. Four of the five outlaws were dead too. Emmett Dalton was the only one of the gang still alive, and he was badly hurt. A court tried him and gave him life in prison. Fourteen years later he was paroled, because his behavior had been good. The Dalton Gang’s end shows how outlaw life often went. It was harsh. It was violent. It was short. Books, movies, and television later made those Wild West deeds look grander than they were.

2The criminals are shown as gunfighters who fear nothing. They are shown as joking figures like Robin Hood. They are shown as cruel villains. The real record was much duller and meaner. A jail in that West was not a place anyone would call grand. Frank James is on the left in one photo. Jesse, the younger brother, is on the right. James and the Youngers The Old West had many dangerous bands. The gang built around the James brothers and the Younger brothers was among the worst. A Missouri farm was where Jesse grew up. Frank, who was older, grew up on that farm too. Enslavement was splitting the region. It was splitting the nation as well. Slavery was legal in Missouri. South of it lay states that also allowed slavery. North of it lay states that did not. People were enslaved by the James family. The family took the South’s side in the Civil War. Both brothers were with guerrilla fighters by 1864, and killing was part of that riding. Frank’s age was twenty-one. Jesse’s age was sixteen. Another photo shows the Younger family. From the left the brothers are Bob, then Jim, then Cole. Henrietta, their sister, stands with them. Fighting ended in 1865. Missouri’s people began putting lives back together. Farm work was not what the James brothers went home to do. Their skills were narrow and specific. A different trade fit those skills. Liberty, Missouri, saw about a dozen riders come in. The date was February 13, 1866. Clay County’s savings bank was the target. The take was 62,000 dollars. That was an enormous amount then. For ten years after that, one robbery followed another. At some of those times the Younger brothers were with them. Cole was one. Jim was one. Bob was one. Still other outlaws came and went. The raids hit dozens of banks. Small towns in Missouri supplied most of the targets. A Kansas City fair lost its ticket office to them in 1872. They planned like a drilled military unit. They hit targets with precision. Bank tellers and townspeople were sometimes left dead or wounded when the riders left.

3The gang shifted from one hideout to another. Friends helped them stay ahead of lawmen. Help also came from people who had sided with the South while that war was fought. Newspapers received letters written by Jesse James. The letters denied what the gang had done, or tried to excuse it. Editors who sympathized with him helped shape what the public believed. He wanted people to see his men as “bold robbers.” He also wanted them seen as Robin Hoods of their own time. Little evidence shows the gang ever gave to anyone except its own members. In 1873 the targets changed. Trains were robbed. Stagecoaches were robbed. Tens of thousands of dollars came out of safes and lockboxes. Money also came from the pockets of passengers. Authorities answered with manhunts that kept growing. Rewards as high as 25,000 dollars were offered for the James brothers. Nothing came of those rewards. In 1876 about ten outlaws traveled to Minnesota. Their target was the First National Bank in the town of Northfield. Local people saw what was happening and armed themselves quickly. Within minutes they poured heavy fire onto outlaws who were stunned. The gang shot a path out of town. Two members of the gang were dead. Two people from town were dead. A huge manhunt followed. Two weeks later the three Younger brothers were caught. They were wounded. A court convicted them and sent them to prison. Frank and Jesse got away and rode back to Missouri. They still did not quit. A new gang was formed. Now and then they robbed a bank, a train, or a stagecoach. On April 3, 1882, a member of Jesse’s own gang killed him. Frank James soon surrendered himself. He thought his brother’s ending would be his own. Dozens of heists were the gang’s total. The dead numbered at least seventeen. More deaths are likely. Frank faced a jury in Missouri. The year was 1885. The jury refused to call him guilty. Books Sold for a Dime Paperbacks known as dime novels were inexpensive, and crowds bought them. Sales ran through the nineteenth century.

4They ran into the early twentieth century as well. Ten cents was a typical price. Some copies cost even less. Made-up stories of frontier bandits and of lawmen were some of the best sellers. Writers produced the tales quickly. Real criminals were often dropped into the plots. To give readers a thrill, events were stretched past the truth. Some plots were invented outright. Indigenous nations were drawn falsely in many of these books. Those peoples already lived in the West when the outlaws arrived. The pages called them violent. The pages called them hostile. The pages called them savage. Jesse James and the riders with him were handled another way. Writers made them antiheroes who excited an audience. An antihero stands at the center of a story. Readers like that character. The character still does not behave as a hero would. The Kid For notoriety, the Jameses and the Youngers may top every other gang of the period. Among single outlaws, one nickname is recognized faster than the rest. That nickname is Billy the Kid. Birth papers name him Henry McCarty. The year was 1859. The city was New York. The New Mexico Territory is where his early teenage years were spent. A laundry in 1875 lost clothes to him, and a jail held him for the theft. He left by climbing out through the chimney. The Arizona Territory was the place he ran to. Reports say that 1877 brought the first time he shot a man. Jail followed once more. So did another escape. New Mexico was where he returned. By then he used the name William H. Bonney. People said “the Kid” because his looks and his manner were boyish. The Lincoln County War is the fight that turned his life fully toward crime. The New Mexico Territory was the setting. Ranchers there fought over land. They fought over money. They fought over power. John Henry Tunstall, young and British, hired him as a hand on a ranch. The two grew close. Tunstall’s enemies had real power. February 1878 is when those enemies’ gang killed Tunstall. Sheriff William J. Brady led the gang. The sheriff’s pay came from a man who competed with Tunstall.

5Soon after that killing, the Kid joined a group called the Regulators. April brought an ambush. Sheriff Brady died in it. A deputy died with him. The Kid was a leading suspect. A warrant called for his arrest. In 1880 a reward of 5,000 dollars was added to make capture more tempting. Sheriff Pat Garrett took over the hunt. December of 1880 is when the Kid fell into Garrett’s hands. April of the next year brought the trial. The court found him guilty of murdering Sheriff Brady. The sentence was hanging. Lincoln was the town where he was locked up. On the way back from the outhouse he slipped out of his handcuffs. The guard’s revolver ended up in the Kid’s hand. That guard did not survive. Another deputy heard the shot and ran toward it. The Kid shot that deputy too. He was free again. Three months later Garrett found the fugitive. Garrett fired twice. The Kid died. Newspapers across the country carried the story. A year after that, Garrett published a book. A ghostwriter helped him. The title started with the words An Authentic Life. The rest of the title named Billy the Kid. Much of the book’s accuracy has been doubted. Even so, the account fixed the Kid’s legend in place. More than fifty movies have been made about him. Not an Ordinary Boy People called Henry McCarty a kid. Twenty-two men still died because of what he did. His life was short and brutal. Pat Garrett, sheriff in Lincoln County, wrote a biography of Billy. He wrote it only eight months after the shooting. The place was Fort Sumner, in New Mexico. Garrett’s shots came in 1881. Billy’s age was twenty-one and no more. Historians did not treat Garrett’s book as accurate. Later editions filled gaps. They also corrected details of Billy’s childhood. Readers still loved the book. The Buck Gang had five members. A photo from the day before the hanging lines them up. Maoma July is at the left. Sam Sampson stands next. Rufus Buck stands next. Lucky Davis stands next. Lewis Davis stands at the right.

6Five Riders Called the Buck Gang Rufus Buck was one of the five. Lucky Davis was another. Sam Sampson was another. Maoma July was another. Lewis Davis was the last. The land they moved through is Oklahoma now. Each man was Black, or he was Indigenous and Creek. White settlers were coming into the territory. Rufus Buck was furious about that. The other four shared his anger. Their crimes were packed into thirteen days during 1895. General stores were robbed. Horses were stolen. They shot a boy whose father served as an official at a boarding school. A deputy marshal was killed. Flatrock Creek was the site of the gun battle that captured every member. Okmulgee lies seven miles south of that creek. Arkansas was the next stop. The city was Fort Smith. A federal courtroom tried them there. Isaac C. Parker was the judge who heard it. He became known for death sentences. The count of people he sent to die was over 150. Those sentences could not be appealed. A conviction came down on each gang member. They asked the country’s highest court, the U.S. Supreme Court, to undo the verdict. That court agreed with Parker. July 1, 1896, was the day all five were hanged. Fort Smith was the place. Officers of the Law Outlaw tales come paired with tales of Old West officers. Sheriffs appear in them. Marshals appear in them. Deputies appear in them. A badge shaped like a star is pinned on the chest in the usual picture. A six-shooter sits on the hip. Some officers were appointed. Some were elected. Keeping the peace was the assignment. The work asked a lot, and danger was sometimes part of it. A number of these officers were little different from criminals. Bass Reeves shows the other kind of person the work could attract. Enslavement was in his past. The year 1875 is when he became a deputy marshal for the United States. No Black man had held that post before him. About three thousand suspects were brought to justice through his work. His mind and his courage were what he relied on. Cassidy’s Wild Bunch Western towns, and western states, wanted to drop a lawless name as the nineteenth century closed.

7Outlaw stories still entertained people. Leaders in politics and in business did not want their banks robbed. They did not want their trains stopped and looted. They did not want their cattle rustled. They did not want their citizens put in fear. Law kept extending its reach toward the gangs. A telegraph, or a newspaper, could report a crime faster than the riders could find a hiding place. Fame for outlaw behavior still came to the Wild Bunch while the frontier era ended. The leader was Butch Cassidy. The Rocky Mountains were the region. The years ran from 1889 through 1901. Robert Leroy Parker was the name given at birth to the man called Butch Cassidy. Utah was the birthplace. The year was 1866. Ranch work is what he left home to find, while he was still in his early teens. The surname Cassidy may have come from a friend who stole cattle. Butch is said to recall a stint spent working where meat was cut. The first bank he robbed, with accomplices beside him, was in 1889. Telluride, Colorado, was the town. The theft was more than 20,000 dollars. A lonely stretch of Wyoming is where they hid after the escape. He repeated a pattern several times. Take the money, ride far, and stay quiet. Horse theft brought an arrest five years later. The prison term was two years. Release is when he pulled the Wild Bunch together. One rider was Elzy Lay. Another was Ben Kilpatrick. Another was Will Carver. Another was Harvey Logan, known as Kid Curry. More riders joined them. Harry Longabaugh came in during 1897. People came to call Longabaugh the Sundance Kid. Trains and banks were the holdup targets. The stolen sums reached the tens of thousands of dollars. Humor, of a defiant kind, was part of Cassidy’s style. A Nevada bank the gang had already robbed once received a photo of the riders in the mail. Cassidy’s note thanked that manager for letting them make a “withdrawal.” Another photo lines the Wild Bunch up. The left-hand man is Harry Longabaugh, also called the Sundance Kid.

8Next is William Carver, who went by News. Next is Ben Kilpatrick, called the Tall Texan. Next is Harvey Logan, or Kid Curry. The man on the right is Robert LeRoy Parker, the one known as Butch Cassidy. A name grew around the gang for keeping clear of violence. The name may not have matched the truth.
