A boast is credited to Cassidy. He claimed no man had ever died by his own hand. The desperadoes who rode with him could not say that. National newspapers gave the Wild Bunch a following, as they did for other gangs that lasted. Officers were drawing closer. Wyoming, in 1899, was where the gang robbed a train. What followed was a fierce hunt by a very large posse. Hunters from the Pinkerton agency, the National Detective Agency, were on the trail as well. Cassidy slipped away once more. Capture or death found several of the others. Argentina was the next move, a year later. Cassidy went. Longabaugh went. Etta Place, a friend to the gang, went too. They bought a ranch and lived there. After that, the record turns unclear. One photo places William A. Pinkerton in the middle. Pat Connell, a special agent for the railroad, is on the left. Sam Finley is on the right. Argentina’s turn came in 1905, when two outlaws from America robbed a bank there. Witnesses described men who matched Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. Bolivia, in 1908, lost a payroll in a robbery. The same pair was blamed. Both of those outlaws died in the shooting that followed. For a long time, historians treated that battle as Cassidy’s last stand, and as the Sundance Kid’s too. Rumors in the years after said the pair had slipped back into this country. The rumors said the outlaw life was over for them. A ranch in Utah was the new start credited to Longabaugh. People close to Cassidy, friends and family, said he came to see them long after the reported deaths. Proof of those visits has never appeared. Women Outlaws, Called Bandit Queens Arizona, in 1899, is where Pearl Hart stopped a stagecoach.

9An accomplice was with her. The take was over 400 dollars. A week was enough time for the law to catch both of them. Papers across the country carried the story. The reason was simple. Hart was a woman. Time with Cassidy’s Wild Bunch included Etta Place. It also included Laura Bullion. The “Bandit Queen” name belonged to Belle Starr. Myra Maybelle Shirley was the name she was born with. Missouri was where she grew up. The James brothers were people she knew. The Younger brothers were people she knew. Sam Starr became her husband. Horse theft brought an arrest for the couple in 1883. A conviction followed. The year 1889 is when she was killed. She was riding toward home. The attack was an ambush. No one ever solved it. Stories That Turned into Legend Only a brief span of American history is what people mean by the Old West. Wagons with covers crossed that span. Drives of cattle crossed it. So did gunfights, and so did frontier towns with little law. A few decades held the whole rise and the whole fade. The year 1900 found it almost finished. What remains is a mythical picture. Heroes fill the tales. Villains fill them. Hardship and courage fill them too. Outlaws stand in the middle of that myth. One version makes them charming desperadoes. That version adds hearts of gold, already worn down. Another version makes them killers with no pity. Survival meant taking what belonged to others. It meant staying about a day of riding ahead of any officer. Excitement is easy to imagine. Fear was the feeling that did not leave. People still ask why these criminals hold attention. One answer is the dream of danger that never stops, and of moments that decide who lives. Another answer is the pleasure of picturing every rule tossed aside. The pull, whatever it was, grabbed many American imaginations in that era. It grabs them now. A map marks where these outlaws struck. All of the places lie west of the Mississippi. The Dalton Gang On June 1, 1892, marked A, they robbed a train at Red Rock, in Indigenous Peoples’ Territory.

10On October 5, 1892, marked B, they attempted a bank robbery in Coffeyville, Kansas. The James-Younger Gang On February 13, 1866, marked C, they robbed a bank in Liberty, Missouri. On September 26, 1872, marked D, they robbed a ticket office at the Kansas City Exposition, in Kansas City, Missouri. On July 21, 1873, marked E, they robbed a train in Adair, Iowa. On September 7, 1876, marked F, they attempted a bank robbery in Northfield, Minnesota. Billy the Kid On August 18, 1877, marked G, he killed a man at Fort Grant, in Arizona. On January 10, 1880, marked H, he killed a gunman at Fort Sumner, in New Mexico. On April 28, 1881, marked I, he killed two lawmen in the New Mexico town of Lincoln. Cassidy’s Gang, Called the Wild Bunch On June 24, 1889, marked J, they robbed a bank in Telluride, Colorado. In 1894, marked K, there was a horse theft in Dubois, Wyoming. On June 2, 1899, marked L, they robbed a train in Wilcox, Wyoming. On September 19, 1900, marked M, they robbed a bank in Winnemucca, Nevada. The Buck Gang On July 30, 1895, marked N, they killed John Garrett, a deputy marshal of the United States, in Okmulgee, Oklahoma. Words to Know stint (n.): a stretch of time spent at a job or an activity. glamorized (v.): made something look more appealing or more exciting than it truly was. guerrilla (n.): a fighter in a small, independent band that usually attacks by surprise. accomplices (n.): people who help someone do a wrong or illegal act. heists (n.): thefts from a person or a place; robberies. ambushed (v.): attacked by surprise from a hiding place. desperadoes (n.): people who take daring, risky actions that are often crimes. notorious (adj.): famous mainly because the thing they are known for is bad. posse (n.): a group a sheriff gathers to help catch criminals or to enforce the law. polarized (v.): split apart by clashing opinions, beliefs, or ideas. exploits (n.): acts that are remarkable or heroic. flaunted (v.): showed something openly so other people would notice.

95. Tusks, Trade, and Living Elephants

1A hippo in one photo is not a living animal. It is a carving made from ivory. The parts of this book come in this order. Treasures that are hard to trust come first. Then comes a definition of ivory. Then comes what elephants are like. Then comes the buying and selling of ivory. Then comes the work of saving elephants. Then comes how little time is left. A word list comes last. Treasures That Are Hard to Trust Your tour of several countries in Asia is nearly done. A perfect souvenir for home is still missing. Tents stand in busy lines, with carts and tables among them. You walk along those lines. The place is an outdoor market. The noise pushes you toward the far end. One table there draws your attention. Sculptures cover the table. Most of them show animals. Two small white pieces are labeled “ivory.” The price is high. They are beautiful. They are small enough to carry on a long flight home. The seller talks about the artist who carved them. He stresses the skill in the work. He says the pieces will last forever. Key facts are left out. He never says what ivory is. He never says how it was obtained. He never mentions the illegal trade in wildlife. That trade is what makes such sculptures available. He never mentions the brutal killing of elephants. What Ivory Is Ivory is a hard substance, cream in color. It forms the tusks of elephants. Less often, the same word is used for tusks of other animals. Walruses have such tusks. Hippos have them. Narwhals, a kind of whale, have them. Wild boars have them. A tusk is a very long tooth. It sticks out of the mouth even when the mouth is shut. In most mammals that have tusks, the tusk is an upper canine tooth. In elephants, the tusks are the front teeth, called incisors. The material is dentine, a hard bony tissue. Enamel, which is harder, covers the tips of an elephant’s tusks. Time wears that enamel away.

2Tusks keep growing for the elephant’s whole life. A photo shows an African elephant skull with the tusks still in place. Living elephants belong to an African kind or an Asian kind. Of the two, the African kind is larger. They divide further into forest elephants and savanna elephants. Both males and females grow tusks in each of those species. Savanna elephants are the bigger species. Their tusks can pass 2.1 meters in length. That is about 7 feet. Among Asian elephants, some males grow tusks that stand out. Other males, and most females, grow tusks that are thin and short. Those short tusks often break off. A tusk is a structural adaptation. It gives an elephant a better chance to survive. Food can be gathered with tusks and carried with them. Roots and minerals can be dug up. Tusks are used for display. They are used as weapons. In the dry season, some elephants dig water holes with them. The trunk gains protection from the tusks. The base of each tusk sits deep in the upper jaw. Killing the elephant is the only way to take those tusks. One photo shows digging. Another shows lifting. Both jobs use the tusks. About Elephants No land animal on Earth is larger. Height at the shoulder can reach 3 meters. That is about 10 feet. Weight for a male of the African kind can reach 6 metric tons. That is about 13,200 pounds. The body lumbers. The ears are huge. The trunk is huge. Even so, these animals are extremely intelligent. Brain size compared with body size matches our own. The complexity matches too. They rank among the most intelligent animals on Earth. Old Relatives Mastodons and mammoths once shared a mammal family with elephants. No other member of that family is still alive. Both of those are extinct. The closest living relatives are hyraxes. A hyrax is small, furred, and a plant-eater. It looks a little like a prairie dog. Manatees are also close relatives. Dugongs are too. Those two look as if dolphins would be nearer kin.

3Even so, elephants, hyraxes, manatees, and dugongs share one ancestor from long ago. A hyrax can weigh up to 5 kilograms. That is about 11 pounds. A dugong can weigh up to 300 kilograms. That is about 661 pounds. Top weight for an elephant is 11,000 kilograms. That is about 24,251 pounds. In South Africa, a matriarch leads her family toward a water hole. Elephants solve problems with skill. They use tools. They often invent new methods by working as a group. Some live into their seventies, as long as some humans. Social bonds are strong. Female family groups last for life and span several generations. An older female, the matriarch, guides them. She keeps the family together. She keeps them safe. She leads them to food and to water. In a drought, a matriarch has been known to find a water hole not visited for decades. Emotions are complex. Elephants have been seen laughing and playing. They show deep compassion. When one is in distress, others stand beside her. Trunks soothe her. Soft sounds comfort her. Humans do something similar for a troubled friend. We use a hand, not a trunk. Grief appears when a family member dies. Two young African elephants mourn an adult female who has died. Intelligence is not the only reason elephants matter in the animal kingdom. Scientists call them a keystone species. Many other species depend on a keystone species. Balance in the ecosystem depends on elephants. Water holes they dig also serve other animals. Trees and bushes they clear open habitat for grassland species. Trails they make can slow a spreading fire. The same trails help water drain. Some seeds will not start to grow until they have passed through an elephant’s gut. Dung can enrich worn-out soil enough for people to raise crops. In short, the ecosystems they live in need them. Around 1925, a hunter in Sudan poses with trophies from elephants. The Ivory Trade People have prized ivory for thousands of years. It has been carved into art. It has been made into jewelry and into many other objects.

4Tusks have been one reason Asian elephants were killed. They have also been killed for meat and for skin. African elephants still suffer more from the trade. Two facts explain that gap. One fact is tusk size. African tusks are bigger. Females grow tusks as well as males, which makes more ivory available. Across two centuries, the drop in numbers is hard to face. An estimate for the year 1800 put Africa’s elephants at twenty-six million. In the early 1900s, wealthy people from the West liked to kill African elephants on safari. Demand was also high for ivory goods. Piano keys were one item. Pool balls were another. Combs and brush handles were others. National Geographic is one source for what came next. By 1913, yearly ivory use in the United States was about 181 metric tons. That is about 200 tons. African elephants were down to about ten million. Demand jumped sharply again in the 1970s and the 1980s. Poachers were taking African elephants at an estimated pace of one hundred thousand a year. Poached means killed against the law. The animals were in serious trouble. Something had to stop the decline, and it had to happen fast. A Word on Poaching Poaching usually means taking a wild animal against a law written to protect wildlife. The act may be a hunt. It may be a capture. It may be a killing. Illegal traps and illegal shooting are included. The land may be public. It may be private. Profit is the most common motive. Sport is another. Rangers and game wardens are the people who enforce the laws against it. In Kenya, rangers and vets try to free an elephant’s feet from a poacher’s snare. A 2016 photo shows a parks official in Zimbabwe looking over ivory the country has stored. In 1989 an international agreement called CITES banned the ivory trade. Say the name SY-teez. The agreement governs trade in plants and animals that are endangered. The ban made the public far more aware of the crisis.

5Prices fell steeply as buyers pulled away. Elephant numbers began to recover. The worldwide ban could have led to a long recovery for African elephants. Ten years of rising numbers changed the politics. Four African countries asked CITES for permission to sell ivory they had stored. Namibia made the request. Botswana made it. Zimbabwe made it. South Africa made it. They said elephant numbers at home were stable, or were going up. They also said the sales would be limited. Only tusks from natural deaths would be sold, they said. Tusks from earlier culling would be included. Culling means killing elephants to hold their numbers down where space is limited. CITES allowed a sale in 1999. Buyers had to be countries with strict rules against illegal trade. No buyer except Japan met the test. A second sale came in 2008. This time both Japan and China bought ivory. That second sale raised demand, which was not the plan. It also suggested that legal trade might return someday. Illegal killing for tusks then shot upward. Many countries began storing ivory. They hoped for huge profits later. Some countries have burned the ivory they stored. Burning means that ivory can never be traded outside the law. A figure of 26 million sits beside this story. The crisis has kept growing. It has reached a tipping point. Each year, poachers now kill more African elephants than are born. If that pattern is not reversed quickly, elephants face doom. Doom would not wait for a far-off age that nobody can picture. It can arrive within the lives of people alive now. WildlifeDirect put the 2018 count of living African elephants under 400,000. The yearly kill was about 35,000. Buyers in Asia were the reason for that ivory. Should the pace stay the same, extinction is guaranteed by 2030. A chart of African elephant numbers uses rough estimates for most years. The counts for 1979 and for 2016 are the exceptions. The Great Elephant Census is the source. Marks on the chart include 1.3 million. They include 600,000.

6They include 352,000. Years on the chart include 1800. They include 1913. They include 1979, 1989, and 2016. One label on the chart reads 10 million. In Kenya, a caretaker walks beside an orphaned elephant calf. Extinction is not the only tragedy tied to this trade. Elephants that survive a killing, and that lose family, carry trauma. Some become aggressive. Some become antisocial. Young males seem especially hurt when mothers are gone. Older males being gone hurts them too. Orphaned adolescents have gone on killing sprees. Other young elephants have been targets. Other species, including rhinoceroses, have been targets. Humans have been targets. Young females who saw killings sometimes grow up without mothering skills. They may reject their babies. Scientists are not surprised. Elephants are highly intelligent, and their social bonds are strong. Another worry is the danger facing rangers who protect them. Long ago, “poacher” usually meant a poor villager. The animals taken were few, and the meat was meant for the family. Rangers often made the arrest without violence. Today’s poachers are nothing like that. They use the newest weapons. The attacks are planned with care. April 2016 brought one such attack. Heavily armed poachers came after elephants in Garamba National Park. The park is in the Congo, in its Democratic Republic. Three rangers were killed. The park’s manager was hurt badly. Similar attacks have happened in other parts of Africa. From 2009 through 2017, wildlife poachers killed more than 450 rangers. A report dated July 2018 came from an international group of rangers. It said 107 rangers had been killed in the year before. Poaching has another result. More elephants are born with no tusks. Mozambique fought a civil war from 1977 to 1992. In Gorongosa National Park, about 2,500 elephants had lived there. Roughly 92 percent were slaughtered. Ivory paid for weapons. Meat fed the fighters. Of the 200 or so that survived, most had no tusks. Under ordinary conditions, only about 4 percent of female African elephants are born without tusks. Since that war, more than 50 percent of females born there have no tusks.

7The same rise shows up elsewhere in Africa, wherever poaching is frequent. Genetics helps explain the shift. Where ivory poaching is common, a tuskless elephant is more likely to live. It is therefore more likely to pass tusklessness to its young. A change like that would normally need a great many generations. Heavy poaching speeds it up. Tuskless elephants get an enormous advantage in staying alive. The situation also raises a question. How does an elephant get by with no tusks? Scientists who study elephants are only starting to look into that. Grasses make up more of the diet when tusks are missing. They eat fewer woody plants than elephants that have tusks. Nobody yet knows what that diet change will do to their health. Nobody yet knows what it will do to survival over a long time. Other Dangers Poaching is a formidable threat. Elephants face other risks too. Habitat loss is one. Long ago, elephants traveled great distances for food and water. They followed migration paths that were already ancient. Humans have pushed farther into that territory. Homes, farms, and roads have been built. Railroads and pipelines have been built. A great deal of the old range is gone. What remains is broken into pieces more and more often. Lost and broken habitat blocks the way to resources. It also separates elephant groups. Mate choice can shrink. Genetic diversity can shrink. That diversity matters for survival. Conflict with humans is another risk. More people nearby means more clashes. Outside protected areas, elephants and people compete. Food is one prize. Water is another. Space is another. Food is what draws elephants into some villages. Crops are damaged. Property is damaged. People trying to chase the animals off often leave them dead or hurt. People are sometimes killed or hurt by the elephants as well. In Kenya, people watch an elephant from the far side of a fence. The fence is there to protect crops. Culling is a third risk. Clashes can grow so severe that wildlife managers kill many elephants at once.

8The aim is to hold the numbers down. Like poaching, culling often leaves trauma in the elephants that survive. Saving Elephants Keeping elephants from extinction takes action across the world. Governments have a part. Organizations have a part. Individuals have a part. A key piece is the law. National rules and international rules need to ban ivory sold as a business. Right now, CITES forbids all commercial international trade in ivory. The ban covers African elephants. It covers Asian elephants. Several countries with large ivory markets already forbid commercial trade, or they will ban it soon. The United States is one. The United Kingdom is one. China is one. Singapore is one. A major step came in December 2017. China had been the world’s largest ivory market. It banned every domestic sale. Carving factories closed. Shops closed. Ivory is still bought and sold in some other Asian countries. Pressure is on them to follow China’s lead. A ban must also be enforced, or it fails. China’s shops stopped offering carvings like the ones in a photo. The 2017 ban is the reason. Desire for ivory is a second piece that must be solved. High demand keeps illegal trade alive even when laws exist. If demand falls sharply, trafficking stops paying. The killing of elephants stops paying with it. Conservation groups work without pause to teach the public about the danger elephants face. The teaching is especially active in Asia, where demand is still high. While they work to lower that demand, several groups report a gap in knowledge. Many people do not know that an elephant must die before its tusks can be taken. Public campaigns are correcting that false idea. In April 2019, people marched in Kenya. They marched against poaching and against the illegal wildlife trade. People Who Fight for Elephants Many people give this rescue effort their full attention. Bryan Christy, an investigative journalist, is one. He had a realistic fake tusk built. A GPS tracker was hidden inside it. He placed the tusk in an African region known for ivory poaching.

9Then he followed the path it traveled. What he found was this. African terrorists were carrying out the poaching. A terrorist group uses violence, or the threat of it, to chase its goals. Support was coming from senior officials. Some of them served in government. Some served in the military. Dr. Sam Wasser is a conservation biologist. Seattle is his base, on the faculty at the University of Washington. He studies elephant DNA in order to fight poaching. For more than twenty years he has used DNA from elephant dung. What he builds is a genetic map of elephant populations. Poached ivory can be traced to a place on that map. Law enforcement can then focus on those places. A large share of illegal ivory leaves Africa for Asia by way of Hong Kong. In 2013, three schoolgirls in Hong Kong formed a group. Nellie Shute was one. Christina Seigrist was another. Lucy Skrine was the third. They taught people that ivory and elephant deaths are connected. A petition gathered more than eighteen thousand signatures. It asked the government in Hong Kong to get rid of a huge ivory store. Smugglers had been the source of that store. The destruction finished in 2016. It was one of the largest ivory-destruction projects known. National Geographic printed his ivory findings in its edition for 2015. Local communities are another part of the rescue. People who have clashed with elephants often feel negatively about them. Those people need support, so that killing is not the only choice left. Conservation groups teach local residents about elephant habits. They teach about habitats. They teach about extinction risk from poaching and from lost habitat. They explain ways to live alongside elephants. Farmers learn from one group to set red pepper plants along the edge of a crop. The plant irritates an elephant’s eyes and nose. The elephant leaves. The groups also ask people to value elephants as a treasure belonging to the country itself. The animals can be a source of pride. They can draw tourists.

10They can bring income. Young people are urged to take part in keeping elephants alive. One photo shows a visit to an elephant orphanage in Kenya. The visitors are schoolchildren. Three elephants in Botswana walk toward a water hole. The time is sunset. Little Time Remains Picture that outdoor market in Asia once more. Beautiful ivory sculptures are still on the table. Buyers who never learn the source of ivory will not stop. Elephant numbers will keep falling. The sharp drop in elephant populations is a complex subject. It is also a controversial one. People disagree about a total ban on ivory trade versus rules that would manage the trade. Some say only a total ban can save elephants. Others say a total ban will push the illegal trade higher. Prices would rise. Poachers would have more reason to keep killing. Will time run out while people argue over the answer? The clock does not stop. For now, two facts are sure. About one hundred elephants die in this killing every day. A world that had no elephants would be a poorer place to live. Words to Know brutal (adj.): cruel, and willing to use violence without pity. essential (adj.): something that cannot be left out. habitat (n.): the outdoor home a plant or an animal is suited to. trafficking (n.): trade that the law does not allow. genetics (n.): the study of traits moving from parents into their young. consumption (n.): the taking and using of goods or resources, at times until little remains. endangered (adj.): facing a real chance of being wiped out entirely. adaptation (n.): a body feature, or a feature of a species, that improves survival in a given setting. slaughter (n.): killing people or animals in large numbers, done with cruelty. trauma (n.): deep emotional pain, most often after a frightening event. conservation (n.): care that keeps wild places safe, along with the plants and creatures in them. extinction (n.): the point at which every member of an animal group or a plant group is gone.

96. Two Species, One Offspring

1Contents. What Makes a Hybrid Animal. Hybrids People Choose to Breed. Wild Mixes and the Hard Meaning of Species. Where Ranges Meet. Why the Mix Matters. Living Things Shaped on Purpose. Hybrid Animals: Harm or Help. Words to Know. What Makes a Hybrid Animal. People in ancient Greece pictured beasts made of two animals at once. They imagined centaurs. They imagined minotaurs. They also imagined griffons and manticores. Those pictured beasts do not live in the real world. Animal hybrids do live in the real world. A hybrid brings together traits from different species. Hybrids show up more often than many people expect. An animal is a hybrid when its two parents belong to different species. Horses are one species. Donkeys are another species. The two animals look similar enough to mate. Their behavior is similar enough for mating as well. If the mother is a horse, people call the baby a mule. If the mother is a donkey, people call the baby a hinny. A mating between species does not always produce a hybrid. Parent species that are too unlike each other may produce no living young. If young are born, those young may be weak. They may be unhealthy. Healthy young from two species, such as the mule and the hinny, usually show a mix of both parents' traits. Closer kinship between the parent species raises the chance of healthy hybrid young. Alike, yet Not Identical. A hybrid's name often depends on which species was the mother. The mother's species often decides many of the hybrid's traits. In donkey-horse mixes, mules are generally larger than hinnies. Mules are also generally hardier than hinnies. Mules and hinnies, like many other hybrids, cannot produce young. They cannot make sperm. They cannot make eggs. They cannot produce offspring. Different animal species often have different numbers of chromosomes. That difference is the reason for the sterility. Mules and hinnies receive genetic information that does not match. One parent supplies thirty-two horse chromosomes. The other parent supplies thirty-one donkey chromosomes. An animal that is not a hybrid ends up with a matched set of chromosomes. A horse receives one set of thirty-two chromosomes from its mother. It receives another set of thirty-two from its father.

2Each of the horse's cells then holds two copies of every chromosome. A donkey receives thirty-one chromosomes from each parent. Each of its cells also holds two copies of every chromosome. In a hybrid, the mother's chromosomes differ from the father's. A mule does not hold two copies of any chromosome. It holds a jumble of sixty-three chromosomes. None of those chromosomes has a partner. Normal cell division does not require matched pairs. Each chromosome makes a copy of itself. One copy is sorted into each new cell. Unmatched chromosomes cause trouble when the mule tries to make reproductive cells. Most cells carry a full paired set. Sperm cells and egg cells carry only one copy of each chromosome. The process that reaches that one-copy state is called meiosis. During meiosis, each chromosome must line up with its match. One member of each pair can then be sorted into a separate cell. Horse chromosomes and donkey chromosomes do not look very much alike. They cannot form neat pairs. The dividing cell has trouble putting the right chromosomes in the right places. Some daughter cells receive too many chromosomes. Others receive too few. These cells rarely survive. Hybrids People Choose to Breed. People sometimes breed hybrids on purpose. They hope for an animal that keeps the best qualities of both parents. Mules have been bred on purpose since ancient times. They are hardier than horses. They are more sure-footed than horses. They are also easier to care for than horses. They are less likely to overeat. They are less bothered by heat. They are less likely to suffer leg injuries. Zebra hybrids are a more recent type. People sometimes call them zebroids. Zebras are wild animals. They are difficult to train for riding. They are also difficult to train to carry packs. They do not catch the same diseases as domesticated equines. A zebroid inherits a gentler personality from its domesticated parent. It inherits disease resistance from its wild parent. Beefalo are another recent hybrid. People created them to combine buffalo, also called bison, with domesticated cattle. Buffalo are hardier than cattle. Their meat is lower in fat than standard beef. Buffalo are difficult to handle. They can sometimes be dangerous.

3Handling a beefalo is as easy as handling ordinary cattle. They are much hardier than ordinary cattle. They are easier to care for. They have an efficient digestive system. That system lets them eat leaves. It also lets them eat bushes. They eat grass as well. Unlike cattle, they can withstand hot temperature extremes. They can also withstand cold temperature extremes. Their meat, like buffalo meat, does not carry much fat. Their meat has more protein than standard beef. Beefalo can have young, which zebroids and mules cannot do. Breeders must stay mindful of the mix. A ratio of three-eighths bison to five-eighths cow is ideal. If the bison share stays at or below three-eighths, reproductive problems are few. There may be none at all. A liger is the hybrid of a male lion and a female tiger. It looks like a supersized lion. It also shows faded tiger stripes. A liger's size reaches about double the size of either parent species. Hercules is the world's biggest male liger. He weighs nearly 1,200 pounds (544 kg). Ligers are usually tawny colored, like lions. They have pale bellies, like tigers. A tigon comes from the opposite pairing of parents. Its mother is a lion. Its father is a tiger. Hercules is called the world's biggest cat. He poses with his little brother Aries. Both animals are ligers. Ligers never occur naturally. Lions and tigers live in different habitats. These strange mixes can draw a crowd. Accredited zoos avoid interbreeding the big cats. Independent breeders have tried to earn money from ligers. Exotic animal preserves have tried as well. Breeders have created other big-cat hybrids. A leopon comes from a leopard and a lion. A jagulep comes from a jaguar and a leopard. A lijagulep comes from a lion and a jagulep. A male from these hybrid lines usually cannot father young. A female from these hybrid lines can usually give birth. Until recently, people could obtain hybrids only from similar species that might be willing to mate. Other species were somewhat similar. They were still unwilling to mate. Camels and llamas, even when given the chance, would rarely mate. A chart can list each hybrid, its parent species, and its traits.

4A mule is a female horse crossed with a male donkey. It has the size of a horse. It has the strength of a horse. It has the endurance of a donkey. It has the hardiness of a donkey. It has the sure-footedness of a donkey. A hinny is a female donkey crossed with a male horse. It is like a mule. It is smaller than a mule. It is less hardy than a mule. Beefalo come from bison crossed with bovine cattle. The ideal ratio is three-eighths bison and five-eighths cow. They have a cattle-like temperament. Like buffalo, they are hardier. They have a more efficient digestive system. They yield meat that is lower in fat. A zedonk is a zebra crossed with a donkey. It has the disease resistance of a zebra. Its temperament sits midway between a zebra and a domestic animal. A zorse is a zebra crossed with a horse. Its appearance is a striking combination of the two parent species. A zony is a zebra crossed with a pony. A liger is a female tiger crossed with a male lion. It grows larger than either parent. Its coat is tawny, like a lion's coat. It shows partial stripes. Some males grow a mane. A tigon is a female lion crossed with a male tiger. It is about the size of a tiger. Its appearance sits midway between a tiger and a lion. A savannah cat is a domestic house cat crossed with an African serval. It is larger than a domestic house cat. It has long legs. Its fur pattern is like a serval's pattern. Its behavior is more dog-like. A cama is a female llama crossed with a male camel. It is strong. It is smaller than a camel. It has a better temper than a camel. It is easier to handle than a camel. Modern medicine provided a way to fertilize an egg in a test tube. Fertilization no longer had to happen inside an animal. That method led to the birth of the first camel-llama hybrid. People call that hybrid the cama. Scientists hope the cama will couple a camel's hardiness with a camel's strength. They also hope it will have the llama's calmer disposition.

5Wild Mixes and the Hard Meaning of Species. Hybrids do not appear only when humans breed them on purpose. Related animal species can interbreed on their own. That can happen any time they live together and interact in the same environment. Telling which animals are hybrids can be surprisingly difficult. Defining what counts as a separate species can be surprisingly difficult too. Scientists often define a species by two important characteristics. The individuals have the potential to interbreed in nature. If they do interbreed, they can produce viable offspring. Viable offspring are healthy enough to produce offspring of their own. A Great Dane and a Chihuahua can look like a puzzle of same species or different species. Appearance alone can make that puzzle hard. These two dog breeds look quite different from each other. They are still considered the same species. The species name is Canis lupus familiaris. Two fruit flies may look like twins. They may actually be different species. Under this definition, most hybrids do not qualify as separate species. They cannot reproduce. Some are unable to reproduce because they are sterile, as mules are. Even a hybrid that can make reproductive cells may still be unable to have offspring. In 2009, off the coast of Greenland, people spotted a hybrid of a narwhal and a beluga whale. Scientists do not know whether it can produce reproductive cells. Even if it can, it needs a mate before it can produce offspring. Narwhal-beluga whale hybrids are rare. Playful names such as narlugas or barwhals have been suggested. A rare animal is unlikely to meet another of its kind. A male hybrid may also have little success with a female narwhal. He lacks the male narwhal's characteristic spiral tusk. That tusk is an important factor when a female narwhal chooses a mate. A picture can set a beluga beside a narwhal and their hybrid. Finding a mate for a narwhal-beluga hybrid depends on which animal is male and which is female. A match with a narwhal is only a maybe. A match with another hybrid is probably not going to happen. These hybrids are extremely rare. Other cases make it harder to say where a hybrid ends and a separate species begins.

6Ring species provide a strong example. Picture a group of preschoolers sitting in a circle. Each preschooler stands for a separate species. Each one sits within arm's reach of two others. Now picture them playing telephone. The first child whispers something to the second child. That child whispers to the next child. The whisper continues until the last child gets the message. The final message is usually completely different from the starting words. Changes in the whispered message are like the changes around a circle of ring species. Each species is similar to the species on either side. That pattern holds until the circle's ends overlap. Neighbors in a ring of species are alike enough to breed with each other. They do interbreed. Interbreeding stops at the overlap point. Seven salamander names help map one ring. They are picta (PIK-tuh), oregonensis (or-e-guh-NEN-sis), and platensis (plah-TEN-sis). They also include xanthoptica (zan-THOP-ti-kuh) and croceater (KROH-see-ay-tur). The last two are klauberi (KLOU-bur-y) and eschscholtzii (es-SHOHLT-zee-y). The San Joaquin Valley lies inside the ring. Every Ensatina salamander in California comes from the same ancestors in Oregon. As the animals spread southward, they adapted to specific environments. Those environments varied. The animals evolved into distinct species. The species formed a ring around the San Joaquin (wah-KEEN) Valley. The species all have slight differences. They are similar enough to interbreed with their immediate neighbors. They do not interbreed where their extremes overlap. Ensatina eschscholtzii and Ensatina klauberi do not breed with each other in southern California. At that place, the ring does not continue. Where Ranges Meet. Evidence suggests that members of ring species have changed slowly. They changed as they adapted to specific environmental conditions. Their ranges overlap in some regions. Hybrids arise where the ranges overlap. Far more animals belong to each parent species than to the hybrid group. Parent populations change very little because of these hybrids. Sometimes two species that were isolated from each other are brought together abruptly. Hybrids can then cause problems for their parent species. They may compete for food. They may compete for territory. They may compete for other resources. They may compete for mates. They may even change the genetic makeup of one original species.

7They may change both original species. In recent decades, shifts in the environment have reunited many species that once lived apart. The Arctic is where climate change has hit hardest. Warming in the Arctic is going two to four times as fast as warming in the rest of the world. Animals that belong to the Arctic are shifting the places where they naturally live. They are responding to rising temperatures. They are also responding to melting sea ice. Animals from farther south once found northern regions too cold. Those animals are extending their ranges northward. Species that used to be geographically separate are now interbreeding. Grizzly bears and polar bears are one pair. One of the first grizzly-polar bear hybrids was spotted in 2006. People call that animal a grolar bear. The bear had thick white fur. It had brown legs. It had brown paws. It had a wide head like a grizzly. Other grolar bears have been identified since that first sighting. They have been identified with increasing frequency. That pattern suggests that grizzlies and polar bears interbreed fairly frequently in the wild. At least one animal was a second-generation hybrid. That fact indicates that the hybrids are able to reproduce. One bear has not been confirmed as a grolar bear. Its body shape suggests a grizzly-polar hybrid when it is compared with other polar bears. Its short neck suggests the same thing. Its odd face suggests it as well. Why the Mix Matters. Grizzlies and polar bears might have little cubs that are brown and white. Does a change like that truly matter? If plenty of polar bears and grizzly bears were roaming the world, the answer might be no. A few hybrids would not be a big deal. That would be especially true if hybrids occurred only in a few overlap areas. Polar bears, though, could disappear as a species. When a species does not have many animals to start with, every birth makes a difference. Every polar bear that breeds with a grizzly is not bringing more polar bears into the world. The situation becomes a numbers game. More interbreeding means more dilution of polar bear genes by grizzly bear genes. Polar bear genes are specialized for surviving in the harsh Arctic environment.

8In time, the polar bear itself might be gone. A grolar bear may also fit poorly in the environment of either parent. Grolar bears kept in a German zoo seem to know, as a polar bear does, how to hunt seals. They do not seem to have its strong swimming ability. Can these hybrids last in the wild as well as animals that are not hybrids? Right now, that answer is unknown. Hybrids and a Species with Few Animals Left. If one species greatly outnumbers another, hybridization can overwhelm the species with fewer numbers. Every breeding between a polar bear, or a polar bear hybrid, and a grizzly dilutes polar bear genes further. Polar bears could simply disappear unless they breed with other polar bears as much as they breed with grizzlies. They would need to do so even more often than that. A polar bear crossed with a grizzly bear can produce young that are one-half polar bear. Those young are also one-half grizzly bear. A later cross with a grizzly bear can produce young that are one-quarter polar bear. Those young are three-quarters grizzly bear. One more cross with a grizzly bear can produce young that are one-eighth polar bear. Those young are seven-eighths grizzly bear. Hybrids are often sterile. Scientists still expect that many arctic mammals will be able to interbreed successfully with their southern cousins. The list includes grizzly bears and polar bears. It includes seals. It includes sea lions. It includes walruses, to name a few. A recent scientific list names thirty-four hybrids among arctic mammals. Climate change is likely to produce those hybrids by bringing once-separated species into contact. On the scale of evolution, northern animal species split from southern relatives not very long ago. Many of the hybrids are therefore likely to be fertile. A picture of a southern flying squirrel can stand for a meeting of cousins. Animal species are starting to meet in other regions besides the Arctic. In Ontario, Canada, southern flying squirrels seem to be using the warmer climate. They are expanding their range northward. They are moving into the domain of their cousins, the northern flying squirrels. The southern flying squirrels are smaller.

9They have white belly fur. Belly fur on the northern squirrels is gray and white. The hybrids have a mash-up of the parents' traits. Scientists studying one band of northern squirrels report a clear share. Hybrids of the two species now make up 4 percent of that group. These squirrels are similar enough genetically for the hybrids to reproduce. Living Things Shaped on Purpose. Some wanted mixes join species so different that even test-tube mating will not work. One wanted trait is the ability to produce spider silk. That ability is unique to spiders. Another wanted trait is the ability to produce large quantities of milk. That ability is limited to mammals. Few fibers in the world are stronger than spider silk. It is stronger than steel. It is more flexible than steel. It is stronger than Kevlar. It is more flexible than Kevlar. It is also hypoallergenic. It has antimicrobial properties. Those properties make it ideal for use in medicine. The fine thread is nearly invisible. It could be used during eye surgery. It could even be used to create artificial ligaments. Fourteen thousand spiders are needed to produce one ounce of spider silk. Spiders tend to eat their neighbors. No one can run a huge farm of spiders. Standard hybridization will not work when species are too different. Scientists used genetic engineering instead. They inserted silk proteins from the golden orb weaver spider into goat DNA. The goats then produce those spider silk proteins in their milk. Scientists extract the proteins in the lab. The process is still imperfect. The results are still imperfect. Someday, researchers hope, engineered goats will yield spider silk in amounts people can use. Two young goats in a picture are twins called spider kids. Armstrong is on the left. Sweet Pea is on the right. Spider genes were introduced by people. The genes were inserted into goat embryos in the laboratory. For that reason, spider goats are considered transgenic. They are not considered hybrid animals. Hybrid Animals: Harm or Help. Scientists used to see animal hybrids as a path that led evolution nowhere. Most hybrid offspring were sterile. Each parent species probably fit its own environment well. Combining their characteristics could leave the hybrid adapted to neither environment.

10In most cases, that is exactly what people see in nature. Hybrid forms tend to be poorly adapted to their environments. They often fail to survive. They often fail to reproduce. Drastic environmental change can make ordinary evolution too slow. A species may not adapt in time. Through hybrids, two species can pass genetic information to each other. The exchange can potentially combine that information in new ways. The new combinations can be useful. Do hybrid animals put the variety of life on Earth at risk today? Or are they nature's way of expediting adaptation when conditions change rapidly? They may be a bit of both. The answer will take time. Words to Know. biodiversity (n.) how many kinds of life share Earth, or share one habitat or ecosystem. chromosomes (n.) rod-shaped parts inside cells that carry genes. diverged (v.) moved apart from one shared point and became different. DNA (n.) a code carrying genetic information about a living thing; a short form of deoxyribonucleic acid. embryos (n.) unborn offspring during the early stages of growth. expediting (v.) speeding something up, especially a process. fertilize (v.) to join male and female reproductive cells so a new animal or plant can start. genetic (adj.) having to do with heredity and with variation in living things. hybrids (n.) offspring that come from two different parent types, breeds, or species. interbreeding (v.) mating two different animal species so the young combine traits from each parent; also called crossbreeding. meiosis (n.) cell division that cuts the chromosome count in half, so each reproductive cell gets one chromosome from every homologous pair. offspring (n.) a person's child, or the young of another animal; also, descendants. reproduce (v.) to make offspring that are similar to the original living thing. species (n.) a group of living things that are physically similar and able to reproduce. sterile (adj.) not able to produce offspring. susceptible (adj.) easily affected or influenced; vulnerable. test tube (n.) a slim glass tube, shut at one end and open at the other, often used in a lab. transgenic (adj.) describing an organism whose DNA was changed by a transfer of genes from another species or breed.

97. When Colors Do Not Look the Same

1A picture sets two crayon boxes side by side. Picking a red crayon is much simpler for someone who sees every color. It is harder for someone whose red and green look alike. Picture a crayon box that shows only grays, blues, and yellows. Picture a traffic signal whose red lamp and green lamp look nearly the same. That is one way the world can look to a person with color blindness. Their view is not the view of people who see the full range of color. Color blindness is the most common genetic condition on Earth. In the United States alone, it affects more than ten million people. The name is misleading. This condition does not make a person blind. Doctors now prefer another name. They say color vision deficiency, often shortened to CVD. Most people who have CVD still see some colors. What they lack is the full ability to see certain colors. Sometimes that ability is only weaker, not gone. CVD is easier to grasp once color is understood as light. Different colors are different wavelengths. A prism can split white light into a rainbow. What the prism really does is sort those wavelengths.

2Longer wavelengths sit at the red end of that spread. Shorter wavelengths sit at the purple end. An object looks a certain color because of what it does with light. It absorbs some wavelengths. It reflects others. A ripe strawberry looks red for a clear reason. It reflects the long wavelengths that we call red. Reflect short wavelengths instead, and that same berry would look blue. Flower petals can look red for the same reason. They send back long red wavelengths. Leaves look green because they send back medium wavelengths, the ones we call green. A diagram of the eye shows the path of sight. The cornea collects light from outside and starts to focus it. Rods and cones line the retina along the rear wall. Those cells note the view. Opening and closing the pupil is the work of the iris. More light enters, or less light enters. The optic nerve carries messages to the brain about the view. The pupil is a hole at the center of the eye. Light passes through that hole. The lens changes shape and finishes the focus. People see color because special cells answer differently to different wavelengths. Light comes into an eye.

3The lens sets that light on the retina. The retina is a thin sheet of tissue inside the eyeball, behind the lens. Light there wakes cells that sense it. Some are rod cells. Some are cone cells. Awake cells send electrical signals. The path is the optic nerve. The brain turns those signals into images. No cells in the retina are more sensitive than rod cells. They let you see when light is extremely dim. They cannot separate one color from another. Color vision is the job of cone cells. Each cone holds one of three light-absorbing molecules. Those molecules are called photopigments. One kind detects blue light. One kind detects green light. One kind detects red light. Mix those three main colors, and thousands of colors become visible. CVD follows when one or more photopigments fail to work properly. A side note compares human sight with other animals. A picture contrasts human vision with honeybee vision. Most animals see fewer colors than people do. Dogs, for instance, see only shades of blue and of yellow. A bull cannot see the color red. Some animals see more colors than humans. Birds are among them.

4Bees are among them. Butterflies are among them. Their extra range includes ultraviolet light and infrared light. Those wavelengths are invisible to people. Animals use color information for several jobs. They signal one another. They hunt prey for food. They defend themselves from predators. The most common form of CVD is the red-green kind. Telling red from green becomes difficult. The condition is hereditary. It shows up most often in Caucasian people whose ancestors lived in northern Europe. Men have it more often than women. Among men, the rate is one out of twelve. Among women, the rate is one in two hundred. The usual cause is a fault in the green photopigment. Without that green pigment, green objects look reddish. Yellow objects look reddish too. A fault in the red photopigment can cause red-green CVD as well. Then red objects look green or black. Orange objects do too. Yellow objects do too. People with this condition still see clearly. Red cones and green cones overlap in the wavelengths they detect. Incoming light can still be detected even if one cone type is missing. Detection can continue even if that cone type is malfunctioning. A comparison picture sets ordinary color sight next to red-green CVD sight.

5Red, yellow, and green are marked in each view. Another comparison picture lines up three views. One is full-color vision. One is red-green CVD. The third view is the blue-yellow form of CVD. That form shows up when the blue photopigment fails or is missing. It is fairly rare. Worldwide, it appears in about one person out of every ten thousand. Unlike the red-green form, it is equally common in men and in women. Blue cone cells are completely absent in some people with this form. They see blue as green. They see yellow as violet, or they see it as gray. More often, the blue cones work only in part. The result is trouble separating yellow from pink. Red is hard to separate from pink too. The harshest form is complete CVD. Defects in this form hit at least two cone types out of the three. One kind of cone might seem like enough for color. It is not. The brain must compare signals from at least two different cone types before it can name a color. A person who has only blue cones can still detect blue wavelengths.

6That person cannot tell colors apart. Some traffic lights add shapes to their colors. Drivers with CVD can read the shape even when the color is unclear. People missing two or more cone types are often very sensitive to light. Clear sight can be hard, especially in bright light. They must lean on rod cells for most of their vision, or for all of it. Rod cells work only when the light is dim. Worldwide, about one person in thirty thousand lacks all three cone types. With no working cones, the world appears in black, in white, and in gray. CVD can bring real challenges. Color-coded information is one example. Maps may be hard to read. Graphs may be hard. Charts may be hard. Children can struggle with schoolwork. The struggle is worse if nobody has found the CVD yet. Chalk that is yellow, written on a chalkboard that is green, is hard to read for someone with red-green CVD. Every type of CVD can make color choice hard. Art projects suffer. Science projects suffer. Safety can suffer too. Fire hydrants are often painted red or yellow so they stand out. Car warning lights often use those colors.

7Emergency equipment often uses them. Someone who sees every color notices those bright marks. Someone with CVD may miss them completely. Sunburns can be hard to spot. Rashes can be hard to spot. Meat that is undercooked can be hard to spot. A job choice can be affected. Some jobs demand full-color vision. A geologist is one example. A commercial airline pilot is another. Other jobs grow much harder without full color. Interior design is one. Photography is one. Food inspection is one. Even so, people with CVD can usually find a way through those problems. Almost any job can still be done well. Testing has a standard tool for red-green conditions. It is called the Ishihara Test. The test uses pictures made of dots. The dots differ in size. They differ in color. Someone who sees every color can find a number inside the picture, or a shape. A person with red-green CVD may not be able to name that hidden mark. The mark may be difficult. It may be impossible. Similar tests look for yellow-blue CVD. A picture of the test asks a simple question. Can you find the hidden numbers or shapes inside the circles?

8A picture shows special sunglasses. With them on, a person who has red-green CVD finds the world much richer in color. No cure for CVD is known today. New tools have still appeared, thanks to modern technology. Phone apps can do useful jobs. One job is naming a color. Another job is suggesting a complementary color, a color that balances or completes the first. Matching clothes becomes easier. Ripe fruit at a store becomes easier to judge. Some apps can name a color only after the user takes a photo. Other apps read the colors in the camera's viewfinder. No photo is required first. The naming happens while they look. Researchers have also built lenses with a high-tech tint. Those lenses filter out particular wavelengths of light. Sunglasses made with the lenses help a person with red-green CVD tell the two colors apart. A true treatment does not exist yet. That may change. Scientists recently tested a workaround on squirrel monkeys that had red-green CVD. The monkeys had no red photopigment. Red and green looked the same to them. The tool the researchers used is called gene therapy. It changes traits.

9They built a special virus. The virus carried the gene for the red photopigment. Green cone cells in the monkeys received that gene. About twenty weeks later, the treated monkeys could tell red dots from green dots. A picture shows a squirrel monkey taking a color test. The news mattered because these monkeys had lived with CVD from birth. Many doctors had predicted full color would be impossible for them. Many scientists had agreed. The needed brain connections, they thought, would never have formed. Those connections usually grow while an animal is young. The connections are what let the brain read color information. Adult squirrel monkeys now show that a workaround exists. People who want full-color vision have a reason to hope. CVD is fairly common. Anyone can inherit it. Maybe you have it. Maybe someone in your family has it. Maybe you know a person who does. Finding CVD early helps. People can understand what they are seeing. They can adjust. Certain activities become harder. Most people with CVD still get along just fine. The world may look a little different to them. That difference does not stop a rich life. It does not stop a fulfilling life.

10A few words help with this topic. Ancestry means family members and relations from earlier times. Molecules are the smallest parts of a substance that can exist on their own. One or more atoms make a molecule. Complementary describes something that completes, balances, or improves something else. Photopigments are natural compounds. They change chemically when they take in light. Cone cells sit in the retina. They sense color, and they work best in bright light. A prism is clear. It bends light until a rainbow of colors appears. Defects are weaknesses, imperfections, or failures. Images land on the retina, a tissue deep inside the eye, and that tissue sends them on to the brain. A genetic condition is a physical condition passed down in a family. The cause is a fault in a gene, or in several genes. Rod cells sit in the retina. They sense light. Dim light is where they work best. Hereditary means a trait traveled from parents down to their children by way of genes. Wavelengths are the distances between one high point of a wave and the next, or between one low point and the next.

98. When Comic Fans Gather

1Batman shares a quiet moment with Robin and with the Joker. The scene is the New York Comic Con of 2014. Imagine an auditorium. Thousands of fans fill it with you. Stars are about to arrive onstage. Your Chewbacca costume feels pretty warm. Two rows down, another fan wears an armored helmet. You guess that helmet is even warmer. Which character is he supposed to be? You turn your head for a clearer view. All at once, people are on their feet and cheering. You leap up. The moment is right. Robert Downey Jr. walks out. Several movies have cast him as Iron Man. A grin is on his face. Roses fly toward people seated in front. With that, the Avengers panel begins. Color, crowds, and pop culture fans are what a comic con is made of. A collector of comic books will find a place here. So will someone who watches cartoons. So will someone who goes to the movies or plays video games. Fans shorten the name of these conventions to cons. The gatherings occur worldwide. Huge venues host some of them. Attendees can number in the thousands, and the schedule can cover multiple days. Other cons are tiny. An afternoon may be all they last, or a single day. Programming reaches every sort of fan. Children are welcome. Adults are welcome. Serious gamers fit in. Obsessive readers fit in. So does everyone between those poles. Attendance at some larger cons passes 130,000 people in a year. Halfway through the twentieth century, comic cons began.

2The purpose was a meeting place. Fans could trade comics there. They could talk about the books. Europe and Japan are where comic books first began. American popular taste did not really catch them until the 1930s. The release of Superman was the moment. Superheroes dominated the books in that period. Devoted fans gathered around them. Organized meetings arrived in the 1960s and the 1970s. Growth of the conventions was quick once that started. One early organizer was Shel Dorf. His own work was drawing comics. Detroit in the 1960s was where he held small fan meetings. He later founded a convention that people now call CCI, or Comic-Con International. The city was San Diego. The year was 1970. Year one drew about 100 fans. Today it is the biggest comic con in the nation. Recent events have seen over 130,000 people attend. After San Diego's success, hundreds of further cons sprang up. Antarctica is the only continent that has no con. Seats disappear quickly. To be certain of a ticket, a few fans sleep outside for several days. A 2015 book fair shows college students browsing comic books. Explosive growth needs an explanation. The first part is a new wave of popularity for the books themselves. Readership was wide in the Golden Age. Those years were the 1930s and the 1940s. After the midpoint of the twentieth century, readership fell. Some readers of that later time called comics poor literature. Others called them something only for kids. Fresh ground opened in the late 1980s and the early 1990s.

3Neil Gaiman wrote the series The Sandman. Watchmen joined Alan Moore with Dave Gibbons. John Higgins joined that same team. Both works drew readers who stayed loyal. Critics praised them. Popular interest has climbed since then. So has interest from critics. New topics and new styles are still being explored by writers and artists. Today's comic books cover more ground than they ever have. Superhero tales of the traditional kind share space with war stories. Family drama is in the mix. Everything between those poles is there too. Graphic novels branched off from comic books. At the moment, young adult fiction counts some of them among its favorite titles. Nonfiction's newest edge includes graphic memoirs. Maus, by Art Spiegelman, is both a graphic memoir and a novel. Interviews with his father, who survived the Holocaust, are the basis. The Pulitzer Prize went to Maus. Few literary awards in the country stand higher. As the topics widened, the audiences widened. A fan of any gender can find a story to relate to. The same is true for any color, any age, and any nationality. Convention crowds have climbed in a dramatic way. The International Berlin Comic Festival is where Spiegelman speaks about Maus. San Diego Comic Con in 2017 puts Black Panther actors on a panel. Michael B. Jordan is one of them. Danai Gurira is the other. Hollywood supplies the second reason for the boom. Movies of recent years, built on comic characters, have succeeded on a huge scale.

4Interest in the comics rose with them. So did the number of people at cons. Favorites with audiences include a 2008 film, Iron Man. They include Spider-Man movies made in the 2000s. They include another 2008 film, The Dark Knight. They include a 2017 film, Wonder Woman. They include a 2018 film, Black Panther. New fans arrived because of those hits. Programming at cons now gives movies a large role. Panels regularly feature famous actors from those films. Writers come too. Directors come too. The crowds they draw are huge. Tripoli hosted the 2017 Libya Comic Convention, and artists there drew illustrations in manga style. The story does not stop at movies. Video games now belong at cons around the world. Television shows belong there. Novels of science fiction and of fantasy belong there. Some fans found the shared audience too broad. They split off and built conventions for one genre. Attendance is strong where the focus is anime and manga. Japan is the source of those animated films and those comic books. Separate cons exist for people who love classic comics and collect them. Separate cons exist for sci-fi fans and for fantasy fans. Steampunk has cons. Horror has cons. Humor has cons. Many other themes do too. The United States holds comic cons in cities from coast to coast. Leave the giant events of San Diego and New York, and the crowds shrink. Enthusiasm among fans stays huge. A town near you may have a con on the way.

5A local newspaper can say so. An online listing can say so. What you find may surprise you. At many smaller cons, local artists and local fans mix with cartoonists whose names are widely known. Movie stars mix with them too. The star of a show you love might be present at any con in the country. The writer of books you love might be present. Meeting local artists is likely. Making new friends is likely. London's 2016 MCM Comic Con shows Captain America in a fight with Loki. CCI: San Diego shows costumed viewers at an early showing of Star Wars Legends. Celebration of creative works and of fandom is only part of the point. Fans also get space to display creativity of their own. An independent film festival joined CCI: San Diego in 2005. Filmmakers who were still aspiring could send in work and compete for prizes. Showings continued across all four days. Categories open to submissions now include action and adventure. They include animation. They include horror and suspense. They include, of course, films drawn from comics. Experts who work in the industry sit on the judging panels. Filmmakers gain a valuable chance to receive feedback. Dressing up is an old comic con custom called cosplay. The costumes portray characters out of comic books. They also portray characters out of anime, manga, animated films, and further fantasy genres. Japan coined the word. It blends two English words, costume and play. Worldwide, fans treat the hobby as serious business. Costume sellers can supply an outfit.

6A builder can make one to order. A fan can sew one by hand. Realistic props are common. A character's weapons and other accessories are examples. While the outfit is on, some fans behave as that character would. Detail can be slight, or it can be astonishing. Eye color can be changed with contact lenses. Temporary tattoos can be designed for a closer likeness. Working out the build of a costume is, for many fans, a large share of the pleasure. Worldwide cons give cosplay a central place. Exhibit halls hold vendors who sell outfits. Costumed fans in the audience can number in the hundreds. Contests are common. Photos, skits, and interviews let cosplayers present their characters. Meeting the makers in person is another draw. Panels regularly include writers, artists, actors, directors, and others who work in the field. A favorite star may describe what it was like to make a comic, a film, or a show. A direct question from the crowd is sometimes allowed. A photo with the celebrity may be possible. An autograph may go onto a comic or a poster. Fans treasure those personal moments as memories. Celebrities, for their part, often report good memories of their own. The fans, they say, tend to be warm. They tend to be friendly. They tend to be devoted. Stan Lee was a legend in three roles. He wrote. He edited. He published. Comic cons saw him often. Many of the best-known superheroes at Marvel Comics exist partly because of him.

7One is the Incredible Hulk. Another is Spider-Man. His death came in 2018. Creative energy at a con gathers in the exhibit hall. Mingling and talk happen there. On display is material tied to comics. Movies are represented. So are TV, games, and further pop culture. Buying comics is possible. Trading them is possible. Action figures, toys, and similar merchandise are for sale too. A seasoned collector may locate an edition that is rare or one of a kind. A new collector may begin a collection with a head start. Artists and writers often meet fans in a signing hall. Publishers sometimes meet hopeful artists and writers in a portfolio review area. The aim for those hopefuls is a contract for a book. Simply standing in the hall still offers plenty. Costumed cosplayers pass by. Trailers and full movies play on a steady schedule. Seeing a celebrity remains possible at any moment. Merchandise in bright colors never seems to run out. A New York Comic Con display is packed with dolls offered for sale. Hayao Miyazaki, at the center of a panel, speaks during the 2009 San Diego comic con. Animation in Japan loves his work. His other roles include director, producer, screenwriter, and author. He draws manga. Studio Ghibli lists him as a co-founder. Controversy has traveled with the growth. Certain fans of comic books say the largest cons grew far past a good size. They say attention drifted too far from the books themselves. Movie fans, TV fans, and game fans, in this view, can bury the spark that started cons.

8A fairer label for many events would be pop culture convention, rather than a convention only about comic books. Devoted fans also argue with one another. The dispute may be who holds the most knowledge of a series, a film, or an invented world. Silly as that sounds, it shows something real. The audience feels a deep emotional tie to these works. Readers of comics, and the people who attend cons, are not the crowd they once were. Men made up most of that crowd in earlier years. Women are about forty percent of recent attendees at CCI: San Diego. Under age thirty, attendance splits by gender at about half and half. Younger fans are finding cons as a generation. Recent cons count more than half their people as younger than twenty-nine. Bigger crowds come with that wider mix. Most fans are glad of it. Portland, Oregon, hosted a Wizard World Comic Con where a girl looks through comics. Larger issues from the wider world can be discussed at a con. Serious subjects appear in some authors' work. Equality of race is one subject. Equality of gender is one. Politics is one. War is one. Not every reader wants those stories. Banned book campaigns have targeted some of them. A community, in such a campaign, asks a school or a library to remove a title from its shelves. Adult language, or adult themes, has brought challenges to Spider-Man comics. The same has happened to Batman comics.

9Recent panels have taken up censorship. The speakers include readers, teachers, and librarians. Those discussions helped two labels spread. One label is graphic novel. The other is graphic memoir. They mark comics aimed at adults. Fiction describes some comics. Nonfiction describes others. Teaching is the goal of some. Fun alone is the goal of others. Big social problems and adult themes fill some pages. A flight into fantasy worlds fills others. A shelf question follows from that mix. Do libraries and schools keep every comic in one place, or do they separate them? A social question follows too. What part should comics play in the wider society? Panels return to these questions often. Some school districts have banned the Sandman series by Neil Gaiman. Boundaries around comics keep moving outward. The shift can be hard. Even so, cons are living through an exciting period. Today's comics, together with other pop culture media, come in vast variety. Audiences for the books and for the conventions have grown bigger. They have grown more varied. Somewhere in a comic, a fan can find a face like their own, whatever their age, gender, or nationality. Superman is one way a hero can look. A young girl from Botswana is another way. A reporter working on the ground in Bosnia is another way. Events inside a comic have no ceiling. The hero's identity has no ceiling either. That openness, in the end, is the pull toward comic cons. Stories, and the cons those stories feed, make worlds in which an everyday person turns into a hero.

10Virtually any person can wear that role. Possibility swallows people up. They put on the clothes of a character they love. They swap books. They swap trivia questions with fans beside them. They greet an artist with a handshake. The experience is one that many people repeat. A young girl at CCI: San Diego models a stormtrooper outfit from Star Wars, colored pink. Words in this book have special uses. Merchandise is the goods people buy and the goods people sell. Censorship is the cutting or blocking of a publication, a play, or a film, in whole or in part, because someone judges the content offensive or threatening. A panel is people asked to speak with knowledge on a subject while an audience listens. A controversy is an argument over some issue. Pop culture is the set of popular ideas that mass media carries, ideas that belong to ordinary modern life. A convention is a big meeting, able to run for several days, where people talk about work or about an interest held in common. Readership is who reads a work, or who reads a kind of writing. Diversity is many different things present at once. A screening is a planned showing of a movie or a television program. Fandom is every follower devoted to one interest. Sports, entertainment, and celebrities are examples. A venue is a site that holds an organized event. A memoir is a written account of experiences a person has had.

99. When the Ocean Climbs the Shore

1Huge blocks of ice calve from the Perito Moreno Glacier in Argentina. They drop into Lake Argentino. The pages ahead move from the encroaching sea to the causes of higher water. They then look at the human share of the problem. Four places are studied in turn. The places are New Orleans in the United States, Kushiro in Japan, Suva in Fiji, and Venice in Italy. A closing section and a word list finish the book. Amsterdam has 105 km (65 mi.) of canals. The city is used to living with water. Scientists expect the sea at Amsterdam to climb about one meter (3.3 ft.) during the coming century. Many people feel drawn to the sea. That is one reason some of the world's largest and most loved cities were built on coasts. A coast is a fine place until the sea begins to rise. In the next hundred years, many coasts can expect a rise of 0.6 meters (2 ft.). For some places, that rise means disaster. For places that are better prepared, it may not. People still have to ask what can be done about the encroaching sea. They also have to ask what should be done. A rise in sea level is not a new event. Water in the oceans has been rising for more than one hundred years. In the last several decades, the speed of that rise has increased. Scientists track tides to measure the change. They also sort through data from satellites. Tide stations show what is happening at particular places. Satellites measure the average height of the whole ocean. All of these records let people judge how sea levels change over time. Two main factors have pushed sea levels up. The first factor is warmth. As ocean water grows warmer, the water itself expands. Its molecules take up more volume. The water then fills more space. For many years, this thermal expansion was the main cause of sea level rise. More recently, a different cause has moved into the lead. Melting of ice that sits on land is now the main reason for the rapid rise. That melting includes glaciers. It also includes the ice sheets that cover much of Greenland and nearly all of the land in Antarctica.

2More than 99 percent of Earth's freshwater ice is locked in those two enormous ice sheets. Since 2003, melting of those sheets has accounted for nearly 80 percent of sea level rise. It is worth asking what would happen if they melted completely. A chart of the 1993 to 2008 average, drawn from the Union of Concerned Scientists and from Church and colleagues in 2011, splits the yearly rise into parts. Greenland ice loss added 0.31 mm each year (0.012 in.). Antarctica ice loss added 0.43 mm each year (0.017 in.). Melting glaciers added 0.99 mm each year (0.039 in.). Thermal expansion added 0.88 mm each year (0.035 in.). For more than a century, thermal expansion was the leading cause. In recent years, ice loss has accounted for twice as much of the rise. If the whole Greenland ice sheet melted, scientists estimate a rise of about 6.7 meters (22 ft.). That alone would swamp many major cities around the world. It would also displace huge numbers of people. If all the ice in Antarctica melted instead, sea levels would rise by 61 meters (200 ft.). Neither event is going to happen overnight. The ice sheet on Greenland is nearly the size of Mexico. The ice sheet on Antarctica is larger than the United States and Mexico combined. Even so, the rise that is happening now is already causing immediate problems worldwide. Maps of Shanghai, China, ask which sea level people will choose. One future shows extreme cuts in carbon. Those cuts would be difficult and expensive, but they are not impossible. The other future shows unchecked pollution, which is the path humans are on now. China is the world's leading carbon polluter. China also faces the greatest risk from coastal flooding. If emission levels stay the same, 145 million people live in places threatened by rising seas. The two maps project two different futures. Which future arrives depends on how people choose to burn fossil fuels in the years ahead. The maps come from Climate Central. A diagram of the Pine Island Glacier Ice Shelf in West Antarctica marks grounded ice, the ice shelf, the grounding line, and a ridge, including the layout from before 1945. The grounding line is the point where the glacier starts to float instead of staying attached to land.

3In 1945, a sudden pulse of warm water created a cavity behind that line. During the 70 years that followed, that grounding line moved back about 48 kilometers (30 mi.). Because of that retreat, a huge iceberg of 583 square kilometers (225 sq. mi.) broke off the thinning glacier in 2015. In July 2017, another ice sheet ten times that size snapped off West Antarctica. Sea levels have fluctuated naturally across Earth's history. At times the swings were dramatic. Human actions now, and across the last century, are adding to a faster rise in a short span of time. From the start of the Industrial Revolution, in the years 1760 to 1840, thermal expansion was the main cause of sea level rise. Humans caused most of that expansion. People caused most of the expansion by burning large amounts of coal and oil. They also cut down huge stretches of tropical forest around the world. Those activities raised the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Emissions of carbon, and emissions of other gases, became a kind of blanket around the planet. The blanket traps heat inside. Once temperatures grew warm enough, subsurface water washing against the West Antarctic Ice Sheet made that ice thin. Most of the glaciers in that part of Antarctica have since melted and retreated. At this point, people could not stop some amount of future sea level rise even if they wanted to. Researchers project a further rise even if every global gas emission stopped tomorrow.
