By the year 2100, seas would still rise 0.36 to 0.79 meters (1.2 to 2.6 ft.). Oceans and land ice would keep adjusting to gases already in the atmosphere. Not every place on Earth is seeing the sea climb. In Juneau, Alaska, the land itself has risen by as much as 3 meters (10 ft.) within the last two hundred years. It may rise another 0.9 meters (3 ft.) by 2100. The same gases that melt ice worldwide are shrinking glaciers in Alaska. As the weight of billions of tons of glacial ice melts away, the land lifts. Tide gauges around the world have measured the long-term rise since 1870.

4From 1880 to 2010, the global rise was about 20 centimeters (8 in.) on average. The observed record in that chart was reproduced from CSIRO Australia. Past 2010, four lines diverge. They show four scenarios for the future, from the most conservative, which is the lowest, to the least conservative, which is the highest. The scenario source is NOAA, 2016. The highest line reaches 200 cm (78.7 in.). That highest rise would come from ocean warming combined with the maximum potential loss of glaciers and ice sheets. An intermediate-high line reaches 160 cm (63 in.). Another line reaches 120 cm (47.2 in.). An intermediate-low line reaches 80 cm (31.5 in.). The lowest line reaches 40 cm (15.8 in.). The lowest path simply continues the historic rate, with no faster rise. The chart scale also marks minus 40 cm (minus 15.8 in.). The years along the chart are 1880, 1920, 1960, 2000, 2040, and 2080. Higher seas will erode shorelines. They will put some places underwater for good. Eight of the world's ten largest cities sit near a coast. Sea level rise will therefore affect urban areas. Roads, bridges, and subways will be at risk. Landfills and sewage treatment plants will be at risk. Schools, businesses, and homes will be at risk too. On the Outer Banks of North Carolina stands the tallest lighthouse in the United States. When it was finished in 1870, it was also the tallest brick building in the world. At that time it stood 457 meters (1,500 ft.) from the ocean. That distance was considered safe. Storm-driven tides and the rising sea later wore away the sand on the ocean side of the cape. Sea levels in the Outer Banks have been rising two to three times faster than the global average. In 1970, only 37 meters (120 ft.) of ground still lay between the lighthouse and the waterline. A structure this large is usually treated as an object that cannot be moved. In 1999, the National Park Service shifted it anyway. The new spot was 488 meters (1,600 ft.) back from the waves. The lighthouse sat on a heavy foundation of hydraulic jacks and steel beams. It moved down a metal runway at only 1.5 meters (5 ft.) per minute.

5The whole operation took twenty-three days. The move meant the lighthouse could keep warning ships about the dangerous offshore Diamond Shoals for another hundred years. The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse survived a major earthquake. It survived more than forty hurricanes. It survived a move of half a mile. It did all of that without a crack. When people picture sea level rise, they often imagine coastal residents fearing water over parts of their cities. Some places far from any ocean are not safe either. Places that are safe from floods today may still face problems with drinking water. Salt water can leak into groundwater sources. Several strategies can help people deal with the water itself. Steps taken now can protect people and property. Those steps can also affect how fast seas rise in the future. Four case studies span the continents and oceans. They include Venice in Italy, New Orleans in the United States, Kushiro in Japan, and Suva in Fiji, set among Europe, North America, Asia, Africa, Australia, the Pacific Ocean, and the Indian Ocean. New Orleans has always been susceptible to storms. The city sits near the Gulf of Mexico. It also sits between the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain. After Hurricane Katrina, many neighborhoods in New Orleans were underwater. The city lies by Lake Pontchartrain. Its average elevation is 0.6 meters (2 ft.) below sea level. In 2005, a storm surge from Hurricane Katrina caused many failures in the levees that had been built to hold the sea out. Eighty percent of the city flooded. After the disaster, workers rebuilt the levees and made them higher. They now have gravel reinforcement. They also have gates that control the flow of water. City experts warn that these barriers can only do so much. As the sea level rises, each storm will arrive on water that is higher than it was when Hurricane Katrina hit. That is why city officials are looking for more solutions. Where it is possible, cities and countries try to use wetlands to absorb floods. Wetlands also slow erosion. Wherever wetlands can be used or made again, they help people deal with sea level rise. New Orleans is considering artificial wetlands to help hold floodwater. Wetlands need a lot of space.

6Making new ones takes a long time. Many houses in New Orleans are built on stilts. For the long term, homes that can float may be the answer. Those homes would normally rest on firm bases. IJburg, a suburb of Amsterdam, has at least seventy-five floating houses. They respond to rising sea levels. They also respond to housing shortages in crowded urban areas. In an enormous flood, the floatable homes could rise as much as 3.7 meters (12 ft.). They would stay anchored to poles. The city is also making better evacuation plans. During a disaster, the most important task is to get people to safety quickly. Kushiro, in Japan, shows why islands face a different kind of problem. When a whole nation is made of islands, sea level rise matters in a special way. From 1970 to 2003, Kushiro had the highest rate of sea level rise in the world. The water there rose more than 0.8 centimeters (0.33 in.) each year. That may not seem like much. Over time the impact becomes enormous. In a hundred years it would be more than 0.9 meters (3 ft.). If the Kushiro rate happened in other parts of Japan, more than 90 percent of Japan's sandy beaches would disappear. Thirty million people who live within 9.7 kilometers (6 mi.) of the sea would be at risk. Strange as it seems, the surface of the ocean is not flat. Sea levels around the world are not changing at the same rate. Many factors shape the rise at any one place. Erosion is one factor. Ocean currents are another. Subsidence is another. Subsidence is the opposite of uplift. Satellites give the average height of the entire ocean. Tide stations give local measurements. The Arakawa River runs right through the heart of Tokyo. Tokyo has a population of more than thirty-seven million. It is the world's largest city. A higher sea is not Tokyo's only problem. A higher sea makes every major threat to coastal communities more likely. Typhoons, tsunamis, and ordinary storm surges would all arrive on top of higher water. The result would be serious damage to property and loss of life. That is why cities such as Tokyo are investing in immense levees to protect their people.

7Disaster can follow when a river flood combines with sea level rise. Along the Arakawa River, officials are paying people to move away for as long as four years. During that time they are building a longer and taller levee. The angle of the levee matters too. The new levees slope gently downward. Floodwater can then flow onto them and away from them bit by bit, instead of breaking them. Fiji is a small island nation east of Australia, in the South Pacific Ocean. Like many of the places most at risk in the world, its coastal cities could see more than 0.6 meters (2 ft.) of sea level rise in the next century. That change will be hard on tourism. The country's economy depends on visitors. Fiji already deals with periods of higher water when El Niño events occur. People are part of the problem as well. Too many people living near the ocean has left much of the coast open to erosion. It has also caused deforestation of catchments. Catchments are habitats, such as mangrove forests, that naturally collect water inside tidal zones and help drain that water back out to sea. After a cyclone in 2009, a father and his children crossed a flooded bridge in Fiji. Future projections show fewer tropical cyclones. They also show stronger ones, with harder wind and more rainfall. Forty-three island states, some of them pictured together, have urged big polluting countries to cut greenhouse emissions. If those cuts do not come, rising seas threaten to wash the islands off the world map. The named places include Hawaii, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Fiji, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, the Maldives, and the Seychelles. A University of Colorado chart compares the change in millimeters per year and in inches per year. Suva, the capital, is looking at natural remedies so it can survive future storms. Officials there are strengthening laws. They are also raising public awareness in order to protect mangrove forests and coral reefs. They hope to plant new mangrove forests. They hope to use artificial reefs to make the coast stronger. Even with these changes, the sea will move forward where people do not want it. The government is encouraging people to settle away from coastal areas.

8It is also planning for the chance that some small rural coastal areas may simply have to be evacuated. This strategy is called managed retreat. It is usually a last resort. In time, moving people may be the only option for many areas, not only for Fiji. In those cases, people can be kept safe if buildings are abandoned, moved, or demolished before a severe storm hits. The same steps can be taken before the sea reaches a dangerous height. Managed retreat can be very expensive where land is heavily developed. There are often hard legal fights over property rights. Venice was built on a group of 117 islands. The islands sit in the middle of a lagoon at the edge of the Adriatic Sea. The engineers who made the city knew the buildings had to handle high tides. They set the buildings on platforms of wood that stay underwater. On top of the wood they placed a kind of rock that does not let water through. This method has worked for centuries. Even so, especially high tides still flood the city at times. As sea levels rise, those floods are becoming more common. These extreme tides are called acqua alta. They happen when a few natural forces come together. One force is a very high tide during a full moon or a new moon. Another is low atmospheric pressure, which makes water flow toward the area. Another is a wind that blows from the south toward the north. That wind is called a scirocco. It pushes water up the Adriatic Sea and into the lagoon. When a strong acqua alta occurs, city squares end up soaked. Businesses end up soaked as well. During an acqua alta in 2010, tourists used planks to get around. Local people went swimming in the city's famous St. Mark's Square. To fight this, the city has been working to install seventy-eight mobile floodgates in the lagoon. The gates rest on heavy concrete foundations. When a high tide is coming, authorities will be able to raise the floodgates. The raised gates will seal the lagoon off from the sea. They will protect the city against tides almost 3 meters (10 ft.) high.

9They are expected to handle sea level concerns through the next century. These mobile gates will help guard Venice against floods and against rising sea levels, at least for a time. Most research looks at what global warming will do by 2100. For humans, one of the biggest impacts will be sea level rise that lasts a long time. That rise will last twice as long as human history. People alive today can still help change the course of that history. Scientists have found the most effective way to combat sea level rise. People must curtail emissions of gases that warm the atmosphere. The main culprit is carbon dioxide. This is easier to say than to do. The growing world population uses energy at a rate that keeps increasing. When governments fail to pass legislation that would reduce emissions, the goal becomes even harder. A 2015 paper in Science Advances links Antarctica's future to our future. The authors are R. Winkelmann, A. Levermann, A. Ridgwell, and K. Caldeira. The paper is dated September 11, 2015. It finds that burning the fossil fuel resources that are available would be enough to eliminate the Antarctic Ice Sheet. The choices drawn on the page are to leave 95 percent underground, to make no further emissions, to burn it all, or to leave half in the ground. How much Antarctic ice melts depends on how much carbon humans bring out of the ground and burn in the years ahead. More burning means more melt. Less burning means less melt. Making no further emissions is impossible at this point. If people burn only another 5 percent, they could keep the rise in global temperature under 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees F). Experts say that anything beyond that is dangerous for humans and for most other living things. Meanwhile, planners and ordinary citizens must prepare now if people and property are to stay safe. Some places have begun. Other places do not appear to have clear plans. As the seas rise around coastal people, those who live on higher and drier ground have to wonder what they can do to help avert this crisis. It is a compelling question. A great deal is at stake. An atmosphere is a layer of gases around a planet, a star, or a moon.

10Encroaching describes something that slowly pushes in, or goes past normal or acceptable limits. Carbon dioxide is an invisible gas. It forms when organic substances, such as fossil fuels, break down chemically or burn. Evacuation is the act or process of moving people out of danger. Fluctuated means changed, or shifted back and forth, or up and down. Catchments are areas or objects that collect water. Glaciers are large bodies of built-up ice and packed snow. They last all year, and they move slowly downhill. Curtailing means limiting, restricting, or reducing something. Deforestation is the clearing away of trees and other plants in an area. The Industrial Revolution was a shift in manufacturing and transportation. Human power and animal power gave way to machine power. The shift started in the late eighteenth century. To displace is to take the place of someone or something, or to force someone or something out. Emissions are things that are produced and given off as part of a process. A lagoon is a shallow, calm body of water. It may lie between a reef and the shoreline, or in the center of an atoll. A storm surge is a quick rise in sea level. Strong storm winds push water toward the shore and cause it. A last resort is a course of action that remains when every other option has failed. Strategies are careful plans for solving problems or reaching goals. Legislation is a law, or a set of laws, made by a government. Susceptible means easily affected or influenced, and it means vulnerable. Levees are ridges or raised areas that keep a river from overflowing. Thermal expansion is the enlarging of a liquid's volume, or of a solid's size, because temperature has increased. Molecules are the smallest parts of a substance that can exist on their own. They are made of one or more atoms. Wetlands are areas of land that are marshy or swampy. Reefs are ridges of coral, rock, or sand that lie very near the surface of the ocean. Sea level is the height of the ocean's surface. It is used as a standard when people measure how deep other things are.

100. When Weather Turns Dangerous

1Contents When the Natural World Turns Harsh Thunderstorms Tornadoes Hurricanes Closing Thoughts Word List Topic List When the Natural World Turns Harsh Many climates stay on one pattern. Daily life stays smoother when that pattern holds. Interest comes from weather that arrives with the seasons. A gentle rain can fall in spring once the air is warm enough. The first snow can fall in winter once the air is cold enough. People often grow bored if one pattern lasts too long. They then wait with impatience for a large shift. Ordinary days gain drama from the weather. Drama is not always the end of the story. Weather can turn dangerous. It can also turn destructive. Thunderstorms, tornadoes, and hurricanes rage with awesome force. That same force is frightening. These three events of nature can cause havoc on Earth. A calm afternoon faces a coming thunderstorm. A diagram shows one path that builds a thunderstorm: clouds, a cold front, and warm, moist air. Thunderstorms No other violent weather event happens as often as the thunderstorm.

2Several inches of rain can fall on one area in little time during a major storm. Stiff winds rise as well. Flash floods, hail, and lightning are hazards these storms create. Lightning ranks as the worst hazard. Every thunderstorm brings it. Formation starts when a huge body of warm, damp air climbs far into the atmosphere and then loses heat. Heat taken up from the ground is one reason that warm air climbs. Summer days often work this way. The Sun pours plentiful heat into the ground. Later the ground gives that heat off. Air above the ground grows warmer. A meeting with a cold front can also shove warm, moist air upward. Cold air packs more densely than warm air. Warm air therefore slides above the leading edge of the cold front. Higher up, the warmer air spreads out. Cooling follows that spreading. Once the chill is great enough, water vapor condenses. The vapor changes from a gas into a liquid. Puffy clouds appear. Their name is cumulus clouds. Some of those clouds grow into cumulonimbus clouds.

3A cumulonimbus cloud is huge. A wide area spreads across its top. Thunderstorms come from these clouds. A great load of condensed water can gather inside a cumulonimbus cloud. The load grows too heavy to remain aloft. Rain then falls. Intense rain from a major storm arrives in a brief span. Flash flooding can follow. Farms and homes can be wiped out. People who are not ready for the massive downpour can die. Strong air also rushes downward from the cloud. At the ground, those downdrafts may become stiff winds. Thunderstorms come in two main kinds. One kind is ordinary. The other kind is severe. Ordinary storms are the usual ones of summer. A typical storm lasts from 30 to 60 minutes. The heat eases, and people welcome that relief. Severe storms are also called supercell thunderstorms. They are huge, and they rotate. Several hours can pass before they end. Extremely heavy rain falls. High winds blow. Anxiety among people rises with those winds. Hail can form in a severe storm.

4The hailstones may be large. Some reach the size of baseballs. Some grow even larger. Severe storms make up about 10 percent of all thunderstorms. Tall towers in Panama City, Panama, take lightning strikes. Buildings there are struck as well. Lightning is the greatest danger in every thunderstorm. Picture a huge spark flashing across the sky. Lightning is that spark. Wildfires can start from it. People can be killed by it. Electric charges build up inside storm clouds. That buildup causes lightning. A bolt is a flow of those charges as they seek opposite charges. The opposite charges may sit in the clouds. They may also sit on the ground. Bolts that leap from cloud to ground put people in danger. Each bolt travels inside a narrow channel of air. Flash heating drives that air to about 54,000 degrees Fahrenheit, or 30,000 degrees C. The Sun's surface is about five times cooler than this. Explosive heat makes the air in the channel expand with violent force. A shockwave follows that expansion. We hear the shockwave as thunder.

5Thunderstorms take their name from that sound. One fire began when lightning struck. Twenty homes were destroyed. Tornadoes Some supercell thunderstorms spawn tornadoes. No other weather event on Earth is more violent. Picture a cloud that spins and drops in a funnel shape. It is large. That cloud is a tornado. It reaches down from the base of a big storm cloud. A narrow, snakelike form is common. Other tornadoes look like wide columns. A column may stretch as far as a mile across, or 1.6 km. Forward speed along the ground averages 30 miles per hour, or 48 km per hour. Some tornadoes move more than twice that fast. A strong updraft forms inside the funnel. Almost anything not fastened firmly to the ground can be sucked up. Vehicles can be lifted. Mobile homes can be lifted too. Once a tornado touches the ground, it usually looks dark. Dirt and debris drawn upward cause that dark look. Tornado Alley takes in these states in this order: Minnesota, then South Dakota, then Iowa, then Wyoming, then Nebraska, then Colorado, then Kansas, then Oklahoma, and then Texas.

6Almost any place in the world can be struck. The United States sees about 75 percent of all tornadoes. About 750 of them happen there every year. On average, 100 people die from them each year. Most tornadoes in the U.S. form in a broad region of the central United States. People call that region Tornado Alley. The Great Plains suit tornado growth very well. The land is flat. Canada sends cold, dry air. The Gulf of Mexico sends air that is moist and warm. Those air masses can meet. Supercell thunderstorms often follow when large masses of those two air types converge. Storms of that kind are ideal makers of tornadoes. Winds inside a major tornado can spin faster than 300 miles per hour, or 480 km per hour. A truly powerful tornado can rip a wood-frame house from its foundations. The house can be lifted far into the air. Destruction along the path may run as far as 50 miles, or 80 km.

7On May 3, 1999, one of the strongest tornadoes ever recorded tore through the suburbs of Oklahoma City. Twisters struck Tornado Alley across four days. This tornado was part of that onslaught. Doppler radar measured the winds at 318 miles per hour, or 512 km per hour. Thirty-six people were killed. Homes and other buildings were destroyed. The count passed 10,000. After that tornado, residents of Oklahoma City search the debris for belongings. Nothing matches a major tornado for sheer violence inside a limited area. People along seacoasts know a wider threat. A hurricane can wreck land across a much broader swath. Hurricanes A hurricane is a huge storm that rotates. It grows over warm ocean water in summer or in fall. Most of them form over the Atlantic Ocean. Many also form over the Gulf of Mexico. The Caribbean Sea is another common birthplace. Some also form in the northeastern Pacific Ocean. Storms of the same kind form in the Western Pacific and in the Indian Ocean.

8People there call them typhoons or severe tropical cyclones. On Reunion, an island in the Indian Ocean, people brace for a severe tropical cyclone. A satellite view shows Hurricane Katrina just before landfall in the southern United States. Low air pressure is where a hurricane begins. Winds circle around that low-pressure area. Warm, moist air is drawn up from the sea underneath. The area grows into a tropical storm. Moisture turns into clouds. A great amount of energy is released. If growth continues, that energy keeps the storm going. Wind speed may reach 74 miles per hour, or 119 km per hour. The storm is then a hurricane. Seen from space, the storm resembles a huge pinwheel. Rapidly circling storm clouds pile up in a towering mass around the outer parts. The center is calm. People call that calm center the eye. Wind and rain are absent there. Width can reach 600 miles, or 965 km. At landfall, coastal places are drenched by hammering rain. Heavy winds buffet those same places. A major hurricane can push winds past 150 miles per hour, or 240 km per hour.

9Roofs can be torn from many houses. Gusts in a major hurricane can equal the wind speed of the strongest tornado. Low-lying communities face a still greater danger. A wall of water, the storm surge, is driven toward land by the winds. In a major hurricane that wall can stand 20 feet high, or 6 m. Flooding can spread far inland. Lives can be lost there. Hurricane Katrina, in August 2005, ranks among the worst recent hurricanes to strike the United States. Severe destruction hit the Gulf Coast. Thousands of people were killed. The states hit were Louisiana and Mississippi. Alabama was hit too. So were Georgia and Florida. Two weeks later, Venice, Louisiana, was still flooded. Every part of town had water at a depth of two feet or more. Closing Thoughts Some parts of devastating weather can be guarded against. A full escape is not possible. Places in the United States that miss tornadoes and hurricanes may still face broiling summers.

10Harsh winters are another possibility. Along the West Coast, moderate weather is often balanced by earthquakes and brush fires. A person choosing a home should weigh the area's usual climate first. Extremes and the worst calamities matter less than that general pattern. The usual weather is what brings both steadiness and drama. Word List Air pressure is the push of air within the atmosphere. A cold front is the leading side where cold air, moving as one mass, meets warmer air. Cumulonimbus clouds tower upward, with flat bases down low and tops that spread out. Thunderstorms often show these clouds. Doppler radar tracks objects by measuring how fast they move. Storms and precipitation are common targets for this tool. A supercell thunderstorm is built from thunderclouds that rotate and reach high into the sky. Tornadoes, hail, and lightning often come from it. Topic List Readers can look up Oklahoma City, the storm surge, Tornado Alley, typhoons, clouds, the eye of a hurricane, the Great Plains, hail, Hurricane Katrina, and lightning.

101. Wild Partners That Share the Work

1In the opening picture, yellow tangs swim as a group and pick algae off a turtle. The turtle is green. This book then explains partnerships in the wild. It looks at food traded for safety, at cleaning, at shared homes, and at hunts made easier by a partner. It looks at animals that hitch a ride, at pollination, and at seeds carried to new ground. A closing thought follows. Word meanings come last. Another picture shows a crocodile holding its jaws open for a small bird, the Egyptian plover. Leftover food is picked from the teeth. Wild life is hard. Food can be scarce. A good home can be scarce. Pests are everywhere. Something is nearly always ready to eat you. Those pressures push many species into unusual partnerships. Each partner does its own task, and both gain. One animal may stand guard against predators. The other may offer a cleaning, or a steady supply of food. Science calls these pairings symbiotic relationships. Symbiosis comes from ancient Greek. One root means with. The other means living. The year 1877 is when scientists first used the word for wild species. They were writing about lichens. A lichen is a complex organism, often full of color. A fungus and a kind of algae usually make it up. Those two live and work tightly together. Researchers have kept finding these partnerships ever since. Deep oceans hold them. Dry deserts hold them. Mountains and forests hold them too. Some pairs surprise everyone. A shrimp that works hard may team with a fish that sees sharply. A colorful clownfish may team with a venomous sea anemone, pronounced uh-NEM-uh-nee. A rodent that lives on the ground may team with a tree that towers overhead. Fascination is only part of the story.

2For the species involved, the partnership can decide life or death. Bees would struggle to live without flower nectar. Those same flowers would struggle to reproduce if bees did not carry their pollen. A home version is easy to picture. A pet dog offers love. It offers companionship and protection. The dog receives meals, notice, and shelter where it can live without harm. Each side gains. Starlings in one picture stay close to a red deer so they can pick insects off its body. The bargain is not always equal. Partnerships that last for thousands of years, or for millions, last for a clear reason. Each species gains enough to make the deal worth keeping. Some scientists think interdependence between different species helps explain Earth's variety of plants and wildlife. Variety inside a species may grow this way too, not only variety across species. An animal may spread into a place that is less than ideal. There it may collaborate with species already native, and survival gets easier. Given time, a subspecies can appear. Kinship with the parent species remains close. Traits, features, or behavior have become different. Examples of the many kinds of partnership come next. The partners themselves are called symbionts. Knowing someone is watching your back can matter. Bright clownfish of the Indian Ocean need every kind of help if hunters are not to catch them. One method is a refuge inside the tentacles of a sea anemone that carries venom. An anemone looks like a plant. It is a marine animal. It fastens itself to rock or to some other surface and waits. Prey has to come to it. A small fish or a shrimp that brushes the soft tentacles meets a toxin.

3Paralysis follows. The anemone pulls the helpless prey into its mouth. Clownfish are a special case. They build immunity on purpose. A tentacle is touched once, or twice. The fish waits. It touches again. Small doses, repeated, slowly lay down a mucus coating on the skin. That coating is protective. A picture shows a striped clownfish, cautious, hiding among those tentacles. Harmful contact is blocked by the mucus, so the fish can swim there and stay unhurt. Lunch for a predator becomes a dive into cover. While the clownfish moves among the tentacles, it also works as a lure. The hunter is drawn into stinging arms. The anemone kills that fish. Both partners then have a meal. On African ground, ostriches and zebras often eat side by side. Eyes and ears are shared. Ostriches see well. Zebras hear extremely well. A lion on the stalk, or some other hunter, is easier to notice together than alone. The pair can flee before the attack lands. Impalas and baboons in Africa keep a similar watch. Hearing in an impala is superb. Vision is excellent. Smell is acute. Danger spotted first by the impalas shows in alert posture and in the shake of horns. Baboons take the warning. Loud screams raise the alarm. Teeth that look intimidating help drive the predator off. A map of this region marks Europe, Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean. One picture shows the mixed herds feeding, each ready to warn the other. Cleaning is another kind of help, aimed at places a body cannot reach. On many reefs a small silvery fish, the cleaner wrasse, does that job. It works almost like a dental hygienist of the deep, serving bigger fish such as butterflyfish or angelfish.

4A cleaning station is the wrasse's post. Large fish wait their turn with patience. Eating the helper would seem easy. It does not happen, because the wrasse dances in a way that soothes and seems to hypnotize. The big fish relaxes and, at last, opens its mouth. The wrasse shoots into the mouth and back out. It does the same at the gills. Fungus is cleared. Parasites are cleared. Dead skin and other debris are cleared. One picture shows a giant moray eel. A bluestreak cleaner wrasse is cleaning the teeth and the mouth. The wrasse leaves with a snack. The larger fish is left clean and healthy. A similar cleaning happens on the Galapagos Islands. Some of Darwin's ground finches do the work, and tortoises receive it. When a tortoise is ready, it takes a particular posture. Neck and legs stretch out. Neighboring finches swoop in and peck parasites the tortoise cannot reach. The tortoise stays absolutely still. It looks as if it has entered a trance while the birds work. Fuller stomachs are the birds' pay. A pest-free body is the tortoise's pay. A map places the islands off the Americas, between the Atlantic and the Pacific. One picture shows the finches clinging to neck and legs, picking ticks. Sharing a house is harder when the roommate is nothing like you. Cliffs high on the New Zealand shore hold one of the oddest pairs. The tuatara, pronounced too-uh-TARR-uh, is a slow reptile that looks like a lizard. Building a nest is usually more effort than it wants. The sooty shearwater is a fast-flying bird. They use one residence, but not at the same hour. Night is the tuatara's active time, so the day is spent in the burrow.

5While it is home it eats burrow bugs. It also eats the parasites the bird hates. That is its housekeeping. A map of this region marks Asia, Australia, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean, and New Zealand. The bird hunts while the reptile tidies. Night brings the shearwater back, and by then the roommate is out. Dirt is loosened. Droppings draw insects the tuatara likes to eat. The odd couple rarely meets. Home is shared anyway, and so is a partnership both of them welcome. North America's tiniest owls are the burrowing owls. They nest under the ground in holes another animal has left. A picture shows that life. They also warn neighbors when a predator comes near. Digging is beyond them. Hiding in a hole is not. Their petite size fits abandoned tunnels once used by prairie dogs or by gopher tortoises. A tiny owl may claim an empty burrow while the former resident has only moved next door. Each animal sounds a warning if danger approaches, and each is safer for it. Forest mice share a home with burrow beetles, and both gain. Fleas in the mouse's fur are a snack for the beetle while the mouse sleeps. An absent mouse gives the beetle time to hunt other bugs through the shared burrow. The beetle eats well. The mouse keeps a home free of pests. The ocean has house-sharers too. Every animal species is playing a survival game. Survival is harder if danger cannot be seen. That is the problem for snapping shrimp on the ocean floor. They are nearly blind, and they dig burrows in the seabed. Moving sand to build the home leaves them open to hungry predators.

6A partner solves it. The goby fish stays alert. Sharp sight lets it notice trouble quickly. As the shrimp shifts sand, the fish hovers near the antennae and keeps watch. A flick of the tail touches those antennae when danger is close. The shrimp gets the signal to take cover. At night the fish may sleep in the burrow. It may also hide there. The shrimp shares that shelter. For these two sea dwellers, the partnership fits perfectly. One picture shows them building a home together. High in America's Rocky Mountains, three lives lock together. A huge grizzly bear, a small red squirrel, and the white bark pine all need one another, and they need the tree's nuts, if their diets are to stay healthy. Pine nuts are a high-calorie food for the bears and for the squirrels. Squirrels eat some nuts at once. They bury others to dig up later. Smell, which is strong in the bears, leads them to those caches. Nuts are eaten. Droppings left after digestion carry some of the seeds away. New trees sprout and grow. Later generations of bears and of red squirrels then find still more nuts. A ride on a hunter is a different bargain. Most small fish stay far from sharks. The remora, a slender fish, does the opposite. It tries to get as close as it can. On top of its head sits a flat disc with ribs. The disc works as a suction cup and locks the remora to a shark's underside. One picture marks that fish with an arrow, stuck to the belly so it can travel and share meals. Swimming alone is possible, and remoras often do it. Sometimes a shark is simply an easier, more efficient ride.

7Another large animal can serve the same way. Once attached, the remora follows every hunt and every meal. Scraps that escape the jaws become its food. A service goes back the other way. Parasites that have hitched on the host are eaten. The host stays clearer of passengers that do less good. The suction disc was not always a disc. It is a dorsal fin that changed. Thousands of years of evolution produced it. Strange headgear is not only a remora trait. Some hermit crabs in the Mediterranean Sea seem to wear an odd hat. The hat is a sea anemone along for the ride. Long tentacles on that anemone carry venom. A hard shell protects the crab from them. Predators meet the anemone instead of an easy crab. The crab's messy eating is the anemone's gain. Scraps hang in the water, and the anemone eats them. Hitchhikers are not only marine. In Africa a small bird, the oxpecker, often rides a hippopotamus rather than spend effort hunting insects alone. Bugs are plucked from the skin and eaten. The bird gets a meal and easy travel. The hippo is picked clean of pests. One picture shows a group of these birds on a hippo's back, doing exactly that work. Bats do more than feed spooky stories. Across much of the world, many plants survive only because a bat visits them. Sweet food is what the plants give back to their furry, winged visitors. Pollinators are the group bats belong to. Pollen is moved from stamens, the male parts of flowers, to pistils, the female parts, while the animal eats. The transfer is inadvertent. It fertilizes the blossoms, so the plant can reproduce and spread.

8Night is when bats often work. Heads sink deep into a flower's center. Sugary nectar is drunk. Pollen rich in protein is eaten. Sticky pollen often dusts the head after a blossom. It dusts the body too. The next flower receives that pollen. Flowers keep exchanging it. Bats keep a steady supply of nectar and of pollen they find delicious. One picture shows a long-nosed bat at an agave plant loaded with pollen. Where these bats live, agaves depend on them more than on other pollinators. Cacti depend on them too. Honeybees, like bats, pollinate actively, and plant reproduction depends on them. Nectar draws a bee into a flower. Flecks of pollen often cover it when it leaves, and the next stop receives that pollen. Hummingbirds work in much the same way. Feathers and bills pick up pollen as the birds dart among blossoms. Some pollinators are offered more than food. A female yucca moth is picky about where eggs go. She prefers to spread her hundreds of eggs across several yucca flowers. The eggs gain a safe home. The flowers gain too, because pollen rides with her from bloom to bloom. One picture shows a honeybee at a dandelion, gathering nectar and leaving pollen on the next bloom it finds. Seeds need their own partners. High in a Brazil nut tree, one picture shows the pods hanging in clusters. A tree or any other plant that cannot move its seeds will grow in only one place. Crowding follows. Light and water become a contest. Survival odds are better if seeds travel far and new plants grow up to make seeds of their own. Animal partners do that dispersing for many plants. In the Amazon rainforest, one remarkable pair is the Brazil nut tree and the agouti, a rodent about the size of a cat.

9The tree can stand 200 feet tall or more, which is 61 meters. Seedpods are about the size of a grapefruit. They are hard and tough. They may drop 100 feet or more, about 30.5 meters. Striking the soil still may not break them. Jaws of the small agouti are strong enough to crack those tough pods. One picture shows that bite. New Brazil nut trees can sprout from droppings the agouti leaves behind. The drop fails. The agouti succeeds. Thick shell yields to its teeth and to the power of its jaws. Some seeds are eaten. Others are buried well away from the parent tree, scattered through the forest. Those buried seeds sprout in time. The long process starts again. Desert mistletoe uses a different carrier, a bird called a phainopepla, pronounced fay-no-PEHP-luh. Seeds sit inside the berries. The bird snacks on them, using its beak to pull skin off the fruit. Undigested seeds leave wherever the droppings fall, and that is how the plant propagates. Without these natural partnerships the world would be very different. Many species would face predators and pests with less defense. Smaller bits of habitat would be more likely to hold them apart from others. Blooming and spreading would be less likely. Food choices would be fewer. Partners would suffer. So would other inhabitants of Earth's ecosystems. Scientists are still learning how these extraordinary relationships work. New ones are still being found. Shallow sunlit water has symbiotic partners. Deep dark caverns have them too. They help each other survive, and they help each other thrive. One closing picture returns to New Zealand. On cliffs above the shore, sooty shearwaters and tuataras keep their unusual shared home.

10Grazing impalas stir insects up, and baboons get an easy meal from that stir. The payback is a warning call if danger comes close. A picture shows that trade. Every symbiotic relationship differs a little. The benefit to each species differs a little too. All of them help hold balance inside their ecosystems. Taken together, their effect on the wider world is a good one. Diversity is promoted. So is sustainability for living things. A better chance then belongs to fish. It belongs to birds, to humans, and to many other organisms. They can survive. They can reproduce. They can live lives that are longer and healthier. Hard words can be read this way. Assume, in this book, means to take on a certain pose or a certain role. To fertilize is to join male and female reproductive cells so a new animal or a new plant can form. A hygienist works as a professional for health and cleanliness. A nurse is one example. A dental assistant is another. Interdependent means depending on one another, as organisms in an ecosystem do. Intimidating means frightening or overwhelming. Mucus is a thick, slimy liquid made in a body. It protects tissues and keeps them wet. Nocturnal describes something active at night rather than in the day. A parasite is a plant or an animal that grows on another and feeds off it. To propagate is to reproduce, creating again and again. A refuge is somewhere safe, somewhere comfortable, or somewhere protected. Symbiotic describes a relationship that benefits different kinds of organisms. Venomous means able to push venom, a poisonous fluid, into another body by striking, biting, or stinging.
